definition 12.3. The ε-packing number, \(\mathcal{D}(\mathcal{F},\varepsilon,d)\) , is the marimal cardinality of an E-separated set.
Note that \(\mathcal{D}(\mathcal{F},\varepsilon,d)\) is decreasing in ε.

definition 12.2. Given \(\varepsilon > 0\) and \(f_{1},\ldots,f_{N}\in\mathcal{F}\) ， we say that \(f_{1},\ldots,f_{N}\) are E-separated if \(d(f_{i},f_{j})>\varepsilon\) for any \(i \neq j\)

Denote \[\triangle_{n}(\mathcal{C})=\sup_{\{x_{1},\ldots,x_{n}\}}\triangle_{n}(\mathcal{C},x_{1},\ldots,x_{n})\leq 2^{n}.\] We will see that for some classes, \(\triangle_{n}(\mathcal{C})=2^{n}\) for \(n \leq V\) and \(\triangle_{n}(\mathcal{C})<2^{n}\) for \(n > V\) for some constant \(V\).

definition 8.1. If \(V < \infty\) , then C is called a VC class. V is called VC dimension of C.

definition 8.0. For any sample \(\{x_{1},\ldots,x_{n}\}\), the ways that \({\mathcal{C}}\) intersects with the sample are \[\{C\cap\{x_{1},\ldots,x_{n}\}:C\in{\mathcal{C}}\}.\] Let \[\triangle_{n}(\mathcal{C},x_{1},\ldots,x_{n})=\mathrm{card}~\{C\cap\{x_{1},\ldots,x_{n}\}:C\in\mathcal{C}\},\] the number of different subsets picked out by \(C\in{\mathcal{C}}\). If \(\triangle_{n}(\mathcal{C})=2^{n}\), this means we can find \(\{x_{1},\ldots,x_{n}\}\) such that \({\mathcal{C}}\) can pick out any subset of it; in this case \({\mathcal{C}}\) shatters \(\{x_{1},\ldots,x_{n}\}\). Equivalently, a set \(A\) is shattered by \({\mathcal{C}}\) when \({\mathcal{C}}\) picks out every subset of \(A\).

Setup. Let \(X'_1,\dots,X'_n\) (the ghost sample) be an independent copy of \(X_1,\dots,X_n\), i.e. i.i.d. \(P\) and independent of \(X_1,\dots,X_n\). Suprema over \(\mathcal{C}\) are assumed measurable; otherwise read \(\mathbb{P}\) as outer probability.

If \(t\geq{\sqrt{\frac{2}{n}}}.\) then
\[\mathbb{P}\left(\operatorname*{sup}_{C\in\mathcal{C}}\left|\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}I(X_{i}\in C)-\mathbb{P}\left(C\right)\right|\geq t\right)\leq 2\mathbb{P}\left(\operatorname*{sup}_{C\in\mathcal{C}}\left|\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}I(X_{i}\in C)-\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}I(X_{i}^{\prime}\in C)\right|\geq t/2\right).\]

steps.claim:
Suppose the event
\[\operatorname*{sup}_{C\in{\mathcal{C}}}\left|{\frac{1}{n}}\sum_{i=1}^{n}I(X_{i}\in C)-\mathbb{P}\left(C\right)\right|\geq t\]
occurs.Let \(\begin{array}{ r }{X=(X_{1},\ldots,X_{n})\in\{\operatorname*{sup}_{C\in\mathcal{C}}\left|\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}I(X_{i}\in C)-\mathbb{P}\left(C\right)\right|\geq t\}}\end{array}\) .

Then
\[\exists C_{X}{\mathrm{~s u c h~t h a t~}}\left|{\frac{1}{n}}\sum_{i=1}^{n}I(X_{i}\in C_{X})-\mathbb{P}\left(C_{X}\right)\right|\geq t .\]
For a fixed C,
\[\begin{array}{ r }{\mathbb{P}_{X^{\prime}}\left(\left|\displaystyle\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}I(X_{i}^{\prime}\in\mathcal{C})-\mathbb{P}(\mathcal{C})\right|\geq t/2\right)=\mathbb{P}\left(\left(\displaystyle\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}I(X_{i}^{\prime}\in\mathcal{C})-\mathbb{P}(\mathcal{C})\right)^{2}\geq t^{2}/4\right)}\\ {\leq\mathrm{~(b y~C h e b y s h e v~s~I n e q)~}\frac{4\mathbb{E}\left(\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}I(X_{i}^{\prime}\in\mathcal{C})-\mathbb{P}(\mathcal{C})\right)^{2}}{t^{2}}}\\ {=\frac{4}{n^{2}t^{2}}\displaystyle\sum_{i,j}\mathbb{E}(I(X_{i}^{\prime}\in\mathcal{C})-\mathbb{P}(\mathcal{C}))(I(X_{j}^{\prime}\in\mathcal{C})-\mathbb{P}(\mathcal{C}))}\\ {=\frac{4}{n^{2}t^{2}}\displaystyle\sum_{i=1}^{n}\mathbb{E}(I(X_{i}^{\prime}\in\mathcal{C})-\mathbb{P}(\mathcal{C}))^{2}=\frac{4 n\mathbb{P}\left(\mathcal{C}\right)\left(1-\mathbb{P}(\mathcal{C})\right)}{n^{2}t^{2}}\leq\frac{1}{n t^{2}}\leq\frac{1}{2}}\end{array}\]
since we chose \(t\geq\sqrt{\textstyle{\frac{2}{n}}}.\)
So,
\[\mathbb{P}_{X^{\prime}}\left(\left|\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}I(X_{i}^{\prime}\in C_{X})-\mathbb{P}\left(C_{X}\right)\right|\leq t/2\Bigg|\exists C_{X}\right)\geq 1/2\]

Since indicators are 0,1-valued,
\[\begin{array}{ r l r }&{}&{\displaystyle\frac{1}{2}T\left(\underbrace{\operatorname*{sup}_{\zeta\in{\mathcal C}}\left|\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}I(X_{i}\in C)-\mathbb{P}(C)\right|\ge t}_{\Im C x}\right)}\\ &{}&{\displaystyle\le\mathbb{P}_{X^{\prime}}\left(\underset{C\in{\mathcal C}}{\operatorname*{sup}}\left|\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}I(X_{i}\in C)-\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}I(X_{i}^{\prime}\in C)\right|\ge t/2\Bigg|\exists C x\right)\cdot I\left(\exists C x\right)}\\ &{}&{\displaystyle\le\mathbb{P}_{X,X^{\prime}}\left(\underset{C\in{\mathcal C}}{\operatorname*{sup}}\left|\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}I(X_{i}\in C)-\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}I(X_{i}^{\prime}\in C)\right|\ge t/2\right).}\end{array}\]

context:
Shared setting for the results below. All definitions, standing assumptions and numbered equations that the proofs rely on are collected here.

Convex set. A set \(K\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) is convex if the line segment between any two points in \(K\) is also contained in \(K\). Formally, for all \(x,y\in K\) and all scalars \(\gamma\in[0,1]\) we have \(\gamma x+(1-\gamma)y\in K\).

Strong convexity. A function \(f\colon\Omega\to\mathbb{R}\) is \emph{\(\alpha\)-strongly convex} if, for all \(x,y\in\Omega\), the following inequality holds for some \(\alpha>0\): \[ f(y) \geqslant f(x) + g(x)^\top(y-x) + \frac{\alpha}{2}\left\lVert x-y\right\rVert^2 \]

Uniform stability. The uniform stability of an algorithm \(A\) is defined as
\[
\Delta_{\sup}(A) = \sup_{S, S' \in (X\times Y)^m } \sup_{i \in [m]} |\ell(A(S), z_i') - \ell(A(S^{(i)}, z_i')|
\]

Local minimum. A point \(x^*\) is an unconstrained \textit{local minimum} if there exists \(\epsilon > 0\) such that \(f(x^*) \leqslant f(x)\) for all \(x\) with \(\|x - x^*\| < \epsilon\).

steps.claim:
We need the following lemma:

Lemma 12.4. Let \(f\) be an \(\alpha\)-strongly convex function w.r.t. a norm \(\|\cdot\|\). Then, \(f(x) - f(x^{*}) \leqslant \frac{1}{2\alpha}\|\nabla f(x)\|_{*}^{2}\).

Lemma 12.4 shows that
\[
\|\nabla f(x_s)\|^{*2}_{[1-\gamma]} \geqslant 2 \alpha \delta_s \ .
\]
On the other hand, Theorem 12.2 showed that
\[
\delta_{t+1} - \delta_t \leqslant -\frac{\|\nabla f(x_t)\|^{*2}_{[1-\gamma]}}{2\sum_{i=1}^n \beta_i^{\gamma}}
\]
Combining these two, we get
\begin{align*}
\delta_{t+1} - \delta_t &\leqslant -\frac{\alpha \delta_t}{\sum_{i=1}^n \beta_i^{\gamma}} \\
\delta_{t+1} &\leqslant \delta_t \left(1 -\frac{\alpha}{\sum_{i=1}^n \beta_i^{\gamma}} \right)~.
\end{align*}
Applying the above inequality recursively and recalling that \(\delta_t = \mathbb{E}[f(x_t) - f(x^*)]\) gives the result.

theorems.statement:
Assume \(\ell(w, z)\) is \(\alpha\)-strongly convex over the domain \(\Omega\) and \(L\)-Lipschitz. Let \(\hat w_S = \arg \min_{w\in \Omega} \frac{1}{m} \sum_{i=1}^m \ell(w, z_i)\) denote the empirical risk minimizer (ERM). Then, ERM satisfies
\[
\Delta_{\sup} (\text{ERM}) \leqslant \frac{4L^2}{\alpha m}\,.
\]

steps.claim:
Denote by \(\hat w_S\) the empirical risk minimizer on a sample \(S.\) Fix arbitrary samples \(S,S'\) of size \(m\) and an index \(i\in[m].\) We need to show that
\[
|(\ell(\hat w_{S^{(i)}},z_i')-\ell(\hat w_{S},z_i'))|\leqslant\frac{4L^2}{\alpha m}\,.
\]
On one hand, by strong convexity we know that
\[
R_S(\hat w_{S^{(i)}}) - R_S(\hat w_{S}) \geqslant \frac{\alpha}{2} \| \hat w_{S} - \hat w_{S^{(i)}} \|^2 \,.
\]
On the other hand,
\begin{align*}
&R_S(\hat w_{S^{(i)}})-R_S(\hat w_{S})\\
&=\frac{1}{m}(\ell(\hat w_{S^{(i)}},z_i)-\ell(\hat w_{S},z_i))+\frac{1}{m}\sum_{i\neq j}(\ell(\hat w_{S^{(i)}},z_j)-\ell(\hat w_{S},z_j))\\
&=\frac{1}{m}(\ell(\hat w_{S^{(i)}},z_i)-\ell(\hat w_{S},z_i))+\frac{1}{m}(\ell(\hat w_{S},z_i')-\ell(\hat w_{S^{(i)}},z_i'))+\left(R_{S^{(i)}}(\hat w_{S^{(i)}})-R_{S^{(i)}}(\hat w_{S})\right)\\
&\leqslant\frac{1}{m}|\ell(\hat w_{S^{(i)}},z_i)-\ell(\hat w_{S},z_i)| +\frac{1}{m}|(\ell(\hat w_{S},z_i')-\ell(\hat w_{S^{(i)}},z_i'))|\\
&\leqslant\frac{2L}{m}\|\hat w_{S^{(i)}}-\hat w_{S}\|\,.
\end{align*}
Here, we used that
\[
R_{S^{(i)}}(\hat w_{S^{(i)}}) - R_{S^{(i)}}(\hat w_{S})) \leqslant 0
\]
and the fact that \(\ell\) is \(L\)-Lipschitz.

Putting it all together \(\| \hat w_{S^{(i)}} - \hat w_{S} \| \leqslant \frac{4 L}{\alpha m}\). Then by the Lipschitz condition we have that
\[
|(\ell(\hat w_{S^{(i)}},z_i')-\ell(\hat w_{S},z_i'))|\leqslant L\|\hat w_{S^{(i)}}-\hat w_{S}\|\leqslant\frac{4L^2}{\alpha m}\,.
\]
Hence, \(\Delta_{\sup}(\text{ERM}) \leqslant \frac{4 L ^ 2}{\alpha m}\).

Fix any direction \(d \in \mathbb{R}^n\).

    \]
    The inequality follows because \(x^*\) is a local minimum, \(0 \leqslant f(x^* + \alpha d) - f(x^*)\) for sufficiently small \(\alpha\). So, we can construct a sequence with only positive \(\alpha\) that converges to \(x^*\) such that each element \(0 \leqslant \frac{f(x^* + \alpha_n d) - f(x^*)}{\alpha_n}\) which implies that statement given that \(f\) is locally differentiable. Since \(d\) is arbitrary, this implies that \(\nabla f(x^*) = 0\).
    \item First we represent \(f(x^* + \alpha d) - f(x^*)\) using the 2nd order Taylor expansion.
    \[
        f(x^* + \alpha d) - f(x^*) = \alpha \nabla f(x^*)^\top d + \frac{\alpha^2}{2} d^\top \nabla^2 f(x^*) d + o(\alpha^2) = \frac{\alpha^2}{2} d^\top \nabla^2 f(x^*) d + o(\alpha^2)
    \]
    Now we do the following
    \[
        0 \leqslant \lim_{\alpha \to 0} \frac{f(x^* + \alpha d) - f(x^*)}{\alpha^2} = \lim_{\alpha \to 0} \frac{1}{2} d^\top \nabla^2 f(x^*) d + \frac{o(\alpha^2)}{\alpha^2} = \frac{1}{2} d^\top \nabla^2 f(x^*) d
    \]
    Because \(d\) is arbitrary, this implies that \(\nabla^2 f(x^*) \succeq 0\) (Positive semidefinite).
\end{enumerate}

theorems.statement: Let \(\Omega \subseteq \mathbb{R}^d\) be a closed convex set. Let \(\mathcal{A}\) denote the affine set \(\{x : Ax = b\}\) for some \(A \in \mathbb{R}^{n \times d}\) and \(b \in \mathbb{R}^n\). Suppose that the set \(\operatorname{ri}(\Omega) \cap \mathcal{A}\) is non-empty. Then for any \(x \in \Omega \cap \mathcal{A}\), \[\mathcal{N}_{\Omega \cap \mathcal{A}}(x) = \mathcal{N}_{\Omega}(x) + \{A^\top \lambda : \lambda \in \mathbb{R}^n\}\,.\]

steps.claim: The ``\(\supseteq\)'' assertion is straightforward.

To see this, suppose \(z \in \Omega \cap \mathcal{A}\) and note that \(z-x \in \operatorname{null}(A)\) so that \((z-x)^\top A^\top \lambda = \lambda^\top A(z-x) = 0\) for all \(\lambda \in \mathbb{R}^n\).

If \(u \in \mathcal{N}_{\Omega}(x)\), then \((z-x)^\top u \leqslant 0\), so for \(\lambda \in \mathbb{R}^n\), we have \[\langle z-x, u + A^\top \lambda \rangle = \langle z-x, u \rangle \leqslant 0\] implying that \(u + A^\top \lambda \in \mathcal{N}_{\Omega \cap \mathcal{A}}(x)\).
For the reverse inclusion, let \(v \in \mathcal{N}_{\Omega \cap \mathcal{A}}(x)\).

Then we have \[v^\top (z-x) \leqslant 0 \text{ for all } z \in \Omega \cap \mathcal{A}.\] Now define the sets \[\begin{aligned} C_1 &= \left\{ (y,\mu) \in \mathbb{R}^{d+1} : y = z-x,\,\, z \in \Omega,\,\, \mu \leqslant v^\top y \right\}\\ C_2 &= \left\{ (y,\mu) \in \mathbb{R}^{d+1} : y \in \operatorname{ker}(A),\,\, \mu = 0 \right\}\,. \end{aligned}\] Note that \(\operatorname{ri}(C_1) \cap C_2 = \emptyset\) because otherwise there would exist a \((\hat{y},\hat{\mu})\) such that \[v^\top \hat{y} > \hat{\mu} = 0\] and \(\hat{y} \in \mathcal{T}_{\Omega \cap \mathcal{A}}(x)\).
This would contradict our assumption that \(v \in \mathcal{N}_{\Omega \cap \mathcal{A}}(x)\).
Since their intersection is empty, we can properly separate \(\operatorname{ri}(C_1)\) from \(C_2\).

Indeed, since \(C_2\) is a subspace and \(C_1\) has nonempty relative interior, there must be a \((w,\gamma)\) such that \[\inf_{(y,\mu)\in C_1} \{ w^\top y + \gamma \mu\} < \sup_{(y,\mu)\in C_1} \{ w^\top y + \gamma \mu\} \leqslant 0\] while \[w^\top u = 0 \text{ for all } u \in \ker(A).\] In particular, this means that \(w = A^\top \lambda\) for some \(\lambda \in \mathbb{R}^n\).
Now, \(\gamma\) must be nonnegative, as otherwise, \[\sup_{(y,\mu)\in C_1} \{ w^\top y + \gamma \mu\} = \infty\] (which can be seen by letting \(\mu\) tend to negative infinity).
If \(\gamma = 0\), then \[\sup_{y \in C_1} w^\top y \leqslant 0\] but the set \(\{y : w^\top y = 0\}\) does not contain the set \(\{z-x : z \in \Omega\}\) as the infimum is strictly negative.
This means that the relative interior of \(\Omega - \{x\}\) cannot intersect the kernel of \(A\) which contradicts our assumptions.
Thus, we can conclude that \(\gamma\) is strictly positive.
By homogeneity, we may as well assume that \(\gamma = 1\).

To complete the argument, note that we now have \[(w+v)^\top (z-x) \leqslant 0 \text{ for all } z \in \Omega.\] This means that \(v+w \in \mathcal{N}_{\Omega}(x)\) and we have already shown that \(w = A^\top \lambda\).
Thus, \[v = (v+w)-w \in \mathcal{N}_{\Omega}(x) + \mathcal{N}_{\mathcal{A}}(x)\,.\]

theorems.statement: For any function \(\varphi(x,z)\), \[\min_x \max_z \varphi(x,z) \geqslant \max_z \min_x \varphi(x,z)\,.\]

steps.claim: The proof is essentially tautological. Note that we always have \[\varphi(x,z) \geqslant \min_x \varphi(x,z).\] Taking the maximization with respect to the second argument verifies that \[\max_z \varphi(x,z) \geqslant \max_z \min_x \varphi(x,z) \quad \forall x\,.\] Now, minimizing the left hand side with respect to \(x\) proves \[\min_x \max_z \varphi(x,z) \geqslant \max_z \min_x \varphi(x,z)\] which is precisely our assertion.

theorem 13.11: We have for any \(\lambda>0\), with probability at least \(1-\delta\), for all \(n\geq 1\) and \(f\in\mathcal{F}\): \[\left[-\sum_{i=1}^{n} f(Z_i)-\frac{1}{\lambda}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\ln\mathbb{E}_{Z_i^{(y)}}e^{-\lambda f(Z_i)}\right]\leq\inf_{\epsilon>0}\left[2n\epsilon+\frac{\ln(M(\epsilon,\mathcal{F},\|\cdot\|_\infty)/\delta)}{\lambda}\right].\]

Shared setting for the results below. All definitions, standing assumptions and numbered equations that the proofs rely on are collected here.

section 13.1 sequential observation setup. In Section 13.1, data are observed sequentially. At each time \(t\), after the history \(S_{t-1}\) has been observed, the next observation \(Z_t\) is drawn according to a distribution that may depend on that history. The observation is decomposed as \(Z_t=(Z_t^{(x)},Z_t^{(y)})\), where \(Z_t^{(x)}\) is the component determined by the past history or the chosen action at time \(t\), and \(Z_t^{(y)}\) is the random response component. The history after time \(t\) is \(S_t=(Z_1,\ldots,Z_t)\), and \(\mathcal{S}_T\) denotes the full sequential experiment/history through time \(T\). For a function depending on \(S_t\), the notation \(\mathbb{E}_{Z_t^{(y)}}[\cdot]\) means conditional expectation over the response component \(Z_t^{(y)}\), conditional on \(S_{t-1}\) and on \(Z_t^{(x)}\). Stopping times are adapted to the filtration generated by the histories \(S_t\).

definition 4.1. Let \((\mathcal{V},d)\) be a pseudometric space with metric \(d(\cdot,\cdot)\). A finite
set \(\mathcal{G}(\epsilon) \subset \mathcal{V}\) is an \(\epsilon\)-cover (or \(\epsilon\)-net) of \(\mathcal{G} \subset \mathcal{V}\) if, for all \(\phi \in \mathcal{G}\), there exists \(\phi' \in \mathcal{G}(\epsilon)\) so that \(d(\phi', \phi) \leq \epsilon\). The \(\epsilon\)-covering number of \(\mathcal{G}\) with metric \(d\) is the smallest cardinality \(N(\epsilon, \mathcal{G}, d)\) of such \(\mathcal{G}(\epsilon)\). The number \(\ln N(\epsilon, \mathcal{G}, d)\) is called the \(\epsilon\)-entropy.
For a function class \(\mathcal{G}\) with seminorm \(L_{p}(\mathcal{D})\) in (3.19), we denote the corresponding \(L_{p}(\mathcal{D})\)-covering number as \(N(\epsilon, \mathcal{G}, L_{p}(\mathcal{D}))\). When \(1 \leq p \leq q\), we have
\[
N(\epsilon,\mathcal{G},L_{p}(\mathcal{D}))\leq N(\epsilon,\mathcal{G},L_{q}(\mathcal{D})).
\]
It is easy to verify the following relationship, which implies that \( L_{p}(\mathcal{D}) \) bracketing cover is a stronger requirement than \( L_{p}(\mathcal{D}) \) cover.

Packing Number. Let \((\mathcal{V},d)\) be a pseudometric space with metric \(d(\cdot,\cdot)\). A finite subset \(\mathcal{G}(\epsilon)\subset \mathcal{G}\) is an \(\epsilon\)-packing of \(\mathcal{G}\) if \(d(\phi,\phi^{\prime})>\epsilon\) for all \(\phi,\phi^{\prime}\in\mathcal{G}(\epsilon)\). The \(\epsilon\)-packing number of \(\mathcal{G}\), denoted by \(M(\epsilon,\mathcal{G},d)\), is the largest cardinality of \(\epsilon\)-packing of \(\mathcal{G}\).
The following results illustrate the equivalence between covering number and packing number. One advantage of using an \(\epsilon\) packing of \(\mathcal{G}\) instead of an \(\epsilon\) cover of \(\mathcal{G}\) is that all members in the \(\epsilon\) packing also belong to \(\mathcal{G}\). There if members in \(\mathcal{G}\) satisfy certain assumptions such as the variance condition, then members of its \(\epsilon\) packing also satisfy such assumptions. For this reason, we will use packing numbers instead of covering numbers in some of the theoretical analysis in later chapters.

theorems.statement:
Assume that for all \( f \in \mathcal{F} \) and \( Z_{t}: -f(Z_{t}) + \mathbb{E}_{Z_{t}^{(y)}}f(Z_{t}) \leq b \), and the following variance condition holds for all \( f \in \mathcal{F} \) and \( S_{t} \):
\[
\operatorname{Var}_{Z_{t}^{(y)}}[f(Z_{t})]\leq c_{0}^{2}+c_{1}\mathbb{E}_{Z_{t}^{(y)}}[f(Z_{t})],
\]
then with probability at least \(1 - \delta\), for all \(f \in \mathcal{F}\):
\[
\begin{array}{l}\left(1-\lambda c_{1}\phi(\lambda b)\right)\sum_{t=1}^{n}\mathbb{E}_{Z_{t}^{(y)}}[f(Z_{t})]\leq\sum_{t=1}^{n}f(Z_{t})+\lambda n c_{0}^{2}\phi(\lambda b)\\ +\inf_{\epsilon>0}\left[2 n\epsilon+\frac{\ln(M(\epsilon,\mathcal{F},\|\cdot\|_{\infty})/\delta)}{\lambda}\right],\\ \end{array}
\]
where \(\phi (z) = (e^{z} - z - 1) / z^{2}\)

steps.claim:
Note that by employing the moment estimation of Bennett's inequality in Lemma 2.20, we obtain
\[
\begin{array}{l}\frac{1}{\lambda}\ln\mathbb{E}_{Z_{t}^{(y)}}e^{-\lambda f(Z_{t})}\\ \leq-\mathbb{E}_{Z_{t}^{(y)}}[f(Z_{t})]+\lambda\phi(\lambda b)\operatorname{Var}_{Z_{t}^{(y)}}[f(Z_{t})]\\ \leq-\mathbb{E}_{Z_{t}^{(y)}}[f(Z_{t})]+\lambda\phi(\lambda b)[c_{0}^{2}+c_{1}\mathbb{E}_{Z_{t}^{(y)}}[f(Z_{t})]].\\ \end{array}
\]
We can now obtain the desired bound from Theorem 13.11.

theorems.statement:
Let \(\{(X_t, \epsilon_t)\}\) be a filtered sequence in \(\mathcal{X} \times \mathbb{R}\) so that \(\epsilon_t\) is conditional zero-mean sub-Gaussian noise: for all \(\lambda \in \mathbb{R}\),
\[
\ln\mathbb{E}\left[e^{\lambda\epsilon_{t}}\mid X_{t},\mathcal{S}_{t-1}\right]\leq\frac{\lambda^{2}}{2}\sigma^{2},
\]
where \( S_{t-1} \) denotes the history data. Assume that \( Y_t = f_*(X_t) + \epsilon_t \), with \( f_*(x) \in \mathcal{F}: \mathcal{X} \to \mathbb{R} \). Let \( \hat{f}_t \) be an approximate ERM solution for some \( \epsilon' > 0 \):
\[
\left(\sum_{s=1}^{t}\left(\hat{f}_{t}\left(X_{s}\right)-Y_{s}\right)^{2}\right)^{1/2}\leq\min_{f\in\mathcal{F}}\left(\sum_{s=1}^{t}\left(f\left(X_{s}\right)-Y_{s}\right)^{2}\right)^{1/2}+\sqrt{t}\epsilon^{\prime}.
\]
Then with probability at least \(1 - \delta\), for all \(t \geq 0\):
\[
\sum_{s=1}^{t}(\hat{f}_{t}(X_{t})-f_{*}(X_{t}))^{2}\leq\inf_{\epsilon>0}\left[8 t(\epsilon+\epsilon^{\prime})(\sigma+2\epsilon+2\epsilon^{\prime})+12\sigma^{2}\ln\frac{2 N(\epsilon,\mathcal{F},\|\cdot\|_{\infty})}{\delta}\right].
\]

steps.claim:
Let \(\eta = \sigma^{-2} / 4\), and for \(f \in \mathcal{F}\), let
\[
\phi(f,Z_{t})=\left[\left(f(X_{t})-Y_{t}\right)^{2}-\left(f_{*}(X_{t})-Y_{t}\right)^{2}\right].
\]
Let \(\mathcal{F}_{\epsilon}\) be an \(\epsilon \| \cdot \|_{\infty}\) cover of \(\mathcal{F}\) with \(N = N(\epsilon, \mathcal{F}, \| \cdot \|_{\infty})\) members.

Given any \(f \in \mathcal{F}_{\epsilon}\),
\[
\begin{array}{l}\ln\mathbb{E}_{Y_{t}|X_{t},S_{t-1}}\exp(-\eta\phi(f,Z_{t}))\\ = -\eta\left(f\left(X_{t}\right)-f_{*}\left(X_{t}\right)\right)^{2}\\ +\ln\mathbb{E}_{Y_{t}\mid X_{t},S_{t-1}}\exp(-2\eta(f(X_{t})-f_{*}(X_{t}))(f_{*}(X_{t})-Y_{t}))\\ \leq-\eta(f(X_{t})-f_{*}(X_{t}))^{2}+\frac{4\eta^{2}\sigma^{2}}{2}(f(X_{t})-f_{*}(X_{t}))^{2}\\ = -\frac{\left(f(X_{t})-f_{*}(X_{t})\right)^{2}}{8\sigma^{2}}.\\ \end{array}
\]
The inequality used the sub-Gaussian noise assumption.
It follows from Theorem 13.11 that with probability at least \( 1 - \delta / 2 \), for all \( f \in \mathcal{F}_{\epsilon} \) and \( t \geq 0 \):

\[
\sum_{i=1}^{t}-\eta\phi(f,Z_{i})\leq-\sum_{i=1}^{t}\frac{\left(f\left(X_{i}\right)-f_{*}\left(X_{i}\right)\right)^{2}}{8\sigma^{2}}+\ln(2 N/\delta).\tag{13.5}
\]
Using Exercise 13.3, we have with probability at least \(1 - \delta /2\), for all \(t\geq 0\)
\[
\underbrace{\sum_{i=1}^{t}\left(f_{*}\left(X_{i}\right)-Y_{i}\right)^{2}}_{A}\leq 2 t\sigma^{2}+3\sigma^{2}\ln(2/\delta).\tag{13.6}
\]
It follows that with probability at least \(1 - \delta\), for all \(t \geq 0\) and \(f \in \mathcal{F}_{\epsilon}\), both (13.5)
and (13.6) hold.
Now, let \( f \in \mathcal{F}_{\epsilon} \) so that \( \| \hat{f}_t - f \|_{\infty} \leq \epsilon \).

This implies that
\[
\begin{array}{l}\sum_{i=1}^{t}\left[(f(X_{i})-Y_{i})^{2}-(f_{*}(X_{i})-Y_{i})^{2}\right]\leq\left(\sqrt{\sum_{i=1}^{t}(\hat{f}_{t}(X_{i})-Y_{i})^{2}}+\sqrt{t}\epsilon\right)^{2}-A\\ \leq\left(\sqrt{A}+\sqrt{t}(\epsilon+\epsilon^{\prime})\right)^{2}-A\\ \stackrel{(a)}{\leq}(\epsilon^{\prime}+\epsilon)^{2}t+2\sqrt{t}(\epsilon^{\prime}+\epsilon)\sigma\sqrt{2 t+3\ln(2/\delta)}\\ \leq 4\left(\epsilon^{\prime}+\epsilon\right)^{2}t+3\sigma t\left(\epsilon^{\prime}+\epsilon\right)+\sigma^{2}\ln(2/\delta).\tag{13.7}\\ \end{array}
\]
In the above derivations, the first inequality used \( |f(X_i) - Y_i| \leq |\hat{f}_t(X_i) - Y_i| + \epsilon \) for all \( i \).
The second inequality used the fact that \( \hat{f}_t \) is approximate ERM. (a) follows from (13.6).
The last inequality used \( 2a\sigma \sqrt{2b + 3c} \leq 3a\sigma \sqrt{b} + 3a^2 + \sigma^2 c \).

We thus obtain
\[
\begin{array}{l}\left(\sum_{i=1}^{t}(\hat{f}(X_{i})-f_{*}(X_{i}))^{2}\right)^{1/2}\\ \leq\sqrt{\epsilon^{2}t}+\left(\sum_{i=1}^{t}\left(f\left(X_{i}\right)-f_{*}\left(X_{i}\right)\right)^{2}\right)^{1/2}\quad(\text{t r i a n g l e i n e q u a l i t y})\\ \leq\sqrt{\epsilon^{2}t}+\left(8\sigma^{2}\ln(2N/\delta)+8\sigma^{2}\sum_{i=1}^{t}\eta\phi(f,Z_{i})\right)^{1/2}\quad(\text{f r o m}(13. 5))\\ =\sqrt{\epsilon^{2}t}+\left(8\sigma^{2}\ln(2N/\delta)+2\sum_{i=1}^{t}\left[\left(f\left(X_{i}\right)-Y_{i}\right)^{2}-\left(f_{*}\left(X_{i}\right)-Y_{i}\right)^{2}\right]\right)^{1/2}\\ \leq\sqrt{\epsilon^{2}t}+\left(10\sigma^{2}\ln(2N/\delta)+8t\left(\epsilon^{\prime}+\epsilon\right)^{2}+6\sigma t\left(\epsilon^{\prime}+\epsilon\right)\right)^{1/2}\quad(\text{f r o m}(13. 7))\\ \leq\left(12\sigma^{2}\ln(2N/\delta)+16t(\epsilon+\epsilon^{\prime})^{2}+8\sigma t(\epsilon+\epsilon^{\prime})\right)^{1/2},\\ \end{array}
\]
where the last inequality used \(\sqrt{a} +\sqrt{b}\leq \sqrt{6a + 1.2b}\) .
This implies the bound.

theorems.statement:
Consider a sequence of real-valued random (measurable) functions \(\xi_1(S_1),\ldots,\xi_T(S_T)\). Let \(\tau \leq T\) be a stopping time so that \(\mathbb{1}(t\leq \tau)\) is measurable in \(S_{t}\). We have
\[
\mathbb{E}_{\mathcal{S}_{T}}\exp\left(\sum_{i=1}^{\tau}\xi_{i}-\sum_{i=1}^{\tau}\ln\mathbb{E}_{Z_{i}^{(y)}}e^{\xi_{i}}\right)=1.
\]

steps.claim: We prove the lemma by induction on \( T \). When \( T = 0 \), the equality is trivial.
Assume that the claim holds at \( T - 1 \) for some \( T \geq 1 \).
Now we will prove the equation at time \( T \) using the induction hypothesis.
Note that \(\tilde{\xi}_i = \xi_i\mathbb{1}(i\leq \tau)\) is measurable in \(S_{i}\).

We have
\[
\sum_{i=1}^{\tau}\xi_{i}-\sum_{i=1}^{\tau}\ln\mathbb{E}_{Z_{i}^{(y)}}e^{\xi_{i}}=\sum_{i=1}^{T}\tilde{\xi}_{i}-\sum_{i=1}^{T}\ln\mathbb{E}_{Z_{i}^{(y)}}e^{\tilde{\xi}_{i}}.
\]
It follows that
\[
\begin{array}{l}\mathbb{E}_{Z_{1},\dots,Z_{T}}\exp\left(\sum_{i=1}^{\tau}\xi_{i}-\sum_{i=1}^{\tau}\ln\mathbb{E}_{Z_{i}^{(y)}}e^{\xi_{i}}\right)\\ =\mathbb{E}_{Z_{1},\dots,Z_{T}}\exp\left(\sum_{i=1}^{T}\tilde{\xi}_{i}-\sum_{i=1}^{T}\ln\mathbb{E}_{Z_{i}^{(y)}}e^{\tilde{\xi}_{i}}\right)\\ =\mathbb{E}_{Z_{1},\ldots,Z_{n-1},Z_{T}^{(x)}}\left[\exp\left(\sum_{i=1}^{T-1}\tilde{\xi}_{i}-\sum_{i=1}^{T-1}\ln\mathbb{E}_{Z_{i}^{(y)}}e^{\tilde{\xi}_{i}}\right)\underbrace{\mathbb{E}_{Z_{T}^{(y)}}\exp(\tilde{\xi}_{T}-\ln\mathbb{E}_{Z_{T}^{(y)}}e^{\tilde{\xi}_{T}})}_{=1}\right]\\ =\mathbb{E}_{Z_{1},\dots,Z_{T-1}}\exp\left(\sum_{i=1}^{T-1}\tilde{\xi}_{i}-\sum_{i=1}^{T-1}\ln\mathbb{E}_{Z_{i}^{(y)}}e^{\tilde{\xi}_{i}}\right)\\ =\mathbb{E}_{Z_{1},\dots,Z_{T-1}}\exp\left(\sum_{i=1}^{\min(\tau,T-1)}\xi_{i}-\sum_{i=1}^{\min(\tau,T-1)}\ln\mathbb{E}_{Z_{i}^{(y)}}e^{\xi_{i}}\right)=1.\\ \end{array}
\]
Note that the last equation follows from the induction hypothesis, and the fact that \(\min(\tau,T-1)\) is a stopping time \(\leq T - 1\).

theorems.statement:
Consider a sequence of random functions \(\xi_1(S_1),\ldots,\xi_t(S_t),\ldots\) with filtration \(\{\mathcal{F}_t\}\). We have for any \(\delta \in (0,1)\) and \(\lambda >0\):
\[
\operatorname*{Pr}\left[\exists n>0: -\sum_{i=1}^{n}\xi_{i}\geq\frac{\ln(1/\delta)}{\lambda}+\frac{1}{\lambda}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\ln\mathbb{E}_{Z_{i}^{(y)}}e^{-\lambda\xi_{i}}\right]\leq\delta .
\]
Moreover, consider a sequence of \(\{z_t\in \mathbb{R}\}\) adapted to \(\{\mathcal{F}_t\}\), and events \(A_{t}\) on \(\mathcal{F}_t\):
\[
\ln\Pr\left[\exists n>0:\sum_{i=1}^{n}\xi_{i}\leq z_{n}\&\mathcal{S}_{n}\in A_{n}\right]\leq\inf_{\lambda>0}\sup_{n>0}\sup_{\mathcal{S}_{n}\in A_{n}}\left[\lambda z_{n}+\sum_{i=1}^{n}\ln\mathbb{E}_{Z_{i}^{(y)}}e^{-\lambda\xi_{i}}\right].
\]

steps.claim: We will prove the result for a finite time sequence \(\xi_1(S_1),\ldots,\xi_T(S_T)\).
It implies the desired result by letting \(T\to \infty\).

Let
\[
\xi_{\tau}(\lambda)= -\sum_{i=1}^{\tau}\ln\mathbb{E}_{Z_{i}^{(y)}}e^{-\lambda\xi_{i}}-\lambda\sum_{i=1}^{\tau}\xi_{i},
\]
where \(\tau\) is a stopping time, then we have from Lemma 13.1:

\(\mathbb{E}e^{\xi_{\tau}(\lambda)} = 1\). Now for any given sequence of \(\tilde{z}_n(S_n)\) and \(A_{n}\), define the stopping time \(\tau\) as either \(T\), or the first time step \(n\) so that
\[
\xi_{n}(\lambda)\geq-\tilde{z}_{n}\left(\mathcal{S}_{n}\right)\&\mathcal{S}_{n}\in A_{n}
\]
for each sequence \(S_T\).

It follows that
\[
\begin{array}{l}\Pr\left(\exists n:\xi_{n}(\lambda)\geq-\tilde{z}_{n}\left(\mathcal{S}_{n}\right)\&\mathcal{S}_{n}\in A_{n}\right)\inf_{n>0,\mathcal{S}_{n}\in A_{n}}e^{-\tilde{z}_{n}\left(\mathcal{S}_{n}\right)}\\ \leq\mathbb{E}\left[e^{\xi_{\tau}(\lambda)+\tilde{z}_{\tau}\left(\mathcal{S}_{\tau}\right)}\mathbb{1}\left(\mathcal{S}_{\tau}\in A_{\tau}\right)\right]\inf_{n>0,\mathcal{S}_{n}\in A_{n}}e^{-\tilde{z}_{n}\left(\mathcal{S}_{n}\right)}\\ \leq\mathbb{E}\left[e^{\xi_{\tau}(\lambda)+\tilde{z}_{\tau}\left(\mathcal{S}_{\tau}\right)}\mathbb{1}\left(\mathcal{S}_{\tau}\in A_{\tau}\right)e^{-\tilde{z}_{\tau}\left(\mathcal{S}_{\tau}\right)}\right]\\ \leq\mathbb{E}e^{\xi_{\tau}(\lambda)}=1.\\ \end{array}
\]
Therefore we obtain
\[
\begin{array}{l}\ln\operatorname*{Pr}\left[\exists n>0: -\lambda\sum_{i=1}^{n}\xi_{i}\geq-\tilde{z}_{n}(\mathcal{S}_{n})+\sum_{i=1}^{n}\ln\mathbb{E}_{Z_{i}^{(y)}}e^{-\lambda\xi_{i}}\&\mathcal{S}_{n}\in A_{n}\right]\\ \leq\sup_{n>0:\mathcal{S}_{n}\in A_{n}}\tilde{z}_{n}(\mathcal{S}_{n}).\\ \end{array}
\]
Let \(\tilde{z}(\mathcal{S}_n) = \ln \delta\), we obtain the first inequality.

Let
\[
\tilde{z}_{n}(\mathcal{S}_{n})=\lambda z_{n}+\sum_{i=1}^{n}\ln\mathbb{E}_{Z_{i}^{(y)}}e^{-\lambda\xi_{i}},
\]
we obtain the second inequality.

theorems.statement:
We have for any \(\lambda >0\), with probability at least \(1 - \delta\), for all \(n\geq 1\) and \(f\in \mathcal{F}\):
\[
\left[-\sum_{i=1}^{n}f(Z_{i})-\frac{1}{\lambda}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\ln\mathbb{E}_{Z_{i}^{(y)}}e^{-\lambda f(Z_{i})}\right]\leq\inf_{\epsilon>0}\left[2 n\epsilon+\frac{\ln(M(\epsilon,\mathcal{F},\|\cdot\|_{\infty})/\delta)}{\lambda}\right].
\]

steps.claim: Let \(\mathcal{F}_{\epsilon} \subset \mathcal{F}\) be an \(\epsilon\) maximal packing of \(\mathcal{F}\), with \(|\mathcal{F}_{\epsilon}| \leq M(\epsilon, \mathcal{F}, \| \cdot \|_{\infty})\).
We obtain from Theorem 13.2, and the uniform bound over \(\mathcal{F}_{\epsilon}\) that with probability at least \(1 - \delta\):

\[
\sup_{f\in\mathcal{F}_{\epsilon}}\left[-\sum_{i=1}^{n}f(Z_{i})-\frac{1}{\lambda}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\ln\mathbb{E}_{Z_{i}^{(y)}}e^{-\lambda f(Z_{i})}\right]\leq\frac{\ln(M(\epsilon,\mathcal{F},\|\cdot\|_{\infty})/\delta)}{\lambda}.
\]
Since \(\mathcal{F}_{\epsilon}\) is also an \(\epsilon L_{\infty}\) cover of \(\mathcal{F}\) (see Theorem 5.2), we obtain
\[
\begin{array}{l}\sup_{f\in\mathcal{F}}\left[-\sum_{i=1}^{n}f(Z_{i})-\frac{1}{\lambda}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\ln\mathbb{E}_{Z_{i}^{(y)}}e^{-\lambda f(Z_{i})}\right]\\ \leq 2 n\epsilon+\sup_{f\in\mathcal{F}_{\epsilon}}\left[-\sum_{i=1}^{n}f(Z_{i})-\frac{1}{\lambda}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\ln\mathbb{E}_{Z_{i}^{(y)}}e^{-\lambda f(Z_{i})}\right].\\ \end{array}
\]
This implies the bound.

In the setting of general online (nonconvex) optimization, the Gibbs distribution can be defined after time \(t\) as follows
\[
p_t(w) \propto p_0(w) \exp \left(-\eta \sum_{s=1}^{t} \ell_s(w)\right), \tag{14.9}
\]
where \(p_0(w)\) is a prior on \(\Omega\).

Hedge Algorithm. Hedge Algorithm
Input: \(T\), prior \(p_{0}(w)\) on \(\Omega\), learning rate \(\eta > 0\)
1 Randomly draw \(w_{0} \sim p_{0}(w)\)
2 for \(t = 1, 2, \ldots, T\) do
3 \quad Observe loss \(\ell_{t}(w_{t-1})\)
4 \quad Randomly draw \(w_{t} \sim p_{t}(w)\) according to \((14.9)\)

We have the following result for the Hedge algorithm, using conditions similar to those of Theorem 7.17.

Online Gradient Descent. Algorithm 14.3: Online Gradient Descent
Input: Sequence of loss functions \(\ell_1,\dots,\ell_T\) defined on \(\Omega\) Output: \(\hat{w}\)   
1 Let \(w_{0} = 0\)   
2 for \(t=1,2,\ldots,T\) do   
3 Observe loss \(\ell_t(w_{t - 1})\)   
4 Let \(\tilde{w}_t = w_{t - 1} - \eta_t\nabla \ell_t(w_{t - 1})\)   
5 Let \(w_{t} = \arg \min_{w\in \Omega}\| w - \tilde{w}_{t}\|_{2}^{2}\)   
6 Let \(\hat{w} = T^{-1}\sum_{t = 1}^{T}w_{t - 1}\) or \(\hat{w} = w_{s}\) for a random \(s\) from O to \(T - 1\) Return: \(\hat{w}\)

example 14.10. Consider the structured-SVM loss of Example 9.32, where

If \( \| \psi(x, y) - \psi(, \ell) \|_2 \leq B \), then we can take \( G = B \). Using Theorem 14.5, we obtain

Shared setting for the results below. All definitions, standing assumptions and numbered equations that the proofs rely on are collected here.

Contextual Bandit Problem. In contextual bandit, we consider a context space \(\mathcal{X}\) and an action space \(\mathcal{A}\). Given context \(x \in \mathcal{X}\), we take an action \(a \in \mathcal{A}\), and observe a reward \(r \in \mathbb{R}\) that can depend on \((x, a)\). The contextual bandit problem is a repeated game: at each time step \(t\):
- The player observes a sample \( x_{t} \in \mathcal{X} \)
- The player chooses precisely one action (or arm) \(a_{t} \in \mathcal{A}\)
- The reward \( r_t \) is revealed.
Note that in this chapter, we will follow the convention in the bandit literature of using \(\mathcal{A}\) to denote the action space instead of the learning algorithm. We may also introduce the notation of policy for contextual bandits. Using the notation of Section 13.4, a bandit learning algorithm returns a policy \(\hat{q}(\mathcal{S}_{t-1})\) based on the history \(\mathcal{S}_{t-1}\).

definition 17.2. A policy \(\pi\) for contextual bandit is a map \(\mathcal{X} \to \Delta(\mathcal{A})\), where \(\Delta(\mathcal{A})\) denotes probability measures over \(\mathcal{A}\) with an appropriately defined \(\sigma\)-algebra. One may also write it as a conditional distribution \(\pi(a|x)\), and the policy draws \(a \sim \pi(\cdot|x)\) when it observes context \(x\). A contextual bandit algorithm \(\hat{q}\) maps historic observations
\[
\mathcal{S}_{t-1}=\left\{\left(x_{1},a_{1},r_{1}\right),\dots,\left(x_{t-1},a_{t-1},r_{t-1}\right)\right\}
\]
to a policy \(\pi_t = \hat{q}(\cdot | \mathcal{S}_{t-1})\) at each time step \(t\), and pulls an arm \(a_t \sim \pi_t(\cdot | x_t)\) based on the observation \(x_t\). In this chapter, we will also write the history dependent policy as \(a_t \sim \hat{q}(a_t | x_t, \mathcal{S}_{t-1})\).
The contextual bandit problem includes the multi-armed bandit problem as a special case if we take \( x = x_0 \) to be a fixed context for all time steps.
Similar to the case of multi-armed bandit problem, we may also consider the adversarial setting with an oblivious adversary as follows. At each time step \( t \), we have the information of all rewards \( [r_t(a) : a \in \mathcal{A}] \), but only reveals the value
of \( r_t(a_t) \) for the chosen arm \( a_t \). The goal is to maximize the expected cumulative reward
\[
\sum_{t=1}^{T}\mathbb{E}_{a_{t}\sim\pi_{t}}[r_{t}(a_{t})].
\]
If we are given a policy class \(\Pi\), then regret of a contextual bandit algorithm with respect to \(\Pi\) can be written as
\[
\operatorname{REG}_{T}=\sup_{\pi\in\Pi}\sum_{t=1}^{T}\mathbb{E}_{a_{t}\sim\pi}[r_{t}(a_{t})]-\sum_{t=1}^{T}\mathbb{E}_{a_{t}\sim\pi_{t}}[r_{t}(a_{t})].\tag{17.1}
\]
If we consider the stochastic contextual bandit setting with unknown value functions
\[
f_{*}(x,a)=\mathbb{E}[r|x,a],\qquad f_{*}(x)=\max_{a\in\mathcal{A}}f(x,a)
\]
that do not change over time, then the goal becomes to maximize the expected reward
\[
\sum_{t=1}^{T}\mathbb{E}_{a_{t}\sim\pi_{t}}[f_{*}(x_{t},a_{t})].
\]
The regret of the algorithm that produces policy sequence \(\{\pi_t\}\) is:
\[
\operatorname{REG}_{T}=\sum_{t=1}^{T}\mathbb{E}_{a_{t}\sim\pi_{t}}\left[f_{*}\left(x_{t}\right)-f_{*}\left(x_{t},a_{t}\right)\right].\tag{17.2}
\]

definition 17.7. Stochastic linear contextual bandit (or stochastic contextual bandit with linear payoff) is a contextual bandit problem, where the reward at each time step \( t \) is given by
\[
r_{t}(a)=r_{t}(x_{t},a)=w_{*}^{\top}\psi(x_{t},a)+\epsilon_{t}(x_{t},a),\tag{17.8}
\]
where \(\epsilon_t(x, a)\) is a zero-mean random variable. We assume that \(\mathcal{H}\) is a known inner product space, \(w_* \in \mathcal{H}\) is the unknown model parameter, and the feature vector \(\psi(x, a) \in \mathcal{H}\) is known.
In the stochastic linear bandit model, the number of arms can be either infinite or finite, and an UCB style algorithm is presented in Algorithm 17.2. Note that the algorithm selects an arm which has the largest confidence bound adjusted reward. This methodology is referred to as the optimism in the face of uncertainty, and is a direct generalization of upper confidence bound (UCB) for MAB. Therefore we call Algorithm 17.2 linear UCB, although it is also referred to as OFUL (optimism in the face of uncertainty linear bandit) in the literature (Abbasi-yadjkori et al., 2011).

EXP4. Algorithm 17.1: EXP4
Input: \(K,T,\mathcal{G},p_0(\cdot),\gamma \in (0,1],\eta >0,b\geq 0\)   
1 Let \(u_{0}(w) = 1\)   
2 for \(t=1,2,\ldots,T\) do   
3 Observe \(x_{t}\)   
4 for \(a=1,\dots,K\) do   
5 Let \(\hat{\pi}_t(a) = (1 - \gamma)\mathbb{E}_{w\sim p_{t - 1}(w)}\hat{q}_t(a|w,x_t) + \gamma /K\)   
6 Sample \(a_{t}\) according to \(\hat{\pi}_t(\cdot)\)   
7 Pull arm \(a_{t}\) and observe reward \(r_t(a_t)\in [0,1]\)   
8 Let \(\hat{r}_t(w,x_t,a_t) = \hat{q}_t(a_t|w,x_t)(r_t(a_t) - b) / \hat{\pi}_t(a_t)\)   
9 Let \(u_{t}(w) = u_{t - 1}(w)\exp (\eta \hat{r}_{t}(w,x_{t},a_{t}))\)   
10 Let \(p_t(w) = p_0(w)u_t(w) / \mathbb{E}_{w\sim p_0(w)}u_t(w)\)

Note that conditioned on the history, the estimator \(\hat{r}_t(w,x_t,a_t)\) is a random estimator that depends on the partial reward \(r_t(a_t)\) received for \(a_t \sim \hat{\pi}_t(a)\). Moreover, it is an unbiased estimator of the following shifted reward of \(w\), according to policy \(\hat{q}_t(\cdot|w,x_t)\):
\[
\mathbb{E}_{a_t \sim \hat{\pi}_t} \hat{r}_t(w,x_t,a_t) = \mathbb{E}_{a \sim \hat{q}_t(a|w,x_t)} (r_t(a) - b). \tag{17.3}
\]
which relies on the full reward vector \([r_t(a)]\) at time step \(t\) over all arms \(a\).

Linear UCB Algorithm. Algorithm 17.2: Linear UCB Algorithm
Input: \(\lambda, T, \{\beta_t\}\)  
1 Let \(A_0 = \lambda I\)  
2 Let \(w_0 = 0\)  
3 Let \(b_0 = 0\)  
4 for \(t = 1, 2, \dots, T\) do  
5 Observe \(x_t\)  
6 Let \(a_t \in \arg \max_a \left[ w_{t-1}^\top \psi(x_t, a) + \beta_{t-1} \sqrt{\psi(x_t, a)^\top A_{t-1}^{-1} \psi(x_t, a)} \right]\)  
7 Pull arm \(a_t\) and observe reward \(r_t(x_t, a_t)\)  
8 Let \(b_t = b_{t-1} + r_t(x_t, a_t) \psi(x_t, a_t)\)  
9 Let \(A_t = A_{t-1} + \psi(x_t, a_t) \psi(x_t, a_t)^\top\)  
10 Let \(w_t = A_t^{-1} b_t\)

theorems.statement:
Let \(\eta = \gamma / K\) and \(b = 0\). Assume that the uniform random policy belongs to \(\Omega\) and \(|\Omega| = N < \infty\). Let \(p_0(w)\) be the uniform prior over \(\Omega\), then
\[
G_{*}-\mathbb{E}\sum_{t=1}^{T}r_{t}(a_{t})\leq(e-1)\gamma G_{*}+\frac{K\ln N}{\gamma},
\]
where the expectation is with respect to the randomization of the algorithm, and
\[
G_{*}=\arg\max_{w}\sum_{t=1}^{T}\mathbb{E}\left.\mathbb{E}_{a\sim\hat{q}_{t}(\cdot|w,x_{t})}[r_{t}(a)]\right..
\]

steps.claim: We have \(\eta \hat{r}_t(w,x_t,a_t)\leq 1\), and thus \(c(\eta,b)=e-2\).

Note that the uniform random policy belongs to \(\Omega\) implies that
\[
\frac{1}{K}\sum_{t=1}^{T}\sum_{a=1}^{K}r_{t}(a)\leq G_{*}.
\]
We consider Theorem 17.4, with \( q \) defined as \( q(w) = \mathbb{1}(w = w_{*}) \), where \( w_{*} \) achieves the maximum of \( G_{*} \).

This implies
\[
\mathbb{E}\sum_{t=1}^{T}r_{t}(a_{t})\geq(1-\gamma)\left[G_{*}-\frac{K}{\gamma}\ln N\right]-(e-2)\gamma G_{*}.
\]
This implies the bound.

theorems.statement:
Assume that in the stochastic linear bandit model, \(r_t(x_t, a_t) \in [0,1]\) and \(\|w_*\|_2 \leq B\) for some constant \(B\). Let \(\mu_t(x, a) = \mathbb{E}_{\epsilon_t(x,a)} r_t(x,a) = w_*^\top \psi(x,a)\). Let \(a_*(x) \in \arg \max_a \mu_t(x,a)\) be the optimal arm for each context \(x\). Then in Algorithm 17.2, with probability at least \(1 - \delta\),
\[
\mathbb{E}\sum_{t=1}^{T}[\mu_{t}(x_{t},a_{*}(x_{t}))-\mu_{t}(x_{t},a_{t})]\leq 3\sqrt{\ln|A_{T}/\lambda|\sum_{t=1}^{T}\beta_{t-1}^{2}}+2\ln|A_{T}/\lambda|,
\]
where \(\{\beta_t\}\) is any sequence that satisfies (17.9).

steps.claim:
We have for \(t \geq 1\): \[
\begin{array}{l}w_{*}^{\top}\psi(x_{t},a_{*}(x_{t}))\\ \leq w_{t-1}^{\top}\psi(x_{t},a_{*}(x_{t}))+\beta_{t-1}\sqrt{\psi(x_{t},a_{*}(x_{t}))^{\top}A_{t-1}^{-1}\psi(x_{t},a_{*}(x_{t}))}\\ \leq w_{t-1}^{\top}\psi(x_{t},a_{t})+\beta_{t-1}\sqrt{\psi(x_{t},a_{t})^{\top}A_{t-1}^{-1}\psi(x_{t},a_{t})}\\ \leq w_{*}^{\top}\psi(x_{t},a_{t})+2\beta_{t-1}\sqrt{\psi(x_{t},a_{t})^{\top}A_{t-1}^{-1}\psi(x_{t},a_{t})},\\ \end{array}
\]
where the first and the third inequalities used Lemma 17.8.
The second inequality is due to the UCB choice of \( a_{t} \) in Algorithm 17.2.
Let \( E_{t} \) be the event of \( \| \psi (x_{t},a_{t})\|_{A_{t - 1}^{- 1}}\leq 1 \).

Since \( w_{*}^{\top}\psi (x_{t},a)\in [0,1] \), we have
\[
w_{*}^{\top}\psi(x_{t},a_{*}(x_{t}))-w_{*}^{\top}\psi(x_{t},a_{t})\leq 2\beta_{t-1}\|\psi(x_{t},a_{t})\|_{A_{t-1}^{-1}}\mathbb{1}(E_{t})+\mathbb{1}(E_{t}^{c}).
\]
By summing over \( t = 1 \) to \( t = T \), we obtain
\[
\begin{array}{l}\sum_{t=1}^{T}\left[\mu_{t}\left(x_{t},a_{*}\left(x_{t}\right)\right)-\mu_{t}\left(x_{t},a_{t}\right)\right]\\ \leq 2\sum_{t=1}^{T}\beta_{t-1}\|\psi\left(x_{t},a_{t}\right)\|_{A_{t-1}^{-1}}\mathbb{1}\left(E_{t}\right)+\sum_{t=1}^{T}\mathbb{1}\left(E_{t}^{c}\right)\\ \leq 2\sum_{t=1}^{T}\beta_{t-1}\sqrt{\frac{2\|\psi(x_{t},a_{t})\|_{A_{t-1}^{-1}}^{2}}{1+\|\psi(x_{t},a_{t})\|_{A_{t-1}^{-1}}^{2}}}+2\sum_{t=1}^{T}\frac{\psi(x_{t},a_{t})^{\top}A_{t-1}^{-1}\psi(x_{t},a_{t})}{1+\psi(x_{t},a_{t})^{\top}A_{t-1}^{-1}\psi(x_{t},a_{t})}\\ \leq 3\sqrt{\sum_{t=1}^{T}\beta_{t-1}^{2}}\sqrt{\sum_{t=1}^{T}\frac{\psi(x_{t},a_{t})^{\top}A_{t-1}^{-1}\psi(x_{t},a_{t})}{1+\psi(x_{t},a_{t})^{\top}A_{t-1}^{-1}\psi(x_{t},a_{t})}}+2\ln|A_{T}/\lambda|.\\ \end{array}
\]
The second inequality used simple algebraic inequalities under \( E_{t} \) and \( E_{t}^{c} \).
The third inequality used the Cauchy-Schwartz inequality and Lemma 13.9.
We can now apply Lemma 13.9 again to obtain the desired bound.

theorems.statement:
Given any function \(U(w)\), we have
\[
\min_{p\in\Delta(\Omega)}\left[\mathbb{E}_{w\sim p}U(w)+\mathrm{KL}(p| |p_{0})\right]= -\ln\mathbb{E}_{w\sim p_{0}}\exp(-U(w)),
\]
and the solution is achieved by the Gibbs distribution \( q(w) \propto p_0(w) \exp(-U(w)) \). Here \( \Delta(\Omega) \) denotes the set of probability distributions on \( \Omega \).

steps.claim:
Let \(C = \mathbb{E}_{w\sim p_0}\exp (-U(w))\) . Then we have
\[
\begin{array}{l}\mathbb{E}_{w\sim p}U(w)+\operatorname{KL}(p| |p_{0})=\mathbb{E}_{w\sim p}\ln\frac{p(w)}{p_{0}(w)\exp(-U(w))}\\ =\mathbb{E}_{w\sim p}\ln\frac{p(w)}{Cq(w)}\geq-\ln C.\\ \end{array}
\]
The inequality used the fact that \(\mathrm{KL}(p||q) \geq 0\), and the equality holds when \(p(w) = q(w)\).

theorems.statement:
Assume that in the stochastic linear bandit model, \(\| w_{*}\|_{\mathcal{H}}\leq B\) for some constant \(B\), and in Algorithm 17.2, assume that \(\{\beta_t\}\) is any sequence so that
\[
\Pr\left[\forall 0\leq t\leq T:\beta_{t}\geq\sqrt{\lambda}B+\left\|\sum_{s=1}^{t}\epsilon_{s}\left(x_{s},a_{s}\right)\psi\left(x_{s},a_{s}\right)\right\|_{A_{t}^{-1}}\right]\geq 1-\delta .\tag{17.9}
\]
Then with probability at least \(1 - \delta\), for all \(t = 0, \dots, T\) and \(u \in \mathcal{H}\):
\[
\left|u^{\top}\left(w_{t}-w_{*}\right)\right|\leq\beta_{t}\sqrt{u^{\top}A_{t}^{-1}u}.
\]

steps.claim:
We have
\[
\begin{array}{l}u^{\top}\left(w_{t}-w_{*}\right)=u^{\top}A_{t}^{-1}\sum_{s=1}^{t}r_{s}\left(x_{s},a_{s}\right)\psi\left(x_{s},a_{s}\right)-u^{\top}w_{*}\\ =u^{\top}A_{t}^{-1}\sum_{s=1}^{t}\epsilon_{s}\left(x_{s},a_{s}\right)\psi\left(x_{s},a_{s}\right)-\lambda u^{\top}A_{t}^{-1}w_{*}\\ \leq\|u\|_{A_{t}^{-1}}\left\|\sum_{s=1}^{t}\epsilon_{s}\left(x_{s},a_{s}\right)\psi\left(x_{s},a_{s}\right)\right\|_{A_{t}^{-1}}+\lambda\|u\|_{A_{t}^{-1}}\|w_{*}\|_{A_{t}^{-1}}\\ \leq\|u\|_{A_{t}^{-1}}\left[\left\|\sum_{s=1}^{t}\epsilon_{s}\left(x_{s},a_{s}\right)\psi\left(x_{s},a_{s}\right)\right\|_{A_{t}^{-1}}+\sqrt{\lambda}B\right]\leq\beta_{t}\|u\|_{A_{t}^{-1}}.\\ \end{array}
\]
The second equality used (17.8).

The first inequality used the Cauchy-Schwartz
inequality.
The last inequality used the definition of \(\beta_{t}\).
This implies the desired bound.

theorems.statement:
For any \(K\), \(T \geq 0\), and any \(\gamma \in (0,1]\), \(\eta > 0\) and \(b \geq 0\). Consider any expert class \(\mathcal{G} = \{[\hat{q}_t(\cdot | w, x)]_{t=1,2,\ldots} : w \in \Omega\}\) with prior \(p_0(w)\). Let
\[
R_{T}(w)=\mathbb{E}\sum_{t=1}^{T}\mathbb{E}_{a\sim\hat{q}_{t}(\cdot|w,x_{t})}r_{t}(a)
\]
be the reward of expert \( w \). Then the expected reward of Algorithm 17.1 satisfies:
\[
\begin{array}{l}\mathbb{E}\sum_{t=1}^{T}r_{t}(a_{t})\geq(1-\gamma)\max_{q}\left[\mathbb{E}_{w\sim q}R_{T}(w)-\frac{1}{\eta}\mathrm{KL}(q| |p_{0})\right]\\ -c(\eta,b)\eta\sum_{t=1}^{T}\sum_{a=1}^{K}|r_{t}(a)-b|,\\ \end{array}
\]
where the expectation is with respect to the randomization of the algorithm,
\[
c(\eta,b)=\phi(z_{0})\max(b,1-b),\quad z_{0}=\max(0,\eta(1-b)K/\gamma),
\]
and \(\phi (z) = (e^{z} - 1 - z) / z^{2}\)

steps.claim:
The proof is similar to that of Theorem 16.17. By the definition of \(\hat{\pi}_t(a_t)\), we have
\[
\tilde{\rho}_{t}\left(a_{t}\right)=\mathbb{E}_{w\sim p_{t-1}(w)}\hat{q}_{t}\left(a_{t}\mid w,x_{t}\right)/\hat{\pi}_{t}\left(a_{t}\right)\leq 1/(1-\gamma).\tag{17.4}
\]
Therefore
\[
\begin{array}{l}\mathbb{E}_{w\sim p_{t-1}(w)}\hat{r}_{t}(w,x_{t},a_{t})=\mathbb{E}_{w\sim p_{t-1}(w)}\hat{q}_{t}(a_{t}|w,x_{t})[r_{t}(a_{t})-b]/\hat{\pi}_{t}(a_{t})\\ \leq\frac{1}{1-\gamma}r_{t}\left(a_{t}\right)-\tilde{\rho}_{t}\left(a_{t}\right)b.\tag{17.5}\\ \end{array}
\]
The first equation used the definition of \(\hat{r}\).

The inequality used (17.4). Moreover
\[
\begin{array}{l}\mathbb{E}_{w\sim p_{t-1}(w)}\hat{r}_{t}(w,x_{t},a_{t})^{2}\\ =\mathbb{E}_{w\sim p_{t-1}(w)}\hat{q}_{t}\left(a_{t}\mid w,x_{t}\right)^{2}\left(\left(r_{t}\left(a_{t}\right)-b\right)/\hat{\pi}_{t}\left(a_{t}\right)\right)^{2}\\ \leq\max(b,1-b)\mathbb{E}_{w\sim p_{t-1}(w)}\hat{q}_{t}\left(a_{t}|w,x_{t}\right)\left(\left|r_{t}\left(a_{t}\right)-b\right| /\hat{\pi}_{t}\left(a_{t}\right)^{2}\right)\\ \leq\frac{\max(b,1-b)}{1-\gamma}\left(\left|r_{t}\left(a_{t}\right)-b\right| /\hat{\pi}_{t}\left(a_{t}\right)\right).\tag{17.6}\\ \end{array}
\]
The first equation used the definition of \(\hat{r}\).
The first inequality used \(|r_t(a_t) - b| \leq \max(b, 1 - b)\).

The second inequality used (17.4). If we let
\[
W_{t}=\mathbb{E}_{w\sim p_{0}(w)}u_{t}(w),
\]
then
\[
\begin{array}{l}\ln\frac{W_{t}}{W_{t-1}}=\ln\mathbb{E}_{w\sim p_{0}(w)}\frac{u_{t}(w)}{W_{t-1}}\\ =\ln\mathbb{E}_{w\sim p_{t-1}(w)}\exp(\eta\hat{r}_{t}(w,x_{t},a_{t}))\\ \leq\ln\mathbb{E}_{w\sim p_{t-1}(w)}\left[1+\left(\eta\hat{r}_{t}\left(w,x_{t},a_{t}\right)\right)+\phi\left(z_{0}\right)\left(\eta\hat{r}_{t}\left(w,x_{t},a_{t}\right)\right)^{2}\right]\\ \leq\mathbb{E}_{w\sim p_{t-1}(w)}\left(\eta\hat{r}_{t}\left(w,x_{t},a_{t}\right)\right)+\phi\left(z_{0}\right)\mathbb{E}_{w\sim p_{t-1}(w)}\left(\eta\hat{r}_{t}\left(w,x_{t},a_{t}\right)\right)^{2}\\ \leq\frac{\eta}{1-\gamma}r_{t}(a_{t})-\eta\tilde{\rho}_{t}(a_{t})b+\frac{c(\eta,b)\eta^{2}}{(1-\gamma)}\frac{|r_{t}(a_{t})-b|}{\hat{\pi}_{t}(a_{t})}.\\ \end{array}
\]
The second equality used the definition of \( u_{t} \).

The first inequality used \( \exp (z) \leq \)
\(1 + z + \phi (z_0)z^2\) when \(z = \eta \hat{r}_t(w,x_t,a_t)\leq z_0\); the second inequality used \(\ln (1 + z)\leq\) \(z\); and the third inequality used (17.5) and (17.6).
Now we can sum over \( t = 1 \) to \( t = T \), and obtain:

\[
\ln\frac{W_{T}}{W_{0}}\leq\frac{\eta}{1-\gamma}\sum_{t=1}^{T}r_{t}(a_{t})-\eta b\sum_{t=1}^{T}\tilde{\rho}_{t}(a_{t})+\frac{c(\eta,b)\eta^{2}}{(1-\gamma)}\sum_{t=1}^{T}\frac{|r_{t}(a_{t})-b|}{\hat{\pi}_{t}(a_{t})}.
\]
Note that \( W_0 = 1 \).

We can take expectation with respect to the randomization of the algorithm, and obtain
\[
\begin{array}{l}\mathbb{E}\ln\mathbb{E}_{w\sim p_{0}(w)}\exp\left(\eta\sum_{t=1}^{T}\hat{r}_{t}(w,x_{t},a_{t})\right)\\ \leq\frac{\eta}{1-\gamma}\mathbb{E}\sum_{t=1}^{T}r_{t}\left(a_{t}\right)-\eta T b+\frac{c(\eta,b)\eta^{2}}{(1-\gamma)}\mathbb{E}\sum_{t=1}^{T}\sum_{a=1}^{K}\left|r_{t}(a)-b\right|.\tag{17.7}\\ \end{array}
\]
The derivation also used \(\mathbb{E}\tilde{\rho}_t(a_t) = \mathbb{E}\mathbb{E}_{a_t\sim \hat{\pi}_t}\tilde{\rho}_t(a_t) = 1\) and
\[
\mathbb{E}\frac{|r_{t}(a_{t})-b|}{\hat{\pi}_{t}(a_{t})}=\mathbb{E}\mathbb{E}_{a_{t}\sim\hat{\pi}_{t}}\frac{|r_{t}(a_{t})-b|}{\hat{\pi}_{t}(a_{t})}=\mathbb{E}\sum_{a=1}^{K}|r_{t}(a)-b|.
\]
We can lower bound the left hand side of (17.7) as:

\[
\begin{array}{l}\mathbb{E}\ln\mathbb{E}_{w\sim p_{0}(w)}\exp\left(\eta\sum_{t=1}^{T}\hat{r}_{t}(w,x_{t},a_{t})\right)\\ =\mathbb{E}\max_{q}\left[\mathbb{E}_{w\sim q}\eta\sum_{t=1}^{T}\hat{r}_{t}(w,x_{t},a_{t})-\operatorname{KL}(q| |p_{0})\right]\\ \geq\max_{q}\left[\mathbb{E}_{w\sim q}\eta\mathbb{E}\sum_{t=1}^{T}\hat{r}_{t}(w,x_{t},a_{t})-\mathrm{KL}(q| |p_{0})\right]\\ =\max_{q}\left[\mathbb{E}_{w\sim q}\eta [R_{T}(w)-bT]-\mathrm{KL}(q| |p_{0})\right].\\ \end{array}
\]
The first equality used Proposition 7.16.
The last equation used (17.3) and the definition of \( R_{T} \).
By plugging this estimate into the left hand side of (17.7), we obtain the desired result.

label: correct

context:
Shared setting for the results below. All definitions, standing assumptions and numbered equations that the proofs rely on are collected here.

assumption 18.12. Given a candidate value function class \(\mathcal{F}\) of functions \(f = \{f^{h}(x^{h},a^{h}):\mathcal{X}\times \mathcal{A}\to \mathbb{R}\}\), with \(f^{H + 1}(\cdot) = 0\). We assume that (realizable assumption)
\[
Q_{*}=f_{*}\in\mathcal{F}.
\]
Moreover, we assume that \( f^1(x^1) \in [0, 1] \) and \( r^h + f^{h+1}(x^{h+1}) \in [0, 1] \) (\( h \geq 1 \)).
Bellman error plays an important role in the analysis of reinforcement learning algorithms. For value function based approach to reinforcement learning, we would like to approximate Bellman error by minimizing least squares loss
\[
\left(f^{h}\left(x^{h},a^{h}\right)-r^{h}-f^{h+1}\left(x^{h+1}\right)\right)^{2}.\tag{18.2}
\]
By taking conditional expectation with respect to \((x^{h},a^{h})\), we obtain
\[
\begin{array}{l}\mathbb{E}_{r^{h},x^{h+1}\mid x^{h},a^{h}}\left(f^{h}\left(x^{h},a^{h}\right)-r^{h}-f^{h+1}\left(x^{h+1}\right)\right)^{2}\\ =\mathcal{E}^{h}(f,x^{h},a^{h})^{2}+\mathbb{E}_{r^{h},x^{h+1}|x^{h},a^{h}}\Bigg(\underbrace{r^{h}+f^{h+1}(x^{h+1})-(\mathcal{T}^{h}f)(x^{h},a^{h})}_{f \text{- d e p e n d e n t z e r o - m e a n n o i s e}}\Bigg)^{2}.\\ \end{array}
\]
Since noise variance depends on \( f \), if we use (18.2) to estimate \( f \), we will favor \( f \) with smaller noise variance, which may not have zero Bellman error. To overcome this issue, one can estimate the noise variance term, and then subtract it from (18.2) to obtain the term \( \mathcal{E}^h (f,x^h,a^h)^2 \). This requires an additional assumption referred to as Bellman completeness (or simply completeness).

Packing Number. Let \((\mathcal{V},d)\) be a pseudometric space with metric \(d(\cdot,\cdot)\). A finite subset \(\mathcal{G}(\epsilon)\subset \mathcal{G}\) is an \(\epsilon\)-packing of \(\mathcal{G}\) if \(d(\phi,\phi^{\prime})>\epsilon\) for all \(\phi,\phi^{\prime}\in\mathcal{G}(\epsilon)\). The \(\epsilon\)-packing number of \(\mathcal{G}\), denoted by \(M(\epsilon,\mathcal{G},d)\), is the largest cardinality of \(\epsilon\)-packing of \(\mathcal{G}\).
The following results illustrate the equivalence between covering number and packing number. One advantage of using an \(\epsilon\) packing of \(\mathcal{G}\) instead of an \(\epsilon\) cover of \(\mathcal{G}\) is that all members in the \(\epsilon\) packing also belong to \(\mathcal{G}\). There if members in \(\mathcal{G}\) satisfy certain assumptions such as the variance condition, then members of its \(\epsilon\) packing also satisfy such assumptions. For this reason, we will use packing numbers instead of covering numbers in some of the theoretical analysis in later chapters.

definition 18.10. We say \( f \) is a candidate \( Q \)-function if \( f = \{f^{h}(x^{h},a^{h}) : \mathcal{X} \times \mathcal{A} \to \mathbb{R} : h \in [H + 1]\} \), with \( f^{H + 1}(\cdot) = 0 \). Define
\[
f^{h}(x^{h})=\arg\max_{a\in\mathcal{A}}f^{h}(x^{h},a),
\]
and define its greedy policy \(\pi_f\) as a deterministic policy that satisfies
\[
\pi_{f}^{h}(x^{h})\in\arg\max_{a\in\mathcal{A}}f^{h}(x^{h},a).
\]
Given an MDP \(M\), we also define the Bellman operator of \(f\) as
\[
\left(\mathcal{T}^{h}f\right)\left(x^{h},a^{h}\right)=\mathbb{E}_{r^{h},x^{h+1}\mid x^{h},a^{h}}\left[r^{h}+f^{h+1}\left(x^{h+1}\right)\right],
\]
and its Bellman error as
\[
\mathcal{E}^{h}(f,x^{h},a^{h})=f^{h}\left(x^{h},a^{h}\right)-\left(\mathcal{T}^{h}f\right)\left(x^{h},a^{h}\right),
\]
where the conditional expectation is with respect to the MDP \(M\).

Bellman Completeness. A candidate value function class \(\mathcal{F}\) is complete with respect to another candidate value function class \(\mathcal{G}\) if for any \(h\in [H]\), \(f\in \mathcal{F}\), there exists \(g\in \mathcal{G}\) so that for all \(h\in [H]\):
\[
g^{h}(x^{h},a^{h})=(\mathcal{T}^{h}f)(x^{h},a^{h})=\mathbb{E}_{r^{h},x^{h+1}|x^{h},a^{h}}\left[r^{h}+f^{h+1}(x^{h+1})\right].
\]
We say \(\mathcal{F}\) is complete if \(\mathcal{F}\) is complete with respect to itself.
Note that if \(\mathcal{F}\) is complete with respect to \(\mathcal{G}\), then we may use the solution of
\[
\min_{g^{h}\in\mathcal{G}^{h}}\sum_{s=1}^{t}\left(g^{h}\left(x_{s}^{h},a_{s}^{h}\right)-r_{s}^{h}-f^{h+1}\left(x_{s}^{h+1}\right)\right)^{2}
\]
to estimate \((\mathcal{T}^h f)(x^h,a^h)\), which can be used to cancel the variance term in (18.2). This motivates the following loss function
\[
\begin{array}{l}L^{h}(f,g,x^{h},a^{h},r^{h},x^{h+1})=\left[\left(f^{h}\left(x^{h},a^{h}\right)-r^{h}-f^{h+1}\left(x^{h+1}\right)\right)^{2}\right.\\ \left.-\left(g^{h}\left(x^{h},a^{h}\right)-r^{h}-f^{h+1}\left(x^{h+1}\right)\right)^{2}\right].\tag{18.3}\\ \end{array}
\]
The following result is a counterpart of Theorem 13.15.

Linear MDP. Let \(\mathcal{H} = \{\mathcal{H}^h\}\) be a sequence of vector spaces with inner products \(\langle \cdot, \cdot \rangle\). An MDP \(M = \mathrm{MDP}(\mathcal{X}, \mathcal{A}, P)\) is a linear MDP with feature maps \(\phi = \{\phi^h(x^h, a^h) : \mathcal{X} \times \mathcal{A} \to \mathcal{H}^h\}_{h=1}^H\) if for all \(h \in [H]\), there exist a map \(\nu^h(x^{h+1}) : \mathcal{X} \to \mathcal{H}^h\) and \(\theta^h \in \mathcal{H}^h\), such that
\[
d P^{h}\left(x^{h+1}\mid x^{h},a^{h}\right)=\left\langle\nu^{h}\left(x^{h+1}\right),\phi^{h}\left(x^{h},a^{h}\right)\right\rangle d\mu^{h+1}\left(x^{h+1}\right),
\]
\[
\mathbb{E}\left[r^{h}\mid x^{h},a^{h}\right]=\langle\theta^{h},\phi^{h}\left(x^{h},a^{h}\right)\rangle .
\]
Here \(\langle \cdot, \cdot \rangle\) denotes the inner product in \(\mathcal{H}^h\) for different \(h\), and the conditional probability measure \(dP^h(\cdot | x^h, a^h)\) is absolute continuous with respect to a measure \(d\mu^{h+1}(\cdot)\) with density \(\langle \nu^h(x^{h+1}), \phi^h(x^h, a^h) \rangle\). In general, we assume that \(\nu^h(\cdot)\) and \(\theta^h\) are unknown. We may assume \(\phi(\cdot)\) to be either known or unknown.

definition 18.8. The optimal value functions starting at step \( h \) are given by
\[
Q_{*}^{h}(x^{h},a^{h})=\sup_{\pi}Q_{\pi}^{h}(x^{h},a^{h}),\qquad V_{*}^{h}(x^{h})=\sup_{\pi}V_{\pi}^{h}(x^{h}).
\]
We also define the optimal value as \( V_{*} = \mathbb{E}_{x^{1}}V_{*}^{1}(x^{1}) \).
In the following, for notation simplicity, we assume that the solution to
\[
\operatorname*{argmax}_{a\in\mathcal{A}}Q_{*}^{h}(x^{h},a)
\]
can be achieved by some \( a \in \mathcal{A} \) so that greedy policy in the Theorem 18.9 can be properly defined. The following theorem describes key properties of optimal value functions and optimal policy for reinforcement learning. The proof is straightforward, and we leave it as an exercise.

V-type Bellman Eluder Coefficient. Given a candidate \(Q\) function class \(\mathcal{F}\), its V-type Bellman eluder coefficient \(\mathrm{EC}_V^h(\epsilon,\mathcal{F},T)\) at step \(h\geq 1\) is the smallest number \(d\) so that for any filtered sequence \(\{f_t,(x_t,r_t,a_t)\sim \pi_{f_t}\}_{t = 1}^T\)
\[
\mathbb{E}\sum_{t=2}^{T}\mathcal{E}^{h}(f_{t},x_{t}^{h},a_{t}^{h})\leq\sqrt{d\mathbb{E}\sum_{t=2}^{T}\left(\epsilon+\sum_{s=1}^{t-1}\mathbb{E}_{\tilde{x}\sim\pi_{f_{s}}}\mathcal{E}^{h}(f_{t},\tilde{x}^{h},\pi_{f_{t}}(\tilde{x}^{h}))^{2}\right)}.
\]
In order to bound the \(Q\)-type Bellman eluder coefficient, we need to assume in Proposition 18.20 that the \(Q\) function class can be embedded in a linear vector space. This is not necessary for the \(V\)-type Bellman eluder coefficient, which allows general nonlinear \(Q\) function class.
We note that for linear MDP, from the proof of Proposition 18.18, we know that for any \( h \geq 2 \), there exists \( u^{h - 1}(f) \in \mathcal{H}^{h - 1} \) so that
\[
\mathbb{E}_{x^{h}\mid x^{h-1},a^{h-1}}\mathcal{E}^{h}(f,x^{h},\pi_{f}(x^{h}))=\langle u^{h-1}(f),\phi^{h-1}(x^{h-1},a^{h-1})\rangle .
\]
If moreover, we assume that \((x^{h - 1},a^{h - 1})\sim \pi^{\prime}\), where \(\pi^\prime\) is referred to as a roll-in policy, then we have the following decomposition,
\[
\mathbb{E}_{x^{h}\sim\pi^{\prime}}\mathcal{E}^{h}(f,x^{h},\pi_{f}(x^{h}))=\langle u^{h-1}(f),\phi^{h-1}(\pi^{\prime})\rangle,
\]
where \(\phi^{h - 1}(\pi^{\prime}) = \mathbb{E}_{x^{h - 1},a^{h - 1}\sim \pi^{\prime}}\phi^{h - 1}(x^{h - 1},a^{h - 1})\)
One may expand this property and define Bellman factorizable MDPs as follows, which includes linear MDP as a special case.

definition 18.30. The coverage coefficient \(\mathrm{CC}^h(\epsilon,\tilde{\pi},\mathcal{F})\) (for \(\epsilon >0\)) of a random policy \(\tilde{\pi}\) at step \(h\) is defined as
\[
\mathrm{CC}^{h}(\epsilon,\tilde{\pi},\mathcal{F})=\sup_{f\in\mathcal{F},x^{h}\in\mathcal{X}}\frac{\mathcal{E}^{h}(f,x^{h},\pi_{f}(x^{h}))^{2}}{\epsilon+\mathbb{E}_{a^{h}\sim\tilde{\pi}^{h}(\cdot|x^{h})}\mathcal{E}^{h}(f,x^{h},a^{h})^{2}}.
\]
We note that Definition 18.30 is consistent with Definition 17.35, which can be regarded as a conditional version of Definition 9.42. Therefore we may employ
a conditional \( G \)-optimal design \( \tilde{\pi}^h(a^h|x^h) \) by conditioning on \( x^h \). The following result shows that if Bellman error is linearly embeddable (with possibly unknown feature map), then good coverage coefficient can be obtained using nonlinear \( G \)-optimal design. It is a direct consequence of Theorem 9.44.

\(V\)-type Bellman Error UCB Algorithm. Algorithm 18.3: \(V\)-type Bellman Error UCB Algorithm
Input: \(\lambda, T, \mathcal{F}, \mathcal{G}, \tilde{\pi}\)  
1 Let \(\mathcal{F}_0 = \{f_0\}\)  
2 Let \(\beta_0 = 0\)  
3 for \(t = 1, 2, \ldots, T\) do  
4 Observe \(x_t^1\)  
5 Let \(f_t \in \arg \max_{f \in \mathcal{F}_{t-1}} f(x_t^1)\)  
6 Let \(\pi_t = \pi_{f_t}\)  
7 Draw \(h_t \sim [H]\) uniformly at random  
8 Play policy \(\pi_t\) and observe trajectory \((x_t, a_t, r_t)\) up to \(x_t^{h_t}\)  
9 Play random policy \(a_t^{h_t} \sim \tilde{\pi}^{h_t}(\cdot | x_t^{h_t})\), and observe \((r_t^{h_t}, x_t^{h_t+1})\)  
10 Let  
\[ \mathcal{F}_t = \left\{ f \in \mathcal{F} : \sup_{g \in \mathcal{G}} \sum_{s=1}^t L^{h_s}(f, g, x_s^{h_s}, a_s^{h_s}, r_s^{h_s}, x_s^{h_s+1}) \leq \beta_t^2 \right\} \] with appropriately chosen \(\beta_t\), where \(L^h(\cdot)\) is defined according to (18.3).

section 13.1 sequential observation setup. In Section 13.1, data are observed sequentially. At each time \(t\), after the history \(S_{t-1}\) has been observed, the next observation \(Z_t\) is drawn according to a distribution that may depend on that history. The observation is decomposed as \(Z_t=(Z_t^{(x)},Z_t^{(y)})\), where \(Z_t^{(x)}\) is the component determined by the past history or the chosen action at time \(t\), and \(Z_t^{(y)}\) is the random response component. The history after time \(t\) is \(S_t=(Z_1,\ldots,Z_t)\), and \(\mathcal{S}_T\) denotes the full sequential experiment/history through time \(T\). For a function depending on \(S_t\), the notation \(\mathbb{E}_{Z_t^{(y)}}[\cdot]\) means conditional expectation over the response component \(Z_t^{(y)}\), conditional on \(S_{t-1}\) and on \(Z_t^{(x)}\). Stopping times are adapted to the filtration generated by the histories \(S_t\).

definition 2.11. A sub-Gaussian random variable \(X\) has quadratic logarithmic moment generating function for all \(\lambda \in \mathbb{R}\):
\[
\ln\mathbb{E}e^{\lambda X}\leq\lambda\mu+\frac{\lambda^{2}}{2}b.\tag{2.10}
\]
Using (2.10), we can obtain an upper bound of the rate function for sub-Gaussian random variables, which imply the following tail inequality.

theorems.statement:
In Algorithm 18.3, we let
\[
\tilde{d}=\sum_{h=1}^{H}\operatorname{EC}_{V}^{h}(\epsilon,\mathcal{F},T)\max(1,\operatorname{CC}^{h}(\epsilon^{\prime},\tilde{\pi},\mathcal{F})),
\]
then
\[
\mathbb{E}\sum_{h=1}^{H}\sum_{t=2}^{T}\mathcal{E}^{h}(f_{t},x_{t}^{h},a_{t}^{h})\leq\sqrt{\tilde{d}\mathbb{E}\sum_{t=2}^{T}\left(\epsilon H+\epsilon^{\prime}H T+\sum_{s=1}^{t-1}\sum_{h=1}^{H}\bar{\mathcal{E}}^{h}(f_{t},\pi_{f_{s}},\tilde{\pi})^{2}\right)},
\]
where
\[
\bar{\mathcal{E}}^{h}(f,\pi,\tilde{\pi})^{2}=\mathbb{E}_{\tilde{x}^{h}\sim\pi}\mathbb{E}_{a^{h}\sim\tilde{\pi}(\cdot|x^{h})}\mathcal{E}^{h}(f_{t},x^{h},a^{h})^{2}.
\]

steps.claim: Let \( d_1^h = \operatorname{EC}_V^h(\epsilon, \mathcal{F}, T) \), and \( d_2^h = \operatorname{CC}^h(\epsilon', \tilde{\pi}, \mathcal{F}) \).

We obtain
\[
\begin{array}{l}\mathbb{E}\sum_{h=1}^{H}\sum_{t=2}^{T}\mathcal{E}^{h}\left(f_{t},x_{t}^{h},a_{t}^{h}\right)\leq\sum_{h=1}^{H}\sqrt{d_{1}^{h}\mathbb{E}\sum_{t=2}^{T}\left(\epsilon+\sum_{s=1}^{t-1}\mathbb{E}_{\tilde{x}\sim\pi_{f_{s}}}\mathcal{E}^{h}\left(f_{t},\tilde{x}^{h},\pi_{f_{t}}(\tilde{x}^{h})\right)^{2}\right)}\\ \leq\sum_{h=1}^{H}\sqrt{d_{1}^{h}\mathbb{E}\sum_{t=2}^{T}\left(\epsilon+d_{2}^{h}\sum_{s=1}^{t-1}\left(\epsilon^{\prime}+\bar{\mathcal{E}}^{h}\left(f_{t},\pi_{f_{s}},\tilde{\pi}\right)^{2}\right)\right)}\\ \leq\sum_{h=1}^{H}\sqrt{d_{1}^{h}\max(1,d_{2}^{h})\mathbb{E}\left.\sum_{t=2}^{T}\left(\epsilon+\epsilon^{\prime}T+\sum_{s=1}^{t-1}\bar{\mathcal{E}}^{h}(f_{t},\pi_{f_{s}},\tilde{\pi})^{2}\right)\right.}.\\ \end{array}
\]
The first inequality used Definition 18.27.
The second inequality used Definition 18.30. We then use the Cauchy Schwartz inequality to obtain the result.

theorems.statement:
Consider a random variable \(X \in [0,1]\) and \(\mathbb{E}X = \mu\). We have the following inequality:
\[
\ln\mathbb{E}e^{\lambda X}\leq\ln [(1-\mu)e^{0}+\mu e^{\lambda}]\leq\lambda\mu+\lambda^{2}/8.
\]

steps.claim: Let \( h_L(\lambda) = \mathbb{E}e^{\lambda X} \) and \( h_R(\lambda) = (1 - \mu)e^0 + \mu e^\lambda \).
We know that \( h_L(0) = h_R(0) \). Moreover, when \( \lambda \geq 0 \):

\[
h_{L}^{\prime}(\lambda)=\mathbb{E}X e^{\lambda X}\leq\mathbb{E}X e^{\lambda}=\mu e^{\lambda}=h_{R}^{\prime}(\lambda),
\]
and similarly \(h_L'(\lambda) \geq h_R'(\lambda)\) when \(\lambda \leq 0\).

This proves the first inequality. Now we let
\[
h(\lambda)=\ln [(1-\mu)e^{0}+\mu e^{\lambda}].
\]
It implies that
\[
h^{\prime}(\lambda)=\frac{\mu e^{\lambda}}{(1-\mu)e^{0}+\mu e^{\lambda}},
\]
and
\[
\begin{array}{l}h^{\prime\prime}(\lambda)=\frac{\mu e^{\lambda}}{(1-\mu)e^{0}+\mu e^{\lambda}}-\frac{(\mu e^{\lambda})^{2}}{[(1-\mu)e^{0}+\mu e^{\lambda}]^{2}}\\ =\left|h^{\prime}(\lambda)\right|\left(1-\left|h^{\prime}(\lambda)\right|\right)\leq 1/4.\\ \end{array}
\]
Using Taylor expansion, we obtain the inequality \( h(\lambda) \leq h(0) + \lambda h'(0) + \lambda^2 / 8 \), which proves the second inequality.

theorems.statement:
Assume that assumption 18.12 holds, \(\mathcal{F}\) is complete with respect to \(\mathcal{G}\), and \(g^{h}(\cdot)\in [0,1]\) for all \(g\in \mathcal{G}\). Consider (18.3), and let
\[
\mathcal{F}_{t}=\left\{f\in\mathcal{F}:\sup_{g\in\mathcal{G}}\sum_{h=1}^{H}\sum_{s=1}^{t}L^{h}(f,g,x_{s}^{h},a_{s}^{h},r_{s}^{h},x_{s}^{h+1})\leq\beta_{t}^{2}\right\},
\]
where
\[
\beta_{t}^{2}\geq 4\epsilon t(4+\epsilon)H+2\ln\left(16 M(\epsilon,\mathcal{F},\|\cdot\|_{\infty})^{2}M(\epsilon,\mathcal{G},\|\cdot\|_{\infty})/\delta^{2}\right),
\]
with \( M(\cdot) \) denotes the \( \| \cdot \|_{\infty} \) packing number, and \( \| f \|_{\infty} = \sup_{h,x,a} |f^{h}(x,a)| \).
Then with probability at least \(1 - \delta\), for all \(t \leq n\): \(Q_{*} \in \mathcal{F}_{t}\) and for all \(f \in \mathcal{F}_{t}\):
\[
\sum_{s=1}^{t}\sum_{h=1}^{H}\mathcal{E}^{h}\left(f,x_{s}^{h},a_{s}^{h}\right)^{2}\leq 4\beta_{t}^{2}.
\]

steps.claim: Let \(\mathcal{F}_{\epsilon}\) be an \(\epsilon \| \cdot \|_{\infty}\) packing subset of \(\mathcal{F}\) of size \(M_1\), and let \(\mathcal{G}_{\epsilon}\) be an \(\epsilon \| \cdot \|_{\infty}\) packing subset of \(\mathcal{G}\) of size \(M_2\).

For all \( f \in \mathcal{F} \) and \( g \in \mathcal{G} \) (or \( g \in \mathcal{F} \)), we introduce the simplified notations
\[
\epsilon_{s}^{h}(f)=r_{s}^{h}+f_{s}^{h+1}\left(x_{s}^{h+1}\right)-\left(\mathcal{T}^{h}f\right)\left(x_{s}^{h},a_{s}^{h}\right),
\]
\[
\Delta_{s}^{h}(f,g)=((\mathcal{T}^{h}f)(x_{s}^{h},a_{s}^{h})-g^{h}(x_{s}^{h},a_{s}^{h})).
\]
We have the following sub-Gaussian inequality (see Lemma 2.15) for any fixed \( f_{\epsilon} \in \mathcal{F}_{\epsilon} \), \( h \in [H] \), and \( \rho \in \mathbb{R} \):

\[
\ln\mathbb{E}_{r_{s}^{h},x_{s}^{h+1}|x_{s}^{h},a_{s}^{h}}\exp(\rho\epsilon_{s}^{h}(f_{\epsilon}))\leq\frac{\rho^{2}}{8}.
\]
Using this logarithmic moment generating function, we can now obtain the following statement from Theorem 13.11, by taking a uniform bound over \(\mathcal{G}_{\epsilon} \times \mathcal{F}_{\epsilon}\) and consider both under and over estimation (for the absolute value on the left hand side).

With probability at least \(1 - \delta / 2\): for all \(f_{\epsilon} \in \mathcal{F}_{\epsilon}\), \(g_{\epsilon} \in \mathcal{G}_{\epsilon}\) and \(t \geq 0\)
\[
\underbrace{\left|\sum_{s=1}^{t}\sum_{h=1}^{H}\Delta_{s}^{h}\left(f_{\epsilon},g_{\epsilon}\right)\epsilon_{s}^{h}\left(f_{\epsilon}\right)\right|}_{A}\leq\sum_{s=1}^{t}\sum_{h=1}^{H}\frac{\Delta_{s}^{h}\left(f_{\epsilon},g_{\epsilon}\right)^{2}}{8}+\ln\left(4 M_{1}M_{2}/\delta\right).\tag{18.4}
\]
In the following for each \(f \in \mathcal{F}\) we choose \(f_{\epsilon} \in \mathcal{F}_{\epsilon}\) so that \(\| f - f_{\epsilon} \|_{\infty} \leq \epsilon\).
Similarly for each \(g \in \mathcal{G}\) we choose \(g_{\epsilon} \in \mathcal{G}_{\epsilon}\) so that \(\| g - g_{\epsilon} \|_{\infty} \leq \epsilon\).

Then
\[
\begin{array}{l}\left|\sum_{s=1}^{t}\sum_{h=1}^{H}\Delta_{s}^{h}(f,g)\epsilon_{s}^{h}(f)\right|\\ \leq\left|\sum_{s=1}^{t}\sum_{h=1}^{H}\Delta_{s}^{h}(f,g)\epsilon_{s}^{h}\left(f_{\epsilon}\right)\right| +2\epsilon\sum_{s=1}^{t}\sum_{h=1}^{H}\left|\Delta_{s}^{h}(f,g)\right|\\ \leq\underbrace{\left|\sum_{s=1}^{t}\sum_{h=1}^{H}\Delta_{s}^{h}(f_{\epsilon},g_{\epsilon})\epsilon_{s}^{h}(f_{\epsilon})\right|}_{A}+4H\epsilon t.\\ \end{array}
\]
The first inequality used \( |\epsilon_s^h (f) - \epsilon_s^h (f_\epsilon)|\leq 2\epsilon \).

The second inequality used the \( \epsilon \)-covering property \( |\Delta_s^h(f,g)-\Delta_s^h(f_\epsilon,g_\epsilon)|\leq 2\epsilon \), \( |\epsilon_s^h (f_\epsilon)|\leq 1 \), and \( |\Delta_s^h (f,g)|\leq 1 \).

We also have
\[
\begin{array}{l}A\leq\frac{1}{8}\sum_{s=1}^{t}\sum_{h=1}^{H}\Delta_{s}^{h}\left(f_{\epsilon},g_{\epsilon}\right)^{2}+\ln\left(4 M_{1}M_{2}/\delta\right)\\ \leq\frac{1}{8}\sum_{s=1}^{t}\sum_{h=1}^{H}\left(\left|\Delta_{s}^{h}(f,g)\right| +2\epsilon\right)^{2}+\ln\left(4 M_{1}M_{2}/\delta\right)\\ \leq\frac{1}{4}\sum_{s=1}^{t}\sum_{h=1}^{H}(\Delta_{s}^{h}(f,g))^{2}+\epsilon^{2}H t+\ln(4 M_{1}M_{2}/\delta).\\ \end{array}
\]
The first inequality used (18.4).
The second inequality used the \(\epsilon\)-covering property \(|\Delta_s^h(f,g)-\Delta_s^h(f_\epsilon,g_\epsilon)|\leq 2\epsilon\).
The last inequality used standard algebra inequalities \(|a + 2\epsilon |^2 /8\leq (a^2 /4) + \epsilon^2\) to simplify the terms.
That is, we have shown that with probability at least \(1 - \delta / 2\): for all \(f \in \mathcal{F}\) and \(g \in \mathcal{G}\) and \(t \geq 0\):

\[
\begin{array}{l}\left|\sum_{s=1}^{t}\sum_{h=1}^{H}\Delta_{s}^{h}(f,g)\epsilon_{s}^{h}(f)\right|\leq\frac{1}{4}\sum_{s=1}^{t}\sum_{h=1}^{H}\Delta_{s}^{h}(f,g)^{2}\\ +\epsilon tH(4+\epsilon)+\ln\left(4M_{1}M_{2}/\delta\right).\qquad(18. 5)\\ \end{array}
\]
Similarly, with probability at least \(1 - \delta /2\): for all \(f\in \mathcal{F}\) and \(t\geq 0\)
\[
\begin{array}{l}\left|\sum_{s=1}^{t}\sum_{h=1}^{H}\Delta_{s}^{h}(f,f)\epsilon_{s}^{h}(f)\right|\leq\frac{1}{4}\sum_{s=1}^{t}\sum_{h=1}^{H}\Delta_{s}^{h}(f,f)^{2}\\ +\epsilon t H(4+\epsilon)+\ln\left(4 M_{1}/\delta\right).\tag{18.6}\\ \end{array}
\]
We have with probability at least \(1 - \delta\), both (18.5) and (18.6) hold.
We obtain with probability at least \(1 - \delta\): for all \(t \geq 0\), \(f \in \mathcal{F}\), \(g \in \mathcal{G}\):

\[
\begin{array}{l}\left|\sum_{h=1}^{H}\sum_{s=1}^{t}\left[\Delta_{s}^{h}(f,f)-\Delta_{s}^{h}(f,g)\right]\epsilon_{s}^{h}(f)\right|\\ \leq\frac{1}{4}\sum_{h=1}^{H}\sum_{s=1}^{t}\left[\Delta_{s}^{h}(f,f)^{2}+\Delta_{s}^{h}(f,g)^{2}\right]+0. 5\beta_{t}^{2}.\tag{18.7}\\ \end{array}
\]
Therefore
\[
\begin{array}{l}\sum_{s=1}^{t}\sum_{h=1}^{H}L^{h}(f,g,x_{s}^{h},a_{s}^{h},r_{s}^{h},x_{s}^{h+1})\\ =\sum_{s=1}^{t}\sum_{h=1}^{H}\left[\Delta_{s}^{h}(f,f)^{2}-\Delta_{s}^{h}(f,g)^{2}+2[\Delta_{s}^{h}(f,f)-\Delta_{s}^{h}(f,g)]\epsilon_{s}^{h}(f)\right]\\ \geq\sum_{s=1}^{t}\sum_{h=1}^{H}\left[0. 5\Delta_{s}^{h}(f,f)^{2}-1. 5\Delta_{s}^{h}(f,g)^{2}\right]-\beta_{t}^{2},\quad(\text{b y})\\ \end{array}
\]
and
\[
\begin{array}{l}\sum_{s=1}^{t}\sum_{h=1}^{H}L^{h}\left(Q_{*},g,x_{s}^{h},a_{s}^{h},r_{s}^{h},x_{s}^{h+1}\right)\\ =\sum_{s=1}^{t}\sum_{h=1}^{H}\left[\Delta_{s}^{h}(Q_{*},Q_{*})^{2}-\Delta_{s}^{h}(Q_{*},g)^{2}+2\left[\Delta_{s}^{h}(Q_{*},Q_{*})-\Delta_{s}^{h}(Q_{*},g)\right]\epsilon_{s}^{h}(f)\right]\\ \leq\sum_{s=1}^{t}\sum_{h=1}^{H}\left[1. 5\Delta_{s}^{h}(Q_{*},Q_{*})^{2}-0. 5\Delta_{s}^{h}(Q_{*},g)^{2}\right]+\beta_{t}^{2}.\quad \tag{by(18.7)}\\ \end{array}
\]
Taking sup over \( g \in \mathcal{G} \), and note that \( \Delta_s^h(Q_*, Q_*) = 0 \), and that \( \mathcal{F} \) is complete with respect to \( \mathcal{G} \), we obtain
\[
\sup_{g\in\mathcal{G}}\sum_{s=1}^{t}\sum_{h=1}^{H}L^{h}\left(Q_{*},g,x_{s}^{h},a_{s}^{h},r_{s}^{h},x_{s}^{h+1}\right)\leq\beta_{t}^{2},
\]
\[
\sup_{g\in\mathcal{G}}\sum_{s=1}^{t}\sum_{h=1}^{H}L^{h}(f,g,x_{s}^{h},a_{s}^{h},r_{s}^{h},x_{s}^{h+1})\geq 0. 5\sum_{s=1}^{t}\sum_{h=1}^{H}\underbrace{\Delta_{s}^{h}(f,f)^{2}}_{\mathcal{E}^{h}(f,x_{s}^{h},a_{s}^{h})^{2}}-\beta_{t}^{2}.
\]
In the two displayed inequalities, the first implies that \( Q_{*} \in \mathcal{F}_{t} \).

The second implies that if \( f \in \mathcal{F}_{t} \), then
\[
\beta_{t}^{2}\geq 0. 5\sum_{s=1}^{t}\sum_{h=1}^{H}\mathcal{E}^{h}(f,x_{s}^{h},a_{s}^{h})^{2}-\beta_{t}^{2},
\]
which implies the second result of the theorem.

theorems.statement:
We have for any \(\lambda >0\), with probability at least \(1 - \delta\), for all \(n\geq 1\) and \(f\in \mathcal{F}\):
\[
\left[-\sum_{i=1}^{n}f(Z_{i})-\frac{1}{\lambda}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\ln\mathbb{E}_{Z_{i}^{(y)}}e^{-\lambda f(Z_{i})}\right]\leq\inf_{\epsilon>0}\left[2 n\epsilon+\frac{\ln(M(\epsilon,\mathcal{F},\|\cdot\|_{\infty})/\delta)}{\lambda}\right].
\]

steps.claim: Let \(\mathcal{F}_{\epsilon} \subset \mathcal{F}\) be an \(\epsilon\) maximal packing of \(\mathcal{F}\), with \(|\mathcal{F}_{\epsilon}| \leq M(\epsilon, \mathcal{F}, \| \cdot \|_{\infty})\).
We obtain from Theorem 13.2, and the uniform bound over \(\mathcal{F}_{\epsilon}\) that with probability at least \(1 - \delta\):

\[
\sup_{f\in\mathcal{F}_{\epsilon}}\left[-\sum_{i=1}^{n}f(Z_{i})-\frac{1}{\lambda}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\ln\mathbb{E}_{Z_{i}^{(y)}}e^{-\lambda f(Z_{i})}\right]\leq\frac{\ln(M(\epsilon,\mathcal{F},\|\cdot\|_{\infty})/\delta)}{\lambda}.
\]
Since \(\mathcal{F}_{\epsilon}\) is also an \(\epsilon L_{\infty}\) cover of \(\mathcal{F}\) (see Theorem 5.2), we obtain
\[
\begin{array}{l}\sup_{f\in\mathcal{F}}\left[-\sum_{i=1}^{n}f(Z_{i})-\frac{1}{\lambda}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\ln\mathbb{E}_{Z_{i}^{(y)}}e^{-\lambda f(Z_{i})}\right]\\ \leq 2 n\epsilon+\sup_{f\in\mathcal{F}_{\epsilon}}\left[-\sum_{i=1}^{n}f(Z_{i})-\frac{1}{\lambda}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\ln\mathbb{E}_{Z_{i}^{(y)}}e^{-\lambda f(Z_{i})}\right].\\ \end{array}
\]
This implies the bound.

theorems.statement:
In a linear MDP with feature map \(\phi^h (x^h,a^h)\) on vector spaces \(\mathcal{H}^h\) \((h\in [H])\). Consider the linear candidate \(Q\) function class
\[
\mathcal{F}=\left\{\langle w^{h},\phi^{h}(x^{h},a^{h})\rangle:w^{h}\in\mathcal{H}^{h},h\in [H]\right\}.
\]
Any function \( g^{h + 1}(x^{h + 1}) \) on \( \mathcal{X} \) satisfies
\[
\left(\mathcal{T}^{h}g^{h+1}\right)\left(x^{h},a^{h}\right)\in\mathcal{F}.
\]
It implies that \(\mathcal{F}\) is complete, and \(Q_{*} \in \mathcal{F}\). Moreover, \(\forall f \in \mathcal{F}\),
\[
\mathcal{E}^{h}(f,x^{h},a^{h})\in\mathcal{F}.
\]

steps.claim:
Let
\[
u_{g}^{h}=\int g^{h+1}(x^{h+1})\nu^{h}(x^{h+1})d\mu^{h+1}(x^{h+1}).
\]
We have
\[
\begin{array}{l}\mathbb{E}_{x^{h+1}\mid x^{h},a^{h}}g^{h+1}\left(x^{h+1}\right)=\int g^{h+1}\left(x^{h+1}\right)\langle\nu^{h}\left(x^{h+1}\right),\phi^{h}\left(x^{h},a^{h}\right)\rangle d\mu^{h+1}\left(x^{h+1}\right)\\ =\langle u_{g}^{h},\phi^{h}(x^{h},a^{h})\rangle .\\ \end{array}
\]
This implies that
\[
\left(\mathcal{T}^{h}g\right)\left(x^{h},a^{h}\right)=\left\langle\theta^{h}+u_{g}^{h},\phi^{h}\left(x^{h},a^{h}\right)\right\rangle\in\mathcal{F}.
\]
Since \( Q_{*}^{h}(x^{h},a^{h}) = (\mathcal{T}^{h}Q_{*})(x^{h},a^{h}) \), we know \( Q_{*}^{h}(x^{h},a^{h})\in \mathcal{F} \)
Similarly, since \((\mathcal{T}^h f)(x^h,a^h)\in \mathcal{F}\), we know that \(f\in \mathcal{F}\) implies
\[
\mathcal{E}^{h}(f,x^{h},a^{h})=f^{h}\left(x^{h},a^{h}\right)-\left(\mathcal{T}^{h}f\right)\left(x^{h},a^{h}\right)\in\mathcal{F}.
\]
This proves the desired result.

Let

It follows that \(0\leq Z-Z^{i}\leq f_{i}^{\circ}\leq 1\) .

Since \(\phi=e^{x}-x-1\) is a convex function of \(x,\)
\[\phi(-\lambda(Z-Z^{i}))=\phi(-\lambda\cdot(Z-Z^{i})+0\cdot(1-(Z-Z^{i})))\leq(Z-Z^{i})\phi(-\lambda)\]
and
\[\begin{array}{ r c l }{\mathbb{E}\left(\lambda Z e^{\lambda Z}\right)-\mathbb{E}e^{\lambda Z}\log\mathbb{E}e^{\lambda Z}}&{\leq}&{\mathbb{E}\left(e^{\lambda Z}\displaystyle\sum_{i=1}^{n}\phi\left(-\lambda(Z-Z^{i})\right)\right)}\\ &{\leq}&{\mathbb{E}\left(e^{\lambda Z}\phi(-\lambda)\displaystyle\sum_{i}\left(Z-Z^{i}\right)\right)}\\ &{\leq}&{\phi(-\lambda)\mathbb{E}\left(e^{\lambda Z}\cdot\displaystyle\sum_{i}f_{i}^{\circ}\right)}\\ &{=}&{\phi(-\lambda)\mathbb{E}\left(Z\cdot e^{\lambda Z}\right).}\end{array}\]
Set \(\tilde{Z}=Z-\mathbb{E}Z\ (\mathrm{i . e .}\) , center Z),and we get
\[\begin{array}{ r l r }{\mathbb{E}\left(\lambda\tilde{Z}e^{\lambda\tilde{Z}}\right)-\mathbb{E}e^{\lambda\tilde{Z}}\log\mathbb{E}e^{\lambda\tilde{Z}}}&{\leq}&{\phi(-\lambda)\mathbb{E}\left(Z\cdot e^{\lambda\tilde{Z}}\right)=\phi(-\lambda)\mathbb{E}\left(\left(\tilde{Z}+\mathbb{E}Z\right)\cdot e^{\lambda\tilde{Z}}\right)}\\ {(\lambda-\phi(-\lambda))\mathbb{E}\left(\tilde{Z}e^{\lambda\tilde{Z}}\right)-\mathbb{E}e^{\lambda\tilde{Z}}\log\mathbb{E}e^{\lambda\tilde{Z}}}&{\leq}&{\phi(-\lambda)\cdot\mathbb{E}Z\cdot\mathbb{E}e^{\lambda\tilde{Z}}.}\end{array}\]
Let \(v=\mathbb{E}Z,F(\lambda)=\mathbb{E}e^{\lambda\tilde{Z}}\) , 亚 = logF,and we get
\[\begin{array}{ r c l }{{(\lambda-\phi(-\lambda)){\displaystyle\frac{F_{\lambda}^{\prime}(\lambda)}{F(\lambda)}}-\log F(\lambda)}}&{{\le}}&{{v\phi(-\lambda)}}\\ {{(\lambda-\phi(-\lambda)){(\log F(\lambda))}_{\lambda}^{\prime}-\log F(\lambda)}}&{{\le}}&{{v\phi(-\lambda).}}\end{array}\tag{41.1}\]
Solving the differential equation
\[(\lambda-\phi(-\lambda))\left(\underbrace{\log F(\lambda)}_{\Psi_{0}}\right)_{\lambda}^{\prime}-\underbrace{\log F(\lambda)}_{\Psi_{0}}=v\phi(-\lambda),\tag{41.2}\]
yields \(\Psi_{0}=v\cdot\phi(\lambda)\) .

We will proceed to show that 亚 satisfying 41.1 has the property \(\Psi\leq\Psi_{0}\)
\[\begin{array}{ r l r }{\mathrm{Substract~41.2~from~41.1,~and~let~\Psi\Psi_1=\Psi-\Psi_0~}}&{}&\\ {(1-e^{-\lambda})\Psi_{1}^{\prime}-\Psi_{1}}&{\le}&{0}\end{array}\]
\[\begin{array}{ r c l }{\displaystyle\big(e^{\lambda}-1\big)\big(1-e^{-\lambda}\big)\frac{1}{e^{\lambda}-1}=1-e^{-\lambda}\mathrm{,a n d}\big(e^{\lambda}-1\big)\big(1-e^{-\lambda}\big)\frac{e^{\lambda}}{(e^{\lambda}-1)^{2}}=1}&&\\ {\displaystyle\big(e^{\lambda}-1\big)\big(1-e^{-\lambda}\big)\underbrace{\Bigg(\frac{1}{e^{\lambda}-1}\Psi_{1}^{\prime}-\frac{e^{\lambda}}{\big(e^{\lambda}-1\big)^{2}}\Psi_{1}\Bigg)}_{\big(\frac{\Psi_{1}}{e^{\lambda}-1}\big)_{\lambda}^{\prime}}}&{\le}&{0}\end{array}\]
\[{\frac{\Psi_{1}(\lambda)}{e^{\lambda}-1}}~\leq~\operatorname*{lim}_{\lambda\to 0}{\frac{\Psi_{1}(\lambda)}{e^{\lambda}-1}}=0 .\]
It follows that \(\Psi\leq v\phi(\lambda)\) ,and \(F=\mathbb{E}e^{\lambda\tilde{Z}}\leq e^{v\phi(\lambda)}\) .

By Chebychev's inequality, \(\mathbb{P}\left(Z\geq\mathbb{E}Z+t\right)\leq e^{-\lambda t+v\phi\left(\lambda\right)}\) Minimizing over all \(\lambda > 0\) ，we get \(\mathbb{P}\left(Z\geq\mathbb{E}Z+t\right)\leq e^{-v\cdot h\left(t/v\right)}\) where \(h(x)=(1+x)\cdot\log(1+x)-x.\)

Setup. Let \(X_1,\dots,X_n\) be i.i.d. copies of a random variable \(X\) with \(0\le X\le 1\) and \(\mu=\mathbb{E}X\), and let \(0<t\le 1-\mu\).

Assume \(0\leq X_{i}\leq 1\) and \(\mu=\mathbb{E}X\) . Then
\[\mathbb{P}\left(\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}X_{i}-\mu\geq t\right)\leq e^{-n\mathcal{D}(\mu+t,\mu)}\]
where the KL-divergence \(\begin{array}{ r }{\mathcal{D}(p,q)=p\log\frac{p}{q}+(1-p)\log\frac{1-p}{1-q}}\end{array}\)

steps.claim:
Note that \(\phi(x)=e^{\lambda x}\) is convex and so \(e^{\lambda x}=e^{\lambda(x\cdot 1+(1-x)\cdot 0)}\leq x e^{\lambda}+(1-x)e^{\lambda\cdot 0}=1-x+x e^{\lambda}\) .Hence,
\[\mathbb{E}e^{\lambda X}\leq 1-\mathbb{E}X+\mathbb{E}X e^{\lambda}=1-\mu+\mu e^{\lambda}.\]
Again,we minimize the following bound with respect to \(\lambda > 0\)
\[\begin{array}{ r c l }{\displaystyle\mathbb{P}\left(\sum_{i=1}^{n}X_{i}\geq n(\mu+t)\right)}&{\leq}&{e^{-\lambda n(\mu+t)}\mathbb{E}e^{\lambda\sum X_{i}}}\\ &&{=}&{e^{-\lambda n(\mu+t)}\left(\mathbb{E}e^{\lambda X}\right)^{n}}\\ &&{\leq}&{e^{-\lambda n(\mu+t)}\left(1-\mu+\mu e^{\lambda}\right)^{n}}\end{array}\]
Take derivative w.r.t. 入:

\[\begin{array}{ c }{{-n(\mu+t)e^{-\lambda n(\mu+t)}(1-\mu+\mu e^{\lambda})^{n}+n(1-\mu+\mu e^{\lambda})^{n-1}\mu e^{\lambda}e^{-\lambda n(\mu+t)}=0}}\\ {{{}}}\\ {{-(\mu+t)(1-\mu+\mu e^{\lambda})+\mu e^{\lambda}=0}}\\ {{{}}}\\ {{e^{\lambda}=\displaystyle\frac{(1-\mu)(\mu+t)}{\mu(1-\mu-t)}.}}\end{array}\]
Substituting,
\[\begin{array}{ r c l }{\mathbb{P}\left(\displaystyle\sum_{i=1}^{n}X_{i}\geq n(\mu+t)\right)}&{\leq}&{\displaystyle\left(\left(\frac{\mu(1-\mu-t)}{(1-\mu)(\mu+t)}\right)^{\mu+t}\left(1-\mu+\frac{(1-\mu)(\mu+t)}{1-\mu-t}\right)\right)^{n}}\\ &{=}&{\displaystyle\left(\left(\frac{\mu}{\mu+t}\right)^{\mu+t}\left(\frac{1-\mu}{1-\mu-t}\right)^{1-\mu-t}\right)^{n}}\\ &{=}&{\displaystyle\exp\left(-n\left((\mu+t)\log\frac{\mu+t}{\mu}+(1-\mu-t)\log\frac{1-\mu-t}{1-\mu}\right)\right),}\end{array}\]
