context:
Shared setting for the results below. All definitions, standing assumptions and numbered equations that the proofs rely on are collected here.

section 13.1 sequential observation setup. In Section 13.1, data are observed sequentially. At each time \(t\), after the history \(S_{t-1}\) has been observed, the next observation \(Z_t\) is drawn according to a distribution that may depend on that history. The observation is decomposed as \(Z_t=(Z_t^{(x)},Z_t^{(y)})\), where \(Z_t^{(x)}\) is the component determined by the past history or the chosen action at time \(t\), and \(Z_t^{(y)}\) is the random response component. The history after time \(t\) is \(S_t=(Z_1,\ldots,Z_t)\), and \(\mathcal{S}_T\) denotes the full sequential experiment/history through time \(T\). For a function depending on \(S_t\), the notation \(\mathbb{E}_{Z_t^{(y)}}[\cdot]\) means conditional expectation over the response component \(Z_t^{(y)}\), conditional on \(S_{t-1}\) and on \(Z_t^{(x)}\). Stopping times are adapted to the filtration generated by the histories \(S_t\).

Sequential Statistical Estimation. Consider a family of environment distributions \(\mathcal{P}_{\mathcal{Z}}\), where each \(q \in \mathcal{P}_{\mathcal{Z}}\) determines the probability for generating \(Z_{t}\) based on policy \(\pi_{t}\) as \(q(Z_{t}|\pi_{t}, S_{t-1})\). Consider also a family of learning algorithms, represented by \(\mathcal{P}_{\mathcal{A}}\). Each learning algorithm \(\hat{q} \in \mathcal{P}_{\mathcal{A}}\) maps the history \(S_{t-1}\) deterministically to the next policy \(\pi_{t} \in \Pi\) as \(\pi_{t} = \hat{q}(S_{t-1})\). Given \(q \in \mathcal{P}_{\mathcal{Z}}\), and \(\hat{q} \in \mathcal{P}_{\mathcal{A}}\), the data generation probability is fully determined as
\[
p(\mathcal{S}_{n}|\hat{q},q)=\prod_{t=1}^{n}q(Z_{t}|\hat{q}(\mathcal{S}_{t-1}),\mathcal{S}_{t-1}).
\]
After observing \( S_{n} \) for some \( n \), the learning algorithm \( \hat{q} \) determines a distribution \( \hat{q}(\theta | S_{n}) \), and draws an estimator \( \theta \in \Theta \) according to \( \hat{q}(\theta | S_{n}) \). The learning algorithm suffers a loss (also referred to as regret) \( Q(\theta, q) \). The overall probability of \( \theta \) and \( S_{n} \) is
\[
p(\theta,\mathcal{S}_{n}|\hat{q},q)=\hat{q}(\theta|\mathcal{S}_{n})\prod_{t=1}^{n}q\left(Z_{t}|\hat{q}\left(\mathcal{S}_{t-1}\right),\mathcal{S}_{t-1}\right).\tag{13.8}
\]
Note that although the notation in Definition 13.16 assumes that \(\pi_t\) is a deterministic function of \(S_{t-1}\), it can also incorporate randomized algorithms. In such case, a policy is simply a distribution over the random choices. Since a random choice can always be characterized by a distribution (over the random choices) that is a deterministic function of \(S_{t-1}\), when we consider random policies in subsequent chapters, it should be understood that such policies can be handled by Definition 13.16. An example is given below.

Packing Number. Let \((\mathcal{V},d)\) be a pseudometric space with metric \(d(\cdot,\cdot)\). A finite subset \(\mathcal{G}(\epsilon)\subset \mathcal{G}\) is an \(\epsilon\)-packing of \(\mathcal{G}\) if \(d(\phi,\phi^{\prime})>\epsilon\) for all \(\phi,\phi^{\prime}\in\mathcal{G}(\epsilon)\). The \(\epsilon\)-packing number of \(\mathcal{G}\), denoted by \(M(\epsilon,\mathcal{G},d)\), is the largest cardinality of \(\epsilon\)-packing of \(\mathcal{G}\).
The following results illustrate the equivalence between covering number and packing number. One advantage of using an \(\epsilon\) packing of \(\mathcal{G}\) instead of an \(\epsilon\) cover of \(\mathcal{G}\) is that all members in the \(\epsilon\) packing also belong to \(\mathcal{G}\). There if members in \(\mathcal{G}\) satisfy certain assumptions such as the variance condition, then members of its \(\epsilon\) packing also satisfy such assumptions. For this reason, we will use packing numbers instead of covering numbers in some of the theoretical analysis in later chapters.

definition 4.1. Let \((\mathcal{V},d)\) be a pseudometric space with metric \(d(\cdot,\cdot)\). A finite
set \(\mathcal{G}(\epsilon) \subset \mathcal{V}\) is an \(\epsilon\)-cover (or \(\epsilon\)-net) of \(\mathcal{G} \subset \mathcal{V}\) if, for all \(\phi \in \mathcal{G}\), there exists \(\phi' \in \mathcal{G}(\epsilon)\) so that \(d(\phi', \phi) \leq \epsilon\). The \(\epsilon\)-covering number of \(\mathcal{G}\) with metric \(d\) is the smallest cardinality \(N(\epsilon, \mathcal{G}, d)\) of such \(\mathcal{G}(\epsilon)\). The number \(\ln N(\epsilon, \mathcal{G}, d)\) is called the \(\epsilon\)-entropy.
For a function class \(\mathcal{G}\) with seminorm \(L_{p}(\mathcal{D})\) in (3.19), we denote the corresponding \(L_{p}(\mathcal{D})\)-covering number as \(N(\epsilon, \mathcal{G}, L_{p}(\mathcal{D}))\). When \(1 \leq p \leq q\), we have
\[
N(\epsilon,\mathcal{G},L_{p}(\mathcal{D}))\leq N(\epsilon,\mathcal{G},L_{q}(\mathcal{D})).
\]
It is easy to verify the following relationship, which implies that \( L_{p}(\mathcal{D}) \) bracketing cover is a stronger requirement than \( L_{p}(\mathcal{D}) \) cover.

theorem 13.11: We have for any \(\lambda>0\), with probability at least \(1-\delta\), for all \(n\geq 1\) and \(f\in\mathcal{F}\): \[\left[-\sum_{i=1}^{n} f(Z_i)-\frac{1}{\lambda}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\ln\mathbb{E}_{Z_i^{(y)}}e^{-\lambda f(Z_i)}\right]\leq\inf_{\epsilon>0}\left[2n\epsilon+\frac{\ln(M(\epsilon,\mathcal{F},\|\cdot\|_\infty)/\delta)}{\lambda}\right].\]

theorems.statement:
Assume that for all \( f \in \mathcal{F} \) and \( Z_{t}: -f(Z_{t}) + \mathbb{E}_{Z_{t}^{(y)}}f(Z_{t}) \leq b \), and the following variance condition holds for all \( f \in \mathcal{F} \) and \( S_{t} \):
\[
\operatorname{Var}_{Z_{t}^{(y)}}[f(Z_{t})]\leq c_{0}^{2}+c_{1}\mathbb{E}_{Z_{t}^{(y)}}[f(Z_{t})],
\]
then with probability at least \(1 - \delta\), for all \(f \in \mathcal{F}\):
\[
\begin{array}{l}\left(1-\lambda c_{1}\phi(\lambda b)\right)\sum_{t=1}^{n}\mathbb{E}_{Z_{t}^{(y)}}[f(Z_{t})]\leq\sum_{t=1}^{n}f(Z_{t})+\lambda n c_{0}^{2}\phi(\lambda b)\\ +\inf_{\epsilon>0}\left[2 n\epsilon+\frac{\ln(M(\epsilon,\mathcal{F},\|\cdot\|_{\infty})/\delta)}{\lambda}\right],\\ \end{array}
\]
where \(\phi (z) = (e^{z} - z - 1) / z^{2}\)

steps.claim:
Note that by employing the moment estimation of Bennett's inequality in Lemma 2.20, we obtain
\[
\begin{array}{l}\frac{1}{\lambda}\ln\mathbb{E}_{Z_{t}^{(y)}}e^{-\lambda f(Z_{t})}\\ \leq-\mathbb{E}_{Z_{t}^{(y)}}[f(Z_{t})]+\lambda\phi(\lambda b)\operatorname{Var}_{Z_{t}^{(y)}}[f(Z_{t})]\\ \leq-\mathbb{E}_{Z_{t}^{(y)}}[f(Z_{t})]+\lambda\phi(\lambda b)[c_{0}^{2}+c_{1}\mathbb{E}_{Z_{t}^{(y)}}[f(Z_{t})]].\\ \end{array}
\]
We can now obtain the desired bound from Theorem 13.11.

theorems.statement:
Let \(\Sigma_0\) be a \(d\times d\) symmetric positive definite matrix, and \(\{\psi (X_t)\}\) be a sequence of vectors in \(\mathbb{R}^d\). Let \(\Sigma_{t} = \Sigma_{0} + \sum_{s = 1}^{t}\psi (X_{s})\psi (X_{s})^{\top}\), then
\[
\sum_{s=1}^{t}\frac{\psi(X_{s})^{\top}\Sigma_{s-1}^{-1}\psi(X_{s})}{1+\psi(X_{s})^{\top}\Sigma_{s-1}^{-1}\psi(X_{s})}\leq\ln|\Sigma_{0}^{-1}\Sigma_{t}|.
\]

steps.claim:
We have
\[
\begin{array}{l}\frac{\psi(X_{s})^{\top}\Sigma_{s-1}^{-1}\psi(X_{s})}{1+\psi(X_{s})^{\top}\Sigma_{s-1}^{-1}\psi(X_{s})}=\psi(X_{s})^{\top}\Sigma_{s}^{-1}\psi(X_{s})\\ =\operatorname{trace}\left(\Sigma_{s}^{-1}\left(\Sigma_{s}-\Sigma_{s-1}\right)\right)\\ =\operatorname{trace}\left(\nabla\ln\left|\Sigma_{s}\right|\left(\Sigma_{s}-\Sigma_{s-1}\right)\right)\\ \leq\ln|\Sigma_{s}| -\ln|\Sigma_{s-1}|.\\ \end{array}
\]
The first equality is due to the Sherman-Morrison formula.
The last inequality used the fact that \(\ln |Z|\) is a concave function of \(Z\) (see Theorem A.18).
Now by summing over \(s = 1\) to \(s = t\), we obtain the desired bound.

theorems.statement:
Let \(\{(X_t, \epsilon_t)\}\) be a filtered sequence in \(\mathcal{X} \times \mathbb{R}\) so that \(\epsilon_t\) is conditional zero-mean sub-Gaussian noise: for all \(\lambda \in \mathbb{R}\),
\[
\ln\mathbb{E}\left[e^{\lambda\epsilon_{t}}\mid X_{t},\mathcal{S}_{t-1}\right]\leq\frac{\lambda^{2}}{2}\sigma^{2},
\]
where \( S_{t-1} \) denotes the history data. Assume that \( Y_t = f_*(X_t) + \epsilon_t \), with \( f_*(x) \in \mathcal{F}: \mathcal{X} \to \mathbb{R} \). Let \( \hat{f}_t \) be an approximate ERM solution for some \( \epsilon' > 0 \):
\[
\left(\sum_{s=1}^{t}\left(\hat{f}_{t}\left(X_{s}\right)-Y_{s}\right)^{2}\right)^{1/2}\leq\min_{f\in\mathcal{F}}\left(\sum_{s=1}^{t}\left(f\left(X_{s}\right)-Y_{s}\right)^{2}\right)^{1/2}+\sqrt{t}\epsilon^{\prime}.
\]
Then with probability at least \(1 - \delta\), for all \(t \geq 0\):
\[
\sum_{s=1}^{t}(\hat{f}_{t}(X_{t})-f_{*}(X_{t}))^{2}\leq\inf_{\epsilon>0}\left[8 t(\epsilon+\epsilon^{\prime})(\sigma+2\epsilon+2\epsilon^{\prime})+12\sigma^{2}\ln\frac{2 N(\epsilon,\mathcal{F},\|\cdot\|_{\infty})}{\delta}\right].
\]

steps.claim:
Let \(\eta = \sigma^{-2} / 4\), and for \(f \in \mathcal{F}\), let
\[
\phi(f,Z_{t})=\left[\left(f(X_{t})-Y_{t}\right)^{2}-\left(f_{*}(X_{t})-Y_{t}\right)^{2}\right].
\]
Let \(\mathcal{F}_{\epsilon}\) be an \(\epsilon \| \cdot \|_{\infty}\) cover of \(\mathcal{F}\) with \(N = N(\epsilon, \mathcal{F}, \| \cdot \|_{\infty})\) members.

Given any \(f \in \mathcal{F}_{\epsilon}\),
\[
\begin{array}{l}\ln\mathbb{E}_{Y_{t}|X_{t},S_{t-1}}\exp(-\eta\phi(f,Z_{t}))\\ = -\eta\left(f\left(X_{t}\right)-f_{*}\left(X_{t}\right)\right)^{2}\\ +\ln\mathbb{E}_{Y_{t}\mid X_{t},S_{t-1}}\exp(-2\eta(f(X_{t})-f_{*}(X_{t}))(f_{*}(X_{t})-Y_{t}))\\ \leq-\eta(f(X_{t})-f_{*}(X_{t}))^{2}+\frac{4\eta^{2}\sigma^{2}}{2}(f(X_{t})-f_{*}(X_{t}))^{2}\\ = -\frac{\left(f(X_{t})-f_{*}(X_{t})\right)^{2}}{8\sigma^{2}}.\\ \end{array}
\]
The inequality used the sub-Gaussian noise assumption.
It follows from Theorem 13.11 that with probability at least \( 1 - \delta / 2 \), for all \( f \in \mathcal{F}_{\epsilon} \) and \( t \geq 0 \):

\[
\sum_{i=1}^{t}-\eta\phi(f,Z_{i})\leq-\sum_{i=1}^{t}\frac{\left(f\left(X_{i}\right)-f_{*}\left(X_{i}\right)\right)^{2}}{8\sigma^{2}}+\ln(2 N/\delta).\tag{13.5}
\]
Using Exercise 13.3, we have with probability at least \(1 - \delta /2\), for all \(t\geq 0\)
\[
\underbrace{\sum_{i=1}^{t}\left(f_{*}\left(X_{i}\right)-Y_{i}\right)^{2}}_{A}\leq 2 t\sigma^{2}+3\sigma^{2}\ln(2/\delta).\tag{13.6}
\]
It follows that with probability at least \(1 - \delta\), for all \(t \geq 0\) and \(f \in \mathcal{F}_{\epsilon}\), both (13.5)
and (13.6) hold.
Now, let \( f \in \mathcal{F}_{\epsilon} \) so that \( \| \hat{f}_t - f \|_{\infty} \leq \epsilon \).

This implies that
\[
\begin{array}{l}\sum_{i=1}^{t}\left[(f(X_{i})-Y_{i})^{2}-(f_{*}(X_{i})-Y_{i})^{2}\right]\leq\left(\sqrt{\sum_{i=1}^{t}(\hat{f}_{t}(X_{i})-Y_{i})^{2}}+\sqrt{t}\epsilon\right)^{2}-A\\ \leq\left(\sqrt{A}+\sqrt{t}(\epsilon+\epsilon^{\prime})\right)^{2}-A\\ \stackrel{(a)}{\leq}(\epsilon^{\prime}+\epsilon)^{2}t+2\sqrt{t}(\epsilon^{\prime}+\epsilon)\sigma\sqrt{2 t+3\ln(2/\delta)}\\ \leq 4\left(\epsilon^{\prime}+\epsilon\right)^{2}t+3\sigma t\left(\epsilon^{\prime}+\epsilon\right)+\sigma^{2}\ln(2/\delta).\tag{13.7}\\ \end{array}
\]
In the above derivations, the first inequality used \( |f(X_i) - Y_i| \leq |\hat{f}_t(X_i) - Y_i| + \epsilon \) for all \( i \).
The second inequality used the fact that \( \hat{f}_t \) is approximate ERM. (a) follows from (13.6).
The last inequality used \( 2a\sigma \sqrt{2b + 3c} \leq 3a\sigma \sqrt{b} + 3a^2 + \sigma^2 c \).

We thus obtain
\[
\begin{array}{l}\left(\sum_{i=1}^{t}(\hat{f}(X_{i})-f_{*}(X_{i}))^{2}\right)^{1/2}\\ \leq\sqrt{\epsilon^{2}t}+\left(\sum_{i=1}^{t}\left(f\left(X_{i}\right)-f_{*}\left(X_{i}\right)\right)^{2}\right)^{1/2}\quad(\text{t r i a n g l e i n e q u a l i t y})\\ \leq\sqrt{\epsilon^{2}t}+\left(8\sigma^{2}\ln(2N/\delta)+8\sigma^{2}\sum_{i=1}^{t}\eta\phi(f,Z_{i})\right)^{1/2}\quad(\text{f r o m}(13. 5))\\ =\sqrt{\epsilon^{2}t}+\left(8\sigma^{2}\ln(2N/\delta)+2\sum_{i=1}^{t}\left[\left(f\left(X_{i}\right)-Y_{i}\right)^{2}-\left(f_{*}\left(X_{i}\right)-Y_{i}\right)^{2}\right]\right)^{1/2}\\ \leq\sqrt{\epsilon^{2}t}+\left(10\sigma^{2}\ln(2N/\delta)+8t\left(\epsilon^{\prime}+\epsilon\right)^{2}+6\sigma t\left(\epsilon^{\prime}+\epsilon\right)\right)^{1/2}\quad(\text{f r o m}(13. 7))\\ \leq\left(12\sigma^{2}\ln(2N/\delta)+16t(\epsilon+\epsilon^{\prime})^{2}+8\sigma t(\epsilon+\epsilon^{\prime})\right)^{1/2},\\ \end{array}
\]
where the last inequality used \(\sqrt{a} +\sqrt{b}\leq \sqrt{6a + 1.2b}\) .
This implies the bound.

theorems.statement:
Consider a sequence of random functions \(\xi_1(S_1),\ldots,\xi_t(S_t),\ldots\) Assume each \(\xi_{i}\) is sub-Gaussian with respect to \(Z_{i}^{(y)}\):
\[
\ln\mathbb{E}_{Z_{i}^{(y)}}e^{\lambda\xi_{i}}\leq\lambda\mathbb{E}_{Z_{i}^{(y)}}\xi_{i}+\frac{\lambda^{2}\sigma_{i}^{2}}{2}
\]
for some \(\sigma_{i}\) that may depend on \(S_{i - 1}\) and \(Z_{i}^{(x)}\). Then for all \(\sigma >0\), with probability at least \(1 - \delta\)
\[
\forall n>0:\sum_{i=1}^{n}\mathbb{E}_{Z_{i}^{(y)}}\xi_{i}<\sum_{i=1}^{n}\xi_{i}+\left(\sigma+\frac{\sum_{i=1}^{n}\sigma_{i}^{2}}{\sigma}\right)\sqrt{\frac{\ln(1/\delta)}{2}}.
\]

steps.claim: We can let \(\lambda = \sqrt{2\ln(1 / \delta)} /\sigma\), and then apply the first inequality of Theorem 13.2.

theorems.statement:
Let \(d \geq 1\) and \(m \geq 2\) be integers, and let \(\mathcal{P}_{\mathcal{Z}} = \{q^{\tau} : \tau \in \{1, \ldots, m\}^{d}\}\) contain \(m^{d}\) probability measures. Suppose that the loss function \(Q\) can be decomposed as
\[
Q(\theta,q)=\sum_{j=1}^{d}Q_{j}(\theta,q),
\]
where \( Q_{j} \geq 0 \) are all non-negative. For each \( j \), \( \tau \sim_{j} \tau' \) if \( \tau = \tau' \) or if \( \tau \) and \( \tau' \) differ by only one component \( j \). Assume that there exists \( \epsilon, \beta \geq 0 \) such that
\[
\forall\tau^{\prime}\sim_{j}\tau,\tau^{\prime}\neq\tau:[Q_{j}(\theta,q^{\tau})+Q_{j}(\theta,q^{\tau^{\prime}})]\geq\epsilon,
\]
and there exists \( q_j^\tau \) such that all \( \tau' \sim_j \tau \) map to the same value: \( q_j^{\tau'} = q_j^\tau \). Given any learning algorithm \( \hat{q} \). If for all \( \tau \), \( j \in [d] \), time step \( t \), and \( S_{t-1} \):
\[
\frac{1}{m}\sum_{\tau^{\prime}\sim_{j}\tau}\mathrm{KL}(q_{j}^{\tau}(\cdot|\hat{q}(\mathcal{S}_{t-1}),\mathcal{S}_{t-1})| |q^{\tau^{\prime}}(\cdot|\hat{q}(\mathcal{S}_{t-1}),\mathcal{S}_{t-1})))\leq\beta_{j,t}^{2},
\]
then
\[
\frac{1}{m^{d}}\sum_{\tau}\mathbb{E}_{\theta,S_{n}\sim p(\cdot|\hat{q},q^{\tau})}Q(\theta,q^{\tau})\geq 0.5 d\epsilon\left(1-\sqrt{\frac{2}{d}\sum_{j=1}^{d}\sum_{t=1}^{n}\beta_{j,t}^{2}}\right).
\]

steps.claim:
We have
\[
\begin{array}{l}\frac{1}{dm^{d}}\sum_{\tau}\sum_{j=1}^{d}\frac{1}{m-1}\sum_{\tau^{\prime}\sim_{j}\tau}\|p(\cdot|\hat{q},q^{\tau})-p(\cdot|\hat{q},q^{\tau^{\prime}})\|_{\mathrm{TV}}\\ \leq\frac{1}{dm^{d}}\sum_{\tau}\sum_{j=1}^{d}\frac{1}{m-1}\sum_{\tau^{\prime}\sim_{j}\tau,\tau^{\prime}\neq\tau}\left[\|p(\cdot|\hat{q},q_{j}^{\tau})-p(\cdot|\hat{q},q^{\tau^{\prime}})\|_{\mathrm{TV}}\right.\\ +\|p(\cdot|\hat{q},q_{j}^{\tau})-p(\cdot|\hat{q},q^{\tau})\|_{\mathrm{TV}}\big]\\ =\frac{2}{dm^{d}}\sum_{\tau}\sum_{j=1}^{d}\frac{1}{m}\sum_{\tau^{\prime}\sim_{j}\tau}\|p(\cdot|\hat{q},q_{j}^{\tau})-p(\cdot|\hat{q},q^{\tau^{\prime}})\|_{\mathrm{TV}}\\ \leq\frac{2}{m^{d}}\sum_{\tau}\sqrt{\frac{1}{dm}\sum_{j=1}^{d}\sum_{\tau^{\prime}\sim_{j}\tau}\|p(\cdot|\hat{q},q_{j}^{\tau})-p(\cdot|\hat{q},q^{\tau^{\prime}})\|_{\mathrm{TV}}^{2}}\\ \leq\frac{2}{m^{d}}\sum_{\tau}\sqrt{\frac{1}{2dm}\sum_{j=1}^{d}\sum_{\tau^{\prime}\sim_{j}\tau}\mathrm{KL}(p(\cdot|\hat{q},q_{j}^{\tau})| |p(\cdot|\hat{q},q^{\tau^{\prime}}))}\\ \leq\sqrt{\frac{2}{d}\sum_{j=1}^{d}\sum_{t=1}^{n}\beta_{t}^{2}}.\\ \end{array}
\]
The first inequality is triangle inequality for TV-norm.
The first equality used \(\hat{q}_j^\tau = \hat{q}_j^{\tau '}\) when \(\tau \sim_{j}\tau^{\prime}\).

The second inequality used Jensen's inequality and the
concavity of \(\sqrt{\cdot}\).
The third inequality used Theorem B.9. The last inequality used Lemma 13.21.
Now in Lemma 12.27, we let \(M_{j}(q^{\tau}) = \{q^{\tau^{\prime}}:\tau^{\prime}\sim_{j}\tau \}\) be the partitions.
The result is a simple application of Lemma 12.27 with \(m_j(q^\tau) = m\), \(|\mathcal{P}| = m^{d}\), and \(d(\mathcal{P}) = dm^{d}\).

context:
Shared setting for the results below. All definitions, standing assumptions and numbered equations that the proofs rely on are collected here.

section 13.1 sequential observation setup. In Section 13.1, data are observed sequentially. At each time \(t\), after the history \(S_{t-1}\) has been observed, the next observation \(Z_t\) is drawn according to a distribution that may depend on that history. The observation is decomposed as \(Z_t=(Z_t^{(x)},Z_t^{(y)})\), where \(Z_t^{(x)}\) is the component determined by the past history or the chosen action at time \(t\), and \(Z_t^{(y)}\) is the random response component. The history after time \(t\) is \(S_t=(Z_1,\ldots,Z_t)\), and \(\mathcal{S}_T\) denotes the full sequential experiment/history through time \(T\). For a function depending on \(S_t\), the notation \(\mathbb{E}_{Z_t^{(y)}}[\cdot]\) means conditional expectation over the response component \(Z_t^{(y)}\), conditional on \(S_{t-1}\) and on \(Z_t^{(x)}\). Stopping times are adapted to the filtration generated by the histories \(S_t\).

Packing Number. Let \((\mathcal{V},d)\) be a pseudometric space with metric \(d(\cdot,\cdot)\). A finite subset \(\mathcal{G}(\epsilon)\subset \mathcal{G}\) is an \(\epsilon\)-packing of \(\mathcal{G}\) if \(d(\phi,\phi^{\prime})>\epsilon\) for all \(\phi,\phi^{\prime}\in\mathcal{G}(\epsilon)\). The \(\epsilon\)-packing number of \(\mathcal{G}\), denoted by \(M(\epsilon,\mathcal{G},d)\), is the largest cardinality of \(\epsilon\)-packing of \(\mathcal{G}\).
The following results illustrate the equivalence between covering number and packing number. One advantage of using an \(\epsilon\) packing of \(\mathcal{G}\) instead of an \(\epsilon\) cover of \(\mathcal{G}\) is that all members in the \(\epsilon\) packing also belong to \(\mathcal{G}\). There if members in \(\mathcal{G}\) satisfy certain assumptions such as the variance condition, then members of its \(\epsilon\) packing also satisfy such assumptions. For this reason, we will use packing numbers instead of covering numbers in some of the theoretical analysis in later chapters.

definition 4.1. Let \((\mathcal{V},d)\) be a pseudometric space with metric \(d(\cdot,\cdot)\). A finite
set \(\mathcal{G}(\epsilon) \subset \mathcal{V}\) is an \(\epsilon\)-cover (or \(\epsilon\)-net) of \(\mathcal{G} \subset \mathcal{V}\) if, for all \(\phi \in \mathcal{G}\), there exists \(\phi' \in \mathcal{G}(\epsilon)\) so that \(d(\phi', \phi) \leq \epsilon\). The \(\epsilon\)-covering number of \(\mathcal{G}\) with metric \(d\) is the smallest cardinality \(N(\epsilon, \mathcal{G}, d)\) of such \(\mathcal{G}(\epsilon)\). The number \(\ln N(\epsilon, \mathcal{G}, d)\) is called the \(\epsilon\)-entropy.
For a function class \(\mathcal{G}\) with seminorm \(L_{p}(\mathcal{D})\) in (3.19), we denote the corresponding \(L_{p}(\mathcal{D})\)-covering number as \(N(\epsilon, \mathcal{G}, L_{p}(\mathcal{D}))\). When \(1 \leq p \leq q\), we have
\[
N(\epsilon,\mathcal{G},L_{p}(\mathcal{D}))\leq N(\epsilon,\mathcal{G},L_{q}(\mathcal{D})).
\]
It is easy to verify the following relationship, which implies that \( L_{p}(\mathcal{D}) \) bracketing cover is a stronger requirement than \( L_{p}(\mathcal{D}) \) cover.

Sequential Statistical Estimation. Consider a family of environment distributions \(\mathcal{P}_{\mathcal{Z}}\), where each \(q \in \mathcal{P}_{\mathcal{Z}}\) determines the probability for generating \(Z_{t}\) based on policy \(\pi_{t}\) as \(q(Z_{t}|\pi_{t}, S_{t-1})\). Consider also a family of learning algorithms, represented by \(\mathcal{P}_{\mathcal{A}}\). Each learning algorithm \(\hat{q} \in \mathcal{P}_{\mathcal{A}}\) maps the history \(S_{t-1}\) deterministically to the next policy \(\pi_{t} \in \Pi\) as \(\pi_{t} = \hat{q}(S_{t-1})\). Given \(q \in \mathcal{P}_{\mathcal{Z}}\), and \(\hat{q} \in \mathcal{P}_{\mathcal{A}}\), the data generation probability is fully determined as
\[
p(\mathcal{S}_{n}|\hat{q},q)=\prod_{t=1}^{n}q(Z_{t}|\hat{q}(\mathcal{S}_{t-1}),\mathcal{S}_{t-1}).
\]
After observing \( S_{n} \) for some \( n \), the learning algorithm \( \hat{q} \) determines a distribution \( \hat{q}(\theta | S_{n}) \), and draws an estimator \( \theta \in \Theta \) according to \( \hat{q}(\theta | S_{n}) \). The learning algorithm suffers a loss (also referred to as regret) \( Q(\theta, q) \). The overall probability of \( \theta \) and \( S_{n} \) is
\[
p(\theta,\mathcal{S}_{n}|\hat{q},q)=\hat{q}(\theta|\mathcal{S}_{n})\prod_{t=1}^{n}q\left(Z_{t}|\hat{q}\left(\mathcal{S}_{t-1}\right),\mathcal{S}_{t-1}\right).\tag{13.8}
\]
Note that although the notation in Definition 13.16 assumes that \(\pi_t\) is a deterministic function of \(S_{t-1}\), it can also incorporate randomized algorithms. In such case, a policy is simply a distribution over the random choices. Since a random choice can always be characterized by a distribution (over the random choices) that is a deterministic function of \(S_{t-1}\), when we consider random policies in subsequent chapters, it should be understood that such policies can be handled by Definition 13.16. An example is given below.

theorem 13.11: We have for any \(\lambda>0\), with probability at least \(1-\delta\), for all \(n\geq 1\) and \(f\in\mathcal{F}\): \[\left[-\sum_{i=1}^{n} f(Z_i)-\frac{1}{\lambda}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\ln\mathbb{E}_{Z_i^{(y)}}e^{-\lambda f(Z_i)}\right]\leq\inf_{\epsilon>0}\left[2n\epsilon+\frac{\ln(M(\epsilon,\mathcal{F},\|\cdot\|_\infty)/\delta)}{\lambda}\right].\]

theorems.statement:

where \( Q_{j} \geq 0 \) are all non-negative. For each \( j \), \( \tau \sim_{j} \tau' \) if \( \tau = \tau' \) or if \( \tau \) and \( \tau' \) differ by only one component \( j \). Assume that there exists \( \epsilon, \beta \geq 0 \) such that
\[
\forall\tau^{\prime}\sim_{j}\tau,\tau^{\prime}\neq\tau:[Q_{j}(\theta,q^{\tau})+Q_{j}(\theta,q^{\tau^{\prime}})]\geq\epsilon,
\]
and there exists \( q_j^\tau \) such that all \( \tau' \sim_j \tau \) map to the same value: \( q_j^{\tau'} = q_j^\tau \). Given any learning algorithm \( \hat{q} \). If for all \( \tau \), \( j \in [d] \), time step \( t \), and \( S_{t-1} \):
\[
\frac{1}{m}\sum_{\tau^{\prime}\sim_{j}\tau}\mathrm{KL}(q_{j}^{\tau}(\cdot|\hat{q}(\mathcal{S}_{t-1}),\mathcal{S}_{t-1})| |q^{\tau^{\prime}}(\cdot|\hat{q}(\mathcal{S}_{t-1}),\mathcal{S}_{t-1})))\leq\beta_{j,t}^{2},

steps.claim:
We have
\[
\begin{array}{l}\frac{1}{dm^{d}}\sum_{\tau}\sum_{j=1}^{d}\frac{1}{m-1}\sum_{\tau^{\prime}\sim_{j}\tau}\|p(\cdot|\hat{q},q^{\tau})-p(\cdot|\hat{q},q^{\tau^{\prime}})\|_{\mathrm{TV}}\\ \leq\frac{1}{dm^{d}}\sum_{\tau}\sum_{j=1}^{d}\frac{1}{m-1}\sum_{\tau^{\prime}\sim_{j}\tau,\tau^{\prime}\neq\tau}\left[\|p(\cdot|\hat{q},q_{j}^{\tau})-p(\cdot|\hat{q},q^{\tau^{\prime}})\|_{\mathrm{TV}}\right.\\ +\|p(\cdot|\hat{q},q_{j}^{\tau})-p(\cdot|\hat{q},q^{\tau})\|_{\mathrm{TV}}\big]\\ =\frac{2}{dm^{d}}\sum_{\tau}\sum_{j=1}^{d}\frac{1}{m}\sum_{\tau^{\prime}\sim_{j}\tau}\|p(\cdot|\hat{q},q_{j}^{\tau})-p(\cdot|\hat{q},q^{\tau^{\prime}})\|_{\mathrm{TV}}\\ \leq\frac{2}{m^{d}}\sum_{\tau}\sqrt{\frac{1}{dm}\sum_{j=1}^{d}\sum_{\tau^{\prime}\sim_{j}\tau}\|p(\cdot|\hat{q},q_{j}^{\tau})-p(\cdot|\hat{q},q^{\tau^{\prime}})\|_{\mathrm{TV}}^{2}}\\ \leq\frac{2}{m^{d}}\sum_{\tau}\sqrt{\frac{1}{2dm}\sum_{j=1}^{d}\sum_{\tau^{\prime}\sim_{j}\tau}\mathrm{KL}(p(\cdot|\hat{q},q_{j}^{\tau})| |p(\cdot|\hat{q},q^{\tau^{\prime}}))}\\ \leq\sqrt{\frac{2}{d}\sum_{j=1}^{d}\sum_{t=1}^{n}\beta_{t}^{2}}.\\ \end{array}
\]
The first inequality is triangle inequality for TV-norm.
The first equality used \(\hat{q}_j^\tau = \hat{q}_j^{\tau '}\) when \(\tau \sim_{j}\tau^{\prime}\).

The second inequality used Jensen's inequality and the
concavity of \(\sqrt{\cdot}\).
The third inequality used Theorem B.9. The last inequality used Lemma 13.21.
Now in Lemma 12.27, we let \(M_{j}(q^{\tau}) = \{q^{\tau^{\prime}}:\tau^{\prime}\sim_{j}\tau \}\) be the partitions.
The result is a simple application of Lemma 12.27 with \(m_j(q^\tau) = m\), \(|\mathcal{P}| = m^{d}\), and \(d(\mathcal{P}) = dm^{d}\).

theorems.statement:
Let \(\Sigma_0\) be a \(d\times d\) symmetric positive definite matrix, and \(\{\psi (X_t)\}\) be a sequence of vectors in \(\mathbb{R}^d\). Let \(\Sigma_{t} = \Sigma_{0} + \sum_{s = 1}^{t}\psi (X_{s})\psi (X_{s})^{\top}\), then
\[
\sum_{s=1}^{t}\frac{\psi(X_{s})^{\top}\Sigma_{s-1}^{-1}\psi(X_{s})}{1+\psi(X_{s})^{\top}\Sigma_{s-1}^{-1}\psi(X_{s})}\leq\ln|\Sigma_{0}^{-1}\Sigma_{t}|.
\]

steps.claim:
We have
\[
\begin{array}{l}\frac{\psi(X_{s})^{\top}\Sigma_{s-1}^{-1}\psi(X_{s})}{1+\psi(X_{s})^{\top}\Sigma_{s-1}^{-1}\psi(X_{s})}=\psi(X_{s})^{\top}\Sigma_{s}^{-1}\psi(X_{s})\\ =\operatorname{trace}\left(\Sigma_{s}^{-1}\left(\Sigma_{s}-\Sigma_{s-1}\right)\right)\\ =\operatorname{trace}\left(\nabla\ln\left|\Sigma_{s}\right|\left(\Sigma_{s}-\Sigma_{s-1}\right)\right)\\ \leq\ln|\Sigma_{s}| -\ln|\Sigma_{s-1}|.\\ \end{array}
\]
The first equality is due to the Sherman-Morrison formula.
The last inequality used the fact that \(\ln |Z|\) is a concave function of \(Z\) (see Theorem A.18).
Now by summing over \(s = 1\) to \(s = t\), we obtain the desired bound.

theorems.statement:
Assume that for all \( f \in \mathcal{F} \) and \( Z_{t}: -f(Z_{t}) + \mathbb{E}_{Z_{t}^{(y)}}f(Z_{t}) \leq b \), and the following variance condition holds for all \( f \in \mathcal{F} \) and \( S_{t} \):
\[
\operatorname{Var}_{Z_{t}^{(y)}}[f(Z_{t})]\leq c_{0}^{2}+c_{1}\mathbb{E}_{Z_{t}^{(y)}}[f(Z_{t})],
\]
then with probability at least \(1 - \delta\), for all \(f \in \mathcal{F}\):
\[
\begin{array}{l}\left(1-\lambda c_{1}\phi(\lambda b)\right)\sum_{t=1}^{n}\mathbb{E}_{Z_{t}^{(y)}}[f(Z_{t})]\leq\sum_{t=1}^{n}f(Z_{t})+\lambda n c_{0}^{2}\phi(\lambda b)\\ +\inf_{\epsilon>0}\left[2 n\epsilon+\frac{\ln(M(\epsilon,\mathcal{F},\|\cdot\|_{\infty})/\delta)}{\lambda}\right],\\ \end{array}
\]
where \(\phi (z) = (e^{z} - z - 1) / z^{2}\)

steps.claim:
Note that by employing the moment estimation of Bennett's inequality in Lemma 2.20, we obtain
\[
\begin{array}{l}\frac{1}{\lambda}\ln\mathbb{E}_{Z_{t}^{(y)}}e^{-\lambda f(Z_{t})}\\ \leq-\mathbb{E}_{Z_{t}^{(y)}}[f(Z_{t})]+\lambda\phi(\lambda b)\operatorname{Var}_{Z_{t}^{(y)}}[f(Z_{t})]\\ \leq-\mathbb{E}_{Z_{t}^{(y)}}[f(Z_{t})]+\lambda\phi(\lambda b)[c_{0}^{2}+c_{1}\mathbb{E}_{Z_{t}^{(y)}}[f(Z_{t})]].\\ \end{array}
\]
We can now obtain the desired bound from Theorem 13.11.

theorems.statement:
Let \(\{(X_t, \epsilon_t)\}\) be a filtered sequence in \(\mathcal{X} \times \mathbb{R}\) so that \(\epsilon_t\) is conditional zero-mean sub-Gaussian noise: for all \(\lambda \in \mathbb{R}\),
\[
\ln\mathbb{E}\left[e^{\lambda\epsilon_{t}}\mid X_{t},\mathcal{S}_{t-1}\right]\leq\frac{\lambda^{2}}{2}\sigma^{2},
\]
where \( S_{t-1} \) denotes the history data. Assume that \( Y_t = f_*(X_t) + \epsilon_t \), with \( f_*(x) \in \mathcal{F}: \mathcal{X} \to \mathbb{R} \). Let \( \hat{f}_t \) be an approximate ERM solution for some \( \epsilon' > 0 \):
\[
\left(\sum_{s=1}^{t}\left(\hat{f}_{t}\left(X_{s}\right)-Y_{s}\right)^{2}\right)^{1/2}\leq\min_{f\in\mathcal{F}}\left(\sum_{s=1}^{t}\left(f\left(X_{s}\right)-Y_{s}\right)^{2}\right)^{1/2}+\sqrt{t}\epsilon^{\prime}.
\]
Then with probability at least \(1 - \delta\), for all \(t \geq 0\):
\[
\sum_{s=1}^{t}(\hat{f}_{t}(X_{t})-f_{*}(X_{t}))^{2}\leq\inf_{\epsilon>0}\left[8 t(\epsilon+\epsilon^{\prime})(\sigma+2\epsilon+2\epsilon^{\prime})+12\sigma^{2}\ln\frac{2 N(\epsilon,\mathcal{F},\|\cdot\|_{\infty})}{\delta}\right].
\]

steps.claim:
Let \(\eta = \sigma^{-2} / 4\), and for \(f \in \mathcal{F}\), let
\[
\phi(f,Z_{t})=\left[\left(f(X_{t})-Y_{t}\right)^{2}-\left(f_{*}(X_{t})-Y_{t}\right)^{2}\right].
\]
Let \(\mathcal{F}_{\epsilon}\) be an \(\epsilon \| \cdot \|_{\infty}\) cover of \(\mathcal{F}\) with \(N = N(\epsilon, \mathcal{F}, \| \cdot \|_{\infty})\) members.

Given any \(f \in \mathcal{F}_{\epsilon}\),
\[
\begin{array}{l}\ln\mathbb{E}_{Y_{t}|X_{t},S_{t-1}}\exp(-\eta\phi(f,Z_{t}))\\ = -\eta\left(f\left(X_{t}\right)-f_{*}\left(X_{t}\right)\right)^{2}\\ +\ln\mathbb{E}_{Y_{t}\mid X_{t},S_{t-1}}\exp(-2\eta(f(X_{t})-f_{*}(X_{t}))(f_{*}(X_{t})-Y_{t}))\\ \leq-\eta(f(X_{t})-f_{*}(X_{t}))^{2}+\frac{4\eta^{2}\sigma^{2}}{2}(f(X_{t})-f_{*}(X_{t}))^{2}\\ = -\frac{\left(f(X_{t})-f_{*}(X_{t})\right)^{2}}{8\sigma^{2}}.\\ \end{array}
\]
The inequality used the sub-Gaussian noise assumption.
It follows from Theorem 13.11 that with probability at least \( 1 - \delta / 2 \), for all \( f \in \mathcal{F}_{\epsilon} \) and \( t \geq 0 \):

\[
\sum_{i=1}^{t}-\eta\phi(f,Z_{i})\leq-\sum_{i=1}^{t}\frac{\left(f\left(X_{i}\right)-f_{*}\left(X_{i}\right)\right)^{2}}{8\sigma^{2}}+\ln(2 N/\delta).\tag{13.5}
\]
Using Exercise 13.3, we have with probability at least \(1 - \delta /2\), for all \(t\geq 0\)
\[
\underbrace{\sum_{i=1}^{t}\left(f_{*}\left(X_{i}\right)-Y_{i}\right)^{2}}_{A}\leq 2 t\sigma^{2}+3\sigma^{2}\ln(2/\delta).\tag{13.6}
\]
It follows that with probability at least \(1 - \delta\), for all \(t \geq 0\) and \(f \in \mathcal{F}_{\epsilon}\), both (13.5)
and (13.6) hold.
Now, let \( f \in \mathcal{F}_{\epsilon} \) so that \( \| \hat{f}_t - f \|_{\infty} \leq \epsilon \).

This implies that
\[
\begin{array}{l}\sum_{i=1}^{t}\left[(f(X_{i})-Y_{i})^{2}-(f_{*}(X_{i})-Y_{i})^{2}\right]\leq\left(\sqrt{\sum_{i=1}^{t}(\hat{f}_{t}(X_{i})-Y_{i})^{2}}+\sqrt{t}\epsilon\right)^{2}-A\\ \leq\left(\sqrt{A}+\sqrt{t}(\epsilon+\epsilon^{\prime})\right)^{2}-A\\ \stackrel{(a)}{\leq}(\epsilon^{\prime}+\epsilon)^{2}t+2\sqrt{t}(\epsilon^{\prime}+\epsilon)\sigma\sqrt{2 t+3\ln(2/\delta)}\\ \leq 4\left(\epsilon^{\prime}+\epsilon\right)^{2}t+3\sigma t\left(\epsilon^{\prime}+\epsilon\right)+\sigma^{2}\ln(2/\delta).\tag{13.7}\\ \end{array}
\]
In the above derivations, the first inequality used \( |f(X_i) - Y_i| \leq |\hat{f}_t(X_i) - Y_i| + \epsilon \) for all \( i \).
The second inequality used the fact that \( \hat{f}_t \) is approximate ERM. (a) follows from (13.6).
The last inequality used \( 2a\sigma \sqrt{2b + 3c} \leq 3a\sigma \sqrt{b} + 3a^2 + \sigma^2 c \).

We thus obtain
\[
\begin{array}{l}\left(\sum_{i=1}^{t}(\hat{f}(X_{i})-f_{*}(X_{i}))^{2}\right)^{1/2}\\ \leq\sqrt{\epsilon^{2}t}+\left(\sum_{i=1}^{t}\left(f\left(X_{i}\right)-f_{*}\left(X_{i}\right)\right)^{2}\right)^{1/2}\quad(\text{t r i a n g l e i n e q u a l i t y})\\ \leq\sqrt{\epsilon^{2}t}+\left(8\sigma^{2}\ln(2N/\delta)+8\sigma^{2}\sum_{i=1}^{t}\eta\phi(f,Z_{i})\right)^{1/2}\quad(\text{f r o m}(13. 5))\\ =\sqrt{\epsilon^{2}t}+\left(8\sigma^{2}\ln(2N/\delta)+2\sum_{i=1}^{t}\left[\left(f\left(X_{i}\right)-Y_{i}\right)^{2}-\left(f_{*}\left(X_{i}\right)-Y_{i}\right)^{2}\right]\right)^{1/2}\\ \leq\sqrt{\epsilon^{2}t}+\left(10\sigma^{2}\ln(2N/\delta)+8t\left(\epsilon^{\prime}+\epsilon\right)^{2}+6\sigma t\left(\epsilon^{\prime}+\epsilon\right)\right)^{1/2}\quad(\text{f r o m}(13. 7))\\ \leq\left(12\sigma^{2}\ln(2N/\delta)+16t(\epsilon+\epsilon^{\prime})^{2}+8\sigma t(\epsilon+\epsilon^{\prime})\right)^{1/2},\\ \end{array}
\]
where the last inequality used \(\sqrt{a} +\sqrt{b}\leq \sqrt{6a + 1.2b}\) .
This implies the bound.

theorems.statement:
Consider a sequence of random functions \(\xi_1(S_1),\ldots,\xi_n(S_n)\). Assume that \(\xi_{i}\geq \mathbb{E}_{Z_{i}^{(y)}}\xi_{i} - b\) for some constant \(b > 0\). Then for any \(\lambda \in (0,3 / b)\), with probability at least \(1 - \delta\):
\[
\forall n>0:\sum_{i=1}^{n}\mathbb{E}_{Z_{i}^{(y)}}\xi_{i}<\sum_{i=1}^{n}\xi_{i}+\frac{\lambda\sum_{i=1}^{n}\mathrm{Var}_{Z_{i}^{(y)}}(\xi_{i})}{2(1-\lambda b/3)}+\frac{\ln(1/\delta)}{\lambda}.
\]

definition 4.1. Let \((\mathcal{V},d)\) be a pseudometric space with metric \(d(\cdot,\cdot)\). A finite
set \(\mathcal{G}(\epsilon) \subset \mathcal{V}\) is an \(\epsilon\)-cover (or \(\epsilon\)-net) of \(\mathcal{G} \subset \mathcal{V}\) if, for all \(\phi \in \mathcal{G}\), there exists \(\phi' \in \mathcal{G}(\epsilon)\) so that \(d(\phi', \phi) \leq \epsilon\). The \(\epsilon\)-covering number of \(\mathcal{G}\) with metric \(d\) is the smallest cardinality \(N(\epsilon, \mathcal{G}, d)\) of such \(\mathcal{G}(\epsilon)\). The number \(\ln N(\epsilon, \mathcal{G}, d)\) is called the \(\epsilon\)-entropy.
For a function class \(\mathcal{G}\) with seminorm \(L_{p}(\mathcal{D})\) in (3.19), we denote the corresponding \(L_{p}(\mathcal{D})\)-covering number as \(N(\epsilon, \mathcal{G}, L_{p}(\mathcal{D}))\). When \(1 \leq p \leq q\), we have
\[
N(\epsilon,\mathcal{G},L_{p}(\mathcal{D}))\leq N(\epsilon,\mathcal{G},L_{q}(\mathcal{D})).
\]
It is easy to verify the following relationship, which implies that \( L_{p}(\mathcal{D}) \) bracketing cover is a stronger requirement than \( L_{p}(\mathcal{D}) \) cover.

definition 3.8. We define
\[
\phi(w,z)=L\left(f(w,x),y\right)-L_{*}(x,y),\tag{3.4}
\]
for \( w \in \Omega \) and \( z = (x, y) \in \mathcal{Z} = \mathcal{X} \times \mathcal{Y} \), and a pre-chosen \( L_{*}(x, y) \) of \( z = (x, y) \) that does not depend on \( w \).
For training data \( S_{n}=\{Z_{i}=(X_{i},Y_{i}):i=1,\ldots,n\} \), we define the training loss for \( w\in \Omega \) as
\[
\phi(w,\mathcal{S}_{n})=\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\phi(w,Z_{i}).\tag{3.5}
\]
Moreover, for a distribution \(\mathcal{D}\) on \(\mathcal{Z}\), we define the test loss for \(w \in \Omega\) as:
\[
\phi(w,\mathcal{D})=\mathbb{E}_{Z\sim\mathcal{D}}\phi(w,Z).\tag{3.6}
\]
Since \( L_{*}(x,y) \) does not depend on \( w \), the ERM solution with respect to the loss \( L(\cdot) \) is equivalent to the ERM solution with respect to \( \phi (w,\cdot) \). Therefore with the simplified notations, the approximate ERM method (3.3) is a special case of the following method:
\[
\phi(\hat{w},\mathcal{S}_{n})\leq\inf_{w\in\Omega}\phi(w,\mathcal{S}_{n})+\epsilon^{\prime}.\tag{3.7}
\]
In general, we may simply take \( L_{*}(x,y) = 0 \) in (3.4). However, for some applications, we may choose a non-zero \( L_{*}(x,y) \) so that
\[
L(f(w,x),y)-L_{*}(x,y)
\]
has a small variance. For least squares loss, this can be achieved with \( L_{*}(x,y) = L(f_{*}(x),y) \) where \( f_{*}(x) \) is the optimal prediction function that minimizes the test loss as shown in Example 3.9. The smaller variance, combined with Bernstein's inequality, implies better generalization bound (see Section 3.6 for more details).

Empirical and Uniform Covering Number. Given an empirical distribution \( S_{n}=\{Z_{1},\ldots,Z_{n}\} \), we define the pseudometric \( d = L_{p}(S_{n}) \) as
\[
d(\phi,\phi^{\prime})=\left[\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}|\phi(Z_{i})-\phi^{\prime}(Z_{i})|^{p}\right]^{1/p}.
\]
The corresponding metric covering number \(N(\epsilon, \mathcal{G}, L_p(\mathcal{S}_n))\) is referred to as the
empirical \( L_{p} \) covering number. Given \( n \), the largest \( L_{p} \) covering number over empirical distribution \( S_{n} \) is referred to as the uniform \( L_{p} \) covering number
\[
N_{p}(\epsilon,\mathcal{G},n)=\sup_{\mathcal{S}_{n}}N(\epsilon,\mathcal{G},L_{p}(\mathcal{S}_{n})).
\]
Since the \(L_{p}(\mathcal{S}_{n})\) pseudometric increases with \(p\), we have the following simple result.

Bracketing Number. Let \(\mathcal{G} = \{\phi(w, \cdot) : w \in \Omega\}\) be a real-valued function class, equipped with a pseudometric \(d\). We say
\[
\mathcal{G}(\epsilon)=\left\{\left[\phi_{1}^{L}(z),\phi_{1}^{U}(z)\right],\dots,\left[\phi_{N}^{L}(z),\phi_{N}^{U}(z)\right]\right\}
\]
is an \(\epsilon\)-bracket of \(\mathcal{G}\) under metric \(d\) if for all \(w \in \Omega\), there exists \(j = j(w)\) such that \(\forall z\):
\[
\phi_{j}^{L}(z)\leq\phi(w,z)\leq\phi_{j}^{U}(z),\quad d(\phi_{j}^{L},\phi_{j}^{U})\leq\epsilon .
\]
The \(\epsilon\)-bracketing number is the smallest cardinality \(N_{\mathbb{I}}(\epsilon, \mathcal{G}, d)\) of such \(\mathcal{G}(\epsilon)\). The quantity \(\ln N_{\mathbb{I}}(\epsilon, \mathcal{G}, d)\) is called \(\epsilon\) bracketing entropy.
In particular, given a distribution \(\mathcal{D}\) and \(p \geq 1\), we define \(L_{p}\)-seminorm in function space as
\[
\left\|f-f^{\prime}\right\|_{L_{p}(\mathcal{D})}=\left[\mathbb{E}_{Z\sim\mathcal{D}}|f(Z)-f^{\prime}(Z)|^{p}\right]^{1/p}.\tag{3.19}
\]
It induces a pseudometric, denoted as \( d = L_{p}(\mathcal{D}) \), and the corresponding bracketing number is \( N_{\parallel}(\epsilon, \mathcal{G}, L_{p}(\mathcal{D})) \).
For \(p = \infty\), the \(L_{\infty}(\mathcal{D})\)-seminorm is defined as the essential supremum seminorm, which leads to the pseudometric
\[
d(f,f^{\prime})=\inf\left\{\omega:\Pr_{\mathcal{D}}[|f(Z)-f^{\prime}(Z)|\leq\omega]=1\right\}.
\]
However, when \( p = \infty \), instead of using the \( L_{\infty} \) bracketing number, it is more conventional to use the equivalent notion of \( L_{\infty} \) covering number (see Proposition 4.3).
We have the following relationship of lower bracketing number and bracketing numbers with different norms.

VC-dimension. We say that \(\mathcal{G}\) shatters \(S_{n}\) if the number of elements \(|\mathcal{G}(S_n)|\) is \(2^{n}\). That is, we can always find \(w\in \Omega\) so that \(\phi (w,z)\) matches any arbitrary possible choice of \(\{0,1\} ^n\) values at the \(n\) points. The maximum \(n\) such that \(\mathcal{G}\) shatters at least one instance of \(S_{n}\in \mathcal{Z}^{n}\), denoted by \(\mathrm{vc}(\mathcal{G})\), is called the VC-dimension of \(\mathcal{G}\).
Note that the maximum number of functions in \(\mathcal{G}(\mathcal{S}_n)\) is \(2^n\). If \(n > d\), then for any \(n\) samples \(\mathcal{S}_n\), \(\mathcal{G}(\mathcal{S}_n)\) contains fewer than \(2^n\) elements. Surprisingly, if a binary-valued function class \(\mathcal{G}\) has VC dimension \(d\), then when \(n > d\), the size of set \(\mathcal{G}(\mathcal{S}_n)\) can grow only polynomially in \(n\). This gives an \(O(d\ln n)\) upper bound on the uniform entropy of the function class \(\mathcal{G}\) with a finite VC-dimension (see Vapnik and Chervonenkis, 1968, 1971; Sauer, 1972).

definition 4.7. Consider a real-valued function family \(\mathcal{F}:\mathcal{Z}\to \mathbb{R}\). Consider \(n\) iid Bernoulli random variables \(\sigma_{i}\in \{\pm 1\}\), where \(\operatorname*{Pr}(\sigma_i=1)=\operatorname*{Pr}(\sigma_i= -1)=0.5\). The symmetrized empirical process is
\[
f(\sigma,\mathcal{S}_{n})=\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\sigma_{i}f(Z_{i})\qquad f\in\mathcal{F},
\]
where the randomness is with respect to both \(S_{n} = \{Z_{i}\}\) and \(\sigma = \{\sigma_{i}\}\).
Note that in order to bound the symmetrized empirical process, we only need a covering number result on \( S_{n} \). Therefore the symmetrization analysis allows us to work with empirical covering numbers. Next we will show that a bound on the symmetrized empirical process can be used to obtain uniform convergence of the empirical process \( \{f(S_{n}): f \in \mathcal{F}\} \) to the corresponding result on the validation data. Since one can relate the validation loss of a learning algorithm to its generalization error on the test data, we can use this result to obtain generalization bounds.
The following lemma shows that if we can obtain an upper bound on the symmetrized empirical process \(\{f(\sigma, S_n) : f \in \mathcal{F}\}\), and the upper bound satisfies a superadditive property, then we can obtain the uniform convergence of the empirical process \(\{f(S_n) : f \in \mathcal{F}\}\) on the training data \(S_n\) to the corresponding result on the validation data \(S_n'\).

theorems.statement:
Let \(\psi_{\mathrm{trn}}: \mathcal{F} \times \mathcal{Z}^n \to \mathbb{R}\), \(\psi_{\mathrm{val}}: \mathcal{F} \times \mathcal{Z}^n \to \mathbb{R}\), \(\psi_{\mathrm{tst}}: \mathcal{F} \times \mathcal{D} \to \mathbb{R}\) be appropriately training (where \(\mathcal{D}\) denotes probability distributions on \(\mathcal{Z}\)), validation, and test statistics. Assume that for any \(\delta_1 \in (0,1)\), the following uniform convergence result holds. With probability at least \(1 - \delta_1\) over randomly drawn training and validation sets \((S_n, S_n') \sim \mathcal{D}^{2n}\):
\[
\forall f\in\mathcal{F}:\psi_{\mathrm{val}}(f,\mathcal{S}_{n}^{\prime})\leq\psi_{\mathrm{trn}}(f,\mathcal{S}_{n})+\epsilon_{n}^{1}(\delta_{1}).
\]
Moreover, assume \(\forall f\in \mathcal{F}\), we have with probability \(1 - \delta_{2}\) over randomly drawn \(\mathcal{S}_n^\prime \sim \mathcal{D}\):
\[
\psi_{\mathrm{tst}}(f,\mathcal{D})\leq\psi_{\mathrm{val}}(f,\mathcal{S}_{n}^{\prime})+\epsilon_{n}^{2}(\delta_{2}).
\]
Then the following uniform convergence statement holds. With probability at least \(1 - \delta_1 - \delta_2\),
\[
\forall f\in\mathcal{F}:\psi_{\mathrm{tst}}(f,\mathcal{D})\leq\psi_{\mathrm{trn}}(f,\mathcal{S}_{n})+\epsilon_{n}^{1}(\delta_{1})+\epsilon_{n}^{2}(\delta_{2}).
\]

steps.claim: Let \( Q(f, \mathcal{S}_n) = \psi_{\mathrm{tst}}(f, \mathcal{D}) - \psi_{\mathrm{trn}}(f, \mathcal{S}_n) - (\epsilon_n^1(\delta_1) + \epsilon_n^2(\delta_2)) \), and let \( E \) be the event that \( \sup_{f \in \mathcal{F}} Q(f, \mathcal{S}_n) \leq 0 \).

We pick \( \hat{f}(\mathcal{S}_n) \in \mathcal{F} \) so that if \( E \) holds, then we choose an arbitrary \( Q(\hat{f}(\mathcal{S}_n), \mathcal{S}_n) \leq 0 \), and if \( E \) does not hold, we choose \( \hat{f}(\mathcal{S}_n) \) so that \( Q(\hat{f}(\mathcal{S}_n), \mathcal{S}_n) > 0 \).
We consider sample \( (\mathcal{S}_n, \mathcal{S}_n') \sim \mathcal{D}^{2n} \).
For simplicity, in the following, we let \( \hat{f} = \hat{f}(\mathcal{S}_n) \).
The uniform convergence condition of the theorem implies that with probability at least \( 1 - \delta_1 \), the following event holds:

\[
{E_{1}:}{\psi_{\mathrm{val}}(\hat{f},\mathcal{S}_{n}^{\prime})\leq\psi_{\mathrm{trn}}(\hat{f},\mathcal{S}_{n})+\epsilon_{n}^{1}(\delta_{1}).}
\]
Note that the validation data \( S_{n}^{\prime} \) is independent of the training data \( S_{n} \).
Therefore \( S_{n}^{\prime} \) is also independent of \( \hat{f} \).
Therefore the condition of the theorem implies that with probability at least \( 1 - \delta_2 \), the following event holds:

\[
E_{2}:\psi_{\mathrm{tst}}(\hat{f},\mathcal{D})\leq\psi_{\mathrm{val}}(\hat{f},\mathcal{S}_{n}^{\prime})+\epsilon_{n}^{2}(\delta_{2}).
\]
If both events \(E_{1}\) and \(E_{2}\) hold, then
\[
\begin{array}{l}\psi_{\mathrm{tst}}(\hat{f},\mathcal{D})\leq\psi_{\mathrm{val}}(\hat{f},\mathcal{S}_{n}^{\prime})+\epsilon_{n}^{2}(\delta_{2})\\ \leq\psi_{\mathrm{trn}}(\hat{f},\mathcal{S}_{n})+\epsilon_{n}^{1}(\delta_{1})+\epsilon_{n}^{2}(\delta_{2}).\\ \end{array}
\]
The definition of \(\hat{f}\) implies that \(E\) holds.
Therefore \(\operatorname*{Pr}(E)\geq \operatorname*{Pr}(E_1\& E_2)\geq 1 - \delta_1 - \delta_2\).
This implies the desired bound.

theorems.statement:
Let \(\sigma_{i} = \{\pm 1\}\) be independent Bernoulli random variables ( each takes value \(\pm 1\) with equal probability). Let \(a_{i}\) be fixed numbers \((i=1,\dots,n)\) Then for all \(\epsilon >0\) ..
\[
\Pr\left(n^{-1}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\sigma_{i}a_{i}\geq\epsilon\right)\leq\exp\left[-\frac{n\epsilon^{2}}{2 n^{-1}\sum_{i=1}^{n}a_{i}^{2}}\right].
\]

steps.claim: Consider \( X_{i} = \sigma_{i}a_{i} \) in Corollary 2.26. We can take \( \mu = 0 \) and \( b_{i} = a_{i}^{2} \) to obtain the desired bound.

theorems.statement:
(Symmetrization) Consider a real valued function family \(F = \{f : Z \rightarrow \mathbb{R}\}\). Assume there exists a function \(\psi : F \times Z^{n} \rightarrow \mathbb{R}\) and \(\epsilon_{n} : (0,1) \rightarrow \mathbb{R}\) so that with probability at least \(1-\delta\):
\[
\forall f \in F, \qquad f(\sigma, S_{n}) \leq \psi(f, S_{n}) + \epsilon_{n}(\delta),
\]
where the randomness is over both \(S_{n} \sim D^{n}\) and \(\sigma\). If there exists \(\tilde{\psi}(f, S_{n} \cup S_{n}^{\prime})\) so that the following superadditive inequality holds for all \((S_{n}, S_{n}^{\prime})\)
\[
\psi(f, S_{n}) + \psi(f, S_{n}^{\prime}) \leq \tilde{\psi}(f, S_{n} \cup S_{n}^{\prime}),
\]
then with probability at least \(1-\delta\) over independent random data \((S_{n}, S_{n}^{\prime}) \sim D^{2n}\):
\[
\forall f \in F, \qquad f(S_{n}^{\prime}) \leq f(S_{n}) + \tilde{\psi}(f, S_{n} \cup S_{n}^{\prime}) + 2\epsilon_{n}(\delta/2).
\]

steps.claim: Consider independent random samples \((S_{n}, S_{n}^{\prime}) \sim D^{2n}\).

The distribution of \(f(S_{n}) - f(S_{n}^{\prime})\) is the same as that of \(f(\sigma, S_{n}) - f(\sigma, S_{n}^{\prime})\), and the latter contains additional randomness from Bernoulli random variables \(\sigma\), drawn independently of \((S_{n}, S_{n}^{\prime})\), as in Definition 4.7.

It follows that
\[
\begin{array}{l}
\Pr\Bigl(\exists f \in F,\ f(S_{n}^{\prime}) > f(S_{n}) + \tilde{\psi}(f, S_{n} \cup S_{n}^{\prime}) + 2\epsilon_{n}(\delta/2)\Bigr) \\
= \Pr\Bigl(\exists f \in F,\ f(\sigma, S_{n}^{\prime}) > f(\sigma, S_{n}) + \tilde{\psi}(f, S_{n} \cup S_{n}^{\prime}) + 2\epsilon_{n}(\delta/2)\Bigr) \\
\stackrel{(a)}{\leq} \Pr\Bigl(\underbrace{\exists f \in F,\ f(\sigma, S_{n}^{\prime}) > f(\sigma, S_{n}) + (\psi(f, S_{n}) + \psi(f, S_{n}^{\prime})) + 2\epsilon_{n}(\delta/2)}_{E_{0}}\Bigr)
\end{array}
\]
\[
\begin{array}{l}
\stackrel{(b)}{\leq} \Pr\Bigl(\underbrace{\exists f \in F,\ f(\sigma, S_{n}^{\prime}) > \psi(f, S_{n}^{\prime}) + \epsilon_{n}(\delta/2)}_{E_{1}}\Bigr) \\
\quad + \Pr\Bigl(\underbrace{\exists f \in F,\ -f(\sigma, S_{n}) > \psi(f, S_{n}) + \epsilon_{n}(\delta/2)}_{E_{2}}\Bigr)
\end{array}
\]
\[
= 2\Pr\Bigl(\exists f \in F,\ f(\sigma, S_{n}) > \psi(f, S_{n}) + \epsilon_{n}(\delta/2)\Bigr) \leq 2(\delta/2).
\]
In the above derivation, the first equation used the fact that \(f(S_{n}) - f(S_{n}^{\prime})\) and \(f(\sigma, S_{n}) - f(\sigma, S_{n}^{\prime})\) have the same distributions. (a) used the assumption \(\psi(S_{n}) + \psi(S_{n}^{\prime}) \leq \widetilde{\psi}(S_{n} \cup S_{n}^{\prime})\). (b) used the union bound, and the fact that if event \(E_{0}\) holds, then either event \(E_{1}\) holds or event \(E_{2}\) holds.
The next equation used the symmetry of \(-f(\sigma, S_{n})\) and \(f(\sigma, S_{n})\), and the last inequality used the assumption of the lemma.
The result implies the desired bound.

theorems.statement:
If \(\operatorname{vc}(\mathcal{G}) = d\), then we have for all \(n > 0\) and empirical samples \(\mathcal{S}_n = \{Z_1, \ldots, Z_n\} \in \mathcal{Z}^n\):
\[
|\mathcal{G}(\mathcal{S}_{n})|\leq\sum_{\ell=0}^{d}\binom{n}{\ell}\leq\max(2,e n/d)^{d}.
\]

steps.claim: First, we prove the statement under the assumption that \(|\mathcal{G}(\mathcal{S}_n)|\) is upper bounded by the number of subsets of \(\mathcal{S}_n\) (including the empty set) that are shattered by \(\mathcal{G}\).

Under this assumption, since any subset shattered by \(\mathcal{G}\) cannot be larger than \(d\) by the definition of VC-dimension, and the number of subsets of size \(\ell\) is \(\binom{n}{\ell}\), we know that the number of subsets shattered by \(\mathcal{G}\) cannot be more than \(\sum_{\ell=0}^{d} \binom{n}{\ell}\).

When \(n \geq d\), we have (see Exercise 4.1)
\[
\sum_{\ell=0}^{d}\binom{n}{\ell}\leq(e n/d)^{d}.\tag{4.2}
\]
When \(n \leq d\), we have \(\sum_{\ell=0}^{d} \binom{n}{\ell} \leq 2^d\).

This implies the desired result. In the following, we only need to prove the statement that \(|\mathcal{G}(\mathcal{S}_n)|\) is upper bounded by the number of subsets of \(\mathcal{S}_n\) that are shattered by \(\mathcal{G}\).
This can be proved by induction on \(n\). When \(n = 1\), one can check that the claim holds trivially.
Now assume that the claim holds for all empirical samples of size no more than \( n - 1 \).
Consider \( n \) samples \( \{Z_1, \ldots, Z_n\} \).

We define
\[
\phi(w,\mathcal{S}_{k})=[\phi(w,Z_{1}),\dots,\phi(w,Z_{k})],
\]
\[
\mathcal{G}_{n-1}(\mathcal{S}_{n})=\left\{\left[\phi(w,\mathcal{S}_{n-1}),1\right]:\left[\phi(w,\mathcal{S}_{n-1}),0\right],\left[\phi(w,\mathcal{S}_{n-1}),1\right]\in\mathcal{G}(\mathcal{S}_{n})\right\}.
\]
Using the induction hypothesis, we know that \(|\mathcal{G}_{n - 1}(\mathcal{S}_n)|\) is bounded by the number of shattered subset \(\mathcal{S}\subset \mathcal{S}_{n - 1}\); for each shattered \(\mathcal{S}\subset \mathcal{S}_{n - 1}\), \(\mathcal{S}\cup \{Z_n\}\) is shattered by \(\mathcal{G}\) because both \([\phi (w,\mathcal{S}_{n - 1}),1]\) and \([\phi (w,S_{n - 1}),0]\) belong to \(\mathcal{G}(\mathcal{S}_n)\).
Therefore \(|\mathcal{G}_{n - 1}(\mathcal{S}_n)|\) is no more than the number of shattered subsets of \(\mathcal{S}_n\) that contains \(Z_{n}\).

Moreover, since for \(\phi(w,\cdot) \in \mathcal{G}(\mathcal{S}_n) - \mathcal{G}_{n-1}(\mathcal{S}_n)\), \(\phi(w,Z_n)\) is uniquely determined by its values at \(\mathcal{S}_{n-1}\) (if not, then both \([\phi(w,\mathcal{S}_{n-1}),0]\) and \([\phi(w,\mathcal{S}_{n-1}),1]\) can be achieved in \(\mathcal{G}(\mathcal{S}_n) - \mathcal{G}_{n-1}(\mathcal{S}_n)\), which is impossible because by definition, we should have put \([\phi(w,\mathcal{S}_{n-1}),1]\) in \(\mathcal{G}_{n-1}(\mathcal{S}_n)\)), it follows that \(|\mathcal{G}(\mathcal{S}_n) - \mathcal{G}_{n-1}(\mathcal{S}_n)|\) is no more than \(|\mathcal{G}(\mathcal{S}_{n-1})|\).
By induction hypothesis, \(|\mathcal{G}(\mathcal{S}_{n-1})|\) is no more than the number of shattered subsets of \(\mathcal{S}_n\) that does not contain \(Z_n\).
By combining the above two facts, \(|\mathcal{G}(\mathcal{S}_n)|\) is no more than the number of shattered subsets of \(\mathcal{S}_n\).

theorems.statement:
Assume that \(\phi(w, z) \in [0,1]\) for all \(w\) and \(z\). Then given \(\delta \in (0,1)\), with probability at least \(1 - \delta\), the following inequality holds:
\[
\forall w\in\Omega:\phi(w,\mathcal{D})\leq\phi(w,\mathcal{S}_{n})+\epsilon_{n}(\delta),
\]
where
\[
\epsilon_{n}(\delta)=\inf_{\epsilon>0}\left[2\epsilon+3\sqrt{\frac{\ln(3 N_{1}(\epsilon,\mathcal{G},2 n)/\delta)}{2 n}}\right].
\]
Moreover, for any \(\gamma \in (0,1)\), with probability at least \(1 - \delta\), the following inequality holds:
\[
\forall w\in\Omega:(1-\gamma)^{2}\phi(w,\mathcal{D})\leq\phi(w,\mathcal{S}_{n})+\epsilon_{n}(\delta),
\]
where
\[
\epsilon_{n}(\delta)=\inf_{\epsilon>0}\left[2\epsilon+\frac{(5-4\gamma)\ln(3 N_{1}(\epsilon,\mathcal{G},n)/\delta)}{2\gamma n}\right].
\]

steps.claim: Let \(\mathcal{F} = \{f(z) = \phi(w,z) - 0.5 : w \in \Omega\}\).
Given \(S_{n}\), we consider an \(\epsilon-L_{1}(S_{n})\) cover \(\mathcal{F}_{\epsilon}(S_{n})\) of \(\mathcal{F}\), of size no more \(N = N_{1}(\epsilon, \mathcal{G}, n)\).
We may assume that \(f(Z_{i}) \in [-0.5, 0.5]\) for \(f \in \mathcal{F}_{\epsilon}(S_{n})\).
From Corollary 2.27 (with \(a_{i} = 0.5\)) and the union bound, we obtain the following uniform convergence result over \(\mathcal{F}_{\epsilon}(S_{n})\).

With probability \(1-\delta\): \[
\forall f\in\mathcal{F}_{\epsilon}(\mathcal{S}_{n}):f(\sigma,\mathcal{S}_{n})\leq\sqrt{\frac{\ln(N/\delta)}{2 n}}.
\]
Since for all \( f \in \mathcal{F} \), we can find \( f' \in \mathcal{F}_{\epsilon}(\mathcal{S}_n) \) so that \( n^{-1} \sum_{Z \in \mathcal{S}_n} |f(Z) - f'(Z)| \leq \epsilon \) for all \( Z \in \mathcal{S}_n \).

It follows that
\[
f(\sigma,\mathcal{S}_{n})\leq f^{\prime}(\sigma,\mathcal{S}_{n})+\epsilon\leq\epsilon+\sqrt{\frac{\ln(N/\delta)}{2 n}}.
\]
Using Lemma 4.8 with \(\psi = 0\), this uniform convergence result for the symmetrized
empirical process implies the following uniform convergence result.
With probability at least \(1 - \delta_{1}\) over \((S_n, S'_n) \sim \mathcal{D}^{2n}\):

\[
\forall w\in\Omega:\underbrace{\phi(w,\mathcal{S}_{n}^{\prime})}_{\psi_{\mathrm{val}}}\leq\underbrace{\phi(w,\mathcal{S}_{n})}_{\psi_{\mathrm{trn}}}+\underbrace{2\epsilon+\sqrt{\frac{2\ln(2 N/\delta_{1})}{n}}}_{\epsilon_{n}^{1}(\delta_{1})}.
\]
The standard additive Chernoff bound implies that for all \( w \in \Omega \), with probability at least \( 1 - \delta_2 \):

\[
\underbrace{\phi(w,\mathcal{D})}_{\psi_{\mathrm{tst}}}\leq\underbrace{\phi(w,\mathcal{S}_{n}^{\prime})}_{\psi_{\mathrm{val}}}+\underbrace{\sqrt{\frac{\ln(1/\delta_{2})}{2 n}}}_{\epsilon_{n}^{2}(\delta_{2})}.
\]
Therefore in Lemma 4.11, we can take symbols as defined above, together with \(\delta_1 = 2\delta /3\) and \(\delta_{2} = \delta /3\) to obtain the desired bound.
Similarly, we consider \(\mathcal{F} = \{f(z) = \phi (w,z):w\in \Omega \}\).
Given \(S_{n}\), we consider an \(\epsilon -L_{1}(S_{n})\) cover \(\mathcal{F}_{\epsilon}(\mathcal{S}_n)\) of \(\mathcal{F}\), of size no more \(N=N_{1}(\epsilon,\mathcal{G},n)\).
We assume that \(f(Z_{i})\in [0,1]\) for all \(f\in \mathcal{F}_{\epsilon}(\mathcal{S}_n)\).
From Corollary 2.27 and the union bound, we obtain the following uniform convergence result over \(\mathcal{F}_{\epsilon}(\mathcal{S}_n)\).

With probability at least \(1 - \delta\): \[
\begin{array}{l}\forall f\in\mathcal{F}_{\epsilon}(\mathcal{S}_{n}):f(\sigma,\mathcal{S}_{n})\leq\sqrt{\frac{2\sum_{Z\in\mathcal{S}_{n}}f(Z)^{2}\ln(N/\delta)}{n^{2}}}\\ \leq\gamma^{\prime}\frac{1}{n}\sum_{Z\in\mathcal{S}_{n}}f(Z)+\frac{\ln(N/\delta)}{2\gamma^{\prime}n}.\\ \end{array}
\]
The first inequality used Corollary 2.27.
The second inequality used \(\sqrt{2ab} \leq \gamma' a + b / (2\gamma')\) and \(f(Z)^2 \leq f(Z)\).
Since for all \(f \in \mathcal{F}\), we can find \(f' \in \mathcal{F}_{\epsilon}(\mathcal{S}_n)\) so that \(\frac{1}{n} \sum_{Z \in \mathcal{S}_n} |f(Z) - f'(Z)| \leq \epsilon\).

It follows that
\[
\begin{array}{l}f(\sigma,\mathcal{S}_{n})\leq f^{\prime}(\sigma,\mathcal{S}_{n})+\epsilon\\ \leq\gamma^{\prime}\frac{1}{n}\sum_{Z\in\mathcal{S}_{n}}f^{\prime}(Z)+\frac{\ln(N/\delta)}{2\gamma^{\prime}n}+\epsilon\\ \leq\gamma^{\prime}\frac{1}{n}\sum_{Z\in\mathcal{S}_{n}}f(Z)+\frac{\ln(N/\delta)}{2\gamma^{\prime}n}+(1+\gamma^{\prime})\epsilon .\\ \end{array}
\]
Now, with \(\psi(f, \mathcal{S}_n) = \widetilde{\psi}(f, \mathcal{S}_n) = \gamma' \frac{1}{n} \sum_{Z \in \mathcal{S}_n} f(Z)\), we obtain from Lemma 4.8 the following uniform convergence result.
With probability at least \(1 - \delta_1\) over \((\mathcal{S}_n, \mathcal{S}_n') \sim \mathcal{D}^{2n}\):

\[
\forall w\in\Omega:(1-\gamma^{\prime})\phi(w,\mathcal{S}_{n}^{\prime})\leq(1+\gamma^{\prime})\phi(w,\mathcal{S}_{n})+2(1+\gamma^{\prime})\epsilon+\frac{\ln(2 N/\delta_{1})}{\gamma^{\prime}n}.
\]
Let \(\gamma' = \gamma / (2 - \gamma)\), then it is easy to check algebraically that \((1 - \gamma') / (1 + \gamma') = 1 - \gamma\)
and \(1 / (\gamma^{\prime}(1 + \gamma^{\prime})) = (2 - \gamma)^{2} / (2\gamma)\).

We thus obtain: \[
\forall w\in\Omega:\underbrace{(1-\gamma)\phi(w,\mathcal{S}_{n}^{\prime})}_{\psi_{\mathrm{val}}}\leq\underbrace{\phi(w,\mathcal{S}_{n})}_{\psi_{\mathrm{trn}}}+\underbrace{2\epsilon+\frac{(2-\gamma)^{2}\ln(2 N/\delta_{1})}{2\gamma n}}_{\epsilon_{n}^{1}(\delta_{1})}.\tag{4.1}
\]
The standard multiplicative Chernoff bound in (2.11) implies that with probability \( 1 - \delta_2 \):

\[
\underbrace{(1-\gamma)(1-\gamma)\phi(w,\mathcal{D})}_{\psi_{\mathrm{tst}}}\leq\underbrace{(1-\gamma)\phi(w,\mathcal{S}_{n}^{\prime})}_{\psi_{\mathrm{val}}}+\underbrace{(1-\gamma)\frac{\ln(1/\delta_{2})}{2\gamma n}}_{\epsilon_{n}^{2}(\delta_{2})}.
\]
Therefore in Lemma 4.11, we can use symbols as displayed above, together with \(\delta_1 = 2\delta /3\) and \(\delta_{2} = \delta /3\) to obtain the desired bound.

context:
Shared setting for the results below. All definitions, standing assumptions and numbered equations that the proofs rely on are collected here.

definition 16.1. In the multi-armed bandit (or MAB) problem, we consider \(K\) arms. The environment generates a sequence of reward vectors for time steps \(t \geq 1\) as \(r_t = [r_t(1), \ldots, r_t(K)]\). Each \(r_t(a)\) is associated with an arm \(a \in \{1, \ldots, K\}\). In the literature, an arm \(a\) is also referred to as an action. At each time step \(t = 1, 2, \ldots, T\),
- The player pulls one of the arms \( a_{t} \in \{1, \dots, K\} \).
- The environment returns the reward \( r_t(a_t) \), but does not reveal information on any other arm \( a \neq a_t \).
At each time \( t \), a (randomized) bandit algorithm takes the historic observations observed so far, and maps it to a distribution \( \hat{\pi}_{t-1} \) over actions \( a \in \{1, \ldots, K\} \). We then draw a random action \( a_t \) (arm) from \( \hat{\pi}_{t-1} \). Here \( \hat{\pi}_{t-1} \) is referred to as policy.
In the adversarial bandit problem, we are given an arbitrary reward sequence \(\{[r_1(1),\ldots,r_t(K)]:t\geq 1\}\) before hand. The adversary in this setting is called oblivious, who decides the rewards of all the rounds before the game starts (but may take advantage of the bandit algorithm's weakness). For this reward se
quence, the expected cumulative reward of a randomized bandit algorithm is
\[
\mathbb{E}\sum_{t=1}^{T}r_{t}(a_{t}),
\]
where the randomization is over the internal randomization of the bandit algorithm. The expected regret is defined as
\[
\operatorname{REG}_{T}=\max_{a}\sum_{t=1}^{T}r_{t}(a)-\mathbb{E}\sum_{t=1}^{T}r_{t}\left(a_{t}\right).\tag{16.1}
\]
If the bandit algorithm is deterministic: i.e. pulling a single arm \(a_{t}\) only at any time step, then the regret is
\[
\mathrm{REG}_{T}=\max_{a}\sum_{t=1}^{T}r_{t}(a)-\sum_{t=1}^{T}r_{t}(a_{t}).
\]
In the adversarial bandit problem, our goal is to minimize the expected regret \(\mathrm{REG}_T\) (and the expectation is with respect to the internal randomization of the algorithm instead of the data).
Another form of bandit problem, called stochastic bandit, assumes that the reward \( r_t(a) \) is drawn independently from a distribution \( \mathcal{D}_a \), with mean \( \mu(a) = \mathbb{E}_{r_t(a) \sim \mathcal{D}_a} [r_t(a)] \). In this setting, the goal of bandit is to find \( a \) that maximizes the expected reward \( \mu(a) \). We are interested in the expected regret defined as:
\[
\operatorname{REG}_{T}=T\max_{a}\mu(a)-\mathbb{E}\sum_{t=1}^{T}\mu\left(a_{t}\right).\tag{16.2}
\]
Again, this regret is defined for each realization of the stochastic rewards, and the expectation is with respect to the randomness of the algorithm. If algorithm is deterministic and outputs \( a_{t} \) at each time \( t \), then
\[
\mathrm{REG}_{T}=T\max_{a}\mu(a)-\sum_{t=1}^{T}\mu(a_{t}).
\]
We can further include randomization over data into the regret of stochastic bandit, by considering expected regret as follows:
\[
\mathbb{E}\operatorname{REG}_{T}=T\max_{a}\mu(a)-\mathbb{E}\sum_{t=1}^{T}\mu(a_{t}),
\]
where the expectation is with respect to both the data and the internal randomization of the learning algorithm.

equation 16.3. For each arm \(a\), define the number of pulls up to time \(t\) and the corresponding empirical mean by
\[
\hat n_t(a)=\sum_{s=1}^{t}\mathbb{1}(a_s=a), \qquad
\hat\mu_t(a)=\frac{1}{\hat n_t(a)}\sum_{s=1}^{t} r_s(a_s)\mathbb{1}(a_s=a),
\]
with the initialization \(\hat n_0(a)=0\) and \(\hat\mu_0(a)=0\). In the UCB algorithm, after the initialization rounds, the arm is selected according to
\[
a_t\in\arg\max_a\left[\hat\mu_{t-1}(a)+\hat c_{t-1}(a)\right]. \tag{16.3}
\]
Here \(\hat c_t(a)\) denotes the confidence width used by the algorithm.

UCB Algorithm. Algorithm 16.1: UCB Algorithm
Input: \(K\) and \(T\geq K\)   
1 for \(a=1,\dots,K\) do   
2 Let \(\hat{n}_0(a) = 0\)   
3 Let \(\hat{\mu}_0(a) = 0\)   
4 for \(t=1,2,\ldots,T\) do   
5 if \(t\leq K\) then   
6 Let \(a_{t} = t\)   
7 else   
8 Let \(a_{t}\in \arg \max_{a}[\hat{\mu}_{t - 1}(a) + \hat{c}_{t - 1}(a)]\) according to (16.3)   
9 Pull arm \(a_{t}\) and observe reward \(r_t(a_t)\)

section 13.1 sequential observation setup. In Section 13.1, data are observed sequentially. At each time \(t\), after the history \(S_{t-1}\) has been observed, the next observation \(Z_t\) is drawn according to a distribution that may depend on that history. The observation is decomposed as \(Z_t=(Z_t^{(x)},Z_t^{(y)})\), where \(Z_t^{(x)}\) is the component determined by the past history or the chosen action at time \(t\), and \(Z_t^{(y)}\) is the random response component. The history after time \(t\) is \(S_t=(Z_1,\ldots,Z_t)\), and \(\mathcal{S}_T\) denotes the full sequential experiment/history through time \(T\). For a function depending on \(S_t\), the notation \(\mathbb{E}_{Z_t^{(y)}}[\cdot]\) means conditional expectation over the response component \(Z_t^{(y)}\), conditional on \(S_{t-1}\) and on \(Z_t^{(x)}\). Stopping times are adapted to the filtration generated by the histories \(S_t\).

theorems.statement:
Let \(a_* \in \arg \max_a \mu(a)\). Let
\[

be the probability that the upper confident bound fails on \( a_* \). Let

be the probability that the lower confident bound fails on \( a \neq a_* \). Then for Algorithm 16.1, we have with probability at least \( 1 - \delta_1 - \delta_2 \):
\[
\operatorname{REG}_{T}\leq\sum_{a=1}^{K}[\mu(a_{*})-\mu(a)]+\sum_{t=K+1}^{T}[\hat{c}_{t-1}(a_{t})+\hat{c}_{t-1}^{\prime}(a_{t})]\mathbb{1}(a_{t}\neq a_{*}).
\]

steps.claim: We have with probability \(1 - \delta_1 - \delta_2\), the following hold for all \(t > K\):

\[
\mu\left(a_{*}\right)\leq\hat{\mu}_{t-1}\left(a_{*}\right)+\hat{c}_{t-1}\left(a_{*}\right),\quad \text{(u p p e r c o n f i d e n c e b o u n d)}
\]
\[

\]
It follows that for all \(t > K\):

\[
\begin{array}{l}\mu\left(a_{*}\right)\mathbb{1}\left(a_{t}\neq a_{*}\right)\\ \leq\left[\hat{\mu}_{t-1}\left(a_{*}\right)+\hat{c}_{t-1}\left(a_{*}\right)\right]\mathbb{1}\left(a_{t}\neq a_{*}\right)\quad(\text{u p p e r c o n f i d e n c e b o u n d})\\ \leq\left[\hat{\mu}_{t-1}\left(a_{t}\right)+\hat{c}_{t-1}\left(a_{t}\right)\right]\mathbb{1}\left(a_{t}\neq a_{*}\right)\quad(\text{U C B a l g o r i t h m})\\ \leq\left[\mu\left(a_{t}\right)+\hat{c}_{t-1}^{\prime}\left(a_{t}\right)+\hat{c}_{t-1}\left(a_{t}\right)\right]\mathbb{1}\left(a_{t}\neq a_{*}\right).\quad \text{(l o w e r c o n f i d e n c e b o u n d)}\\ \end{array}

For \(t \leq K\), we have

steps.claim: We would like to apply Theorem 13.24 with \(d = 1\) and \(m = K\).

We consider a family of \(K\) distributions \(\mathcal{P}_{\mathcal{Z}} = \{q^{\tau}, \tau = 1, \ldots, K\}\), and for each arm \(a\), the distribution \(q^{\tau}(a)\) is a Bernoulli distribution \(r \in \{0, 1\}\) with mean \(\mathbb{E}[r] = 0.5 + \epsilon \mathbb{1}(a = \tau)\) with \(\epsilon \in (0, 0.1]\) to be determined later.
We also define \(q_0(a)\) as a Bernoulli distribution \(r \in \{0, 1\}\) with mean \(\mathbb{E}[r] = 0.5\).
Since by construction, \(q^{\tau} \sim_{1} q^{\tau'}\) for all \(\tau, \tau' \in [K]\), we can map them all to \(q_1^\tau = q_0\).

If we pull an arm \(\theta\), we have
\[
Q(\theta,q^{\tau})=\epsilon\mathbb{1}(\theta\neq\tau).
\]
It is clear that \([Q(\theta, q^{\tau}) + Q(\theta, q^{\tau'})] \geq \epsilon\) for \(\tau \neq \tau'\).

Consider \(n \leq T\) samples generated sequentially by an arbitrary bandit algorithm and \(q^{\tau}(a)\), and let the resulting distribution that generates \(\mathcal{S}_n\) as \(p^{\tau}(\mathcal{S}_n)\), where \(\mathcal{S}_n = \{a_1, r_1, \ldots, a_n, r_n\}\).
Let \(\epsilon = \min (0.1, 0.24\sqrt{K / T})\). We have for all \(a_{t}\):

\[
\begin{array}{l}\frac{1}{K}\sum_{\tau=1}^{K}\mathrm{KL}\left(q_{0}\left(a_{t}\right)| |q^{\tau}\left(a_{t}\right)\right)=\frac{1}{K}\sum_{\tau=1}^{K}\mathrm{KL}\left(q_{0}\left(a_{t}\right)| |q^{\tau}\left(a_{t}\right)\right)\mathbb{1}\left(a_{t}=\tau\right)\\ =\frac{1}{K}\mathrm{KL}(0. 5| |0. 5+\epsilon)\leq\frac{0.5\epsilon^{2}}{K(0.5+\epsilon)(0.5-\epsilon)}\leq\frac{2.1}{K}\epsilon^{2}.\\ \end{array}
\]
The first inequality is left as Exercise 16.4.

The second inequality used \(\epsilon \leq 0.1\). Theorem 13.24 (with \(d = 1\), \(m = K\), and \(\beta_{1,t}^2 = \frac{2.1}{K}\epsilon^2\)) implies that at the end of the \(n\)-th iteration, \(\hat{\theta}\) of any learning algorithm satisfies
\[
\begin{array}{l}\frac{1}{K}\sum_{\tau=1}^{K}\mathbb{E}_{q^{\tau}}\mathbb{E}_{\hat{\theta}}Q(\hat{\theta},q^{\tau})\geq 0. 5\epsilon\left(1-\sqrt{2\times 2.1(n/K)\epsilon^{2}}\right)\\ \geq 0. 25\epsilon=0. 25\min\left(0. 1,0. 24\sqrt{K/T}\right).\\ \end{array}
\]
The second inequality used \((n / K)\epsilon^2\leq 0.24^2\).
Since this holds for all steps \(n\leq T\) we obtain the desired bound.

theorems.statement:
Let \(a_* \in \arg \max_a \mu(a)\). Let
\[
\delta_{1}=\Pr\left[\exists t>K:\mu\left(a_{*}\right)>\hat{\mu}_{t-1}\left(a_{*}\right)+\hat{c}_{t-1}\left(a_{*}\right)\right],
\]
\[
\delta_{2}=\Pr\left[\exists t>K,a\in\{1,\dots,K\}\backslash\{a_{*}\}:\mu(a)<\hat{\mu}_{t-1}(a)-\hat{c}_{t-1}^{\prime}(a)\right].
\]
Define \(\Delta(a) = \mu(a_{*}) - \mu(a)\), and
\[
T(a)=\max\left\{m:\Delta(a)\leq\hat{c}_{t-1}(a)+\hat{c}_{t-1}^{\prime}(a),\hat{n}_{t-1}(a)=m,K<t\leq T\right\}\cup\{0\}.
\]
Then for Algorithm 16.1, we have with probability at least \(1 - \delta_{1} - \delta_{2}\):
\[
\operatorname{REG}_{T}\leq\inf_{\Delta_{0}>0}\left[\sum_{a=1}^{K}T(a)\Delta(a)\mathbb{1}(\Delta(a)>\Delta_{0})+(T-K)\Delta_{0}\right]+\sum_{a=1}^{K}\Delta(a).
\]

steps.claim: The proof of Lemma 16.2 shows that with probability at least \(1 - \delta\), for all \(t \geq K + 1\):

\[
\mu(a_{*})\leq\mu(a_{t})+[\hat{c}_{t-1}^{\prime}(a_{t})+\hat{c}_{t-1}(a_{t})]\mathbb{1}(a_{t}\neq a_{*}),
\]
which implies that
\[
\Delta(a_{t})\leq [\hat{c}_{t-1}^{\prime}(a_{t})+\hat{c}_{t-1}(a_{t})]\mathbb{1}(a_{t}\neq a_{*}).
\]
Using the assumption of the lemma, we obtain for all \(a \neq a_*\) and \(1 \leq t \leq T\), \(\hat{n}_{t-1}(a) \mathbb{1}(a_t = a) \leq T(a)\).
It follows that for all \( a \neq a_* \), let \( t \) be the last time such that \( a_t = a \), then \( t \leq T \) and \( \hat{n}_T(a) = \hat{n}_{t-1}(a_t) + 1 \leq T(a) + 1 \).
We thus obtain the following regret bound for any \( \Delta_0 \geq 0 \):

\[
\begin{array}{l}\sum_{t=1}^{T}\left[\mu\left(a_{*}\right)-\mu\left(a_{t}\right)\right]=\sum_{a=1}^{K}\hat{n}_{T}(a)\Delta(a)\\ \leq\sum_{a=1}^{K}\Delta(a)+\sum_{a=1}^{K}(\hat{n}_{T}(a)-1)\Delta_{0}+\sum_{a=1}^{K}(\hat{n}_{T}(a)-1)\Delta(a)\mathbb{1}(\Delta(a)>\Delta_{0})\\ \leq\sum_{a=1}^{K}\Delta(a)+(T-K)\Delta_{0}+\sum_{a=1}^{K}T(a)\Delta(a)\mathbb{1}(\Delta(a)>\Delta_{0}).\\ \end{array}
\]
The second inequality used \(\sum_{a=1}^{K} (\hat{n}_T(a) - 1) = T - K\) and \(\hat{n}_T(a) - 1 \leq T(a)\).
This implies the bound.

steps.claim: Given any integer \( m \geq 1 \) and \( a \in \{1, \ldots, K\} \).
We know that the sequence \( r(a_{t})\mathbb{1}(a_{t} = a) \) satisfies the sub-Gaussian bound in Theorem 13.3 with \( \sigma_{i} = 0.5\mathbb{1}(a_{i} = a) \).
This means that \( \sum_{i=1}^{t}\sigma_{i}^{2} = 0.25\hat{n}_{t}(a) \).
By letting \( \sigma = 0.5\sqrt{m} \) for a constant \( m \), and considering the event \( \hat{n}_{t}(a) = m \), we obtain with probability at most \( 0.5\delta / (m + 1)^{2} \):

\[
\exists t\geq 1:\mu(a)>\hat{\mu}_{t}(a)+\hat{c}_{t}(a)\&\hat{n}_{t}(a)=m.
\]
Similarly, with probability at most \((0.5 / K)\delta /(m + 1)^2\)
\[
\exists t\geq 1:\mu(a)<\hat{\mu}_{t}(a)-\hat{c}_{t}^{\prime}(a)\&\hat{n}_{t}(a)=m,
\]
where the lower confidence interval size is defined as
\[
\hat{c}_{t}^{\prime}(a)=\sqrt{\frac{\ln(2 K(\hat{n}_{t}(a)+1)^{2}/\delta)}{2\hat{n}_{t}(a)}}.
\]
It follows that the failure probability of upper confidence bound is given by
\[
\begin{array}{l}\Pr\left[\exists t>K:\mu\left(a_{*}\right)>\hat{\mu}_{t}\left(a_{*}\right)+\hat{c}_{t}\left(a_{*}\right)\right]\\ \leq\sum_{m=1}^{\infty}\Pr\left[\exists t>K:\hat{n}_{t}\left(a_{*}\right)=m\&\mu\left(a_{*}\right)>\hat{\mu}_{t}\left(a_{*}\right)+\hat{c}_{t}\left(a_{*}\right)\right]\\ \leq\sum_{m=1}^{\infty}0. 5\delta/(m+1)^{2}\leq 0. 5\delta .\\ \end{array}
\]
Moreover, the failure probability of lower confidence bound is given by
\[
\begin{array}{l}\Pr\left[\exists t>K\&a\in\{1,\dots,K\}:\mu(a)<\hat{\mu}_{t}(a)-\hat{c}_{t}^{\prime}(a)\right]\\ \leq\sum_{a=1}^{K}\Pr\left[\exists t>K:\mu(a)<\hat{\mu}_{t}(a)-\hat{c}_{t}^{\prime}(a)\right]\\ \leq\sum_{a=1}^{K}\sum_{m=1}^{\infty}\Pr\left[\exists t>K:\hat{n}_{t}(a)=m\&\mu(a)<\hat{\mu}_{t}(a)-\hat{c}_{t}^{\prime}(a)\right]\\ \leq\sum_{a=1}^{K}\sum_{m=1}^{\infty}\frac{\delta}{2 K(m+1)^{2}}\leq\delta/2.\\ \end{array}
\]
The following bound follows from Lemma 16.2.

With probability at least \(1 - \delta\): \[
\begin{array}{l}\sum_{t=1}^{T}[\mu(a_{*})-\mu(a_{t})]-\sum_{a=1}^{K}[\mu(a_{*})-\mu(a)]\leq\sum_{t=K+1}^{T}[\hat{c}_{t-1}(a_{t})+\hat{c}_{t-1}^{\prime}(a_{t})]\\ \leq 2\sum_{t=K+1}^{T}\sqrt{\frac{\ln(2 K(\hat{n}_{t-1}(a_{t})+1)^{2}/\delta)}{2\hat{n}_{t-1}(a_{t})}}\\ =2\sum_{a=1}^{K}\sum_{t=K+1}^{T}\sqrt{\frac{\ln\left(2 K\left(\hat{n}_{t-1}\left(a_{t}\right)+1\right)^{2}/\delta\right)}{2\hat{n}_{t-1}\left(a_{t}\right)}}\mathbb{1}\left(a_{t}=a\right)\\ \stackrel{(a)}{=}2\sum_{a=1}^{K}\sum_{m=1}^{\hat{n}_{T}(a)-1}\sqrt{\frac{\ln(2 K(m+1)^{2}/\delta)}{2 m}}\\ \leq 2\sum_{a=1}^{K}\int_{0}^{\hat{n}_{T}(a)-1}\sqrt{\frac{\ln\left(2 K\hat{n}_{T}(a)^{2}/\delta\right)}{2 t}}d t\\ =4\sum_{a=1}^{K}\sqrt{\frac{\ln(2 K\hat{n}_{T}(a)^{2}/\delta)(\hat{n}_{T}(a)-1)}{2}}\\ \leq 4\sqrt{\frac{\ln(2 K T^{2}/\delta)(T-K)K}{2}}.\\ \end{array}
\]
Equation (a) used the fact that for each arm \( a \), with \( a_{t} = a \), \( \hat{n}_{t-1}(a_{t}) \) takes values from \( m = 1 \) to \( m = \hat{n}_T(a) - 1 \), once for each value.

In the derivation of the last inequality, we used Jensen's inequality and the concavity of \( \sqrt{z} \), which implies that
\[
\sum_{a=1}^{K}\sqrt{\hat{n}_{T}(a)-1}\leq\sqrt{K\sum_{a=1}^{K}(\hat{n}_{T}(a)-1)}=\sqrt{K(T-K)}.
\]
This implies the desired bound.

theorems.statement:
Assume \(\ell(w, z)\) is \(\alpha\)-strongly convex over the domain \(\Omega\) and \(L\)-Lipschitz. Let \(\hat w_S = \arg \min_{w\in \Omega} \frac{1}{m} \sum_{i=1}^m \ell(w, z_i)\) denote the empirical risk minimizer (ERM). Then, ERM satisfies
\[
\Delta_{\sup} (\text{ERM}) \leqslant \frac{4L^2}{\alpha m}\,.
\]

steps.claim:
Denote by \(\hat w_S\) the empirical risk minimizer on a sample \(S.\) Fix arbitrary samples \(S,S'\) of size \(m\) and an index \(i\in[m].\) We need to show that
\[
|(\ell(\hat w_{S^{(i)}},z_i')-\ell(\hat w_{S},z_i'))|\leqslant\frac{4L^2}{\alpha m}\,.
\]
On one hand, by strong convexity we know that
\[
R_S(\hat w_{S^{(i)}}) - R_S(\hat w_{S}) \geqslant \frac{\alpha}{2} \| \hat w_{S} - \hat w_{S^{(i)}} \|^2 \,.
\]
On the other hand,
\begin{align*}
&R_S(\hat w_{S^{(i)}})-R_S(\hat w_{S})\\
&=\frac{1}{m}(\ell(\hat w_{S^{(i)}},z_i)-\ell(\hat w_{S},z_i))+\frac{1}{m}\sum_{i\neq j}(\ell(\hat w_{S^{(i)}},z_j)-\ell(\hat w_{S},z_j))\\
&=\frac{1}{m}(\ell(\hat w_{S^{(i)}},z_i)-\ell(\hat w_{S},z_i))+\frac{1}{m}(\ell(\hat w_{S},z_i')-\ell(\hat w_{S^{(i)}},z_i'))+\left(R_{S^{(i)}}(\hat w_{S^{(i)}})-R_{S^{(i)}}(\hat w_{S})\right)\\
&\leqslant\frac{1}{m}|\ell(\hat w_{S^{(i)}},z_i)-\ell(\hat w_{S},z_i)| +\frac{1}{m}|(\ell(\hat w_{S},z_i')-\ell(\hat w_{S^{(i)}},z_i'))|\\
&\leqslant\frac{2L}{m}\|\hat w_{S^{(i)}}-\hat w_{S}\|\,.
\end{align*}
Here, we used that
\[
R_{S^{(i)}}(\hat w_{S^{(i)}}) - R_{S^{(i)}}(\hat w_{S})) \leqslant 0
\]
and the fact that \(\ell\) is \(L\)-Lipschitz.

Putting it all together \(\| \hat w_{S^{(i)}} - \hat w_{S} \| \leqslant \frac{4 L}{\alpha m}\). Then by the Lipschitz condition we have that
\[
|(\ell(\hat w_{S^{(i)}},z_i')-\ell(\hat w_{S},z_i'))|\leqslant L\|\hat w_{S^{(i)}}-\hat w_{S}\|\leqslant\frac{4L^2}{\alpha m}\,.
\]
Hence, \(\Delta_{\sup}(\text{ERM}) \leqslant \frac{4 L ^ 2}{\alpha m}\).

If \(f\) is in addition \(\alpha\)-strongly convex w.r.t to \(\|\cdot\|_{[1-\gamma]}\), then we get
\[

steps.claim:
We need the following lemma:

Lemma 12.4. Let \(f\) be an \(\alpha\)-strongly convex function w.r.t. a norm \(\|\cdot\|\). Then, \(f(x) - f(x^{*}) \leqslant \frac{1}{2\alpha}\|\nabla f(x)\|_{*}^{2}\).

Lemma 12.4 shows that
\[
\|\nabla f(x_s)\|^{*2}_{[1-\gamma]} \geqslant 2 \alpha \delta_s \ .
\]
On the other hand, Theorem 12.2 showed that
\[
\delta_{t+1} - \delta_t \leqslant -\frac{\|\nabla f(x_t)\|^{*2}_{[1-\gamma]}}{2\sum_{i=1}^n \beta_i^{\gamma}}
\]
Combining these two, we get
\begin{align*}
\delta_{t+1} - \delta_t &\leqslant -\frac{\alpha \delta_t}{\sum_{i=1}^n \beta_i^{\gamma}} \\
\delta_{t+1} &\leqslant \delta_t \left(1 -\frac{\alpha}{\sum_{i=1}^n \beta_i^{\gamma}} \right)~.
\end{align*}
Applying the above inequality recursively and recalling that \(\delta_t = \mathbb{E}[f(x_t) - f(x^*)]\) gives the result.

definition 8.0. For any sample \(\{x_{1},\ldots,x_{n}\}\), the ways that \({\mathcal{C}}\) intersects with the sample are \[\{C\cap\{x_{1},\ldots,x_{n}\}:C\in{\mathcal{C}}\}.\] Let \[\triangle_{n}(\mathcal{C},x_{1},\ldots,x_{n})=\mathrm{card}~\{C\cap\{x_{1},\ldots,x_{n}\}:C\in\mathcal{C}\},\] the number of different subsets picked out by \(C\in{\mathcal{C}}\). theorems.statement: The number \(\triangle_{n}(\mathcal{C},x_{1},\ldots,x_{n})\) of subsets picked out by C is bounded by the number of subsets shattered by C.

steps.claim:
Without loss of generality, we restrict C to \({\mathcal{C}}: =\{C\cap\{x_{1},\ldots,x_{n}\}:C\in{\mathcal{C}}\}\) , and we have \(\operatorname{card}({\mathcal{C}})=\) \(\Delta_{n}({\mathcal{C}},x_{1},\cdots,x_{n})\)
We will say that C is hereditary if and only if whenever \(B\subseteq C\in{\mathcal{C}},B\in{\mathcal{C}}\) .If C is hereditary, then every \(C\in{\mathcal{C}}\) is shattered by C,and the lemma is obvious.
Otherwise,we will transform \({\mathcal{C}}\to{\mathcal{C}}^{\prime}\) ,hereditary, without changing the cardinality of C and without increasing the number of shattered subsets.

Define the operators \(T_{i}\) for \(i=1,\cdots,n\) as the following,
\[\begin{array}{ r c l }{T_{i}(C)}&{=}&{\left\{\begin{array}{ l l }{C-\{x_{i}\}}&{\mathrm{~i f~}C-\{x_{i}\}\mathrm{~i s~n o t~i n~}\mathcal{C}}\\ {C}&{\mathrm{~o t h e r w i s e}}\end{array}\right.}\\ {T_{i}(\mathcal{C})}&{=}&{\{T_{i}(C):C\in\mathcal{C}\}.}\end{array}\]
It follows that card \(T_{i}({\mathcal{C}})=\operatorname{card}{\mathcal{C}}\) Moreover, every \(A\subseteq\{x_{1},\cdots,x_{n}\}\) that is shattered by \(T_{i}(\mathcal{C})\) is also shattered by \({\mathcal{C}}.{\mathrm{~I f~}}x_{i}\notin A .\) ,then \(\forall C\in\mathcal{C},A\bigcap C=A\bigcap T_{i}(C)\) , thus C and \(T_{i}(\mathcal{C})\) both or neither shatter A.

On the other hand, if \(x_{i}\in A\) and A is shattered by \(T_{i}(\mathcal{C})\) , then \(\forall B\subseteq A,\exists C\in{\mathcal{C}}\) ,such that \(B\bigcup\{x_{i}\}=A\bigcap T_{i}(C)\) This means that \(x_{i}\in T_{i}(C)\) ，and that \(C\backslash\{x_{i}\}\in\mathcal{C}\) Thus both \(B\bigcup\{x_{i}\}\) and \(B\backslash\{x_{i}\}\) are picked out by C.
Since either \(B=B\cup\{x_{i}\}\) or \(B=B\backslash\{x_{i}\}\) , B is picked out by C.
Thus A is shattered by C. Apply the operator \(T=T_{1}\circ\dots\circ T_{n}\) until \(T^{k+1}({\mathcal{C}})=T^{k}({\mathcal{C}})\) .

This will happen for at most \(\scriptstyle\sum_{C\in{\mathcal{C}}}\operatorname{card}(C)\) times,since \(\begin{array}{ r }{\sum_{C\in\mathcal{C}}\operatorname{card}(T_{i}(C))<\sum_{C\in\mathcal{C}}\operatorname{card}(C)\mathrm{~i f~}T_{i}(\mathcal{C})\neq\mathcal{C}}\end{array}\) ，The resulting collection \(\scriptstyle{\mathcal{C}}^{\prime}\) is hereditary.
This proves the lemma.
