In this section, we introduce our notation, data generation process, neural network architecture and the optimization algorithm.

Notations. We use lower case letters to denote scalars and boldface letters and symbols (e.g. x) to denote vectors and matrices. We use $\odot$ to denote element-wise product. For an integer n, we use [n] to denote the set of integers $\{1,2,\ldots,n\}$ . We use $x=O(y),x=$ $\Omega(y),x=\Theta(y)$ to denote that there exists a constant C such that $x\leq Cy,\ x\geq Cy,x=Cy$ respectively. We use $\widetilde{O},\widetilde{\Omega}$ and Θe to hide polylogarithmic factor in these notations. Finally, we use $x=\mathrm{poly}(y)$ if $x=O(y^{C})$ for some positive constant $C_{i}$ , and $x={\mathrm{poly}}\log y$ if $x=\operatorname{poly}(\log y)$

Definition 1 (Data distribution of K classes) Consider we are given the set of signal vectors $\{\mu\mathbf{e}_{i}\}_{i=1}^{K}$ , where $\mu > 0$ denotes the strength of the signal, and $\mathbf{e}_{i}\in\mathbb{R}^{d}$ (with $d>K)$ denotes the $_{i-t h}$ standard basis vector with its i-th entry being 1 and all other coordinates being 0. Each data point $\left(\mathbf{x},y\right)$ with $\mathbf{x}=[\mathbf{x}_{1}^{\top},\mathbf{x}_{2}^{\top}]^{\top}\in\mathbb{R}^{2\bar{d}}$ and $y \in [ K ]$ is generated from the following distribution $\mathcal{D}.$ :

1. The label y is generated from a uniform distribution over $[ K ]$  
2. A noise vector $\boldsymbol{\xi}$ is generated from the Gaussian distribution ${\mathcal{N}}(\mathbf{0},\sigma_{n}^{2}\mathbf{I})$  
3. With probability $1/2_{;}$ , assign $\mathbf{x}_{1}=\pmb{\mu}_{y},\ \mathbf{x}_{2}=\pmb{\xi}$ ; with probability $1/2_{;}$ , assign ${\bf x}_{2}=$ $\mu_{y},~\mathbf{x}_{1}=\pmb{\xi}$ where $\mu_{y}=\mu\mathbf{e}_{y}$

Network architecture and random pruning. We consider a two-layer convolutional neural network model with polynomial ReLU activation $\sigma(z)=(\operatorname*{max}\{0,z\})^{q}$ , where we focus on the case when $q=3\AA^{1}$ The network is pruned at the initialization by mask M where each entry in the mask M is generated i.i.d. from Bernoulli(p). Given the data $\left(\mathbf{x},y\right)$ , the output of the neural network can be written as $F(\mathbf{W}\odot\mathbf{M},\mathbf{x})=(F_{1}(\mathbf{W}_{1}\odot\mathbf{M}_{1},\mathbf{x}),F_{2}(\mathbf{W}_{2}\odot$ $\mathbf{M}_{2},\mathbf{x}),\ldots,F_{K}(\mathbf{W}_{K}\odot\mathbf{M}_{K},\mathbf{x}))$ where the j-th output is given by

$$
\begin{array}{l}F_{j}(\mathbf{W}_{j}\odot\mathbf{M}_{j},\mathbf{x})=\sum_{r=1}^{m}[\sigma(\langle\mathbf{w}_{j,r}\odot\mathbf{m}_{j,r},\mathbf{x}_{1}\rangle)+\sigma(\langle\mathbf{w}_{j,r}\odot\mathbf{m}_{j,r},\mathbf{x}_{2}\rangle)]\\ =\sum_{r=1}^{m}[\sigma(\langle\mathbf{w}_{j,r}\odot\mathbf{m}_{j,r},\boldsymbol{\mu}_{y}\rangle)+\sigma(\langle\mathbf{w}_{j,r}\odot\mathbf{m}_{j,r},\boldsymbol{\xi}\rangle)],\\ \end{array}
$$

where $\mathbf{m}_{j,r}$ denotes the r-th row of $\mathbf{M}_{j}$ . The mask M is only sampled once at the initialization and remains fixed through the entire training process. From now on, we use tilde over a symbol to denote its masked version, e.g., $\widetilde{\mathbf{W}}=\mathbf{W}\odot\mathbf{M}$ and $\widetilde{\mathbf{w}}_{j,r}=\mathbf{w}_{j,r}\odot\mathbf{m}_{j,r}$

Since we have $\pmb{\mu}_{j}\odot\mathbf{m}_{j,r}=\mathbf{0}$ , with probability $1-p,$ some neurons will not receive the corresponding signal at all and will only learn noise. Therefore, for each class $j \in [ K ]$ , we split the neurons into two sets based on whether it receives its corresponding signal or not:

$$
\mathcal{S}_{\text{signal}}^{j}=\{r\in [m]:\boldsymbol{\mu}_{j}\odot\mathbf{m}_{j,r}\neq\mathbf{0}\},
$$

$$
\mathcal{S}_{\mathrm{noise}}^{j}=\{r\in [m]:\boldsymbol{\mu}_{j}\odot\mathbf{m}_{j,r}=\mathbf{0}\}.
$$

Gradient descent algorithm. We consider the network is trained by cross-entropy loss with softmax. We denote by $\begin{array}{ r }{\mathrm{logit}_{i}(F,\mathbf{x}): =\frac{e^{F_{i}(\mathbf{x})}}{\sum_{j\in [K]}e^{F_{j}(\mathbf{x})}}}\end{array}$ and the cross-entropy loss can be written as $\ell(F(\mathbf{x},y))= -\log\log\mathrm{i}\mathbf{\xi}_{y}(F,\mathbf{x})$ . The convolutional neural network is trained by minimizing the empirical cross-entropy loss given by

$$
L_{S}(\mathbf{W})=\underset{S}{\mathbb{E}}\ell [F(\mathbf{W}\odot\mathbf{M};\mathbf{x}_{i},y_{i})]=\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\ell [F(\mathbf{W}\odot\mathbf{M};\mathbf{x}_{i},y_{i})],
$$

where $S=\{(\mathbf{x}_{i},y_{i})\}_{i=1}^{n}$ is the training data set. Similarly, we define the generalization loss as

$$
L_{\mathcal{D}}:=\underset{(\mathbf{x},y)}{\mathbb{E}}[\ell(F(\mathbf{W}\odot\mathbf{M};\mathbf{x},y))].
$$

The model weights are initialized from a i.i.d. Gaussian $\mathcal{N}(0,\sigma_{0}^{2})$ . The gradient of the cross-entropy loss is given by $\ell_{j,i}^{\prime}: =\ell_{j}^{\prime}(\mathbf{x}_{i},y_{i})=\mathrm{logit}_{j}(F,\mathbf{x}_{i})-\mathbb{I}(j=y_{i})$

Since

$$
\begin{array}{l}\nabla_{\mathbf{w}_{j,r}}L_{S}(\mathbf{W}\odot\mathbf{M})=\nabla_{\mathbf{w}_{j,r}\odot\mathbf{m}_{j,r}}L_{S}(\mathbf{W}\odot\mathbf{M})\odot\mathbf{m}_{j,r}\\ =\nabla_{\widetilde{\mathbf{w}}_{j,r}}L_{S}(\widetilde{\mathbf{W}})\odot\mathbf{m}_{j,r},\\ \end{array}
$$

we can write the full-batch gradient descent update of the weights as

$$
\begin{array}{l}\widetilde{\mathbf{w}}_{j,r}^{(t+1)}=\widetilde{\mathbf{w}}_{j,r}^{(t)}-\eta\nabla_{\widetilde{\mathbf{w}}_{j,r}}L_{S}(\widetilde{\mathbf{W}})\odot\mathbf{m}_{j,r}\\ =\widetilde{\mathbf{w}}_{j,r}^{(t)}-\frac{\eta}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\ell_{j,i}^{\prime(t)}\cdot\sigma^{\prime}\left(\left\langle\widetilde{\mathbf{w}}_{j,r}^{(t)},\boldsymbol{\xi}_{i}\right\rangle\right)\cdot\widetilde{\boldsymbol{\xi}}_{j,r,i}\\ -\frac{\eta}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\ell_{j,i}^{\prime(t)}\sigma^{\prime}\left(\left\langle\widetilde{\mathbf{w}}_{j,r}^{(t)},\boldsymbol{\mu}_{y_{i}}\right\rangle\right)\boldsymbol{\mu}_{y_{i}}\odot\mathbf{m}_{j,r},\\ \end{array}
$$

for $j \in [ K ]$ and $r \in [ m ]$ , where $\widetilde{\pmb{\xi}}_{j,r,i}=\pmb{\xi}_{i}\odot\mathbf{m}_{j,r}$

Condition 2 We consider the parameter regime described as follows: (1) Number of classes $K=O(\log d).\quad(2)$ Total number of training samples n = poly log d. (3) Dimension $d\geq C_{d}$ for some suficiently large constant $\it C_{d}.\it(4)$ Relationship between signal strength and noise strength: $\mu=\Theta(\sigma_{n}\sqrt{d}\log d)=\Theta(1)$ . (5) The number of neurons in the network $m=\Omega({\mathrm{poly}}\log d).\ (6)$ Initialization variance: $\begin{array}{ r }{\sigma_{0}=\widetilde{\Theta}(m^{-4}n^{-1}\mu^{-1})}\end{array}$ . (7) Learning rate: $\Omega(1/\operatorname{poly}(d))\leq\eta\leq\widetilde{O}(1/\mu^{2})$ . (8) Target training loss: $\epsilon=\Theta(1/\operatorname{poly}(d))$ ).

Conditions (1) ensures that there are not too many classes which is a mild assumption and can be satisfied by real world dataset like MNIST. Condition (2) ensure that there are enough samples in each class with high probability and at the same time not too many samples such that the noise will interfere with the neural network learning the signals. Condition (3) ensures that our setting is in high-dimensional regime. Condition (4) ensures that the full model can be trained to exhibit good generalization. Condition (5), (6) and (7) ensures that the neural network is suficiently overparameterized and can be optimized eficiently by gradient descent. Condition (7) and (8) further ensures that training time is polynomial in d. We further discuss the practical consideration of η and ε to justify their condition in Theorem 23.

Our second result shows that there exists a relatively large pruning fraction (i.e., small p) such that the learned model yields poor generalization, although gradient descent is still able to drive the training error toward zero. The full proof is defered to Appendix D.

Theorem 9 (Main theorem for over pruning, informal version of Theorem 41 ) Under Condition 2 if $\begin{array}{ r }{p\ =\ \Theta(\frac{1}{K m\log d})}\end{array}$ , then with probability at least $1 - 1 /$ poly log d over the randomness in the data, network initialization and pruning, there exists $T =$ $O(\eta^{-1}n\sigma_{0}^{q-2}\sigma_{n}^{-q}(p d)^{-q/2}+\eta^{-1}\epsilon^{-1}m^{4}n\sigma_{n}^{-2}(p d)^{-1})$ such that

1. The training loss is below $\epsilon\colon L_{S}(\widetilde{\mathbf{W}}^{(T)})\le\epsilon$  
2. The generalization loss is large: $L_{\mathcal{D}}(\widetilde{\mathbf{W}}^{(T)})\ge\Omega(\log K)$

In this section, we introduce the following signal-noise decomposition of each neuron weight from Cao et al. (2022), and some useful properties for the terms in such a decomposition, which are useful in our analysis.

Definition 14 (signal-noise decomposition) For each neuron weight $j\in [K],\ r\in [m]$ • there exist coeficients $\gamma_{j,r,k}^{(t)},\zeta_{j,r,i}^{(t)},\omega_{j,r,i}^{(t)}$ such that

$$
\begin{array}{l}\widetilde{\mathbf{w}}_{j,r}^{(t)}\\ =\widetilde{\mathbf{w}}_{j,r}^{(0)}+\sum_{k=1}^{K}\gamma_{j,r,k}^{(t)}\cdot\|\boldsymbol{\mu}_{k}\|_{2}^{-2}\cdot\boldsymbol{\mu}_{k}\odot\mathbf{m}_{j,r}+\sum_{i=1}^{n}\zeta_{j,r,i}^{(t)}\cdot\left\|\widetilde{\boldsymbol{\xi}}_{j,r,i}\right\|_{2}^{-2}\cdot\widetilde{\boldsymbol{\xi}}_{j,r,i}+\sum_{i=1}^{n}\omega_{j,r,i}^{(t)}\left\|\widetilde{\boldsymbol{\xi}}_{j,r,i}\right\|_{2}^{-2}\cdot\widetilde{\boldsymbol{\xi}}_{j,r,i},\\ \end{array}
$$

where $\gamma_{j,r,j}^{(t)}\geq 0,\gamma_{j,r,k}^{(t)}\leq 0,\zeta_{j,r,i}^{(t)}\geq 0,\omega_{j,r,i}^{(t)}\leq 0 .$

It is straightforward to see the following:

$$
\begin{array}{l}\gamma_{j,r,k}^{(0)},\zeta_{j,r,i}^{(0)},\omega_{j,r,i}^{(0)}=0,\\ \gamma_{j,r,j}^{(t+1)}=\gamma_{j,r,j}^{(t)}-\mathbb{I}(r\in\mathcal{S}_{\mathrm{signal}}^{j})\frac{\eta}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\ell_{j,i}^{\prime(t)}\cdot\sigma^{\prime}\left(\left\langle\widetilde{\mathbf{w}}_{j,r}^{(t)},\boldsymbol{\mu}_{y_{i}}\right\rangle\right)\|\boldsymbol{\mu}_{y_{i}}\|_{2}^{2}\mathbb{I}(y_{i}=j),\\ \gamma_{j,r,k}^{(t+1)}=\gamma_{j,r,k}^{(t)}-\mathbb{I}((\mathbf{m}_{j,r})_{k}=1)\frac{\eta}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\ell_{j,i}^{\prime(t)}\cdot\sigma^{\prime}\left(\left\langle\widetilde{\mathbf{w}}_{j,r}^{(t)},\boldsymbol{\mu}_{y_{i}}\right\rangle\right)\left\|\boldsymbol{\mu}_{y_{i}}\right\|_{2}^{2}\mathbb{I}(y_{i}=k),\forall j\neq k,\\ \end{array}
$$

$$
\zeta_{j,r,i}^{(t+1)}=\zeta_{j,r,i}^{(t)}-\frac{\eta}{n}\cdot\ell_{j,i}^{\prime(t)}\cdot\sigma^{\prime}\left(\left\langle\widetilde{\mathbf{w}}_{j,r}^{(t)},\boldsymbol{\xi}_{i}\right\rangle\right)\left\|\widetilde{\boldsymbol{\xi}}_{j,r,i}\right\|_{2}^{2}\mathbb{I}(j=y_{i}),
$$

$$
\omega_{j,r,i}^{(t+1)}=\omega_{j,r,i}^{(t)}-\frac{\eta}{n}\cdot\ell_{j,i}^{\prime(t)}\cdot\sigma^{\prime}\left(\left\langle\widetilde{\mathbf{w}}_{j,r}^{(t)},\boldsymbol{\xi}_{i}\right\rangle\right)\left\|\widetilde{\boldsymbol{\xi}}_{j,r,i}\right\|_{2}^{2}\mathbb{I}(j\neq y_{i}),

We begin by introducing some fundamental notations that will frequently appear. Suppose that the data $D_{n}: =\{X_{1},\ldots,X_{n}\}$ are independent and identically distributed (i.i.d.) and drawn from an unknown distribution P that is absolutely continuous with respect to the Lebesgue measure $\mu$ and admits a unique density function $f .$ . In this paper, we assume that $f$ is supported on $[0,1]^{d}$ , which we denote as X . Recall that for $1 \leq p < \infty$ and a vector $x\in\mathbb{R}^{d}$ , the $\ell_{p}{\mathrm{-norm}}$ is defined as $\|x\|_{p}: =(x_{1}^{p}+\cdot\cdot\cdot+x_{d}^{p})^{1/p}$ , and the $\ell_{\infty}{\mathrm{-norm}}$ is defined as $\|x\|_{\infty}: =\operatorname*{max}_{i=1,\ldots,d}|x_{i}|$ . For a measurable function $g:\mathcal{X}\mathbb{R}$ , we define the $L_{p}{\mathrm{-norm}}$ as $\begin{array}{ r }{\|g\|_{p}: =\big(\int_{\mathcal X}|g(x)|^{p}dx\big)^{1/p}}\end{array}$ . Let $B(x,r): =\{x^{\prime}\in\mathbb{R}^{d}:\|x^{\prime}-x\|_{2}\leq r\}$ denote a ball in Euclidean space $\mathbb{R}^{d}$ centered at $x\in\mathbb{R}^{d}$ with radius $r\in(0,+\infty)$ . We use $V_{d}$ to denote the volume of the d-dimensional closed unit ball. In addition, for $n\in\mathbb{N}_{+}$ , we write $[n]: =\{1,\dots,n\}$ as the set containing integers from 1 to n and $\mathcal{W}_{n}: =\{(w_{1},\ldots,w_{n})\in\mathbb{R}^{n}$ $\begin{array}{ r }{\sum_{i=1}^{n}w_{i}=1,~w_{i}\ge 0,~i\in [n]\}}\end{array}$ . For any $x\in\mathbb{R}$ , let bxc be the largest integer less than or equal to x and dxe be the smallest ingeter larger than or equal to x. Throughout this paper, we use $a\vee b=\operatorname*{max}\{a,b\}$ and $a\wedge b=\operatorname*{min}\{a,b\}$ . Moreover, we use the following notations to compare the magnitudes of quantities: $a_{n}\lesssim b_{n}$ or $a_{n}={\mathcal{O}}(b_{n})$ indicates that there exists a positive constant $c > 0$ that is independent of n such that $a_{n}\leq cb_{n};a_{n}\gtrsim b_{n}$ implies that there exists a positive constant $c > 0$ such that $a_{n}\geq cb_{n};$ and $a_{n}\asymp b_{n}$ means that $a_{n}\lesssim b_{n}$ and $b_{n}\lesssim a_{n}$ hold simultaneously. In this paper, we focus on the case of a fixed dimension, allowing the constant c to depend on the dimension $d .$ Finally, we use $C,C^{\prime},c,$ and $c^{\prime}$ to represent positive constants. Assumption 1 The data $D_{n}$ consists ofi.i.d. samples drawn from a distribution P satisfying the contamination model: $$ \mathrm{P}=(1-\Pi)\cdot\mathrm{P}_{0}+\Pi\cdot\mathrm{P}_{1},\tag{1} $$ where $\mathrm{P_{0}}$ and $\mathrm{P_{1}}$ denote the distributions of normal and anomalies, respectively, and $\Pi \in$ (0, 1) is the contamination proportion. Additionally, we assume that $\mathrm{P_{0}}$ has a probability density function $f_{0}$ , while $\mathrm{P_{1}}$ is uniformly distributed over $[0,1]^{d}$ with density function $f_{1}$ Building on this framework, we explore the distance-based method for unsupervised anomaly detection, motivated by the connection between distance functions and k-nearest neighbor (kNN) density estimations highlighted by Biau et al. (2011). This method leverages the distances between data points and their nearest neighbors to assess anomalies. For any $\boldsymbol{x}\in\mathbb{R}^{d}$ and a dataset $D_{n}.$ , we denote $X_{(k)}(x;D_{n})$ as the k-th nearest neighbor of x in $D_{n}$ We then define $R_{n,(k)}(x): =\left\|x-X_{(k)}(x;D_{n})\right\|_{2}$ as the distance between x and $X_{(k)}(x;D_{n})$ referred to as the k-nearest neighbor distance, or k-distance of x in $D_{n}$ Distance-based methods are important and efective for anomaly detection. However, when handling large datasets, the number of nearest neighbors that need to be searched grows substantially, leading to significant computational overhead. To mitigate this issue, we incorporate the bagging technique by averaging the weighted k-distances computed on multiple disjoint sub-datasets randomly drawn from the original dataset $D_{n}$ without replacement. Let B be the number of bagging rounds pre-specified by the user, and $\{D_{s}^{b}\}_{b=1}^{B}$ be B disjoint subsets of $D_{n}$ , each of size s. Since the sub-samples are disjoint and the data $D_{n}$ is supposed i.i.d., this procedure is mathematically equivalent to taking the first s samples for bag 1, the following s samples for bag 2, etc. In each subset $D_{s}^{b},\ b\in [B]$ ， let $R_{s,(k)}^{b}(x): =\left. x-X_{(k)}(x;D_{s}^{b})\right._{2}$ be the k-distance of x in $D_{s}^{b}$ for any integer $k\leq s,$ , and let the weighted k-distance be defined as $\begin{array}{ r }{R_{s}^{w,b}(x): =\sum_{i=1}^{s}w_{i}^{b}R_{s,(i)}^{b}(x)}\end{array}$ , with $w^{b}\in\mathcal{W}_{s}$ . The bagged weighted k-distances are obtained by averaging these weighted k-distances across the B sub-datasets: $$ R_{n}^{B}(x):=\frac{1}{B}\sum_{b=1}^{B}R_{s}^{w,b}(x). $$ Then, we introduce the bagged weighted k-distances for density estimation (BWDDE) as $$ f_{n}^{B}(x):=\frac{1}{V_{d}R_{n}^{B}(x)^{d}}\left(\frac{1}{B}\sum_{b=1}^{B}\sum_{i=1}^{s}w_{i}^{b}\gamma_{s,i}\right)^{d},\tag{2} $$ where $V_{d}={\pi}^{d/2}/\Gamma(d/2+1)$ is the volume of the unit ball and $$ \gamma_{s,i}:=\frac{\Gamma(i+1/d)\Gamma(s+1)}{\Gamma(i)\Gamma(s+1+1/d)}.\tag{3} $$ Since the underlying density function f in (4) is unknown, standard optimization techniques for parameter selection cannot be directly applied to weight selection in density estimation. To address this, we seek a surrogate for the empirical risk in (4) and minimize it to determine the nearest neighbor weights. To proceed, we introduce the following regularity assumptions on the underlying probability distribution P. Assumption 2 Assume that P has a Lebesgue density f with support $\mathcal{X}=[0,1]^{d}$ (i) [Lipschitz Continuity] The density f is Lipschitz continuous on $[0,1]^{d}$ , i.e., for all x, $,y\in [0,1]^{d}$ , there exists a constant $c_{L}>0$ such that $|f(x)-f(y)|\leq c_{L}\|x-y\|_{2}$ (ii) [Boundness] There exist constants $\overline{{c}}\geq\underline{{c}}>0$ such that $\underline{{c}}\le f(x)\le\overline{{c}}$ for all $x\in\mathcal{X}$ Under these assumptions, along with additional conditions on the weights, the next proposition presents a surrogate for the empirical risk (4). Proposition 1 (Surrogate Risk) Let Assumption 2 hold, and let L denote the absolute value loss. Let $\{D_{s}^{\bar{b}}\}_{b=1}^{B}$ be B disjoint subsets randomly drawn from $D_{n},$ with $D_{s}^{b}= $ $\{X_{1}^{b},\ldots,X_{s}^{b}\}$ , and define $\begin{array}{ r }{\overline{{R}}_{s,(i)}^{b}: =\sum_{j=1}^{s}R_{s,(i)}^{b}(X_{j}^{b})/s}\end{array}$ as the average i-distances for any integer $i \leq s$ on the subset $D_{s}^{b}$ . Furthermore, let f be the true density function and $f_{n}^{B}$ be the BWDDE as in (2). Moreover, let $k^{b}: =k(w^{b}): =\operatorname*{sup}\{i\in [s]:w_{i}^{b}\neq 0\},\ :\underline{{k}}: =\operatorname*{min}_{b\in [B]}k^{b}$ and $\overline{{k}}: =\operatorname*{max}_{b\in [B]}k^{b}$ . Finally, suppose that the following four conditions hold: (i) There exists a sequence $c_{n}\asymp$ log n such that $\sum_{i=1}^{cn}w_{i}^{b}\lesssim(\log n)/k^{b}$ for all $b \in \left[ B \right]$ (ii) $\begin{array}{ r }{\underline{{k}}\gtrsim(\log n)^{2},\underline{{k}}\asymp\overline{{k}},B\geq 2(d^{2}+4)(\log n)/3,B\lesssim(\overline{{k}}/(\log n))^{1+2/d}}\end{array}$ , log $s \asymp \log n$ , and $s\geq\operatorname*{max}\{c_{1}^{\prime},2\overline{{k}}\}$ , where $c_{1}^{\prime}$ is a constant defined in Lemma ${\mathit{12}};$ (iii) $\|w^b\|_2 \gtrsim (k^b)^{-1/2}$ and $\sum_{i=1}^s i^{1/d} w_i^b \asymp (k^b)^{1/d}$ for $b \in [B]$; (iv) There exist constants $C_{n,i}$ such that $\max_{b\in[B]} w_i^b \lesssim C_{n,i}$ for $i\in[s]$ and $\sum_{i=1}^s i^{1/d-1/2} C_{n,i} \lesssim \overline{k}^{1/d-1/2}$. Then, there exists $N_{1}^{*}\in\mathbb{N}$ , specified in the proof, such that for all $n\geq N_{1}^{*}$ and $X_{i}^{b}$ satisfying $B(X_{i}^{b},R_{s,(k^{b^{\prime}})}^{b^{\prime}}(X_{i}^{b}))\stackrel{^{\prime}}{\subset}[0,1]^{d}$ for all $b^{\prime}\in [B]$ , there holds $$ L(X_{i}^{b},f_{n}^{B})\lesssim\sqrt{(\log s)/B}\cdot\|w^{b}\|_{2}+R_{s}^{w,b}(X_{i}^{b}),\qquad i\in [s],b\in [B],\tag{5} $$ with probability $\mathrm{P}^{Bs}$ at least $1-4/n^{2}$ . Furthermore, we have $$ \begin{array}{l}\mathcal{R}_{L,D_{s}^{B}}(f_{n}^{B})\lesssim\mathcal{R}_{L,D_{s}^{B}}^{\text{sur}}(f_{n}^{B}):=\frac{1}{B}\sum_{b=1}^{B}\left(\sqrt{(\log s)/B}\cdot\|w^{b}\|_{2}+\frac{1}{s}\sum_{i=1}^{s}R_{s}^{w,b}(X_{i}^{b})\right)\\ =\frac{1}{B}\sum_{b=1}^{B}\left(\sqrt{(\log s)/B}\cdot\|w^{b}\|_{2}+\sum_{i=1}^{s}w_{i}^{b}\overline{{R}}_{s,(i)}^{b}\right).\tag{6}\\ \end{array} $$ Surrogate risk minimization (SRM). From the expression of the surrogate risk in (6), minimizing the surrogate risk is equivalent to solving the following optimization problems: $$ w^{b,*}:=\underset{w^{b}\in\mathcal{W}_{s}}{\arg\min}\sqrt{(\log s)/B}\cdot\|w^{b}\|_{2}+\sum_{i=1}^{s}w_{i}^{b}\overline{{R}}_{s,(i)}^{b},\quad b\in [B].\tag{7} $$ Density estimation. The discussions above indicate that the minimization problem (7) provides a practical method for determining the weights of nearest neighbors in density estimation. However, these weights depend on the data, introducing statistical dependence between the weights $w_{i}^{b,*}$ and the i-distance $R_{s,(i)}^{b}(x)$ for $i \in [ s ]$ in each bag $b \in [ B ]$ . Such dependence complicates the theoretical analysis of weighted k-distances and density estimation within the framework of statistical learning theory. To address this issue, we employ distinct subsets of the data for computing the kdistances, ensuring their independence from the optimized weights. For simplicity, we assume that $n = 2 B s$ , which facilitates a more straightforward theoretical derivation without loss of generality. This assumption ensures that each subset is of equal size; if n is not exactly divisible by 2B, minor modifications to the partitioning scheme can be applied without afecting the theoretical conclusions. We randomly partition $D_{n}$ into B disjoint pairs of subsets $\{(D_{s}^{b},\widetilde{D}_{s}^{b})\}_{b=1}^{B}$ , where each subset has size s and $D_{s}^{b}\cap\widetilde{D}_{s}^{b}=\varnothing$ for each b. Let $w^{b,*}$ represent the weights obtained by solving the optimization problem (7) using $\{D_{s}^{b}\}_{b=1}^{B},$ and let $\widetilde{R}_{s,(i)}^{b}(x)$ denote the i-distance of x computed using $\{\widetilde{D}_{s}^{b}\}_{b=1}^{B}$ for $i \in [ s ]$ . Then, we define the regularized k-distances as follows: $$ R_{s}^{b,*}(x):=R_{s}^{w^{b,*},b}(x)=\sum_{i=1}^{s}w_{i}^{b,*}\widetilde{R}_{s,(i)}^{b}(x).\tag{9} $$ We refer to the weighted average of these k-distances as the bagged regularized k-distance $$ R_{n}^{B,*}(x):=\frac{1}{B}\sum_{b=1}^{B}R_{s}^{b,*}(x).\tag{10} $$ By incorporating the $w^{b,*}$ and $R_{n}^{B,*}(x)$ into the BWDDE formula (2), we are able to obtain a new nearest-neighbor-based density estimator called bagged regularized k-distances for density estimation (BRDDE), expressed as $$ f_{n}^{B,*}(x):=\frac{1}{V_{d}R_{n}^{B,*}(x)^{d}}\left(\frac{1}{B}\sum_{b=1}^{B}\sum_{i=1}^{s}w_{i}^{b,*}\gamma_{s,i}\right)^{d}.\tag{11} $$
Algorithm 2: Bagged Regularized $k$-Distances for Anomaly Detection (BRDAD) Input: Data $D = \{X_1, \cdots, X_n\}$; Number of anomalies $m$; Bagging rounds $B$; Subsampling size $s$. Randomly partition $D_n$ into $B$ disjoint pairs of subsets, denoted as $\{(D_s^b, \widetilde{D}_s^b)\}_{b=1}^B$, such that $D_s^b \cap \widetilde{D}_s^b = \emptyset$ for each $b$. for $b \in [B]$ do Compute weights $w^{b,*}$ using $D_s^b$ by (7); Compute the regularized $k$-distances $R_s^{b,*}(X_i)$ for $1 \leq i \leq n$ using (9), based on $w^{b,*}$ and $\widetilde{D}_s^b$. end Compute the bagged regularized $k$-distances $R_n^{B,*}(X_i)$ by (10) for $1 \leq i \leq n$. Sort the data $D_n = \{X_1, \ldots, X_n\}$ as $\{X_1', \ldots, X_n'\}$ in descending order according to their bagged regularized $k$-distances, i.e., $R_n^{B,*}(X_1') \geq \cdots \geq R_n^{B,*}(X_n')$. Output: Anomalies $\{X_i'\}_{i=1}^m$.
Anomaly Detection. By applying BRDDE to all samples, anomalies can be identified as instances with lower BRDDE values. However, explicit density estimation is not necessary for anomaly detection. Since density estimates serve as anomaly scores, any monotone transformation preserves their ranking (possibly in reverse) and maintains the same family of level sets, leading to identical AUC values. Thus, bagged regularized k-distances provide a suficient and practical alternative for anomaly detection. They can be accurately computed in high-dimensional spaces, and their associated weights can be eficiently optimized from (7), making them an efective approach for density-based anomaly detection. We now introduce our anomaly detection algorithm, bagged regularized k-distances for anomaly detection (BRDAD). The dataset $D_{n}$ is sorted into the sequence $\{X_{1}^{\prime},\ldots,X_{n}^{\prime}\}$ based on their bagged regularized k-distances in descending order, i.e. $R_{n}^{B,*}(X_{1}^{\prime})\geq\cdots\geq$ $R_{n}^{B,*}(X_{n}^{\prime})$ . Given the pre-specified number of anomalies $m,$ the first m instances $\{X_{i}^{\prime}\}_{i=1}^{m},$ are considered as the m anomalies. The complete procedure of our BRDAD algorithm is presented in Algorithm 2. As illustrated above, SRM mitigates the challenge of hyperparameter selection in density estimation. Consequently, BRDAD retains the advantages of BRDDE by using the same weights to address the sensitivity of hyperparameter selection in nearest-neighbor-based methods for unsupervised anomaly detection. In this section, we present theoretical results related to our BRDAD algorithm. We first investigate the Huber contamination model in Section 3.1, in which we can analyze the performance of the bagged regularized k-distances from a learning theory perspective. Then, we present the convergence rates of BRDDE and BRDAD in Section 3.2 and 3.3, respectively. Finally, we provide comments and discussions on our algorithms and theoretical results in Section 3.4. We also compare our theoretical findings on the convergences of both BRDDE and BRDAD with other nearest-neighbor-based methods in this section. In the Huber contamination model (HCM) in Assumption 1, for every instance X from $\mathrm{P}{\mathrm{,}}$ we can use a latent variable $Y\in\{0,1\}$ that indicates which distribution it is from. More specifically, $Y = 0$ and $Y = 1$ indicate that the instance is from the normal and the anomalous distribution, respectively. As a result, the anomaly detection problem can be converted into a bipartite ranking problem where instances are labeled positive or negative implicitly according to whether it is normal or not. Let $\widetilde{\mathrm{P}}$ represent the joint probability distribution of $\mathcal{X}\times\mathcal{Y}$ In this case, our learning goal is to learn a score function that minimizes the probability of mis-ranking a pair of normal and anomalous instances, i.e. that maximizes the area under the ROC curve (AUC). Therefore, we can study regret bounds for the AUC of the bagged regularized k-distances to evaluate its performance from the learning theory perspective. Let $r:\mathcal{X}\mathbb{R}$ be a score function, then the AUC of r can be written as $$ \mathrm{AUC}(r)=\mathbb{E}\big [\mathbf{1}\{(Y-Y^{\prime})(r(X)-r(X^{\prime})>0)\}+\mathbf{1}\{r(X)=r(X^{\prime})\}/2|Y\neq Y^{\prime}\big], $$ where $(X,Y),(X^{\prime},Y^{\prime})$ are assumed to be drawn i.i.d. from $\widetilde{\mathrm{P}}$ . In other words, the AUC of $r$ is the probability that a randomly drawn anomaly is ranked higher than a randomly drawn normal instance by the score function $r .$ . Given the HCM in (1) and the assumption that $\mathrm{P_{1}}$ is uniformly distributed over $[0,1]^{d}$ in Assumption 1, the posterior probability function with respect to $\widetilde{\mathrm{P}}$ is given by $$ \eta(x):=\widetilde{\mathrm{P}}(Y=1|X=x)=\frac{\Pi f_{1}(x)}{(1-\Pi)f_{0}(x)+\Pi f_{1}(x)}=\Pi f(x)^{-1}.\tag{12} $$ Then, the optimal AUC is defined as $$ \mathrm{AUC}^{*}:=\sup_{r:\mathcal{X}\to\mathbb{R}}\mathrm{AUC}(r)=1-\frac{1}{2\Pi(1-\Pi)}\mathbb{E}_{X,X^{\prime}}\big [\min\big(\eta(X)(1-\eta(X^{\prime})),\eta(X^{\prime})(1-\eta(X))\big)\big]. $$ Finally, the AUC regret of a score function r is defined as $$ \mathrm{Reg}^{\mathrm{AUC}}(r):=\mathrm{AUC}^{*}-\mathrm{AUC}(r). $$ As discussed in Section 2.2, BRDAD is a density-based anomaly detection method. To establish its convergence rates under the Huber contamination model, we first derive the theoretical convergence rates of BRDDE in (11), which are presented in the next subsection. In this section, we first provide the error decomposition for the BWDDE $f_{n}^{B}(x)$ in (2). Then, we present the upper bounds for these error terms. Let the term (I) be defined as $$ (I):=\frac{1}{V_{d}R_{n}^{B}(x)^{d}}\sum_{j=0}^{d-1}\left(\frac{1}{B}\sum_{b=1}^{B}\sum_{i=1}^{s}w_{i}^{b}\gamma_{s,i}\right)^{j}\left(V_{d}^{1/d}f(x)^{1/d}R_{n}^{B}(x)\right)^{d-1-j}.\tag{14} $$ If the terms (II) and (III) are defined respectively as $$ (II):=\sum_{i=1}^{s}\left|\frac{1}{B}\sum_{b=1}^{B}w_{i}^{b}\left(\gamma_{s,i}-\mathrm{P}\left(B\left(x,R_{s,(i)}^{b}(x)\right)\right)^{1/d}\right)\right|,\tag{17} $$ $$ (III):=\sum_{i=1}^{s}\left|\frac{1}{B}\sum_{b=1}^{B}w_{i}^{b}\big(\mathrm{P}(B(x,R_{s,(i)}^{b}(x)))^{1/d}-V_{d}^{1/d}f(x)^{1/d}R_{s,(i)}^{b}(x)\big)\right|,\tag{18} $$ then applying the triangle inequality to (16) yields the error decomposition $$ \left|f_{n}^{B}(x)-f(x)\right|\leq(I)\cdot(II)+(I)\cdot(III).\tag{19} $$ We emphasize that $\gamma_{s,i}=\mathbb{E}[\mathrm{P}(B(x,R_{s,(i)}^{b}(x)))^{1/d}]$ for a fixed $x\in\mathcal{X},b\in [B]$ , and $i \in [ s ]$ Therefore, standard concentration inequalities can be applied to establish the convergence rates for term (II). The derivation of this equality is explained as follows: Since P has a density over $[0,1]^{d}$ with respect to the Lebesgue measure, the random variable $\|X-x\|_{2}$ is continuous for a fixed $x\in\mathcal{X}$ . By the probability integral transform, $\operatorname{P}(B(x,\|X-x\|_{2}))$ is uniformly distributed over $[0,1]$ . For any $b \in [ B ]$ , note that $X_{1}^{b},\ldots,X_{s}^{b}$ are i.i.d. with the same distribution P. Let $U_{1}^{b},\ldots,U_{s}^{b}$ be i.i.d. uniform [0, 1] random variables. Then $$ \bigl(\mathrm{P}(x,\|X_{1}^{b}-x\|_{2}),\dots,\mathrm{P}(x,\|X_{s}^{b}-x\|_{2})\bigr)\stackrel{{\mathcal{D}}}{{=}}\bigl(U_{1}^{b},\dots,U_{s}^{b}\bigr). $$ Reordering the samples such that $\|X_{(1)}^{b}(x)-x\|_{2}\leq\cdot\cdot\cdot\leq\|X_{(s)}^{b}(x)-x\|_{2}$ , we obtain $$ \left(\mathrm{P}(B(x,R_{s,(1)}^{b}(x))),\dots,\mathrm{P}(B(x,R_{s,(s)}^{b}(x)))\right)\stackrel{{\mathcal{D}}}{{=}}\left(U_{(1)}^{b},\dots,U_{(s)}^{b}\right),\tag{20} $$ where $U_{(i)}^{b}$ is the i-th order statistic of $U_{1}^{b},\ldots,U_{s}^{b}$ . This reduces the study of $\mathrm{P}(B(x,R_{s,(i)}^{b}(x)))$ to the study of $U_{(i)}^{b}$ . By Corollary 1.2 in Biau and Devroye (2015), $U_{(i)}^{b}\sim\mathrm{Beta}(i,s+1-i)$ Hence, $\mathbb{E}[\mathrm{P}(B(x,R_{s,(i)}^{b}(x)))^{1/d}]=\mathbb{E}[(U_{(i)}^{b})^{1/d}]=\gamma_{s,i}.$ The following proposition provides the upper bounds for the error terms $(I),(II)$ , and (III), respectively. \Delta_{n}:=[c_{3}^{\prime}(c_{8}^{\prime}(n/\log n)^{1/(d+2)}/(2 s))^{1/d},1-c_{3}^{\prime}(c_{8}^{\prime}(n/\log n)^{1/(d+2)}/(2 s))^{1/d}]^{d}.
$$

On the event $\Omega_{6}$ , for all $x\in\Delta_{n}$ and any $b \in [ B ]$ , we have

$$
\widetilde{R}_{s,(k^{b,*})}^{b}(x)\leq c_{3}^{\prime}(k^{b,*}/s)^{1/d}\leq c_{3}^{\prime}(c_{8}^{\prime}(n/\log n)^{1/(d+2)}/(2 s))^{1/d}.
$$

Thus, for any $y\in B\big(x,\widetilde{R}_{s,(k^{b,*})}^{b}(x)\big)$ , we have

$$
d(y,\mathbb{R}^{d}\setminus [0,1]^{d})\geq c_{3}^{\prime}(c_{8}^{\prime}(n/\log n)^{1/(d+2)}/(2 s))^{1/d}-\widetilde{R}_{s,(k^{b,*})}^{b}(x)\geq 0.
$$

This implies that $B\left(x,\widetilde{R}_{s,(k^{b,*})}^{b}(x)\right)\subset [0,1]^{d}$ for all $x\in\Delta_{n}$ and $b \in [ B ]$ . Therefore, from Proposition 21 and inequality (82), we obtain

$$
\left|f_{n}^{B,*}(x)-f(x)\right|\lesssim((\log n)/\overline{{k}})^{1+1/d}+\big((\log n)/(\overline{{k}}B)\big)^{1/2}+(\overline{{k}}/s)^{1/d},\quad x\in\Delta_{n}.
$$

Using $k^{b,*}\asymp(n/\log n)^{1/(d+2)}$ from Proposition 5 and substituting the choices of B and $s,$ we obtain

$$
\big|f_{n}^{B,*}(x)-f(x)\big|\lesssim n^{-1/(d+2)}(\log n)^{(d+3)/(d+2)},\qquad x\in\Delta_{n}
$$

Integrating over $\Delta_{n}$ , we get

$$
\int_{\Delta_{n}}|f_{n}^{B,*}(x)-f(x)|d x\lesssim n^{-1/(d+2)}(\log n)^{(d+3)/(d+2)}.\tag{83}
$$

On the other hand, on the event $\Omega_{5}$ , condition (iii) in Proposition 1 holds for $w^{b,*}$ and $k^{b,*}$ , which implies that $\textstyle\sum_{i=1}^{s}w_{i}^{b,*}i^{1/d}\lesssim(k^{b,*})^{1/d}$ for all $b \in [ B ]$ . Since $\gamma_{s,i}<((i+1/d)/(s+$ $1/d))^{1/d}\leq(2 i\bar{/}s)^{1/d}$ by (38), we have

$$
\frac{1}{B}\sum_{b=1}^{B}\sum_{i=1}^{s}w_{i}^{b,*}\gamma_{s,i}\lesssim\frac{1}{B}\sum_{b=1}^{B}\sum_{i=1}^{s}w_{i}^{b,*}(i/s)^{1/d}\lesssim\frac{1}{B}\sum_{b=1}^{B}(k^{b,*}/s)^{1/d}\lesssim(\overline{{k}}/s)^{1/d}.
$$

Following similar arguments as in (47) from Proposition 4, we obtain $R_{n}^{B,*}(x)\gtrsim(\underline{{k}}/s)^{1/d}$ for all $x\in\mathcal{X}$ on the event $\Omega_{5}\cap\Omega_{6}$ . This implies

$$
f_{n}^{B,*}(x)=\frac{1}{V_{d}R_{n}^{B,*}(x)^{d}}\bigg(\frac{1}{B}\sum_{b=1}^{B}\sum_{i=1}^{s}w_{i}^{b,*}\gamma_{s,i}\bigg)^{d}\lesssim\overline{{k}}/\underline{{k}}\lesssim 1,\qquad x\in\mathcal{X}.
$$

Since $\|f\|_{\infty}\leq\overline{{c}}$ from Assumption 2, we conclude that $\|f_{n}^{B,*}-f\|_{\infty}$ is bounded by a constant. Therefore, we have

$$
\begin{array}{l}\int_{\mathcal{X}\backslash\Delta_{n}}|f_{n}^{B,*}(x)-f(x)|d x\lesssim\mu(\mathcal{X}\setminus\Delta_{n})\lesssim((n/\log n)^{1/(d+2)}/s)^{1/d}\\ \lesssim n^{-1/(d+2)}(\log n)^{(d+3)/(d+2)}.\\ \end{array}
$$

Finally, combining this with (83), we have

$$
\int_{\mathcal{X}}\left|f_{n}^{B,*}(x)-f(x)\right|d x=\left(\int_{\Delta_{n}}+\int_{\mathcal{X}\backslash\Delta_{n}}\right)\left|f_{n}^{B,*}(x)-f(x)\right|d x\lesssim n^{-1/(d+2)}(\log n)^{(d+3)/(d+2)},
$$

which completes the proof.

Theorem 3 Let Assumptions 1 and 2 hold. Suppose the conditions in Theorem 2 hold, including the dataset partitioning and choice of parameters s and B. Let $R_{n}^{B,*}$ be the bagged regularized k-distances returned by Algorithm 2. Then there exists $N_{2}^{*}\in\mathbb{N}$ , as specified in Theorem ${\mathcal{Q}},$ such that for all $n>N_{2}^{*}$ , with probability $\mathrm{P}^{n}$ at least $1-4/n^{2}$ , we have

$$
\mathrm{Reg}^{\mathrm{AUC}}(R_{n}^{B,*})\lesssim n^{-1/(2+d)}(\log n)^{(d+3)/(d+2)}.
$$

steps.claim:
Proof [of Theorem 3] Let $\Omega_{5},\Omega_{6}$ , and $\Omega_{7}$ be the events defined in the proof of Proposition 21. Following the arguments therein, the event $\Omega_{5}\cap\Omega_{6}\cap\Omega_{7}$ holds with probability $\mathrm{P}^{n}$ at least $1-4/n^{2}$ for all $n\geq N_{4}$ . For the subsequent arguments, we assume that $\Omega_{5}\cap\Omega_{6}\cap\Omega_{7}$ holds and that $n>N_{2}^{*}=N_{4}$

Let $\left\{c_{n}\right\}$ denote the sequence from Lemma 12. On the event $\Omega_{6},$ , for all $x\in\mathcal{X}$ , we have

$$
\begin{array}{l}R_{s}^{b,*}(x)=\sum_{i=1}^{s}w_{i}^{b,*}\widetilde{R}_{s,(i)}^{b}(x)=\sum_{i=1}^{c_{n}}w_{i}^{b,*}\widetilde{R}_{s,(i)}^{b}(x)+\sum_{i=c_{n}+1}^{s}w_{i}^{b,*}\widetilde{R}_{s,(i)}^{b}(x)\\ \leq\widetilde{R}_{s,(c_{n})}^{b,*}(x)+\sum_{i=c_{n}+1}^{s}w_{i}^{b,*}\widetilde{R}_{s,(i)}^{b}(x)\lesssim(c_{n}/s)^{1/d}+\sum_{i=1}^{s}w_{i}^{b,*}(i/s)^{1/d},\\ \end{array}
$$

By Proposition 5, on the event $\Omega_{5}$ , we have $\textstyle\sum_{i=1}^{s}w_{i}^{b,*}i^{1/d}\lesssim\overline{{k}}^{1/d}$ and $\underline{{k}}\gtrsim(\log n)^{2}$ . This implies that $R_{s}^{b,*}(x)\lesssim(c_{n}/s)^{1/d}+(\overline{{k}}/s)^{1/d}\lesssim(\overline{{k}}/s)^{1/d}$ . Averaging over b in $[ B ]$ , we obtain

$$
R_{n}^{B,*}(x)=\frac{1}{B}\sum_{b=1}^{B}R_{s}^{b,*}(x)\lesssim(\bar{k}/s)^{1/d}\tag{85}
$$

On the other hand, using (38), we have

$$
\sum_{i=1}^{s}w_{i}^{b,*}\gamma_{s,i}>\sum_{i=1}^{s}w_{i}^{b,*}\bigg(\frac{i+1/d-1}{s+1+1/d}\bigg)^{1/d}\gtrsim\sum_{i=1}^{s}w_{i}^{b,*}(i/s)^{1/d},
$$

where we use the inequality $(i+1/d-1)/(s+1+1/d)\geq(i-1)/(s+2)\geq(i-1)/(2s)$ Applying Proposition 5 again, we get $\textstyle\sum_{i=1}^{s}w_{i}^{b,*}i^{1/d}\gtrsim\overline{{k}}^{1/d}$ . Averaging over b in [B], we have

$$
\frac{1}{B}\sum_{b=1}^{B}\sum_{i=1}^{s}w_{i}^{b,*}\gamma_{s,i}\gtrsim(\overline{{k}}/s)^{1/d}.
$$
Combining this with (85), we conclude that $f_{n}^{B,*}(x)$ is lower bounded by a constant for $x\in\mathcal{X}$ . Consequently, by Theorem 2 and Proposition 6, we obtain the desired assertion.

Proposition 6 Let Assumptions 1 and 2 hold, and let f be the true density function. Let $R_{n}^{B,*}$ be the bagged regularized k-distances as in (10) and $f_{n}^{B,*}(x)$ be the BRDDE as in (11). Suppose that there exists a constant $c > 0$ such that $\|f_{n}^{B,*}\|_{\infty}\overset{\cdot}{\geq}c$ . Then, we have

steps.claim:
Proof [of Proposition 6] Under the Huber contamination model in Assumption 1, let $\eta(x)$ be defined as in (12), and define $\widehat{\eta}(x)=\Pi\cdot f_{n}^{B,*}(x)^{-1}$ . By the expression of $f_{n}^{^{\prime}{},*}(x)$ in (11), it follows that ${\bf 1}\{R_{n}^{B,*}(X)-R_{n}^{B,*}(X^{\prime})>0\}={\bf 1}\{\widehat{\eta}(X)-\widehat{\eta}(X^{\prime})>0\}$ and $\mathbf{1}\{R_{n}^{B,*}(X)=$ ${\cal{R}}_{n}^{B,*}(X^{\prime})\}=\mathbf{1}\{{\widehat\eta}(X){=}{\widehat\eta}(X^{\prime})\}$ . Consequently, we obtain

$$
\begin{array}{l}\mathrm{AUC}(R_{n}^{B,*})\\ =\mathbb{E}\left[\mathbf{1}\left\{\left(Y-Y^{\prime}\right)\left(R_{n}^{B,*}(X)-R_{n}^{B,*}\left(X^{\prime}\right)>0\right)\right\}+\mathbf{1}\left\{R_{n}^{B,*}(X)=R_{n}^{B,*}\left(X^{\prime}\right)\right\}/2\mid Y\neq Y^{\prime}\right]\\ =\mathbb{E}\big [\mathbf{1}\{(Y-Y^{\prime})(\widehat{\eta}(X)-\widehat{\eta}(X^{\prime})>0)\}+\mathbf{1}\{\widehat{\eta}(X)=\widehat{\eta}(X^{\prime})\}/2|Y\neq Y^{\prime}\big]=\mathrm{AUC}(\widehat{\eta}).\\ \end{array}
$$

Therefore, we have $\mathrm{Reg}^{\mathrm{AUC}}(R_{n}^{B,*})=\mathrm{Reg}^{\mathrm{AUC}}(\widehat\eta)$ . Applying Agarwal (2013, Corollary 11), we obtain

$$
\mathrm{Reg}^{\mathrm{AUC}}(R_{n}^{B,*})=\mathrm{Reg}^{\mathrm{AUC}}(\widehat{\eta})\leq\frac{1}{\Pi(1-\Pi)}\int_{\mathcal{X}}|\widehat{\eta}(x)-\eta(x)|d\mathrm{P}_{X}(x).\tag{84}
$$

From Assumption 2, we have $\|f\|_{\infty}\geq\underline{{c}},$ and given that $\|f_{n}^{B,*}\|_{\infty}\geq c$ , it follows that

$$
|\widehat{\eta}(x)-\eta(x)| =\frac{\Pi\big|f_{n}^{B,*}(x)-f(x)\big|}{f_{n}^{B,*}(x)f(x)}\lesssim\big|f_{n}^{B,*}(x)-f(x)\big|.
$$
Combining this with (84) and the condition $\|f\|_{\infty}\leq\overline{{c}}$ from Assumption 2, we establish the desired result. ■

context:
In this work, we tackle feature learning and function estimation jointly through the paradigm of empirical risk minimisation. We consider a classical supervised learning problem. We have i.i.d. samples $(x_{i},y_{i})_{i\in [n]}$ from a random variable $(X,Y)\in\mathcal{X}\times\mathcal{Y}\subset\mathbb{R}^{d}\times\mathbb{R}$ Our goal is to minimise the expected risk, which is defined as $\mathcal{R}(f): =\mathbb{E}_{X,Y}[\ell(Y,f(X))]$ over some class of functions ${\mathcal{F}}_{:}$ where \` is a loss function mapping from $\mathbb{R}\times\mathbb{R}$ to R. This can be achieved through the framework of regularised empirical risk minimisation, where the empirical risk is defined as $\begin{array}{ r }{\widehat{\mathcal{R}}(f): =\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\ell(y_{i},f(x_{i}))}\end{array}$ . Our interest in regularised empirical risk minimisation stems from its flexibility, allowing it to be applied to a wide range of problems as long as the objective can be defined as the optimisation of an expected loss. Our primary objective is to achieve the lowest possible risk, which we study in theory and in practice, while we explore the recovery of underlying features in numerical experiments. Our method draws inspiration from several lines of work, namely positive definite kernels and neural networks with their mean field limit, which we briefly review, together with the main limitations we aim to alleviate.

Mean-field limit. To apply a similar framework to our future estimator, we introduce the mean-field limit of an over-parameterised one-hidden layer neural network (Nitanda and Suzuki, 2017; Mei et al., 2019; Chizat and Bach, 2022; Sirignano and Spiliopoulos, 2020). When the number of neurons m is very large, the network can be rescaled as follows

$$
f(x)=\frac{1}{m}\sum_{j=1}^{m}\eta_{j}\sigma(w_{j}^{\top}x+b_{j}),\text{which approximates}\int\eta\sigma(w^{\top}x+b)\mathrm{d}\mu(\eta,w,b),\tag{1}
$$

where $\mu$ is a probability distribution, and we can take the weights and constant terms $(w,b)$ to be constrained when the activation is 1-homogeneous,<sup>1</sup> such as the ReLU or step func tion. This approach is valuable because, as noted by Chizat and Bach (2022), under certain conditions (convexity of the loss and penalty functions, homogeneity of the activation function), the regularised empirical risk problem optimised via gradient descent in the infinitely small step-size limit converges to the minimiser of the corresponding problem with infinitely many particles. This allows us to use a finite number of particles m in practice while still leveraging the theoretical benefits derived from the continuous framework.

We use the following notations. For a positive integer m, we define $[m]: =\{1,\dots,m\}$ For a d-dimensional vector α and $i\in [d],\alpha_{i}$ denotes its i-th element. For a matrix A, tr A denotes its trace when A is square, $A^{-1}$ its inverse when well defined, while $A_{i,j}$ the element in its i-th row and j-th column, and $A^{\top}$ its transpose. $I_{d}$ is the $d \times d$ identity matrix. We use $S^{d-1}$ to denote the unit sphere in $\mathbb{R}^{d}$ for $\| \cdot \|$ a generic norm and $\| \cdot \| .$ <sub>∗</sub> its dual norm. The $\ell_{2},\ell_{1}$ , and $\ell_{\infty}$ norms are denoted as $\|\cdot\|_{2},\|\cdot\|_{1}$ , and $\|\cdot\|_{\infty}$ respectively. We use $O(\cdot)$ to denote the asymptotic behaviour of functions, indicating the order of growth. The set of probability measures on a given space S is denoted by ${\mathcal{P}}(S)$ . A normal random variable is denoted as following the law N(mean, variance). 1 is the indicator function. For two spaces $S_{1},S_{2},S_{1}^{S_{2}}$ is the set of functions from $S_{2}$ to $S_{1}$

Building on the limitations of current methods discussed in the introduction, we propose a novel architecture that integrates neural networks with kernel methods. This approach can be interpreted in two ways: as learning with a kernel that is itself learned during training, or as employing a one-hidden layer neural network where the weights from the input layer to the hidden layer are learned through gradient descent, while the weights and non-linearity from the hidden layer to the output are optimised explicitly. In this section, we introduce the custom function space we propose, revisit key properties of reproducing kernel Hilbert spaces (RKHS), and explore the connections between BKerNN model, kernel methods, and neural networks. Additionally, we present the various regularisation penalties we consider throughout our analysis.

We begin by considering the continuous setting, which mirrors the mean-field limit of overparameterised one-hidden layer neural networks discussed in Section 1.

Definition 1 (Infinite-Width Function Space) Let

$$
\mathcal{F}_{\infty}:=\left\{f\mid f(\cdot)=c+\int_{\mathcal{H}\times\mathcal{S}^{d-1}}g(w^{\top}\cdot)\mathrm{d}\mu(g,w),\quad\Omega_{0}(f)<\infty\right\},
$$

where $c$ is a constant in $\mathbb{R},S^{d-1}$ is the unit sphere for some norm $\| \cdot \|$ on $\mathbb{R}^{d}$ (typically either $\ell_{2}$ or $\ell_{1}\ j$ , H is a space of functions, and µ is a probability measure on $\mathcal{H}\times S^{d-1}$ . We define H as $\{g:\mathbb{R}\to\mathbb{R}\mid g(0)=0$ , g has a weak derivative $g^{\prime}$ $\textstyle\int_{\mathbb{R}}(g^{\prime})^{2}<\infty\}$ . H is a Hilbert space and a Sobolev space, with the inner product defined as $\begin{array}{ r }{\langle\tilde{g},\bar{g}\rangle_{\mathcal{H}}=\int\tilde{g}^{\prime}g^{\prime}}\end{array}$ . We define $\Omega_{0}$ as the infimum over all measures which can be used to define f, i.e.

$$
\Omega_{0}(f):=\inf_{\mu\in\mathcal{P}(\mathcal{H}\times\mathcal{S}^{d-1})}\int_{\mathcal{H}\times\mathcal{S}^{d-1}}\|g\|_{\mathcal{H}}\mathrm{d}\mu(g,w),\tag{2}
$$

with the infimum over $\mu$ such that $\begin{array}{ r }{f=c+\int_{\mathcal{H}\times S^{d-1}}g(w^{\top}\cdot)\mathrm{d}\mu(g,w)}\end{array}$ , where $\begin{array}{ r }{\|g\|_{\mathcal{H}}^{2}: =\int_{-\infty}^{+\infty}(g^{\prime})^{2}}\end{array}$

Note that c corresponds to the value of the function f evaluated at the null vector and is therefore unique, which is not necessarily the case of the measure $\mu .\_F_{\infty}$ is well-defined using a “variation norm” on couples $(g,w)$ integrated w.r.t a Borel measure on $\mathcal{H}\times S^{d-1}$ This is the variation norm associated to the map $(g,w)\in\mathcal{H}\times{\mathcal{S}}^{d-1}\to g(w^{\top}.)$ (which is a function from $\mathbb{R}^{d}$ to $\mathbb{R},$ , see Kurkova and Sanguineti (2001) and Bach (2024, Section 9.3.2).

The function space $\mathcal{F}_{\infty}$ is inspired by infinite-width single hidden layer neural networks: with the addition of the intercept c, each function in this space can be seen as the integral of a linear part w and a non-linearity g over some probability distribution, as in Equation (1) where the non-linearity is $\eta\sigma(\cdot)$ . Thus here the activation functions are learnt.

The approximation of $\mathcal{F}_{\infty}$ with m particles can then be obtained as follows.

Definition 2 (Finite-Width Function Space) Let

$$
\mathcal{F}_{m}:=\left\{f\mid f(\cdot)=c+\frac{1}{m}\sum_{j=1}^{m}g_{j}(w_{j}^{\top}\cdot),w_{j}\in\mathcal{S}^{d-1},g_{j}\in\mathcal{H},c\in\mathbb{R}\right\}.
$$

Remark that $\forall m\in\mathbb{N}^{*},\mathcal{F}_{m}\subset\mathcal{F}_{\infty}.$ , by taking the discrete probability measure uniformly supported by the particles $w_{1},\ldots,w_{m}$

We now consider regularised empirical risk minimisation starting with the basic penalty $\Omega_{0}$ This penalty enforces the regularity of the function and, because we use penalisation with non-squared norms, limits the cardinality of the support of $\mu$ on the space H. While this penalty is not specifically aimed at feature learning, by limiting the number of non-zero particles, it indirectly promotes feature learning to some extent. This serves as a starting point, and we introduce more targeted penalties in Section 2.5 with a stronger feature learning behaviour. For $f\in\mathcal{F}_{m}$ written as in Definition 2, the penalty simplifies to $\begin{array}{ r }{\Omega_{0}(f)=\frac{1}{m}\sum_{j=1}^{m}\|g_{j}\|_{\mathcal{H}}}\end{array}$ . The learning objective is thus defined as

$$
\hat{f}_{\lambda}:=\underset{f\in\mathcal{F}}{\arg\min}\widehat{\mathcal{R}}(f)+\lambda\Omega(f),\tag{3}
$$

where $\lambda > 0$ is a regularisation parameter and Ω is currently $\Omega_{0}$ from Equation (2). The function space $\mathcal{F}$ is either $\mathcal{F}_{\infty}$ or $\mathcal{F}_{m}$ . For statistical analysis in Section 4, we consider $\mathcal{F}_{\infty}$ while in practice, we compute the estimator using $\mathcal{F}_{m}$ as discussed in Section 3. The rationale for using $\mathcal{F}_{m}$ and expecting the statistical properties of $\mathcal{F}_{\infty}$ is elaborated in Section 3.2.

In the continuous setting, Equation (3) corresponds to

$$
\min_{c\in\mathbb{R},\mu\in\mathcal{P}(\mathcal{H}\times\mathcal{S}^{d-1})}\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\ell\left(y_{i},c+\int_{\mathcal{H}\times\mathcal{S}^{d-1}}g(w^{\top}x_{i})\mathrm{d}\mu(g,w)\right)+\lambda\int_{\mathcal{H}\times\mathcal{S}^{d-1}}\|g\|_{\mathcal{H}}\mathrm{d}\mu(g,w),\tag{4}
$$

while in the m-particles setting, Equation (3) becomes

$$
\min_{c\in\mathbb{R},w_{1},\dots,w_{m}\in\mathcal{S}^{d-1},g_{1},\dots,g_{m}\in\mathcal{H}}\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\ell\left(y_{i},c+\frac{1}{m}\sum_{j=1}^{m}g_{j}\left(w_{j}^{\top}x_{i}\right)\right)+\lambda\frac{1}{m}\sum_{j=1}^{m}\|g_{j}\|_{\mathcal{H}},\tag{5}
$$

where we clearly see a sparsity-inducing “grouped” penalty (Yuan and Lin, 2006).

In this subsection, we succinctly present some properties of reproducing kernel Hilbert spaces (RKHS) that are essential for our analysis. See Aronszajn (1950); Berlinet and Thomas-Agnan (2011) for an introduction to RKHS. Recall that we defined the Hilbert space H as

$$
\mathcal{H}:=\left\{g:\mathbb{R}\to\mathbb{R}\mid g(0)=0,\int_{\mathbb{R}}(g^{\prime})^{2}<   +\infty\right\},
$$

with the inner product $\begin{array}{ r }{\langle\tilde{g},g\rangle_{\mathcal{H}}=\int_{\mathbb{R}}\tilde{g}^{\prime}g^{\prime}}\end{array}$ . This space is a reproducing kernel Hilbert space with the reproducing kernel $k^{(B)}(a,b)=(|a| + |b| - |a-b|)/2=\mathrm{min}(|a|,|b|)\mathbb{1}_{a b>0}$ . This kernel, which can be referred to as the “Brownian” kernel, corresponds to the covariance of the Brownian motion at times a and b (Mishura and Shevchenko, 2017). To see that $k^{(B)}$ is the reproducing kernel of H, it sufices to check that we have the reproducing property, i.e. that

$$
\forall g\in\mathcal{H},\forall a\in\mathbb{R},g(a)=\langle g,k_{a}^{(B)}\rangle_{\mathcal{H}},
$$

where $k_{a}^{(B)}:b\in\mathbb{R}\to k^{(B)}(a,b)\in\mathbb{R}^{2}$ As a reproducing kernel, it is positive definite, meaning that for any $n\in\mathbb{N},\alpha\in\mathbb{R}^{n}$ , and $a\in\mathbb{R}^{n}$ , we have $\begin{array}{ r }{\sum_{i,j=1}^{n}\alpha_{i}k^{(B)}(a_{i},a_{j})\alpha_{j}\geq 0}\end{array}$

Additionally, we observe that $\lVert\boldsymbol{k}_{a}^{(B)}\rVert_{\mathcal{H}}^{2}=\langle\boldsymbol{k}_{a}^{(B)},\boldsymbol{k}_{a}^{(B)}\rangle=k^{(B)}(a,a)= |a|$ and we can obtain $\|\boldsymbol{k}_{a}^{(B)}-\boldsymbol{k}_{b}^{(B)}\|_{\mathcal{H}}^{2}= |a-b|$ in a similar manner. It is also noteworthy that by definition, the functions in H are necessarily continuous, in fact even $1 / 2 \cdot$ -Hölder continuous as we see in Lemma 3.

We first transform the optimisation problem before considering our setup from two diferent perspectives: one through kernel learning and the other through neural networks. To transform the optimisation problem, we use the representer theorem, a well-known result in RKHS theory that allows us to replace the optimisation over functions in the RKHS with optimisation over a finite weighted sum of the kernel at the data points.

In summary, we aim to perform multiple kernel learning with a kernel parametrized by a probability measure (Lemma 6), and approximate it using particles (Lemma 5).

Lemma 5 shows that we are solving a regularised kernel ridge regression problem where the kernel $\begin{array}{ r }{\frac{1}{m}\sum_{j=1}^{m}(|w_{j}^{\top}x| + |w_{j}^{\top}x^{\prime}| - |w_{j}^{\top}(x-x^{\prime})|)/2}\end{array}$ is also learnt through the weights $(w_{j})_{j\in [m]}$ and the third term $\begin{array}{ r }{\frac{\lambda}{2}\frac{1}{m}\sum_{j=1}^{m}\|w_{j}\|\quad}\end{array}$ serves as a penalty to improve kernel learning.

The homogeneity of the kernel $k^{(B)}$ leads to well-behaved optimisation, as we discuss in Section 3.2 and see in Experiment 1 in Section 5.2. The kernel matrix K is indeed positively 1-homogeneous in the particles $(w_{j})_{j\in [m]}$ . If we had chosen H to be the RKHS corresponding to the exponential kernel (or the Gaussian kernel), we would have faced the challenge of learning the kernel $\begin{array}{ r }{\sum_{j=1}^{m}e^{- |w_{j}^{\top}(x-x^{\prime})|}}\end{array}$ , which exhibits a complex and nonhomogeneous dependency on the weights $(w_{j})_{j\in [m]}$ . By using the Brownian kernel instead of the exponential kernel, we only slightly change the regularisation, regularising with $\int_{\mathbb{R}}(g^{\prime})^{2}$ instead of $\begin{array}{ r }{\int_{\mathbb{R}}g^{2}+\int_{\mathbb{R}}(g^{\prime})^{2}}\end{array}$ while making the optimisation more tractable.

We now present other penalties designed to achieve diferent efects. The three terms in Equation (8) correspond to the empirical risk, the standard penalty from KRR on the RKHS norm of the function, and an extra regularisation term on the learnt kernel weights. This additional term, $\begin{array}{ r }{\frac{\lambda}{2 m}\sum_{j=1}^{m}\|w_{j}\|}\end{array}$ , originates from the penalty $\Omega_{0}(f)$ in Equation (2). However, we can explore other penalties on $w_{1},\ldots,w_{m}$ that induce various additional sparsity efects, even if they do not directly correspond to penalties on $f\in\mathcal{F}_{m}$ . Let $W\in\mathbb{R}^{d\times m}$ be the matrix with $(w_{1},\ldots,w_{m})$ as columns, denote by $W^{(a)}$ the a-th row of $W$ , and let $W=U S V^{\top}$ be its singular value decomposition, with S a diagonal matrix composed of $S_{1},\ldots,S_{\operatorname*{min}(m,d)}$ Recall that ν is a probability distribution on $\mathbb{R}^{d}$

1. Basic penalty: $\begin{array}{ r }{\Omega_{\mathrm{basic}}(w_{1},\dots,w_{m})=\frac{1}{2 m}\sum_{j=1}^{m}\left| |w_{j}|\right|}\end{array}$ , which we discussed in Section 2.1. In the continuous setting, it corresponds to $\begin{array}{ r }{\frac{1}{2}\int_{\mathbb{R}^{d}}\|w\|\mathrm{d}\nu(w)}\end{array}$ . This penalty, which does not target any specific pattern in the data-generating mechanism, is the one for which we provide theoretical results in Section 4. However, it does not work as well in practice as the following penalties.

2. Variable penalty: $\begin{array}{ r }{\Omega_{\mathrm{variable}}(w_{1},\dots,w_{m})=\frac{1}{2}\sum_{a=1}^{d}\big(\frac{1}{m}\sum_{j=1}^{m}(w_{j})_{a}^{2}\big)^{1/2}}\end{array}$ , which is also equal to $\begin{array}{ r }{\frac{1}{2\sqrt{m}}\sum_{a=1}^{\operatorname*{min}(m,d)}\|W^{(a)}\|_{2}}\end{array}$ . This penalty, inspired by the group Lasso (Yuan and Lin, 2006), is designed for variable selection, pushing quantities $\lVert W^{(a)}\rVert_{2}$ towards zero, thus encouraging dependence on a few variables. In the continuous setting, it corresponds to $\begin{array}{ r }{\frac{1}{2}\sum_{a=1}^{\operatorname*{min}(m,d)}\big(\int_{\mathbb{R}^{d}}|w_{a}|^{2}{\mathrm{d}}\nu(w)\big)^{1/2}}\end{array}$

3. Feature penalty: $\begin{array}{ r }{\Omega_{\mathrm{feature}}(w_{1},\ldots,w_{m})=\frac{1}{2}\mathrm{tr}\left(\left(\frac{1}{m}\sum_{j=1}^{m}w_{j}w_{j}^{\top}\right)^{1/2}\right)}\end{array}$ , which is also equal to ${\frac{1}{2}}\sum_{a=1}^{\operatorname*{min}(m,d)}{\frac{S_{a}}{\sqrt{m}}}$ and to the nuclear norm of W divided by $2\sqrt{m}$ . It is used for feature learning as it is a convex relaxation of the rank, encouraging W to have low rank and thus dependence on only a few linear transformations of the data. Regularisation using the nuclear norm in the context of feature learning is wellestablished in the literature, as demonstrated by Argyriou et al. (2008). It corresponds to $\begin{array}{ r }{\frac 12\operatorname{tr}\big(\big(\int_{\mathbb R^{d}}ww^{\top}\mathrm{d}\nu(w)\big)^{1/2}\big)}\end{array}$ in the continuous setting.

4. Concave variable penalty: The concave version of the penalty for variable selection, Ω<sub>concave</sub> <sub>variable</sub> $\begin{array}{ r }{(w_{1},\ldots,w_{m})=\frac{1}{2 s}\sum_{a=1}^{d}\log\left(1+\frac{s}{\sqrt{m}}\|W^{(a)}\|_{2}\right)}\end{array}$ , with $s \geq 0$ . The appeal of the added concavity is discussed below. In the continuous setting, it corresponds to $\begin{array}{ r }{\frac{1}{2 s}\sum_{a=1}^{d}\log\left(1+s\int_{\mathbb{R}^{d}}(w_{a})^{2}{\mathrm{d}\nu}(w)\right)^{1/2})}\end{array}$

5. Concave feature penalty: The concave version of the penalty intended for feature learning, $\Omega_{\mathrm{concave}}$ feature $\begin{array}{ r }{(w_{1},\ldots,w_{m})=\frac{1}{2 s}\sum_{a=1}^{\operatorname*{min}(m,d)}\log\left(1+\frac{s}{\sqrt{m}}S_{a}\right)}\end{array}$ for feature selection, with $s \geq 0$ . The appeal of the added concavity is discussed below. In the continuous setting it corresponds to $\begin{array}{ r }{\frac{1}{2 s}\sum_{a=1}^{d}\log\big(1+s\big(\big(\int_{\mathbb{R}^{d}}w w^{\top}\mathrm{d}\nu(w)\big)^{1/2}\big)_{a,a}\big)}\end{array}$

The first penalty is convex in both ν and W, making it straightforward to optimise. The second and third penalties, while not convex in $\nu,$ are convex in W due to the presence of squared and square root terms on the components of W, easing optimisation in the m particles setting. The fourth and fifth penalties are neither convex in ν nor $W .$ , instead, they are concave in W. As s approaches zero, these penalties revert to their non-concave versions. Convex penalties, while easier to handle, can be detrimental by diminishing relevant variables or features to achieve sparsity. Mitigating this efect can involve retraining with the selected variables/features or employing concave penalties, which is the choice we made here. Although concave penalties are more complex to analyse, they often yield better performance because they drive the solution towards the boundary, promoting sparsity (Fan and Li, 2001; Bach et al., 2012). We discuss the impact of the choice of regularisation in Experiment 3 in Section 5.3.

Note that the link with infinite-dimensional normed function spaces and the theoretical analysis of Section 4. only applies to the first “basic” penalty. Extending the analysis of concave penalties from finite dimension (Fan and Li, 2001; Zhang, 2010) to infinite dimension remains an open problem.

In this section, we detail the process of computing the estimator for each of the penalties presented in Section 2.5. We then discuss the importance of the homogeneity of the Brownian kernel and how the optimisation with particles relates to the continuous setting.

In this section, we focus on the square loss $\ell(y,y^{\prime})=\textstyle{\frac{1}{2}}(y-y^{\prime})^{2}$ , which allows for explicit computations. However, the method can be extended to other loss functions using gradientbased techniques, (see Bach, 2024, Chapter 5). Recalling Equation (8) and the penalties described in Section 2.5, the optimisation problem we aim to solve is

$$
\min_{w_{1},\dots,w_{m}\in\mathbb{R}^{d},c\in\mathbb{R},\alpha\in\mathbb{R}^{n}}\frac{1}{2 n}\|Y-K\alpha-c\mathbb{1}_{n}\|_{2}^{2}+\frac{\lambda}{2}\alpha^{\top}K\alpha+\lambda\Omega_{\text{weights}}\left(w_{1},\dots,w_{m}\right),\tag{10}
$$

where $\begin{array}{ r }{K=\frac{1}{m}\sum_{j=1}^{m}K^{(w_{j})}}\end{array}$ and $\Omega_{\mathrm{weights}}$ represents any of the penalties from Section 2.5.

To solve this problem, we alternate between exact minimisation with respect to α and $c,$ which is done in closed-form, and one improvement step for the minimisation with respect to $w_{1},\ldots,w_{m}$ which is done using one step of proximal gradient descent. This corresponds to minimizing with respect to the $w_{1},\ldots,w_{m}$ the infimum with respect to c and $\alpha .$

When the weights $w_{1},\ldots,w_{m}$ are fixed, the kernel matrix K is also fixed, allowing us to find the solution for the constant c and the coeficients α in closed-form. By centring both the kernel matrix and the response $Y$ , we transform the problem into a classical kernel ridge regression problem, for which explicit solutions are well-known.

Next, we focus on optimising $w_{1},\ldots,w_{m}$ while keeping c and α fixed. The goal is to solve

$$
\min_{w_{1},\dots,w_{m}\in\mathbb{R}^{d}}G(w_{1},\dots,w_{m})+\lambda\Omega_{\text{weights}}(w_{1},\dots,w_{m}),\tag{11}
$$

where the dependence on $(w_{j})_{j\in [m]}$ in the first term is through the kernel matrix K. Note that G is convex in K but not in $w_{1},\ldots,w_{m}$ . Additionally, G is diferentiable almost everywhere, except where $w_{j}^{\top}(x_{i}-x_{i^{\prime}})$ for some $j\in [m],i\neq i^{\prime}\in [n]$ . However, standard practice assumes that these non-diferentiabilities average out with many data points. Meanwhile, the penalties $\Omega_{\mathrm{weights}}$ are not diferentiable at certain fixed points, independently of the data, similarly to the Lasso penalty. Therefore, we use proximal gradient descent to solve Equation (11). With a step-size $\gamma > 0$ , this involves minimising

$$
\sum_{j=1}^{m}\frac{\partial G}{\partial w_{j}}(w^{\mathrm{old}})^{\top}(w_{j}-w_{j}^{\mathrm{old}})+\frac{1}{2\gamma}\sum_{j=1}^{m}\|w_{j}-w_{j}^{\mathrm{old}}\|_{2}^{2}+\lambda\Omega_{\mathrm{weights}}(w_{1},\ldots,w_{m}),
$$

over $w_{1},\ldots,w_{m}\in\mathbb{R}^{d}$ . This corresponds to the simultaneous proximal gradient descent steps $\begin{array}{ r }{w_{j}\mathrm{prox}_{\lambda\gamma\Omega}(w_{j}-\gamma\frac{\partial G}{\partial w_{i}})}\end{array}$ . We therefore compute the gradient and the proximal operator. For the gradient, we have the following lemma.

theorems.statement:
Lemma 5 (Kernel Formulation of Finite-Width) Equation (5) is equivalent to

$$
\min_{w_{1},\dots,w_{m}\in\mathbb{R}^{d},c\in\mathbb{R},\alpha\in\mathbb{R}^{n}}\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\ell(y_{i},(K\alpha)_{i}+c)+\frac{\lambda}{2}\alpha^{\top}K\alpha+\frac{\lambda}{2}\frac{1}{m}\sum_{j=1}^{m}\|w_{j}\|,\tag{8}
$$

where $\begin{array}{ r }{K=\frac{1}{m}\sum_{j=1}^{m}K^{(w_{j})}}\end{array}$ , and $K^{(w_{j})}\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times n}$ is the kernel matrix $f o r$ kernel $k^{(B)}$ and projected data $(w_{j}^{\top}x_{1},\ldots,w_{j}^{\top}x_{n}),\ i . e .,K_{i,i^{\prime}}^{(w_{j})}=(|w_{j}^{\top}x_{i}| + |w_{j}^{\top}x_{i^{\prime}}| - |w_{j}^{\top}(x_{i}-x_{i^{\prime}})|)/2$ . Notice that there are no constraints on the particles $(w_{j})_{j\in [m]}$ to belong to the unit sphere anymore.

steps.claim:
Proof [Proof of Lemma 5] Our goal is to transform Equation (5). We begin with the following trick for the m particles setting

$$
\frac{1}{m}\sum_{j=1}^{m}\|g_{j}\|_{\mathcal{H}}=\inf_{\beta\in\mathbb{R}_{+}^{m}}\frac{1}{2 m}\sum_{j=1}^{m}\left(\frac{\|g_{j}\|_{\mathcal{H}}^{2}}{\beta_{j}}+\beta_{j}\right).
$$

This allows us to rewrite Equation 5 in the following way

$$
\min_{c\in\mathbb{R},w_{1},\dots,w_{m}\in\mathcal{S}^{d-1},g_{1},\dots,g_{m}\in\mathcal{H},\beta\in\mathbb{R}_{+}^{m}}\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\ell\left(y_{i},c+\frac{1}{m}\sum_{j=1}^{m}g_{j}(w_{j}^{\top}x_{i})\right)+\lambda\frac{1}{2 m}\sum_{j=1}^{m}\left(\frac{\|g_{j}\|_{\mathcal{H}}^{2}}{\beta_{j}}+\beta_{j}\right).
$$

Now if we fix $(w_{j})_{j\in [m]}$ and $(\beta_{j})_{j\in [m]}$ in the equation above, the minimisation problem is equivalent to

$$
\min_{c\in\mathbb{R},g_{1},\dots,g_{m}\in\mathcal{H}}\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\ell(y_{i},c+\frac{1}{m}\sum_{j=1}^{m}g_{j}(w_{j}^{\top}x_{i}))+\frac{\lambda}{2}\frac{1}{m}\sum_{j=1}^{m}\frac{\|g_{j}\|_{\mathcal{H}}^{2}}{\beta_{j}}.\tag{17}
$$

Using the representer theorem (Schölkopf et al., 2001), we express each $x  g_{j}(w_{j}^{\top}x)$ as

$$
x\to\sum_{i=1}^{n}\alpha_{i}^{(j)}k^{(B)}(w_{j}^{\top}x_{i},w_{j}^{\top}x),
$$

which leads to

$$
\|g_{j}\|_{\mathcal{H}}^{2}=\sum_{i,i^{\prime}=1}^{n}\alpha_{i}^{(j)}\alpha_{i^{\prime}}^{(j)}k^{(B)}(w_{j}^{\top}x_{i},w_{j}^{\top}x_{i^{\prime}}).
$$

Rewriting the norm and evaluation in kernel form with $K_{i,i^{\prime}}^{(w_{j})}=k^{(B)}(w_{j}^{\top}x_{i},w_{j}^{\top}x_{i^{\prime}})$ , we obtain

$$
\|g_{j}\|_{\mathcal{H}}^{2}=(\alpha^{(j)})^{\top}K^{(w_{j})}\alpha^{(j)},
$$

and

$$
g_{j}(w_{j}^{\top}x_{i})=(K^{(w_{j})}\alpha^{(j)})_{i}.
$$

Thus, we transform Equation (17) into

$$
\min_{c\in\mathbb{R},\alpha^{(1)},\dots,\alpha^{(m)}\in\mathbb{R}^{n}}\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\ell(y_{i},\frac{1}{m}\sum_{j=1}^{m}(K^{(w_{j})}\alpha^{(j)})_{i}+c)+\frac{\lambda}{2}\frac{1}{m}\sum_{j=1}^{m}\frac{(\alpha^{(j)})^{\top}K^{(w_{j})}\alpha^{(j)}}{\beta_{j}}.
$$

We show that minimisation is attained for vectors $\alpha^{(j)}$ equal to $\beta_{j}\alpha$ for a single vector $\alpha .$ Consider the convex problem

$$
\min_{\alpha^{(1)},\dots,\alpha^{(m)}\in\mathbb{R}^{n}}\frac{1}{2}\frac{1}{m}\sum_{j=1}^{m}\frac{(\alpha^{(j)})^{\top}K^{(w_{j})}\alpha^{(j)}}{\beta_{j}},
$$

subject to $\begin{array}{ r }{\frac{1}{m}\sum_{j=1}^{m}K^{(w_{j})}\alpha^{(j)}=z}\end{array}$ where $z\in\mathbb{R}^{d}$ . We define the Lagrangian

$$
\mathcal{L}(\alpha^{(1)},\dots,\alpha^{(m)},\alpha)=\frac{1}{2}\frac{1}{m}\sum_{j=1}^{m}\frac{(\alpha^{(j)})^{\top}K^{(w_{j})}\alpha^{(j)}}{\beta_{j}}+\alpha^{\top}\left(z-\frac{1}{m}\sum_{j}K^{(w_{j})}\alpha^{(j)}\right).
$$

By taking the diferential of L with respect to $\alpha^{(j)}$ at the optimum, we get

$$
\frac{\partial\mathcal{L}}{\partial\alpha^{(j)}}=\frac{1}{m}K^{(w_{j})}\left(\frac{\alpha^{(j)}}{\beta_{j}}-\alpha\right)=0.
$$

The diferential with respect to α yields that at the optimum, the constraint is verified, $\begin{array}{ r }{\mathrm{i . e .,}z=\frac{1}{m}\sum_{i}K^{(w_{j})}\alpha^{(j)}}\end{array}$ . We note that for $\alpha^{(j)}=\beta_{j}\alpha$ , all equations are satisfied, yielding the desired result.

We can then write Equation (5) as

$$
\min_{w_{1},\dots,w_{m}\in\mathbb{R}^{d},c\in\mathbb{R},\beta\in\mathbb{R}_{+}^{m},\alpha\in\mathbb{R}^{n}}\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\ell(y_{i},(K\alpha)_{i}+c)+\frac{\lambda}{2}\alpha^{\top}K\alpha+\frac{\lambda}{2}\frac{1}{m}\sum_{j=1}^{m}\beta_{j},
$$

with the constraints $\forall j\in [m],w_{j}\in S^{d-1}$ , and $\begin{array}{ r }{K=\frac{1}{m}\sum_{j=1}^{m}\beta_{j}K^{(w_{j})}}\end{array}$

We notice that $\beta_{j}K^{(w_{j})}=K^{(\beta_{j}w_{j})}$ due to the positive homogeneity of the Brownian kernel. We therefore introduce the change of variable $\beta_{j}w_{j}=\tilde{w}_{j}$

$$
\min_{\tilde{w}_{1},\dots,\tilde{w}_{m}\in\mathbb{R}^{d},c\in\mathbb{R},\alpha\in\mathbb{R}^{n}}\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\ell(y_{i},(K\alpha)_{i}+c)+\frac{\lambda}{2}\alpha^{\top}K\alpha+\frac{\lambda}{2}\frac{1}{m}\sum_{j=1}^{m}\|\tilde{w}_{j}\|,
$$

with $\begin{array}{ r }{K=\frac{1}{m}\sum_{j=1}^{m}K^{(\tilde{w}_{j})}}\end{array}$ and no constraint on the norm of $\tilde{w}_{j}$ . For ease of exposition in the main text, we replace w˜ by w. ■

theorems.statement:
Lemma 6 (Kernel Formulation of Infinite-Width) Equation (4) is equivalent to:

$$
\min_{\nu\in\mathcal{P}(\mathbb{R}^{d}),c\in\mathbb{R},\alpha\in\mathbb{R}^{n}}\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\ell(y_{i},(K\alpha)_{i}+c)+\frac{\lambda}{2}\alpha^{\top}K\alpha+\frac{\lambda}{2}\int_{\mathbb{R}^{d}}\|w\|\mathrm{d}\nu(w),\tag{9}
$$

with $\begin{array}{ r }{K=\int_{\mathbb{R}^{d}}K^{(w)}\mathrm{d}\nu(w)}\end{array}$ and and $K^{(w)}\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times n}$ is the kernel matrix for kernel $k^{(B)}$ and data $(w^{\top}x_{1},\ldots,w^{\top}x_{n})$

steps.claim:
Proof [Proof of Lemma 6] The proof follows the same steps as the proof of Lemma $5,$ systematically replacing any $\textstyle{\frac{1}{m}}\sum_{j=1}^{m}$ with the appropriate integral over $\mathcal{H}\times\mathcal{S}^{d-1}$ with respect to measure $\mu .$ . Before the change of variables, the problem is

$$
\min_{\mu\in\mathcal{P}(\mathcal{H}\times\mathcal{S}^{d-1}),c\in\mathbb{R},(\beta_{g})_{g}\in\mathbb{R}_{+}^{\mathcal{H}},\alpha\in\mathbb{R}^{n}}\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\ell(y_{i},(K\alpha)_{i}+c)+\frac{\lambda}{2}\alpha^{\top}K\alpha+\frac{\lambda}{2}\int_{\mathcal{H}\times\mathcal{S}^{d-1}}\beta_{g}\mathrm{d}\mu(g,w),
$$

where $\begin{array}{ r }{K=\int_{\mathcal{H}\times S^{d-1}}\beta_{g}K^{(w)}d\mu(g,w)=\int_{\mathcal{H}\times S^{d-1}}K^{(\beta_{g}w)}d\mu(g,w)}\end{array}$ .

The change of variables $\beta_{g}w=\tilde{w}$ transforms the problem into

$$
\min_{(\beta_{g})_{g}\in\mathbb{R}_{+}^{\mathcal{H}},\nu\in\mathcal{P}(\{\beta_{g}w,g\in\mathcal{H},w\in\mathcal{S}^{d-1}\}),c\in\mathbb{R},\alpha\in\mathbb{R}^{n}}\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\ell(y_{i},(K\alpha)_{i}+c)+\frac{\lambda}{2}\alpha^{\top}K\alpha+\frac{\lambda}{2}\int_{\mathbb{R}^{d}}\|\tilde{w}\|\mathrm{d}\nu(\tilde{w}),
$$

with $\begin{array}{ r }{K=\int_{\mathbb{R}^{d}}K^{(\tilde{w})}\mathrm{d}\nu(\tilde{w})}\end{array}$ . We can consider the integral over R<sup>d</sup> instead of $\{\beta_{g}w,g\in\mathcal{H},w\in$ $S^{d-1}\bigr\}$ by extending ν with $\nu(\mathbb{R}^{d}\setminus\{\beta_{g}w,g\in\mathcal{H},w\in\mathcal{S}^{d-1}\})=0$ .

This is equivalent to considering the minimum over $\nu\in\mathcal{P}(\mathbb{R}^{d})$ instead of the minimum over $(\beta_{g})_{g\in\mathcal{H}}\in\mathbb{R}_{+}^{\mathcal{H}}$ and $\nu\in\mathcal{P}(\{\beta_{g}w,g\in\mathcal{H},w\in\mathcal{S}^{d-1}\})$ , as we discuss now.

Indeed, the first minimum is smaller as it is considered over a larger space, but they are equal because both the norm $\| \cdot \|$ and the kernel K are positively homogeneous. Hence, the problem finally becomes

$$
\min_{\nu\in\mathcal{P}(\mathbb{R}^{d}),c\in\mathbb{R},\alpha\in\mathbb{R}^{n}}\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\ell(y_{i},(K\alpha)_{i}+c)+\frac{\lambda}{2}\alpha^{\top}K\alpha+\frac{\lambda}{2}\int_{\mathbb{R}^{d}}\|\tilde{w}\|\mathrm{d}\nu(\tilde{w}),
$$

with $\begin{array}{ r }{K=\int_{\mathbb{R}^{d}}K^{(\tilde{w})}\mathrm{d}\nu(\tilde{w})}\end{array}$ . For ease of exposition in the main text, we replace $\tilde{w}$ by w.

theorems.statement:
Lemma 7 (Optimisation for Fixed Particles) For fixed $w_{1},\ldots,w_{m}$ and hence a fixed $K$ , define

$$
G(w_{1},\dots,w_{m}):=\min_{\alpha\in\mathbb{R}^{n},c\in\mathbb{R}}\frac{1}{2 n}\|Y-K\alpha-c\mathbb{1}_{n}\|_{2}^{2}+\frac{\lambda}{2}\alpha^{\top}K\alpha .
$$

The optimisation problem defining G is solved by

$$
\alpha=(\tilde{K}+n\lambda I)^{-1}\tilde{Y}\quad\mathrm{and}\quad c=\frac{\mathbb{1}^{\top}Y}{n}-\frac{\mathbb{1}^{\top}K\alpha}{n},
$$

where $\tilde{K}: =\Pi K\Pi$ and $\begin{array}{ r }{\tilde{Y}: =Y-\frac{\mathbb{1}\mathbb{1}^{\top}Y}{n}}\end{array}$ , with $\begin{array}{ r }{\Pi=I-\frac{\mathbb{1}\mathbb{1}^{\top}}{n}}\end{array}$ being the centring matrix. The objective value is then

$$
G(w_{1},\dots,w_{m})=\frac{\lambda}{2}\tilde{Y}^{\top}(\tilde{K}+\lambda n I)^{-1}\tilde{Y}.
$$

steps.claim:
Proof [Proof of Lemma 7] For a fixed $\alpha,$ , the optimal c is given by $\begin{array}{ r }{c=\frac{\mathbb{1}^{\top}Y}{n}-\frac{\mathbb{1}^{\top}K\alpha}{n}}\end{array}$ Substituting this back into the objective function, we obtain

$$
\min_{\alpha\in\mathbb{R}^{n}}\frac{1}{2 n}\|\Pi Y-\Pi K\alpha\|_{2}^{2}+\frac{\lambda}{2}\alpha^{\top}K\alpha,
$$

which is minimised for α satisfying $(K\Pi K+n\lambda K)\alpha=K\Pi Y$ . We can further simplify this by observing that if $(\Pi K+n\lambda I)\alpha=\Pi Y$ , then the previous condition is satisfied.

From the equation nλα $= \Pi Y - \Pi K \alpha$ , we can deduce that $\Pi \alpha = \alpha$ because $\Pi^{2}=\Pi$ Therefore, we can express α as $\alpha=\Pi\tilde{\alpha}$ . Substituting this change of variable into the original problem, we define $\tilde{K}: =\Pi K\Pi$ and $\tilde{Y}: =\Pi Y$ , transforming the problem into

$$
\min_{\tilde{\alpha}\in\mathbb{R}^{n}}\frac{1}{2 n}\|\tilde{Y}-\tilde{K}\tilde{\alpha}\|_{2}^{2}+\frac{\lambda}{2}\tilde{\alpha}^{\top}\tilde{K}\tilde{\alpha}.
$$

This is a standard kernel ridge regression problem (noting that $\tilde{K}$ is still a valid kernel matrix), for which the solution is known to be $\tilde{\alpha}=(\tilde{K}+n\lambda I)^{-1}\tilde{Y}$ . We also have $\Pi\tilde{\alpha}=\tilde{\alpha}.$ implying $\alpha=\tilde{\alpha}$ because one can show that $\mathbb{1}^{\top}\tilde{\alpha}=0$ . To see why, note that $\mathbb{1}^{\top}\tilde{\alpha}=\langle\mathbb{1},\tilde{\alpha}\rangle=$ $\langle(\tilde{K}+n\lambda I)^{-1}\mathbf{1},\tilde{Y}\rangle$ . Since $(\tilde{K}+n\lambda I)^{-1}\mathbf{1}$ is proportional to 1 (as 1 is an eigenvector of $\tilde{K}+n\lambda I$ and its inverse), and $\langle\tilde{Y},\mathbb{1}\rangle=0$ , we obtain the desired result.

Finally, we verify the optimal condition $(K\Pi K+n\lambda K)\alpha=K\Pi Y$ . Given $(\Pi K\Pi+$ $n\lambda I)\tilde{\alpha}=\Pi Y$ by definition, multiplying by K yields $(K\Pi K\Pi+n\lambda K)\tilde{\alpha}=K\Pi Y$ . Since $\tilde{\alpha}=\alpha=\Pi\alpha$ , the desired result follows. ■

theorems.statement:
Lemma 8 (Gradient of G) Let $j \in [ m ]$ , then

$$
\frac{\partial G}{\partial w_{j}}=\frac{\lambda}{4}\frac{1}{m}\sum_{i,i^{\prime}=1}^{n}z_{i}z_{i^{\prime}}\mathrm{sign}(w_{j}^{\top}(x_{i}-x_{i^{\prime}}))(x_{i}-x_{i^{\prime}}),
$$

where $z=(\tilde{K}+n\lambda I)^{-1}\tilde{Y}$

steps.claim:
Proof [Proof of Lemma 8] First, we compute the derivative of $\begin{array}{ r }{G=\frac{\lambda}{2}\tilde{Y}^{\top}(\tilde{K}+\lambda n I)^{-1}\tilde{Y}}\end{array}$ with respect to $w_{j}$

$$
\begin{array}{l}\frac{\partial G}{\partial w_{j}}=\sum_{i,i^{\prime}=1}^{n}\frac{\partial G}{\partial K_{i,i^{\prime}}}\frac{\partial K_{i,i^{\prime}}}{\partial w_{j}}\\ =\frac{1}{m}\sum_{i,i^{\prime}=1}^{n}\frac{\partial G}{\partial K_{i,i^{\prime}}}\frac{\left(\operatorname{sign}\left(w_{j}^{\top}x_{i}\right)x_{i}+\operatorname{sign}\left(w_{j}^{\top}x_{i^{\prime}}\right)x_{i^{\prime}}-\operatorname{sign}\left(w_{j}^{\top}\left(x_{i}-x_{i^{\prime}}\right)\right)\left(x_{i}-x_{i^{\prime}}\right)\right)}{2}.\tag{18}\\ \end{array}
$$

We know that

$$
\frac{\partial G}{\partial(\tilde{K}+\lambda n I)}= -\frac{\lambda}{2}(\tilde{K}+\lambda n I)^{-1}\tilde{Y}\tilde{Y}^{\top}(\tilde{K}+\lambda n I)^{-1},
$$

thus

$$
\begin{array}{l}\frac{\partial G}{\partial K_{i,i^{\prime}}}=\sum_{l,k}\frac{\partial G}{\partial(\tilde{K}+\lambda n I)_{l,k}}\frac{\partial(\Pi K\Pi+\lambda n I)_{l,k}}{\partial K_{i,i^{\prime}}}\\ =\sum_{l,k}-\frac{\lambda}{2}((\tilde{K}+\lambda n I)^{-1}\tilde{Y}\tilde{Y}^{\top}(\tilde{K}+\lambda n I)^{-1})_{l,k}\Pi_{l,i}\Pi_{i^{\prime},k}\\ = -\frac{\lambda}{2}\left(\Pi(\tilde{K}+\lambda n I)^{-1}\tilde{Y}\tilde{Y}^{\top}(\tilde{K}+\lambda n I)^{-1}\Pi\right)_{i,i^{\prime}}\\ = -\frac{\lambda}{2}(\Pi(\tilde{K}+\lambda n I)^{-1}\tilde{Y})_{i}(\Pi(\tilde{K}+\lambda n I)^{-1}\tilde{Y})_{i^{\prime}}.\\ \end{array}
$$

Substituting this back into Equation (18) and introducing $S_{j}\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times n}$ with $(S_{j})_{i,i^{\prime}}=$ $(\mathrm{sign}(w_{j}^{\top}x_{i})x_{i}+\mathrm{sign}(w_{j}^{\top}x_{i^{\prime}})x_{i^{\prime}}-\mathrm{sign}(w_{j}^{\top}(x_{i}-x_{i^{\prime}}))(x_{i}-x_{i^{\prime}}))/2,$ , we get

$$
\begin{array}{l}\frac{\partial G}{\partial w_{j}}= -\frac{\lambda}{2 m}\sum_{i,i^{\prime}=1}^{n}(\Pi(\tilde{K}+\lambda n I)^{-1}\tilde{Y})_{i}(\Pi(\tilde{K}+\lambda n I)^{-1}\tilde{Y})_{i^{\prime}}(S_{j})_{i,i^{\prime}}\\ = -\frac{\lambda}{2 m}\operatorname{tr}\left((\Pi(\tilde{K}+\lambda n I)^{-1}\tilde{Y})^{\top}S_{j}(\Pi(\tilde{K}+\lambda n I)^{-1}\tilde{Y})\right)\\ = -\frac{\lambda}{2 m}\operatorname{tr}\left(((\tilde{K}+\lambda n I)^{-1}\tilde{Y})^{\top}\Pi S_{j}\Pi((\tilde{K}+\lambda n I)^{-1}\tilde{Y})\right).\\ \end{array}
$$

This implies that we can replace $(S_{j})_{i,i^{\prime}}$ with the i-th, i<sup>0</sup>-th component of any matrix with the same centred version, such as ${\tilde{S}}_{j}$ where $(\tilde{S}_{j})_{i,i^{\prime}}= -\mathrm{sign}(w_{j}^{\top}(x_{i}-x_{i}^{\prime}))(x_{i}-x_{i}^{\prime})$ 2 yielding the desired result.

$$

Given the privacy parameter $\alpha > 0$ , we write $z_{\alpha}: =e^{2\alpha}-e^{-2\alpha}=2\sinh(2\alpha)$ .
