Given a pair of distributions $(P_{Y},P_{Z})\in\mathcal{P}$ , for each $i\in [n_{1}]$ , the ith data owner draws $Y_{i}$ from $P_{Y}$ independently from the others. Similarly, for each $j\in [n_{2}]$ , the jth data owner independently draws $Z_{j}$ from $P_{Z}$ We allow the sample sizes $n_{1}$ and $n_{2}$ to difer, and assume $n_{1}~\leq~n_{2}$ , without loss of generality, throughout this paper. We denote the pooled sample size as $n: =n_{1}+n_{2}$ Under the LDP constraint, each owner releases only a randomized transformation of their raw sample, formally referred to as an LDP view:

Definition 1 (Local diferential privacy) Given a privacy level $\alpha > 0$ , let $X_{i}$ and ${\tilde{X}}_{i}$ be random elements mapped to measurable spaces $(\mathcal{X},\mathcal{F})$ and $(\tilde{\mathcal{X}}_{i},\tilde{\mathcal{F}}_{i})$ , respectively, for each $i \in [ n ]$ . Then ${\tilde{X}}_{i}$ is an α-local diferentially private $\left(\alpha-LDP\right)$ view of $X_{i}$ if there exists a bivariate function $Q_{i}({\cdot}\mid\cdot):\tilde{\mathcal{F}}_{i}\times\mathcal{X}\mapsto [0,1]$ such that:

1. For any $x\in\mathcal{X},Q_{i}(\cdot|x)$ is a conditional distribution of ${\tilde{X}}_{i}$ given $X_{i}=x_{\mathrm{~}}$  
2. For any $A\in\tilde{\mathcal{F}}_{i},x\mapsto Q_{i}(A\vert x)$ is a measurable function on $\mathcal{X}_{i}$ , and  
3. For any $x,x^{\prime}\in\mathcal{X}\times\mathcal{X}$ and $A\in\tilde{\mathcal{F}}_{i}$ , the inequality $Q_{i}(A\mid x)\le e^{\alpha}Q_{i}(A\mid x^{\prime})$ holds.

Let ${\mathcal{Q}}_{\alpha}$ denote the collection of function sets $\{Q_{i}\}_{i=1}^{n}$ satisfying the above properties. Then $Q\in\mathcal{Q}_{\alpha}$ is called an α-LDP mechanism (or channel) associated with $\{X_{i}\}_{i=1}^{n}$

Let $\mathcal{P}_{0}$ and $\mathcal{P}_{1}$ denote the collections of null and alternative distributions, respectively, corresponding to $H_{0}$ and $H_{1}$ introduced in (1). In the minimax framework, we focus on a subset of $\mathcal{P}_{1}$ , denoted as $\mathcal{P}_{1}(\rho_{n_{1},n_{2}})$ , where $\rho_{n_{1},n_{2}}$ indicates a minimum separation between $\mathcal{P}_{1}(\rho_{n_{1},n_{2}})$ and $\mathcal{P}_{0}$

Given a privacy mechanism $Q,$ the curator evaluates a test function $\begin{array}{ r }{\Delta_{Q}:\prod_{i=1}^{n}\tilde{\mathcal{X}}_{i}\mapsto}\end{array}$ $\{0,1\}$ on the α-LDP views and rejects $H_{0}$ if $\Delta_{Q}\ =\ 1$ and accepts $H_{0}$ otherwise. Our objective is to design the private test $\Delta_{Q}$ that controls the type I and II errors uniformly over distributions in $\mathcal{P}_{0}$ and $\mathcal{P}_{1}(\rho_{n_{1},n_{2}})$ , respectively. In particular, for fixed $\gamma,\beta\in(0,1)$ ， we aim for the private test $\Delta_{Q}$ to satisfy the following conditions:

$$
\text{Type I error:}\sup_{(P_{Y},P_{Z})\in\mathcal{P}_{0}}\mathbb{E}[\Delta_{Q}]\leq\gamma\quad \text{and}\quad \text{Type II error:}\sup_{(P_{Y},P_{Z})\in\mathcal{P}_{1}(\rho_{n_{1},n_{2}})}\mathbb{E}[1-\Delta_{Q}]\leq\beta .\tag{2}
$$

Let $\Phi_{\gamma}^{\alpha}$ be the set of α-LDP level-γ tests, which take α-LDP views as inputs and control the type I error as in (2). The quality of a level-γ test $\Delta_{Q,\gamma}\in\Phi_{\gamma}^{\alpha}$ is measured by its uniform separation, which quantifies how close two hypotheses can be while still being reliably distinguished by $\Delta_{Q,\gamma}$ . In more technical terms, the uniform separation $\tilde{\rho}_{n_{1},n_{2}}(\Delta_{Q,\gamma})$ is the smallest separation $\rho_{n_{1},n_{2}}$ which accomplishes the type II error control as in (2), namely,

$$
\tilde{\rho}_{n_{1},n_{2}}\left(\Delta_{Q,\gamma}\right):=\inf\left\{\rho_{n_{1},n_{2}}>0:\sup_{\left(P_{Y},P_{Z}\right)\in\mathcal{P}_{1}\left(\rho_{n_{1},n_{2}}\right)}\mathbb{E}\left[1-\Delta_{Q,\gamma}\right]\leq\beta\right\}.\tag{3}
$$

Since diferent α-LDP mechanism $Q$ may assume diferent $\tilde{\mathcal{X}}_{i}^{\flat}\mathrm{s}$ , a test $\Delta_{Q,\gamma}$ depends on a particular LDP mechanism $Q .$ . Therefore, an optimal private level-γ test can be described as a pair of an α-LDP mechanism and a test function, designed to achieve the minimal uniform separation (3). We define this minimal uniform separation as the optimal testing separation under LDP, which we refer to as the minimax testing separation:

Definition 2 (α-LDP non-asymptotic minimax testing separation) For a fixed privacy level $\alpha > 0$ , the α-LDP non-asymptotic minimax separation of testing is defined as

$$
\rho_{n_{1},n_{2},\alpha}^{*}:=\inf_{Q\in\mathcal{Q}_{\alpha}}\inf_{\Delta_{Q,\gamma}\in\Phi_{\gamma}^{\alpha}}\tilde{\rho}_{n_{1},n_{2}}(\Delta_{Q,\gamma}).\tag{4}
$$

In this section, we switch gears to testing for equality between two multivariate densities under the LDP constraint. To this end, we consider two classes of smooth densities, namely the Hölder ball and Besov ball, and establish the minimax testing separation in terms of the $\mathbb{L}_{2}$ distance for each class. Especially, we derive the upper bound for the minimax testing separation by building on the multinomial permutation test introduced in Section 3.2 with a careful discretization scheme. We also introduce an aggregated test, which is adaptive to the unknown smoothness parameter.

We start by formally defining the Hölder ball and Besov ball. The Hölder ball generalizes Lipschitz continuity and can be thought of as functions with bounded fractional derivatives. The following definition of the Hölder ball rephrases the one stated in Section 2.1 of Arias-Castro et al. (2018).

Definition 8 (Hölder ball) The Hölder ball with smoothness parameter $s > 0$ and radius $R > 0$ , denoted as $B_{d,s}^{\mathrm{H}}(R)$ , is the class of functions $f:[0,1]^{d}\mapsto\mathbb{R}$ satisfying the following conditions:

1. $\left|f^{(\lfloor s\rfloor)}(\mathbf{x})-f^{(\lfloor s\rfloor)}(\mathbf{x}^{\prime})\right|\leq R\left\|\mathbf{x}-\mathbf{x}^{\prime}\right\|^{s-\lfloor s\rfloor}$ , for all $\mathbf{x},\mathbf{x}^{\prime}\in [0,1]^{d}$ .  
2. $\|f^{(s^{\prime})}\|_{\infty}\leq R$ , for each $s^{\prime}\in [\left\lfloor s\right\rfloor]$

where $f^{(\lfloor s\rfloor)}$ denotes the $\lfloor s \rfloor$ -order derivative of $f .$

The Besov ball, on the other hand, measures the smoothness of a function by capturing its abrupt oscillations through wavelets. In this respect, it can address spatially inhomogeneous functions whose smoothness can vary across their domain. To elaborate, we consider an orthonormal wavelet basis of $\mathbb{L}_{2}([0,1]^{d})$ at a fixed prime resolution level $J\in{\mathbb{N}}_{0}$ . We denote this basis as ${\overline{{\Phi}}}_{J}\cup(\cup_{j\geq J}{\overline{{\Psi}}}_{j})$ , which are classified into two distinct categories. For $\phi\in\overline{{\Phi}}_{J}$ the scaling coeficient $\begin{array}{ r }{\mathbf{\bar{\theta}}_{\phi}(\mathbf{\bar{f}}): =\int_{[0,1]^{d}}f(\mathbf{x})\phi(\mathbf{x})}\end{array}$ dx detects an overall trend of $f .$ On the other hand, for $\psi\in\overline{{\Psi}}_{j}$ with its resolution level $j \geq J$ , the wavelet coeficient $\theta_{\psi}(f): =$ $\begin{array}{ r }{\int_{[0,1]^{d}}f(\mathbf{x})\psi(\mathbf{x})}\end{array}$ dx captures abrupt oscillations from the general trend. As J and $j$ increase, the coeficients capture more detailed behaviors. Among many existing types of wavelet basis, this paper focuses on Haar multivariate wavelet basis. It is useful because projecting densities onto a subset of this basis is equivalent to applying equal-sized binning, as used in our test proposed in Section 4.3. Consequently, the discretization error inherent in the test can be characterized by the corresponding wavelet coeficients. This basis is constructed by taking tensor products of many rescaled and shifted versions of two basic univariate functions (see Appendix B.3 for the details).

The Besov ball can be defined through the magnitudes of wavelet coeficients. The following definition paraphrases the one presented in Section 3 of Tang and Yang (2023).

Definition 9 (Besov seminorm and Besov ball) Fix a smoothness parameter $s > 0$ , a microscopic parameter $1 \leq q \leq \infty$ , and a wavelet basis $\overline{{\Phi}}_{0}\cup(\bigcup_{j\geq 0}\overline{{\Psi}}_{j})$ . The Besov seminorm of $f\in\mathbb{L}_{2}([0,1]^{d})$ is defined using the sequences of its wavelet coeficients $\left(\theta_{\psi}(f)\right)_{\psi\in\overline{{\Psi}}_{j}}$ as follows:

$$
\|f\|_{s,2,q}:=\left\{\begin{array}{l l}\left[\sum_{j=0}^{\infty}2^{j s q}\big(\sum_{\psi\in\overline{{\Psi}}_{j}}|\theta_{\psi}(f)|^{2}\big)^{\frac{q}{2}}\right]^{\frac{1}{q}},&1\leq q<\infty,\\ \sup_{j\in\mathbb{N}_{0}}2^{j s}\big(\sum_{\psi\in\overline{{\Psi}}_{j}}|\theta_{\psi}(f)|^{2}\big)^{\frac{1}{2}},&q=\infty .\end{array}\right.
$$

For a radius $R > 0$ , we define the Besov ball $B_{d,s,q}^{\mathrm{B}}(R)$ as

$$
\mathcal{B}_{d,s,q}^{\mathrm{B}}(R):=\{f\in\mathbb{L}_{2}([0,1]^{d}):\|f\|_{s,2,q}\leq R\}.
$$

Building on the smooth distribution classes defined in Definition 10, we formally define the two density testing problems of interest and present the minimax testing rate applicable to both. In this subsection, we assume that the smoothness parameter s for Hölder ball and Besov ball is known, addressing the case of unknown s in Section 4.4.

Assume that the pair of data-generating distributions $(P_{\mathbf{Y}},P_{\mathbf{Z}})$ is contained in a class $\mathcal{P}.$ The curator uses two sets of α-LDP views $\{\tilde{\mathbf{Y}}_{i}\}_{i\in [n_{1}]}$ and $\{\tilde{\mathbf{Z}}_{j}\}_{j\in [n_{2}]}$ , privatized as described in Section 2.1, to decide whether $(P_{\mathbf{Y}},P_{\mathbf{Z}})$ came from

$$
\mathcal{P}_{0}:=\left\{\left(P_{\mathbf{Y}},P_{\mathbf{Z}}\right)\in\mathcal{P}:f_{\mathbf{Y}}=f_{\mathbf{Z}}\right\}\text{or}\mathcal{P}_{1}\left(\rho_{n_{1},n_{2}}\right):=\left\{\left(P_{\mathbf{Y}},P_{\mathbf{Z}}\right)\in\mathcal{P}:\|f_{\mathbf{Y}}-f_{\mathbf{Z}}\|_{\mathbb{L}_{2}}\geq\rho_{n_{1},n_{2}}\right\},\tag{12}
$$

where $f_{\mathbf{Y}}$ and $f_{\mathbf{Z}}$ are densities of $P_{\mathbf{Y}}$ and $P_{\mathbf{Z}}.$ , respectively. We consider the problems of $\mathcal{P}=\mathcal{P}_{d,s}^{\mathrm{H,2}}(R)$ and $\mathcal{P}=\mathcal{P}_{d,s,q}^{\mathrm{B},2}(R)$ . Notably, while we focus on the class of either being Hölder or Besov smooth distributions, the permutation-based test presented in Section 4.3 guarantees type I error control over a broader class of null distributions beyond those defined over Hölder or Besov balls.

Let us fix the type I error $\gamma\in(0,1)$ and the type II error $\beta\in(0,1)$ such that $2 \gamma + \beta < 1$ as in Section 3.1, and assume further that $n_{\mathrm{1}}\alpha^{2}\geq 1$ , similarly considered in Lam-Weil et al. (2022). The main result of this section, stated below, establishes a lower bound as well as an upper bound for the minimax separation for two-sample density testing under the LDP constraint.

We outline the construction of multivariate Haar wavelets, following Giné and Nickl (2015), Section 4.3.6, and Autin et al. (2010), Section 2. For $f:[0,1]\to\mathbb{R}$ and integers $u,v,$ define the re-scaled and shifted version as $f_{u,v}(x): =2^{u/2}f(2^{u}x-v)$ . Define the univariate Haar scaling and wavelet functions from [0, 1] to $\mathbb{R}$ as

$$
\phi(x):=\mathbb{1}(0\leq x<1)\quad \text{and}\quad\psi(x):=\mathbb{1}(0\leq x<1/2)-\mathbb{1}(1/2\leq x<1),
$$

respectively. A multivariate Haar wavelet basis is indexed by its prime resolution level $J\in{\mathbb{N}}_{0}$ , with each element characterized by up to three (multi) indices that range over:

1. Re-scaling: $\mathbb{N}\setminus [J-1]$ 2  
2. Shifting: $\Lambda(j): =\{0,1,\ldots,(2^{j}-1)\}^{d}$ , for an integer $j \geq J$  
3. On-of: $\mathcal{T}: =\{0,1\}^{d}\backslash\{0$

respectively. For any $\pmb{k}=(k_{1},\dots,k_{d})\in\Lambda(J)$ , let $\phi_{J,k}:[0,1]^{d}\to\mathbb{R}$ be a tensor product of the re-scaled and shifted $\phi^{\prime}\mathrm{s},$ , evaluated at $\mathbf{x}=(x_{1},\ldots,x_{d})\in [0,1]^{d}\mathrm{.}$

$$
\phi_{J,\boldsymbol{k}}(\mathbf{x}):=\prod_{p=1}^{d}\phi_{J,k_{p}}(x_{p}).
$$

For a resolution level $j\geq J,$ , and for any $\ell=(\ell_{1},\dots,\ell_{d})\in\Lambda(j)$ , let $\psi_{i,\ell}^{\epsilon}:[0,1]^{d}\to\mathbb{R}$ be a mixed tensor product of re-scaled and shifted $\phi^{\prime}\mathrm{s}$ and $\psi\mathrm{s}$ , evaluated at $\mathbf{x}=(x_{1},\ldots,x_{d})\in$ $[0,1]^{d}$ :

$$
\psi_{j,\ell}^{\epsilon}(\mathbf{x}):=\prod_{p=1}^{d}\left\{\phi_{j,\ell_{p}}(x_{p})\right\}^{1-\epsilon_{p}}\left\{\psi_{j,\ell_{p}}(x_{p})\right\}^{\epsilon_{p}}.
$$

The Haar multivariate wavelet basis at prime resolution level J is defined as

$$
\Phi_{J}\cup\left(\bigcup_{j\geq J}\Psi_{j}\right),\text{where}\Phi_{J}:=\left\{\phi_{J,\boldsymbol{k}}\right\}_{\boldsymbol{k}\in\Lambda(J)}\text{and}\Psi_{j}:=\left\{\psi_{j,\ell}^{\epsilon}\right\}_{\ell\in\Lambda(j),\epsilon\in\mathcal{I}}.\tag{26}
$$

This section analyzes the error arising from comparing discretized multinomial probability vectors instead of the original multivariate densities. Given the number of bins $\kappa,$ let $B_{1},\ldots,B_{\kappa^{d}}$ enumerate d-dimensional hypercubes with side length $1 / \kappa$ . For a density $f_{\mathbf{Y}}.$ its step function approximation is defined as:

$$
\hat{f}_{\mathbf{Y}}(\mathbf{y}):=\sum_{m\in [\kappa^{d}]}\mathbb{1}(\mathbf{y}\in B_{m})\kappa^{d}\int_{B_{m}}f_{\mathbf{Y}}(\mathbf{t})d\mathbf{t}.\tag{27}
$$

By the argument in Arias-Castro et al. (2018), the lower bound for the minimax testing rate in the one-sample problem, denoted as $\rho_{n_{1},\alpha}^{*}$ , also provides a lower bound for the minimax separation in two-sample case, denoted as $\rho_{n_{1},n_{2},\alpha}^{*}.$ . Thus, we focus on bounding $\rho_{n_{1},\alpha}^{*}$ in the following proof.

Proof In the one-sample setting, let $f_{0}$ denote the known density $f_{\mathbf{Z}}$ , and assume that the data-generating distribution $P\mathbf{\hat{Y}}$ lies within the following class:

Definition 23 (Smooth distribution classes) Let $\mathcal{P}_{d,s}^{\mathrm{H},1}(R)$ denote the set of distributions $P\mathbf{\hat{Y}}$ whose density function $f_{\mathbf{Y}}$ satisfies $(f_{\mathbf{Y}}-f_{0})\in B_{d,s}^{\mathrm{H}}(R)$ and $\|f_{\mathbf{Y}}-f_{0}\|_{\mathbb{L}_{2}}\leq R$ Similarly, define $\mathcal{P}_{d,s,q}^{\mathrm{B},1}(R)$ by replacing $B_{d,s}^{\mathrm{H}}(R)$ with $B_{d,s,q}^{\mathrm{B}}(R)$

The one-sample density testing problem is defined as follows: Given $\{\tilde{\mathbf{Y}}_{i}\}_{i\in [n_{1}]}$ generated from $P\mathbf{\hat{Y}}$ and privatized via α-LDP mechanism $Q,$ , decide whether $P\mathbf{\hat{Y}}$ came from

$$
\mathcal{P}_{0}=\{P_{\mathbf{Y}}\in\mathcal{P}:f_{\mathbf{Y}}=f_{0}\}\quad \text{or}\quad\mathcal{P}_{1}(\rho_{n_{1}})=\{P_{\mathbf{Y}}\in\mathcal{P}:\|f_{\mathbf{Y}}-f_{0}\|_{\mathbb{L}_{2}}\geq\rho_{n_{1}}\}.\tag{72}
$$

We consider two problems: (i) $\mathcal{P}=\mathcal{P}_{d,s}^{\mathrm{H},1}(R)$ , and (ii) $\mathcal{P}=\mathcal{P}_{d,s,q}^{\mathrm{B},1}(R)$ , with significant overlap in most of the proof steps.

We derive the lower bound by testing the uniform null hypothesis against a carefully constructed mixture alternative. This alternative balances two objectives regarding the distances between the distributions: achieving suficient separation in $\mathbb{L}_{2}$ distance without the $\alpha{\mathrm{-}}\mathrm{LDP}$ constraint, and ensuring indistinguishability in the total variation distance under the $\alpha{\mathrm{-}}\mathrm{LDP}$ constraint. The mixture construction follows the approach in Appendix A.2.2 of Lam-Weil et al. (2022), where uniform densities are perturbed by eigenfunctions of the integral operator created from the $\alpha{\mathrm{-}}\mathrm{LDP}$ mechanism. We generalize this construction to multivariate Besov and Hölder smoothness classes.

As defined in Definition 1, let $Q\in\mathcal{Q}_{\alpha}$ be a non-interactive $\alpha{\mathrm{-}}\mathrm{LDP}$ mechanism, and $\{Q_{i}\}_{i\in [n_{1}]}$ be its marginals. By Lemma B.1 of Lam-Weil et al. (2022), for each $i\in [n_{1}]$ , there exists a probability measure $\mu_{i}$ such that $Q_{i}(\cdot|\mathbf{y}_{i})$ is absolutely continuous with respect to $\mu_{i}$ for all $\mathbf{y}_{i}\in [0,1]^{d}$ . Denote its density with respect to $\mu_{i}$ by $q_{i}(\tilde{\mathbf{y}}_{i}|\mathbf{y}_{i})$ . Using this, we define the private counterpart of a density function on $[0,1]^{d};$

Definition 24 (Private counterpart of density) Let f be a probability density on $[0,1]^{d}$ and Q be an $\alpha{-}L D P$ mechanism with marginal conditional densities $q_{i}(\tilde{\bf y}_{i}\mid\bf y)$ with respect to $\mu_{i}$ . The private counterpart of f is defined as

$$
\tilde{f}_{i}(\tilde{\mathbf{y}}_{i}):=\int_{[0,1]^{d}}q_{i}(\tilde{\mathbf{y}}_{i}\mid\mathbf{y})f(\mathbf{y})d\mathbf{y}.
$$

Let $f_{0}$ denote the uniform density supported on $[0,1]^{d}$ . Using its private counterpart, we introduce the following integral operator whose kernel resembles the likelihood ratio of the privatized densities:

Definition 25 (Privacy mechanism integral operator) For each $i\in [n_{1}]$ , define an operator $L_{i}:[0,1]^{d}\times\tilde{\mathcal{X}}\mathbb{R}$ as:

$$
L_{i}(\mathbf{s},\mathbf{t}):=\frac{q_{i}(\mathbf{t}|\mathbf{s})}{\sqrt{\tilde{f}_{0,i}(\mathbf{t})}}.
$$

Using $L_{i}$ as a kernel function, we define an integral operator $K_{i}:\mathbb{L}_{2}([0,1]^{d})\to\mathbb{L}_{2}(\tilde{\mathcal{X}},d\mu_{i})$ as:

$$
(K_{i}f)(\cdot):=\int_{[0,1]^{d}}L_{i}(\mathbf{y},\cdot)f(\mathbf{y})d\mathbf{y}.
$$

Let $K_{i}^{*}$ denote the adjoint of $K_{i}$ . Finally, by aggregating all the operators for $i\in [n_{1}]$ , we define a symmetric and positive semidefinite integral operator:

$$
K:=\sum_{i=1}^{n_{1}}\frac{1}{n_{1}}K_{i}^{*}K_{i}.
$$

For $f\in\mathbb{L}_{2}\big([0,1]^{d}\big)$ , the operator K yields the expected squared privatized likelihood ratio:

$$
\begin{array}{l}\langle K f,f\rangle=\frac{1}{n_{1}}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\int_{\tilde{\mathcal{X}}_{i}}\frac{\left(\int_{[0,1]^{d}}q_{i}(\tilde{\mathbf{y}}_{i}|\mathbf{y})f(\mathbf{y})d\mathbf{y}\right)^{2}}{\tilde{f}_{0,i}(\tilde{\mathbf{y}}_{i})}d\mu_{i}(\tilde{\mathbf{y}}_{i})\\ =\frac{1}{n_{1}}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\int_{\tilde{\mathcal{X}}_{i}}\frac{\tilde{f}_{i}(\tilde{\mathbf{y}}_{i})^{2}}{\tilde{f}_{0,i}(\tilde{\mathbf{y}}_{i})}\frac{d Q_{f_{0}}}{\tilde{f}_{0,i}(\tilde{\mathbf{y}}_{i})}=\frac{1}{n_{1}}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\mathbb{E}_{Q_{f_{0}}}\left[\frac{\tilde{f}_{i}^{2}(\tilde{\mathbf{y}}_{i})}{\tilde{f}_{0,i}^{2}(\tilde{\mathbf{y}}_{i})}\right].\tag{73}\\ \end{array}
$$

We construct each mixture element by adding carefully chosen eigenfunctions of K as bumps to $f_{0},$ , ensuring the resulting densities belong to the Hölder or Besov classes. Specifically, we define two orthonormal sets of smoothness-inducing functions—one for Besov smoothness and one for Hölder smoothness. For a positive integer J and $\omega{>}0$ , we set $\kappa=2^{J}$ and determine the number of functions as $\kappa^{d}$ . The parameter $\omega$ controls the perturbation height. The value of $J$ and $\omega$ will be optimized later to achieve a tight lower bound. Both orthonormal sets have cardinality $\kappa^{d}$ , the supports of their elements partition $[0,1]^{d}$ without overlap, each element has the $\mathbb{L}_{\infty}$ norm bounded by $\kappa^{d/2}$ , and is orthogonal to $f_{0}$ . We start by defining the orthonormal set for the Besov ball, consisting of bounded step functions from the multivariate Haar basis.

Definition 26 (Orthonormal set for the Besov ball) Consider the Haar wavelet basis on $[0,1]^{d}$ with a prime resolution level $J\in\mathbb{N}$ , as defined in Appendix B.3. Set $\kappa=2^{J}$ and define $\Lambda(\bar{J}): =\{0,1,\ldots,(\kappa{-}1)\}^{d}.$ . Fix a d-dimensional on-of multi-index $\epsilon^{*}: =\{1,0,0,\dots,0\}$ Let B $B$ represent the elements with this multi-index, drawn from the mixed tensor product set at the lowest resolution level J. Specifically, we define:

$$
\mathbb{B}_{B}:=\{\psi_{J,\ell}^{\epsilon^{*}}\}_{\ell\in\Lambda(J)}.
$$

Since all results ahead hold for any non-zero $\epsilon^{*}$ , the specific choice in Definition 26 is arbitrary. Each element of $\mathbb{B}_{B}$ is orthogonal to $f_{0}$ because its multi-index has at least one non-zero entry. In that dimension of non-zero entry, the scaled and shifted Haar wavelet function $\psi(x)=\mathbb{1}_{[0,1/2)}(x)-\mathbb{1}_{[1/2,1)}(x)$ , which integrates to zero, contributes to the integral. By Fubini’s theorem, this ensures that the entire integral equals zero. Next we define the orthonormal set for Hölder ball:

Definition 27 (Orthonormal set for the Hölder ball) For a smoothness parameter $s >$ 0, let $\bar{\varphi}:\mathbb{R}^{d}\to$ R be an infinitely diferentiable function supported on $[0,1]^{d}$ satisfying $\begin{array}{ r }{\|\bar{\varphi}\|_{\mathbb{L}_{2}}=1,\ \|\bar{\varphi}\|_{\mathbb{L}_{\infty}}<\infty,\int_{[0,1]^{d}}\bar{\varphi}=0}\end{array}$ , and $\|\bar{\varphi}^{(s^{\prime})}\|_{\infty}<\infty$ for $s^{\prime}\in\{1,\ldots,(\lfloor s\rfloor+1)\}$ . For $J\in\mathbb{N}_{.}$ , set $\kappa=2^{J}$ and define $\Lambda(J): =\{0,1,...,(\kappa-1)\}^{d},\varphi_{J,\ell}(\mathbf{y}): =\kappa^{d/2}\bar{\varphi}(\kappa\mathbf{y}-\ell)$ for $\ell\in\Lambda(J)$ , and $\mathbb{B}_{H}: =\{\varphi_{J,\ell}\}_{\ell\in\Lambda(J)}$ , meaning scaled and shifted copies $o f\bar{\varphi}$

Now we are ready to define the mixtures, one for Besov and one for Hölder ball.

Definition 28 (Mixture alternatives) For the Hölder ball, let $V=\operatorname{Span}(\{f_{0}\}\cup\mathbb{B}_{H})$ Construct an orthonormal basis of V as $\{f_{0}\}\cup\{u_{t}\}_{t=1}^{\kappa^{d}}$ , where each $u_{t}$ is an eigenfunction of K with eigenvalue $\lambda_{t}$ . For each $t\in [\kappa^{d}]$ , since u<sub>t</sub> is orthogonal to $f_{0}$ , it integrates to zero. Recall that $z_{\alpha}=e^{2\alpha}-e^{-2\alpha}~f o r~\alpha>0$ , and set $\widetilde{\lambda}_{t}=(\lambda_{t}/z_{\alpha}^{2})\vee\kappa^{-d}$ . Fix $\omega > 0$ . For any $\pmb{\eta}=(\eta_{1},\dots,\eta_{\kappa^{d}})\in\{-1,1\}^{\kappa^{d}}$ , define the perturbed density as:

$$
f_{\omega,\kappa}^{\eta}:=f_{0}+\omega\sum_{t=1}^{\kappa^{d}}\eta_{t}\tilde{\lambda}_{t}^{-1/2}u_{t}.\tag{74}
$$

Since $u_{t}\in V$ for each $t\in [\kappa^{d}]$ , we can also write:

$$
f_{\omega,\kappa}^{\eta}=f_{0}+\omega\sum_{t=1}^{\kappa^{d}}\eta_{t}\tilde{\lambda}_{t}^{-1/2}\sum_{\psi\in\mathbb{B}_{H}}\theta_{\psi}(u_{t})\psi,\tag{75}
$$

where $\theta_{\psi}(u_{t})$ is the Fourier coeficient of $u_{t}$ with respect to $\psi$ . The mixture for Hölder ball, denoted as $\nu_{\rho}^{H}$ , is defined as the uniform probability measure over $\{f_{\omega,\kappa}^{\eta}:\eta\in\{-1,1\}^{\kappa^{d}}\}$ $T h e$ mixture for the Besov ball, denoted as $\nu_{\rho}^{B}$ , is defined through the same procedure as above, with B $H$ replaced by $\mathbb{B}_{B}$

We next establish a series of conditions on κ and $\omega$ to ensure that the mixture elements belong to the smooth density class with high probability.

Lemma 30 (Nonnegativity) For any $f_{\omega,\kappa}^{\eta}$ drawn from either the distribution $\nu_{\rho}^{H}$ or $\nu_{\rho}^{B}$ 2 we always have $\begin{array}{ r }{\int_{[0,1]^{d}}f_{\omega,\kappa}^{\eta}(\mathbf{y})d\mathbf{y}=1}\end{array}$ . Also, $f_{\omega,\kappa}^{\eta}\geq 0$ with a probability greater than $1 - \gamma$ if

$$
\omega\leq\frac{\kappa^{-d}}{\sqrt{2\log(2\kappa^{d}/\gamma)}}.\tag{77}
$$

Lemma 32 (Besov class) With probability at least $1 - \gamma$ , a function drawn from $\nu_{\rho}^{\mathrm{B}}$ lies in $B_{d,s,q}^{\mathrm{B}}(R)$ if

$$
\omega\leq\frac{R\kappa^{-(s+d)}}{\sqrt{2\log(\kappa^{d}/\gamma)}}.\tag{78}
$$

Finally, we characterize the condition for κ and $\omega$ that ensures any valid private test fails.

Verification of nonnegativeness with high probability. The proof follows the approach of Lemma B.5 in Lam-Weil et al. (2022), with an adjustment for the change of basis. Since the proof is the same for $\nu_{\rho}^{H}$ and $\nu_{\rho}^{B}$ , we state if only for $\nu_{\rho}^{B}$ . For each $\boldsymbol{\psi}\in\mathbb{B}_{B}$ , define an

event $A_{\psi}$ as:

$$
A_{\psi}:=\left[\left|\omega\sum_{t=1}^{\kappa^{d}}\eta_{t}\tilde{\lambda}_{t}^{-1/2}\theta_{\psi}(u_{t})\right|\geq\kappa^{-d/2}\right],
$$

which belongs to σ-algebra generated by $\eta .$ . Since the sum of independent scaled Rademacher variables inside $A_{\psi}$ is sub-Gaussian with variance proxy $\begin{array}{ r }{\omega^{2}\tilde{\lambda}_{t}^{-1}\sum_{t=1}^{\kappa^{d}}\theta_{\psi}^{2}(u_{t})}\end{array}$ , by the union bound, we have:

$$
\begin{array}{l}\mathbb{P}_{\nu_{\rho}^{B}}\left(\bigcup_{\psi\in\mathbb{B}_{B}}A_{\psi}\right)\leq\sum_{\psi\in\mathbb{B}_{B}}2\exp\left(\frac{-\kappa^{-d}}{2\omega^{2}\tilde{\lambda}_{t}^{-1}\sum_{t=1}^{\kappa^{d}}\theta_{\psi}^{2}(u_{t})}\right)\\ \stackrel{(a)}{\leq}2\sum_{\psi\in\mathbb{B}_{B}}\exp\left(\frac{-\kappa^{-2 d}}{2\omega^{2}\sum_{t=1}^{\kappa^{d}}\theta_{\psi}^{2}(u_{t})}\right)\\ \stackrel{(b)}{=}2\kappa^{d}\exp\left(\frac{-\kappa^{-2 d}}{2\omega^{2}}\right),\tag{81}\\ \end{array}
$$

where step (a) uses $\tilde{\lambda_{t}}\leq\kappa^{-d}$ and step (b) uses the following equality that stems from the fact that $u_{t}\mathrm{'s}$ are orthonormal eigenbasis of V and the orthonormality of $\mathbb{B}_{B}$ :

$$
\sum_{t=1}^{\kappa^{d}}\theta_{\psi}^{2}(u_{t})=\langle\psi,\sum_{t=1}^{\kappa^{d}}\langle\psi,u_{t}\rangle_{\mathbb{L}_{2}}u_{t}\rangle_{\mathbb{L}_{2}}=\langle\psi,\psi\rangle_{\mathbb{L}_{2}}=1.
$$

steps.claim: Proof We verify the two steps mentioned above in order.

Hölder continuity of derivatives with high probability. Fix arbitrary $\mathbf{y}_{1},\mathbf{y}_{2}\in [0,1]^{d}$ . Since each $\varphi\in\mathbb{B}_{H}$ has disjoint support, we can specify the element of $\mathbb{B}_{H}$ whose $\lfloor s \rfloor -$ derivative has support containing $\mathbf{y}_{1}$ and $\mathbf{y}_{2}$ , say $\varphi_{\mathbf{y}_{1}}$ and $\varphi_{\mathbf{y}_{2}}$ . Then using the fact that $\varphi_{\mathbf{y}_{1}}^{(\lfloor s\rfloor)}(\mathbf{y}_{2})-$ $\varphi_{\mathbf{y}_{2}}^{(\lfloor s\rfloor)}(\mathbf{y}_{1})=0$ , we can write the diference of the s -derivative of $f_{\omega,\kappa}^{\eta}$ as

$$
\begin{array}{l}|(f_{\omega,\kappa}^{\eta})^{(\lfloor s\rfloor)}(\mathbf{y}_{1})-(f_{\omega,\kappa}^{\eta})^{(\lfloor s\rfloor)}(\mathbf{y}_{2})|\\ =\omega\left|\sum_{t=1}^{\kappa^{d}}\eta_{t}\tilde{\lambda}_{t}^{-1/2}\left\{\theta_{\varphi_{\mathbf{y}_{1}}}(u_{t})\varphi_{\mathbf{y}_{1}}^{(\lfloor s\rfloor)}(\mathbf{y}_{1})-\theta_{\varphi_{\mathbf{y}_{2}}}(u_{t})\varphi_{\mathbf{y}_{2}}^{(\lfloor s\rfloor)}(\mathbf{y}_{2})\right\}\right|\\ \leq\omega\left|\sum_{t=1}^{\kappa^{d}}\theta_{\varphi_{\mathbf{y}_{1}}}\left(u_{t}\right)\eta_{t}\tilde{\lambda}_{t}^{-1/2}\left(\varphi_{\mathbf{y}_{1}}^{(\lfloor s\rfloor)}\left(\mathbf{y}_{1}\right)-\varphi_{\mathbf{y}_{1}}^{(\lfloor s\rfloor)}\left(\mathbf{y}_{2}\right)\right)\right|(82)\\ +\omega\left|\sum_{t=1}^{\kappa^{d}}\theta_{\varphi_{\mathbf{y}_{2}}}\left(u_{t}\right)\eta_{t}\tilde{\lambda}_{t}^{-1/2}\left(\varphi_{\mathbf{y}_{2}}^{(\lfloor s\rfloor)}\left(\mathbf{y}_{1}\right)-\varphi_{\mathbf{y}_{2}}^{(\lfloor s\rfloor)}\left(\mathbf{y}_{2}\right)\right)\right|,(83)\\ \end{array}

where the last inequality uses the triangle inequality.

We separately bound the terms (82) and (83), starting with (82). For $\mathbf{y}~\in~[0,1]^{d}$ , recall from (27) that $\varphi_{\mathbf{y}_{1}}$ has the form $\kappa^{d/2}\varphi(\kappa\mathbf{y}-\pmb{\ell})$ . By the chain rule, its $\lfloor s \rfloor$ -mixed partial derivatives are written as

$$
\varphi_{\mathbf{y}_{1}}^{(\lfloor s\rfloor)}(\mathbf{y})=\kappa^{(d/2)+\lfloor s\rfloor}\bar{\varphi}^{(\lfloor s\rfloor)}(\kappa\mathbf{y}-\boldsymbol{\ell}).\tag{84}

Using the above equality, the mean value theorem and the boundedness of all partial mixed derivatives specified in Definition 27, the term (82) is upper bounded by

\omega\kappa^{(d/2)+\lfloor s\rfloor}\bigg|\sum_{t=1}^{\kappa^{d}}\theta_{\varphi_{\mathbf{y}_{1}}}(u_{t})\eta_{t}\tilde{\lambda}_{t}^{-1/2}\bigg|\left(2\|\bar{\varphi}^{(\lfloor s\rfloor)}\|_{\infty}\wedge\|\bar{\varphi}^{(\lfloor s+1\rfloor)}\|_{\infty}\kappa\|\mathbf{y}_{1}-\mathbf{y}_{2}\|\right),

Bounding the term (83) using the same argument, we obtain the following bound:

$$
\begin{array}{l}\left|\left(f_{\omega,\kappa}^{\boldsymbol{\eta}}\right)^{(\lfloor s\rfloor)}\left(\mathbf{y}_{1}\right)-\left(f_{\omega,\kappa}^{\boldsymbol{\eta}}\right)^{(\lfloor s\rfloor)}\left(\mathbf{y}_{2}\right)\right|\\ \leq\omega\kappa^{(d/2)+\lfloor s\rfloor}\left(\left|\sum_{t=1}^{\kappa^{d}}\theta_{\varphi_{\mathbf{y}_{1}}}\left(u_{t}\right)\eta_{t}\tilde{\lambda}_{t}^{-1/2}\right| +\left|\sum_{t=1}^{\kappa^{d}}\theta_{\varphi_{\mathbf{y}_{2}}}\left(u_{t}\right)\eta_{t}\tilde{\lambda}_{t}^{-1/2}\right|\right)\left(2\|\bar{\varphi}^{(\lfloor s\rfloor)}\|_{\infty}\wedge\|\bar{\varphi}^{(\lfloor s+1\rfloor)}\|_{\infty}\kappa\|\mathbf{y}_{1}-\mathbf{y}_{2}\|\right).\tag{85}\\ \end{array}
$$

For each $\varphi\in\mathbb{B}_{H}$ , let $A_{\varphi}$ be an event within the σ-algebra generated by $\eta_{\mathrm{:}}$ , defined as follows:

$$
A_{\varphi}:=\left[\left|\sum_{t=1}^{\kappa^{d}}\eta_{t}\tilde{\lambda}_{t}^{-1/2}\theta_{\varphi}(u_{t})\right|\geq\sqrt{2\kappa^{d}\log(2\kappa^{d}/\gamma)}\right].\tag{86}
$$

$1 - \gamma / 2$ . Under the event $\cap_{\varphi\in\mathbb{B}_{H}}A_{\varphi}^{c}$ , the bound (85) continues to

$$
\begin{array}{l}|(f_{\omega,\kappa}^{\boldsymbol{\eta}})^{(\lfloor s\rfloor)}(\mathbf{y}_{1})-(f_{\omega,\kappa}^{\boldsymbol{\eta}})^{(\lfloor s\rfloor)}(\mathbf{y}_{2})|\stackrel{(a)}{\leq}\omega\kappa^{\frac{d}{2}+\lfloor s\rfloor}2\sqrt{2\kappa^{d}\log(2\kappa^{d}/\gamma)}\left(2\|\bar{\varphi}^{(\lfloor s\rfloor)}\|_{\infty}\wedge\|\bar{\varphi}^{(\lfloor s+1\rfloor)}\|_{\infty}\kappa\|\mathbf{y}_{1}-\mathbf{y}_{2}\|\right)\\ \stackrel{(b)}{\leq}\omega\kappa^{\frac{d}{2}+\lfloor s\rfloor}\sqrt{2\kappa^{d}\log(2\kappa^{d}/\gamma)}C_{2}(s,\bar{\varphi})(1\wedge\kappa\|\mathbf{y}_{1}-\mathbf{y}_{2}\|)\\ \stackrel{(c)}{\leq}\omega\kappa^{\frac{d}{2}+\lfloor s\rfloor}\sqrt{2\kappa^{d}\log(2\kappa^{d}/\gamma)}C_{2}(s,\bar{\varphi})\kappa^{(s-\lfloor s\rfloor)}\|\mathbf{y}_{1}-\mathbf{y}_{2}\|^{s-\lfloor s\rfloor}\\ =\omega\kappa^{d+s}\sqrt{2\log(2\kappa^{d}/\gamma)}C_{2}(s,\bar{\varphi})\|\mathbf{y}_{1}-\mathbf{y}_{2}\|^{s-\lfloor s\rfloor},\tag{87}\\ \end{array}
$$

where $C_{2}(s,\bar{\varphi}): =\big(4\||\bar{\varphi}^{(\lfloor s\rfloor)}\|_{L_{\infty}}\vee 2\||\bar{\varphi}^{(\lfloor s+1\rfloor)}\|_{L_{\infty}}\big)$ , step (a) uses the event $\cap_{\varphi\in{\mathbb B}_{H}}A_{\varphi}^{c}$ , step (b) uses the basic inequality that

$$
(a\times 1)\land(b\times c)\leq(a\lor b)\times(1\land c)\quad \text{for} a,b,c\geq 0,
$$

and step (c) holds by the following fact: When $(1\land c)\leq 1$ and $0 \leq s - \lfloor s \rfloor < 1$ , it holds that

$$
(1\land c)\leq(1\land c)^{s-\lfloor s\rfloor}\leq c^{s-\lfloor s\rfloor}.
$$

Starting from inequality (87), we solve for $\omega$ in $\omega\kappa^{d+s}\sqrt{2\log(2\kappa^{d}/\gamma)}C_{2}(s,\bar{\varphi})\leq R .$ Solving for $\omega,$ we obtain

$$
\omega\leq\frac{R\kappa^{-(d+s)}}{C_{2}(s,\bar{\varphi})\sqrt{2\log(2\kappa^{d}/\gamma)}}.\tag{88}
$$

Therefore, if $\omega$ satisfies this inequality, then with probability at least $1 - \gamma / 2$ , the Lipschitz property from Definition 8 holds for a function $f_{\omega,\kappa}^{\eta}$ drawn from $\nu_{\rho}^{H}$

Bounded derivatives with high probability. Fix an integer $s^{\prime}\in\left[\left\lfloor s\right\rfloor\right]$ and an arbitrary ${\textbf{ y }}\in$ $[0,1]^{d}$ . Since each $\varphi\in\mathbb{B}_{H}$ has disjoint support, we can specify the element of $\mathbb{B}_{H}$ whose s<sup>0</sup>-derivative has support containing y, say $\varphi_{\mathbf{y}}$ . Using (84) to the basis expansion of $f_{\omega,\kappa}^{\eta}$ with respect to $\mathbb{B}_{H}$ , we compute the $s^{\prime}.$ -derivative of $f_{\omega,\kappa}^{\eta}$ as:

$$
(f_{\omega,\kappa}^{\pmb{\eta}})^{(s^{\prime})}(\mathbf{y})=\omega\kappa^{\frac{d}{2}+s^{\prime}}\biggl(\sum_{t=1}^{\kappa^{d}}\eta_{t}\tilde{\lambda}_{t}^{-1/2}\theta_{\varphi_{\mathbf{y}}}(u_{t})\biggr)\bar{\varphi}^{(s^{\prime})}(\kappa\mathbf{y}-\pmb{\ell}).
$$

Under the event $\cap_{\varphi\in{\mathbb{B}}_{H}}A_{\varphi}^{c}$ as defined in (86), the derivative above is bounded by

$$
(f_{\omega,\kappa}^{\eta})^{(s^{\prime})}(\mathbf{y})\leq\kappa^{d+s^{\prime}}\||\varphi^{(s^{\prime})}\||_{\infty}\omega\sqrt{2\log(2\kappa^{d}/\gamma)}.
$$

We solve for $\omega$ in $\kappa^{d+s^{\prime}}\|\varphi^{(s^{\prime})}\|_{\infty}\omega\sqrt{2\log(2\kappa^{d}/\gamma)}\leq R$ . Solving for $\omega,$ , we obtain

$$
\omega\leq\frac{R\kappa^{-(d+s^{\prime})}}{\|\|\varphi^{(s^{\prime})}\|\|_{\infty}\sqrt{2\log(2\kappa^{d}/\gamma)}}.\tag{89}
$$

Therefore, if ω satisfies this inequality, then with probability at least $1 - \gamma / 2$ , the s<sup>0</sup>-derivative of $f_{\omega,\kappa}^{\eta}$ drawn from $\nu_{\rho}^{H}$ is bounded by R. Combining the above condition for $s^{\prime}\in [\left\lfloor s\right\rfloor]$ , we conclude that if

$$
\omega\leq\frac{R\kappa^{-(d+s)}}{C_{3}(s,\bar{\varphi})\sqrt{2\log(2\kappa^{d}/\gamma)}},\tag{90}
$$

where $\begin{array}{ r }{C_{3}(s,\bar{\varphi}): =\operatorname*{max}_{s^{\prime}\in\{1,\dots,\lfloor s\rfloor\}}\||\bar{\varphi}^{(s^{\prime})}\||_{\infty}}\end{array}$ , then with probability at least $1 - \gamma / 2$ , the bounded derivatives property of Definition 8 holds for a function $f_{\omega,\kappa}^{\eta}$ drawn from $\nu_{\rho}^{H}$

Conclusion.

Combining the conditions (88) and (90), we conclude that if

$$
\omega\leq\frac{R\kappa^{-(d+s)}}{C_{4}(s,\bar{\varphi})\sqrt{2\log(2\kappa^{d}/\gamma)}},\tag{91}
$$

where $\begin{array}{ r }{C_{4}(s,\bar{\varphi}): =\operatorname*{max}_{s^{\prime}\in\{1,\dots,(\lfloor s\rfloor+1)\}}4\||\bar{\varphi}^{(s^{\prime})}\|_{\infty}}\end{array}$ , then with probability at least $1 - \gamma$ , for a function $f_{\omega,\kappa}^{\eta}$ drawn from $\nu_{\rho}^{H}$ , we have $f_{\omega,\kappa}^{\eta}\in\mathcal{B}_{d,s}^{\mathrm{H}}(R)$ . This completes the proof Lemma 31.

Notation. Scalars are denoted in lower-case and vectors in lower-case bold, e.g. $x\in\mathbb{R}$ and $\mathbf{x}\in\mathbb{R}^{n}$ . Note that these will sometimes denote random variables depending on the context. We maintain an analogous notation for scalar-valued and vector-valued functions, e.g., $f$ and $f .$ . The ith coordinate of the vector x is denoted by $\mathbf{\mathcal{x}}_{i}$ . The set containing the first n integers excluding 0 is denoted by [n]. Given a subset of indices $S \subseteq [ n ]$ , x denotes the subvector consisting of entries $\mathbf{\nabla}_{\mathbf{x}_{i}}$ for $i \in S$ . Given a sequence of T random vectors $(\pmb{x}^{1},\dots,\pmb{x}^{T})$ , the subsequence consisting of the first t elements is denoted by $\pmb{x}^{\le t}: =(\pmb{x}^{1},...,\pmb{x}^{t})$ , and analogously for $\scriptstyle{\pmb x}^{<t}$ . We will sometimes combine these notation to get $\pmb{x}_{S}^{\le t}: =(\pmb{x}_{S}^{1},\ldots,\pmb{x}_{S}^{t})$ . Given a function $f:\mathbb{R}^{n}\mathbb{R}^{m}$ , its Jacobian matrix evaluated at $\mathbf{\boldsymbol{x}}\in\mathbb{R}^{n}$ is denoted by $D f(\pmb{x})\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times n}$ . See Table 5 in the Appendix for more.

In this section, we introduce the latent variable model under consideration (Section 2.1), entanglement graphs (Section 2.2), identifiability and observational equivalence (Section 2.3), equivalence up to diffeomorphism (Section 2.4) as well as permutation equivalence (Section 2.5).

We now specify the setting under consideration. Assume that we observe the realization of a sequence of $d_{x}$ -dimensional random vectors $\{x^{t}\}_{t=1}^{T}$ and a sequence of $d_{a}$ -dimensional auxiliary vectors $\{a^{t}\}_{t=0}^{T-1}$ . The coordinates of $\pmb{a}^{t}$ are discrete or continuous and can potentially represent, for example, an action taken by an agent or the index of an intervention or environment (see Section 3.4.1). Observations $\{x^{t}\}$ are assumed to be explained by a sequence of continuous random vectors $d_{z}$ of hidden dimensions $\{z^{t}\}_{t=1}^{T}$ using a ground-truth decoder function $f$

Assumption 1 (Observation model) For all $t \in [ T ]$ , the observations ${\boldsymbol{x}}^{t}$ are given by

$$
\boldsymbol{x}^{t}=\boldsymbol{f}(\boldsymbol{z}^{t})+\boldsymbol{n}^{t},
$$

where $\pmb{n}^{t}\sim\mathcal{N}(0,\sigma^{2}\pmb{I})$ are mutually independent across time and independent ofall $z^{t}$ and $\pmb{a}^{t}$ with $\sigma^{2}\geq 0 .$ . Moreover, $d_{z}\ \leq\ d_{x}$ and $\pmb{f}:\mathbb{R}^{d_{z}}\mathbb{R}^{d_{x}}$ is a diffeomorphism onto its image<sup>2</sup>. Lastly, assume that $f(\mathbb{R}^{d_{z}})$ is closed in $\mathbb{R}^{d_{x}}$

Importantly, we suppose that each factor $\boldsymbol{z}_{i}^{t}$ contains interpretable information about the observation, e.g., for high-dimensional images, the coordinates $\boldsymbol{z}_{i}^{t}$ might be the position of an object, its color, or its orientation in space. This idea that there exists a ground-truth decoder $f$ that captures the relationship between the so-called “natural factors of variations” and the observations x is of capital importance, since it is the very basis for a mathematical definition of disentanglement (Definition 7). Appendix D.1 discusses the implications of the diffeomorphism assumption (see also Mansouri et al. (2022)). We denote $\boldsymbol{z}^{\le t}: =\left[\boldsymbol{\bar{z}}^{1}\ \cdot\ \cdot\ \boldsymbol{z}^{t}\right]\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{z}\times t}$ and analogously for $z^{<t}$ and other random vectors.

In a similar spirit to previous works on nonlinear ICA (Hyvarinen et al.¨ , 2019; Khemakhem et al., 2020a), we assume that the latent factors $\boldsymbol{z}_{i}^{t}$ are conditionally independent given the past.

Assumption 2 (Conditionally independent latent factors) The latent factors $\boldsymbol{z}_{i}^{t}$ are conditionally mutually independent given $z^{<t}$ and $\mathbf{\pmb{a}}^{<t}$ :

$$
p(\boldsymbol{z}^{t}\mid\boldsymbol{z}^{<t},\boldsymbol{a}^{<t})=\prod_{i=1}^{d_{z}}p(\boldsymbol{z}_{i}^{t}\mid\boldsymbol{z}^{<t},\boldsymbol{a}^{<t}),\tag{1}
$$

where $p(z^{t}\mid z^{<t},\pmb{a}^{<t})$ is a density function w.r.t. the Lebesgue measure on $\mathbb{R}^{d_{z}}$ . We assume that the support $o f p(z_{i}^{t}\mid z^{<t},\pmb{a}^{<t})$ is R for all $z^{<t}$ and $\pmb{a}^{<t}$ . The support of $p(z^{t}\mid z^{<t},\pmb{a}^{<t})$ is thus given by $\mathbb{R}^{d_{z}}$ . At $t = 1$ , we set $\begin{array}{ r }{p(z^{1}\mid z^{<1},{\pmb a}^{<1})=p(z^{1}\mid{\pmb a}^{0})=\prod_{i=1}^{d_{z}}p(z_{i}^{1}\mid{\pmb a}^{0})}\end{array}$

We will refer to the l.h.s. of (1) as the transition model and to the factors $p(\pmb{z}_{i}^{t}\ |\ \pmb{z}^{<t},\pmb{a}^{<t})$ as mechanisms. In a causal setting, this conditional independence assumption states that latent variables cannot exert influence on other latent variables instantaneously. We believe this to be a reasonable assumption when the time steps are sampled at a sufficiently high rate since, at a fundamental level, causal effects cannot travel faster than the speed of light. Of course in many practical scenarios, a low sampling rate can entail instantaneous dependencies which, if too strong, might result in model misspecification. In Section 7, we discuss and contrast with causal representation learning methods which allow for instantaneous influence.

Notice that we do not assume the dynamical system to be $M a r k o\nu i a n^{3}.$ , i.e. the distribution over future states can depend on the whole history of latents and auxiliary variables $(z^{<t},a^{<t})$ ). In addition, this model can represent non-homogeneous processes by taking the auxiliary variable a to be a time index (Hyvarinen et al.¨ , 2019).

We are going to describe the dependency structure of the latent and auxiliary variables over time using a probabilistic directed graphical model composed of two bipartite graphs, $G^{z}\in\{0,1\}^{d_{z}\times d_{z}}$ which relates $z^{<t}$ to $z^{t},$ , and $G^{a}\in\{0,1\}^{d_{z}\times d_{a}}$ , which relates $\pmb{a}^{<t}$ to $z^{t}$ . A directed edge points from $z_{i}^{<t}$ to $\boldsymbol{z}_{i}^{t}$ if and only if $G_{i,j}^{z}=1$ . Analogously, a directed edge points from $\pmb{a}_{\ell}^{<t}$ to $z_{i}^{t}.$ , if and only $\mathrm{if}^{\prime}G_{i,\ell}^{a}=1$ . Figure 1 shows an example of such graphs together with its adjacency matrix $G: =[G^{z},G^{a}]$ . The following assumption specifies the relationship between these graphs and the transition model.

Assumption 3 (Transition model $p$ follows G) For every mechanism $i\in [d_{z}]$

$$
p(\boldsymbol{z}_{i}^{t}\mid\boldsymbol{z}^{<t},\boldsymbol{a}^{<t})=p(\boldsymbol{z}_{i}^{t}\mid\boldsymbol{z}_{\mathbf{Pa}_{i}^{z}}^{<t},\boldsymbol{a}_{\mathbf{Pa}_{i}^{a}}^{<t}),\tag{2}
$$

where $\mathbf{Pa}_{i}^{z}\subseteq [d_{z}]$ and $\mathbf{Pa}_{i}^{a}\subseteq [d_{a}]$ are the sets of parents of $\cdot_{z_{i}^{t}}$ in $G^{z}$ and $G^{a}$ , respectively.

The graph G thus encodes a set of conditional independence statements about the latent and auxiliary variables.<sup>4</sup> We will say that mechanisms are sparse when the graphs $G^{a}$ and $G^{z}$ are sparse.

This model has three components that need to be learned: (i) the decoder function f, (ii) the transition model over latent variables $p,$ and (iii) the dependency graph $G$ . We gather all these components into $\pmb\theta: =(\pmb f,p,\pmb G)$ . Everything else in the model, i.e. $d_{z}$ and $\sigma^{2}$ , is assumed to be known. We assume that $\sigma^{2}$ is known here mainly for simplicity, since, when it is not, it can be identified as shown by Lachapelle et al. (2022, Appendix A.4.1), as long as $d_{x}>d_{z}$

Notice how we have not specified any model for the auxiliary variable $\pmb{a}^{t}$ . We do not intend to do so in this work, as we are solely interested in modeling the conditional distribution of $\mathbf{\boldsymbol{x}}^{\le T}$ and $z^{\le T}$ given $\mathbf{\pmb{a}}^{<T}$ . We denote by $\mathcal{A}\subseteq\mathbb{R}^{d_{a}}$ the set of possible values for the auxiliary variable $\pmb{a}^{t}$ . We thus have that, for all values of $\pmb{a}^{<T}\in\mathcal{A}^{T}$ , our model induces a conditional distribution

$$
p(\boldsymbol{x}^{\leq T}\mid\boldsymbol{a}^{<T})=\int\prod_{t=1}^{T}p(\boldsymbol{x}^{t}\mid\boldsymbol{z}^{t})p(\boldsymbol{z}^{t}\mid\boldsymbol{z}^{<t},\boldsymbol{a}^{<t})d\boldsymbol{z}^{\leq T},
$$

where $p(\pmb{x}^{t}\mid z^{t})=\mathcal{N}(\pmb{x}^{t};\pmb{f}(z^{t}),\sigma^{2}\pmb{I})$ . We note that if $\sigma^{2}=0;$ , the conditional distribution of ${\boldsymbol{x}}^{t}$ given $z^{t}$ is a Dirac centered at $\pmb{f}(\pmb{z}^{t})$ and thus has no density w.r.t. the Lebesgue measure. Even if, in that case, the above integral does not make sense, the conditional distribution of $\mathbf{\boldsymbol{x}}^{\le T}$ given $\pmb{a}^{<T}$ is still well-defined and all the results of this work still hold since none of the proofs requires $\sigma^{2}>0$

In this section, we define entanglement maps, which describe the functional relationship between the learned and ground-truth representations, and entanglement graphs, which describe their entanglement structure.

Definition 1 (Entanglement maps) Let f and $\tilde{f}$ be two diffeomorphisms from $\mathbb{R}^{d_{z}}$ to their images such that $\pmb{f}(\mathbb{R}^{d_{z}})=\tilde{\pmb{f}}(\mathbb{R}^{d_{z}})$ . The entanglement map of the pair $(f,{\tilde{f}})$ is given by

$$
\boldsymbol{v}:=\boldsymbol{f}^{-1}\circ\tilde{\boldsymbol{f}}.\tag{3}
$$

We now define the dependency graph of some function h so that each edge indicates that some input i influences some output j:

Definition 2 (Functional dependency graph) Let h be a function from $\mathbb{R}^{n}$ to $\mathbb{R}^{m}$ . The dependency graph of h is a bipartite directed graph from [n] to [m] with adjacency matrix $\pmb{H}\in\{0,1\}^{m\times n}$ such that

$$
\boldsymbol{H}_{i,j}=0\iff \text{There is a function}\bar{\boldsymbol{h}}\text{such that, for all}\boldsymbol{a}\in\mathbb{R}^{n},\boldsymbol{h}_{i}(\boldsymbol{a})=\bar{\boldsymbol{h}}_{i}(\boldsymbol{a}_{-j}),
$$

where $\pmb{a}_{-j}$ is a with its jth coordinate removed.

We will be particularly interested in the dependency graph of the entanglement map $\pmb{v}: =\pmb{f}^{-1}$ ◦ ${\hat{f}},$ denoted by V.

Definition 3 (Entanglement graphs) Let f and $\tilde{f}$ be two diffeomorphisms from $\mathbb{R}^{d_{z}}$ to their images such that $\pmb{f}(\mathbb{R}^{d_{z}})=\tilde{\pmb{f}}(\mathbb{R}^{d_{z}})$ . The entanglement graph of the pair $(f,{\tilde{f}})$ is the dependency graph (Definition 2) of their entanglement map $\pmb{v}: =\pmb{f}^{-1}\circ\tilde{\pmb{f}},$ , which we denote $V\in\{0,1\}^{d_{z}\times d_{z}}$

To analyze formally whether a specific algorithm is expected to yield a disentangled representation, we will rely on the notion of identifiability. Before we define what we mean by identifiability, we need the notion of observationally equivalent models. Two models are observationally equivalent if both models represent the same distribution over observations. The following formalizes this definition.

Definition 4 (Observational equivalence) We say that two models $\pmb\theta: =(\pmb f,p,\pmb G)$ and $\tilde{\pmb{\theta}}: =(\tilde{f},\tilde{p},\tilde{G})$ satisfying Assumption 1 are observationally equivalent, denoted $\theta\sim_{\mathrm{obs}}\theta,$ , if and only if, for all $\mathbf{\Psi}_{\mathbf{\lambda}}\mathbf{a}^{<T}\in\mathcal{\bar{A}}^{T}$ and all $\pmb{x}^{\le T}\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{x}\times T}$

$$
p(\boldsymbol{x}^{\leq T}\mid\boldsymbol{a}^{<T})=\tilde{p}(\boldsymbol{x}^{\leq T}\mid\boldsymbol{a}^{<T}).
$$

We start by defining equivalence up to diffeomorphism. This equivalence relation is important since we will show later on that it is actually the same as observational equivalence and will thus be our first step in all our identifiability results. In what follows, we overload the notation and write $\pmb{v}(z^{<t}): =[\pmb{v}(z^{1}),\dots,\pmb{v}(z^{t-1})]$ , and similarly for other functions.

In this section, we show that without further assumptions the model introduced so far is unidentifiable (Section 3.1), provide a first insight as to why mechanism sparsity can make the model identifi able and thus lead to disentanglement (Section 3.2), introduce the machinery of G-preserving maps (Section 3.3) which leads up to theorems showing identifiability up to a-consistency (Section 3.4) and z-consistency (Section 3.5), which corresponds to partial disentanglement. Finally, we introduce the sufficient influence assumptions and prove the identifiability results (Section 3.8), and provide multiple examples to build intuition (Sec tion 3.9).

Proof [of Theorem 1] Recall equation (13), which we derived in Section 3.2:

$$

$$

Notice that Assumption 6 holds only “almost everywhere”, i.e. on a set $\mathbb{R}^{d_{z}}\setminus E_{0}$ where $E_{0}$ has zero Lebesgue measure. Fix an arbitrary $\boldsymbol{z}\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{z}}\setminus E_{0}$ . For notational convenience, define

$$
\Lambda(\boldsymbol{z},\gamma):=H_{z,a}^{t,\tau}q(\boldsymbol{v}(\boldsymbol{z})\mid\boldsymbol{v}(\boldsymbol{z}^{<t}),\boldsymbol{a}^{<t})\qquad\hat{\Lambda}(\boldsymbol{z},\gamma):=H_{z,a}^{t,\tau}\hat{q}(\boldsymbol{z}\mid\boldsymbol{z}^{<t},\boldsymbol{a}^{<t}),
$$

where $\gamma:=(t,\tau,\boldsymbol{z}^{<t},\boldsymbol{a}^{<t})$ . This allows us to rewrite (16) with a much lighter notation:

$$
\hat{\Lambda}(\boldsymbol{z},\gamma)=D\boldsymbol{v}(\boldsymbol{z})^{\top}\Lambda(\boldsymbol{z},\gamma).\tag{17}
$$

Now, notice that the sufficient influence assumption (Assumption 6) requires that, for all $\ell\in[d_{a}]$ there exists $\{\gamma_{(r)}\}_{r=1}^{|\mathbf{Ch}_{\ell}^{a}|}$ such that $\mathrm{span}\{\Lambda(\boldsymbol{z},\gamma_{(r)})_{\cdot,\ell}\}_{r=1}^{|\mathbf{Ch}_{\ell}^{a}|}=\mathbb{R}_{\mathbf{Ch}_{\ell}^{a}}^{d_{z}}$ . We can thus write

$$
D\boldsymbol{v}(\boldsymbol{z})^{\top}\mathbb{R}_{\boldsymbol{G}_{\cdot,\ell}^{a}}^{d_{z}}=D\boldsymbol{v}(\boldsymbol{z})^{\top}\mathrm{span}\{\Lambda(\boldsymbol{z},\gamma_{(r)})_{\cdot,\ell}\}_{r=1}^{|\mathbf{Ch}_{\ell}^{a}|}=\mathrm{span}\{\hat{\Lambda}(\boldsymbol{z},\gamma_{(r)})_{\cdot,\ell}\}_{r=1}^{|\mathbf{Ch}_{\ell}^{a}|}\subseteq\mathbb{R}_{\hat{\boldsymbol{G}}_{\cdot,\ell}^{a}}^{d_{z}}\tag{18}
$$

Since $D\boldsymbol{v}(\boldsymbol{z})$ is invertible, there exists a permutation $\boldsymbol{P}(\boldsymbol{z})$ such that $D\boldsymbol{v}(\boldsymbol{z})\boldsymbol{P}(\boldsymbol{z})$ has no zero on its diagonal (Lemma 2). Let $\boldsymbol{C}(\boldsymbol{z}):=D\boldsymbol{v}(\boldsymbol{z})\boldsymbol{P}(\boldsymbol{z})$ . By left-multiplying (18) by $\boldsymbol{P}(\boldsymbol{z})^{\top}$ , we get

$$
\boldsymbol{C}(\boldsymbol{z})^{\top}\mathbb{R}_{\boldsymbol{G}_{\cdot,\ell}^{a}}^{d_{z}}\subseteq\mathbb{R}_{\boldsymbol{P}(\boldsymbol{z})^{\top}\hat{\boldsymbol{G}}_{\cdot,\ell}^{a}}^{d_{z}}.\tag{19}
$$

We would like to show that $\boldsymbol{C}(\boldsymbol{z})$ is $\boldsymbol{G}^{a}$ -preserving. Notice how the above equation is almost exactly the definition of $\boldsymbol{G}^{a}$ -preserving. All that is left to prove is that $\boldsymbol{P}(\boldsymbol{z})^{\top}\hat{\boldsymbol{G}}^{a}=\boldsymbol{G}^{a}$ .

We start by showing $\boldsymbol{P}(\boldsymbol{z})^{\top}\hat{\boldsymbol{G}}^{a}\supseteq\boldsymbol{G}^{a}$ . Take $(i,\ell)\in\boldsymbol{G}^{a}$ . Since $\boldsymbol{e}_{i}\in\mathbb{R}_{\boldsymbol{G}_{\cdot,\ell}^{a}}^{d_{z}}$ , equation (19) implies

$$
\boldsymbol{C}(\boldsymbol{z})^{\top}\boldsymbol{e}_{i}=\boldsymbol{C}(\boldsymbol{z})_{i,\cdot}\in\mathbb{R}_{\boldsymbol{P}(\boldsymbol{z})^{\top}\hat{\boldsymbol{G}}_{\cdot,\ell}^{a}}^{d_{z}}.
$$

Since $\boldsymbol{C}(\boldsymbol{z})_{i,i}\neq0$ (all elements on its diagonal are nonzero), we must have that $(i,\ell)\in\boldsymbol{P}(\boldsymbol{z})^{\top}\hat{\boldsymbol{G}}^{a}$ .

Now, since $||\boldsymbol{P}(\boldsymbol{z})^{\top}\hat{\boldsymbol{G}}^{a}||_{0}=||\hat{\boldsymbol{G}}^{a}||_{0}\leq||\boldsymbol{G}^{a}||_{0}$ , we have $\boldsymbol{P}(\boldsymbol{z})^{\top}\hat{\boldsymbol{G}}^{a}=\boldsymbol{G}^{a}$ . This implies

$$
\boldsymbol{C}(\boldsymbol{z})^{\top}\mathbb{R}_{\boldsymbol{G}^{a}}^{d_{z}\times d_{a}}\subseteq\mathbb{R}_{\boldsymbol{G}^{a}}^{d_{z}\times d_{a}},
$$

i.e. $\boldsymbol{C}(\boldsymbol{z})$ is a $\boldsymbol{G}^{a}$ -preserving matrix, as desired.

To recap, we now have that, for all $\boldsymbol{z}\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{z}}\setminus E_{0}$ , there exists a permutation $\boldsymbol{P}(\boldsymbol{z})$ s.t. $D\boldsymbol{v}(\boldsymbol{z})\boldsymbol{P}(\boldsymbol{z})$ is $\boldsymbol{G}^{a}$ -preserving. We are not done yet, since, a priori, the permutation $\boldsymbol{P}(\boldsymbol{z})$ can be different for different values of $\boldsymbol{z}$ , and we do not know what happens on the measure-zero set $E_{0}$ . What we need to show is that there exists a permutation $\boldsymbol{P}$ such that, for all $\boldsymbol{z}$ , $D\boldsymbol{v}(\boldsymbol{z})\boldsymbol{P}$ is $\boldsymbol{G}^{a}$ -preserving. Lemma 12 in Appendix A.5 shows precisely this, by leveraging the continuity of $D\boldsymbol{v}(\boldsymbol{z})$ ( $\boldsymbol{v}$ is a diffeomorphism and thus $C^{1}$ ).

Notice that $D(\boldsymbol{v}\circ\boldsymbol{P})(\boldsymbol{z})=D\boldsymbol{v}(\boldsymbol{P}\boldsymbol{z})\boldsymbol{P}$ , which is $\boldsymbol{G}^{a}$ -preserving everywhere. Using Lemma 1, we conclude that the function $\boldsymbol{c}:=\boldsymbol{v}\circ\boldsymbol{P}$ is $\boldsymbol{G}^{a}$ -preserving. This concludes the proof.

We will assume that the conditional densities $p(z_{i}^{t}\mid z^{<t},\pmb{a}^{<t})$ are from an exponentialfamily (Wainwright and Jordan, 2008):

Assumption 9 (Exponential family transition model) For all $i\in [d_{z}]$ , we have

$$
p(\boldsymbol{z}_{i}^{t}\mid\boldsymbol{z}^{<t},\boldsymbol{a}^{<t})=h_{i}(\boldsymbol{z}_{i}^{t})\exp\{\boldsymbol{s}_{i}(\boldsymbol{z}_{i}^{t})^{\top}\boldsymbol{\lambda}_{i}(\boldsymbol{z}^{<t},\boldsymbol{a}^{<t})-\psi_{i}(\boldsymbol{z}^{<t},\boldsymbol{a}^{<t})\}.\tag{30}
$$

Well-known distributions which belong to this family include the Gaussian and beta distributions. In the Gaussian case, the sufficient statistic is $\pmb{s}_{i}(z): =(z,z^{2})$ and the base measure is $\begin{array}{ r }{h_{i}(z): =\frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi}}}\end{array}$ . The function $\lambda_{i}(z^{<t},\pmb{a}^{<t})$ outputs the vectors of natural parameters for the conditional distribution and can be itself parametrized, for instance, by a multi-layer perceptron (MLP) or a recurrent neural network (RNN). We will refer to the functions $\lambda_{i}$ as the mechanisms or the transition functions. In the Gaussian case, the natural parameter is two-dimensional and is related to the usual parameters $\mu$ and $\sigma^{2}$ via the equation $\begin{array}{ r }{(\lambda_{1},\lambda_{2})=(\frac{\mu}{\sigma^{2}},-\frac{1}{2\sigma^{2}})}\end{array}$ . We will denote by k the dimensionality of the natural parameter and that of the sufficient statistic (which are equal). Thus, $k = 2$ in the Gaussian case. The remaining term $\psi_{i}(z^{<t},\pmb{a}^{<t})$ acts as a normalization constant.

We define $\pmb{\lambda}(\pmb{z}^{<t},\pmb{a}^{<t})~\in~\mathbb{R}^{k d_{z}}$ as the concatenation of all $\lambda_{i}(z^{<t},\pmb{a}^{<t})$ and similarly for $\pmb{s}(z^{t})\in\mathbb{R}^{k d_{z}}$ . Similarly to the nonparameteric case, the learnable parameters are $\pmb\theta: =(f,\lambda,G)$ Note that throughout, we assume that the sufficient statistic s is not learned and known in advance. With this notation, we can write the full transition model as

$$
p(\boldsymbol{z}^{t}\mid\boldsymbol{z}^{<t},\boldsymbol{a}^{<t})=h(\boldsymbol{z}^{t})\exp\{\boldsymbol{s}(\boldsymbol{z}^{t})^{\top}\boldsymbol{\lambda}(\boldsymbol{z}^{<t},\boldsymbol{a}^{<t})-\psi(\boldsymbol{z}^{<t},\boldsymbol{a}^{<t})\},
$$

where $\begin{array}{ r }{h: =\prod_{i=1}^{d_{z}}h_{i}}\end{array}$ and $\begin{array}{ r }{\psi=\sum_{i=1}^{d_{z}}\psi_{i}}\end{array}$

In this section, we follow Khemakhem et al. (2020a) and show that the exponential family assumption combined with an additional sufficient variability assumption allows us to go from identifiability up to diffeomorphism (Definition 5) to identifiability up to quasi-linearity, which we define next:

Definition 17 (Quasi-linear equivalence) We say that two models $\pmb\theta: =(f,\lambda,G)$ and $\tilde{\pmb{\theta}}: =(\tilde{f},\tilde{\lambda},\tilde{G})$ satisfying Assumptions $I,2\&9$ are equivalent up to quasi-linearity, denoted $\theta\sim_{\mathrm{lin}}\tilde{\theta},$ if and only $i f\theta\sim_{\mathrm{diff}}\tilde{\theta}$ and there exist an invertible matrix $\pmb{L}\in\mathbb{R}^{k d_{z}\times k d_{z}}$ and a vector $\pmb{b}\in\mathbb{R}^{k d_{z}}$ such that the map $\pmb{v}: =\pmb{f}^{-1}\circ\tilde{\pmb{f}}$ satisfies

$$
\boldsymbol{s}(\boldsymbol{v}(\boldsymbol{z}))=\boldsymbol{L}\boldsymbol{s}(\boldsymbol{z})+\boldsymbol{b},\forall\boldsymbol{z}\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{z}}.
$$

Ifthe sufficient statistic s is invertible, one obtains

$$
\boldsymbol{v}(\boldsymbol{z})=\boldsymbol{s}^{-1}(\boldsymbol{L}\boldsymbol{s}(\boldsymbol{z})+\boldsymbol{b}),\forall\boldsymbol{z}\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{z}}.\tag{31}
$$

The following theorem provides conditions to guarantee identifiability up to quasi-linearity. This is an adaptation and minor extension of Theorem 1 from Khemakhem et al. (2020a). For completeness, we provide a proof in Appendix B.2.

Theorem 4 (Conditions for linear identifiability - Adapted from Khemakhem et al. (2020a)) Let $\pmb\theta: =(f,\lambda,G)$ and $\hat{\pmb\theta}: =(\hat{f},\hat{\lambda},\hat{G})$ be two models satisfying Assumptions 1, 2 & 9. Further assume that

1. [Observational equivalence] $\theta\sim_{\mathrm{obs}}\hat{\theta}(D e f i n i t i o n 4).$  
2. [Minimal sufficient statistics] For all i, the sufficient statistic $\mathbf{\delta}_{s_{i}}$ is minimal (see below).  
3. [Sufficient variability] The natural parameter λ varies “sufficiently” as formalized by Assumption 10 (see below).

Then, $\pmb\theta\sim_{\mathrm{lin}}\hat{\pmb\theta}(D e f . I 7).$

Assumption 10 (Sufficient variability in exponential families) There exist $(z_{(r)},\mathbf{a}_{(r)})_{p=0}^{k d_{z}}$ in their respective supports such that the $k d_{z}$ -dimensional vectors $(\lambda(z_{(r)},\pmb{a}_{(r)})-\lambda(z_{(0)},\pmb{a}_{(0)}))_{r=1}^{k d_{z}}$ are linearly independent.

Notice that $z_{(r)}$ represents values of $z^{<t}$ for potentially different values of t and therefore can vary in shape.

We now provide a (partial) disentanglement guarantee that takes advantage of sparsity regularization of $\hat{G}^{z}$ and is specialized for exponential families with a one-dimensional sufficient statistic $(k=1)$ . We will see that this extra parametric assumption on the transition model allows us to weaken the sufficient influence assumption of Theorem 3 (Assumption 8). In particular, this is going to allow for Markovian transitions without auxiliary variables, which was not allowed by the nonparametric result (Remark 7).

The sufficient influence assumption for z specialized to exponential families with $k = 1$ is directly taken from Lachapelle et al. (2022):

Assumption 11 (Sufficient influence of z (Lachapelle et al., 2022)) Assume $k = 1$ and $Ds(z)$ is invertible everywhere. There exist $\{(z_{(r)},\pmb{a}_{(r)},\tau_{(r)})\}_{r=1}^{| |\pmb{G}^{z}| |_{0}}$ belonging to their respective support such that

$$
\mathrm{span}\left\{D_{z}^{\tau_{(r)}}\pmb{\lambda}(\pmb{z}_{(r)},\pmb{a}_{(r)})D\pmb{s}(\pmb{z}_{(r)}^{\tau_{(r)}})^{-1}\right\}_{r=1}^{| |\pmb{G}^{z}| |_{0}}=\mathbb{R}_{\pmb{G}^{z}}^{d_{z}\times d_{z}},
$$

where $D_{z}^{\tau_{(r)}}\lambda$ and Ds are Jacobians with respect to $z^{\tau_{(r)}}$ and $z,$ respectively

The goal of the next result is to relax the conditions of Lemma 11 so that $\pmb{L}(z)\pmb{P}(z)$ is $\mathbf{G}\mathrm{-}$ preserving for almost all $\boldsymbol{z}\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{z}}$

Lemma 12 Let $G\in\{0,1\}^{m\times n}$ and let $\pmb{L}:\mathbb{R}^{d_{z}}\mathbb{R}^{m\times m}$ be a continuous function such that $\pmb{L}(z)$ is invertible for all $z\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{z}}$ . Suppose that, for almost all $z\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{z}}$ (i.e. except on a set E of Lebesgue measure zero), there exists a permutation matrix $P(z)$ such that $\pmb{L}(z)\pmb{P}(z)$ is G-preserving. Then, there exists a permutation matrix P such that, for all $z\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{z}},\pmb{L}(z)\pmb{P}$ is G-preserving.

We recall the definition of a minimal sufficient statistic in an exponential family, which can be found in Wainwright and Jordan (2008, p. 40).

Definition 20 (Minimal sufficient statistic) Given a parameterized distribution in the exponential family, as in (30), we say that its sufficient statistic $\mathbf{\delta}_{s_{i}}$ is minimal when there is no $v \neq 0$ such that $v^{\top}s_{i}(z)$ is constantfor all $z\in{\mathcal{Z}}$

Lemma 15 Let $\pmb\theta: =(\pmb f,p,\pmb G)$ satisfy Assumptions 1, 2, 3, 4 & 9 and let $q : = \log p .$ . Then

$$
\begin{array}{l}D_{z}^{t}q(\boldsymbol{z}^{t}\mid\boldsymbol{z}^{<t},\boldsymbol{a}^{<t})=\boldsymbol{\lambda}(\boldsymbol{z}^{<t},\boldsymbol{a}^{<t})^{\top}D\boldsymbol{s}(\boldsymbol{z}^{t})+D(\log h)(\boldsymbol{z}^{t})\\ H_{z,a}^{t,\tau}q(\boldsymbol{z}^{t}\mid\boldsymbol{z}^{<t},\boldsymbol{a}^{<t})=D\boldsymbol{s}(\boldsymbol{z}^{t})^{\top}D_{a}^{\tau}\boldsymbol{\lambda}(\boldsymbol{z}^{<t},\boldsymbol{a}^{<t})\\ H_{z,z}^{t,\tau}q(\boldsymbol{z}^{t}\mid\boldsymbol{z}^{<t},\boldsymbol{a}^{<t})=D\boldsymbol{s}(\boldsymbol{z}^{t})^{\top}D_{z}^{\tau}\boldsymbol{\lambda}(\boldsymbol{z}^{<t},\boldsymbol{a}^{<t}).\\ \end{array}
$$

steps.claim:
Proof [of Theorem 2] We recall equation (8) derived in Section 3.2:

$$
D_{z}^{t}\hat{q}(\boldsymbol{z}^{t}\mid\boldsymbol{z}^{<t},\boldsymbol{a}^{<t})=D_{z}^{t}q(\boldsymbol{v}(\boldsymbol{z}^{t})\mid\boldsymbol{v}(\boldsymbol{z}^{<t}),\boldsymbol{a}^{<t})D\boldsymbol{v}(\boldsymbol{z}^{t})+\eta(\boldsymbol{z}^{t})\in\mathbb{R}^{1\times d_{z}}.\tag{20}
$$

Now, instead of differentiating w.r.t. $\pmb{a}_{\ell}^{\tau}$ for some $\tau < t$ and $\ell\in [d_{a}]$ , we are going to take a partial difference. That is, we evaluate the above equation on at $\pmb{a}^{<t}$ and $\pmb{a}^{<t}+\epsilon\pmb{E}^{(\ell,\tau)}$ and $\epsilon\in\mathbb{R}$ , where $\pmb{E}^{(\ell,\tau)}$ is a “one-hot matrix”, while keeping everything else constant, and take the difference.

This yields:

$$
\begin{array}{l}[D_{z}^{t}\hat{q}(\boldsymbol{z}^{t}\mid\boldsymbol{z}^{<t},\boldsymbol{a}^{<t}+\epsilon\boldsymbol{E}^{(\ell,\tau)})-D_{z}^{t}\hat{q}(\boldsymbol{z}^{t}\mid\boldsymbol{z}^{<t},\boldsymbol{a}^{<t})]^{\top}\\ =D\boldsymbol{v}(\boldsymbol{z}^{t})^{\top}[D_{z}^{t}q(\boldsymbol{v}(\boldsymbol{z}^{t})\mid\boldsymbol{v}(\boldsymbol{z}^{<t}),\boldsymbol{a}^{<t}+\epsilon\boldsymbol{E}^{(\ell,\tau)})-D_{z}^{t}q(\boldsymbol{v}(\boldsymbol{z}^{t})\mid\boldsymbol{v}(\boldsymbol{z}^{<t}),\boldsymbol{a}^{<t})]^{\top}\\ \Delta_{a,\ell}^{\tau,\epsilon}D_{z}^{t}\hat{q}\left(\boldsymbol{z}^{t}\mid\boldsymbol{z}^{<t},\boldsymbol{a}^{<t}\right)^{\top}=D\boldsymbol{v}\left(\boldsymbol{z}^{t}\right)^{\top}\Delta_{a,\ell}^{\tau,\epsilon}D_{z}^{t}q\left(\boldsymbol{v}\left(\boldsymbol{z}^{t}\right)\mid\boldsymbol{v}\left(\boldsymbol{z}^{<t}\right),\boldsymbol{a}^{<t}\right)^{\top},\tag{21}\\ \end{array}
$$

where we used the notation for partial differences introduced in Definition 16.

Notice that the difference on the left is $\subseteq\hat{G}_{\cdot,\ell}^{a}$ and the difference on the right $\mathrm{is}\subseteq G_{\cdot,\ell}^{a}.$ This equation is thus analogous to (16) from the continuous case. For that reason, we can employ a completely analogous strategy. Hence, we define

$$
\hat{\Lambda}(\boldsymbol{z}^{t},\gamma)_{\cdot,\ell}:=\Delta_{a,\ell}^{\tau,\epsilon}D_{z}^{t}\hat{q}(\boldsymbol{z}^{t}\mid\boldsymbol{z}^{<t},\boldsymbol{a}^{<t})^{\top}\quad\Lambda(\boldsymbol{z}^{t},\gamma)_{\cdot,\ell}:=\Delta_{a,\ell}^{\tau,\epsilon}D_{z}^{t}q(\boldsymbol{v}(\boldsymbol{z}^{t})\mid\boldsymbol{v}(\boldsymbol{z}^{<t}),\boldsymbol{a}^{<t})^{\top},
$$

where $\gamma=(t,\tau,z^{<t},\pmb{a}^{<t},\vec{\epsilon})$ .

This notation allows us to rewrite (21) more compactly as

$$
\underbrace{\hat{\Lambda}(\boldsymbol{z}^{t},\gamma)}_{\subseteq\hat{\boldsymbol{G}}^{a}}=\boldsymbol{L}(\boldsymbol{z}^{t})^{\top}\underbrace{\Lambda(\boldsymbol{z}^{t},\gamma)}_{\subseteq\boldsymbol{G}^{a}}.
$$
From here, the rest of the argument is exactly analogous to the proof of Theorem 1.

1. [Observational equivalence] $\pmb{\theta}\sim_{\mathrm{obs}}\hat{\pmb{\theta}}(D e f . 4),$  
2. [Sufficient influence of z] The Hessian matrix $H_{z,z}^{t,\tau}$ log $p(z^{t}\mid z^{<t},\pmb{a}^{<t})$ varies “sufficiently”, asformalized in Assumption $\mathbf{\nabla}_{\delta,\cdot}$

Then, there exists a permutation matrix P such that $P G^{z}P^{\top}\subseteq\hat{G}^{z}$ . Further assume that

Then, $\theta\sim_{\mathrm{con}}^{z}\hat{\pmb{\theta}}(D e f . I 4)$

steps.claim:
Proof [of Theorem 3] We recall equation (15) derived in Section 3.2:

$$
\underbrace{H_{z,z}^{t,\tau}\hat{q}(\boldsymbol{z}^{t}\mid\boldsymbol{z}^{<t},\boldsymbol{a}^{<t})}_{\subseteq\hat{\boldsymbol{G}}^{z}}=D\boldsymbol{v}(\boldsymbol{z}^{t})^{\top}\underbrace{H_{z,z}^{t,\tau}q(\boldsymbol{v}(\boldsymbol{z}^{t})\mid\boldsymbol{v}(\boldsymbol{z}^{<t}),\boldsymbol{a}^{<t})}_{\subseteq\boldsymbol{G}^{z}}D\boldsymbol{v}(\boldsymbol{z}^{\tau}).
$$

This equation holds for all pairs of $z^{t}$ and $z^{\tau}$ in $\mathbb{R}^{d_{z}}$ . We can thus evaluate it at a point such that $z^{t}=z^{\tau}$ , which yields

$$
H_{z,z}^{t,\tau}\hat{q}(\boldsymbol{z}^{t}\mid\boldsymbol{z}^{<t},\boldsymbol{a}^{<t})=D\boldsymbol{v}(\boldsymbol{z}^{t})^{\top}H_{z,z}^{t,\tau}q(\boldsymbol{v}(\boldsymbol{z}^{t})\mid\boldsymbol{v}(\boldsymbol{z}^{<t}),\boldsymbol{a}^{<t})D\boldsymbol{v}(\boldsymbol{z}^{t}).\tag{22}
$$

Recall that Assumption 8 holds for all $\boldsymbol{z}^{t}\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{\boldsymbol{z}}}\setminus E_{0}$ where $E_{0}$ has Lebesgue measure zero. Fix an arbitrary $z^{t}\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{z}}\setminus E_{0}$ and set $z^{\tau}=z^{t}$ . Let us define

$$
\Lambda(\pmb{z}^{t},\gamma):=H_{z,z}^{t,\tau}q(\pmb{v}(\pmb{z}^{t})\mid\pmb{v}(\pmb{z}^{<t}),\pmb{a}^{<t})\qquad\hat{\Lambda}(\pmb{z}^{t},\gamma):=H_{z,z}^{t,\tau}\hat{q}(\pmb{z}^{t}\mid\pmb{z}^{<t},\pmb{a}^{<t}),
$$

where $\gamma: =(t,\tau,z_{-\tau}^{<t},\pmb{a}^{<t})$ and $ {\boldsymbol{z}}_{-\tau}^{<t}$ is $z^{<t}$ but without $z^{\tau}$ . We can now rewrite (22) compactly as

$$
\hat{\Lambda}(\boldsymbol{z}^{t},\gamma)=D\boldsymbol{v}(\boldsymbol{z}^{t})^{\top}\Lambda(\boldsymbol{z}^{t},\gamma)D\boldsymbol{v}(\boldsymbol{z}^{t}).
$$

Now, notice that the sufficient influence assumption (Assumption 8) requires that, there exists $\{\gamma_{(r)}\}_{r=1}^{| |G^{z}| |_{0}}$ such that span $\{\Lambda(z^{t},\gamma_{(r)})\}_{r=1}^{| |G^{z}| |_{0}}=\bar{\mathbb{R}}_{G^{z}}^{d_{z}\times d_{z}}$ . We can thus write

$$
D\boldsymbol{v}(\boldsymbol{z}^{t})^{\top}\mathrm{span}\{\Lambda(\boldsymbol{z}^{t},\gamma_{(r)})\}_{r=1}^{| |\boldsymbol{G}^{z}| |_{0}}D\boldsymbol{v}(\boldsymbol{z}^{t})=\mathrm{span}\{\hat{\Lambda}(\boldsymbol{z}^{t},\gamma_{(r)})\}_{r=1}^{| |\boldsymbol{G}^{z}| |_{0}}\subseteq\mathbb{R}_{\hat{\boldsymbol{G}}^{z}}^{d_{z}\times d_{z}}
$$

$$
\Longrightarrow D\boldsymbol{v}\left(\boldsymbol{z}^{t}\right)^{\top}\mathbb{R}_{\boldsymbol{G}^{z}}^{d_{z}\times d_{z}}D\boldsymbol{v}\left(\boldsymbol{z}^{t}\right)\subseteq\mathbb{R}_{\hat{\boldsymbol{G}}^{z}}^{d_{z}\times d_{z}}\tag{23}
$$

Since $Dv(z)$ is invertible, there exists a permutation $P(z)$ such that $D{\pmb v}({\pmb z})P({\pmb z})$ has no zero on its diagonal (Lemma 2). Let $C(z): =Dv(z)P(z)$ . If we left and right-multiply (23) by $P(z)^{\top}$ and $P(z)$ , respectively, we obtain

$$
\boldsymbol{C}(\boldsymbol{z}^{t})^{\top}\mathbb{R}_{\boldsymbol{G}^{z}}^{d_{z}\times d_{z}}\boldsymbol{C}(\boldsymbol{z}^{t})\subseteq\mathbb{R}_{\boldsymbol{P}(\boldsymbol{z})^{\top}\hat{\boldsymbol{G}}^{z}\boldsymbol{P}(\boldsymbol{z})}^{d_{z}\times d_{z}}.\tag{24}
$$

We now show that $\pmb{G}^{z}\subseteq\pmb{P}(\pmb{z})^{\top}\hat{G}^{z}\pmb{P}(\pmb{z})$ . Take $(i,j)\in G^{z}$ . Since $e_{i}e_{j}^{\top}\in\mathbb{R}_{G^{z}}^{d_{z}\times d_{z}}$ , equation (24) implies

$$
\boldsymbol{C}(\boldsymbol{z}^{t})^{\top}\boldsymbol{e}_{i}\boldsymbol{e}_{j}^{\top}\boldsymbol{C}(\boldsymbol{z}^{t})=\left(\boldsymbol{C}(\boldsymbol{z}^{t})_{i,\cdot}\right)^{\top}\boldsymbol{C}(\boldsymbol{z}^{t})_{j,\cdot}\subseteq\mathbb{R}_{\boldsymbol{P}(\boldsymbol{z})^{\top}\hat{\boldsymbol{G}}^{z}\boldsymbol{P}(\boldsymbol{z})}^{d_{z}\times d_{z}}\tag{25}
$$

Since $C(z^{t})_{i,i}C(z^{t})_{j,j}~\ne~0$ (recall the diagonal of $C(\boldsymbol{z}^{t})$ has no zero), we must have $(i,j)\in$ $P(z)^{\top}\hat{G}^{z}P(z)$ . This shows that $\pmb{G}^{z}\subseteq\pmb{P}(\pmb{z})^{\top}\hat{G}^{z}\pmb{P}(\pmb{z})$

Since $| |P(z)^{\top}\hat{G}^{z}P(z)| |_{0}= | |\hat{G}^{z}| |_{0}\leq| |G^{z}| |_{0}$ , we must have $\pmb{G}^{z}=\pmb{P}(\pmb{z})^{\top}\hat{G}^{z}\pmb{P}(\pmb{z})$ , which yields

$$
\boldsymbol{C}(\boldsymbol{z}^{t})^{\top}\mathbb{R}_{\boldsymbol{G}^{z}}^{d_{z}\times d_{z}}\boldsymbol{C}(\boldsymbol{z}^{t})\subseteq\mathbb{R}_{\boldsymbol{G}^{z}}^{d_{z}\times d_{z}}.\tag{26}
$$

We are now going to show that the above implies that $C(\boldsymbol{z}^{t})$ is both $G^{z}$ -preserving and $(G^{z})^{\top}$ preserving. Start by rewriting (25) as follows:

$$
\text{for all}(i,j)\in\boldsymbol{G}^{z},\left(\boldsymbol{C}(\boldsymbol{z}^{t})_{i,\cdot}\right)^{\top}\boldsymbol{C}(\boldsymbol{z}^{t})_{j,\cdot}\subseteq\mathbb{R}_{\boldsymbol{G}^{z}}^{d_{z}\times d_{z}}.\tag{27}
$$

We showed that $C(\boldsymbol{z}^{t})$ is G<sup>z</sup>-preserving and $\left(G^{z}\right)^{\top}$ -preserving. It is easy to verify that this is equivalent to being $[G^{z}\ (G^{z})^{\top}]$ -preserving (where [· ·] stands for column concatenation). This remark will be useful below.

Similarly to the proof of Theorem 1, we must now show that there exists a single permutation that works for all $\boldsymbol{z}^{t}\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{z}}$ . To achieve this, we use Lemma 12 with $G: =[\bar{G}^{z}\bar{(}G^{z})^{\top}]$ and $\pmb{L}(z): =D\pmb{v}(z)$ . This allows us to say that there exists a permutation P such that $D{\pmb v}({\pmb z})P$ is $[G^{z}\left(G^{z}\right)^{\top}]$ ]-preserving for all z (not “almost all”).

Notice that $D(\pmb{v}\circ\pmb{P})(z)=D\pmb{v}(\pmb{P}z)\pmb{P}$ , which is $[G^{z}\ (G^{z})^{\top}]$ ]-preserving everywhere. Using Lemma 1, we conclude that the function $c: =v\circ P{\mathrm{~i s~}}[G^{z}\left(G^{z}\right)^{\top}]$ -preserving.

Then, $\theta\sim_{\mathrm{con}}^{z}\hat{\theta}$ (Def. 14) & $\pmb{\theta}\sim_{\mathrm{lin}}\hat{\pmb{\theta}}(D e f . I 7)$ , which together implies that

\boldsymbol{v}(\boldsymbol{z})=\boldsymbol{s}^{-1}(\boldsymbol{CP}^{\top}\boldsymbol{s}(\boldsymbol{z})+\boldsymbol{b}),

where $\pmb{b}\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{z}}$ and $C\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{z}\times d_{z}}$ is invertible, $G^{z}.$ and $(G^{z})^{\top}$ -preserving (Definition 11).

Proof Recall the equation we derived in Section 3.2:

$$
H_{z,z}^{t,\tau}\hat{q}(\boldsymbol{z}^{t}\mid\boldsymbol{z}^{<t},\boldsymbol{a}^{<t})=D\boldsymbol{v}(\boldsymbol{z}^{t})^{\top}H_{z,z}^{t,\tau}q(\boldsymbol{v}(\boldsymbol{z}^{t})\mid\boldsymbol{v}(\boldsymbol{z}^{<t}),\boldsymbol{a}^{<t})D\boldsymbol{v}(\boldsymbol{z}^{\tau}).
$$

Using Lemma 15, we get

$$
D\boldsymbol{s}(\boldsymbol{z}^{t})^{\top}D_{z}^{\tau}\hat{\boldsymbol{\lambda}}(\boldsymbol{z}^{<t},\boldsymbol{a}^{<t})=D\boldsymbol{v}(\boldsymbol{z}^{t})^{\top}D\boldsymbol{s}(\boldsymbol{v}(\boldsymbol{z}^{t}))^{\top}D_{z}^{\tau}\boldsymbol{\lambda}(\boldsymbol{v}(\boldsymbol{z}^{<t}),\boldsymbol{a}^{<t})D\boldsymbol{v}(\boldsymbol{z}^{\tau}).\tag{65}
$$

Note that Assumption 3 requires that $D_{z}^{\tau}\lambda(z^{<t},\pmb{a}^{<t})\subseteq\pmb{G}^{z}$ and $D_{z}^{\tau}\hat{\lambda}(z^{<t},{\pmb a}^{<t})\subseteq\hat{\pmb{G}}^{z}$ . Theorem 4 implies that there exist an invertible matrix $\pmb{L}\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{z}\times d_{z}}$ and a vector $\pmb{b}\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{z}}$ such that

$$
\boldsymbol{v}(\boldsymbol{z})=\boldsymbol{s}^{-1}(\boldsymbol{L}\boldsymbol{s}(\boldsymbol{z})+\boldsymbol{b}).
$$

Taking the derivative of the above w.r.t. z, we obtain

$$
\begin{array}{l}D\boldsymbol{v}(\boldsymbol{z})=D\boldsymbol{s}^{-1}(\boldsymbol{L}\boldsymbol{s}(\boldsymbol{z})+\boldsymbol{b})\boldsymbol{L}D\boldsymbol{s}(\boldsymbol{z})(66)\\ =D\boldsymbol{s}^{-1}(\boldsymbol{s}(\boldsymbol{v}(\boldsymbol{z})))\boldsymbol{L}D\boldsymbol{s}(\boldsymbol{z})(67)\\ =D\boldsymbol{s}(\boldsymbol{v}(\boldsymbol{z}))^{-1}\boldsymbol{L}D\boldsymbol{s}(\boldsymbol{z}),(68)\\ \end{array}
$$

where we used $\pmb{\mathscr{s}}(\pmb{v}(z))=\pmb{L\mathscr{s}}(z)+\pmb{b}$ to go from the first to the second line and used the inverse function theorem to go from the second to the third line.

Plugging (68) into (65) yields

$$
\begin{array}{l}D\boldsymbol{s}(\boldsymbol{z}^{t})^{\top}D_{z}^{\tau}\hat{\boldsymbol{\lambda}}(\boldsymbol{z}^{<t},\boldsymbol{a}^{<t})\\ =D\boldsymbol{s}(\boldsymbol{z}^{t})^{\top}\boldsymbol{L}^{\top}D\boldsymbol{s}(\boldsymbol{v}(\boldsymbol{z}^{t}))^{-\top}D\boldsymbol{s}(\boldsymbol{v}(\boldsymbol{z}^{t}))^{\top}D_{z}^{\tau}\boldsymbol{\lambda}(\boldsymbol{v}(\boldsymbol{z}^{<t}),\boldsymbol{a}^{<t})D\boldsymbol{s}(\boldsymbol{v}(\boldsymbol{z}^{\tau}))^{-1}\boldsymbol{L}D\boldsymbol{s}(\boldsymbol{z}^{\tau})\\ =D\boldsymbol{s}(\boldsymbol{z}^{t})^{\top}\boldsymbol{L}^{\top}D_{z}^{\tau}\boldsymbol{\lambda}(\boldsymbol{v}(\boldsymbol{z}^{<t}),\boldsymbol{a}^{<t})D\boldsymbol{s}(\boldsymbol{v}(\boldsymbol{z}^{\tau}))^{-1}\boldsymbol{L}D\boldsymbol{s}(\boldsymbol{z}^{\tau}),\\ \end{array}
$$

which implies

$$
D\boldsymbol{s}\left(\boldsymbol{z}^{t}\right)^{\top}D_{z}^{\tau}\hat{\boldsymbol{\lambda}}\left(\boldsymbol{z}^{<t},\boldsymbol{a}^{<t}\right)=D\boldsymbol{s}\left(\boldsymbol{z}^{t}\right)^{\top}\boldsymbol{L}^{\top}D_{z}^{\tau}\boldsymbol{\lambda}\left(\boldsymbol{v}\left(\boldsymbol{z}^{<t}\right),\boldsymbol{a}^{<t}\right)D\boldsymbol{s}\left(\boldsymbol{v}\left(\boldsymbol{z}^{\tau}\right)\right)^{-1}\boldsymbol{L}D\boldsymbol{s}\left(\boldsymbol{z}^{\tau}\right)\tag{69}
$$

$$
D_{z}^{\tau}\hat{\boldsymbol{\lambda}}(\boldsymbol{z}^{<t},\boldsymbol{a}^{<t})D\boldsymbol{s}(\boldsymbol{z}^{\tau})^{-1}=\boldsymbol{L}^{\top}D_{z}^{\tau}\boldsymbol{\lambda}(\boldsymbol{v}(\boldsymbol{z}^{<t}),\boldsymbol{a}^{<t})D\boldsymbol{s}(\boldsymbol{v}(\boldsymbol{z}^{\tau}))^{-1}\boldsymbol{L},\tag{70}
$$

where we left- and right-multiplied by $D s(z^{t})^{-\top}$ and $D s(z^{\tau})^{-1}$ , respectively.

Let us define

$$
\Lambda(\gamma):=D_{z}^{\tau}\boldsymbol{\lambda}(\boldsymbol{v}(\boldsymbol{z}^{<t}),\boldsymbol{a}^{<t})D\boldsymbol{s}(\boldsymbol{v}(\boldsymbol{z}^{\tau}))^{-1}\quad\hat{\Lambda}(\gamma):=D_{z}^{\tau}\hat{\boldsymbol{\lambda}}(\boldsymbol{z}^{<t},\boldsymbol{a}^{<t})D\boldsymbol{s}(\boldsymbol{z}^{\tau})^{-1},
$$

where $\gamma=(t,\tau,z^{<t},\pmb{a}^{<t})$ . Note that because Ds is diagonal, we have that $\Lambda(\gamma)\subseteq G^{z}$ and $\hat{\boldsymbol{\Lambda}}(\gamma)\subseteq\hat{\boldsymbol{G}}^{z}$ . Using this notation, we can rewrite (70) as

$$
\underbrace{\hat{\Lambda}(\gamma)}_{\subseteq\hat{G}^{z}}=\boldsymbol{L}^{\top}\underbrace{\Lambda(\gamma)}_{\subseteq\boldsymbol{G}^{z}}\boldsymbol{L}.
$$

Thanks to Assumption 11, we can apply the same argument as in Theorem 3 to show that $\pmb{L}=\pmb{C P}^{\top}$ where C is a matrix that is both $G^{z}$ -preserving and $\left(G^{z}\right)^{\top}$ -preserving, as desired.
