context:
Learning a model using several machines over their collective data is appealing. The motivation behind this distributed machine learning (ML) scheme (a.k.a. federated learning (Kairouz et al., 2021)) is usually eficiency. Another motivation is data protection, as each machine retains control over its local data. The distributed ML problem can be precisely stated as follows in a standard server-based system comprising n machines (referred as workers), represented by set $[n]: =\{1,\dots,n\}$ , and a server. Each worker i has access to a common data space $\mathcal{X}$ through a local distribution $\mathcal{D}^{(i)}$ . A model parameterized by $\boldsymbol{\theta}\in\mathbb{R}^{d}$ incurs a loss for each data point $x\in\mathcal{X}$ measured by a real-valued loss function $q:\mathbb{R}^{d}\times\mathcal{X}\mathbb{R}$ Then, for each worker $i \in [ n ]$ , the local loss function is given by $$ Q^{(i)}(\theta):=\mathbb{E}_{x\sim\mathcal{D}^{(i)}}[q(\theta,x)].\tag{1} $$ The server aims to compute a model parameter $\theta^{*}\in\mathbb{R}^{d}$ minimizing the global loss function $$ Q(\theta):=\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}Q^{(i)}(\theta).\tag{2} $$ We assume that the gradient of the loss function $q(\theta,x)$ with respect to $\theta,$ denoted by $\nabla q(\theta,x)$ , exists and is continuous at all $\theta\in\mathbb{R}^{d}$ and $x\in\mathcal{X}$ , which is standard in machine learning (Bottou et al., 2018). Solution to Byzantine failure is tight with respect to data poisoning. We consider the class of ML problems that can be solved by optimizing L-Lipschitz smooth loss functions satisfying the $\mu{\mathrm{-}}\mathrm{P}\mathrm{L}$ inequality, where the local gradients (of honest workers) have bounded covariance trace of $\sigma^{2}$ . These conditions are satisfied in many cases (Bottou et al., 2018). We further assume that the global gradient dissimilarity that characterizes data heterogeneity is bounded by $\zeta^{2}$ , which is essential to tackling misbehaving workers of either type (Karimireddy et al., 2022; Allouah et al., 2023a). We assume that the total number of fully corrupted workers is bounded by f. Note that the case of $f \geq n / 2$ is trivial as the learning error can be arbitrarily large (Lemma 1 in (Liu et al., 2021)): we thus assume $f < n / 2$ in all our results. We consider a server-based system architecture with n workers and a central server. The workers only communicate with the server and there is no communication between workers. We assume that at most f out of n workers may be faulty, either as per Byzantine failure or fully-poisonous local data. We denote by H the set of $n - f$ honest workers, and let $Q^{(\mathcal{H})}(\theta)$ denote their average loss, i.e., $$ Q^{(\mathcal{H})}(\theta)=\frac{1}{|\mathcal{H}|}\sum_{i\in\mathcal{H}}Q^{(i)}(\theta),\quad\forall\theta\in\mathbb{R}^{d}.\tag{5} $$ We assume that ${Q}^{(\mathcal{H})}$ admits a minimum, i.e., $\exists\theta^{*}\in\mathbb{R}^{d}$ such that for all $\theta\in\mathbb{R}^{d},Q^{(\mathcal{H})}(\theta)\geq$ $Q^{(\mathcal{H})}(\theta^{\ast})$ . We let $Q^{*}: =Q^{(\mathcal{H})}(\theta^{*})$ . Furthermore, we consider the class of smooth loss functions satisfying the Polyak-Łojasiewicz (PL) inequality, which is more general than strong convexity (Bottou et al., 2018) and can indeed be satisfied by some non-convex functions (Karimi et al., 2016). Assumption 1 (Smoothness) There exists $L < \infty$ such that for all $i \in [ n ]$ and θ, $,\theta^{\prime}\in\mathbb{R}^{d}$ $$ \left\|\nabla Q^{(i)}(\theta)-\nabla Q^{(i)}(\theta^{\prime})\right\|\leq L\left\|\theta^{\prime}-\theta\right\|. $$ Assumption 2 (PL-condition) There exists $\mu \geq 0$ such that for all $\boldsymbol{\theta}\in\mathbb{R}^{d}$ $$ \left\|\nabla Q^{(\mathcal{H})}(\theta)\right\|^{2}\geq 2\mu\left(Q^{(\mathcal{H})}(\theta)-Q^{*}\right). $$ As stated below, we also assume that the stochastic gradients computed by the honest workers have a bounded local covariance trace. This assumption is standard for analyzing the convergence of stochastic first-order methods (Tang et al., 2018). For all $i\in\mathcal{H}$ , by definition of $Q^{(i)}$ , and the assumption that $\nabla q\left(\theta,x\right)$ is continuous in θ and x, we have $\mathbb{E}_{\boldsymbol{x}\sim\mathcal{D}^{(i)}}\left[\nabla q\left(\theta,\boldsymbol{x}\right)\right]=\nabla Q^{(i)}(\theta)$ Assumption 3 (Stochasticity) There exists $\sigma < \infty$ such that for all $i\in\mathcal{H}$ and $\boldsymbol{\theta}\in\mathbb{R}^{d}$ $$ \mathbb{E}_{x\sim\mathcal{D}^{(i)}}\left[\left\|\nabla q(\theta,x)-\nabla Q^{(i)}(\theta)\right\|^{2}\right]\leq\sigma^{2}. $$ Lastly, as stated below, we assume the local gradients of the honest workers to have bounded diversity (or heterogeneity) over the parameter space. Without this assumption we cannot obtain meaningful guarantees in the threat models we consider, as shown by Karimireddy et al. (2022). Assumption 4 (Heterogeneity) There exists $\zeta < \infty$ such that for all $\theta\in\mathbb{R}^{d}$ $$ \frac{1}{|\mathcal{H}|}\sum_{i\in\mathcal{H}}\left\|\nabla Q^{(i)}(\theta)-\nabla Q^{(\mathcal{H})}(\theta)\right\|^{2}\leq\zeta^{2}. $$ We present here a matching upper bound (up to a multiplicative factor of condition number) for Theorem 1, considering a Byzantine adversary. We first describe the algorithm we consider, and then present its convergence guarantee. The algorithm follows the skeleton of DSGD and imparts robustness to the learning procedure by applying a momentum operation at the workers’ level and a trimmed mean operation at the server (instead of averaging), as described in Algorithm 1. Essentially, in each iteration $t \geq 0$ , each honest worker i computes a stochastic gradient $$ g_{t}^{(i)}:=\nabla q(\theta_{t},x^{(i)}),\quad \text{where} x^{(i)}\sim\mathcal{D}^{(i)},\tag{6} $$ and returns a Polyak’s momentum of its stochastic gradients, denoted by ${m}_{t}^{\left(i\right)}$ and defined: $$ m_{t}^{(i)}=\beta_{t}m_{t-1}^{(i)}+(1-\beta_{t})g_{t}^{(i)},\tag{7} $$
Algorithm 1: DSGD with distributed momentum and trimmed mean aggregation Input : $T \geq 2$, $(\gamma_0, \ldots, \gamma_{T-1})$ and $(\beta_0, \ldots, \beta_{T-1})$. Server chooses arbitrarily $\theta_0 \in \mathbb{R}^d$. Each honest worker $i$ sets $m_{-1}^{(i)} = 0$. for $t = 0$ to $T - 1$ do Server broadcasts $\theta_t$ to all workers; for each honest worker $i$ (in parallel) do Compute a stochastic gradient $g_t^{(i)}$, as defined in (6); Send to the server the momentum $m_t^{(i)}$, as defined in (7); end % A corrupted worker $i$ may send an arbitrary value for $m_t^{(i)}$ to the server. Server updates the parameter vector $\theta_{t+1}=\theta_t-\gamma_t \text{TM}^{(f)}\left(m_t^{(1)},\ldots,m_t^{(n)}\right)$; end Output: $\hat{\theta} = \theta_T$
where $\beta_{t}\in [0,1)$ is the momentum coeficient, and $m_{-1}^{(i)}=0$ by convention. The server updates its current parameter vector $\theta_{t}$ by aggregating the workers’ momentums using coordinate-wise trimmed mean (TM), defined below. Hereafter, for any $z\in\mathbb{R}^{d}$ and $k \in [ d ] .$ we denote by $[z]_{k}$ the k-th coordinate of $z .$ . Then, given n input vectors $z_{1},...,z_{n}\in\mathbb{R}^{d}$ 2 for all $k \in [ d ]$ , we denote by $\tau_{k}$ the permutation on [n] that sorts the k-th coordinates of the input vectors in non-decreasing order, i.e., $[z_{\tau_{k}(1)}]_{k}\leq [z_{\tau_{k}(2)}]_{k}\leq ...\leq [z_{\tau_{k}(n)}]_{k}$ . Then, the trimmed mean of $z_{1},\ldots,z_{n},$ with trimming parameter $f$ is a vector in $\mathbb{R}^{d}$ whose k-th coordinate is defined as follows, $$ \left[\mathrm{TM}^{(f)}(z_{1},\dots,z_{n})\right]_{k}:=\frac{1}{n-2 f}\sum_{j\in [f+1,n-f]}[z_{\tau_{k}(j)}]_{k}. $$ Theorem 3 below establishes the convergence of Algorithm 1, with a Byzantine adversary, assuming a scheduled decreasing step sizes and increasing momentum coeficients. Note that the algorithm is oblivious to the identity of faulty workers that may send arbitrary values to the server. We denote by E [·] the expectation on the randomness of the algorithm, formally defined in Appendix B. We present here the key steps involved in proving Theorem 3. Our proof is based on a new Lyapunov function, denoted by $V_{t}$ . We first motivate the design of $V_{t}.$ , and define it formally. We then analyze the growth of $V_{t}$ along the trajectory of Algorithm 1. Lastly, we show the convergence of the sequence $(V_{t})_{t=0}^{\bar{T}-1}$ for the specified diminishing step sizes, thereby proving our result. Analyzing the growth of the loss function. We analyze the growth of the loss function ${Q^{(\mathcal{H})}(\boldsymbol{\theta}_{t})}$ along the trajectory of Algorithm 1. For any $t \geq 0$ we denote the average momentum of the honest workers as $\begin{array}{ r }{\overline{{m}}_{t}: =\frac{1}{(n-f)}\sum_{i\in\mathcal{H}}m_{t}^{(i)}}\end{array}$ . Combining the result of Allouah et al. (2023a) on the robustness of TM with the standard decomposition of the loss function under smoothness assumption (Bottou et al., 2018), we get the following bound on the growth of the loss function. Incorporating the drift and deviation in the Lyapunov function. In the remaining, for any $t \geq 0$ , we denote the deviation and the drift of each worker i as $$ \delta_{t}:=\overline{{m}}_{t}-\nabla Q^{(\mathcal{H})}(\theta_{t})\quad \text{and}\quad\Delta m_{t}^{(i)}:=m_{t}^{(i)}-\overline{{m}}_{t},\forall i\in\mathcal{H}.\tag{8} $$ Due to the time-varying step size and momentum coeficient in Algorithm 1, it is dificult to derive a uniform bound (i.e., a bound that holds true for any $t\geq 0)$ on the second and third terms in the right hand side of Lemma 5. Accordingly, we cannot simply and directly analyze the variation of E $\left[Q^{(\mathcal{H})}\left(\theta_{t}\right)-Q^{\ast}\right]$ with t. Instead, we have to incorporate the drift and the deviation in the analysis. Specifically, we define the following Lyapunov function for our problem. $$ V_{t}:=\mathbb{E}\left[Q^{(\mathcal{H})}(\theta_{t})-Q^{*}+\rho\|\delta_{t}\|^{2}+\rho\frac{\lambda}{n-f}\sum_{i\in\mathcal{H}}\left\|\Delta m_{t}^{(i)}\right\|^{2}\right],\tag{9} $$ where $\begin{array}{ r }{\rho=\frac{1}{12L}}\end{array}$ . Then, by definition of $V_{t}.$ , we have E $\left[Q^{(\mathcal{H})}(\theta_{T})-Q^{*}\right]\leq V_{T}$ . Hence an upper bound on $V_{T}$ gives us an upper bound on E $\left[Q^{(\mathcal{H})}(\theta_{T}^{\mathsf{^{*}}})-Q^{*}\right]$ . With this Lyapunov function at hand, we can construct the proof by following three critical steps: (i) determining a recursive bound on the Lyapunov function Vt, (ii) choosing a desirable sequence $(\gamma_{0},\dots,\gamma_{T-1})$ to obtain tight convergence rate, and (iii) combining (i) and (ii) to derive the final bound on E $\left[Q^{(\mathcal{H})}(\theta_{T})-Q^{\ast}\right]$ Before proving a few simple lemmas that will be used in the subsequent proofs, let us introduce some useful notations. Notation: We denote by $\mathcal{P}_{t}$ the history of nodes from steps 0 to t. Specifically, we define $$ \mathcal{P}_{t}:=\left\{\theta_{0},\dots,\theta_{t};m_{1}^{(i)},\dots,m_{t-1}^{(i)};i=1,\dots,n\right\}. $$ By convention, ${\mathcal P}_{0}=\{\theta_{0}\}$ . Furthermore, we denote by $\mathbb{E}_{t}\left[\cdot\right]: =\mathbb{E}\left[\cdot\mid\mathcal{P}_{t}\right]$ the conditional expectation given the history $\mathcal{P}_{t}$ , and by E [·] the total expectation over the randomness of the algorithm; thus, $\mathbb{E}\left[\cdot\right]: =\mathbb{E}_{0}\left[\cdot\cdot\cdot\mathbb{E}_{T}\left[\cdot\right]\right]$ . Also denote by $$ R_{t}:=\mathrm{TM}\left(m_{t}^{(1)},\dots,m_{t}^{(n)}\right),\tag{27} $$ the output of trimmed mean operation. Note that by decomposing the update rule computed by the server at step t, we can treat Algorithm 1 as DSGD with a momentum term and a bias $\gamma_{t}\left(R_{t}-{\overline{{m}}}_{t}\right)$ . Specifically, we have $$ \theta_{t+1}=\theta_{t}-\gamma_{t}R_{t}=\theta_{t}-\gamma_{t}\overline{{m}}_{t}-\gamma_{t}(R_{t}-\overline{{m}}_{t}).\tag{28} $$ The key to better understand the bias term in (28) is the analysis of TM, that attempts to robustly estimate the average of the honest momentums at every step. Using a recent result in (Allouah et al., 2023a), we can actually bound the bias $\left(R_{t}-{\overline{{m}}}_{t}\right)$ from above by the spread of honest nodes’ momentums. Specifically, we have the following lemma. Lemma 15 (Proposition 2 in (Allouah et al., 2023a)) Let $n > 2 f$ . Consider $A l g o -$ rithm 1 and $R_{t}$ as defined in (27). For any $t \geq 0$ , we have $$ \|R_{t}-\overline{{m}}_{t}\|^{2}\leq\frac{\lambda}{n-f}\sum_{i\in\mathcal{H}}\left\|m_{t}^{(i)}-\overline{{m}}_{t}\right\|^{2},\quad w i t h\quad\lambda=\frac{6 f}{n-2 f}\left(1+\frac{f}{n-2 f}\right). $$ Lemma 17 Consider an arbitrary non-empty set $S\subseteq\{1,\dots,n\}$ . For any set $o f \left| S \right|$ realvalued vectors $\{x^{(i)}\}_{i\in S}$ , we obtain that $$ \frac{1}{|S|}\sum_{i\in S}\left\|x^{(i)}-\bar{x}\right\|^{2}=\frac{1}{2|S|^{2}}\sum_{i,j\in S}\left\|x^{(i)}-x^{(j)}\right\|^{2},\quad w h e r e\quad\bar{x}=\frac{1}{|S|}\sum_{i\in S}x^{(i)}. $$

Lemma 5. Suppose Assumption 1 holds true. Consider Algorithm 1 with $T \geq 2$ , and $\gamma_{t}\leq 1/L$ for all $t\in\{0,\ldots,T-1\}$ . Let λ be as defined in Lemma 15. Then, for all $t,$ the following holds true

$$
\begin{array}{l}\mathbb{E}\left[Q^{(\mathcal{H})}(\theta_{t+1})-Q^{(\mathcal{H})}(\theta_{t})\right]\leq-\frac{\gamma_{t}}{2}\mathbb{E}\left[\left\|\nabla Q^{(\mathcal{H})}(\theta_{t})\right\|^{2}\right]+\gamma_{t}\frac{\lambda}{n-f}\sum_{i\in\mathcal{H}}\mathbb{E}\left[\left\|m_{t}^{(i)}-\overline{{m}}_{t}\right\|^{2}\right]\\ +\gamma_{t}\mathbb{E}\left[\left\|\nabla Q^{(\mathcal{H})}(\theta_{t})-\overline{{m}}_{t}\right\|^{2}\right].\\ \end{array}
$$

steps.claim:
Proof Consider an arbitrary step t. Note that Assumption 1 implies the Lipschitz continuity of $\nabla Q^{(\mathcal{H})}({\boldsymbol{\theta}})$ with coeficient L. Thus, we have

$$
Q^{(\mathcal{H})}(\theta_{t+1})-Q^{(\mathcal{H})}(\theta_{t})\leq\left\langle\theta_{t+1}-\theta_{t},\nabla Q^{(\mathcal{H})}(\theta_{t})\right\rangle+\frac{L}{2}\left\|\theta_{t+1}-\theta_{t}\right\|^{2}.
$$

Substituting from Algorithm 1, $\theta_{t+1}=\theta_{t}-\gamma_{t}R_{t}$ , we obtain that

$$
Q^{(\mathcal{H})}(\theta_{t+1})-Q^{(\mathcal{H})}(\theta_{t})\leq-\gamma_{t}\left\langle R_{t},\nabla Q^{(\mathcal{H})}(\theta_{t})\right\rangle+\frac{L\gamma_{t}^{2}}{2}\left\|R_{t}\right\|^{2}.
$$

Using the fact that $2\left. a,b\right.=\left\|a\right\|^{2}+\left\|b\right\|^{2}-\left\|a-b\right\|^{2}$ , we obtain that

$$
\begin{array}{l}Q^{(\mathcal{H})}(\theta_{t+1})-Q^{(\mathcal{H})}(\theta_{t})\leq-\frac{\gamma_{t}}{2}\left\|R_{t}\right\|^{2}-\frac{\gamma_{t}}{2}\left\|\nabla Q^{(\mathcal{H})}(\theta_{t})\right\|^{2}+\frac{\gamma_{t}}{2}\left\|R_{t}-\nabla Q^{(\mathcal{H})}(\theta_{t})\right\|^{2}+\frac{L\gamma_{t}^{2}}{2}\left\|R_{t}\right\|^{2}\\ =\left(\frac{L\gamma_{t}^{2}}{2}-\frac{\gamma_{t}}{2}\right)\|R_{t}\|^{2}-\frac{\gamma_{t}}{2}\left\|\nabla Q^{(\mathcal{H})}(\theta_{t})\right\|^{2}+\frac{\gamma_{t}}{2}\left\|R_{t}-\nabla Q^{(\mathcal{H})}(\theta_{t})\right\|^{2}.\\ \end{array}
$$

As $\gamma_{t}\leq 1/L$ , we obtain that

$$
\begin{array}{l}Q^{(\mathcal{H})}(\theta_{t+1})-Q^{(\mathcal{H})}(\theta_{t})\leq-\frac{\gamma_{t}}{2}\left\|\nabla Q^{(\mathcal{H})}(\theta_{t})\right\|^{2}+\frac{\gamma_{t}}{2}\left\|R_{t}-\nabla Q^{(\mathcal{H})}(\theta_{t})\right\|^{2}\\ \leq-\frac{\gamma_{t}}{2}\left\|\nabla Q^{(\mathcal{H})}(\theta_{t})\right\|^{2}+\gamma_{t}\left\|R_{t}-\overline{{m}}_{t}\right\|^{2}+\gamma_{t}\left\|\nabla Q^{(\mathcal{H})}(\theta_{t})-\overline{{m}}_{t}\right\|^{2}.\\ \end{array}
$$

Using Lemma 15, we then obtain that

$$
Q^{(\mathcal{H})}(\theta_{t+1})-Q^{(\mathcal{H})}(\theta_{t})\leq-\frac{\gamma_{t}}{2}\left\|\nabla Q^{(\mathcal{H})}(\theta_{t})\right\|^{2}+\gamma_{t}\frac{\lambda}{n-f}\sum_{i\in\mathcal{H}}\left\|m_{t}^{(i)}-\overline{{m}}_{t}\right\|^{2}+\gamma_{t}\left\|\nabla Q^{(\mathcal{H})}(\theta_{t})-\overline{{m}}_{t}\right\|^{2}.
$$

Taking the total expectation from both sides we then have

$$
\begin{array}{l}\mathbb{E}\left[Q^{(\mathcal{H})}(\theta_{t+1})-Q^{(\mathcal{H})}(\theta_{t})\right]\leq-\frac{\gamma_{t}}{2}\mathbb{E}\left[\left\|\nabla Q^{(\mathcal{H})}(\theta_{t})\right\|^{2}\right]+\gamma_{t}\frac{\lambda}{n-f}\sum_{i\in\mathcal{H}}\mathbb{E}\left[\left\|m_{t}^{(i)}-\overline{{m}}_{t}\right\|^{2}\right]\\ +\gamma_{t}\mathbb{E}\left[\left\|\nabla Q^{(\mathcal{H})}(\theta_{t})-\overline{{m}}_{t}\right\|^{2}\right],\\ \end{array}
$$

which is the desired result.

Lemma 7. Suppose assumptions $\begin{array}{ r }{I,~\mathcal{3},}\end{array}$ and 4 hold true, consider Algorithm 1 with $T \geq 2$ 2 and λ as defined in Lemma 5. Then for any $t\in\{0,\ldots,T-1\}$ , the following holds true

$$
\begin{array}{l}\mathbb{E}\left[\left\|\delta_{t+1}\right\|^{2}\right]\leq\beta_{t+1}^{2}\left(1+4\gamma_{t}L+3\gamma_{t}^{2}L^{2}\right)\mathbb{E}\left[\left\|\delta_{t}\right\|^{2}\right]+(1-\beta_{t+1})^{2}\frac{\sigma^{2}}{n-f}\\ \left.+3\beta_{t+1}^{2}\left(\gamma_{t}^{2}L^{2}+\gamma_{t}L\right)\left(\frac{\lambda}{n-f}\sum_{i\in\mathcal{H}}\mathbb{E}\left[\left\|\Delta m_{t}^{(i)}\right\|^{2}\right]+\mathbb{E}\left[\left\|\nabla Q^{(\mathcal{H})}\left(\theta_{t}\right)\right\|^{2}\right]\right)\right).\\ \end{array}
$$

steps.claim:
Proof We recall that at any round $t\in\{0,\ldots,T-1\}$ and any worker $i\in\mathcal{H}$ , the momentum ${m}_{t}^{\left(i\right)}$ is computed as follows

$$
m_{t}^{(i)}=\beta_{t}m_{t-1}^{(i)}+(1-\beta_{t})g_{t}^{(i)}.
$$

Hence, we have

$$
\delta_{t+1}=\overline{{m}}_{t+1}-\nabla Q^{(\mathcal{H})}(\theta_{t+1})=\beta_{t+1}\overline{{m}}_{t}+(1-\beta_{t+1})\overline{{g}}_{t+1}-\nabla Q^{(\mathcal{H})}(\theta_{t+1}).
$$

where for any $\begin{array}{ r }{t\in\{0,\ldots,T-1\},\ :\overline{{m}}_{t}: =\frac{1}{(n-f)}\sum_{i\in\mathcal{H}}m_{t}^{(i)}}\end{array}$ and $\begin{array}{ r }{\overline{{g}}_{t}: =\frac{1}{(n-f)}\sum_{i\in\mathcal{H}}g_{t}^{(i)}}\end{array}$

Adding and subtracting $\beta_{t+1}\nabla Q^{(\mathcal{H})}(\theta_{t})$ , we obtain that

$$
\begin{array}{l}\delta_{t+1}=\beta_{t+1}\left(\overline{{m}}_{t}-\nabla Q^{(\mathcal{H})}(\theta_{t})\right)+(1-\beta_{t+1})\overline{{g}}_{t+1}-\nabla Q^{(\mathcal{H})}(\theta_{t+1})+\beta_{t+1}\nabla Q^{(\mathcal{H})}(\theta_{t})\\ =\beta_{t+1}\left(\overline{{m}}_{t}-\nabla Q^{(\mathcal{H})}(\theta_{t})\right)+(1-\beta_{t+1})\left(\overline{{g}}_{t+1}-\nabla Q^{(\mathcal{H})}(\theta_{t+1})\right)+\beta_{t+1}\left(\nabla Q^{(\mathcal{H})}(\theta_{t})-\nabla Q^{(\mathcal{H})}(\theta_{t+1})\right).\\ \end{array}
$$

Now by Assumption 3, we have $\begin{array}{ r }{\mathbb{E}_{t+1}\left[\overline{{g}}_{t+1}\right]=\nabla Q^{(\mathcal{H})}(\theta_{t+1})\mathrm{and}\mathbb{E}_{t+1}\left[\left.\overline{{g}}_{t+1}-\nabla Q^{(\mathcal{H})}(\theta_{t+1})\right.^{2}\right]\leq}\end{array}$ $\frac{\sigma^{2}}{n-f}$ . Therefore,

$$
\mathbb{E}_{t+1}\left[\left\|\delta_{t+1}\right\|^{2}\right]\leq\beta_{t+1}^{2}\left\|\delta_{t}+\nabla Q^{(\mathcal{H})}(\theta_{t})-\nabla Q^{(\mathcal{H})}(\theta_{t+1})\right\|^{2}+(1-\beta_{t+1})^{2}\frac{\sigma^{2}}{n-f}.
$$

Now as $(a+b)^{2}\leq(1+c)a^{2}+(1+1/c)b^{2}$ for any c, we obtain that

$$
\begin{array}{l}\mathbb{E}_{t+1}\left[\left\|\delta_{t+1}\right\|^{2}\right]\leq\beta_{t+1}^{2}(1+\gamma_{t}L)\left\|\delta_{t}\right\|^{2}+\beta_{t+1}^{2}(1+\frac{1}{\gamma_{t}L})\left\|\nabla Q^{(\mathcal{H})}(\theta_{t})-\nabla Q^{(\mathcal{H})}(\theta_{t+1})\right\|^{2}\\ +(1-\beta_{t+1})^{2}\frac{\sigma^{2}}{n-f}.\\ \end{array}
$$

From Assumption 1, we have $\left\|\nabla Q^{(\mathcal{H})}(\theta_{t})-\nabla Q^{(\mathcal{H})}(\theta_{t+1})\right\|\le L\left\|\theta_{t}-\theta_{t+1}\right\|$ . Using this above, we obtain that

$$
\begin{array}{l}\mathbb{E}_{t+1}\left[\left\|\delta_{t+1}\right\|^{2}\right]\leq\beta_{t+1}^{2}(1+\gamma_{t}L)\left\|\delta_{t}\right\|^{2}+\beta_{t+1}^{2}\left(1+\frac{1}{\gamma_{t}L}\right)L^{2}\left\|\theta_{t}-\theta_{t+1}\right\|^{2}\\ +(1-\beta_{t+1})^{2}\frac{\sigma^{2}}{n-f}.\tag{29}\\ \end{array}
$$

Now recall that $\theta_{t}-\theta_{t+1}=\gamma_{t}R_{t}$ . Therefore,

$$

Notation. Throughout this paper, we denote by $\Delta(\boldsymbol{S})$ the probability simplex over a set , and $[K]: =\{1,\cdots,K\}$ for any positive integer $K > 0$ . In addition, $f(\cdot)=\widetilde O(g(\cdot))$ or $f \lesssim g$ (resp. $f(\cdot)=\widetilde\Omega(g(\cdot))$ or $f\gtrsim g)$ means that $f(\cdot)$ is orderwise no larger than (resp. no smaller than) $g(\cdot)$ modulo some logarithmic factors. The notation $f \asymp g$ means $f \lesssim g$ and $f \gtrsim g$ hold simultaneously. In this section, we introduce the mathematical model and background of Markov decision processes. Infinite-horizon Markov decision process. We consider an infinite-horizon Markov decision process (MDP), which is represented by $\boldsymbol{\mathcal{M}}=(\boldsymbol{\mathcal{S}},\boldsymbol{\mathcal{A}},\boldsymbol{P},\boldsymbol{r},\boldsymbol{\gamma})$ . Here, and $\mathcal{A}$ denote the state space and the action space, respectively, $P:\mathcal{S}\times\mathcal{A}\times\mathcal{S}[0,1]$ indicates the transition kernel such that $P(s^{\prime}\mid s,a)$ denotes the probability that action a in state s leads to state $s^{\prime},r:\mathcal{S}\times\mathcal{A}\to [0,1]$ denotes a deterministic reward function, where $r(s,a)$ is the immediate reward for action a in state s, and $\gamma\in [0,1)$ is the discount factor. Policy, value function, and Q-function. A policy is an action-selection rule denoted by the mapping $\pi:S\Delta({\mathcal{A}})$ , such that $\pi(a|s)$ is the probability of taking action a in state s. For a given policy $\pi_{\ i}$ the value function $V^{\pi}:{\mathcal{S}}\mathbb{R}$ , which measures the expected discounted cumulative reward from an initial state $s,$ is defined as $$ \forall s\in\mathcal{S}:\quad V^{\pi}(s):=\mathbb{E}\left[\sum_{t=0}^{\infty}\gamma^{t}r(s_{t},a_{t})\mid s_{0}=s\right].\tag{6} $$ Here, the expectation is taken with respect to the randomness of the trajectory $\{s_{t},a_{t},r_{t}\}_{t=0}^{\infty},$ sampled based on the transition kernel $(\mathrm{i . e .,~}s_{t+1}\sim P(\cdot|s_{t},a_{t}))$ and the policy $\pi\ \left(\mathrm{i . e .}\right.$ 2 $a_{t}\sim\pi(\cdot|s_{t}))$ for any $t \geq 0$ . Similarly, the state-action value function $(\mathrm{i . e .,~}Q\mathrm{-}f u n c t i o n)$ $Q^{\pi}:\mathcal{S}\times\mathcal{A}\mathbb{R}$ , which measures the expected discounted cumulative reward from an initial state-action pair $(s,a)$ , is defined as $$ \forall(s,a)\in\mathcal{S}\times\mathcal{A}:\qquad Q^{\pi}(s,a):=r(s,a)+\mathbb{E}\left[\sum_{t=1}^{\infty}\gamma^{t}r(s_{t},a_{t})\mid s_{0}=s,a_{0}=a\right]. $$ Again here, the expectation is taken with respect to the randomness of the trajectory $\{s_{t},a_{t},r_{t}\}_{t=1}^{\infty}$ generated similarly as above. Since the rewards lie within $[0,1]$ ], it follows that for any policy $\pi .$ $$ 0\leq V^{\pi}\leq\frac{1}{1-\gamma},\quad 0\leq Q^{\pi}\leq\frac{1}{1-\gamma}.\tag{7} $$ Optimal policy and Bellman’s principle of optimality. A policy that maximizes the value function uniformly over all states is called an optimal policy and denoted by $\pi^{\star}$ . Note that the existence of such an optimal policy is always guaranteed (Puterman, 2014), which also maximizes the Q-function simultaneously. The corresponding optimal value function and Q-function are denoted by $V^{\star}: =V^{\pi^{\star}}$ and $Q^{\star}: =Q^{\pi^{\star}}$ , respectively. It is well-known that the optimal Q-function $Q^{\star}$ can be determined as the unique fixed point of the Bellman operator $\tau$ , given by $$ \mathcal{T}(Q)(s,a):=r(s,a)+\gamma\underset{s^{\prime}\sim P(\cdot|s,a)}{\mathbb{E}}\left[\max_{a^{\prime}\in\mathcal{A}}Q(s^{\prime},a^{\prime})\right].\tag{8} $$ In this section, we begin with understanding federated synchronous Q-learning, where all the state-action pairs are updated simultaneously assuming access to a generative model or simulator at all the agents. In the synchronous setting, each agent $k \in [ K ]$ has access to a generative model, and generates a new sample $$ s_{t}^{k}(s,a)\sim P(\cdot|s,a)\tag{9} $$ for every state-action pair $(s,a)\in\mathcal{S}\times\mathcal{A}$ independently at every iteration t. Our goal is to learn the optimal Q-function $Q^{\star}$ collaboratively by aggregating the local Q-learning estimates periodically. We propose a natural federated synchronous Q-learning algorithm called FedSynQ that alternates between local updates at agents and periodic averaging at a central server. The complete description is summarized in Algorithm 1. FedSynQ initializes a local Q-function as $Q_{0}^{k}=Q_{0}$ at each agent $k \in [ K ]$ . Suppose at the beginning of each iteration $t \geq 1$ , each agent maintains a local Q-function estimate $Q_{t-1}^{k}$ and a local value function estimate $V_{t-1}^{k}$ 2 which are related via $$ \forall s\in\mathcal{S}:\quad V_{t}^{k}(s):=\max_{a\in\mathcal{A}}Q_{t}^{k}(s,a).\tag{11} $$ FedSynQ proceeds according to the following steps in the rest of the t-th iteration. 1. Local updates: Each agent first independently updates all entries of its Q-estimate $Q_{t-1}^{k}$ to reach some intermediate estimate following the update rule: $$ \forall(s,a)\in\mathcal{S}\times\mathcal{A}:\quad Q_{t-\frac{1}{2}}^{k}(s,a)=(1-\eta)Q_{t-1}^{k}(s,a)+\eta\left(r(s,a)+\gamma V_{t-1}^{k}(s_{t}^{k}(s,a))\right),\tag{12} $$ where $s_{t}^{k}(s,a)$ is drawn according to (9), and $\eta \geq 0$ is the learning rate. 2. Periodic averaging: These intermediate estimates will be periodically averaged by the server to form the updated estimate $Q_{t}^{k}$ at the end of the t-th iteration. Formally, denoting $\tau \geq 1$ as the synchronization period, it follows $$ \forall(s,a)\in\mathcal{S}\times\mathcal{A}:\quad Q_{t}^{k}(s,a)=\left\{\begin{array}{l l}\frac{1}{K}\sum_{k=1}^{K}Q_{t-\frac{1}{2}}^{k}(s,a)&\text{if} t\equiv 0(\bmod\tau)\\ Q_{t-\frac{1}{2}}^{k}(s,a)&\text{otherwise}\end{array}.\right.\tag{13} $$ Denoting the number of total iterations by $T_{i}$ , the algorithm outputs the final Q-estimate as the average of all local estimates, i.e. $\begin{array}{ r }{Q_{T}=\frac{1}{K}\sum_{k}Q_{T}^{k}}\end{array}$ . Without loss of generality, we assume the total number of iterations T is divisible by $\tau_{\ast}$ where $C_{\sf r o u n d}=T/\tau$ is the rounds of communication. Algorithm 1: Federated Synchronous Q-learning (FedSynQ)
inputs: learning rate $\eta$, discount factor $\gamma$, number of agents $K$, synchronization period $\tau$, number of iterations $T$. initialization: $Q_0^k = Q_0$ for all $k$. for $t = 1, \cdots, T$ do for $k \in [K]$ do Draw $s_t^k(s, a) \sim P(\cdot | s, a)$ for all $(s, a) \in \mathcal{S} \times \mathcal{A}$. Compute $Q_{t-\frac{1}{2}}^k$ according to (12). Compute $Q_t^k$ according to (13). end for end for return: $Q_T = \frac{1}{K} \sum_k Q_T^k$.
We are ready to provide the finite-time convergence analysis of Algorithm 1. Theorem 1 (Finite-time convergence of FedSynQ) Consider any given $\delta\in(0,1)$ and $\varepsilon\in(0,\frac{1}{1-\gamma}]$ . Suppose that the initialization of Algorithm 1 satisfies $\begin{array}{ r }{0\leq Q_{0}\leq\frac{1}{1-\gamma}}\end{array}$ , and the synchronization period τ obeys $$ \tau\leq 1+\frac{1}{\eta}\min\left\{\frac{1-\gamma}{8\gamma},\frac{1}{K}\right\}.\tag{14a} $$ There exist some suficiently large constant $c_{T}>0$ and suficiently small constant $c_{\eta}>0$ 2 both independent of problem parameters, such that with probability at least $1 - \delta$ , the output of Algorithm 1 satisfies $\|Q_{T}-Q^{\star}\|_{\infty}\leq\varepsilon$ , provided that the sample size per agent T and the learning rate η satisfy $$ T\geq\frac{c_{T}}{K(1-\gamma)^{5}\varepsilon^{2}}(\log((1-\gamma)^{2}\varepsilon))^{2}\log\frac{|\mathcal{S}| |\mathcal{A}|K T}{\delta},\tag{14b} $$ $$ \eta=c_{\eta}K(1-\gamma)^{4}\varepsilon^{2}\frac{1}{\log\frac{|\mathcal{S}| |\mathcal{A}|K T}{\delta}}.\tag{14c} $$ In this section, we study the sample complexity of federated asynchronous Q-learning, where K agents sample local trajectories using diferent behavior policies. In particular, we propose a novel aggregation algorithm FedAsynQ-ImAvg that leverages the heterogeneity of these policies and dramatically improves the sample complexity. In the asynchronous setting, each agent $k \in [ K ]$ independently collects a sample trajectory $\{s_{t}^{k},a_{t}^{k},r_{t}^{k}\}_{t=0}^{\infty}$ from the same underlying MDP following some stationary local behavior policy $\pi_{\mathfrak{b}}^{k}$ such that $$ a_{t}^{k}\sim\pi_{\mathsf{b}}^{k}(\cdot|s_{t}^{k}),\quad r_{t}^{k}=r(s_{t}^{k},a_{t}^{k}),\quad s_{t+1}^{k}\sim P(\cdot|s_{t}^{k},a_{t}^{k})\tag{15} $$ for all $t \geq 0 .$ , where the initial state is initialized as $s_{0}^{k}$ for each agent k. Note that the behavior policies $\{\pi_{\mathfrak{b}}^{k}\}_{k\in [K]}$ are heterogeneous across agents and can be diferent from the optimal policy $\pi^{\star}$ . Contrary to the generative model considered in the synchronous setting, the samples collected under the asynchronous setting are no longer independent across time but are Markovian, making the analysis significantly more challenging. The sample trajectory at each agent can be viewed as sampling a time-homogeneous Markov chain over the set of state-action pairs. Throughout this paper, we make the following standard uniform ergodicity assumption (Paulin, 2015; Li et al., 2021b). Assumption 1 (Uniform ergodicity) For every agent $k \in [ K ]$ , the Markov chain induced by the stationary behavior policy $\pi_{\mathfrak{b}}^{k}$ is uniformly ergodic over the entire state-action space $\mathcal{S}\times\mathcal{A}$ Uniform ergodicity guarantees that the distribution of the state-action pair $(s_{t},a_{t})$ of a trajectory converges to the stationary distribution of the Markov chain geometrically fast regardless of the initial state-action pair, and eventually, each state-action pair is visited in proportion to the stationary distribution. Key parameters. Two important quantities concerning the resulting Markov chains will govern the performance guarantees. The first one is the stationary state-action distribution $\mu_{\mathrm{b}}^{k}$ , which is the stationary distribution of the Markov chain induced by $\pi_{\mathfrak{b}}^{k}$ over all stateaction pairs; the second one is $t_{\mathrm{mix}}^{k}$ , which is the mixing time of the same Markov chain given by $$ t_{\text{mix}}^{k}:=\min\left\{t\mid\max_{(s_{0},a_{0})\in\mathcal{S}\times\mathcal{A}}d_{\mathrm{TV}}\left(P_{t}^{k}(\cdot\mid s_{0},a_{0}),\mu_{\mathrm{b}}^{k}\right)\leq\frac{1}{4}\right\},\tag{16} $$ where $P_{t}^{k}(\cdot|s_{0},a_{0})$ denote the distribution of $(s_{t},a_{t})$ conditioned on $(s_{0},a_{0})$ for agent $k,$ and $d_{\mathsf{TV}}(\cdot,\cdot)$ is the total variation distance. Further, let the largest mixing time of all the Markov chains induced by local behavior policies be $$ t_{\text{mix}}^{\max}:=\max_{k\in [K]}t_{\text{mix}}^{k}.\tag{17} $$ Let us further define a few key parameters that measure the coverage and heterogeneity of the stationary state-action distribution $\mu_{\mathrm{b}}^{k}$ across agents. First, define $$ \mu_{\min}:=\min_{k\in [K]}\mu_{\min}^{k},\quad \text{where}\quad\mu_{\min}^{k}:=\min_{(s,a)\in\mathcal{S}\times\mathcal{A}}\mu_{\mathrm{b}}^{k}(s,a).\tag{18} $$ State-action pairs with small stationary probabilities are visited less frequently, and therefore can become bottlenecks in improving the quality of Q-function estimates. Clearly, $\mu_{\mathrm{{m i n}}}\leq{\frac{1}{|S| |A|}}$ . In addition, denote $$ \mu_{\mathrm{avg}}:=\min_{(s,a)\in\mathcal{S}\times\mathcal{A}}\frac{1}{K}\sum_{k=1}^{K}\mu_{\mathrm{b}}^{k}(s,a).\tag{19} $$ In words, $\mu_{\mathsf{avg}}$ is the minimum entry of the average stationary state-action distribution of all agents. The diference between $\mu_{\sf a v g}$ and $\mu_{\mathrm{{m i n}}}$ stands out when an individual agent fails to cover the entire state-action space. While $\mu_{\mathrm{{m i n}}}=0$ in such a case, $\mu_{\mathsf{avg}}$ can still be positive as long as each state-action pair is explored by at least one of the agents, i.e., $\textstyle\sum_{k=1}^{K}\mu_{\mathsf{b}}^{k}(s,a)>0$ . Note that $\mu_{\sf a v g}$ is always greater than or equal to $\mu_{\mathrm{{m i n}}}$ since $$ \mu_{\mathrm{avg}}=\min_{(s,a)\in\mathcal{S}\times\mathcal{A}}\frac{1}{K}\sum_{k=1}^{K}\mu_{\mathrm{b}}^{k}(s,a)\geq\min_{(s,a)\in\mathcal{S}\times\mathcal{A},k\in [K]}\mu_{\mathrm{b}}^{k}(s,a)=\mu_{\min}.\tag{20} $$ Last but not least, we measure the heterogeneity of the stationary state-action distributions across agents by $$ C_{\mathrm{het}}:=\max_{k\in [K]}\max_{(s,a)\in\mathcal{S}\times\mathcal{A}}\frac{\mu_{\mathrm{b}}^{k}(s,a)}{\frac{1}{K}\sum_{k=1}^{K}\mu_{\mathrm{b}}^{k}(s,a)},\tag{21} $$ which satisfies $1\leq C_{\mathsf{het}}\leq\operatorname*{min}\{K,1/\mu_{\mathsf{avg}}\}$ , and in particular, $C_{\mathsf{het}}=1$ when $\mu_{b}^{k}=\mu_{b}$ are all equal. Similar to the synchronous setting, we describe a federated asynchronous Q-learning algorithm, called FedAsynQ (see Algorithm 2), that learns the optimal Q-function by periodically averaging the local Q-estimates with the aid of a central server. See Figure 1 for an illustration. Inheriting the notation of $Q_{t}^{k}$ and $V_{t}^{k}$ from the synchronous setting (cf. (11)), FedAsynQ proceeds as follows in the rest of the t-th iteration. 1. Local updates: Each agent k samples a transition $(s_{t-1}^{k},a_{t-1}^{k},r_{t-1}^{k},s_{t}^{k})$ from its Markovian trajectory generated by the behavior policy $\pi_{\mathfrak{b}}^{k}$ according to (15) and updates a single Figure 1: Federated asynchronous Q-learning with K agents and a parameter server. For each state-action $(s,a)\in\mathcal{S}\times\mathcal{A}$ and agent $k,$ by invoking the recursive relation (49) derived from the local Q-learning update in (23), $\Delta_{u}^{k}$ is decomposed as follows:

$$
\begin{array}{l}\Delta_{u}^{k}(s,a)=\underbrace{(1-\eta)^{N_{\iota(u),u}^{k}(s,a)}\Delta_{\iota(u)}^{k}(s,a)}_{=:D_{1}}+\underbrace{\gamma\sum_{v\in\mathcal{U}_{\iota(u),u}^{k}(s,a)}\eta(1-\eta)^{N_{v+1,u}^{k}(s,a)}(P(s,a)-P_{v+1}^{k}(s,a))V^{\star}}_{=:D_{2}}\\ +\underbrace{\gamma\sum_{v\in\mathcal{U}_{\iota(u),u}^{k}(s,a)}\eta\left(1-\eta\right)^{N_{v+1,u}^{k}(s,a)}P_{v+1}^{k}(s,a)\left(V^{\star}-V_{v}^{k}\right)}_{=:D_{3}}.\tag{169}\\ \end{array}
$$
Now, we obtain the bound on the three decomposed terms separately.

Bounding $D_{1}$ . The term $D_{1}$ can be bounded by

$$
|D_{1}|\leq(1-\eta)^{N_{\iota(u),u}^{k}(s,a)}\|\Delta_{\iota(u)}^{k}\|_{\infty}.\tag{170}
$$

Bounding $D_{2}$ . By applying the Hoefding bound using the independence of transitions, the second term is bounded as follows:

$$
|D_{2}|\leq\gamma\sqrt{\sum_{v\in\mathcal{U}_{\iota(u),u}^{k}(s,a)}(\eta(1-\eta)^{N_{v+1,u}^{k}(s,a)})^{2}(\|V^{\star}\|_{\infty})^{2}\log\frac{|\mathcal{S}| |\mathcal{A}|T K}{\delta}}
$$

$$
\leq\frac{\gamma}{1-\gamma}\sqrt{\eta\log\frac{|\mathcal{S}| |\mathcal{A}|T K}{\delta}}:=\rho \tag{171}
$$

with probability at least $1-\delta,$ where the last inequality holds due to the fact that $\begin{array}{ r }{\|V^{\star}\|_{\infty}\leq\frac{1}{1-\gamma}}\end{array}$ and

$$
\sum_{v\in\mathcal{U}_{\iota(u),u}^{k}(s,a)}(\eta(1-\eta)^{N_{v+1,u}^{k}(s,a)})^{2}\leq\eta^{2}(1+(1-\eta)^{2}+(1-\eta)^{4}+\dots)\leq\eta .
$$
See (Li et al., 2021b, Lemma 1) for the detailed explanation of the bound.

Bounding $D_{3}$ . Lastly, we bound the third term as follows:

$$
\begin{array}{l}|D_{3}|\leq\gamma\sum_{v\in\mathcal{U}_{\iota(u),u}^{k}(s,a)}\eta(1-\eta)^{N_{v+1,u}^{k}(s,a)}\|P_{v+1}^{k}(s,a)\|_{1}\|V^{\star}-V_{v}^{k}\|_{\infty}\\ \leq\gamma\sum_{v\in\mathcal{U}_{\iota(u),u}^{k}(s,a)}\eta(1-\eta)^{N_{v+1,u}^{k}(s,a)}\|\Delta_{v}^{k}\|_{\infty},\tag{172}\\ \end{array}
$$

where the last inequality follows from the fact that $\|P_{v+1}^{k}(s,a)\|_{1}=1$ and

$$
Q_{v}^{k}(s,a^{\star}(s))-Q^{\star}(s,a^{\star}(s))\leq V_{v}^{k}(s)-V^{\star}(s)\leq Q_{v}^{k}(s,a_{v}^{k}(s))-Q^{\star}(s,a_{v}^{k}(s))
$$

for any $s \in S$ , where we denote $\begin{array}{ r }{a^{\star}(s)=\arg\operatorname*{max}_{a}Q^{\star}(s,a),\ a_{v}^{k}(s)=\arg\operatorname*{max}_{a}Q_{v}^{k}(s,a)}\end{array}$

By combining the bounds of the above three terms, we obtain the following recursive relation:

$$
\left|\Delta_{u}^{k}(s,a)\right|\leq(1-\eta)^{N_{\iota(u),u}^{k}(s,a)}\|\Delta_{\iota(u)}^{k}\|_{\infty}+\rho+\gamma\sum_{v\in\mathcal{U}_{\iota(u),u}^{k}(s,a)}\eta(1-\eta)^{N_{v+1,u}^{k}(s,a)}\|\Delta_{v}^{k}\|_{\infty}.\tag{173}
$$

Using the recursive relation, we will prove that the following claim holds for any $0 \leq m < \tau$ by induction:

$$
\|\Delta_{\iota(u)+m}^{k}\|_{\infty}\leq\|\Delta_{\iota(u)}^{k}\|_{\infty}+2\rho,\tag{174}
$$

which completes the proof of Lemma 20. First, if $m = 0$ , the claim is obviously true. Suppose the claim holds for $\iota(u),\iota(u)+1,\cdot\cdot\cdot,\iota(u)+m-1$ . Then, for $u=\iota(u)+m$ , by invoking the recursive relation (173), we can show that the claim (174) holds for m as follows:

$$
\begin{array}{l}|\Delta_{\iota(u)+m}^{k}(s,a)|\\ \leq(1-\eta)^{N_{\iota(u),u}^{k}(s,a)}\|\Delta_{\iota(u)}^{k}\|_{\infty}+\rho+\gamma\sum_{v\in\mathcal{U}_{\iota(u),u}^{k}(s,a)}\eta(1-\eta)^{N_{v+1,u}^{k}(s,a)}(\|\Delta_{\iota(u)}^{k}\|_{\infty}+2\rho)\\ =((1-\eta)^{N_{\iota(u),u}^{k}(s,a)}+\gamma\sum_{v\in\mathcal{U}_{\iota(u),u}^{k}(s,a)}\eta(1-\eta)^{N_{v+1,u}^{k}(s,a)})\|\Delta_{\iota(u)}^{k}\|_{\infty}\\ \end{array}
$$

$$
\begin{array}{l}+(1+2\gamma\sum_{v\in\mathcal{U}_{\iota(u),u}^{k}(s,a)}\eta(1-\eta)^{N_{v+1,u}^{k}(s,a)})\rho\\ =((1-\eta)^{N_{\iota(u),u}^{k}(s,a)}+\gamma(1-(1-\eta)^{N_{\iota(u),u}^{k}(s,a)})\|\Delta_{\iota(u)}^{k}\|_{\infty}+(1+2\gamma(1-(1-\eta)^{N_{\iota(u),u}^{k}(s,a)}))\rho\\ \leq\|\Delta_{\iota(u)}^{k}\|_{\infty}+2\rho,\tag{175}\\ \end{array}
$$

where the last inequality holds since

$$
(1-\eta)^{N_{\iota(u),u}^{k}(s,a)}\geq(1-\eta)^{\tau}\geq(\frac{1}{4})^{\eta\tau}\geq\frac{1}{2}
$$

provided that $\begin{array}{ r }{\eta\tau\leq\frac{1}{2}}\end{array}$

context:
Throughout the paper we limit the discussion to estimation of $\mathcal{M}\in\mathcal{C}^{k}$ , k-times smooth, compact submanifolds of $\mathbb{R}^{D}$ without boundary. This limitation is important for the analysis, but the algorithm we present is local and thus from a practical perspective, a local version of these assumptions should sufice. The smoothness requirement is also crucial for the algorithm. However, it is shown in Kouˇrimsk´a et al. (2024) that a non-smooth manifold can be approximated arbitrarily well by a smooth manifold without a significant change to the reach. This implies that the method presented in this paper is useful for non-smooth manifolds as well. A key concept in the analysis of manifold estimates is the reach of a manifold (e.g., see the analyses at Aamari and Levrard (2018, 2019); Feferman et al. (2018); Niyogi et al. (2008)), which was introduced by Federer in Federer (1959) and is defined as the maximal distance for which there exists a unique projection onto M.

Definition 1 (Reach Federer (1959)) The reach of a subset A $o f\mathbb{R}^{D}$ , is the largest τ (possibly ∞) such that for any $\boldsymbol{x}\in\mathbb{R}^{D}$ that maintains dis $t(A,x)\leq\tau$ , there exists a unique point $P r o j_{A}(x)\in A$ , nearest to x.

Our noise model in the analysis is as follows: We assume that we are given a finite set of samples $\{r_{i}\}_{i=1}^{n}$ drawn independently from

$$
\mathcal{M}_{\sigma}\triangleq\{q\in\mathbb{R}^{D}\mid d i s t(q,\mathcal{M})<\sigma\},\tag{1}
$$

a tubular neighborhood of M. Explicitly, we assume that $r_{i}\sim\mathrm{Unif}(\mathcal{M}_{\sigma})$ , which is the uniform distribution on $\mathcal{M}_{\sigma};$ i.e., the normalized Lebesgue measure with respect to $\mathbb{R}^{D}$

Finally, let $p\in\mathcal{M}$ , we wish to describe $W_{p}\subset{\mathcal{M}}$ a neighborhood of p as a graph of a function

$$
\varphi_{p}:W_{T_{p}\mathcal{M}}\to\mathcal{M}\tag{2}
$$

where $W_{T_{p},M}=P r o j_{T_{p},M}(W_{p})$ , the projection of $W_{p}$ onto the tangent, and $\varphi_{p}$ is defined by

$$
\varphi_{p}(x)=p+(x,\phi_{p}(x))_{T_{p}\mathcal{M}},\tag{3}
$$

where $\boldsymbol{x}\in\mathbb{R}^{d}\simeq T_{p}\boldsymbol{\mathcal{M}},\phi_{p}(\boldsymbol{x})\in\mathbb{R}^{D-d}\simeq T_{p}\boldsymbol{\mathcal{M}}^{\perp}$ , and $(x,y)_{T_{p}\mathcal{M}}\in\mathbb{R}^{D}$ denotes that $\boldsymbol{x}\in\mathbb{R}^{d}$ and $\boldsymbol{y}\in\mathbb{R}^{D-d}$ represent a point in some basis of $T_{p}{\mathcal{M}}$ and $T_{p}\mathcal{M}^{\perp}$ correspondingly. Then, we define the graph of $\phi_{p}$ to be

$$
\Gamma_{\phi_{p},W_{p}}\triangleq\{p+(x,\phi_{p}(x))_{T_{p}\mathcal{M}}|x\in W_{T_{p}\mathcal{M}}\}.\tag{4}
$$

For simplicity, throughout the paper we identify the graph of $\phi_{p}$ with $\Gamma_{\phi_{p},W_{p}}$ . That is, we refer to M as locally a graph of $\phi_{p}$ (see Figure 1).

We would like to stress that throughout the paper there is a slight misuse of notation. Explicitly, when we refer to $T_{p}{\mathcal{M}}$ and $T_{p}{\mathcal{M}}^{\perp}$ , we sometimes look at it as elements in the Grassmannian $Gr(d,D)$ and $Gr(D-d,D)$ ; i.e., subspaces of $\mathbb{R}^{D}$ with dimensions d and $D - d$ correspondingly. On the other hand, in some other occasions (as in (4)) we neglect the fact that these are subsets of ${\mathbb R}^{D}$ which is equivalent to choosing some basis and working in it.

Throughout this paper we assume that the (unknown) manifold M and the samples $\{r_{i}\}_{i=1}^{n}$ satisfy the following requirements:

1. $M\in{\mathcal{C}}^{k}$ is a compact d-dimensional sub-manifold of $\mathbb{R}^{D}$ without boundary  
2. $\begin{array}{ r }{M=\frac{\tau}{\sigma}}\end{array}$ is large enough, where τ is the reach of M and $\sigma > 0$ is the noise level.  
3. $\{r_{i}\}_{i=1}^{n}$ are samples drawn independently and uniformly from $\mathcal{M}_{\sigma}\left(\mathrm{i . e .,}r_{i}\sim\mathrm{Unif}(\mathcal{M}_{\sigma})\right)$

Given $(\boldsymbol{q},H)\in\mathbb{R}^{D}\times G r(\boldsymbol{d},D)$ we define the following minimization scheme, known as local polynomial regression $\left(\mathrm{e . g .}\right.$ , Cleveland (1979); McLain (1976)): Find $\pi\in\Pi_{k-1}^{d\mapsto D}$ a polynomial of total degree $deg(\pi)\leq k-1$ from $\mathbb{R}^{d}$ to R $_{\cdot}^{D-d}$ which minimizes

$$
J_{2}(\pi\mid q,H)=\frac{1}{N_{q,H}}\sum_{r_{i}\in U_{\mathrm{ROI}}^{n}}\|r_{i}-(x_{i},\pi(x_{i}))_{H}\|^{2},\tag{8}
$$

where $x_{i}\in\mathbb{R}^{d}$ are the projections of $r_{i}-q$ onto $H,(x,y)_{H}\in\mathbb{R}^{d}\times\mathbb{R}^{D-d}$ are coeficients in a basis of $H\times H^{\perp},U_{\mathrm{ROI}}^{n}(q,H)$ is defined through a bandwidth $\epsilon_{n}$

$$
U_{\mathrm{ROI}}^{n}(q,H)=\left\{r_{i}\in U_{\mathrm{ROI}}\mid\|x_{i}\|<\epsilon_{n}\right\},\tag{9}
$$

and $N_{q,H}$ denotes the number of samples in $U_{\mathrm{ROI}}^{n}(q,H)$ . Explicitly, the local polynomial regression is defined through

$$
\pi_{q,H}^{*}=\underset{\pi\in\Pi_{k-1}^{d\mapsto D}}{\operatorname{argmin}}J_{2}(\pi\mid q,H).\tag{10}
$$

As required to ensure convergence in probability for local polynomial regression Aizenbud and Sober (2021a); Stone (1980), we demand that the bandwidth $\epsilon_{n}\to 0$ as n → ∞ is such that

$$
0<\lim_{n\to\infty}n^{1/(2 k+d)}\cdot\epsilon_{n}<\infty .\tag{11}
$$

Unfortunately, the minimization problem stated in Equation (10) could not be used as-is, since we need an explicit relation between the failure probability, the error bound, and the number of samples. The analysis of convergence of local polynomial regression of vector-valued functions in Theorem 3.2 of Aizenbud and Sober (2021a), uses a variant of local polynomial regression, namely some sort of “median trick” Alon et al. (1999) on (10)

to unveil such an explicit connection. For simplicity of notations, we abuse the definition of $\pi_{q,H}^{*}$ in (10), and define

$$
\pi_{q,H}^{*}=\text{Algorithm 2 of Aizenbud and Sober (2021a)}(x_{i},y_{i}),\tag{12}
$$

where $y_{i}$ are the projection of $r_{i}-q$ onto $H^{\perp}$ . Any derivative of $\pi_{q,H}^{*}$ can also be estimated by means of Algorithm 2 of Aizenbud and Sober (2021a). For simplicity of presentation, throughout the paper when we write $\partial\pi_{q,H}^{*}$ or $\mathcal{D}_{\pi_{q_{\ell},H_{\ell}}^{*}}$ what we actually mean is the estimate of the derivative rather than the derivative of $\pi_{q,H}^{*}.$

We begin with $q^{*}$ (a coarse approximation of a point on the manifold) and $H_{0}=H^{*}$ (the initial tangent estimate) resulting from Algorithm 1. Then, we update iteratively the directions of H with respect to a tangent of M. Explicitly, in iteration $\ell,$ we define $H_{\ell+1}$ to be the subspace coinciding with Im $(\mathcal{D}_{\pi_{r,H_{\ell}}^{*}}[0])$ the image of the diferential of $(\mathrm{I}_{d},\pi_{r,H_{\ell}}^{*})$ $\mathbb{R}^{d}\mathbb{R}^{D}$ at 0 (i.e., the tangent to the graph of $\pi_{r,H_{\ell}}^{*})$ . In other words, we look at the manifold as a local graph of a function

$$
f_{\ell}:\mathbb{R}^{d}\simeq H_{\ell}\to\mathbb{R}^{D-d}\simeq H_{\ell}^{\perp}.\tag{13}
$$

That is, we define a local patch of the manifold through the graph

$$
\Gamma_{f_{\ell},r,H_{\ell}}=\{r+(x,f_{\ell}(x))_{H_{\ell}}|x\in B_{H_{\ell}}(0,\rho)\}\subset\mathcal{M},\tag{14}
$$

where $\rho$ is some radius where this function is defined (see Lemma 17 for more details regarding the existence of such $\rho>0)$ . Then, we estimate the first order diferential of $f_{\ell}$ through taking the diferential of the local polynomial regression estimate $\pi_{r,H_{\ell}}^{*}$ . The image of the diferential determines d-directions in $\mathbb{R}^{D}$ (i.e., an element in the Grassmannian $Gr(d,D))$ , by which we define $H_{\ell+1}$ . Following this, we define

$$
f_{\ell+1}:(r,H_{\ell+1})\rightarrow H_{\ell+1}^{\perp}\simeq\mathbb{R}^{D-d}\tag{15}
$$

Definition 4 (Principal Angles) Let V be an inner product space. Given two sub-spaces U, W of dimensions dim $(\mathcal{U})=k,d i m(\mathcal{W})=l$ , where $k \leq l$ there exists a sequence of k angles $0\le\beta_{1}\le ...\le\beta_{k}\le\pi/2$ called the principal angles and their corresponding principal pairs of vectors $(u_{i},w_{i})\in\mathcal{U}\times\mathcal{W}\ f o r\ i=1,\dots,k$ such that $\angle(u_{i},w_{i})=\beta_{i}$ are defined by:

$$
u_{1},w_{1}\triangleq\operatorname*{argmin}_{\substack{u\in\mathcal{U},w\in\mathcal{W}\\ \|u\|=\|w\|=1}}\arccos\left(|\langle u,w\rangle|\right),\beta_{1}\triangleq\angle(u_{1},w_{1}),

$$

where

In other words, given two linear subspaces of $\mathbb{R}^{D}$ of the same dimension d we can measure the distance between them based upon the principal angles. In our case, we measure the distance between two subspaces by taking the maximal principal angle (maximal angle) , and denote it as

For $\pmb{v}\in\mathbb{C}^{n}$ , its $\ell_{2}$ norm is denoted as $\begin{array}{ r }{\|\pmb{v}\|_{2}=\sqrt{\sum_{i}|v_{i}|^{2}}}\end{array}$ and we use $\ell_{0}$ norm to denote the number of nonzero elements in v. The spectral norm of a matrix A is denoted as $\|A\|=\operatorname*{max}_{i}\sigma_{i}(A)$ , where $\sigma_{i}(A)\ '_{\mathrm{i}}$ s are the singular values of A. The matrix nuclear norm of A is $\begin{array}{ r }{\|\pmb{A}\|_{*}=\sum_{i}\sigma_{i}(\pmb{A})}\end{array}$

The framework of tensor singular value decomposition (t-SVD) is based on the t-product under an invertible linear transform L (Kernfeld et al., 2015). In this paper, the transformation matrix Φ defining the transform L is restricted to be orthogonal, i.e., $\Phi\in\mathbb{C}^{n_{3}\times n_{3}}$ satisfying

$$
\boldsymbol{\Phi}\boldsymbol{\Phi}^{H}=\boldsymbol{\Phi}^{H}\boldsymbol{\Phi}=\ell\boldsymbol{I}_{n_{3}},\tag{5}
$$

where $\ell > 0$ is a constant. We define the associated linear transform $L(\cdot)$ with its inverse mapping $L^{-1}(\cdot)$ on any $\pmb{\mathcal{A}}\in\mathbb{R}^{n_{1}\times n_{2}\times n_{3}}$ as

$$
\bar{\boldsymbol{\mathcal{A}}}:=L(\boldsymbol{\mathcal{A}})=\boldsymbol{\mathcal{A}}\times_{3}\boldsymbol{\Phi}\quad \text{and}\quad L^{-1}(\boldsymbol{\mathcal{A}}):=\boldsymbol{\mathcal{A}}\times_{3}\boldsymbol{\Phi}^{-1},\tag{6}
$$

where $\times{}_{3}$ denotes the mode-3 tensor-matrix product (Kolda and Bader, 2009), i.e., for any $\pmb{\mathcal{A}}\in\mathbb{C}^{n_{1}\times n_{2}\times n_{3}}$ and $\begin{array}{ r }{M\in\mathbb{C}^{n_{4}\times n_{3}},\mathcal{B}=\pmb{\mathcal{A}}\times_{3}\pmb{M}\in\mathbb{C}^{n_{1}\times n_{2}\times n_{4}}}\end{array}$ such that

$$
\boldsymbol{\mathcal{B}}_{i,j,l}=\sum_{k=1}^{n_{3}}\boldsymbol{\mathcal{A}}_{i,j,k}\boldsymbol{M}_{l,k},\quad i\in [n_{1}],j\in [n_{2}],l\in [n_{4}].
$$

Definition 1 (t-product (Kernfeld et al., 2015)) The t-product of any $\pmb{\mathcal{A}}\in\mathbb{C}^{n_{1}\times n_{2}\times n_{3}}$ and $\pmb{{\cal B}}\in\mathbb{C}^{n_{2}\times n_{4}\times n_{3}}$ under transform L in (6), is a unique tensor $\pmb{\mathcal{C}}=\pmb{\mathcal{A}}*_{\Phi}\pmb{\mathcal{B}}\in\mathbb{C}^{n_{1}\times n_{4}\times n_{3}}$ such that $L(\pmb{C})=L(\pmb{A})\triangle L(\pmb{B})$

We denote $\ b{\overline{{A}}}\in\mathbb{C}^{n_{1}n_{3}\times n_{2}n_{3}}$ as the block diagonal matrix with its i-th diagonal block corresponding to the i-th frontal slice $\bar{A}^{(i)}$ of A in (6), i.e.,

$$
\overline{{\boldsymbol{A}}}=\operatorname{bdiag}(\overline{{\boldsymbol{A}}})=\left[\begin{array}{c c c}\overline{{\boldsymbol{A}}}^{(1)}&&\\ &\ddots&\\ &&\overline{{\boldsymbol{A}}}^{(n_{3})}\end{array}\right],\tag{7}
$$

where bdiag is an operator that maps $\bar{A}$ to $\bar{A}$ . Using (5), we have the following properties:

$$
\|\boldsymbol{\mathcal{A}}\|_{F}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{\ell}}\|\bar{\boldsymbol{\mathcal{A}}}\|_{F}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{\ell}}\|\bar{\boldsymbol{A}}\|_{F}\quad \text{and}\quad\langle\boldsymbol{\mathcal{A}},\boldsymbol{\mathcal{B}}\rangle=\frac{1}{\ell}\langle\bar{\boldsymbol{\mathcal{A}}},\bar{\boldsymbol{\mathcal{B}}}\rangle=\frac{1}{\ell}\langle\bar{\boldsymbol{A}},\bar{\boldsymbol{B}}\rangle .\tag{8}
$$

Definition 2 (Conjugate transpose (Song et al., 2020)) The conjugate transpose of a tensor $\pmb{\mathcal{A}}\in\mathbb{C}^{n_{1}\times n_{2}\times n_{3}}$ under L is the tensor $\pmb{\mathcal{A}}^{H}\in\mathbb{C}^{n_{2}\times n_{1}\times n_{3}}$ satisfying $L(\mathcal{A}^{\bar{H}})^{(i)}\stackrel{.}{=}$ $(L(\pmb{A})^{(i)})^{H},i=1,2,...,n_{3}$

Definition 3 (Identity tensor (Song et al., 2020)) The identity tensor $\pmb{\mathcal{I}}_{n}\in\mathbb{C}^{n\times n\times n_{3}}$ under L is a tensor such that each frontal slice of $L(\pmb{\mathcal{I}}_{n})=\bar{\pmb{\mathcal{I}}}_{n}$ is the identity matrix $\boldsymbol{I}_{n}$ Then $\pmb{\mathcal{I}}_{n}=L^{-1}(\bar{\pmb{\mathcal{I}}}_{n})$ gives the identity tensor under L.

Definition 4 (Orthogonal tensor (Song et al., 2020)) A tensor $\pmb{\mathcal{Q}}\in\mathbb{C}^{n\times n\times n_{3}}$ is orthogonal if it satisfies $\pmb{\mathcal{Q}}*_{\Phi}\pmb{\mathcal{Q}}^{H}=\pmb{\mathcal{Q}}^{H}*_{\Phi}\pmb{\mathcal{Q}}=\pmb{\mathcal{I}}_{n}$

Definition 5 (Invertible tensor) A tensor $\pmb{\mathcal{A}}\in\mathbb{R}^{r\times r\times n_{3}}$ is invertible if there exists a tensor $\pmb{\mathcal{B}}\in\mathbb{R}^{r\times r\times n_{3}}$ such that $\pmb{\mathcal{A}}*_{\Phi}\pmb{\mathcal{B}}=\pmb{\mathcal{B}}*_{\Phi}\pmb{\mathcal{A}}=\pmb{\mathcal{I}}_{r}$ . In this paper, we study the two-time-scale SA (Borkar, 1997), a variant of the classical SA algorithm, designed to identify the roots of systems comprising two coupled, potentially nonlinear equations. We focus on two unknown Lipschitz operators, $F:\mathbb{R}^{d_{x}}\times\mathbb{R}^{d_{y}}\mathbb{R}^{d_{x}}$ and $G:\mathbb{R}^{d_{x}}\times\mathbb{R}^{d_{y}}\mathbb{R}^{d_{y}}$ , with the aim of finding the root pair $(x^{\star},y^{\star})$ satisfying

$$
\left\{\begin{array}{l}F(x^{\star},y^{\star})=0,\\ G(x^{\star},y^{\star})=0.\end{array}\right.\tag{1}
$$

Given that $F$ and $G$ are unknown, we assume access to a stochastic oracle that provides noisy evaluations of $F(x,y)$ and $G(x,y)$ at any input pair $(x,y)$ . Specifically, for any x and $y,$ the oracle returns $F(x,y)+\xi$ and $G(x,y)~+~\psi$ where $\xi$ and $\psi$ represent noise components. Utilizing this stochastic oracle, we apply the nonlinear two-time-scale $\mathrm{SA}$ to solve the problem defined in (1) by iteratively updating estimates $x_{t}$ and $y_{t}$ for $x^{\star}$ and $y^{\star}$ , respectively, as follows

$$
x_{t+1}=x_{t}-\alpha_{t}\left(F(x_{t},y_{t})+\xi_{t}\right),\tag{2a}
$$

$$
y_{t+1}=y_{t}-\beta_{t}\left(G(x_{t},y_{t})+\psi_{t}\right),\tag{2b}
$$

where $x_{0}$ and $y_{0}$ are initialized arbitrarily in $\mathbb{R}^{d_{x}}$ and $\mathbb{R}^{d_{y}}$ . The noise components $\xi_{t}$ and $\psi_{t}$ are modeled as martingale diference sequences. The step sizes $\alpha_{t}$ and $\beta_{t}$ are chosen such that $\beta_{t}\ll\alpha_{t}$ , making $y_{t}$ “quasi-static” relative to $x_{t}$ . This diference in step sizes simulates a setting where $y_{t}$ remains nearly fixed while $x_{t}$ undergoes rapid updates, as discussed in Konda and Tsitsiklis (2004).

Assuming that for a given y, the equation $F(x,y)=0 $ has a unique solution $H(y)$ , where H is a Lipschitz operator. Under this assumption, we can regard two-time-scale SA as a single-loop approximation of the following double-loop process

Inner loop: compute $x=H(y)$ , or equivalently, solve $F(x,y)=0 $ for a fixed $y,$ (3)

Outer loop: iteratively find the root of $G(H(y),y)=0$

This formulation ensures that the solution to (1) satisfies $x^{\star}=H(y^{\star})$ ; in other words, for $y=y^{\star},x^{\star}$ is precisely the root of the inner loop. We designate the update of $x_{t}$ as the “fast-time-scale” update and that of $y_{t}$ as the “slow-time-scale” update, referring $x_{t}$ and $y_{t}$ as the fast iterate and slow iterate, respectively.

Notation. For a vector $x,\ \|x\|$ denotes the Euclidean norm; for a matrix $A,\parallel A\parallel$ to denote the spectral norm. We use $o(\cdot),\mathcal{O}(\cdot),\Omega(\cdot)$ , and $\Theta(\cdot)$ to hide universal constants and $\widetilde{\mathcal{O}}(\cdot)$ to hide both universal constants and log factors. We denote max $\{a,b\}$ as $a \vee b$ and min{a, b} as $a \wedge b .$ . The ceiling function ⌈·⌉ denotes the smallest integer greater than or equal to the input number. For two non-negative numbers a and $b,a\lesssim b(a\propto b)$ indicates the existence of a positive number C such that $a\leq Cb(a=Cb)$ with $C$ depending on parameters of no interest. For two positive sequence $\left\{a_{n}\right\}$ and $\{b_{n}\},a_{n}\sim b_{n}$ signifies lim $_{1}{_{n\to\infty}}a_{n}/b_{n}=1$ $\operatorname{By}{\stackrel{a.s.}{\to}}$ we denote almost sure convergence; by $\xrightarrow{d}$ we denote the convergence in distribution. We abbreviate $\{1,2,\ldots,n\}$ as [n].

Assumption 1 (Lipschitz conditions of F and H) For any fixed $\boldsymbol{y}\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{y}}$ , there exists an operator $H:\mathbb{R}^{d_{y}}\mathbb{R}^{d_{x}}$ such that $x=H(y)$ is the unique solution of $F(x,y)=0$ . H and F satisfy that for $\forall x\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{x}},y_{1},y_{2}\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{y}}$

$$
\|H(y_{1})-H(y_{2})\|\leq L_{H}\|y_{1}-y_{2}\|,\tag{11}
$$

$$
\|F(x,y_{1})-F(H(y_{1}),y_{1})\|\leq L_{F}\|x-H(y_{1})\|.\tag{12}
$$

Condition (12) introduces a star-type Lipschitz condition, which is less restrictive and allows for greater flexibility in modeling and analysis.

Assumption 2 (Nested Lipschitz condition of G) The operator G satisfies that ∀ $\boldsymbol{\mathscr{r}}_{\mathcal{X}}\in$ $\mathbb{R}^{d_{x}},y\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{y}}$

$$
\|G(x,y)-G(H(y),y)\|\leq L_{G,x}\|x-H(y)\|,\tag{13}
$$

$$
\|G(H(y),y)-G(H(y^{\star}),y^{\star})\|\leq L_{G,y}\|y-y^{\star}\|.\tag{14}
$$

Here $y^{\star}$ is the unique solution to $G(H(y),y)=0$

Assumption 3 (Star-type strong monotonicity) For any fixed $y~\in~\mathbb{R}^{d_{y}},~F(\cdot,y)$ is strongly monotone at $H(y),i.e.,$ there exists a constant $\mu_{F}>0$ such that

$$
\langle x-H(y),F(x,y)-F(H(y),y)\rangle\geq\mu_{F}\|x-H(y)\|^{2},\quad\forall x\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{x}}.\tag{15}

$G(H(\cdot),\cdot)$ is strongly monotone at $y^{\star},i . e .$ , there exists a constant $\mu_{G}>0$ such that

$$
\langle y-y^{\star},G(H(y),y)-G(H(y^{\star}),y^{\star})\rangle\geq\mu_{G}\|y-y^{\star}\|^{2},\quad\forall y\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{y}}.\tag{16}
$$

The star-type strong monotonicity assumption of F and G also appears in previous work (Doan, 2022; Shen and Chen, 2022). A direct consequence of the above assumptions is $L_{F}\geq\mu_{F}$ and $L_{G,y}\geq\mu_{G}$

Although a finite-time decoupled convergence rate for nonlinear two-time-scale SA is not established in the literature, asymptotic decoupled convergence has been explored under a local linearity assumption (Mokkadem and Pelletier, 2006). Next, we focus on noise models. We denote by $\mathcal{F}_{t}$ the filtration containing all the history generated by (2) before time t, i.e., $\mathcal{F}_{t}=\sigma\{x_{0},y_{0},\xi_{0},\psi_{0},\xi_{1},\psi_{1},\hdots,\xi_{t-1},\psi_{t-1}\}$

In this section, we outline the framework of our proof for Theorem 3. We first present the high-level idea and comparison with prior works, with the detailed procedure developed in Sections 5.1–5.4.

High-level idea. Our main technical contribution is a systematic framework for handling the cross term $\|\mathbb{E}\hat{x}_{t}\hat{y}_{t}^{\top}\|$ in the nonlinear setting. It’s crucial for the sharp convergence characterization of the interacting sequences $\{x_{t}\}_{t=0}^{\infty}$ and $\{y_{t}\}_{t=0}^{\infty}$ . While similar analysis exists for the linear case (e.g., Kaledin et al. 2020), the nonlinear case is harder due to the nonlinearity of F, G, and H. We approximate these mappings by their linear parts, which introduces residual errors. The key challenge is that the cross term’s dynamics intertwine with these (higher-order) residuals. Our framework systematically tracks this interaction and controls the error accumulation via a fourth-moment analysis, showing the residuals are indeed higher-order.

The whole proof is organized into the following four steps:

Step 1: Derive Convergence Rates without Local Linearity of F and G

Step 2: Introduce the Matrix Cross Term and Derive Refined One-Step Descent Lemmas

Step 3: Analyze the Convergence Rates of Fourth-Order Moments

Step 4: Integrate the Above Ingredients and Derive Decoupled Convergence Rates

Comparison with prior works. Overall, the nonlinear setting requires several additional components beyond those in Doan (2022) and Kaledin et al. (2020), even though a few individual steps are similar in spirit to these earlier analyses. The first step is close in spirit to Doan (2022), but it only provides a preliminary convergence rate and serves as a starting point for our later analysis. The second step is partly inspired by Kaledin et al. (2020), where we introduce the matrix cross term $\|\mathbb{E}\hat{x}_{t}\hat{y}_{t}^{\top}\|$ to refine the one-step descent analysis for the slow iterate; however, in the nonlinear setting, the local linear approximations of $F .$ , $G,$ and H also produce higher-order error terms, which require additional control arguments. The third step, namely the convergence analysis of fourth-order moments, does not appear in either Doan (2022) or Kaledin et al. (2020), and is needed to handle the higher-order terms caused by nonlinearity. Finally, the last step integrates all these ingredients to establish decoupled convergence, while simultaneously handling the nonlinear remainder terms and the matrix cross term.

To this end, we first present the one-step descent lemmas for the squared errors The analysis in this step does not require the local linearity of $F$ and G in Assumption 5, nor does it require the bounded fourth-order moments in Assumption 6. \begin{array}{l}\|\hat{x}_{t+1}\|^{2}=\|\hat{x}_{t}-\alpha_{t}F(x_{t},y_{t})\|^{2}+\|H(y_{t})-H(y_{t+1})-\alpha_{t}\xi_{t}\|^{2}\\ +2\left\langle\hat{x}_{t}-\alpha_{t}F\left(x_{t},y_{t}\right),H\left(y_{t}\right)-H\left(y_{t+1}\right)\right\rangle-2\alpha_{t}\left\langle\hat{x}_{t}-\alpha_{t}F\left(x_{t},y_{t}\right),\xi_{t}\right\rangle .\tag{61}\\ \end{array}
$$

For the first term, noting that $F(H(y_{t}),y_{t})=0$ , we have

$$
\begin{array}{l}\|\hat{x}_{t}-\alpha_{t}F(x_{t},y_{t})\|^{2}\\ =\|\hat{x}_{t}\|^{2}-2\alpha_{t}\langle\hat{x}_{t},F(x_{t},y_{t})-F(H(y_{t}),y_{t})\rangle+\alpha_{t}^{2}\|F(x_{t},y_{t})-F(H(y_{t}),y_{t})\|^{2}\\ \leq\|\hat{x}_{t}\|^{2}-2\mu_{F}\alpha_{t}\|\hat{x}_{t}\|^{2}+L_{F}^{2}\alpha_{t}^{2}\|\hat{x}_{t}\|^{2}\leq\left(1-\frac{7\mu_{F}\alpha_{t}}{4}\right)\|\hat{x}_{t}\|^{2},\tag{62}\\ \end{array}
$$

where the inequality uses strong monotone and Lispchitz continuity of F in (15) and (12) respectively.

For the second term, recall that $\mathcal{F}_{t}=\sigma\{x_{0},y_{0},\xi_{0},\psi_{0},\xi_{1},\psi_{1},\hdots,\xi_{t-1},\psi_{t-1}\}$ . We then take the conditional expectation of the second term on the right-hand side of (61) w.r.t. $\mathcal{F}_{t}$ and using Assumption 8 to have

$$
\begin{array}{l}\mathbb{E}\left[\|H(y_{t})-H(y_{t+1})-\alpha_{t}\xi_{t}\|^{2}\mid\mathcal{F}_{t}\right]\\ \leq 2L_{H}^{2}\beta_{t}^{2}\left\|G(x_{t},y_{t})\right\|^{2}+2L_{H}^{2}\beta_{t}^{2}\mathbb{E}\left[\left\|\psi_{t}\right\|^{2}\mid\mathcal{F}_{t}\right]+2\alpha_{t}^{2}\mathbb{E}\left[\left\|\xi_{t}\right\|^{2}\mid\mathcal{F}_{t}\right]\\ \leq 4L_{H}^{2}L_{G,x}^{2}\beta_{t}^{2}\|\hat{x}_{t}\|^{2}+4L_{H}^{2}L_{G,y}^{2}\beta_{t}^{2}\|\hat{y}_{t}\|^{2}+2\beta_{t}^{2}L_{H}^{2}\Gamma_{22}+2\alpha_{t}^{2}\Gamma_{11},\tag{63}\\ \end{array}
$$

where the last inequality uses the following inequality that depends on the fact $G(H(y^{\star}),y^{\star})=$ 0 and Assumption 2

$$
\|G(x_{t},y_{t})\|\leq\|G(x_{t},y_{t})-G(H(y_{t}),y_{t})\|+\|G(H(y_{t}),y_{t})-G(H(y^{\star}),y^{\star})\|
$$

$$
\leq L_{G,x}\|\hat{x}_{t}\|+L_{G,y}\|\hat{y}_{t}\|,\tag{64}
$$

and thus $\Vert G(x_{t},y_{t})\Vert^{2}\leq 2 L_{G,x}^{2}\Vert\hat{x}_{t}\Vert^{2}+2 L_{G,y}^{2}\Vert\hat{y}_{t}\Vert^{2}$

Combing these two inequalities, we then obtain the preceding relation

$$
\mathbb{E}\left[\langle\hat{x}_{t}-\alpha_{t}F(x_{t},y_{t}),H(y_{t})-H(y_{t+1})\rangle|\mathcal{F}_{t}\right]
$$

$$
\begin{array}{l}\leq 7L_{H}\beta_{t}\sqrt{1-\alpha_{t}\mu_{F}}\|\hat{x}_{t}\|\|G(x_{t},y_{t})\|+4S_{H}\sqrt{1-\alpha_{t}\mu_{F}}\beta_{t}^{1+\delta_{H}}\|\hat{x}_{t}\|\Gamma_{22}^{\frac{1+\delta_{H}}{2}}\\ \stackrel{(64)}{\leq}7L_{H}\beta_{t}\left(L_{G,x}\sqrt{1-\alpha_{t}\mu_{F}}\|\hat{x}_{t}\|^{2}+L_{G,y}\sqrt{1-\alpha_{t}\mu_{F}}\|\hat{x}_{t}\|\|\hat{y}_{t}\|\right)+4S_{H}\sqrt{1-\alpha_{t}\mu_{F}}\beta_{t}^{1+\delta_{H}}\|\hat{x}_{t}\|\Gamma_{22}^{\frac{1+\delta_{H}}{2}}\\ \leq\frac{\mu_{F}\alpha_{t}}{2}\|\hat{x}_{t}\|^{2}+7L_{H}L_{G,y}\beta_{t}\sqrt{1-\alpha_{t}\mu_{F}}\|\hat{x}_{t}\|\|\hat{y}_{t}\|+\frac{16S_{H}^{2}\Gamma_{22}^{1+\delta_{H}}}{\mu_{F}}\frac{\beta_{t}^{2+2\delta_{H}}}{\alpha_{t}}\tag{67}\\ \end{array}
$$

where the last inequality uses the relation obtained from the choices of step sizes $7 L_{H}L_{G,x}\beta_{t}\leq$ $\frac{\mu_{F}\alpha_{t}}{4}$ and Cauchy–Schwarz inequality.

Proof [Proof of Lemma 7] Recall that $\hat{y}=y-y^{\star}$ . Using (2) we consider

$$
\hat{y}_{t+1}=\hat{y}_{t}-\beta_{t}G(H(y_{t}),y_{t})+\beta_{t}\left(G(H(y_{t}),y_{t})-G(x_{t},y_{t})\right)-\beta_{t}\psi_{t},\tag{68}
$$

which implies that

$$
\begin{array}{l}\|\hat{y}_{t+1}\|^{2}=\|\hat{y}_{t}-\beta_{t}G(H(y_{t}),y_{t})\|^{2}+\|\beta_{t}\left(G(H(y_{t}),y_{t})-G(x_{t},y_{t})\right)-\beta_{t}\psi_{t}\|^{2}\\ +2\beta_{t}\langle\hat{y}_{t}-\beta_{t}G(H(y_{t}),y_{t}),G(H(y_{t}),y_{t})-G(x_{t},y_{t})\rangle-2\beta_{t}\langle\hat{y}_{t}-\beta_{t}G(H(y_{t}),y_{t}),\psi_{t}\rangle .\tag{69}\\ \end{array}
$$

We next analyze each term on the right-hand side of (69).

For the first term, we have that

$$
\begin{array}{l}\|\hat{y}_{t}-\beta_{t}G(H(y_{t}),y_{t})\|^{2}\stackrel{(16)}{\leq}\|\hat{y}_{t}\|^{2}-2\mu_{G}\beta_{t}\|\hat{y}_{t}\|^{2}+\beta_{t}^{2}\|G(H(y_{t}),y_{t})-G(H(y^{\star}),y^{\star})\|^{2}\\ \leq(1-2\mu_{G}\beta_{t})\|\hat{y}_{t}\|^{2}+L_{G,y}^{2}\beta_{t}^{2}\|\hat{y}_{t}\|^{2}\leq(1-\mu_{G}\beta_{t})\|\hat{y}_{t}\|^{2},\tag{70}\\ \end{array}
$$

where the first inequality also uses $G(H(y^{\star}),y^{\star})=0$ and the last inequality uses the relation $L_{G,y}^{2}\beta_{t}^{2}\le\mu_{G}\beta_{t}$

For the second term, taking the conditional expectation on its both sides w.r.t $\mathcal{F}_{t}$ and using Assumptions 8 and 2, we have

$$
\mathbb{E}\left[\|\beta_{t}\left(G(H(y_{t}),y_{t})-G(x_{t},y_{t})\right)-\beta_{t}\psi_{t}\|^{2}\mid\mathcal{F}_{t}\right]\leq L_{G,x}^{2}\beta_{t}^{2}\|\hat{x}_{t}\|^{2}+\beta_{t}^{2}\Gamma_{22}.\tag{71}
$$

For the third term, it follows that

$$
\begin{array}{l}2\beta_{t}\langle\hat{y}_{t}-\beta_{t}G(H(y_{t}),y_{t}),G(H(y_{t}),y_{t})-G(x_{t},y_{t})\rangle\\ \stackrel{(13)}{\leq}2\beta_{t}\|\hat{y}_{t}-\beta_{t}G(H(y_{t}),y_{t})\|\cdot L_{G,x}\|\hat{x}_{t}\|\stackrel{(70)}{\leq}2L_{G,x}\beta_{t}\sqrt{1-\mu_{G}\beta_{t}}\|\hat{x}_{t}\|\|\hat{y}_{t}\|.\tag{72}\\ \end{array}
$$

Finally, taking the conditional expectation of (69) w.r.t $\mathcal{F}_{t}$ and using (70)–(72) yields

$$
\mathbb{E}\left[\|\hat{y}_{t+1}\|^{2}\mid\mathcal{F}_{t}\right]\leq(1-\mu_{G}\beta_{t})\|\hat{y}_{t}\|^{2}+L_{G,x}^{2}\beta_{t}^{2}\|\hat{x}_{t}\|^{2}+\beta_{t}^{2}\Gamma_{22}+2L_{G,x}\beta_{t}\sqrt{1-\mu_{G}\beta_{t}}\|\hat{x}_{t}\|\|\hat{y}_{t}\|,
$$

which concludes our proof.

Before present the detailed proof, we first give an operator decomposition lemma, which states that with Assumption 5, we could decompose the nonlinear operators F and G as the linear parts plus higher-order error terms.

Lemma 19 (Operator decomposition) Suppose that Assumption 5 holds. With $\hat{x}_{t}$ and $\hat{y}_{t}$ defined in (24), we have the following results.

(i) $F(x_{t},y_{t})=B_{1}\hat{x}_{t}+R_{t}^{F}$ with $\lvert|R_{t}^{F}\rvert|\leq S_{B,F}(\lvert|\hat{x}_{t}\rvert|^{1+\delta_{F}}+\lvert|\hat{y}_{t}\rvert|^{1+\delta_{F}})$ . It follows that $\hat{x}_{t}-\alpha_{t}F(x_{t},y_{t})=(I-\alpha_{t}B_{1})\hat{x}_{t}-\alpha_{t}R_{t}^{F}$ . We further have $\|I-\alpha_{t}B_{1}\|\le 1-\mu_{F}\alpha_{t}$ if $\begin{array}{ r }{0\leq\alpha_{t}\leq\frac{\mu_{F}}{L_{F}^{2}}.}\end{array}$  
(ii) G $(H(y_{t}),y_{t})~=~B_{3}\hat{y}_{t}+R_{t}^{G H}$ with $\|R_{t}^{G H}\|~\le~S_{B,G}\|\hat{y}_{t}\|^{1+\delta_{G}}$ . It follows that $\hat{y}_{t}-$ $\beta_{t}G(H(y_{t}),y_{t})=(I-\beta_{t}B_{3})\hat{y}_{t}-\beta_{t}R_{t}^{G H}$ . We further have $\|I-\beta_{t}B_{3}\|\le 1-\mu_{G}\beta_{t}$ $\begin{array}{ r }{i f 0\le\beta_{t}\le\frac{\mu_{G}}{L_{G,y}^{2}}.}\end{array}$  
(iii) G(x<sub>t</sub>, y<sub>t</sub>) = B<sub>2</sub>xˆ<sub>t</sub> + B<sub>3</sub>yˆ<sub>t</sub> + R<sup>G</sup> with ∥R<sup>G</sup>∥ ≤ S<sub>B,G</sub>(∥xˆ<sub>t</sub>∥<sup>1+δ</sup>G + ∥yˆ<sub>t</sub>∥<sup>1+δ</sup>G ).

Lemma 10 (Refined one-step descent of the slow iterate $\hat{y}_{t})$ Suppose that Assumptions 2–3 and 5–7 hold. We have for any $t \geq 0$

$$
\begin{array}{l}\mathbb{E}\|\hat{y}_{t+1}\|^{2}\leq\left(1-\frac{2\mu_{G}\beta_{t}}{3}\right)\mathbb{E}\|\hat{y}_{t}\|^{2}+2L_{G,x}^{2}\beta_{t}^{2}\mathbb{E}\|\hat{x}_{t}\|^{2}+2d_{y}L_{G,x}\beta_{t}\|\mathbb{E}\hat{x}_{t}\hat{y}_{t}^{\top}\|\tag{38}\\ +\Gamma_{22}\beta_{t}^{2}+\Delta_{y,t},\\ \end{array}
$$

where $\Delta_{y,t}$ is a higher-order residual given in the following

$$
\Delta_{y,t}=S_{B,G}^{2}\beta_{t}\left(15d_{y}^{2}/\mu_{G}+d_{y}^{2}\beta_{t}+8d_{y}\beta_{t}\right)\mathcal{Z}_{t,2+2\delta_{G}}.\tag{39}
$$

steps.claim:
Proof [Proof of Lemma 10] The decomposition in (69) implies that

$$
\begin{array}{l}\mathbb{E}\|\hat{y}_{t+1}\|^{2}\stackrel{(70)+(71)}{\leq}(1-\mu_{G}\beta_{t})\mathbb{E}\|\hat{y}_{t}\|^{2}+L_{G,x}^{2}\beta_{t}^{2}\mathbb{E}\|\hat{x}_{t}\|^{2}+\beta_{t}^{2}\Gamma_{22}\tag{97}\\ +2\beta_{t}\mathbb{E}\langle\hat{y}_{t}-\beta_{t}G(H(y_{t}),y_{t}),G(H(y_{t}),y_{t})-G(x_{t},y_{t})\rangle\\ \end{array}
$$
The proof is almost identical to that of Lemma $7$ except that we take additional care on the last term.

By Lemma 19, we have

$$
\hat{y}_{t}-\beta_{t}G(H(y_{t}),y_{t})=(I-\beta_{t}B_{3})\hat{y}_{t}-\beta_{t}R_{t}^{G H}
$$

$$
G(H(y_{t}),y_{t})=B_{3}\hat{y}_{t}+R_{t}^{G H}
$$

$$
G(x_{t},y_{t})=B_{2}\hat{x}_{t}+B_{3}\hat{y}_{t}+R_{t}^{G}
$$

with $\lVert R_{t}^{G H}\rVert\leq S_{B,G}\rVert\hat{y}_{t}\rVert^{1+\delta_{G}}$ and $\lVert R_{t}^{G}\rVert\leq S_{B,G}(\lVert\hat{x}_{t}\rVert^{1+\delta_{G}}+\lVert\hat{y}_{t}\rVert^{1+\delta_{G}})$ . Therefore, we have

$$
\begin{array}{l}\mathbb{E}\langle\hat{y}_{t}-\beta_{t}G(H(y_{t}),y_{t}),G(H(y_{t}),y_{t})-G(x_{t},y_{t})\rangle\\ \leq d_{y}\left\|\mathbb{E}((I-\beta_{t}B_{3})\hat{y}_{t}-\beta_{t}R_{t}^{GH})(-B_{2}\hat{x}_{t}+R_{t}^{GH}-R_{t}^{G})^{\top}\right\|\\ \leq d_{y}\Big [(\sqrt{1-\mu_{G}\beta_{t}})\|B_{2}\|\|\mathbb{E}\hat{y}_{t}\hat{x}_{t}^{\top}\|+(\sqrt{1-\mu_{G}\beta_{t}})\mathbb{E}\|\hat{y}_{t}\|(\|R_{t}^{GH}\|+\|R_{t}^{G}\|)\\ \left.+\beta_{t}\|B_{2}\|\mathbb{E}\|R_{t}^{GH}\|\|\hat{x}_{t}\|+\beta_{t}\mathbb{E}\|R_{t}^{GH}\|(\|R_{t}^{GH}\|+\|R_{t}^{G}\|)\right]\\ \leq d_{y}L_{G,x}\left\|\mathbb{E}\hat{x}_{t}\hat{y}_{t}^{\top}\right\|+\frac{\mu_{G}}{6}\mathbb{E}\left\|\hat{y}_{t}\right\|^{2}+\frac{L_{G,x}^{2}}{2}\beta_{t}\mathbb{E}\|\hat{x}_{t}\|^{2}\tag{98}\\ +S_{B,G}^{2}\left(\frac{15d_{y}^{2}}{2\mu_{G}}+\frac{d_{y}^{2}}{2}\beta_{t}+4d_{y}\beta_{t}\right)\left(\mathbb{E}\|\hat{x}_{t}\|^{2+2\delta_{G}}+\mathbb{E}\|\hat{y}_{t}\|^{2+2\delta_{G}}\right),\\ \end{array}
$$

where the second inequality uses $\|I-\beta_{t}B_{3}\|\le\sqrt{1-\mu_{G}\beta_{t}}$ and the last inequality uses Cauchy–Schwarz inequality.

Plugging (98) into (97) yields

$$
\begin{array}{l}\mathbb{E}\|\hat{y}_{t+1}\|^{2}\stackrel{(97)}{\leq}(1-\mu_{G}\beta_{t})\mathbb{E}\|\hat{y}_{t}\|^{2}+L_{G,x}^{2}\beta_{t}^{2}\mathbb{E}\|\hat{x}_{t}\|^{2}+\beta_{t}^{2}\Gamma_{22}\\ +2\beta_{t}\mathbb{E}\langle\hat{y}_{t}-\beta_{t}G(H(y_{t}),y_{t}),G(H(y_{t}),y_{t})-G(x_{t},y_{t})\rangle\\ \stackrel{(98)}{\leq}\left(1-\frac{2\mu_{G}\beta_{t}}{3}\right)\mathbb{E}\|\hat{y}_{t}\|^{2}+2L_{G,x}^{2}\beta_{t}^{2}\mathbb{E}\|\hat{x}_{t}\|^{2}+2d_{y}L_{G,x}\beta_{t}\|\mathbb{E}\hat{x}_{t}\hat{y}_{t}^{\top}\|+\Gamma_{22}\beta_{t}^{2}+\Delta_{y,t},\\ \end{array}
$$

where we use $\Delta_{y,t}$ defined in (39) to collect the remaining terms.

Lemma 12 (One-step descent of the fourth-order moment of the fast iterate $\hat{x}_{t})$ Suppose that Assumptions $1-4,\ 6,$ , and 7† hold. We have for any $t \geq 0$ ，

$$
\begin{array}{l}\mathbb{E}\left[\|\hat{x}_{t+1}\|^{4}\mid\mathcal{F}_{t}\right]\leq(1-\mu_{F}\alpha_{t})\|\hat{x}_{t}\|^{4}+c_{xx,1}^{de}\beta_{t}\|\hat{x}_{t}\|^{3}\|\hat{y}_{t}\|+c_{xx,2}^{de}\beta_{t}^{2}\|\hat{x}_{t}\|^{2}\|\hat{y}_{t}\|^{2}\\ +c_{xx,3}^{de}\beta_{t}^{4}\|\hat{y}_{t}\|^{4}+32\alpha_{t}^{4}\Gamma_{11}^{2}+224L_{H}^{4}\beta_{t}^{4}\Gamma_{22}^{2}\tag{42}\\ +\left(20\Gamma_{11}\alpha_{t}^{2}+20L_{H}^{2}\Gamma_{22}\beta_{t}^{2}+c_{xx,4}^{de}\frac{\beta_{t}^{2+2\delta_{H}}}{\alpha_{t}}\right)\|\hat{x}_{t}\|^{2},\\ \end{array}
$$

where $\{c_{x x,i}\}_{i\in [5]}$ are problem-dependent constants defined in (107).

steps.claim:
Proof [Proof of Lemma 12] We first present the specific forms of the constants:

$$
c_{xx,1}^{de}=28L_{H}L_{G,y},c_{xx,2}^{de}=40L_{H}^{2}L_{G,y}^{2},c_{xx,3}^{de}=1280L_{H}^{4}L_{G,y}^{4},c_{xx,4}^{de}=\frac{64S_{H}^{2}\Gamma_{22}^{1+\delta_{H}}}{\mu_{F}}.\tag{107}
$$

From the proof of Lemma 6, we have

$$
\begin{array}{l}\|\hat{x}_{t+1}\|^{2}\stackrel{(61)}{=}\underbrace{\|\hat{x}_{t}-\alpha_{t}F(x_{t},y_{t})\|^{2}}_{\mathcal{C}_{1}}+\underbrace{\|H(y_{t})-H(y_{t+1})-\alpha_{t}\xi_{t}\|^{2}}_{\mathcal{C}_{2}}\\ +\underbrace{2\langle\hat{x}_{t}-\alpha_{t}F(x_{t},y_{t}),H(y_{t})-H(y_{t+1})\rangle}_{\mathcal{C}_{3}}+\underbrace{2\alpha_{t}\langle\hat{x}_{t}-\alpha_{t}F(x_{t},y_{t}),-\xi_{t}\rangle}_{\mathcal{C}_{4}}.\\ \end{array}
$$

Taking the square of both sides yields

$$
\|\hat{x}_{t+1}\|^{4}\leq\mathcal{C}_{1}^{2}+4\mathcal{C}_{2}^{2}+4\mathcal{C}_{3}^{2}+4\mathcal{C}_{4}^{2}+2\mathcal{C}_{1}(\mathcal{C}_{2}+\mathcal{C}_{3}+\mathcal{C}_{4}),\tag{108}
$$

where the last inequality is due to $(a+b+c)^{2}\leq 3(a^{2}+b^{2}+c^{2})$ for any $a,b\in\mathbb{R}$ . We then analyze these terms respectively in the following.

• For $\mathcal{C}_{1}^{2}$ , we have

$$
\mathcal{C}_{1}^{2}\stackrel{(62)}{\leq}\left(1-\frac{7\mu_{F}\alpha_{t}}{2}+\frac{49\mu_{F}^{2}\alpha_{t}^{2}}{16}\right)\|\hat{x}_{t}\|^{4}.\tag{109}
$$

• For $\mathcal{C}_{2}^{2}$ , taking the expectation w.r.t. $\mathcal{F}_{t}$ , we have

$$
\begin{array}{l}\mathbb{E}\left[\mathcal{C}_{2}^{2}\mid\mathcal{F}_{t}\right]\stackrel{(11)}{\leq}8\left(L_{H}^{4}\beta_{t}^{4}\mathbb{E}\left[\|G(x_{t},y_{t})+\psi_{t}\|^{4}\mid\mathcal{F}_{t}\right]+\alpha_{t}^{4}\Gamma_{11}^{2}\right)\\ \stackrel{(111)}{\leq}8\left(5L_{H}^{4}\beta_{t}^{4}\|G(x_{t},y_{t})\|^{4}+7L_{H}^{4}\beta_{t}^{4}\Gamma_{22}^{2}+\alpha_{t}^{4}\Gamma_{11}^{2}\right),\tag{110}\\ \end{array}
$$

where the first inequality also uses $(a+b)^{4}\leq 8(a^{4}+b^{4})$ for any $a,b\in\mathbb{R}$ and the last inequality uses (111) below

$$
\mathbb{E}\left[\|G(x_{t},y_{t})+\psi_{t}\|^{4}\right]\leq 5\|G(x_{t},y_{t})\|^{4}+7\Gamma_{22}^{2}.\tag{111}
$$

To derive (111), we first notice that

$$
\begin{array}{l}\|G(x_{t},y_{t})+\psi_{t}\|^{4}\leq\|G(x_{t},y_{t})\|^{4}+6\|G(x_{t},y_{t})\|^{2}\|\psi_{t}\|^{2}+4\|G(x_{t},y_{t})\|\|\psi_{t}\|^{3}+\|\psi_{t}\|^{4}\\ +4\|G(x_{t},y_{t})\|^{2}\langle G(x_{t},y_{t}),\psi_{t}\rangle\\ \leq 5\|G(x_{t},y_{t})\|^{4}+7\|\psi_{t}\|^{4}+4\|G(x_{t},y_{t})\|^{2}\langle G(x_{t},y_{t}),\psi_{t}\rangle,\\ \end{array}
$$

where the last inequality follows from Young’s inequality. Taking the conditional expectation gives (111).

Then we plug (64) into (110) and obtain

$$
\mathbb{E}\left[\mathcal{C}_{2}^{2}\mid\mathcal{F}_{t}\right]\leq 320L_{H}^{4}L_{G,x}^{4}\beta_{t}^{4}\|\hat{x}_{t}\|^{4}+320L_{H}^{4}L_{G,y}^{4}\beta_{t}^{4}\|\hat{y}_{t}\|^{4}+56L_{H}^{4}\beta_{t}^{4}\Gamma_{22}^{2}+8\alpha_{t}^{4}\Gamma_{11}^{2},\tag{112}
$$

where the inequality also uses $(a+b)^{4}\leq 8(a^{4}+b^{4})$ for any $a,b\in\mathbb{R}$

• For $\mathcal{C}_{3}^{2}$ , taking the expectation w.r.t. $\mathcal{F}_{t}$ , we have

$$
\begin{array}{l}\mathbb{E}\left[\mathcal{C}_{3}^{2}\mid\mathcal{F}_{t}\right]\stackrel{(11)+(62)}{\leq}4L_{H}^{2}\|\hat{x}_{t}\|^{2}\mathbb{E}\left[\|y_{t}-y_{t+1}\|^{2}\mid\mathcal{F}_{t}\right]\\ \stackrel{(64)}{\leq}4L_{H}^{2}\beta_{t}^{2}\|\hat{x}_{t}\|^{2}\left(2L_{G,x}^{2}\|\hat{x}_{t}\|^{2}+2L_{G,y}^{2}\|\hat{y}_{t}\|^{2}+\Gamma_{22}\right)\\ =8L_{H}^{2}L_{G,x}^{2}\beta_{t}^{2}\|\hat{x}_{t}\|^{4}+8L_{H}^{2}L_{G,y}^{2}\beta_{t}^{2}\|\hat{x}_{t}\|^{2}\|\hat{y}_{t}\|^{2}+4L_{H}^{2}\Gamma_{22}\beta_{t}^{2}\|\hat{x}_{t}\|^{2}.\tag{113}\\ \end{array}
$$

• For $\mathcal{C}_{4}^{2}$ , taking the expectation w.r.t. $\mathcal{F}_{t}$ , we have

$$
\mathbb{E}\left[\mathcal{C}_{4}^{2}\mid\mathcal{F}_{t}\right]\leq 4\alpha_{t}^{2}\|\hat{x}_{t}-\alpha_{t}F(x_{t},y_{t})\|^{2}\mathbb{E}\left[\|\xi_{t}\|^{2}\mid\mathcal{F}_{t}\right]\stackrel{(62)}{\leq}4\alpha_{t}^{2}\Gamma_{11}\|\hat{x}_{t}\|^{2}.\tag{114}
$$

• For $\mathcal{C}_{1}\mathcal{C}_{2}$ , taking the expectation w.r.t. $\mathcal{F}_{t}$ , we have

$$
\begin{array}{l}\mathbb{E}\left[\mathcal{C}_{1}\mathcal{C}_{2}\mid\mathcal{F}_{t}\right]=\mathcal{C}_{1}\mathbb{E}\left[\mathcal{C}_{2}\mid\mathcal{F}_{t}\right]\\ \stackrel{(62)+(63)}{\leq}\|\hat{x}_{t}\|^{2}\left(4L_{H}^{2}L_{G,x}^{2}\beta_{t}^{2}\|\hat{x}_{t}\|^{2}+4L_{H}^{2}L_{G,y}^{2}\beta_{t}^{2}\|\hat{y}_{t}\|^{2}+2\beta_{t}^{2}L_{H}^{2}\Gamma_{22}+2\alpha_{t}^{2}\Gamma_{11}\right)\\ \leq 4L_{H}^{2}L_{G,x}^{2}\beta_{t}^{2}\|\hat{x}_{t}\|^{4}+4L_{H}^{2}L_{G,y}^{2}\beta_{t}^{2}\|\hat{x}_{t}\|^{2}\|\hat{y}_{t}\|^{2}+2L_{H}^{2}\Gamma_{22}\beta_{t}^{2}\|\hat{x}_{t}\|^{2}+2\Gamma_{11}\alpha_{t}^{2}\|\hat{x}_{t}\|^{2}.\tag{115}\\ \end{array}
$$

• For $\mathcal{C}_{1}\mathcal{C}_{3}$ , taking the expectation w.r.t. $\mathcal{F}_{t}$ , we have

$$
\begin{array}{l}\mathbb{E}\left[\mathcal{C}_{1}\mathcal{C}_{3}\mid\mathcal{F}_{t}\right]=\mathcal{C}_{1}\mathbb{E}\left[\mathcal{C}_{3}\mid\mathcal{F}_{t}\right]\\ \stackrel{(62)+(67)}{\leq}\|\hat{x}_{t}\|^{2}\left(\mu_{F}\alpha_{t}\|\hat{x}_{t}\|^{2}+14L_{H}L_{G,y}\beta_{t}\|\hat{x}_{t}\|\|\hat{y}_{t}\|+\frac{32S_{H}^{2}\Gamma_{22}^{1+\delta_{H}}}{\mu_{F}}\frac{\beta_{t}^{2+\delta_{H}}}{\alpha_{t}}\right)\\ \leq\mu_{F}\alpha_{t}\|\hat{x}_{t}\|^{4}+14L_{H}L_{G,y}\beta_{t}\|\hat{x}_{t}\|^{3}\|\hat{y}_{t}\|+\frac{32S_{H}^{2}\Gamma_{22}^{1+\delta_{H}}}{\mu_{F}}\frac{\beta_{t}^{2+2\delta_{H}}}{\alpha_{t}}\|\hat{x}_{t}\|^{2}.\tag{116}\\ \end{array}
$$

• For $\mathcal{C}_{1}\mathcal{C}_{4}$ , taking the expectation w.r.t. $\mathcal{F}_{t}$ , we have

$$
\mathbb{E}\left[\mathcal{C}_{1}\mathcal{C}_{4}\mid\mathcal{F}_{t}\right]=\mathcal{C}_{1}\mathbb{E}\left[\mathcal{C}_{4}\mid\mathcal{F}_{t}\right]=0.\tag{117}
$$

Moreover, since $\begin{array}{ r }{\alpha_{t}\leq\frac{1}{12\mu_{F}}}\end{array}$ and $\begin{array}{ r }{\frac{\beta_{t}^{2}}{\alpha_{t}}\leq\frac{\mu_{F}}{200L_{H}^{2}L_{G,x}^{2}}}\end{array}$ , we have

$$
1-\frac{3\mu_{F}\alpha_{t}}{2}+\frac{49\mu_{F}^{2}\alpha_{t}^{2}}{16}+40L_{H}^{2}L_{G,x}^{2}\beta_{t}^{2}+1280L_{H}^{4}L_{G,x}^{4}\beta_{t}^{4}\leq 1-\mu_{F}\alpha_{t}.
$$

Taking the expectation on both sides of (108) w.r.t. $\mathcal{F}_{t}$ and plugging (109), (112) to (117) into it, together with the above inequality and the definition of $\{c_{x x,i}\}_{i\in [4]}$ in (107), we obtain (42).
