The limitations of dimension reduction and the potential applications of manifold fitting underline the value of formulating the manifold fitting problem, as follows. Suppose the observed data samples $X=\{x_{i}\in\mathbb{R}^{D}\}_{i=1}^{N}$ are in the form

$$
x_{i}=y_{i}+\xi_{i},
$$

where $y_{1},\cdots,y_{N}$ are unobserved variables drawn from the uniform distribution supported on the latent manifold M with dimension $d < D$ . Generally, M is assumed to be a compact and smooth sub-manifold embedded in the ambient space $\mathbb{R}^{D}$ . The precise conditions on M will be detailed in Section 2.1. The uniform distribution assumption of $y_{i}$ sampled from M is the same as those used in the related works (Genovese et al., 2012c, 2014; Mohammed and

Narayanan, 2017). Here, $\xi_{1},\cdots\xi_{N}$ are drawn from a distribution G. The assumptions about the noisy distribution G difer among the related work. The simplest assumption is that the observed samples are noiseless (Feferman et al., 2016; Mohammed and Narayanan, 2017). However, some literature assumes that the noise is distributed in a bounded region centered at the origin, which means that the observed samples are located in a tube centered at M (Genovese et al., 2012b). Other literature, such as Genovese et al. (2012c, 2014); Feferman et al. (2018), assumes $G$ to be a Gaussian distribution supported on $\mathbb{R}^{D}$ , whose density at ξ is

$$
(\frac{1}{2\pi\sigma^{2}})^{\frac{D}{2}}\exp(-\frac{\|\xi\|_{2}^{2}}{2\sigma^{2}}).\tag{1.1}
$$

The tail of the Gaussian distribution might make the theoretical analysis more challenging than in the previous two cases. Strictly speaking, previous manifold fitting methods have not directly addressed this problem, nor have they proved the convergence of the fitted manifold under this assumption. In this paper, we are concerned with the Gaussian assumption of noisy distribution, denoting it as $G_{\sigma}$ to stress the deviation parameter σ hereafter. Under the above settings, the goal is to produce a smooth manifold $\mathcal{M}_{\mathrm{out}}$ convergent to M. Specifically, if $\sigma$ is suficiently small, one could derive $M_{\mathrm{out}}$ such that $d(x,{\mathcal{M}})\leq O(\sigma)$ holds for any arbitrary $x\in\mathcal{M}_{\mathrm{out}}$ . In particular, $\mathcal{M}_{\mathrm{out}}$ converges to M when $\sigma  0$ The convergence with respect to $\sigma$ is the domain that Feferman et al. (2018) is built on, although its final theoretical result is expressed through sample complexity.

Throughout this paper, the latent manifold is denoted as M and our approximation to M is denoted as $\mathcal{M}_{\mathrm{out}}$ . For a set $A\subset\mathbb{R}^{D}$ and a point $\boldsymbol{x}\in\mathbb{R}^{D}$ 2 $\Pi_{A}x$ denotes the projection of x onto $A,$ namely the nearest point in A to x. Hence $\Pi_{\mathcal{M}}x$ is the projection of x onto the latent manifold. If there is no ambiguity, we might use $x^{*}$ instead of $\Pi_{\mathcal{M}}x$ for simplicity. The distance between x and A, denoted by $d(x,A)$ , is the Euclidean distance between $\Pi_{A}{x}$ and x. For any $x^{*}\in\mathcal{M},T_{x^{*}}\mathcal{M}$ denotes the tangent space of M at $x^{*}$ and $\Pi_{x^{*}}$ denotes the orthogonal projection onto the normal space of M at $x^{*}$ . We will make frequent use of the lower-cases $c,c_{0},c_{1}$ , etc. and upper-cases $C,C_{0},C_{1}$ etc., in the rest of this paper with the lower-cases denoting generic constants less than 1, while the upper-cases denote generic constants greater than 1. Values of the generic constants may change from line to line. By constants, we mean they are independent of the radius r, the standard deviation σ or x, while the constants may depend on some other constants used to characterize the manifold, such as the reach of M.

We denote $B_{D}(x,r)$ as the Euclidean ball in $\mathbb{R}^{D}$ centered at x of radius r, which defines a neighborhood of x. The index set $I_{x,r}$ is defined as the indices of the sample points in $B_{D}(x,r)$ , and $\left|I_{x,r}\right|$ denotes the cardinality of $I_{x,r}$ . As given in (1.1), σ represents the standard deviation of noise. Throughout this paper, we assume

$$
r=O(\sqrt{\sigma}),\quad\sigma<1 \tag{2.1}
$$

without loss of generality, otherwise the data could be rescaled so that $\sigma < 1$ holds. Here $r=O({\sqrt{\sigma}})$ means that there exist constants c and C such that $c{\sqrt{\sigma}}\leq r\leq C{\sqrt{\sigma}}$ . Noticing $\sigma < 1$ , we obtain

$$
r\leq C\sqrt{\sigma}<C.\tag{2.2}
$$

This means r can be bounded above by certain constant. In subsequent proofs, under the premise that it does not afect the final precision of conclusive upper bound, we will relax some r to C in order to simplify the proof.

The latent manifold M is supposed to be boundaryless, compact, d-dimensional, and twice diferentiable, with a reach bounded by $\tau > 0$ . The concept reach is a measure of the regularity of the manifold, first introduced by Federer (Federer, 1959) as follows:

Definition 1 (Reach). Let M be a closed subset of $\mathbb{R}^{D}$ . The reach of M, denoted by reach(M), is the largest number τ to have the property that any point at a distance $r < \tau$ from M has a unique nearest point in M.

This section introduces a novel method for estimating the bias $f(x)$ from a point x to the latent manifold M, and defines the approximated manifold $\mathcal{M}_{\mathrm{out}}$ as the points satisfying $f(x)=\mathbf{0}$ . Unlike the aforementioned methods, which rely on discs centered at sample points to estimate the bias $f(x)$ , here we build upon the fact that a Riemannian manifold can be locally treated as an afine space and calculate the bias from x to $T_{x^{*}}{\mathcal{M}}$ as an equivalent measure of the bias $f(x)$ from x to $\mathcal{M}$ . Thus, the key to addressing such a bias is to find an afine space $\{x^{\prime}:\Psi_{x}^{\alpha}(x^{\prime}-\mathbf{b})\}$ approximating $T_{x^{*}}{\mathcal{M}}$ , where $\Psi_{x}^{\alpha}$ estimates the orthogonal projection onto the normal space at $x^{*}$ and b estimates one points in $T_{x^{*}}{\mathcal{M}}$

In order to approximate the orthogonal projection onto the normal space of $\mathcal{M}$ at $x^{*}$ $\Psi_{x}^{\alpha}$ is defined as the weighted average of $\{P_{x_{i}}\}_{i\in I_{x,r}}$ , where $P_{x_{i}}$ is the orthogonal projection perpendicular to the first d principal components in $B_{D}(x_{i},r^{\prime})$ . Mathematically, $P_{x_{i}}=$ $V_{\perp}V_{\perp}^{T}$ , where $V_{\perp}$ is the orthogonal component of V and V is the $D \times d$ matrix whose columns are the eigenvectors corresponding to the largest d eigenvalues of $\begin{array}{ r }{\sum_{j\in I_{x_{i},r^{\prime}}}(x_{j}-x_{i})(x_{j}-x_{i})^{T}}\end{array}$ The radius $r^{\prime}$ should be suficiently large, so that the intersection of $B_{D}(x_{i},r^{\prime})$ and M is nonempty. Further analysis in Section 3.1 explains that we need $r^{\prime}\geq 2 r$

As the weighted average of $\{P_{x_{i}}\}_{i\in I_{x,r}}$

$$
\Psi_{x}^{\alpha}=\Pi_{\mathrm{hi}}(A_{x}),\quad A_{x}=\sum_{i\in I_{x,r}}\alpha_{i}(x)P_{x_{i}}.\tag{2.4}
$$

Here, $\Pi_{\mathrm{hi}}(A)$ denotes the projection onto the span of the eigenvectors corresponding to the largest $D - d$ eigenvalues of A. Specifically, $\Pi_{\mathrm{hi}}(A)=V{\bar{V}}^{T}$ , V is a $D\times(D-d)$ matrix whose columns are the eigenvectors corresponding to the largest $D - d$ eigenvalues of A. Further, the weights $\alpha_{i}:\mathbb{R}^{D}\mathbb{R}$ in (2.4) are defined as follows:

$$

$$

with $\beta \geq 2$ a fixed integer guaranteeing $f(x)$ in (2.6) to be twice diferentiable.

Under the assumption that a manifold can be approximated well by an afine space locally, samples in the neighborhood of x lie close to $T_{x^{*}}{\mathcal{M}}$ , with the exception of noise. Therefore, a convex combination of these samples also lies close to $T_{x^{*}}{\mathcal{M}}$ . Thus, we can estimate b using the average of sample points in the neighborhood of x. Recalling the weights in (2.5), we formulate b $\textstyle=\sum_{i\in I_{x,r}}\alpha_{i}(x)x_{i}$ as the weighted average of sample points in the neighborhood of $x .$ Then the bias from x to the space $\{x^{\prime}:\Psi_{x}^{\alpha}(x^{\prime}-\mathbf{b})\}$ is

context: In this section we establish notation for reference in the rest of the text. We let S be a countably infinite set with the discrete topology. In sections 4 and 5 where we study guarantees for kernels on arbitrary infinite discrete spaces, S can be any countable infinite set; in the rest of the paper we will specifically be interested in the case when S is the space of sequences (defined below). For any finite set B we will define |B| as its cardinality. We let N be the set of natural numbers $\{0,1,2,\ldots\}$ . We also define $\mathbb{1}(P)$ to be the indicator function, which is 1 if P is true and 0 if it is false. If $y,z\in\mathbb{R}$ , we define $y \vee z$ as their maximum and $y\wedge z{\mathrm{~a s}}$ their minimum. For $X \ \in \ S$ , by $\delta_{X}$ we either mean the function or measure that is 1 on X and 0 everywhere else. We call $C_{0}(S)$ the space of functions on S that vanish at infinity and $\|\cdot\|_{\infty}$ the infinity norm on $C_{0}(S)$ . We define $C_{C}(S)$ to be the set of functions on S that are non-zero at only finitely many points. We define ${\mathcal{P}}(S)$ to be the space of probability distributions on S. A kernel is a function $k:S\times S\to\mathbb{R}$ such that for any finite set of $Y_{1},\dots,Y_{N}\ \in$ S and $\begin{array}{ r }{\alpha_{1},\dots,\alpha_{N}\in\mathbb{R},\sum_{n,m}\alpha_{n}\alpha_{m}k(Y_{n},Y_{m})\geq 0}\end{array}$ We define the inner product $(\cdot|\cdot)_{k}$ on linear combinations of functions $k_{Y}=k(Y,\cdot)$ so that $\begin{array}{ r l }{{\bigl(\sum_{n=1}^{N}\alpha_{n}k_{X_{n}}\big|\sum_{m=1}^{M}\beta_{m}k_{Y_{m}}\bigr)_{k}=}\qquad}&{{}}\end{array}$ $\begin{array}{ r }{\sum_{n,m}\alpha_{n}\beta_{m}k(X_{n},Y_{m})}\end{array}$ for $X_{n},Y_{m}\in S$ and $\alpha_{n},\beta_{m}\in\mathbb{R}$ . We denote the associated norm as $\|\cdot\|_{k}$ . We say that a kernel is strictly positive definite if $\textstyle\sum_{n=1}^{N}\alpha_{n}k_{X_{n}}\neq 0$ when the $X_{n}$ are distinct and $\alpha_{n}$ are non-zero. We define the reproducing kernel Hilbert space (RKHS) of the kernel $\mathcal{H}_{k}$ as the Hilbert space completion using the inner product $(\cdot|\cdot)_{k}$ . We can write every $f\in\mathcal{H}_{k}$ as a function on S given by $f(X)=(f|k_{X})_{k}$ . For a set of vectors $\{v_{\lambda}\}_{\lambda}\subset{\mathcal{H}}_{k}$ we define span $\{v_{\lambda}\}_{\lambda}$ as the set of finite linear combinations of elements of $\{v_{\lambda}\}_{\lambda}$ Say µ is a signed measure on S such that $\begin{array}{ r }{\int d|\mu|(X)\sqrt{k(X,X)}<\infty}\end{array}$ . Then there is a $\textit{ f }\in\mathcal{H}_{k}$ such that for all $\textit{ g }\in\mathcal{H}_{k}$ we have $(f|g)_{k}\ =\ \textstyle\int d\mu(X)g(X)$ and $\|f\|_{k}^{2}=$ $\begin{array}{ r }{\int d\mu(X)\int d\mu(Y)k(X,Y)}\end{array}$ . This element of $\mathcal{H}_{k}$ is called the “kernel embedding” of the measure $\mu,$ denoted $\textstyle{\int d\mu(X)k_{X}}$ Let B be a finite set, the “alphabet” (for example, this would be the four nucleotides for DNA, or the twenty amino acids for proteins). We define the set of sequences as $\cup_{L=0}^{\infty}B^{L}$ where $B^{0}$ is defined to be the set containing just the sequence of length zero, ∅. For a sequence X, and numbers ${\mathit{l}},{{\mathit{l}}^{\prime}}.$ , we define $X_{(:l)}$ as the first l letters in X, $X_{(l:l^{\prime})}$ as the l0 − l letters after the first l letters and $X_{(l:)}$ as all letters after the first l letters, which is potentially the empty sequence ∅. We call $X_{(l)}$ the l-th letter of X, starting counting at 0. The concatenation of sequences X, Y is denoted $X + Y$ . For any number l, the sequence X concatenated to itself l times is denoted $l \times X$ . We call $d_{H}(X,Y)$ the Hamming distance between the sequences X and Y , that is the total number of mismatches between the two sequences after they have been padded with an infinite tail of stop symbols \$. In this section we introduce the discrete mass property and describe its implications for kernel flexibility. We focus on properties necessary for procedures useful in biological sequence analysis. In particular, we show that if a kernel has discrete masses, it is (1) universal (an important property for consistent regression), (2) characteristic (important for consistent two-sample testing (Gretton et al., 2012; Fukumizu et al., 2007)) and (3) metrizes the space of distributions (important for optimizing sequence distributions (Li et al., 2017; Pronzato and Zhigljavsky, 2020; Husz´ar and Duvenaud, 2012; Futami et al., 2019)). Later, we will design biological sequence kernels that have discrete masses to satisfy these three properties. We say a kernel has discrete masses if its Hilbert space includes delta functions at all points in the space S. Note that in this section we take S to be an arbitrary discrete space; later (starting in Section 6) we will specialize to the setting where S is sequence space. Definition 1 (The discrete mass property) We say k has discrete masses if $C_{C}(S)\subset$ $\mathcal{H}_{k}$ , where $C_{C}(S)$ is the set of all functions on S that are non-zero at only finitely many points. Since $\mathcal{H}_{k}$ is a linear space, this is equivalent to $\delta_{X}\in\mathcal{H}_{k}$ for all $X \in S$ Next we consider re-weighting kernels to emphasize or de-emphasize certain areas of sequence space. More precisely, we consider tilting a kernel k by some function $A:S\to(0,\infty)$ to obtain a new kernel $k^{A}(X,Y)=A(X)k(X,Y)A(Y)$ for $X,Y\in S$ . The discrete mass property is preserved after tilting. Proposition 16 If k is a kernel on S that has discrete masses, then $k^{A}$ has discrete masses. Finally, we look at a novel transformation of kernels, specific to biological sequences, that involves “reparameterizing” the alphabet B. The basic idea starts from representing letters in the alphabet B as one-hot encoded vectors, i.e. we treat each $b \in B$ as a vector of length |B| with zeros everywhere except at one position. The alphabet B thus forms a basis of $\mathbb{R}^{B}$ However, we may also consider an alternative basis $\tilde{B}$ of $\mathbb{R}^{B}$ . This alternative basis gives rise to an alternative set of sequences $\tilde{S}=\cup_{L=0}^{\infty}\tilde{B}^{L}$ . By treating S and $\tilde{S}$ as sets of vectors, there will be a natural way to extend a kernel on S to $\tilde{S}.$ . We will see that the property of discrete masses is invariant to this change in basis: if the kernel has discrete masses over $S,$ it also has discrete masses over ${\tilde{S}}_{;}$ , and vice versa. (Note in this section and all following sections, S will be the set of sequences, rather than an arbitrary infinite discrete space.) To be more precise, we must define what it means to apply a sequence kernel to vector encoding of a sequence. Any sequence $Y$ in $S=\cup_{{\cal L}=0}^{\infty}B^{L}$ can be represented as a one-hot encoding, which consists of a vector $V\in\mathbb{R}^{|Y|\times B}$ such that $V_{(l)}\in\mathbb{R}^{B}$ is the one-hot encoding of the letter $Y_{(l)}$ . If the vector $V\in\mathbb{R}^{L\times B}$ is a one-hot encoding of a sequence then we define its embedding into $\mathcal{H}_{k}$ as the embedding of the sequence it encodes. We can write this using the formula $$ k_{V}=\sum_{X\in S: |X| =L}\left(\prod_{l=0}^{L-1}V_{(l),X_{(l)}}\right)k_{X}.\tag{3} $$ Thus if V is a one-hot encoding of $Y$ , we recover $k_{V}=k_{Y}$ . The kernel has not changed; all we have done is rewrite it to embed vector encoded sequences. We now apply the same kernel to diferent sequences that use diferent encodings, which are not one-hot. In particular, let $\tilde{B}$ be an alternative basis of $\mathbb{R}^{B}$ . Each sequence $\tilde{Y}$ in $\tilde{S}=\cup_{L=0}^{\infty}\tilde{B}^{L}$ can be represented by a vector encoding $\tilde{V}\in\mathbb{R}^{|\tilde{Y}|\times B}$ , where $\tilde{V}_{(l)}$ is the encoding of the letter $\tilde{Y}_{(l)}$ . We define the kernel embedding of $\tilde{Y}$ by plugging $\tilde{V}$ into Equation $s ;$ it consists of a linear combination of kernel embeddings $k_{X}$ from each sequence $X \in S$ with $|X| = |{\tilde{V}}|$ . We will show that if the kernel k has discrete masses over $S,$ and we apply k to ${\tilde{S}}_{:}$ it will still have discrete masses. We call this shift from the alphabet B to $\tilde{B}$ a “reparameterization” of the kernel’s alphabet. Proposition 17 Say k is a strictly positive definite kernel on $S_{i}$ , and $\tilde{B}$ is a basis $o f\mathbb{R}^{B}$ Then k has discrete masses as a kernel on $\tilde{S}$ if and only if it has discrete masses as a kernel on $S$ Throughout the rest of the paper, for any kernel on S and any $V,W\in\cup_{L=0}^{\infty}\mathbb{R}^{L\times B}$ we will write $k(V,W)=(k_{V}|k_{W})_{k}$ where $k_{V}$ and kW are defined by Eqn 3. In this section, we design kernels with discrete masses that compare sequences based on pairwise alignments. Whereas position-wise comparison kernels judge two sequences X and Y to be similar only if there are a small number of substitutions that can transform X into Y, alignment kernels judge two sequences to be similar if there are a small number of substitutions, insertions and/or deletions that can transform X into Y. Biologically, sequences that are similar in this way often share similar phenotypes, and are closely related evolutionarily. However, this notion of similarity is poorly captured by position-wise comparison kernels. For example, the sequence $X = A T G C$ difers from the sequence $Y = T G C$ only by the insertion of a single A at the start of the sequence, but kernels based on the Hamming distance will judge the two sequences to be completely diferent, with distance $d_{H}(X,Y)=4= |X|$ One popular, but problematic, technique for dealing with insertions and deletions is to pre-process the data set using a multiple sequence alignment algorithm, which adds gap symbols to each sequence to make it the same length. In essence, the idea behind multiple sequence alignment algorithms is to construct a point estimate of which letters in each sequence are evolutionarily related to one another via substitutions, and place each related letter in the same position, i.e. in the same column of the pre-processed data matrix. Once sequences have been aligned, it is more reasonable to apply a position-wise comparison kernel; insertions and deletions are compared by including the gap symbol in the alphabet B. The problem with multiple sequence alignment pre-processing is that (a) it does not take into account uncertainty in which positions are related to one another, instead relying on a point estimate, and (b) it prevents downstream machine learning methods from generalizing to unseen sequences, since adding new sequences to the data set can change the multiple sequence alignment, for instance, if the new sequence is longer than those previously observed (Weinstein and Marks, 2021). Alignment kernels ofer an alternative approach to accounting for insertions and deletions (Haussler, 1999). Rather than transform the entire data set, they consider two sequences X and Y to be similar if they difer by a small number of insertions and deletions, as well as substitutions. Alignment kernels are of special relevance to problems involving sequences with high length variation, such as in the analysis of human antibodies or of distantly related evolutionary homologs. Alignment kernels are typically computed with a dynamic programming procedure – comparing two sequences of length L costs $\mathcal{O}(L^{2})$ (Watkins, 2000). However, the algorithm can be made much more eficient in practice with modest assumptions and the use of GPUs (Rush, 2020). In this section we define the alignment kernel and show that it has discrete masses if and only if its hyperparameters are set to values in a certain range. In biological sequence analysis, a pairwise alignment between two sequences is a matching between a subset of positions in each sequence, with the restrictions that (a) each position in each sequence can be matched to at most one position in the other sequence, and (b) matchings must be ordered, such that if site $l_{X}$ in sequence $X$ is matched to $l_{Y}$ in sequence $Y,$ site $l_{X}^{\prime}>l_{X}$ in $X$ cannot match to a site $l_{Y}^{\prime}ATGC|||AC-C where vertical lines | denote a matching. Here, - is a gap symbol, denoting the fact that the nucleotide G in X is unmatched; we can interpret the G as an insertion in X relative to $Y,\mathrm{or},$ conversely, interpret the gap - as a deletion in Y relative to X. The alignment kernel $k(X,Y)$ considers all possible pairwise alignments between X and Y, scores each alignment according to a position-wise comparison kernel applied to the aligned sequences, and sums up those scores to produce its value. Mathematically, to define the alignment kernel, we start with two simpler kernels and then convolve them, following the construction of Haussler (1999). The first kernel, $k_{s}.$ evaluates matches between aligned letters. The second kernel, $k_{I}$ , evaluates insertions and deletions; it applies an “afine” gap penalty, which separately penalizes the presence of a gap and the gap’s total length. For any two kernels $k_{1}$ and $k_{2}$ on $S_{;}$ , the convolution kernel $k_{1}\star k_{2}$ is, $$ (k_{1}\star k_{2})(X,Y) = \sum_{X^{(1)} + X^{(2)} = X}\sum_{Y^{(1)} + Y^{(2)} = Y}k_{1}(X^{(1)},Y^{(1)})k_{2}(X^{(2)},Y^{(2)}) $$ where the sum is over all sequences $X^{(1)},X^{(2)},Y^{(1)},Y^{(2)}\in S$ such that $X^{(1)}+X^{(2)}=X$ and $Y^{(1)}+Y^{(2)}=Y$ . Recall that S includes the sequence of length zero, so the sum includes such terms as $X^{(1)}=X,X^{(2)}=\varnothing$ Definition 20 (Alignment kernel) Let $k_{s}^{\prime}$ be a strictly positive definite kernel on B. Define $k_{s}\ b y$ extending $k_{s}^{\prime}$ to S with $k_{s}(X,Y)=0\ i f\ |X|\neq 1\ o r\ |Y|\neq 1$ Let $\Delta \mu > 0$ be the penalty for starting an insertion and let $\mu > 0$ be the penalty for the insertion’s length. The insertion penalty function g is then defined as $g(X)=1$ if $| X | = 0$ and $g(X)=\exp\left(-\Delta\mu- |X|\mu\right)$ otherwise. Define the non-negative-definite kernel $k_{I}(X,Y)=g(X)g(Y)~f o r~X,Y\in S$ The alignment kernel k is, $$ k=\sum_{l=0}^{\infty}k_{I}\star(k_{s}\star k_{I})^{\star l}, $$ where the exponent ?l denotes the convolution of l kernels $k_{s}\star k_{I}$ We start by connecting alignment kernels to kmer spectrum kernels. The basic connection between the two kernels has led to similar dynamic programming methods to compute each (Lodhi et al., 2002) and has been noted in a special case to motivate neural network architectures (Chen et al., 2019). Here we formally describe the connection in terms of an orthonormal basis of the RKHS. We show that, for a particular tilting, the features of the alignment kernel are a weighted sum of kmer counts, allowing for some kmer mismatches. More precisely, we show that the tilted alignment kernel is equivalent to an infinite-dimensional gapped kmer spectrum kernel. Since tilting preserves discrete masses (Proposition 16), this gapped kmer spectrum kernel has discrete masses. Intuitively, a “gapped kmer” is a kmer that includes gaps; it matches another sequence if each of the non-gap characters match, regardless of the letters at the gap positions. For example, the gapped kmer sequence $\mathtt{AT}\mathtt{-G}$ matches ATCG, ATGG, ATAG and ATTG. Formally, a gapped kmer of length L, with M non-gap letters, is defined by an ordered set of indices $J=\left(j_{0},\ldots,j_{M+1}\right)$ , with $-1=j_{-1}˜, inducing the set of sequences $\tilde{S}$ , such that k applied to S˜ is an alignment kernel with parameters $\mu,\Delta\mu$ and $k_{s}(\tilde{b},\tilde{b}^{\prime})=\sigma^{-1}|B|\delta_{\tilde{b}}(\tilde{b}^{\prime})$ for all $\tilde{b},\tilde{b}^{\prime}\in\tilde{B}$ . As well, for any $\begin{array}{ r }{b\in\mathcal{B},\sum_{\tilde{b}\in\tilde{\mathcal{B}}}k_{s}(\tilde{b},b)=\sigma^{-1}|\mathcal{B}|}\end{array}$ . We call $\tilde{B}$ a rectified alphabet for k and $\tilde{S}$ a rectified set of sequences for k. In this section we show that alignment kernels have discrete masses under certain parameter settings when the alphabet size is one. This result is crucial for proving the more general result, covering arbitrary alphabet sizes, in Theorem 21 and Appendix C. It builds on the feature representation described in Theorem 24 and Appendix E. The result will depend on the theory of the Riordan group, for which we will need to introduce some notation. If $\textstyle f(x)=\sum_{i=0}^{\infty}C_{i}x^{i}$ is a formal power series, define $[x^{n}]f=C_{n}$ For two formal power series $f(y),g(y)$ we define the Riordan array of $f$ and $g$ as the infinite upper triangular matrix with entries $$ Q_{L^{\prime},L}=[x^{L^{\prime}}y^{L}]\frac{g(y)}{1-x y f(y)}=[x^{L^{\prime}}y^{L}]\sum_{l=0}^{\infty}g(y)x^{l}y^{l}f(y)^{l}=[y^{L}]y^{L^{\prime}}g(y)f(y)^{L^{\prime}} $$ for numbers $L,L^{\prime}\ge 0$ . We say that $Q$ is in the Bell subgroup if $f = g$ . The result we will need is that one can invert a Riordan array by inverting the power series $f$ and $g$ (Shapiro et al., 1991). Proposition 38 (Shapiro et al., 1991) Let $$ Q_{L^{\prime},L}=[x^{L^{\prime}}y^{L}]\frac{g(y)}{1-x y f(y)} $$ and let $\bar{f}$ be the unique power series such that the equation $y\bar{f}(y)f(y\bar{f}(y))=y~h o l d s .^{\mathrm{\tiny~8}}$ Then, letting $\bar{g}(y)=\left(g(y\bar{f}(y))\right)^{-1}$ ， $$ Q_{L^{\prime},L}^{-1}=[x^{L^{\prime}}y^{L}]\frac{\bar{g}(y)}{1-x y\bar{f}(y)}. $$ Note $i f Q$ is in the Bell subgroup, $g(y)=f(y)$ and $\bar{f}(y)f(y\bar{f}(y))=1\ s o\ \bar{g}(y)=\bar{f}(y)$ Thus $Q^{-1}$ is also in the Bell subgroup.

3. Consistency up to mixing with parents: The estimator $\hat{\mathbf{Z}}(\mathbf{X})$ satisfies consistency up to mixing with parents if there exists a permutation π of [n] and a constant matrix $\mathbf{C}_{\mathrm{pa}}\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times n}$ such that

$$
\hat{\mathbf{Z}}(\mathbf{X})=\mathbf{P}_{\pi}\cdot\mathbf{C}_{\mathrm{pa}}\cdot\mathbf{Z},\quad\forall\mathbf{z}\in\mathbb{R}^{n},\tag{22}
$$

where $\mathbf{C}_{\mathrm{{p a}}}$ has nonzero diagonal entries and for all $j\notin\overline{{\mathrm{pa}}}(i),[\mathbf{C}_{\mathrm{pa}}]_{i,j}=0$ . Equivalently, $\hat{Z}_{\pi_{i}}$ is a linear function of $\{Z_{j}:j\in\overline{{\mathrm{pa}}}(i)\}$ for all $i \in [ n ]$

Definition 6 (Node-level Partial Identifiability) For identifiability of a single latent variable, we define:

1. Partial latent recovery: The estimator $\hat{\mathbf{Z}}(\mathbf{X})$ satisfies partial latent recovery for node i if

$$
\left[\hat{\mathbf{Z}}(\mathbf{X})\right]_{i}=\phi_{k}(Z_{k}),\tag{24}
$$

for some $k \in [ n ]$ where $\phi_{k}:\mathbb{R}\mathbb{R}$ is a difeomorphism.

2. Partial consistency up to mixing with parents: The estimator $\hat{\mathbf{Z}}(\mathbf{X})$ satisfies partial consistency up to mixing with parents for node i if

$$
[\hat{\mathbf{Z}}(\mathbf{X})]_{i}=\sum_{j\in\overline{{\mathrm{pa}}}(k)}c_{k}\cdot Z_{k},\tag{25}
$$

for some $k \in [ n ]$ and constants $\{c_{j}:j\in\overline{{\mathrm{pa}}}(k)\}$

For formalizing the achievability results and designing the associated algorithms, generating the estimates $\hat{\mathbf{Z}}(\mathbf{X})$ and $\hat{\mathcal G}$ is facilitated by estimating the inverse of $g$ based on the observed data X. Specifically, an estimate of $g^{-1}$ , where $g^{-1}$ denotes the inverse of $g,$ facilitates recovering Z via ${\bf Z}=g^{-1}({\bf X})$ . Throughout the rest of this paper, we refer to $g^{-1}$ as the true encoder. To formalize the procedures of estimating $g^{-1}$ , we define $\mathcal{H}$ as the set of possible valid encoders, i.e., candidates for $g^{-1}$ . A function $h \in \mathcal H$ can be such a candidate if it is invertible, that is, there exists an associated decoder $h^{-1}$ such that $(h^{-1}\circ h)(\mathbf{X})=\mathbf{X}$ . Hence, the set of valid encoders is specified by

$$
\mathcal{H}\triangleq\{h:\mathcal{X}\to\mathbb{R}^{n}:\exists h^{-1}:\mathbb{R}^{n}\to\mathbb{R}^{d}\text{such that}(h^{-1}\circ h)(\mathbf{x})=\mathbf{x},\forall\mathbf{x}\in\mathcal{X}\}.\tag{26}
$$

Next, corresponding to any pair of observation X and valid encoder $h \in \mathcal H$ , we define $\hat{\mathbf{Z}}(\mathbf{X};h)$ as an auxiliary estimate of $\mathbf{Z}$ generated by applying the valid encoder h on X, i.e.,

$$
\hat{\mathbf{Z}}(\mathbf{X};h)\triangleq h(\mathbf{X})=(h\circ g)(\mathbf{Z}),\quad\forall h\in\mathcal{H}.\tag{27}
$$

The estimate $\hat{\mathbf{Z}}(\mathbf{X};h)$ inherits its randomness from X, and its statistical model is governed by that of Z under the chosen h. To emphasize the dependence on $h,$ we denote the score functions associated with the pdfs of $\hat{\mathbf{Z}}(\mathbf{X};h)$ under environments $\mathcal{E}^{0},\mathcal{E}^{m}$ , and $\tilde{\mathcal{E}}^{m}$ respectively, by

$$
\boldsymbol{s}_{\hat{\mathbf{Z}}}(\cdot;h),\quad\boldsymbol{s}_{\hat{\mathbf{Z}}}^{m}(\cdot;h),\quad\mathrm{and}\quad\tilde{\boldsymbol{s}}_{\hat{\mathbf{Z}}}^{m}(\cdot;h).\tag{28}
$$

We will be addressing both general and linear transformations $g .$ In the linear transformation setting, the true linear transformation $g$ is denoted by the matrix $\mathbf{G}\in\mathbb{R}^{d\times n}$ . Accordingly, we denote a valid linear encoder by $\mathbf{H}\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times d}$ . For a given valid encoder H, the associated valid decoder is given by its Moore-Penrose inverse, i.e., $\mathbf H^{\dagger}\triangleq\mathbf H^{\top}\cdot(\mathbf H\cdot\mathbf H^{\top})^{-1}$

Score functions and their variations across diferent interventional environments play pivotal roles in our approach to identifying latent representations. In this section, we present the key properties of the score functions that will be leveraged in Section 5 and Section 6 to construct identifiability results, along with the corresponding algorithms.

We first investigate score variations across pairs of environments, such as the observational environment and an interventional one (under both soft and hard atomic interventions) or two interventional environments, either coupled or uncoupled. The key insight is that an intervention causes changes in only certain coordinates of the score function, as indicated by the sparse changes in the decompositions of the score functions in (18) and (19). These sparse changes further reflect the graph structure in the score diferences. For instance, for a single-node intervention $I^{m}=\{i\}$ in m-th environment, j-th coordinate of the score diference $s-s^{m}$ becomes

$$
\left[\boldsymbol{s}(\mathbf{z})-\boldsymbol{s}^{m}(\mathbf{z})\right]_{j}=\frac{\partial}{\partial z_{j}}\log p_{i}(z_{i}\mid\mathbf{z}_{\mathrm{pa}(i)})-\frac{\partial}{\partial z_{j}}\log q_{i}(z_{i}\mid\mathbf{z}_{\mathrm{pa}(i)}),\tag{29}
$$

which is zero if $j\not\in\overline{{\mathrm{pa}}}(i)$ . The following lemma formalizes this property for all relevant cases.

Lemma 7 (Score Changes under Interventions) Consider the observational environment $\mathcal{E}^{0}$ and an interventional environment $\mathcal{E}^{m}$ with unknown intervention target $I^{m}$ . Then, for any causal model and intervention type, $\mathbb{E}\Big [\big|\pmb{s}(\mathbf{Z})-\pmb{s}^{m}(\mathbf{Z})\big|_{i}\Big]\neq 0$ implies that $i\in\overline{{\mathrm{pa}}}(I^{m})$ . For the reverse direction, we have the following results specified for each relevant case.

(i) Hard interventions: If the intervention in $\mathcal{E}^{m}~(o r~\tilde{\mathcal{E}}^{m})$ is hard, then score functions s and $\pmb{s}^{m}\left(o r\tilde{\pmb{s}}^{m}\right)$ difer in their i-th coordinate if and only if node i or one of its children is intervened in $\mathcal{E}^{m}$ (or in $\tilde{\mathcal{E}}^{m})$

$$
\mathbb{E}\left[\left|\boldsymbol{s}(\mathbf{Z})-\boldsymbol{s}^{m}(\mathbf{Z})\right|_{i}\right]\neq 0\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad i\in\overline{{\mathrm{pa}}}(I^{m}),\tag{30}
$$

$$
a n d\quad\mathbb{E}\Big [\big|\boldsymbol{s}(\mathbf{Z})-\tilde{\boldsymbol{s}}^{m}(\mathbf{Z})\big|_{i}\Big]\neq 0\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad i\in\overline{{\mathrm{pa}}}(\tilde{I}^{m}).\tag{31}
$$

(ii) Soft interventions: If the intervention in $\mathcal{E}^{m}$ is soft and the latent causal model is an additive noise model, then score functions s and $s^{m}$ difer in their i-th coordinate if and only if node i or one of its children is intervened in $\mathcal{E}^{m}$

$$
\mathbb{E}\left[\left|\boldsymbol{s}(\mathbf{Z})-\boldsymbol{s}^{m}(\mathbf{Z})\right|_{i}\right]\neq 0\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad i\in\overline{{\mathrm{pa}}}(I^{m}).\tag{32}
$$

(iii) Coupled environments $I^{m}=\tilde{I}^{m}$ : In the coupled environment setting, $s^{m}$ and $\tilde{\pmb{s}}^{m}$ difer in their i-th coordinate if and only $i f i$ is intervened.

$$
\mathbb{E}\left[\left|\boldsymbol{s}^{m}(\mathbf{Z})-\tilde{\boldsymbol{s}}^{m}(\mathbf{Z})\right|_{i}\right]\neq 0\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad i=I^{m}.\tag{33}
$$

(iv) Uncoupled environments $I^{m}\neq\tilde{I}^{m}$ : Consider two interventional environments $\mathcal{E}^{m}$ and $\tilde{\mathcal{E}}^{m}$ with diferent intervention targets ${\cal I}^{m}\ne{\tilde{\cal I}}^{m}$ , and consider additive noise models specified in (7). Given that $p(\mathbf{Z})$ is twice diferentiable, the score functions $s^{m}$ and $\tilde{\pmb{s}}^{m}$ difer in their i-th coordinate if and only if node i or one of its children is intervened.

$$
\mathbb{E}\left[\left|\boldsymbol{s}^{m}(\mathbf{Z})-\tilde{\boldsymbol{s}}^{m}(\mathbf{Z})\right|_{i}\right]\neq 0\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad i\in\overline{{\mathrm{pa}}}(I^{m},\tilde{I}^{m}).\tag{34}
$$

Theorem 7 provides the necessary and suficient conditions for the invariance of the coordinates of the score functions of latent variables. The core idea of the score-based framework is that tracing these sparse changes in the score functions of the latent variables guides finding reliable estimates for the inverse of the transformation g, which in turn facilitates estimating $\mathbf{Z}.$ Intuitively, we will look for the encoders $h \in \mathcal H$ such that the variations between the score estimates $\begin{array}{ r }{{\pmb{s}}_{\hat{\mathbf{Z}}}(\hat{\bf{z}};h),{\pmb{s}}_{\hat{\mathbf{Z}}}^{m}(\hat{\bf{z}};h)}\end{array}$ , and $\tilde{\pmb{s}}_{\hat{\mathbf{z}}}^{m}(\hat{\mathbf{z}};h)$ will be similar to the true score variations given by Theorem 7. However, the scores of the latent variables are not directly accessible. To circumvent this, we need to understand the connection between score functions of X and Z. In the following lemma, we leverage the change of variables formula for injective mappings and establish this relationship for any injective mapping f from latent to observed space.

Lemma 8 (Score Diference Transformation) Consider random vectors $\mathbf{Y}_{1},\mathbf{Y}_{2}\in\mathbb{R}^{r}$ and $\mathbf{W}_{1},\mathbf{W}_{2}\in\mathbb{R}^{s}$ that are related through

$$
\mathbf{Y}_{1}=f(\mathbf{W}_{1}),\quad a n d\quad\mathbf{Y}_{2}=f(\mathbf{W}_{2}),\tag{35}
$$

such that $r\geq s,$ probability measures of $\mathbf{W}_{1},\mathbf{W}_{2}$ are absolutely continuous with respect to the s-dimensional Lebesgue measure, and $f:\mathbb{R}^{s}\mathbb{R}^{r}$ is an injective and continuously diferentiable function. The diference of the score functions of Y<sub>1</sub> and $\mathbf{Y}_{2}$ , and that of W<sub>1</sub> and $\mathbf{W}_{2}$ are related as

$$
s_{\mathbf{W}_{1}}(\mathbf{w})-s_{\mathbf{W}_{2}}(\mathbf{w})=\left[J_{f}(\mathbf{w})\right]^{\top}\cdot\left[s_{\mathbf{Y}_{1}}(\mathbf{y})-s_{\mathbf{Y}_{2}}(\mathbf{y})\right],\quad \text{where}\mathbf{y}=f(\mathbf{w}),\tag{36}
$$

where $J_{f}(\mathbf{w})$ denotes the Jacobian of f at point w. Furthermore, for the reverse direction, we have

$$
s_{\mathbf{Y}_{1}}(\mathbf{y})-s_{\mathbf{Y}_{2}}(\mathbf{y})=\left[\left[J_{f}(\mathbf{w})\right]^{\dagger}\right]^{\top}\cdot\left[s_{\mathbf{W}_{1}}(\mathbf{w})-s_{\mathbf{W}_{2}}(\mathbf{w})\right],\quad \text{where}\mathbf{y}=f(\mathbf{w}).\tag{37}
$$

For CRL under linear transformations in Section 5, we use the following corollary of Theorem 8.

Corollary 9 In Theorem 8, if f is a linear transform, that is Y = F W for a full-rank matrix $\mathbf{F}\in\mathbb{R}^{r\times s}$ , then the score functions of Y and W are related through $\begin{array}{ r }{s_{\mathbf{W}}(\mathbf{w})=\mathbf{F}^{\top}\cdot s_{\mathbf{Y}}(\mathbf{y})}\end{array}$ and $s_{\mathbf{Y}}(\mathbf{y})=\left[\mathbf{F}^{\dagger}\right]^{\top}\cdot s_{\mathbf{W}}(\mathbf{w})$ , where $\mathbf{y}=\mathbf{F}\cdot\mathbf{w}$

In this section, we consider CRL under linear transformation, in which the general transformation model in (3) becomes:

$$
\mathbf{X}=\mathbf{G}\cdot\mathbf{Z},\tag{41}
$$

where $\mathbf{G}\in\mathbb{R}^{d\times n}$ is an unknown full-rank matrix mapping the latent variables to the observed ones. We will present steps for leveraging the properties of the score functions presented in Section 4 to design an algorithm that identifies the true encoder and recovers the true causal representations. The algorithm is referred to as Linear Score-based Causal Latent Estimation via Interventions (LSCALE-I). The theoretical guarantees associated with the algorithm steps will also be presented, serving as constructive proof of identifiability.

LSCALE-I consists of three stages outlined in Algorithm 1. In the first stage, we will learn an encoder $\begin{array}{ r }{\hat{\bf H},}\end{array}$ row by row, where each row is an estimate of a row of the true encoder $\mathbf{G}^{\dagger}$ . This encoder estimate will recover each $Z_{i}$ up to mixing with $\mathbf{Z}_{\mathrm{pa}(i)}$ . In the second <sub>stage, we will use the estimated latent variables H</sub>ˆ <sub>to obtain the transitive closure of the</sub> latent graph . Finally, as an optional third stage for hard interventions, we will leverage the independence statements implied by the hard interventions to refine our encoder estimate. We will demonstrate that this refinement yields scaling consistency and perfect DAG recovery. We will also discuss the relevance and distinctions of our results vis-à-vis the results in the existing literature.

Statistical diversity. Similarly to the existing identifiability results, it is necessary to have some regularity conditions <sup>5</sup> on the probability distributions of observational and interventional environments. We adopt the following assumption for the case of linear transformations.

Assumption 1 For every possible pair $(i,k)$ where $i\in [n],k\in\mathrm{pa}(i)$ , the following term cannot be a constant function in z,

$$
\frac{\partial}{\partial z_{k}}\left(\log\frac{p_{i}(z_{i}\mid\mathbf{z}_{\mathrm{pa}(i)})}{q_{i}(z_{i}\mid\mathbf{z}_{\mathrm{pa}(i)})}\right)\left[\frac{\partial}{\partial z_{i}}\log\frac{p_{i}(z_{i}\mid\mathbf{z}_{\mathrm{pa}(i)})}{q_{i}(z_{i}\mid\mathbf{z}_{\mathrm{pa}(i)})}\right]^{-1}.\tag{42}
$$

Essentially, $\begin{array}{ r }{\frac{\partial}{\partial z_{k}}\big(\log\frac{p_{i}\left(z_{i}\left|\mathbf{z}_{\mathrm{pa}(i)}\right.\right)}{q_{i}\left(z_{i}\left|\mathbf{z}_{\mathrm{pa}(i)}\right.\right)}\big)}\end{array}$ captures the efect of intervening on node i on the score associated with node k. Therefore, Assumption 1 ensures that an intervention suficiently diferentiates the target variable and its parents in the score function. We note that this is a very mild assumption and holds for a wide range of commonly used models (including additive noise models under hard interventions) and is discussed in more detail in Section 5.5.

Before we explain the details of LSCALE-I and establish identifiability results in the following subsections, we first present the rationale and derive the partial identifiability result, which will serve as the building block. In the rest of the paper, for brevity, we denote the score diference functions for each $m \in [ n ]$ by

$$
\boldsymbol{d}_{\mathbf{Z}}^{m}(\mathbf{z})\triangleq\boldsymbol{s}^{m}(\mathbf{z})-\boldsymbol{s}(\mathbf{z})\quad \text{and}\quad\boldsymbol{d}_{\mathbf{X}}^{m}(\mathbf{x})\triangleq\boldsymbol{s}_{\mathbf{X}}^{m}(\mathbf{x})-\boldsymbol{s}_{\mathbf{X}}(\mathbf{x}).\tag{43}
$$

To construct an algorithm that achieves identifiability under linear transformations, we first analyze the score diferences for the linear transformation. Note that for linear transformation ${\mathbf{X}}={\mathbf{G}}\cdot{\mathbf{Z}}.$ Jacobian $J_{\mathbf{G}}(\mathbf{z})$ is independent of z and equal to matrix G. Also, we have $\mathbf{z}=\mathbf{G}^{\dagger}\cdot\mathbf{x}$ for all $\mathbf{x}\in\mathrm{col}(\mathbf{G})$ . Then, using Theorem 9 we have

$$
\boldsymbol{d}_{\mathbf{X}}^{m}(\mathbf{x})=[\mathbf{G}^{\dagger}]^{\top}\cdot\boldsymbol{d}_{\mathbf{Z}}^{m}(\mathbf{z}).\tag{44}
$$

Let us denote the correlation matrices of $d_{\mathbf{X}}^{m}(\mathbf{x})$ and $d_{\mathbf{Z}}^{m}(\mathbf{z})$ , respectively, by

$$
\mathbf{R}_{\mathbf{X}}^{m}\triangleq\mathbb{E}\big [\pmb{d}_{\mathbf{X}}^{m}(\mathbf{x})\cdot [\pmb{d}_{\mathbf{X}}^{m}(\mathbf{x})]^{\top}\big]\quad\mathrm{and}\quad\mathbf{R}_{\mathbf{Z}}^{m}\triangleq\mathbb{E}\big [\pmb{d}_{\mathbf{Z}}^{m}(\mathbf{z})\cdot [\pmb{d}_{\mathbf{Z}}^{m}(\mathbf{z})]^{\top}\big].(45)
$$

Note that (44) implies that $\mathbf{R}_{\mathbf{X}}^{m}=[\mathbf{G}^{\dagger}]^{\top}\cdot\mathbf{R}_{\mathbf{Z}}^{m}\cdot\mathbf{G}^{\dagger}$ . The next lemma specifies that the structure of the column space of correlation matrix R<sup>m</sup> is heavily constrained by the true encoder $\mathbf{G}^{\dagger}$ , the graph $\mathcal{G}_{:}$ and the intervention target $I^{m}$ in m-th environment.

After obtaining the partial identifiability result from a single interventional environment, our goal is to construct an algorithm that uses the complete set of interventional environments $\mathcal{E}=\{\mathcal{E}^{1},\ldots,\mathcal{E}^{n}\}$ with targets $\cup_{m\in [n]}I^{m}=[n]$ to form estimates of the true encoder $\mathbf{G}^{\dagger}$ and the latent graph $\mathcal{G}$ .

Encoder estimation. In Stage L1 of Algorithm 1, we form an encoder estimate $\hat{\bf H}$ via using the column spaces of $\{\mathbf{R}_{\mathbf{X}}^{m}:m\in [n]\}$ . Specifically, for each $m \in [ n ]$ we select a vector randomly from $\mathrm{col}(\mathbf{R}_{\mathbf{X}}^{m})$ and assign its transpose to m-th row of Hˆ .

Latent graph estimation. Next, we use the encoder estimate $\hat{\bf H}$ to recover the transitive closure of the latent graph $\mathcal{G}$ . Motivated by Theorem $7(\mathrm{ii})$ , we form $\hat{\mathcal G}$ with parent sets

$$
\hat{\mathrm{pa}}(m)\triangleq\left\{i\neq m:\mathbb{E}\left[|\boldsymbol{s}_{\hat{\mathbf{Z}}}(\hat{\mathbf{Z}};\hat{\mathbf{H}})-\boldsymbol{s}_{\hat{\mathbf{Z}}}^{m}(\hat{\mathbf{Z}};\hat{\mathbf{H}})|_{i}\right]\neq 0\right\}.\tag{53}
$$

Using the result that $\hat{\mathbf{Z}}(\mathbf{X};\hat{\mathbf{H}})$ recovers Z up to mixing with parents, we show that the transitive closures of the estimate $\hat{\mathcal G}$ and the true graph $\mathcal{G}$ are the same under a graph isomorphism.

First, we provide a linear algebraic property, which will be used in the proofs.

Lemma 33 Consider the latent causal graph , and a matrix $\mathbf{L}\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times n}$

[\mathbf{L}_{\mathrm{pa}}]_{i,j}\triangleq\left\{\begin{array}{l l}1,&\text{if}\quad j\in\overline{{\mathrm{pa}}}(i)\\ 0,&\text{otherwise}\end{array},\text{and}\quad [\mathbf{L}_{\mathrm{an}}]_{i,j}\triangleq\left\{\begin{array}{l l}1,&\text{if}\quad j\in\overline{{\mathrm{an}}}(i)\\ 0,&\text{otherwise}\end{array}.\right.\right.\tag{170}
$$

Then, $if\mathbf{I}_{n\times n}\preccurlyeq\mathbf{1}\{\mathbf{L}\}\preccurlyeq\mathbf{L}_{\mathrm{pa}}$ , we also have ${\bf\cal I}_{n\times n}\preccurlyeq 1\{{\bf L}^{-1}\}\preccurlyeq{{\bf L}}_{\mathrm{an}}$

[\mathbf{L}_{\text{sur}}]_{i,j}\triangleq\left\{\begin{array}{l l}1,&\text{if}\overline{{\operatorname{ch}}}(i)\subseteq\overline{{\operatorname{ch}}}(j),\\ 0,&\text{otherwise}\end{array}.\right.\tag{171}

$$

Using 𝔼<sub>𝑡</sub> $\left(\hat{\mathbf{H}}^{-1}(\bar{\mathbf{g}}_{t}-\mathbf{g}_{t})\right)=\hat{\mathbf{H}}^{-1}\mathbb{E}_{t}\left(\bar{\mathbf{g}}_{t}-\mathbf{g}_{t}\right)=0\mathrm{~a n d~}\Delta_{t}-\eta\hat{\mathbf{H}}^{-1}\mathbf{g}_{t}=\mathbb{E}_{t}\Delta_{t+1},\mathrm{~w e~g e t},$

$$
\mathbb{E}_{t}\left(\left\|\Delta_{t+1}\right\|_{\mathbf{H}}-\mathbb{E}_{t}\left\|\Delta_{t+1}\right\|_{\mathbf{H}}\right)^{2}=\left\|\mathbb{E}_{t}\Delta_{t+1}\right\|_{\mathbf{H}}^{2}+\eta^{2}\mathbb{E}_{t}\left\|\hat{\mathbf{H}}^{-1}(\bar{\mathbf{g}}_{t}-\mathbf{g}_{t})\right\|_{\mathbf{H}}^{2}-(\mathbb{E}_{t}\left\|\Delta_{t+1}\right\|_{\mathbf{H}})^{2}.
$$

Using Jensen’s inequality on the first term, we have $\left\|\mathbb{E}_{t}\Delta_{t+1}\right\|_{\mathbf{H}}\leq\mathbb{E}_{t}\left\|\Delta_{t+1}\right\|_{\mathbf{H}}$ , from which it follows that,

$$
\begin{array}{l}\mathbb{E}_{t}\left(\left\|\Delta_{t+1}\right\|_{\mathbf{H}}-\mathbb{E}_{t}\left\|\Delta_{t+1}\right\|_{\mathbf{H}}\right)^{2}\leq\left(\mathbb{E}_{t}\left\|\Delta_{t+1}\right\|_{\mathbf{H}}\right)^{2}+\eta^{2}\mathbb{E}_{t}\left\|\hat{\mathbf{H}}^{-1}(\bar{\mathbf{g}}_{t}-\mathbf{g}_{t})\right\|_{\mathbf{H}}^{2}-(\mathbb{E}_{t}\left\|\Delta_{t+1}\right\|_{\mathbf{H}})^{2}\\ =\eta^{2}\mathbb{E}_{t}\left\|\hat{\mathbf{H}}^{-1}(\bar{\mathbf{g}}_{t}-\mathbf{g}_{t})\right\|_{\mathbf{H}}^{2}\\ =\eta^{2}\mathbb{E}_{t}\|\mathbf{H}^{1/2}\hat{\mathbf{H}}^{-1/2}\hat{\mathbf{H}}^{-1/2}(\bar{\mathbf{g}}_{t}-\mathbf{g}_{t})\|^{2}\\ \leq\eta^{2}\cdot\|\mathbf{H}^{1/2}\hat{\mathbf{H}}^{-1/2}\|^{2}\cdot\mathbb{E}_{t}\|\hat{\mathbf{H}}^{-1/2}(\bar{\mathbf{g}}_{t}-\mathbf{g}_{t})\|^{2}.\tag{6}\\ \end{array}

Definition 5 A subspace A of X is called a deformation retract of X if there is a continuous $F:X\times [0,1]\to X$ such that for all $x \in X$ and $a \in A$ •

$F(x,0)=x$  
$F(x,1)\in A$  
$F(a,1)=a.$

The function F is then called a (deformation) retraction from X to A.

A deformation retraction F from X to A ensures that X and A are “homotopy equivalent” (see Hatcher, 2000, pages 2–3), and thus are topologically similar. The idea behind persistent homology is to encode the evolution of the topology (in the homology sense) of a nested family of topological spaces, called a filtration. As we move along indices, topological features (connected components, cycles, cavities, ...) can appear or disappear (existing connected components merge, cycles or cavities are filled, ...). Two keys to formalize this idea, which we use throughout this paper, are the notions of filtration and of persistence module.

Definition 6 Let $\Lambda\subset\mathbb{R}$ be a set of indices. A filtration indexed by Λ is a family $(\kappa_{\lambda})_{\lambda\in\Lambda}$ of topological spaces satisfying, for all $\lambda,\lambda^{\prime}\in\Lambda,\lambda\leqslant\lambda^{\prime}$

$$
\mathcal{K}_{\lambda}\subset\mathcal{K}_{\lambda^{\prime}}.
$$

The typical filtration that we will consider in this paper is, for a function $f:\mathbb{R}^{d}\mathbb{R}$ , the family of sublevel sets $({\mathcal{F}}_{\lambda})_{\lambda\in\mathbb{R}}=\left(f^{-1}(]-\infty,\lambda])\right)_{\lambda\in\mathbb{R}}$

Definition 7 Let $\Lambda\subset\mathbb{R}$ be a set of indices. A persistence module over Λ is a family $\mathbb{V}=(\mathbb{V}_{\lambda})_{\lambda\in\Lambda}$ of vector spaces equipped with linear maps $v_{\lambda}^{\lambda^{\prime}}:\mathbb{V}_{\lambda}\to\mathbb{V}_{\lambda^{\prime}}$ such that, for all $\lambda\leqslant\lambda^{\prime}\leqslant\lambda^{\prime\prime}\in\Lambda$

$$
v_{\lambda}^{\lambda}=i d
$$

and

$$
v_{\lambda^{\prime}}^{\lambda^{\prime\prime}}\circ v_{\lambda}^{\lambda^{\prime}}=v_{\lambda}^{\lambda^{\prime\prime}}.
$$

The typical persistence module that we will consider in this paper is, for a function $f:\mathbb{R}^{d} $ R and $s \in \mathbb N$ , the family of homology groups $\mathbb{V}_{f,s}=(H_{s}\left(\mathcal{F}_{\lambda}\right))_{\lambda\in\mathbb{R}}$ equipped with $v_{\lambda}^{\lambda^{\prime}}$ the linear maps induced by the inclusion $\mathcal{F}_{\lambda}\subset\mathcal{F}_{\lambda^{\prime}}$ . Under the q-tameness assumption (see Definition 10 in Appendix A), a persistence module V can be fully described by a multi-set in $\mathbb{R}^{2}$ , known as its persistence diagram:

$$
\mathrm{dgm}(\mathbb{V})=\{(b_{j},d_{j})\mid j\in J\}\subset\overline{{\mathbb{R}}}^{2}.
$$

In this representation, each $b_{j}$ represents the birth time of a topological feature $(\mathrm{e . g .}$ , the emergence of a connected component or the formation of a cycle), while $d_{j}$ represents its death time $(\mathrm{e . g .}$ , the merging of two components or the filling of a cycle). The diference $d_{j}-b_{j}$ corresponds to the feature’s lifetime. For a detailed construction of persistence diagrams, we refer the reader to Chazal et al. (2016). We consider the least-squares criterion $\begin{array}{ r }{\frac 12\|\pmb{y}-\pmb{X}\pmb{\beta}\|_{2}^{2}}\end{array}$ for the estimation of $\beta^{*}$ . For the minimization, we adopt a constant learning-rate gradient descent algorithm with random dropouts in each iteration. Following the seminal work on dropout by Srivastava et al. (2014), we call a $d \times d$ random diagonal matrix D a p-dropout matrix if its diagonal entries satisfy $D_{i i}\stackrel{\mathrm{i . i . d .}}{\sim}$ Bernoulli(p), with some retaining probability $p\in(0,1)$ . On average, D has pd diagonal entries equal to 1 and $(1-p)d$ diagonal entries equal to 0. For simplicity, the dependence of D on p will only be stated if unclear from the context. For a sequence of independent and identically distributed (i.i.d.) dropout matrices $D_{k},k=1,2,\ldots,$ and some constant learning rate $\alpha > 0$ , the k-th step gradient descent iterate with dropout takes the form

$$
\begin{array}{l}\tilde{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{k}(\alpha)=\tilde{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{k-1}(\alpha)-\alpha\nabla_{\tilde{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{k-1}}\frac{1}{2}\big\|\boldsymbol{y}-X D_{k}\tilde{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{k-1}(\alpha)\big\|_{2}^{2}\\ =\tilde{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{k-1}(\alpha)+\alpha D_{k}X^{\top}\big(\boldsymbol{y}-X D_{k}\tilde{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{k-1}(\alpha)\big),\end{array}\tag{2}
$$

with $\tilde{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{0}$ a given initial vector.

In the previous section, we considered a fixed design matrix and (full) gradient descent with dropout. Computing the gradient over the entire dataset can be computationally expensive, especially with large datasets. We now investigate stochastic gradient descent with dropout regularization.

Consider i.i.d. covariate vectors $\pmb{x}_{k}\in\mathbb{R}^{d},k=1,2,....$ from some distribution Π, and the realizations $y_{k}|\pmb{x}_{k}$ from a linear regression model

$$
y_{k}=\boldsymbol{x}_{k}^{\top}\boldsymbol{\beta}^{*}+\epsilon_{k},\tag{31}
$$

with unknown regression vector $\beta^{*}\in\mathbb{R}^{d}$ . We assume that the model is in reduced form, which here means that min $_i(\mathbb{E}[\pmb{x}_{1}\pmb{x}_{1}^{\top}])_{i i}>0$ . In addition, we assume that the i.i.d. random noises $\epsilon_{k}$ satisfy $\mathbb{E}[\epsilon_{k}]=0$ and $\mathrm{Var}(\epsilon_{k})=1$ . In this paper, we focus on the classical case where the SGD computes the gradient based on an individual observation $(y_{k},\pmb{x}_{k})$ and a dropout matrix $D_{k}$ . For constant learning rate α and initialization $\breve{\beta}_{0}$ , the k-th step SGD iterate with Bernoulli dropout is

$$
\begin{array}{l}\breve{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{k}(\alpha)=\breve{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{k-1}(\alpha)-\alpha\nabla_{\breve{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{k-1}}\frac{1}{2}\big(y_{k}-\boldsymbol{x}_{k}^{\top}D_{k}\breve{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{k-1}(\alpha)\big)^{2}\\ =\breve{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{k-1}(\alpha)+\alpha D_{k}\boldsymbol{x}_{k}\left(y_{k}-\boldsymbol{x}_{k}^{\top}D_{k}\breve{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{k-1}(\alpha)\right).\tag{32}\\ \end{array}
$$

This is a sequential estimation, or online learning scheme, as computing $\breve{\beta}_{k}(\alpha)$ from $\breve{\beta}_{k-1}(\alpha)$ only requires the k-th sample $(y_{k},\pmb{x}_{k})$ and the dropout matrix $D_{k}$ . To study the contraction property of the SGD dropout iterates $\breve{\beta}_{k}(\alpha)$ , we express the recursion (32) by an iterated random function $\breve{f}:\mathbb{R}^{d\times\hat{d}}\times\mathbb{R}\times\mathbb{R}^{d}\times\mathbb{R}^{d}\mapsto\mathbb{R}^{d}$ with

$$
f_{D,(y,\boldsymbol{x})}(\boldsymbol{u})=\boldsymbol{u}+\alpha D\boldsymbol{x}(y-\boldsymbol{x}D\boldsymbol{u}),
$$

that is,

$$
\begin{array}{l}\breve{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{k}(\alpha)=\breve{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{k-1}(\alpha)+\alpha D_{k}\boldsymbol{x}_{k}\big(y_{k}-\boldsymbol{x}_{k}^{\top}D_{k}\breve{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{k-1}(\alpha)\big)\\ =:\check{f}_{D_{k},(y_{k},\boldsymbol{x}_{k})}(\check{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{k-1}(\alpha)).\tag{33}\\ \end{array}
$$

We shall show that this iterated random function $\breve{f}$ is geometrically contracting under suitable conditions, and therefore, there exists a unique stationary distribution $\breve{\pi}_{\alpha}$ such that $\breve{\beta}_{k}(\alpha)\Rightarrow\breve{\pi}_{\alpha}$ , where ⇒ denotes the convergence in distribution.

From now on, let $(y,x)$ be a sample with the same distribution as $(y_{k},\pmb{x}_{k})$ . By marginalizing over all randomness, we can view the SGD dropout in (32) as a minimizer of the $\ell^{2}.$ -regularized least-squares loss

$$
\breve{\boldsymbol{\beta}}:=\arg\min_{\boldsymbol{\beta}\in\mathbb{R}^{d}}\mathbb{E}_{(y,\boldsymbol{x})}\mathbb{E}_{D}\left[\frac{1}{2}\left(y-\boldsymbol{x}^{\top}D\boldsymbol{\beta}\right)^{2}\right].\tag{34}
$$

Here, the expectation is take over both the random sample $(y,x)$ and the dropout matrix $D$ . Throughout the rest of the paper, we shall write $\mathbb{E}[\cdot]=\mathbb{E}_{(y,\pmb{x})}\mathbb{E}_{D}[\cdot]$ when no confusion should be caused.

Lemma 26 (Gaussian approximation (Karmakar and Wu, 2020)) Suppose that we have a sequence of nonstationary mean-zero random vectors $\pmb{x}_{k}=g_{k}(\epsilon_{k},\epsilon_{k-1},...)\in\mathbb{R}^{d}$ , for $k=1,\ldots,n$ , where the $\epsilon_{k}$ ’s are i.i.d. random variables, and $g_{k}(\cdot)$ is a measurable function such that each $\scriptstyle{\mathbf{{\mathit{x}}}}_{k}$ is a proper random vector. Let $\begin{array}{ r }{S_{j}=\sum_{k=1}^{j}\pmb{x}_{k}}\end{array}$ . Assume the following conditions hold for some $q > 2$

(i) The series $(\|\pmb{x}_{k}\|_{2}^{q})_{k\ge 1}$ is uniformly integrable: $\begin{array}{ r }{\operatorname*{sup}_{k\geq 1}\mathbb{E}\big [\|\pmb{x}_{k}\|_{2}^{q}\mathbf{1}_{\|\pmb{x}_{k}\|_{2}\geq u}\big]0}\end{array}$ as $u $ $\infty_{i}$  
(ii) The eigenvalues of covariance matrices of increment processes are lower-bounded, that is, there exists $\lambda_{*}>0$ and $l_{*}\in\mathbb{N}$ , such that for all $t\geq 1,l\geq l_{*}$ ，

$$
\lambda_{\mathrm{min}}\big(\mathrm{Cov}(S_{t+l}-S_{t})\big)\geq\lambda_{*}l;
$$

(iii) There exist constants $\chi>\chi_{0}$ and $\kappa > 0$ , where

$$
\chi_{0}=\frac{q^{2}-4+(q-2)\sqrt{q^{2}+20q+4}}{8q},
$$

such that the tail cumulative dependence measure

$$
\Theta_{m,q}(\alpha)=\sum_{k=m}^{\infty}\theta_{k,q}(\alpha)=O\big\{m^{-\chi}\big(\log(m)\big)^{-\kappa}\big\}.\tag{124}
$$

Then, for all $q > 2$ , there exists a probability space $(\Omega^{\star},{\mathcal{A}}^{\star},\mathbb{P}^{\star})$ on which we can define random vectors $\boldsymbol{x}_{k}^{\star},$ , with the partial sum process $\begin{array}{ r }{S_{i}^{\star}=\sum_{k=1}^{i}{\pmb x}_{k}^{\star}}\end{array}$ and a Gaussian process $\begin{array}{ r }{G_{i}^{\star}=\sum_{k=1}^{i}z_{k}^{\star}}\end{array}$ . Here $z_{k}^{\star}$ is a mean-zero independent Gaussian vector, such that $(S_{i}^{\star})_{1\leq i\leq n}\stackrel{\mathcal{D}}{=}$ $(S_{i})_{1\leq i\leq n}$ and

$$
\max_{i\leq n}|S_{i}^{\star}-G_{i}^{\star}| =o_{\mathbb{P}}(n^{1/q})\quad i n(\Omega^{\star},\mathcal{A}^{\star},\mathbb{P}^{\star}).
$$

We notice that condition (ii) in Lemma 26 on the non-singularity is required when the sequence $\{\pmb{x}_{k}\}_{k\in\mathbb{N}}$ is non-stationary. However, if the function $g_{k}(\cdot)\equiv g(\cdot)$ , that is, the sequence $\{\pmb{x}_{k}\}_{k\in\mathbb{N}}$ is stationary, then the covariance matrix of the increments is allowed to be singular. To see this, consider a stationary partial sum $\boldsymbol{S_{l}}=(S_{l,1},\ldots,S_{l,d})^{\top}$ with a singular covariance matrix $\Sigma\in\mathbb{R}^{d\times d}$ and assume $\operatorname{rank}(\Sigma)=d-1$ . Then, there exists a unit vector $\pmb{v}\in\mathbb{R}^{d}$ such that $\Sigma{\boldsymbol{v}}=0$ , which indicates that $S_{l,1}$ can be written into a linear combination of $S_{l,2},\ldots,S_{l,d};$ and the covariance matrix of this linear combination is non-singular. Hence, condition (ii) in Lemma 26 is not required for stationary processes.

That is, for all $\tilde{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{0}^{\circ},\tilde{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{0}^{\circ^{\prime}}\in\mathbb{R}^{d}$ , such that $\tilde{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{0}^{\circ}\neq\tilde{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{0}^{\circ^{\prime}}$ , we have

$$
\begin{array}{l}\big(\mathbb{E}\|f_{D_{k}}\circ\cdots\circ f_{D_{1}}(\tilde{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{0}^{\circ})-f_{D_{k}}\circ\cdots\circ f_{D_{1}}(\tilde{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{0}^{\circ^{\prime}})\|_{2}^{q}\big)^{1/q}\\ =\big(\mathbb{E}\|h_{\alpha}(D_{k},\ldots,D_{1},D_{0},D_{-1},\ldots)-h_{\alpha}(D_{k},\ldots,D_{1},D_{0}^{\prime},D_{-1}^{\prime},\ldots)\|_{2}^{q}\big)^{1/q}\\ =\big(\mathbb{E}\|h_{\alpha}(\mathcal{F}_{k})-h_{\alpha}(\mathcal{F}_{k,\{0,-1,\ldots\}})\|_{2}^{q}\big)^{1/q}\\ \leq c_{q}r_{\alpha,q}^{k},\end{array}\tag{126}
$$

where we recall the filtration $\mathcal{F}_{i,\{j\}}=\sigma(D_{i},\ldots,D_{j+1},D_{j}^{\prime},D_{j-1},\ldots)$ , and $c_{q}>0$ is some constant independent of k. Moreover, since $h_{\alpha}(\mathcal{F}_{k})$ is stationary over k and $D_{i}$ and $D_{j}^{\prime}$ are i.i.d. random matrices, for all $i,j\in\mathbb{Z},$ , it follows that

$$
\begin{array}{l}\mathbb{E}\|h_{\alpha}(\mathcal{F}_{k,\{0\}})-h_{\alpha}(\mathcal{F}_{k,\{0,-1,\dots\}})\|_{2}^{q}\\ =\mathbb{E}\|h_{\alpha}(\mathcal{F}_{k})-h_{\alpha}(\mathcal{F}_{k,\{-1,-2\dots\}})\|_{2}^{q}\\ =\mathbb{E}\|h_{\alpha}(\mathcal{F}_{k+1})-h_{\alpha}(\mathcal{F}_{k+1,\{0,-1,\dots\}})\|_{2}^{q}\leq c_{q}^{\prime}r_{\alpha,q}^{k},\tag{127}\\ \end{array}
$$

where the constant $c_{q}^{\prime} > 0$ is also independent of k.

Next, we bound the diference between $\tilde{S}_{t}^{\circ}(\alpha)$ and $\tilde{S}_{t}^{\tilde{\beta}_{0}}(\alpha)$ for any arbitrarily fixed $\tilde{\beta}_{0}\in$ $\mathbb{R}^{d}$ in the q-th moment, for all $q \geq 2$ . For the constant learning rate $\alpha > 0$ satisfying $\alpha\|\mathbb{X}\|<2$ , applying Theorem 3 yields

$$
\begin{array}{l}\left(\mathbb{E}\big\|\tilde{S}_{t}^{\circ}(\alpha)-\tilde{S}_{t}^{\tilde{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{0}}(\alpha)\big\|_{2}^{q}\right)^{1/q}\\ =\left(\mathbb{E}\big\|\left[f_{D_{1}}\left(\tilde{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{0}^{\circ}(\alpha)\right)+f_{D_{2}}\circ f_{D_{1}}\left(\tilde{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{0}^{\circ}(\alpha)\right)+\dots+f_{D_{t}}\circ\dots\circ f_{D_{1}}\left(\tilde{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{0}^{\circ}(\alpha)\right)\right]\right.\\ \left.-\left[f_{D_{1}}\left(\tilde{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{0}(\alpha)\right)+f_{D_{2}}\circ f_{D_{1}}\left(\tilde{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{0}(\alpha)\right)+\dots+f_{D_{t}}\circ\dots\circ f_{D_{1}}\left(\tilde{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{0}(\alpha)\right)\right]\|_{2}^{q}\right)^{1/q}\\ \leq\left(\sum_{k=1}^{t}r_{\alpha,q}^{k}\right)\|\tilde{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{0}^{\circ}-\tilde{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{0}\|_{2}.\tag{131}\\ \end{array}
$$

Since the contraction constant $r_{\alpha,q}\in(0,1)$ , we can derive the limit for the sum of the geometric series $\{r_{\alpha,q}^{k}\}_{k=1}^{t}$ as follows

$$
\lim_{t\rightarrow\infty}\sum_{k=1}^{t}r_{\alpha,q}^{k}=\lim_{t\rightarrow\infty}\frac{r_{\alpha,q}\left(1-r_{\alpha,q}^{t}\right)}{1-r_{\alpha,q}}=\frac{r_{\alpha,q}}{1-r_{\alpha,q}}.\tag{132}
$$

This, together with (131) gives

$$
\left(\mathbb{E}\big\|\tilde{S}_{t}^{\circ}(\alpha)-\tilde{S}_{t}^{\tilde{\beta}_{0}}(\alpha)\big\|_{2}^{q}\right)^{1/q}=O(1)=o(\sqrt{t}),\tag{133}
$$

which yields the quenched central limit theorem for the partial sum $\tilde{S}_{t}^{\tilde{\beta}_{0}}(\alpha)$ defined in (114), that is, for any fixed initial point $\tilde{\beta}_{0}\in\mathbb{R}^{d}$ 2

$$
t^{-1/2}\tilde{S}_{t}^{\tilde{\beta}_{0}}(\alpha)\Rightarrow\mathcal{N}(0,\Sigma(\alpha)).\tag{134}
$$

Moreover, we notice that by Markov’s inequality and (143), for any $u\in\mathbb{R}$ and $\delta > 0$ , we have

$$
\begin{array}{l}\sup_{k\geq 1}\mathbb{E}\big [\|\tilde{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{k}^{\circ}(\alpha)-\tilde{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{\text{mean}}(\alpha)\|_{2}^{q}\mathbf{1}_{\|\tilde{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{k}^{\circ}(\alpha)-\tilde{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{\text{mean}}(\alpha)\|_{2}\geq u}\big]\\ \leq\sup_{k\geq 1}\mathbb{E}\Big [\|\tilde{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{k}^{\circ}(\alpha)-\tilde{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{\text{mean}}(\alpha)\|_{2}^{q}\cdot\|\tilde{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{k}^{\circ}(\alpha)-\tilde{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{\text{mean}}(\alpha)\|_{2}^{\delta}/u^{\delta}\Big]\\ =\sup_{k\geq 1}\mathbb{E}\big [\|\tilde{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{k}^{\circ}(\alpha)-\tilde{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{\text{mean}}(\alpha)\|_{2}^{q+\delta}\big]/u^{\delta}\\ =O\bigl\{\alpha^{(q+\delta)/2}/u^{\delta}\bigr\},\tag{144}\\ \end{array}
$$

which converges to 0 as $u  \infty$ . Therefore, condition (i) in Lemma 26 is satisfied. Since $\{\tilde{\beta}_{k}^{\circ}(\alpha)\}_{k\in\mathbb{N}}$ is stationary, following the arguments below Lemma 26, condition (ii) is not required. Regarding condition (iii), for the constant learning rate $\alpha > 0$ satisfying $\alpha\|\mathbb{X}\|<2$ it follows from (128) that the functional dependence measure $\begin{array}{ r }{\theta_{k,q}(\alpha)\leq c\cdot r_{\alpha,q}^{k},}\end{array}$ for all $q > 2$ and $k \in \mathbb N$ , where the constant $c > 0$ is independent of $k .$ . Consequently, there exists a constant $\kappa > 0$ such that the tail cumulative dependence measure of $\{\tilde{\beta}_{k}^{\circ}(\alpha)\}_{k\in\mathbb{N}}$ can be bounded by

$$
\Theta_{m,q}(\alpha)=\sum_{k=m}^{\infty}\theta_{k,q}(\alpha)=O\big\{m^{-\chi}\big(\log(m)\big)^{-\kappa}\big\},\tag{145}
$$

where $\chi>0$ is some constant that can be taken to be arbitrarily large.

Next, recall the partial sum $\begin{array}{ r }{\tilde{S}_{i}^{\tilde{\beta}_{0}}(\alpha)=\sum_{k=1}^{i}[\tilde{\beta}_{k}(\alpha)-\tilde{\beta}_{\mathrm{mean}}(\alpha)]}\end{array}$ as defined in (114), given an arbitrarily fixed initial point $\tilde{\beta}_{0}\in\mathbb{R}^{d}$ . It follows from the triangle inequality that

$$
\begin{array}{l}\left(\mathbb{E}\Big [\max_{1\leq i\leq t}\big\|\tilde{S}_{i}^{\tilde{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{0}}(\alpha)-\Sigma^{1/2}(\alpha)\tilde{G}_{i}^{\star}\big\|_{2}\Big]^{q}\right)^{1/q}\\ =\left(\mathbb{E}\left[\max_{1\leq i\leq t}\left\|\tilde{S}_{i}^{\tilde{\beta}_{0}}(\alpha)-\tilde{S}_{i}^{\circ}(\alpha)+\tilde{S}_{i}^{\circ}(\alpha)-\Sigma^{1/2}(\alpha)\tilde{G}_{i}^{\star}\right\|_{2}\right]^{q}\right)^{1/q}\\ \leq\left(\mathbb{E}\left[\max_{1\leq i\leq t}\left\|\tilde{S}_{i}^{\tilde{\beta}_{0}}(\alpha)-\tilde{S}_{i}^{\circ}(\alpha)\right\|_{2}+\max_{1\leq i\leq t}\left\|\tilde{S}_{i}^{\circ}(\alpha)-\Sigma^{1/2}(\alpha)\tilde{G}_{i}^{\star}\right\|_{2}\right]^{q}\right)^{1/q}\\ \leq\left(\mathbb{E}\left[\max_{1\leq i\leq t}\left\|\tilde{S}_{i}^{\tilde{\beta}_{0}}(\alpha)-\tilde{S}_{i}^{\circ}(\alpha)\right\|_{2}\right]^{q}\right)^{1/q}+\left(\mathbb{E}\left[\max_{1\leq i\leq t}\left\|\tilde{S}_{i}^{\circ}(\alpha)-\Sigma^{1/2}(\alpha)\tilde{G}_{i}^{\star}\right\|_{2}\right]^{q}\right)^{1/q}.\tag{148}\\ \end{array}
$$

Therefore, to show the invariance principle for $\big(\tilde{S}_{i}^{\tilde{\beta}_{0}}(\alpha)\big)_{1\leq i\leq t},$ it sufices to bound the difference part max $_{1\le i\le t}\|\tilde{S}_{i}^{\tilde{\beta}_{0}}(\alpha)-\tilde{S}_{i}^{\scriptscriptstyle\mathrm{o}}(\alpha)\|_{2}$ in terms of the $q\mathrm{-}$ -th moment. To this end, recall the iterative function $f_{D}(\beta)=\beta+\alpha D X^{\top}({\pmb y}-X D\beta)$ in (9) that rewrites the GD dropout recursion (2). We note that

$$
\begin{array}{l}\max_{1\leq i\leq t}\left\|\tilde{S}_{i}^{\tilde{\beta}_{0}}(\alpha)-\tilde{S}_{i}^{\circ}(\alpha)\right\|_{2}\\ =\max_{1\leq i\leq t}\left\|\left[f_{D_{1}}\left(\tilde{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{0}\right)-f_{D_{1}}\left(\tilde{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{0}^{\circ}\right)\right]+\dots+\left[f_{D_{i}}\circ\dots\circ f_{D_{1}}\left(\tilde{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{0}\right)-f_{D_{i}}\circ\dots\circ f_{D_{1}}\left(\tilde{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{0}^{\circ}\right)\right]\right\|_{2}\\ \leq\max_{1\leq i\leq t}\left(\left\|f_{D_{1}}\left(\tilde{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{0}\right)-f_{D_{1}}\left(\tilde{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{0}^{\circ}\right)\right\|_{2}+\dots+\left\|f_{D_{i}}\circ\dots\circ f_{D_{1}}\left(\tilde{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{0}\right)-f_{D_{i}}\circ\dots\circ f_{D_{1}}\left(\tilde{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{0}^{\circ}\right)\right\|_{2}\right)\\ =\left\|f_{D_{1}}\left(\tilde{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{0}\right)-f_{D_{1}}\left(\tilde{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{0}^{\circ}\right)\right\|_{2}+\dots+\left\|f_{D_{t}}\circ\dots\circ f_{D_{1}}\left(\tilde{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{0}\right)-f_{D_{t}}\circ\dots\circ f_{D_{1}}\left(\tilde{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{0}^{\circ}\right)\right\|_{2}.\tag{149}\\ \end{array}
$$

This, along with the triangle inequality and Theorem 3 yields

$$
\begin{array}{l}\left(\mathbb{E}\left[\max_{1\leq i\leq t}\left\|\tilde{S}_{i}^{\tilde{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{0}}(\alpha)-\tilde{S}_{i}^{\circ}(\alpha)\right\|_{2}\right]^{q}\right)^{1/q}\\ \leq\left(\mathbb{E}\big\|f_{D_{1}}(\tilde{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{0})-f_{D_{1}}(\tilde{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{0}^{\circ})\big\|_{2}^{q}\right)^{1/q}+\dots+\left(\mathbb{E}\big\|f_{D_{t}}\circ\dots\circ f_{D_{1}}(\tilde{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{0})-f_{D_{t}}\circ\dots\circ f_{D_{1}}(\tilde{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{0}^{\circ})\big\|_{2}^{q}\right)^{1/q}\\ \leq\frac{r_{\alpha,q}\left(1-r_{\alpha,q}^{t}\right)}{1-r_{\alpha,q}}\|\tilde{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{0}-\tilde{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{0}^{\circ}\|_{2}=o\left(t^{1/q}\right).\tag{150}\\ \end{array}
$$

We insert this result back into (149), which together with (148) gives the invariance principle for the partial sum $\begin{array}{ r }{\tilde{S}_{i}^{\tilde{\beta}_{0}}(\alpha)=\sum_{k=1}^{i}[\tilde{\beta}_{k}(\alpha)-\tilde{\beta}_{\mathrm{mean}}(\alpha)]}\end{array}$

Finally, let the partial sum $\begin{array}{ r }{S_{i}^{\beta_{0}}(\alpha)=\sum_{k=1}^{i}[\tilde{\beta}_{k}(\alpha)-\tilde{\beta}]}\end{array}$ be as defined in Theorem 9. We shall bound the diference between $S_{i}^{\tilde{\beta}_{0}}(\alpha)$ and $\tilde{S}_{i}^{\tilde{\beta}_{0}}(\alpha)$ . Since $\widetilde{\beta}_{\mathrm{mean}}(\alpha)=\mathbb{E}_{D}[\widetilde{\beta}_{1}^{\circ}(\alpha)]$ as defined in (111) and $\tilde{\beta}_{\mathrm{mean}}(\alpha)-\tilde{\beta}=\mathbb{E}_{D}\widetilde [\tilde{\beta}_{1}^{\circ}(\alpha)-\tilde{\beta}]\stackrel{\circ}{=}0$ by (137), it follows that

$$
\left(\mathbb{E}\Big [\max_{1\leq i\leq t}\big\|\tilde{S}_{i}^{\tilde{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{0}}(\alpha)-S_{i}^{\tilde{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{0}}(\alpha)\big\|_{2}\Big]^{q}\right)^{1/q}=\left(\mathbb{E}\Big [\max_{1\leq i\leq t}\big\|\sum_{k=1}^{i}\tilde{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{\mathrm{mean}}(\alpha)-\tilde{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\big\|_{2}\Big]^{q}\right)^{1/q}=0.\tag{151}
$$

Proof The recursion in (36) is $\breve{\beta}_{k}(\alpha)-\breve{\beta}=\breve{A}_{k}(\alpha)(\breve{\beta}_{k-1}(\alpha)-\breve{\beta})+\breve{b}_{k}(\alpha)$ , with random matrix $\breve{A}_{k}(\alpha)=I_{d}-\alpha D_{k}\mathbb{X}_{k}D_{k}$ , and random vector $\breve{\pmb{b}}_{k}(\alpha)=\alpha D_{k}\pmb{x}_{k}(y_{k}-\pmb{x}_{k}^{\top}D_{k}\breve{\beta})$ . Recall $\begin{array}{ r }{\breve{\beta}=\arg\operatorname*{min}_{\beta\in\mathbb{R}^{d}}\mathbb E[(y-\pmb{x}^{\top}D\beta)^{2}/2]}\end{array}$ in (34), where the expectation is taken over both $(y,x)$ and D. By Lemma 21 (ii),

$$
\begin{array}{l}\mathbb{E}_{(y,\pmb{x})}\mathbb{E}_{D}[\breve{\pmb{b}}_{k}(\alpha)]=\mathbb{E}_{(y,\pmb{x})}\mathbb{E}_{D}[\alpha D_{k}\pmb{x}_{k}(y_{k}-\pmb{x}_{k}^{\top}D_{k}\breve{\pmb{\beta}})]\\ =\mathbb{E}_{(y,\boldsymbol{x})}[\alpha p I_{d}y_{k}\boldsymbol{x}_{k}-\alpha p\mathbb{X}_{k,p}\breve{\boldsymbol{\beta}}]\\ =\alpha p\mathbb{E}[\mathbb{X}_{1,p}]\breve{\boldsymbol{\beta}}-\alpha p\mathbb{E}[\mathbb{X}_{1,p}]\breve{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\\ =0.\tag{193}\\ \end{array}
$$

The proofs of the quenched CLT and the invariance principle for averaged SGD dropout follow similar arguments as the ones for averaged GD dropout. The key diferences lie in the functional dependence measures, because for SGD settings, both the dropout matrix $D_{k}$ and the sequential observation $\mathbf{{x}}_{k}$ are random. We shall first introduce some necessary definitions and then proceed with the rigorous proofs.

Recall the generic dropout matrix $D\in\mathbb{R}^{d\times d}$ and random sample $(y,\pmb{x})\in\mathbb{R}\times\mathbb{R}^{d}$ . For the SGD dropout sequence $\{\breve{\beta}_{k}(\alpha)\}_{k\in\mathbb{N}}$ , we define the centering term

$$
\breve{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{\text{mean}}(\alpha)=\lim_{k\rightarrow\infty}\mathbb{E}[\breve{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{k}(\alpha)]=\mathbb{E}[\breve{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{1}^{\circ}(\alpha)],\tag{204}
$$

where the expectation is taken over both $(y,x)$ and D, and $\breve{\beta}_{1}^{\circ}(\alpha)$ defined in (44) follows the unique stationary distribution $\breve{\pi}_{\alpha}$ . We first use Lemma 25 to prove the CLT for the partial sum of the stationary sequence $\{\breve{\beta}_{k}^{\circ}(\alpha)-\breve{\beta}_{\mathrm{mean}}(\alpha)\}_{k\in\mathbb{N}}$ , and then apply the geometricmoment contraction in Theorem 12 to show the quenched CLT for the partial sum of the non-stationary one $\{\breve{\beta}_{k}(\alpha)-\breve{\beta}_{\mathrm{mean}}(\alpha)\}_{k\in\mathbb{N}}$ . Finally, we extend the quenched CLT to the partial sum of $\{\breve{\beta}_{k}(\alpha)-\breve{\beta}_{\mathrm{mean}}(\alpha)\}_{k\in\mathbb{N}}$ by providing the upper bound of $\breve{\beta}_{\mathrm{mean}}(\alpha)-\breve{\beta}$ in terms of the q-th moment for some $q \geq 2$

Similar to Section D.1, we introduce the functional dependence measure in Wu (2005) for the stationary SGD dropout sequence $\{\breve{\beta}_{k}^{\circ}(\alpha)\}_{k\in\mathbb{N}}$ . However, the randomness in $\breve{\beta}_{k}^{\circ}(\alpha)$ is induced from both the dropout matrix $D_{k}$ and the random sample $(y_{k},\pmb{x}_{k})$ . Therefore, we define a new filtration $\breve{\mathcal{F}}_{k}$ by

$$
\breve{\mathcal{F}}_{k}=\sigma(\boldsymbol{\xi}_{k},\boldsymbol{\xi}_{k-1},\dots),\quad k\in\mathbb{Z},\tag{205}
$$

where the i.i.d. random elements $\pmb{\xi}_{k}=(D_{k},(y_{k},\pmb{x}_{k})),k\in\mathbb{Z},$ are defined in (45). For any random vector $\zeta\in\mathbb{R}^{d}$ satisfying $\mathbb{E}\|\zeta\|_{2}<\infty$ , define projection operators

$$
\breve{\mathcal{P}}_{k}[\boldsymbol{\zeta}]=\mathbb{E}[\boldsymbol{\zeta}\mid\breve{\mathcal{F}}_{k}]-\mathbb{E}[\boldsymbol{\zeta}\mid\breve{\mathcal{F}}_{k-1}],\quad k\in\mathbb{Z}.\tag{206}
$$

By Theorem 12 and (44), there exists a measurable function $\breve{h}_{\alpha}(\cdot)$ such that the stationary SGD dropout sequence $\{\breve{\beta}_{k}^{\circ}(\alpha)\}_{k\in\mathbb{N}}$ can be represented by a causal process

$$
\breve{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{k}^{\circ}(\alpha)=\breve{h}_{\alpha}\left(\boldsymbol{\xi}_{k},\boldsymbol{\xi}_{k-1},\dots\right)=\breve{h}_{\alpha}\left(\breve{\mathcal{F}}_{k}\right).\tag{207}
$$

We denote the coupled version of $\breve{\mathscr{F}}_{i}$ by

$$
\breve{\mathcal{F}}_{i,\{j\}}=\sigma(\boldsymbol{\xi}_{i},\dots,\boldsymbol{\xi}_{j+1},\boldsymbol{\xi}_{j}^{\prime},\boldsymbol{\xi}_{j-1}\dots),\tag{208}
$$

and let $\breve{\mathcal{F}}_{i,\{j\}}=\breve{\mathcal{F}}_{i}\mathrm{~i f~}j>i$ , where $\xi_{j}^{\prime}$ is an i.i.d. copy of $\xi_{i}$ . For $q > 1$ , define the functional dependence measure of $\breve{\beta}_{k}(\alpha)$ as

$$
\check{\theta}_{k,q}(\alpha)=\left(\mathbb{E}\|\check{\beta}_{k}^{\circ}(\alpha)-\check{\beta}_{k,\{0\}}^{\circ}(\alpha)\|_{2}^{q}\right)^{1/q},\quad \text{where}\check{\beta}_{k,\{0\}}^{\circ}(\alpha)=\check{h}_{\alpha}(\check{\mathcal{F}}_{k,\{0\}}).\tag{209}
$$

In addition, if $\begin{array}{ r }{\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}\breve{\theta}_{k,q}(\alpha)<\infty .}\end{array}$ , we define the tail of cumulative dependence measure as

$$
\check{\Theta}_{m,q}(\alpha)=\sum_{k=m}^{\infty}\check{\theta}_{k,q}(\alpha),\quad m\in\mathbb{N}.\tag{210}
$$

Both $\breve{\theta}_{k,q}(\alpha)$ and $\check{\Theta}_{k,q}(\alpha)$ are useful to study the dependence structure of the stationary SGD dropout iteration $\breve{\beta}_{k}^{\circ}(\alpha)=f_{D_{k},(y_{k},{\pmb x}_{k})}(\breve{\beta}_{k-1}^{\circ}(\alpha))$ . To apply Lemma 25, we only need to show that the stationary SGD dropout sequence $\{\breve{\beta}_{k}^{\circ}(\alpha)\}_{k\in\mathbb{N}}$ is short-range dependent in the sense that $\check{\Theta}_{0,q}(\alpha)<\infty$ , for some $q \geq 2$

Proof For any fixed unit vector $\pmb{u}\in\mathbb{R}^{d}$ , since $\breve{A}_{k}(\alpha)=I_{d}-\alpha D_{k}\mathbb{X}_{k}D_{k}$ as defined in (36) with $\mathbb{X}_{k}=\pmb{x}_{k}\pmb{x}_{k}^{\top}$ , it follows that

$$
\begin{array}{l}\|\breve{A}_{k}(\alpha)\boldsymbol{v}\|_{2}^{2}=\|(I_{d}-\alpha D_{k}\boldsymbol{x}_{k}\boldsymbol{x}_{k}^{\top}D_{k})\boldsymbol{v}\|_{2}^{2}\\ =\|\boldsymbol{v}\|_{2}^{2}-2\alpha\boldsymbol{v}^{\top}D_{k}\boldsymbol{x}_{k}\boldsymbol{x}_{k}^{\top}D_{k}\boldsymbol{v}+\alpha^{2}\boldsymbol{v}^{\top}D_{k}\boldsymbol{x}_{k}\boldsymbol{x}_{k}^{\top}D_{k}^{2}\boldsymbol{x}_{k}\boldsymbol{x}_{k}^{\top}D_{k}\boldsymbol{v}\\ =1-2\alpha(\boldsymbol{x}_{k}^{\top}D_{k}\boldsymbol{v})^{2}+\alpha^{2}\|D_{k}\boldsymbol{x}_{k}\|_{2}^{2}(\boldsymbol{x}_{k}^{\top}D_{k}\boldsymbol{v})^{2}.\tag{180}\\ \end{array}
$$

Write $\pmb{v}=(v_{1},\ldots,v_{d})^{\top}$ and $\pmb{x}_{k}=(x_{k 1},\ldots,x_{k d})^{\top}$ . Let $D_{k,j j}$ be the j-th diagonal element in $D_{k}$ . Since $\pmb{x}_{k}\sim\mathcal{N}(0,I_{d})$ and $D_{k}$ is independent of $\scriptstyle{\mathbf{{\mathit{x}}}}_{k}$ , it follows that

$$
\mathbb{E}(\boldsymbol{x}_{k}^{\top}D_{k}\boldsymbol{v})^{2}=\sum_{j=1}^{d}v_{j}^{2}\mathbb{E}[D_{k,j j}x_{k j}^{2}]=\sum_{j=1}^{d}v_{j}^{2}p=p.\tag{181}
$$

Moreover,

$$
\begin{array}{l}\|D_{k}\boldsymbol{x}_{k}\|_{2}^{2}(\boldsymbol{x}_{k}^{\top}D_{k}\boldsymbol{v})^{2}=\Big(\sum_{i=1}^{d}D_{k,i i}x_{k i}^{2}\Big)\Big(\sum_{j,l=1}^{d}D_{k,j j}D_{k,l l}v_{j}v_{l}x_{k j}x_{k l}\Big)\\ =\sum_{i,j,l=1}^{d}D_{k,i i}D_{k,j j}D_{k,l l}v_{j}v_{l}x_{k i}^{2}x_{k j}x_{k l}.\tag{182}\\ \end{array}
$$

For $j\neq l,\mathbb{E}[x_{k i}^{2}x_{k j}x_{k l}]=0$ . For $j = l$ and $i\neq j,\mathbb{E}[x_{k i}^{2}x_{k j}^{2}]=1$ . For $j = l$ and $i = j$ , $\mathbb{E}[x_{k i}^{4}]=3$ . Therefore, by the independence of the diagonal elements in $D_{k}$ , we have

$$
\begin{array}{l}\mathbb{E}\big [\|D_{k}\boldsymbol{x}_{k}\|_{2}^{2}(\boldsymbol{x}_{k}^{\top}D_{k}\boldsymbol{v})^{2}\big]=\sum_{j=1}^{d}v_{j}^{2}\mathbb{E}\Big(3 D_{k,j j}+\sum_{i\neq j}D_{k,i i}D_{k,j j}\Big)\\ =\sum_{j=1}^{d}v_{j}^{2}\big(3 p+p^{2}(d-1)\big)\\ =3 p+p^{2}(d-1).\tag{183}\\ \end{array}
$$

Finally, we obtain

$$
\mathbb{E}\|\breve{A}_{k}(\alpha)\pmb{v}\|_{2}^{2}=1-2\alpha p+\alpha^{2}[3 p+(d-1)p^{2}],
$$

for all unit vectors $\pmb{v}\in\mathbb{R}^{d}$ . This completes the proof.
