Proof [Theorem 15] Consider two initial vectors $\breve{\beta}_{0}^{\circ},\breve{\beta}_{0}^{\circ^{\prime}}$ following the stationary distribution $\breve{\pi}_{\alpha}$ defined in Theorem 12. By the recursion in (36), we obtain two stationary SGD dropout sequences $\{\breve{\beta}_{k}^{\circ}(\alpha)\}_{k\in\mathbb{N}}$ and $\{\breve{\beta}_{k}^{\circ^{\prime}}(\alpha)\}_{k\in\mathbb{N}}$ . It follows from Theorem 12 that for all $q \geq 2$ 2

$$
\sup_{\check{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{0}^{\circ},\check{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{0}^{\circ^{\prime}}\in\mathbb{R}^{d},\check{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{0}^{\circ}\neq\check{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{0}^{\circ^{\prime}}}\frac{\left(\mathbb{E}\|\check{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{k}^{\circ}(\alpha)-\check{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{k}^{\circ^{\prime}}(\alpha)\|_{2}^{q}\right)^{1/q}}{\|\check{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{0}^{\circ}-\check{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{0}^{\circ^{\prime}}\|_{2}}\leq\check{r}_{\alpha,q}^{k},\quad k\in\mathbb{N},\tag{211}
$$

with $\begin{array}{ r }{\breve{r}_{\alpha,q}=\left(\operatorname*{sup}_{{\pmb v}\in\mathbb{R}^{d}:\|{\pmb v}\|_{2}=1}\mathbb{E}\|\breve{A}_{1}(\alpha){\pmb v}\|_{2}^{q}\right)^{1/q}}\end{array}$ as defined in (38) and random matrix $\breve{A}_{1}(\alpha)=$ $I_{d}-\alpha D_{1}\mathbb{X}_{1}D_{1}$ .

When the constant learning rate $\alpha > 0$ satisfies the condition in (37), we have $\breve{r}_{\alpha,q}~\in~(0,1)$ as shown in Theorem 12. Recall the coupled filtration $\breve{\mathcal{F}}_{i,\{j\}}=$ $\sigma(\pmb{\xi}_{i},\dots,\pmb{\xi}_{j+1},\pmb{\xi}_{j}^{\prime},\pmb{\xi}_{j-1}\dots)$ as defined in (208). Then, (44) and (211) show that

$$
\begin{array}{l}\left(\mathbb{E}\|\breve{f}_{\boldsymbol{\xi}_{k}}\circ\dots\circ\breve{f}_{\boldsymbol{\xi}_{1}}\left(\breve{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{0}^{\circ}\right)-\breve{f}_{\boldsymbol{\xi}_{k}}\circ\dots\circ\breve{f}_{\boldsymbol{\xi}_{1}}\left(\breve{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{0}^{\circ^{\prime}}\right)\|_{2}^{q}\right)^{1/q}\\ =\left(\mathbb{E}\|\breve{h}_{\alpha}\left(\boldsymbol{\xi}_{k},\dots,\boldsymbol{\xi}_{1},\boldsymbol{\xi}_{0},\boldsymbol{\xi}_{-1},\dots\right)-\breve{h}_{\alpha}\left(\boldsymbol{\xi}_{k},\dots,\boldsymbol{\xi}_{1},\boldsymbol{\xi}_{0}^{\prime},\boldsymbol{\xi}_{-1}^{\prime},\dots\right)\|_{2}^{q}\right)^{1/q}\\ =\left(\mathbb{E}\|\breve{h}_{\alpha}(\breve{\mathcal{F}}_{k})-\breve{h}_{\alpha}(\breve{\mathcal{F}}_{k,\{0,-1,\dots\}})\|_{2}^{q}\right)^{1/q}\\ \leq\check{c}_{q}\check{r}_{\alpha,q}^{k},\tag{212}\\ \end{array}
$$

for some constant $\breve{c}_{q}>0$ that is independent of k.

Following a similar argument in (127), for all $q \geq 2$ and $k \in \mathbb N$ , we can bound the functional dependence measure $\cup_{k,q}(\alpha)$ in (209) as follows

$$
\begin{array}{l}\breve{\theta}_{k,q}(\alpha)=\left(\mathbb{E}\|\breve{h}_{\alpha}(\breve{\mathcal{F}}_{k})-\breve{h}_{\alpha}(\breve{\mathcal{F}}_{k,\{0\}})\|_{2}^{q}\right)^{1/q}\\ \leq\left(\mathbb{E}\|\breve{h}_{\alpha}(\breve{\mathcal{F}}_{k})-\breve{h}_{\alpha}(\breve{\mathcal{F}}_{k,\{0,-1,\dots\}})\|_{2}^{q}\right)^{1/q}+\left(\mathbb{E}\|\breve{h}_{\alpha}(\breve{\mathcal{F}}_{k,\{0,-1,\dots\}})-\breve{h}_{\alpha}(\breve{\mathcal{F}}_{k,\{0\}})\|_{2}^{q}\right)^{1/q}\\ \leq\check{c}_{q}^{\prime}\check{r}_{\alpha,q}^{k},\tag{213}\\ \end{array}
$$

for some constant $\breve{c}_{q}^{\prime}>0$ that is independent of k.

Consequently, the cumulative dependence measure $\breve{\Theta}_{m,q}(\alpha)$ in (210) is also bounded for all $q \geq 2$ and $m\in\mathbb{N}$ , that is,

$$
\breve{\Theta}_{m,q}(\alpha)=\sum_{k=m}^{\infty}\breve{\theta}_{k,q}(\alpha)=O\left(\check{r}_{\alpha,q}^{m}\right)<\infty .\tag{214}
$$

The inequality in (119) derived by Wu (2005) holds for a general class of functional dependence measures, as long as the inputs of the functional system (i.e., the measurable function $\breve{h}(\xi_{k},\xi_{k-1},...))$ are i.i.d. elements. Thus, we can apply (119) to the projection operator $\breve{\mathcal{P}}_{k}[\cdot]$ in (206) and obtain

$$
\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}\left(\mathbb{E}\|\check{\mathcal{P}}_{0}[\check{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{k}^{\circ}(\alpha)]\|_{2}^{q}\right)^{1/q}\leq\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}\check{\theta}_{k,q}(\alpha)=\check{\Theta}_{0,q}(\alpha)<\infty,\tag{215}
$$

implying the short-range dependence of the stationary SGD dropout sequence $\{\breve{\beta}_{k}^{\circ}(\alpha)\}_{k\in\mathbb{N}}$ Then, it follows from Lemma 25 that

$$
t^{-1/2}\sum_{k=1}^{t}\left(\breve{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{k}^{\circ}(\alpha)-\breve{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{\text{mean}}(\alpha)\right)\Rightarrow\mathcal{N}(0,\breve{\Sigma}(\alpha)),\tag{216}
$$

where the long-run covariance matrix $\breve{\Sigma}(\alpha)$ is defined in Theorem 15.

Following similar arguments as in (131)–(133), for any initial vector $\breve{\beta}_{0}\in\mathbb{R}^{d}$ , we can leverage the geometricmoment contraction in Theorem 12 and achieve the quenched CLT for the corresponding SGD dropout sequence $\{\breve{\beta}_{k}(\alpha)\}_{k\in\mathbb{N}}$ , that is,

$$
t^{-1/2}\sum_{k=1}^{t}\left(\breve{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{k}(\alpha)-\breve{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{\text{mean}}(\alpha)\right)\Rightarrow\mathcal{N}(0,\breve{\Sigma}(\alpha)).\tag{217}
$$

Recall the $\ell^{2}.$ -minimizer $\breve{\beta}$ in (34) and the centering term $\begin{array}{ r }{\breve{\beta}_{\mathrm{mean}}(\alpha)=\operatorname*{lim}_{k\to\infty}\mathbb{E}(\breve{\beta}_{k}(\alpha))=}\end{array}$ $\mathbb{E}(\breve{\beta}_{1}^{\circ}(\alpha))$ in (204). We shall prove $\begin{array}{ r }{\|\sum_{k=1}^{t}\mathbb{E}[\breve{\beta}_{k}(\alpha)-\breve{\beta}]\|_{2}=o(\sqrt{t})}\end{array}$ . For any two initial vectors $\breve{\beta}_{0}$ and $\breve{\beta}_{0}^{\circ}$ , where $\breve{\beta}_{0}^{\circ}$ follows the stationary distribution $\breve{\pi}_{\alpha}$ in Theorem 12, while $\breve{\beta}_{0}$ is an arbitrary initial vector in $\mathbb{R}^{d}$ , it follows from the triangle inequality that

$$
\begin{array}{l}\left\|\sum_{k=1}^{t}\mathbb{E}[\breve{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{k}(\alpha)-\breve{\boldsymbol{\beta}}]\right\|_{2}=\left\|\mathbb{E}\left[\sum_{k=1}^{t}\left(\breve{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{k}(\alpha)-\breve{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{k}^{\circ}(\alpha)+\breve{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{k}^{\circ}(\alpha)-\breve{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\right)\right]\right\|_{2}\\ \leq\left\|\mathbb{E}\left[\sum_{k=1}^{t}\left(\breve{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{k}(\alpha)-\breve{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{k}^{\circ}(\alpha)\right)\right]\right\|_{2}+\left\|\mathbb{E}\left[\sum_{k=1}^{t}\left(\breve{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{k}^{\circ}(\alpha)-\breve{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\right)\right]\right\|_{2}\\ =:\check{\mathrm{I}}_{1}+\check{\mathrm{I}}_{2}.\tag{218}\\ \end{array}
$$

For the part $\breve{\mathrm{I}}_{1}$ , Jensen’s inequality and a similar argument as for (131) yield

$$
\begin{array}{l}\breve{\mathrm{I}}_{1}=\left\|\mathbb{E}\left[\sum_{k=1}^{t}\left(\breve{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{k}(\alpha)-\breve{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{k}^{\circ}(\alpha)\right)\right]\right\|_{2}\\ \leq\left(\mathbb{E}\left\|\sum_{k=1}^{t}\left(\breve{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{k}(\alpha)-\breve{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{k}^{\circ}(\alpha)\right)\right\|_{2}^{2}\right)^{1/2}\\ \leq\left(\sum_{k=1}^{t}\check{r}_{\alpha,2}^{k}\right)\left\|\breve{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{0}-\breve{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{0}^{\circ}\right\|_{2}.\tag{219}\\ \end{array}
$$

For the part $\breve{\mathrm{I}}_{2}$ , we recall the random matrix $\breve{A}_{1}(\alpha)=I_{d}-\alpha D_{1}\mathbb{X}_{1}D_{1}$ in (36) with $\mathbb{X}_{1}=\pmb{x}_{1}\pmb{x}_{1}^{\top}$ Recall the notation $\mathbb{X}_{1,p}=p\mathbb{X}_{1}+(1-p)\mathrm{Diag}(\mathbb{X}_{1})$ in (35). Notice that by Lemma 21 (ii), we have $\begin{array}{ r }{\mathbb{E}_{(y,x)}\mathbb{E}_{D}[\check{A}_{1}(\boldsymbol{\hat{\alpha}})]=\mathbb{E}_{(y,x)}\mathbb{E}_{D}[I_{d}-\alpha D_{1}\mathbb{X}_{1}D_{1}]=\mathbb{E}_{(y,x)}[I_{d}-\alpha p\mathbb{X}_{1,p}]=I_{d}-\alpha p\mathbb{E}[\mathbb{X}_{1,p}]}\end{array}$ which along with E $[\breve{b}_{k}]=0$ in (193) gives $\mathbb{E}[\breve{\beta}_{k}^{\circ}(\alpha)-\breve{\beta}]=\bigl(I_{d}-\alpha p\mathbb{E}[\mathbb{X}_{1,p}]\bigr)\mathbb{E}[\breve{\beta}_{k-1}^{\circ}(\alpha)-\breve{\beta}]$ Since $\{\breve{\beta}_{k}^{\circ}(\alpha)\}_{k\in\mathbb{N}}$ is stationary and $\mathbb{E}[\mathbb{X}_{1,p}]$ is non-singular by the reduced-form condition mi $\mathbf{\sigma}_{\mathfrak{i}}(\mathbb{E}[\pmb{x}_{1}\pmb{x}_{1}^{\top}])_{i i}>0$ imposed on model (31), it follows that

$$
\mathbb{E}[\breve{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{k}^{\circ}(\alpha)-\breve{\boldsymbol{\beta}}]=0,\quad \text{for all} k\in\mathbb{N}.\tag{220}
$$

This further yields

$$
\check{\mathrm{I}}_{2}=\left\|\mathbb{E}\left[\sum_{k=1}^{t}\left(\check{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{k}^{\circ}(\alpha)-\check{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\right)\right]\right\|_{2}=\left\|\sum_{k=1}^{t}\mathbb{E}\left[\check{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{k}^{\circ}(\alpha)-\check{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\right]\right\|_{2}=0.\tag{221}
$$

By applying the results for $\breve{\mathrm{I}}_{1}$ and $\breve{\mathrm{I}}_{2}$ to (218), we obtain

$$
\left\|\sum_{k=1}^{t}\mathbb{E}\left[\check{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{k}(\alpha)-\check{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\right]\right\|_{2}\leq\left(\sum_{k=1}^{t}\check{r}_{\alpha,2}^{k}\right)\left\|\check{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{0}-\check{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{0}^{\circ}\right\|_{2}.\tag{222}
$$

When the constant learning rate $\alpha > 0$ satisfies the condition in (37), $\breve{r}_{\alpha,2}\in(0,1)$ by Theorem 12, and hence (222) remains bounded as $t \to \infty$ . By this result and (217), the desired quenched CLT for the partial sum $\scriptstyle\sum_{k=1}^{t}({\check{\beta}}_{k}^{\circ}(\alpha)-{\check{\beta}})$ follows.

Proof Consider a stationary SGD dropout sequence $\{\breve{\beta}_{k}^{\circ}(\alpha)\}_{k\in\mathbb{N}}$ following the stationary distribution $\breve{\pi}_{\alpha}$ in Theorem 12. Define the mean-zero stationary partial sum

$$
\breve{S}_{i}^{\circ}(\alpha)=\sum_{k=1}^{i}\left(\breve{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{k}^{\circ}(\alpha)-\breve{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{\text{mean}}\right),\quad i\in\mathbb{N}.\tag{223}
$$

Recall that $\breve{\beta}_{\mathrm{mean}}(\alpha)=\mathbb{E}[\breve{\beta}_{1}^{\circ}(\alpha)]$ as defined in (204). Due to the stationarity, we have $\mathbb{E}[\breve{\beta}_{k}^{\circ}(\alpha)-\breve{\beta}]=0$ for all $k \in \mathbb N$ by (220). This gives

$$
\left(\mathbb{E}\|\breve{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{\text{mean}}(\alpha)-\breve{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\|_{2}^{q}\right)^{1/q}=\left(\mathbb{E}\|\mathbb{E}[\breve{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{1}^{\circ}(\alpha)-\breve{\boldsymbol{\beta}}]\|_{2}^{q}\right)^{1/q}=0.\tag{224}
$$

Since we supposed in Theorem 17 that Assumption 1 holds for some $q > 2$ , it follows from Lemma 14 that, for all $q > 2$ 2

$$
\left(\mathbb{E}\|\breve{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{k}^{\circ}(\alpha)-\breve{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{\text{mean}}(\alpha)\|_{2}^{q}\right)^{1/q}\leq\left(\mathbb{E}\|\breve{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{k}^{\circ}(\alpha)-\breve{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\|_{2}^{q}\right)^{1/q}+\left(\mathbb{E}\|\breve{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{\text{mean}}(\alpha)-\breve{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\|_{2}^{q}\right)^{1/q}=O(\sqrt{\alpha}).\tag{225}
$$

Following a similar argument as for (144), we can show that $\breve{\beta}_{k}^{\circ}(\alpha)-\breve{\beta}_{\mathrm{mean}}(\alpha)$ satisfies condition (i) on the uniform integrability in Lemma 26. Due to the stationarity of $\{\breve{\beta}_{k}^{\circ}(\alpha)\}_{k\in\mathbb{N}}.$ condition (ii) in Lemma 26 is not required (see the discussion below Lemma 26 for details). Condition (iii) is also satisfied, since when the constant learning rate $\alpha > 0$ satisfies condition (37), the stationary SGD dropout sequence $\{\breve{\beta}_{k}^{\circ}(\alpha)\}_{k\in\mathbb{N}}$ is shown to be short-range dependent by (215), i.e., the tail of cumulative dependence measure $\begin{array}{ r }{\breve{\Theta}_{m,q}(\alpha)=\sum_{k=m}^{\infty}\breve{\theta}_{k,q}(\alpha)<}\end{array}$ ∞.

Hence, by Lemma 26, there exists a (richer) probability space $(\breve{\Omega}^{\star},\breve{A}^{\star},\breve{\mathbb{P}}^{\star})$ on which we can define random vectors $\breve{\beta}_{k}^{\star}\mathrm{s}$ with the partial sum process $\begin{array}{ r }{\breve{S}_{i}^{\star}=\sum_{k=1}^{i}(\breve{\beta}_{k}^{\star}-\breve{\beta}_{\mathrm{mean}})}\end{array}$ , and a Gaussian process $\begin{array}{ r }{\breve{G}_{i}^{\star}=\sum_{k=1}^{i}\breve{z}_{k}^{\star}}\end{array}$ , where $\breve{z}_{k}^\star\}\mathrm{s}$ are independent Gaussian random vectors in $\mathbb{R}^{d}$ following $\mathcal{N}(0,I_{d})$ , such that

$$
(\breve{S}_{i}^{\star})_{1\leq i\leq t}\stackrel{{\mathcal{D}}}{{=}}(\breve{S}_{i}^{\circ})_{1\leq i\leq t},\tag{226}
$$

and

$$
\max_{1\leq i\leq t}\left\|\check{S}_{i}^{\star}-\check{\Sigma}^{1/2}(\alpha)\check{G}_{i}^{\star}\right\|_{2}=o_{\mathbb{P}}(t^{1/q}),\quad \text{in}(\check{\Omega}^{\star},\check{\mathcal{A}}^{\star},\check{\mathbb{P}}^{\star}),\tag{227}
$$

where the long-run covariance matrix $\breve{\Sigma}(\alpha)$ is defined in Theorem 15.

Following similar arguments as for (148)–(150), we can leverage the geometric-moment contraction in Theorem 12 to show the same Gaussian approximation rate, i.e., $O_{\mathbb{P}}(t^{1/q})$ , for the partial sum sequence $\begin{array}{ r }{\big(\sum_{k=1}^{i}(\breve{\beta}_{k}(\alpha)-\breve{\beta}_{\mathrm{mean}}(\alpha))\big)_{1<i<t},}\end{array}$ for any arbitrarily fixed initial vector $\breve{\beta}_{0}\in\mathbb{R}^{d}$ . Finally, recall the partial sum process $\begin{array}{ r }{\breve{S}_{i}^{\breve{\beta}_{0}}(\alpha)=\sum_{k=1}^{i}(\breve{\beta}_{k}(\alpha)-\breve{\beta})}\end{array}$ . By a similar argument in (151), the desired Gaussian approximation result for the partial sum process $(\breve{S}_{i}^{\breve{\beta}_{0}}(\alpha))_{1\leq i\leq t}$ follows. ■

context:
Throughout, we assume $f(x; S)$ is convex in $x$ where $S$ is a random variable with sample space $\mathcal{S}$ . For conciseness, we denote $f(x; S_i)$ by $f_i(x)$ where $S_i$ represents the $i$ th sample. Define $F(x) := \mathbb{E}[f(x; S)]$ , $F^{\star} := \inf_{x \in \mathcal{X}} F(x) > -\infty$ , $\bar{F}(x) := \frac{1}{n} \sum_{i=1}^{n} f_i(x)$ . Let $\mathcal{X}$ be a closed convex set with $\mathcal{X} \subseteq \mathbb{R}^d$ . In most practical cases, $\mathcal{X} = \mathbb{R}^d$ . Let $\mathcal{X}^{\star} := \arg \min_{x \in \mathcal{X}} F(x)$ and $R^{\star} := \inf_{x \in \mathcal{X}^{\star}} \|x\|$ . If $\mathcal{X}^{\star}$ is empty, then $R^{\star} = \infty$ . The dual norm is $\|z\|_* = \sup\{z \cdot x : \|x\| \leq 1\}$ . Let $\nabla h(x)$ be any subgradient of a function $h(x)$ and $\nabla_j h(x)$ be the $j$ th coordinate of $\nabla h(x)$ . Define $a \wedge b := \min\{a, b\}$ and $a \vee b := \max\{a, b\}$ . For a scalar $K$ , we let $[K] := \{0, 1, \ldots, K\}$ and, with slight abuse of notation, for a vector $v$ we let $[v]_j$ be the $j$ th coordinate of $v$ . Let $\mathbf{0}$ be a vector of zeros. We say the function $h(x)$ is $L$ -Lipschitz if and only if for all $x, x' \in \mathcal{X}$ , we have $|h(x) - h(x')| \leq L \|x - x' \|$ . An equivalent definition is that $\| \nabla h(x)\|_* \leq L$ for all $x \in \mathcal{X}$ . We say the function $f$ is $L$ -Lipschitz if and only if $h(x) = f(x; S)$ is $L$ -Lipschitz almost surely. We say the function $h: \mathcal{X} \to \mathbb{R}$ is $\mu$ -strongly convex if and only if for all $u, v \in \mathcal{X}$ we have $h(u) - h(v) \geq \nabla h(v) \cdot (u - v) + \frac{\mu}{2} \|u - v\|^2$ . We say the function $f$ is $\mu$ -strongly convex if and only if $h(x) = f(x; S)$ is $\mu$ -strongly convex almost surely. We assume there exists some reference model $x_{0}$ , a model the user identifies as a reasonable baseline. In the theory (Section 2 and Section 3), for simplicity we set the reference model to be the origin, i.e., $x_{0} = 0$ . Nonetheless, our results hold for an arbitrary reference model by shifting the origin.

In this section, we consider the case where there is a finite set of models $x_{0}, x_{1}, \ldots, x_{K}$ . In this setting, our goal is to find the best model among these $K + 1$ models. We will also explore applications of these techniques to selecting hyperparameters for stochastic optimization methods.

Section 2.1 studies the performance of standard model selection which chooses the model that minimizes the validation error. In particular, we show that it can effectively tune hyperparameters when strong convexity is present but otherwise may perform poorly compared to parameter-free optimization methods. Section 2.2 studies the performance of a new algorithm called RELIABLEMODELSELECTION, which obtains good worst-case performance both with and without strong convexity.

Conversely, without strong convexity, standard model selection can perform poorly at tuning learning rates. For a concrete example, consider adaptive SGD (also known as isotropic AdaGrad (Gupta et al., 2017)), which is a scalar variant of ADAGRAD (Duchi et al., 2011). While we chose adaptive SGD as an example, similar issues occur for tuning other standard stochastic optimization methods such as regularized ERM or SGD with a fixed step size. The formula for adaptive SGD is

$$
u_{t+1}\leftarrow\mathbf{proj}_{R}\left(u_{t}-R\frac{\boldsymbol{\nabla}f_{n+t}\left(u_{t}\right)}{\sqrt{\sum_{j=1}^{t}\left\|\boldsymbol{\nabla}f_{n+j}\left(u_{j}\right)\right\|_{2}^{2}}}\right),\bar{u}_{t}\leftarrow\frac{1}{t}\sum_{j=1}^{t}u_{j},\text{for} t=1,\dots,n \tag{4}
$$

where $u_1 = \mathbf{0}$ , $\text{proj}_R(\hat{u}) := \arg\min_{u \in \mathcal{X}: \|u\|_2 \leq R} \|u - \hat{u}\|_2$ and $R > 0$ is the learning rate which represents our estimated distance to optimality. We add the constraint $\|u\|_2 \leq R$ to ensure the domain is bounded proportionally to the learning rate. To clearly separate the validation set and training set, Equation (4) uses gradient $\nabla f_{n+t}(u_t)$ instead of $\nabla f_t(u_t)$ . Thus, we can think of $f_1, \ldots, f_n$ as the validation set and $f_{n+1}, \ldots, f_{2n}$ as the training set. Denote ADASGD(R) = $\bar{u}_n$ . It is well-known, e.g., Orabona (2019, Theorem 3.9 & 4.14), that assuming $f$ is $L$ -Lipschitz, adaptive SGD starting from $u_1 = \mathbf{0}$ , with probability $1 - \delta$ obtains

$$
F(\mathrm{ADASGD}(R))-\min_{x\in\mathcal{X}:\|x\|_{2}\leq R}F(x)\leq O\left(\frac{L R}{\sqrt{n}}\sqrt{\ln 2/\delta}\right)\tag{5}
$$

Setting $R = R^{\star}$ yields the optimal $O(LR^{\star}\sqrt{\ln 2 / \delta} /\sqrt{n})$ suboptimality guarantee. However, this approach relies on $R^{\star}$ being known.

Next, we consider how to reliably select high-quality models and avoid the issues that plagued standard model selection for tuning learning rates in Section 2.1. Our method, described in Algorithm 1, requires a list of confidence interval widths $\tau_{1},\ldots,\tau_{K}$ that satisfy Condition 1. The algorithm identifies a set of safe models $\mathcal{F}$ over which we minimize the validation error. The algorithmic parameter $\gamma \in [1,\infty)$ controls the size of $\mathcal{F}$ , with larger values of $\gamma$ behaving more like standard model selection. When $\gamma = 1$ , the algorithm reduces to minimizing the upper confidence bound on the function value, but this can be overly conservative, heavily favoring models that make predictions similar to the reference model.

Condition 1 Let $\tau_1, \ldots, \tau_K$ be nonnegative scalars such that for some $\delta \in (0,1)$ , $\mathbb{P}(\exists k \in \{1, \ldots, K\}) : |F(x_k) - \bar{F}(x_k) - (F(\mathbf{0}) - \bar{F}(\mathbf{0}))| > \tau_k) \leq \delta$ .

Condition 1 supposes that we have confidence intervals on the closeness of our validation loss to the population loss relative to the reference model, $x_0 = \mathbf{0}$ . Depending on the problem at hand, there are multiple ways to generate such confidence intervals. For example, if $f$ is $L$ -Lipschitz and some upper bound $\hat{L} \geq L$ is known, then a result of Maurer and Pontil (2009) (Theorem 14 in Appendix A) with $Z_i = f_i(x_k) - f_i(\mathbf{0})$ gives that with probability at most $\delta_k \in (0,1)$ , $|F(x_k) - F(\mathbf{0}) - (\bar{F}(x_k) - \bar{F}(\mathbf{0}))| > \sqrt{\frac{2\mathbb{V}_k}{n}\ln\frac{4}{\delta_k}} + \frac{14\hat{L}\|x_k\|}{3(n-1)}\ln\frac{4}{\delta_k}$ where

$$
\mathbb{V}_{k}:=\frac{1}{n-1}\sum_{i=1}^{n}(f_{i}(x_{k})-f_{i}(\mathbf{0})-(\bar{F}(x_{k})-\bar{F}(\mathbf{0})))^{2}
$$

is the sample variance of the paired differences $f_{i}(x_{k}) - f_{i}(\mathbf{0})$ . Setting $\delta_{k} = \frac{\delta}{K}$ and applying a union bound shows Condition 1 holds with

$$
\tau_{k}=\sqrt{\frac{2\tilde{c}\mathbb{V}_{k}}{n}}+\tilde{c}\frac{14\hat{L}\|x_{k}\|}{3(n-1)}\text{where}\tilde{c}:=\ln\frac{4K}{\delta}.\tag{6}
$$

Black dots show the validation errors of candidate models $x_{0}$ to $x_{4}$ . Orange and red intervals depict $\tau_{k}$ and $\gamma\tau_{k}$ , respectively, which are smaller for models with predictions more similar to the reference model, $x_{0}$ . The threshold $\theta$ (red dashed line) is the smallest extended upper bound $\bar{F}(x_{k}) + \gamma\tau_{k}$ . Models with $\bar{F}(x_{k}) + \tau_{k} \leq \theta$ form the candidate set F (in this example $F = \{1, 2\}$ ). Among these, $x_{2}$ has the lowest error and thus $k_{rely} = 2$ . Standard model selection chooses the lowest validation error across all models, $k_{std} = 4$ .

input A scalar $\gamma \in [1,\infty)$

input Candidate solutions $x_0, \ldots, x_K$

input Sample functions $f_{1},\ldots,f_{n}$

input $\tau_{1},\ldots,\tau_{K}$ satisfying Condition 1.

1: $\tau_{0} := 0$  
2: $\theta \leftarrow \min_{k\in [K]}\bar{F} (x_k) + \gamma \tau_k$  
3: $\mathcal{F} \leftarrow \{k \in [K] : \bar{F}(x_k) + \tau_k \leq \theta\}$  
4: $k_{\mathrm{rely}} := \arg \min_{k \in \mathcal{F}} \bar{F}(x_k)$

output The chosen index: $k_{\mathrm{rely}}$ .

Theorem 4 Suppose that $f$ is $L$ -Lipschitz and $\tau_{k}$ is defined as per Equation (6). Let $\delta \in (0,1)$ and $\tilde{c} := \ln \frac{4K}{\delta}$ . Then, with probability at least $1 - \delta$ ,

$$
F(x_{k_{\mathrm{rely}}})\leq\min_{k\in [K]}F(x_{k})+(1+\gamma)\left(L\sqrt{\frac{2\tilde{c}}{n-1}}+\frac{14\hat{L}\tilde{c}}{3(n-1)}\right)\|x_{k}\|.\tag{7}
$$

Additionally, if $F$ is $\mu$ -strongly convex and $\gamma \geq 3$ , then, with probability at least $1 - 2\delta$ ,

$$
F(x_{k_{\mathrm{rely}}})-F^{\star}\leq 4\Big(\min_{k\in [K]}F(x_{k})-F^{\star}\Big)+\frac{128}{\mu}\left(2L\sqrt{\frac{2\tilde{c}}{n-1}}+\frac{14\hat{L}\tilde{c}}{3(n-1)}\right)^{2}.\tag{8}
$$

We can use Equation (7) to generically obtain sample complexity bounds for parameter-free stochastic optimization. For example, Corollary 5 shows how to obtain such bounds by applying RELIABLEMODELSELECTION to tune the learning rate for adaptive SGD. To interpret Corollary 5, recall that $f_1, \ldots, f_{2n}$ are i.i.d. samples where $f_1, \ldots, f_n$ is the validation set (i.e., used by RELIABLEMODELSELECTION) and $f_{n+1}, \ldots, f_{2n}$ is the training set, i.e., used by adaptive SGD, see Equation (4).

This section develops a method with perfect adaptivity to unknown distance to optimality, matching optimal known-parameter high-probability bounds. Our results hold for p-norms with three values of p: 1, 2, and $\infty$ . While our method requires an estimate of the Lipschitz constant (Assumption 1), we show that for a sample of size n, an estimate within $\tilde{O}(\sqrt{n})$ of the true Lipschitz constant suffices to match optimal known-parameter high-probability bounds.

Assumption 1 (Upper bound on Lipschitz constants) Suppose that $f$ is differentiable, convex in $x$ , and satisfies $\| \nabla f(x; S) \|_2 \leq L \leq \hat{L}$ and $|\nabla_j f(x; S)| \leq \mathbf{L}_j \leq \hat{\mathbf{L}}_j$ almost surely for all $j \leq d$ and $x \in \mathcal{X}$ , where $\hat{L}$ and $\hat{\mathbf{L}}$ are known.

Assumption 1 treats $f$ as differentiable only for the sake of simplicity: our results extend to nondifferentiable functions via a smoothing argument, e.g., using the Moreau envelope (Moreau, 1965). Our optimal adaptive method consists of two stages. First, using half our sample, we apply regularized empirical risk minimization (ERM) to find a radius $R$ such that, with high probability, the minimum of $F$ in a ball of radius $R$ is close to its global minimum, and also $R = O(R^{\star})$ . Second, using the other half of our sample, we apply an off-the-shelf optimal known-parameter stochastic optimization method to approximately minimize $F$ in a ball of radius $R$ . Since $R$ is given to the method, it need not be adaptive to the distance to optimality. Our approach is summarized in Algorithm 2.

STAGE 1: LOCALIZATION VIA ERM. The key component of our approach is (non-squared) norm regularization. For a given regularization parameter $\lambda_{n}$ , consider the following regularized ERM and regularized population risk minimizers:

$$
\hat{x}_{\lambda_{n}}\in\underset{x\in\mathcal{X}}{\arg\min}\left\{\bar{F}(x)+\lambda_{n}\|x\|\right\}\text{and} x_{\lambda_{n}}^{\star}\in\underset{x\in\mathcal{X}}{\arg\min}\left\{F(x)+\lambda_{n}\|x\|\right\}.
$$

To obtain our results, it will suffice to choose $\lambda_{n}$ such that the following condition holds.

Let $(\mathcal{X},d)$ be a finite metric space with finite cardinality $M: = |{\mathcal{X}}|$ and denote by $\mathcal{M}_{+}(\mathcal{X}): =$ $\{\mu\in\mathbb{R}^{M}\mid\mu(x)\geq 0\forall x\in\mathcal{X}\}$ the set of non-negative measures<sup>1</sup> on $\mathcal{X}$ . The total mass of a measure $\mu\in\mathcal{M}_{+}(\mathcal{X})$ is defined as $\begin{array}{ r }{\mathbb{M}(\mu): =\sum_{x\in\mathcal{X}}\mu(x)}\end{array}$ and the subset $\mathcal{P}(\mathcal{X})\subset\mathcal{M}_{+}(\mathcal{X})$

of measures with total mass one is the set of probability measures. If $\pi\in\mathcal{M}_{+}(\mathcal{X}\times\mathcal{X})$ is a measure on the product space $\mathcal{X}\times\mathcal{X}$ its marginals are defined as $\textstyle\pi(x,\mathcal{X}): =\sum_{x^{\prime}}\pi(x,x^{\prime})$ and $\begin{array}{ r }{\pi(\boldsymbol{\mathcal{X}},\boldsymbol{x}^{\prime}): =\sum_{\boldsymbol{x}^{\prime}\in\mathcal{X}}\pi(\boldsymbol{x},\boldsymbol{x}^{\prime})}\end{array}$ , respectively. For two measures $\mu,\nu\in\mathcal{M}_{+}(\mathcal{X})$ define the set of non-negative sub-couplings as

$$
\Pi_{\leq}(\mu,\nu):=\{\pi\in\mathcal{M}_{+}(\mathcal{X}\times\mathcal{X})\mid\pi(x,\mathcal{X})\leq\mu(x),\pi(\mathcal{X},x^{\prime})\leq\nu(x^{\prime})\forall x,x^{\prime}\in\mathcal{X}\}.\tag{1}
$$

Following Heinemann et al. (2023), for $p \geq 1$ and a parameter $C > 0$ , the $(p,C){-}Kanto-$ rovich-Rubinstein distance (KRD) between two measures $\mu,\nu\in\mathcal{M}_{+}(\mathcal{X})$ is defined as

$$
\mathrm{KR}_{p,C}(\mu,\nu):=\left(\min_{\pi\in\Pi_{\leq}(\mu,\nu)}\sum_{x,x^{\prime}\in\mathcal{X}}d^{p}(x,x^{\prime})\pi(x,x^{\prime})+C^{p}\left(\frac{\mathbb{M}(\mu)+\mathbb{M}(\nu)}{2}-\mathbb{M}(\pi)\right)\right)^{\frac{1}{p}}.\tag{2}
$$

For $p \geq 1$ , it defines a distance on $\mathcal{M}_{+}(\mathcal{X})$ robust to spatial outliers<sup>2</sup> and naturally extends the well-known $p { - } t h$ order OT distance defined for measures of equal total mass (Heinemann et al., 2023). Notably, by compactness of $\Pi_{\le}(\mu,\nu)$ and continuity of the objective, an optimizer $\pi\in\Pi_{\leq}(\mu,\nu)$ of (2) always exists and is called unbalanced optimal transport plan (UOT plan).

$$
\mathbf{P}_{p,C}^{*}(\mu,\nu):=\left\{\pi\cdot\mathbb{1}(\cdot\in\mathcal{D}(C))\mid\pi\in\overline{{\mathbf{P}}}_{p,C}^{*}(\mu,\nu)\right\}.\tag{21}
$$

Lemma 36 in Appendix D.4 shows that $\mathbf{P}_{p,C}^{*}(\mu,\nu)$ is a subset of $\overline{{\mathbf{P}}}_{p,C}^{*}(\mu,\nu)$ , and that every sub-coupling in $\Pi_{\le}(\mu,\nu)$ which is the sum of an element in $\overline{{\mathbf{P}}}_{p,C}^{*}(\mu,\nu)$ and a non-negative measure supported on $\{(x,x^{\prime})\in\mathcal{X}\times\mathcal{X}|d(x,x^{\prime})=C\}$ is contained in $\overline{{\mathbf{P}}}_{p,C}^{*}(\mu,\nu)$ . Based on this insight, we restrict our attention to the set of restricted UOT plans for empirical and population measures,

$$
\mathbf{P}_{p,C}^{*}(\widehat{\mu}_{t,s},\widehat{\nu}_{t,s})\quad\mathrm{and}\quad\mathbf{P}_{p,C}^{*}(\mu,\nu),
$$

and quantify the accuracy in estimating the latter in terms of the former via the Hausdorf distance induced by the total variation norm. Crucial for our analysis is the following novel stability bound of the UOT plans.

For our stability bound of the UOT plan we establish a novel stability bound for the vanilla OT plan between measures with equal mass which might be of independent interest. To formalize these results, we employ the following notation. Let $\mu,\nu\in\mathcal{M}_{+}(\mathcal{X})$ be measures with identical mass $\mathbb{M}(\mu)=\mathbb{M}(\nu)$ , let c : ${\mathcal{X}}\times{\mathcal{X}}\to [0,\infty)$ be a cost function and denote the respective collection of OT plans as

$$
\widetilde{\mathbf{P}}_{c}^{*}(\mu,\nu):=\underset{\pi\in\Pi=(\mu,\nu)}{\operatorname{argmin}}\sum_{x,x^{\prime}\in\mathcal{X}}c(x,x^{\prime})\pi(x,x^{\prime}).\tag{22}
$$

Note that the assumption of identical masses ensures that the collection of transport plans is always non-empty and compact, hence $\widetilde{\mathbf{P}}_{c}^{*}(\mu,\nu)$ is always non-empty.

Theorem 14 (Stability bound for balanced OT plans) Let X be a finite discrete space and $\mu_{1},\nu_{1},\mu_{2},\nu_{2}\in\mathcal{M}_{+}(\mathcal{X})$ such that $\mathbb{M}(\mu_{1})=\mathbb{M}(\nu_{1})$ and $\mathbb{M}(\mu_{2})=\mathbb{M}(\nu_{2})$ . Then, for every cost function c: ${\mathcal{X}}\times{\mathcal{X}}\to [0,\infty)$ it holds that

$$
\mathcal{H}_{\mathrm{TV}}\left(\widetilde{\mathbf{P}}_{c}^{*}(\mu_{1},\nu_{1}),\widetilde{\mathbf{P}}_{c}^{*}(\mu_{2},\nu_{2})\right)\leq 4|\mathcal{X}|\left(\mathrm{TV}(\mu_{1},\mu_{2})+\mathrm{TV}(\nu_{1},\nu_{2})\right).
$$

A key tool in establishing properties of the $(p,C)\mathrm{-K R D}$ and the $(p,C)$ -barycenter is the lift of these problems to the space of probability measures by augmenting the space X with a dummy point having a fixed distance to all points in $\mathcal{X}_{:}$ , see (Heinemann et al., 2023, Section 3.1) for details. For a fixed parameter $C > 0$ , consider a dummy point d and define the augmented space ${\tilde{x}}: ={\mathcal{X}}\cup\{{\mathfrak{o}}\}$ with metric cost

$$
\widetilde{d}_{C}^{p}(x,x^{\prime})=\left\{\begin{array}{l l}d^{p}(x,x^{\prime})\wedge C^{p},&\text{if} x,x^{\prime}\in\mathcal{X},\\ \frac{C^{p}}{2},&\text{if} x\in\mathcal{X},x^{\prime}=\mathfrak{d},\\ \frac{C^{p}}{2},&\text{if} x=\mathfrak{d},x^{\prime}\in\mathcal{X},\\ 0,&\text{if} x=x^{\prime}=\mathfrak{d}.\end{array}\right.\tag{27}
$$

Consider the subset $\mathcal{M}_{+}^{B}(\mathcal{X})\ : =\ \{\mu\in\mathcal{M}_{+}(\mathcal{X})\ |\ \mathbb{M}(\mu)\leq B\}\ \subset\ \mathcal{M}_{+}(\mathcal{X})$ of non-negative measures whose total mass is bounded by $B .$ Setting $\widetilde{\mu}: =\mu+(B-\mathbb{M}(\mu))\delta_{\mathfrak{d}}$ , any measure $\mu\in\mathcal{M}_{+}^{B}(\mathcal{X})$ defines an augmented measure $\widetilde{\mu}$ on $\mathcal{X}$ such that $\mathbb{M}(\widetilde{\mu})=B$ . For any $\mu,\nu\in$ $\mathcal{M}_{+}(\mathcal{X})$ and their augmented versions $\widetilde{\mu},\widetilde{\nu}\in\mathcal{M}_{+}(\mathcal{X})$ it holds

$$
\mathrm{KR}_{C,p}^{p}(\mu,\nu)=\widetilde{\mathrm{OT}}_{\widetilde{d}_{C}^{p}}(\widetilde{\mu},\widetilde{\nu}).\tag{28}
$$

Here, $\widetilde{\mathrm{OT}}_{\widetilde{d}_{C}^{p}}$ denotes the OT cost defined for measures $\mu,\nu$ on $(\widetilde{\mathcal{X}},\widetilde{d})$ with $\mathbb{M}(\mu)=\mathbb{M}(\nu)$ as

$$
\widetilde{\mathrm{OT}}_{\widetilde{d}_{C}^{p}}(\mu,\nu):=\min_{\pi\in\Pi_{=}(\mu,\nu)}\sum_{x,x^{\prime}\in\mathcal{X}}\widetilde{d}_{C}^{p}(x,x^{\prime})\pi(x,x^{\prime}),
$$

where the set of couplings $\scriptstyle\Pi=(\mu,\nu)$ is the set $\Pi_{\le}(\mu,\nu)$ with inequalities replaced by equalities.

$$

Throughout the paper, we make the following assumption:

Assumption 1 Suppose that $\mathcal{H}~=~\mathcal{H}_{d}$ is a separable reproducing kernel Hilbert space (RKHS) on $\boldsymbol{\mathcal{X}}\subset\mathbb{R}^{d}$ with respect to a continuous kernel function $k=k_{d}$ satisfying

$$
\sup_{\boldsymbol{x}\in\mathcal{X}}k_{d}(\boldsymbol{x},\boldsymbol{x})\leq\kappa^{2},
$$

where κ is an absolute constant.

For example, in Section 3.2, we consider $k_{d}$ as the inner product kernel on the unit sphere, which takes the form $k_{d}({\pmb x},{\pmb x}^{\prime})=\Phi(\langle{\pmb x},{\pmb x}^{\prime}\rangle)$ , where $\pmb{x},\pmb{x}^{\prime}\in\mathbb{S}^{d}$ and $\Phi(\cdot)$ is a function independent of the dimension d (see Assumption 4).

By convention in statistical learning, we consider the large-sample-size limit, i.e., the case where the sample size n is suficiently large, although our results are non-asymptotic. This paper allows the dimension d to grow as n grows, meaning that we consider $d=d(n)$ and a sequence of estimation problems:

Estimating {f<sup>∗</sup><sub>ρ</sub> }<sub>d≥1</sub> using the RKHS {H<sub>d</sub>}<sub>d≥1</sub> or kernel {k<sub>d</sub>}<sub>d≥1</sub>.

In Section 3.1, we will consider the general case $d=d(n)$ , where d can be fixed or vary with n. In Section 3.2 and Section 3.3, we consider a specific large-dimensional setting, where $n\asymp d^{\gamma}$ for some $\gamma > 0$ . In both cases, we suppose that Assumption 1 holds uniformly for all $d \geq 1$ . For brevity, in the remainder of this paper, we frequently omit the subscript d in $\mu_{d},\rho_{d},f_{\rho_{d}}^{*},k_{d},\mathcal{H}_{d}.$ and other quantities that depend on d.

Suppose that the samples $\{(x_{i},y_{i})\}_{i=1}^{n}$ are i.i.d. sampled from $\rho .$ Kernel ridge regression (KRR) constructs an estimator ${\ddot{f}}_{\lambda}$ by solving the penalized least squares problem

$$
\hat{f}_{\lambda}=\underset{f\in\mathcal{H}}{\arg\min}\left(\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\left(y_{i}-f(\boldsymbol{x}_{i})\right)^{2}+\lambda\|f\|_{\mathcal{H}}^{2}\right),
$$

where $\lambda > 0$ is referred to as the regularization parameter.

Denote the samples as $\pmb{X}=(\pmb{x}_{1},\cdots,\pmb{x}_{n})$ and $\mathbf{y}=\left(y_{1},\ldots,y_{n}\right)^{\top}$ . The representer theorem (see, e.g., Steinwart and Christmann 2008) provides an explicit formula for the KRR estimator:

$$
\hat{f}_{\lambda}(\boldsymbol{x})=\mathbb{K}(\boldsymbol{x},\boldsymbol{X})(\mathbb{K}(\boldsymbol{X},\boldsymbol{X})+n\lambda\mathbf{I})^{-1}\mathbf{y},\tag{1}
$$

where

$$
\mathbb{K}(\pmb{X},\pmb{X})=(k(\pmb{x}_{i},\pmb{x}_{j}))_{n\times n},\mathbb{K}(\pmb{x},\pmb{X})=(k(\pmb{x},\pmb{x}_{1}),\dots,k(\pmb{x},\pmb{x}_{n})).
$$

We aim to analyze the convergence rate of the generalization error (excess risk) of $\hat{f}_{\lambda};$

$$
\mathbb{E}_{\pmb{x}\sim\mu}\left[\left(\hat{f}_{\lambda}(\pmb{x})-f_{\rho}^{*}(\pmb{x})\right)^{2}\right]=\left\|\hat{f}_{\lambda}-f_{\rho}^{*}\right\|_{L^{2}(\mathcal{X},\mu)}^{2}.
$$

Notations. We use the standard asymptotic notations $O(\cdot),\ o(\cdot),\ \Omega(\cdot)$ , and $\Theta(\cdot)$ . We also write $a_{n}\asymp b_{n}$ for $a_{n}=\Theta(b_{n});a_{n}\lesssim b_{n}$ for $a_{n}=O(b_{n});a_{n}\gtrsim b_{n}$ for $a_{n}=\Omega(b_{n});a_{n}\ll b_{n}$ for $a_{n}=o(b_{n})$ . We will also use the probability versions of the asymptotic notations such as $O_{\mathbb{P}}(\cdot),o_{\mathbb{P}}(\cdot),\Omega_{\mathbb{P}}(\cdot)$ , and $\Theta_{\mathbb{P}}(\cdot)$ . For instance, we say the random variables $X_{n},Y_{n}$ satisfying $X_{n}={\cal O}_{\mathbb{P}}(Y_{n})$ if and only if for any $\varepsilon > 0$ , there exist a constant $C_{\varepsilon}$ and $N_{\varepsilon}$ such that $P\left(|X_{n}|\geq C_{\varepsilon}|Y_{n}|\right)\leq\varepsilon,\forall n>N_{\varepsilon}$

Let $S_{k}:\mathcal{H}\to L^{2}(\mathcal{X},\mu)$ denote the natural embedding operator. Its adjoint operator $S_{k}^{*}:L^{2}(\mathcal{X},\mu)\to\mathcal{H}$ is an integral operator. Specifically, for $f\in L^{2}(\mathcal{X},\mu)$ and $\mathbf{\boldsymbol{x}}\in\mathcal{X}$ ，

$$
(S_{k}^{*}f)(\pmb{x})=\int_{\mathcal{X}}k(\pmb{x},\pmb{x}^{\prime})f(\pmb{x}^{\prime})\mathrm{d}\mu(\pmb{x}^{\prime}).
$$

Under Assumption $1,S_{k}$ and $S_{k}^{*}$ are Hilbert-Schmidt (HS) operators and therefore compact. Their HS norms (denoted as $\|{\cdot}\|_{2})$ satisfy

$$
\|S_{k}^{*}\|_{2}=\|S_{k}\|_{2}=\|k\|_{L^{2}(\mathcal{X},\mu)}:=\left(\int_{\mathcal{X}}k(\boldsymbol{x},\boldsymbol{x})\mathrm{d}\mu(\boldsymbol{x})\right)^{1/2}\leq\kappa .
$$

Next, we define two integral operators:

$$
L_{k}:=S_{k}S_{k}^{*}:L^{2}(\mathcal{X},\mu)\to L^{2}(\mathcal{X},\mu),\quad T:=S_{k}^{*}S_{k}:\mathcal{H}\to\mathcal{H}.\tag{2}
$$

$L_{k}$ and $T$ are self-adjoint, positive-definite and trace class (hence Hilbert-Schmidt and compact). Their trace norms (denoted as $\left.\cdot\right._{1})$ satisfy

$$
\|L_{k}\|_{1}=\|T\|_{1}=\|S_{k}\|_{2}^{2}=\|S_{k}^{*}\|_{2}^{2}.
$$

The spectral theorem for self-adjoint compact operators yields that there is an at most countable index set $N .$ , a non-increasing summable sequence $\{\lambda_{i}\}_{i\in N}\subseteq(0,\infty)$ and a family $\{e_{i}\}_{i\in N}\subseteq\mathcal{H}$ , such that $\{e_{i}\}_{i\in N}$ is an orthonormal basis (ONB) of Ran ${\overline{{S_{k}}}}\subseteq L^{2}({\mathcal{X}},{\mu})$ and $\{\lambda_{i}^{1/2}e_{i}\}_{i\in N}$ is an ONB of H. Further, the integral operators can be written as

$$
L_{k}=\sum_{i\in N}\lambda_{i}\left\langle\cdot,e_{i}\right\rangle_{L^{2}}e_{i}\quad \text{and}\quad T=\sum_{i\in N}\lambda_{i}\left\langle\cdot,\lambda_{i}^{1/2}e_{i}\right\rangle_{\mathcal{H}}\lambda_{i}^{1/2}e_{i}.
$$

We refer to $\{e_{i}\}_{i\in N}$ and $\{\lambda_{i}\}_{i\in N}$ as the eigenfunctions and eigenvalues. Mercer’s theorem $(\mathrm{see},\mathrm{e . g .}$ , Steinwart and Christmann 2008, Theorem 4.49) states that

$$
k\left(\boldsymbol{x},\boldsymbol{x}^{\prime}\right)=\sum_{i\in N}\lambda_{i}e_{i}(\boldsymbol{x})e_{i}\left(\boldsymbol{x}^{\prime}\right),\quad\boldsymbol{x},\boldsymbol{x}^{\prime}\in\mathcal{X},
$$

where the convergence is absolute and uniform in $\boldsymbol{x},\boldsymbol{x}^{\prime}$.

Since we are going to consider the source condition in subsequent sections, we now introduce the interpolation spaces (power spaces) of RKHS. For any $s \geq 0$ , the fractional power operator $L_{k}^{s}:L^{2}(\mathcal X,\mu)\to L^{2}(\mathcal X,\mu)$ is defined as

$$
L_{k}^{s}(f)=\sum_{i\in N}\lambda_{i}^{s}\left\langle f,e_{i}\right\rangle_{L^{2}}e_{i}.
$$

Then the interpolation space (power space) $[\mathcal{H}]^{s}$ is given by

$$
\left[\mathcal{H}\right]^{s}:=\operatorname{Ran}L_{k}^{s/2}=\left\{\sum_{i\in N}a_{i}\lambda_{i}^{s/2}e_{i}:(a_{i})_{i\in N}\in\ell_{2}(N)\right\}\subseteq L^{2}(\mathcal{X},\mu),\tag{3}
$$

equipped with the inner product

$$
\langle f,g\rangle_{[\mathcal{H}]^{s}}=\left\langle L_{k}^{-s/2}f,L_{k}^{-s/2}g\right\rangle_{L^{2}}.
$$

It follows that $[{\mathcal{H}}]^{s}$ is also a separable Hilbert space with orthogonal basis $\{\lambda_{i}^{s/2}e_{i}\}_{i\in N}$ . In particular, we have $[\mathcal{H}]^{1}=\mathcal{H}$ . For $0<s_{1}<s_{2}$ , the embeddings $[\mathcal{H}]^{s_{2}}\hookrightarrow [\mathcal{\dot{H}}]^{\check{s}_{1}}\hookrightarrow [\mathcal{H}]^{0}\hookrightarrow$ $L^{2}(\mathcal{X},\mu)$ are well-defined and compact (Fischer and Steinwart, 2020). For the functions in $[{\mathcal{H}}]^{s}$ with larger $s,$ we say they have higher regularity (smoothness) with respect to the RKHS. In the remainder of this paper, we assume $| N | = \infty$ . Also note that $\{\lambda_{i}\}_{i=1}^{\infty}$ and $\{e_{i}\}_{i=1}^{\infty}$ are dependent on ${\mathcal{H}},$ and hence depend on d.

Given the RKHS H and the corresponding eigenvalues and eigenfunctions, the true function can be decomposed as $\begin{array}{ r }{f_{\rho}^{*}=\sum_{i=1}^{\infty}f_{i}e_{i}({\pmb x})\in L^{2}({\pmb\chi},{\mu})}\end{array}$ for some sequence $\{f_{i}\}_{i=1}^{\infty}$ . We define the following important quantities, which are determined by $\{\lambda_{i}\}_{i=1}^{\infty},\{e_{i}\}_{i=1}^{\infty},\{f_{i}\}_{i=1}^{\infty}$ and regularization parameter λ:

$$
\mathcal{N}_{1}(\lambda)=\sum_{i=1}^{\infty}\left(\frac{\lambda_{i}}{\lambda_{i}+\lambda}\right);\quad\mathcal{N}_{2}(\lambda)=\sum_{i=1}^{\infty}\left(\frac{\lambda_{i}}{\lambda_{i}+\lambda}\right)^{2};\tag{4}
$$

$$
\mathcal{M}_{1}(\lambda)=\operatorname*{esssup}_{\boldsymbol{x}\in\mathcal{X}}\left|\sum_{i=1}^{\infty}\left(\frac{\lambda}{\lambda_{i}+\lambda}f_{i}e_{i}(\boldsymbol{x})\right)\right|;\mathcal{M}_{2}(\lambda)=\sum_{i=1}^{\infty}\left(\frac{\lambda}{\lambda_{i}+\lambda}f_{i}\right)^{2}.
$$

Assumption 2 Suppose that for some absolute constant $\sigma > 0$ ，

$$
\mathbb{E}_{(\boldsymbol{x},y)\sim\rho}\left[\left(y-f_{\rho}^{*}(\boldsymbol{x})\right)^{2}\Big|\boldsymbol{x}\right]=\sigma^{2},\quad\mu \text{-a.e.}\boldsymbol{x}\in\mathcal{X}.
$$

Assumption 2 ensures that the noise is non-vanishing, a condition satisfied in the standard nonparametric regression model $y=f_{\rho}^{*}(\pmb{x})+\epsilon$ where ε is an independent nonzero noise.

Assumption 3 Suppose that

$$
\operatorname*{esssup}_{\boldsymbol{x}\in\mathcal{X}}\sum_{i=1}^{\infty}\left(\frac{\lambda_{i}}{\lambda_{i}+\lambda}\right)^{2}e_{i}^{2}(\boldsymbol{x})\leq\mathcal{N}_{2}(\lambda),\tag{5}
$$

and

$$
\operatorname*{esssup}_{\boldsymbol{x}\in\mathcal{X}}\sum_{i=1}^{\infty}\frac{\lambda_{i}}{\lambda_{i}+\lambda}e_{i}^{2}(\boldsymbol{x})\leq\mathcal{N}_{1}(\lambda).\tag{6}
$$

Similar to Assumption 1, we suppose that Assumption 2 and 3 hold uniformly for all $d \geq 1$ . Assumption 3 naturally holds for RKHSs with uniformly bounded eigenfunctions, i.e., $\begin{array}{ r }{\operatorname*{sup}_{i\geq 1}\operatorname*{sup}_{{\pmb x}\in{\mathcal{X}}}|e_{i}({\pmb x})|\leq 1}\end{array}$ . Additionally, RKHSs associated with the inner product kernel on the unit sphere under the uniform distribution satisfy Assumption 3 (see Lemma 22).

In this subsection, we consider the inner product kernel on the unit sphere $\mathbb{S}^{d}$ with uniform distribution. In the large-dimensional setting $n\asymp d^{\gamma},\gamma\searrow 0$ , and under an additional source condition assumption, we apply Theorem 1 to establish the convergence rates of the generalization error of the KRR estimator. We then derive the corresponding minimax lower bound, allowing us to discuss the minimax optimality and the saturation efect of KRR.

Suppose that $\mathcal{X}=\mathbb{S}^{d}$ and $\mu$ is the uniform distribution on $\mathbb{S}^{d}$ . We consider the inner product kernel, i.e., there exists a function $\Phi(t):[-1,1]\ \to\ \mathbb{R}$ such that $k_{d}({\pmb x},{\pmb x}^{\prime})=$ Φ $\ L\left(\left.\pmb{x},\pmb{x}^{\prime}\right.\right),\forall\pmb{x},\pmb{x}^{\prime}\in\mathbb{S}^{d}$ . Then Mercer’s decomposition for the inner product kernel is then expressed in the basis of spherical harmonics:

$$
k_{d}(\boldsymbol{x},\boldsymbol{x}^{\prime})=\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}\mu_{k}\sum_{l=1}^{N(d,k)}Y_{k,l}(\boldsymbol{x})Y_{k,l}(\boldsymbol{x}^{\prime}),
$$

where $\{Y_{k,l}\}_{l=1}^{N(d,k)}$ are spherical harmonic polynomials of degree $k;\mu_{k}$ are the eigenvalues (also depending on d) with multiplicity $\begin{array}{ r }{N(d,0)=1;N(d,k)=\frac{2 k+d-1}{k}\frac{(k+d-2)!}{(d-1)!(k-1)!},k=1,2,\cdot\cdot\cdot}\end{array}$

Assumption 4 (Inner product kernel) Suppose that $k=\{k_{d}\}_{d=1}^{\infty}$ satisfies

$$
k_{d}(\pmb{x},\pmb{x}^{\prime})=\Phi\left(\langle\pmb{x},\pmb{x}^{\prime}\rangle\right),\forall\pmb{x},\pmb{x}^{\prime}\in\mathbb{S}^{d},
$$

where $\Phi(t)\in\mathcal{C}^{\infty}\left([-1,1]\right)$ is a fixed function independent of d and

$$
\Phi(t)=\sum_{j=0}^{\infty}a_{j}t^{j},a_{j}>0,\forall j=0,1,2,\dots
$$

Assumption 4 formally defines the kernel considered in this subsection. We assume all coeficients $\{a_{j}\}_{j=0}^{\infty}$ are positive to simplify the main results and proofs. In fact, the proof remains similar for other inner product kernels, provided that the positive coeficients can be identified, for example, the neural tangent kernel in Section 3.3. We assume $\Phi(t)$ to be fixed (i.e., assume $\{a_{j}\}_{j=0}^{\infty}$ to be independent of $d)$ and ignore the dependence of constants on $\{a_{j}\}_{j=0}^{\infty}$ in the rest of our paper.

Assumption 5 (Source condition)

(a) Suppose that $f_{\rho}^{*}(\pmb{x})=f_{\rho_{d}}^{*}(\pmb{x})=\sum_{i=1}^{\infty}f_{i}e_{i}(\pmb{x})\in [\mathcal{H}]^{s}$ for some $s > 0$ and satisfies that,

$$

$$

where $R_{\gamma}$ is a constant only depending on $\gamma .$

(b) Denote q as the smallest integer such that $q > \gamma$ and $\mu_{q}\neq 0$ . For $k \in \mathbb N$ , define $\mathcal{T}_{k}$ as the index set satisfying $\lambda_{i}\equiv\mu_{k},i\in\mathcal{I}_{k}$ . Further suppose that there exists an absolute constant $c_{0}>0$ such that for any d and $k\in\{0,1,\cdots,q\}$ with $\mu_{k}\neq 0$ , we have

$$
\sum_{i\in\mathcal{I}_{k}}\mu_{k}^{-s}f_{i}^{2}\geq c_{0}.\tag{10}

Note that $f_{\rho}^{\ast}$ and H vary with $d,$ thus $\{f_{i}\}_{i=1}^{\infty},\{\mu_{k}\}_{k=0}^{\infty},\{\mathcal{T}_{k}\}_{k=0}^{\infty}$ also depend on d. We omit the subscript d and assume Assumption 5 to hold uniformly for all $d \geq 1$

The proof of Theorem 1 is based on the traditional bias-variance decomposition. The contribution in this paper is that we refine the tools in Li et al. (2024) and Li et al. (2023b) to extend the applicability to the large-dimensional case. Throughout the proof, we denote

$$
T_{\lambda}=T+\lambda;\quad T_{\boldsymbol{X}\lambda}=T_{\boldsymbol{X}}+\lambda,\tag{14}
$$

where λ is the regularization parameter. $T + \lambda$ actually means $T + \lambda I$ , where I is the identity operator. We use $\|\cdot\|_{\mathcal{B}(B_{1},B_{2})}$ to denote the operator norm of a bounded linear operator from a Banach space $B_{1}$ to $B_{2}$ , i.e., $\|A\|_{\mathcal{B}(B_{1},B_{2})}=\operatorname*{sup}_{\|f\|_{B_{1}}=1}\|A f\|_{B_{2}}$ . For brevity, we denote it simply as $\| \cdot \|$ where no ambiguity arises. In addition, we use trA and $\|A\|_{1}$ to denote the trace and the trace norm of an operator. We denote $\|A\|_{2}$ as the Hilbert-Schmidt norm. In addition, we use $L^{2}(\mathcal{X},\mu)$ and $L^{\infty}(\mathcal{X},\mu)$ simply as $L^{2}$ and $L^{\infty}$ throughout the proof for brevity.

We also need the following essential notations, which are frequently used in related literature. Denote the samples $\pmb{Z}=\{(\pmb{x}_{i},y_{i})\}_{i=1}^{n}$ . Define the sampling operator $K_{x}:\mathbb{R} $ $\mathcal{H},\ y\mapsto\ y k(\pmb{x},\cdot)$ and its adjoint operator $K_{\pmb{x}}^{*}:\mathcal{H}\mathbb{R},\ f\mapsto f(\pmb{x})$ . Then we can define $T_{x}=K_{x}K_{x}^{*}$ . Furthermore, we define the sample covariance operator $T_{X}:{\mathcal{H}}\to{\mathcal{H}}$ as

$$
T_{\boldsymbol{X}}:=\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}K_{\boldsymbol{x}_{i}}K_{\boldsymbol{x}_{i}}^{*}.\tag{15}
$$

Then we know that $\|T_{\mathbf{\mathbf{X}}}\|\le\|T_{\mathbf{\mathbf{X}}}\|_{1}\le\kappa^{2}$ and $T_{X}$ is a trace class thus compact operator. Furthermore, define the sample basis function

$$
g_{\boldsymbol{Z}}:=\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}K_{\boldsymbol{x}_{i}}y_{i}\in\mathcal{H}.
$$

Following Caponnetto and de Vito (2007), the KRR estimator (1) can be expressed in operator form as

$$
\hat{f}_{\lambda}=(T_{\boldsymbol{X}}+\lambda)^{-1}g_{\boldsymbol{Z}},
$$

In order to derive the bias term, we define

$$
\tilde{g}_{\boldsymbol{Z}}:=\mathbb{E}\left(g_{\boldsymbol{Z}}|\boldsymbol{X}\right)=\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}K_{\boldsymbol{x}_{i}}f_{\rho}^{*}(\boldsymbol{x}_{i})\in\mathcal{H};
$$

$$
\tilde{f}_{\lambda}:=\mathbb{E}\left(\hat{f}_{\lambda}|\boldsymbol{X}\right)=(T_{\boldsymbol{X}}+\lambda)^{-1}\tilde{g}_{\boldsymbol{Z}}\in\mathcal{H}.\tag{16}
$$

We also need to define the expectation of $g z$ as

$$
g=\mathbb{E}g_{\boldsymbol{Z}}=\int_{\mathcal{X}}k(\boldsymbol{x},\cdot)f_{\rho}^{*}(\boldsymbol{x})d\mu(\boldsymbol{x})=S_{k}^{*}f_{\rho}^{*}\in\mathcal{H},
$$

and

$$
f_{\lambda}=(T+\lambda)^{-1}g=(T+\lambda)^{-1}S_{k}^{*}f_{\rho}^{*}.\tag{17}
$$

Our next goal is to prove that second term in (41) is higher order infinitesimal, i.e., $\Big\|\tilde{f}_{\lambda}-f_{\lambda}\Big\|_{L^{2}}=o_{\mathbb{P}}(\mathcal{M}_{2}(\lambda)^{\frac{1}{2}})$

Lemma 17 Suppose that Assumption 1, 2 and 3 hold. If the following approximation conditions hold for some $\lambda=\lambda(d,n)\to 0$ :

$$
\frac{\mathcal{N}_{1}(\lambda)}{n}\ln n=o(1);\quad n^{-1}\mathcal{N}_{1}(\lambda)^{\frac{1}{2}}\mathcal{M}_{1}(\lambda)=o\left(\mathcal{M}_{2}(\lambda)^{\frac{1}{2}}\right),\tag{43}

$$

Proof To begin with, by definition, we rewrite $\left\|\tilde{f}_{\lambda}-f_{\lambda}\right\|_{L_{2}}$ as follows

$$
\begin{array}{l}\left\|\tilde{f}_{\lambda}-f_{\lambda}\right\|_{L_{2}}=\left\|S_{k}\left(\tilde{f}_{\lambda}-f_{\lambda}\right)\right\|_{L^{2}}\\ =\left\|S_{k}T_{\lambda}^{-\frac{1}{2}}\cdot T_{\lambda}^{\frac{1}{2}}T_{\boldsymbol{X}\lambda}^{-1}T_{\lambda}^{\frac{1}{2}}\cdot T_{\lambda}^{-\frac{1}{2}}T_{\boldsymbol{X}\lambda}\left(\tilde{f}_{\lambda}-f_{\lambda}\right)\right\|_{L^{2}}\\ \leq\left\|S_{k}T_{\lambda}^{-\frac{1}{2}}\right\|_{\mathscr{B}(\mathcal{H},L^{2})}\cdot\left\|T_{\lambda}^{\frac{1}{2}}T_{\boldsymbol{X}\lambda}^{-1}T_{\lambda}^{\frac{1}{2}}\right\|_{\mathscr{B}(\mathcal{H},\mathcal{H})}\cdot\left\|T_{\lambda}^{-\frac{1}{2}}\left(\tilde{g}_{\boldsymbol{Z}}-T_{\boldsymbol{X}\lambda}f_{\lambda}\right)\right\|_{\mathcal{H}}.\tag{44}\\ \end{array}

Proof If $p \leq l \leq p + 1$ for some $p\in\{0,1,2\cdot\cdot\cdot\}$ , Lemma 19 and Lemma 21 show that there exist constants ${\mathfrak{C}},{\mathfrak{C}}_{1},{\mathfrak{C}}_{2},{\mathfrak{C}}_{3}$ and ${\mathfrak{C}}_{4}$ only depending on $p$ (recall that we ignore the dependence on $\{a_{j}\}_{j=0}^{\infty})$ , such that for any $d\geq\mathfrak{C}$ , we have

$$
\mathfrak{C}_{2}^{-1}\mu_{p+1}\leq\lambda\leq\mathfrak{C}_{1}^{-1}\mu_{p};
$$

and for $k=0,1,\cdots,p+1$ 2

$$
\mathfrak{C}_{1}d^{-k}\leq\mu_{k}\leq\mathfrak{C}_{2}d^{-k};\quad\mathfrak{C}_{3}d^{k}\leq N(d,k)\leq\mathfrak{C}_{4}d^{k}.
$$

We first prove (57). On the one hand, for any $d\geq\mathfrak{C}$ , we have

$$
\begin{array}{l}\mathcal{N}_{1}(\lambda)=\sum_{k=0}^{p}\frac{\mu_{k}}{\mu_{k}+\lambda}N(d,k)+\sum_{k=p+1}^{\infty}\frac{\mu_{k}}{\mu_{k}+\lambda}N(d,k)\\ \leq\sum_{k=0}^{p}\frac{\mu_{k}}{\mu_{k}}N(d,k)+\sum_{k=p+1}^{\infty}\frac{\mu_{k}}{\lambda}N(d,k)\\ \leq(p+1)\mathfrak{C}_{4}d^{p}+\lambda^{-1}\sum_{k=p+1}^{\infty}\mu_{k}N(d,k)\\ \leq(p+1)\mathfrak{C}_{4}d^{p}+\lambda^{-1}\kappa^{2}\\ \lesssim\lambda^{-1},\tag{59}\\ \end{array}
$$

where we use the fact that $\begin{array}{ r }{\sum_{k=p+1}^{\infty}\mu_{k}N(d,k)\le\sum_{i=1}^{\infty}\lambda_{i}\le\operatorname*{sup}_{x\in\mathcal{X}}k(x,x)\le\kappa^{2}}\end{array}$ for the third inequality.

On the other hand, for any $d\geq\mathfrak{C}$ , we have

$$
\begin{array}{l}\mathcal{N}_{1}(\lambda)=\sum_{k=0}^{p}\frac{\mu_{k}}{\mu_{k}+\lambda}N(d,k)+\sum_{k=p+1}^{\infty}\frac{\mu_{k}}{\mu_{k}+\lambda}N(d,k)\\ \geq\frac{\mu_{p}}{\mu_{p}+\lambda}N(d,p)+\frac{\mu_{p+1}}{\mu_{p+1}+\lambda}N(d,p+1)\\ \geq\frac{\mu_{p}}{\mu_{p}+\mathfrak{C}_{1}^{-1}\mu_{p}}N(d,p)+\frac{\mu_{p+1}}{\mathfrak{C}_{2}\lambda+\lambda}N(d,p+1)\\ \geq\frac{\mathfrak{C}_{3}}{1+\mathfrak{C}_{1}^{-1}}d^{p}+\frac{\mathfrak{C}_{1}\mathfrak{C}_{3}}{\mathfrak{C}_{2}+1}\lambda^{-1}\\ \gtrsim\lambda^{-1}.\tag{60}\\ \end{array}
$$
Combining (59) and (60), we finish the proof of (57).

Now we begin to prove (58). On the one hand, for any $d\geq\mathfrak{C}$ we have

$$
\begin{array}{l}\mathcal{N}_{2}(\lambda)=\sum_{k=0}^{p}\left(\frac{\mu_{k}}{\mu_{k}+\lambda}\right)^{2}N(d,k)+\sum_{k=p+1}^{\infty}\left(\frac{\mu_{k}}{\mu_{k}+\lambda}\right)^{2}N(d,k)\\ \leq\sum_{k=0}^{p}\left(\frac{\mu_{k}}{\mu_{k}}\right)^{2}N(d,k)+\sum_{k=p+1}^{\infty}\left(\frac{\mu_{k}}{\lambda}\right)^{2}N(d,k)\\ \leq(p+1)\mathfrak{C}_{4}d^{p}+\lambda^{-2}\sum_{k=p+1}^{\infty}\mu_{k}^{2}N(d,k)\\ \leq(p+1)\mathfrak{C}_{4}d^{p}+\lambda^{-2}\mu_{p+1}\sum_{k=p+1}^{\infty}\mu_{k}N(d,k)\\ \leq(p+1)\mathfrak{C}_{4}d^{p}+\lambda^{-2}\mathfrak{C}_{2}d^{-(p+1)}\kappa^{2}.\tag{61}\\ \end{array}
$$

Note that for the forth equation, we use the fact that $\mu_{k}\leq\mu_{p+1},\forall k\geq p+1$ (when d is suficiently large), which can be proved by Lemma 20. On the other hand, for any $d\geq\mathfrak{C}.$ , we have

$$
\begin{array}{l}\mathcal{N}_{2}(\lambda)=\sum_{k=0}^{p}\left(\frac{\mu_{k}}{\mu_{k}+\lambda}\right)^{2}N(d,k)+\sum_{k=p+1}^{\infty}\left(\frac{\mu_{k}}{\mu_{k}+\lambda}\right)^{2}N(d,k)\\ \geq\left(\frac{\mu_{p}}{\mu_{p}+\mathfrak{C}_{1}^{-1}\mu_{p}}\right)^{2}N(d,p)+\left(\frac{\mu_{p+1}}{\mathfrak{C}_{2}\lambda+\lambda}\right)^{2}N(d,p+1)\\ \geq\frac{\mathfrak{C}_{3}}{\left(1+\mathfrak{C}_{1}^{-1}\right)^{2}}d^{p}+\lambda^{-2}\left(\frac{\mathfrak{C}_{1}}{\mathfrak{C}_{2}+1}\right)^{2}\mathfrak{C}_{3}d^{-(p+1)}.\tag{62}\\ \end{array}
$$
Combining (61) and (62), we prove that $\displaystyle{\mathcal{N}}_{2}(\lambda)=\Theta\left(d^{p}+\lambda^{-2}d^{-(p+1)}\right)$

Lemma 25 Consider $\mathcal{X}=\mathbb{S}^{d}$ and the marginal distribution µ to be the uniform distribution. Let $k=k_{d}$ be the inner product kernel on $\mathbb{S}^{d}$ satisfying Assumption 1 and 4. Further suppose that Assumption 5 holds for some $s > 0$ . Define $\tilde{s}=\operatorname*{min}\{s,2\}$ . By choosing $\lambda=d^{-l}$ for some $0 < l < \gamma$ , we have: if $p \leq l \leq p + 1$ for some $p\in\{0,1,2,\cdots\}$ , we have

$$
\mathcal{M}_{2}(\lambda)=\Theta\left(\lambda^{2}d^{(2-\tilde{s})p}+d^{-(p+1)\tilde{s}}\right).\tag{66}
$$

The notation Θ involves constants only depending on $s,p,c_{0}$ and $R_{\gamma}$ , where $c_{0}$ and $R_{\gamma}$ are the constants from Assumption 5.

steps.claim:
Proof When $0<s\leq 2,\mathcal{M}_{2}(\lambda)$ can be viewed as $\lambda^{2}{\mathcal{M}}_{\alpha,\beta}(\lambda)$ in Lemma 24 with $\alpha=0,\beta=2$ The conditions (63) are satisfied and Lemma 24 shows that

$$
\mathcal{M}_{2}(\lambda)=\Theta\left(\lambda^{2}d^{(2-s)p}+d^{-(p+1)s}\right).\tag{67}
$$

When $s > 2$ , without loss of generality, we can assume $\lambda_{i}\leq 1,\forall i$ and $\lambda \leq 1$ . Recall we have proved in Lemma 19 that $\mu_{0}$ remains as a constant as $d \to \infty$ . On the one hand, Assumption 5 (b) also implies $f_{1}^{2}\geq c_{0}$ , which further implies

$$
\mathcal{M}_{2}(\lambda)=\lambda^{2}\sum_{i=1}^{\infty}\frac{f_{i}^{2}}{(\lambda_{i}+\lambda)^{2}}\geq\frac{1}{4}\lambda^{2}\sum_{i=1}^{\infty}f_{i}^{2}\geq\frac{1}{4}\lambda^{2}c_{0}.\tag{68}
$$

On the other hand, since $s > 2$ , we have

$$
\begin{array}{l}\mathcal{M}_{2}(\lambda)=\lambda^{2}\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}\left(\frac{\mu_{k}^{s}}{(\mu_{k}+\lambda)^{2}}\sum_{i\in\mathcal{I}_{k}}\mu_{k}^{-s}f_{i}^{2}\right)\\ \leq\lambda^{2}\left(\sup_{k\geq 0}\frac{\mu_{k}^{s}}{(\mu_{k}+\lambda)^{2}}\cdot\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}\sum_{i\in\mathcal{I}_{k}}\mu_{k}^{-s}f_{i}^{2}\right)\\ \leq\lambda^{2}\cdot\sup_{k\geq 0}\frac{\mu_{k}^{s}}{(\mu_{k}+\lambda)^{2}}\cdot R_{\gamma}^{2}\\ \leq\lambda^{2}R_{\gamma}^{2}.\tag{69}\\ \end{array}
$$

Further note that since $s > 2$ and $p \leq l \leq p + 1$ , (68) and (69) implies

$$
\mathcal{M}_{2}(\lambda)=\Theta(\lambda^{2})=\Theta(\lambda^{2}d^{(2-\tilde{s})p}+d^{-(p+1)\tilde{s}}).
$$

We finish the proof.

Lemma 26 Consider $\mathcal{X}=\mathbb{S}^{d}$ and the marginal distribution µ to be the uniform distribution. Let $k=k_{d}$ be the inner product kernel on $\mathbb{S}^{d}$ satisfying Assumption 1 and $\it 4 .$ . Further suppose that Assumption 5 holds for some $s \geq 1$ . Define $\tilde{s}=\operatorname*{min}\{s,2\}$ . By choosing $\lambda=d^{-l}$ for some $0 < l < \gamma$ , we have: if $p \leq l \leq p + 1$ for some $p\in\{0,1,2\cdot\cdot\cdot\}$ , we have

$$
\mathcal{M}_{1}(\lambda)=O\left(\lambda^{\frac{1}{2}}d^{\frac{(2-\tilde{s})p}{2}}+d^{-\frac{(\tilde{s}-1)(p+1)}{2}}\right).\tag{70}
$$

The notation O involves constants only depending on $s,\kappa,p$ and $R_{\gamma}$ , where $R_{\gamma}$ is the constant from Assumption 5.

steps.claim:
Proof First, Cauchy-Schwarz inequality shows that

$$
\begin{array}{l}\mathcal{M}_{1}(\lambda)^{2}=\underset{\boldsymbol{x}\in\mathcal{X}}{\text{ess sup}}\left|\sum_{i=1}^{\infty}\left(\frac{\lambda}{\lambda_{i}+\lambda}f_{i}e_{i}(\boldsymbol{x})\right)\right|^{2}\\ \leq\left(\sum_{i=1}^{\infty}\frac{\lambda^{2}\lambda_{i}^{-1}}{\lambda_{i}+\lambda}f_{i}^{2}\right)\cdot\operatorname{ess}\sup_{\boldsymbol{x}\in\mathcal{X}}\sum_{i=1}^{\infty}\left(\frac{\lambda_{i}}{\lambda_{i}+\lambda}e_{i}(\boldsymbol{x})^{2}\right)\\ \leq\left(\sum_{i=1}^{\infty}\frac{\lambda^{2}\lambda_{i}^{-1}}{\lambda_{i}+\lambda}f_{i}^{2}\right)\cdot\sum_{i=1}^{\infty}\left(\frac{\lambda_{i}}{\lambda_{i}+\lambda}\right)\\ :=\mathcal{Q}_{1}(\lambda)\cdot\mathcal{N}_{1}(\lambda),\tag{71}\\ \end{array}
$$

where we use (6) in Assumption 3 for the second inequality.

When $1\leq s\leq 2,\mathcal{Q}_{1}(\lambda)$ defined above can be viewed as $\lambda^{2}{\mathcal{M}}_{\alpha,\beta}(\lambda)$ in Lemma 24 with $\alpha= -1,\beta=1$ . In addition, the conditions (63) are satisfied, thus Lemma 24 shows that

$$
\mathcal{Q}_{1}(\lambda)=\Theta\left(\lambda^{2}d^{(2-s)p}+\lambda d^{-(s-1)(p+1)}\right).\tag{72}
$$

Since we assume the kernel to be bounded in Assumption 1, we can assume $\lambda_{i}\leq 1$ , ∀i and $\lambda \leq 1$ without loss of generality. When $s > 2$ , on the one hand, Assumption $5\ (\mathrm{b})$ also implies

$$
\mathcal{Q}_{1}(\lambda)=\lambda^{2}\sum_{i=1}^{\infty}\frac{f_{i}^{2}}{(\lambda_{i}+\lambda)\lambda_{i}}\geq\frac{1}{2}\lambda^{2}\sum_{i=1}^{\infty}f_{i}^{2}\geq\frac{1}{2}\lambda^{2}c_{0}.\tag{73}
$$

On the other hand, since $s > 2$ , we have

$$
\begin{array}{l}\mathcal{Q}_{1}(\lambda)=\lambda^{2}\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}\left(\frac{\mu_{k}^{s-1}}{\mu_{k}+\lambda}\sum_{i\in\mathcal{I}_{k}}\mu_{k}^{-s}f_{i}^{2}\right)\\ \leq\lambda^{2}\left(\sup_{k\geq 0}\frac{\mu_{k}^{s-1}}{\mu_{k}+\lambda}\cdot\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}\sum_{i\in\mathcal{I}_{k}}\mu_{k}^{-s}f_{i}^{2}\right)\\ \leq\lambda^{2}\cdot\frac{\mu_{k}^{s-1}}{\mu_{k}+\lambda}\cdot R_{\gamma}^{2}\\ \leq\lambda^{2}R_{\gamma}^{2}.\tag{74}\\ \end{array}
$$

Further note that since $s > 2$ and $p \leq l \leq p + 1$ , (73) and (74) implies

$$
\mathcal{Q}_{1}(\lambda)=\Theta(\lambda^{2})=\Theta(\lambda^{2}d^{(2-\tilde{s})p}+\lambda d^{-(\tilde{s}-1)(p+1)}).
$$

Therefore, we have $\mathcal{Q}_{1}(\lambda)=\Theta\left(\lambda^{2}d^{(2-\tilde{s})p}+\lambda d^{-(\tilde{s}-1)(p+1)}\right)$ for any $s > 0$

Further recalling that Lemma 23 proves $\mathcal{N}_{1}(\lambda)=\Theta\left(\lambda^{-1}\right)$ , use (71) and we finish the proof.

Lemma 28 Suppose that Assumption 1, 2 and 3 hold. Further suppose that Assumption 5 holds for some $0 < s < 1$ . If the following approximation conditions hold for some $\lambda=\lambda(d,n)\to 0$:

$$
\frac{\mathcal{N}_{1}(\lambda)}{n}\ln n=o(1);\quad n^{-1}\mathcal{N}_{1}(\lambda)^{\frac{1}{2}}\left\|f_{\lambda}\right\|_{L^{\infty}}=o\left(\mathcal{M}_{2}(\lambda)^{\frac{1}{2}}\right);\tag{80}
$$

and there exists $\varepsilon > 0$ , such that

$$
n^{-1}\mathcal{N}_{1}(\lambda)^{\frac{1}{2}}n^{\frac{1-s}{2}+\varepsilon}=o\left(\mathcal{M}_{2}(\lambda)^{\frac{1}{2}}\right),\tag{81}
$$

then we have

$$
\left\|\tilde{f}_{\lambda}-f_{\lambda}\right\|_{L^{2}}=o_{\mathbb{P}}(\mathcal{M}_{2}(\lambda)^{\frac{1}{2}}),
$$

where the notation $o_{\mathbb{P}}$ involves constants only depending on s and $\kappa .$

steps.claim:
Proof Recall the decomposition (44) in the proof of Lemma 17. The first two terms in (44) can be handled without any diference. Our goal here is to prove the following equation and we will finish the proof:

$$
\left\|T_{\lambda}^{-\frac{1}{2}}\left(\tilde{g}_{\boldsymbol{Z}}-T_{\boldsymbol{X}\lambda}f_{\lambda}\right)\right\|_{\mathcal{H}}=o_{\mathbb{P}}\left(\mathcal{M}_{2}(\lambda)^{\frac{1}{2}}\right).\tag{82}
$$

Similarly as (47), we rewrite the left hand side of (82) as

$$
\left\|T_{\lambda}^{-\frac{1}{2}}\left(\tilde{g}_{\mathbf{Z}}-T_{\mathbf{X}\lambda}f_{\lambda}\right)\right\|_{\mathcal{H}}=\left\|T_{\lambda}^{-\frac{1}{2}}\left[\left(\tilde{g}_{\mathbf{Z}}-T_{\mathbf{X}}f_{\lambda}\right)-(g-T f_{\lambda})\right]\right\|_{\mathcal{H}}.\tag{83}
$$

Denote $\xi_{i}=\xi({\pmb x}_{i})=T_{\lambda}^{-\frac 12}(K_{{\pmb x}_{i}}f_{\rho}^{*}({\pmb x}_{i})-T_{{\pmb x}_{i}}f_{\lambda})$ . Further consider the subset $\Omega_{1}=\{{\pmb x}\in\mathcal{X}$ $|f_{\rho}^{*}({\pmb x})|\leq t\}$ and $\Omega_{2}=\mathcal{X}\backslash\Omega_{1}$ , where t will be chosen appropriately later. Decompose $\xi_{i}$ as $\xi_{i}I_{{\pmb x}_{i}\in\Omega_{1}}+\xi_{i}I_{{\pmb x}_{i}\in\Omega_{2}}$ and we have the following decomposition of (83):

$$
\begin{array}{l}\left\|\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\xi_{i}-\mathbb{E}\xi_{x}\right\|_{\mathcal{H}}\leq\left\|\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\xi_{i}I_{\boldsymbol{x}_{i}\in\Omega_{1}}-\mathbb{E}\xi_{\boldsymbol{x}}I_{\boldsymbol{x}\in\Omega_{1}}\right\|_{\mathcal{H}}+\|\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\xi_{i}I_{\boldsymbol{x}_{i}\in\Omega_{2}}\|_{\mathcal{H}}+\|\mathbb{E}\xi_{\boldsymbol{x}}I_{\boldsymbol{x}\in\Omega_{2}}\|_{\mathcal{H}}\\ :=\mathrm{I}+\mathrm{II}+\mathrm{III}.\tag{84}\\ \end{array}
$$

Next we choose $\begin{array}{ r }{t=n^{\frac{1-s}{2}+\varepsilon_{t}},q=\frac{2}{1-s}-\varepsilon_{q}}\end{array}$ such that

$$
\varepsilon_{t}<\varepsilon;\text{and}\frac{1-s}{2}+\varepsilon_{t}>1/\left(\frac{2}{1-s}-\varepsilon_{q}\right),\tag{85}
$$

where $\varepsilon$ is given in (81). Then we can bound the three terms in (84) as follows:

(i) For the first term in (84), denoted as I, notice that

$$
\left\|\left(f_{\lambda}-f_{\rho}^{*}\right)I_{\pmb{x}_{i}\in\Omega_{1}}\right\|_{L^{\infty}}\leq\|f_{\lambda}\|_{L^{\infty}}+n^{\frac{1-s}{2}+\varepsilon_{t}}.
$$

Imitating the procedure (iii) in the proof of Lemma 17 and using (80), (81), we have

$$
\mathrm{I}=o_{\mathbb{P}}\left(\mathcal{M}_{2}(\lambda)^{\frac{1}{2}}\right).\tag{86}
$$

(ii) For the second term in (84), denoted as II. Since $\begin{array}{ r }{q=\frac{2}{1-s}-\varepsilon_{q}<\frac{2}{1-s}}\end{array}$ , Lemma 44 shows that,

$$
[\mathcal{H}]^{s}\hookrightarrow L^{q}(\mathcal{X},\mu),
$$

with embedding norm less than a constant $C_{s,\kappa}$ . Then Assumption 5 (a) implies that there exists $0<C_{q}<\infty$ only depending on $\gamma,s$ and κ such that $\|f_{\rho}^{*}\|_{L^{q}(\mathcal{X},\mu)}\leq C_{q}$ . Using the Markov inequality, we have

$$
P(\pmb{x}\in\Omega_{2})=P\Big(|f_{\rho}^{*}(\pmb{x})| >t\Big)\leq\frac{\mathbb{E}|f_{\rho}^{*}(\pmb{x})|^{q}}{t^{q}}\leq\frac{(C_{q})^{q}}{t^{q}}.
$$

Further, since (85) guarantees $t^{q}\gg n$ , we have

$$
\begin{array}{l}\tau_{n}:=P\left(\mathrm{II}\geq\mathcal{M}_{2}(\lambda)^{\frac{1}{2}}\right)\leq P\Big(\exists\boldsymbol{x}_{i}\text{s.t.}\boldsymbol{x}_{i}\in\Omega_{2},\Big)=1-P\Big(\boldsymbol{x}_{i}\notin\Omega_{2},\forall\boldsymbol{x}_{i},i=1,2,\dots,n\Big)\\ =1-P\left(\boldsymbol{x}\notin\Omega_{2}\right)^{n}\\ =1-P\Big(|f_{\rho}^{*}(\boldsymbol{x})|\leq t\Big)^{n}\\ \leq 1-\left(1-\frac{\left(C_{q}\right)^{q}}{t^{q}}\right)^{n}\rightarrow 0.\tag{87}\\ \end{array}
$$

(iii) For the third term in (84), denoted as III. Since Lemma 39 implies that $\|T_{\lambda}^{-\frac{1}{2}}k(\pmb{x},\cdot)\|_{\mathcal{H}}\leq$ $\mathcal{N}_{1}(\lambda)^{\frac{1}{2}},\mu\mathrm{{\mathrm{-}}a . e .}~\pmb{x}\in\mathcal{X}$ , so

$$
\begin{array}{l}\mathrm{III}\leq\mathbb{E}\|\xi_{\boldsymbol{x}}I_{\boldsymbol{x}\in\Omega_{2}}\|_{\mathcal{H}}\leq\mathbb{E}\left[\|T_{\lambda}^{-\frac{1}{2}}k(\boldsymbol{x},\cdot)\|_{\mathcal{H}}\cdot\left|\left(f_{\rho}^{*}-f_{\lambda}(\boldsymbol{x})\right)I_{\boldsymbol{x}\in\Omega_{2}}\right|\right]\\ \leq\mathcal{N}_{1}(\lambda)^{\frac{1}{2}}\mathbb{E}\big|\big(f_{\rho}^{*}-f_{\lambda}(\boldsymbol{x})\big)I_{\boldsymbol{x}\in\Omega_{2}}\big|\\ \leq\mathcal{N}_{1}(\lambda)^{\frac{1}{2}}\left\|f_{\rho}^{*}-f_{\lambda}\right\|_{L^{2}}^{\frac{1}{2}}\cdot P\left(\boldsymbol{x}\in\Omega_{2}\right)^{\frac{1}{2}}\\ \leq\mathcal{N}_{1}(\lambda)^{\frac{1}{2}}\mathcal{M}_{2}(\lambda)^{\frac{1}{2}}t^{-\frac{q}{2}},\tag{88}\\ \end{array}
$$

where we use Cauchy-Schwarz inequality for the third inequality and (16) for the forth inequality.

Recalling that the choices of t, q satisfy $t^{-q}\ll n^{-1}$ and we have assumed $\mathcal{N}_{1}(\lambda)$ ln $n/n=o(1)$ , we have

$$
\mathrm{III}=o\left(\mathcal{M}_{2}(\lambda)^{\frac{1}{2}}\right).\tag{89}
$$
Plugging (86), (87) and (89) into (84), we finish the proof.

context:
We consider a two-state HMM with real-valued emissions, in which we observe the first n entries of a sequence $\pmb{Y}=(Y_{1},Y_{2},\dots)\in [0,1]^{\mathbb{N}}$ which, under a parameter $\theta=(p,q,f_{0},f_{1})$ satisfies

$$
\mathbb{P}_{\theta}(Y_{n}\in A\mid\boldsymbol{X})=\int_{A}f_{X_{n}}(y)\mathrm{d}y,\tag{1}
$$

$$
\boldsymbol{X}=(X_{n})_{n\in\mathbb{N}}\sim\operatorname{Markov}(\pi,Q_{\theta}),
$$

with the $Y_{n},\ n\in\mathbb{N}$ conditionally independent given X. The vector X of ‘hidden states’, which we assume is started from its invariant distribution $X_{1}\sim\pi$ , takes values in $\{0,1\}^{\mathbb{N}}$ The transition matrix of the chain is given by

$$
Q=Q_{\theta}:=\left(\begin{array}{c c}1-p&p\\ q&1-q\end{array}\right),\tag{2}
$$

with the convention that for $j\geq 1,\mathbb{P}_{\theta}(X_{j+1}=0\mid X_{j}=0)=1-p<1$ and $\mathbb{P}_{\theta}(X_{j+1}=0\ |$ $X_{i}=1)=q>0$ . The functions $f_{0},f_{1}\in L^{2}([0,1])$ are density functions. Thus all $Y_{k},k\geq 1$ follow the mixture distribution $\pi_{0}f_{0}+\pi_{1}f_{1}$

The goal is to estimate the parameter θ. This is a nonlinear inverse problem known to be solvable, up to a label-switching issue, even without any modelling assumptions on $f_{0}$ and $f_{1}$ (Gassiat et al., 2016; Alexandrovich et al., 2016): specifically, given that the highly non-identifiable i.i.d. nonparametric mixture is a degenerate submodel of a HMM, under conditions which rule out independence. There are three ways in which the data $(Y_{n})_{n\in\mathbb{N}}$ can fail to exhibit dependence: when the hidden states themselves are in reality independently distributed; when the emission distributions are identical; or when only one population is observed. We adopt the minimax paradigm and we analyse the smallest maximum risk attainable over the following class of parameters. We define for some $\delta,\epsilon\in(0,1)$ and some $\zeta,s_{0},s_{1},R>0$

$$
\Theta_{\delta,\epsilon,\zeta}^{s_{0},s_{1}}(R):=\{\theta:p,q\geq\delta,|1-p-q|\geq\epsilon,\|f_{0}-f_{1}\|_{L^{2}}\geq\zeta,\|f_{i}\|_{B_{2,\infty}^{s_{i}}}\leq R\}.\tag{3}
$$

Here $\|\cdot\|_{B_{2,\infty}^{s}}$ denotes a Besov norm whose precise definition as used in this paper is delayed to equation (15) below. The space $B_{2,\infty}^{s}$ can be thought to be similar to the subspace of s-times diferentiable functions with continuous s-derivative that are square-integrable, but it allows for slightly more general functions with comparable smoothness. We refer to Triebel (1983) for a thorough introduction to Besov spaces and their history. The quantities $\delta,\epsilon$ and ζ lower bound the “distance” to the i.i.d. submodel. Indeed if $\delta = 0$ , we may be unable to estimate both $f_{0}$ and $f_{1}$ since we may see data from one of these alone; if $\zeta = 0$ we may be unable to estimate $p$ and $q ;$ and if $\epsilon = 0$ then we may be unable to identify the contributions of $f_{0}$ and $f_{1}$ to the mixture $\pi_{0}f_{0}+\pi_{1}f_{1}$ . We use concentration inequalities for Markov chains (Paulin, 2015) to build our estimators. This requires us to slightly shrink the set $\Theta_{\delta,\epsilon,\zeta}^{s_{0},s_{1}}(R)$ ) and restrict our attention to parameters that are also in

$$
\Sigma_{\gamma^{*}}(L):=\{\theta:1- |1-p-q|\geq\gamma^{*},\max_{j=0,1}\|f_{j}\|_{\infty}\leq L\},\tag{4}
$$

i.e. parameters with uniformly bounded emission densities (here $\|\cdot\|_{\infty}$ denotes the usual supremum norm) and having an absolute spectral gap. The assumption that the Markov chain starts from its stationary distribution could be relaxed as explained in (Paulin, 2015, Section 3.3), at the price of increasing the constants in the upper bounds, and longer proofs. We throughout use $\mathbb{P}_{\theta}$ to denote the law of $(X,Y)$ , and all induced marginal and conditional laws.

In this section we construct estimators whose maximum risk over $\Theta_{\delta,\epsilon,\zeta}^{s_{0},s_{1}}(R)\cap\Sigma_{\gamma^{*}}(L)$ match those established in the lower bounds of Theorems 2 and 3 in most cases.

Here we describe the heuristic we use to build a near minimax optimal estimator of $\theta =$ $(p,q,f_{0},f_{1})$ . As noted previously (Gassiat et al., 2016), understanding the law of three consecutive observations is key to recovering the model parameters. A reparametrisation simplifies the expression for said law, and allows the dependence on the parameters $\delta,\epsilon$ and ζ to appear more naturally. Set

$$
\phi(\theta)=\big(\frac{q-p}{p+q},1-p-q,\|f_{0}-f_{1}\|_{L^{2}}\big),\quad\psi(\theta)=\big(\frac{q f_{0}+p f_{1}}{p+q},\frac{f_{0}-f_{1}}{\|f_{0}-f_{1}\|_{L^{2}}}\big).\tag{7}
$$

For $m \geq 1$ , let $P_{\phi,\psi}^{(m)}$ denote the law of $(Y_{1},\ldots,Y_{m})$ under parameter $(\phi,\psi)$ , and let $p_{\phi,\psi}^{(m)}$ denote the corresponding density with respect to Lebesgue measure on $[0,1]^{m}$ . In the parametrisation (7), defining for $\phi=\left(\phi_{1},\phi_{2},\phi_{3}\right)$

$$
r(\phi)=\frac{1}{4}(1-\phi_{1}^{2})\phi_{2}\phi_{3}^{2},\tag{8}
$$

one computes, with $f \otimes g$ defined by $(f\otimes g)(x,y)=f(x)g(y)$ 2

$$
\begin{array}{l}p_{\phi,\psi}^{(3)}=\psi_{1}\otimes\psi_{1}\otimes\psi_{1}+r(\phi)\big(\psi_{2}\otimes\psi_{2}\otimes\psi_{1}+\psi_{1}\otimes\psi_{2}\otimes\psi_{2}\big)\\ +\phi_{2}r(\phi)\psi_{2}\otimes\psi_{1}\otimes\psi_{2}-\phi_{1}\phi_{2}\phi_{3}r(\phi)\psi_{2}\otimes\psi_{2}\otimes\psi_{2}.\tag{9}\\ \end{array}
$$

We propose to estimate $(p,q)$ and the wavelet coeficients of $f_{0}$ and $f_{1}$ using the method of moments. In the inversion procedure described above we replace the moments by their empirical versions computed using

$$
\mathbb{P}_{n}^{(s)}(H):=\frac{1}{n-s+1}\sum_{i=1}^{n-s+1}H(Y_{i},\dots,Y_{i+s-1}),\quad H:[0,1]^{s}\rightarrow\mathbb{R},s\geq 1.\tag{13}
$$

As suggested by equation (12), the formula for computing (φ, ψ) given the moments is unstable if the function h is chosen poorly, so that the estimates may be far from the true values if $\langle\psi_{2},h\rangle$ is too small even if empirical moments are close to their means. No fixed choice of h works uniformly over the parameter space: given $h,$ there exists a parameter $(\phi,\psi)$ such that $\langle\psi_{2},h\rangle$ is arbitrarily small, resulting in an arbitrarily large maximum risk over $\Theta_{\delta,\epsilon,\zeta}^{s_{0},s_{1}}(R)$ . To avoid a deteriorated maximum risk, it is therefore necessary to estimate h from the data. The oracle choice for h would maximize $\begin{array}{ r }{h\mapsto\frac{|\langle\psi_{2},h\rangle|}{\|h\|}}\end{array}$ and hence be given by $h=\psi_{2}$ . Thus, a crucial step in our estimation procedure is to provide an initial (crude) estimator $\tilde{\psi}_{2}$ of $\psi_{2}$ such that $\|\tilde{\psi}_{2}\|_{L^{2}}=1$ and such that

$$
\tilde{\mathcal{I}}:=\left\langle\psi_{2},\tilde{\psi}_{2}\right\rangle \tag{14}
$$

is suficiently bounded away from zero with high probability under each parameter $(\phi,\psi)\in$ $\Theta_{\delta,\epsilon,\zeta}^{s_{0},s_{1}}(R)\cap\Sigma_{\gamma^{*}}(L)$ . For this reason we describe $\tilde{\psi}_{2}$ as a separating function: since $\psi_{2}= $ $(f_{0}-f_{1})/\|f_{0}-f_{1}\|_{L^{2}}$ , finding $\tilde{\psi}_{2}$ is tantamount to finding an hyperplane in $L^{2}[0,1]$ which separates $f_{0}$ and $f_{1}$ suficiently well. The estimator $\tilde{\psi}_{2}$ is built in Section 3.3.

As explained in Section 3.1, our estimation procedure is based on computing empirical averages of the type $\begin{array}{ r }{\mathbb{P}_{n}^{(2)}(\tilde{\psi}_{2}\otimes f)=\frac{1}{n-1}\sum_{i=1}^{n-1}\tilde{\psi}_{2}(Y_{i})f(Y_{i+1})}\end{array}$ where $\tilde{\psi}_{2}$ is a crude estimator of $\psi_{2}$ . If $\tilde{\psi}_{2}$ is also estimated from $(Y_{1},\ldots,Y_{n})$ , it is not clear at all that these empirical average approach $\mathbb{E}_{\theta}(\psi_{2}(Y_{1})f(Y_{2}))$ , as they are sum of somewhat complex dependent random variables, each term of which depends on the whole sample $(Y_{1},\ldots,Y_{n})$ . A classical trick is to estimate $\tilde{\psi}_{2}$ using a sample $({\tilde{Y}}_{1},\dots,{\tilde{Y}}_{n})$ that is independent from the sample $(Y_{1},\ldots,Y_{n})$ used to compute the average $\begin{array}{ r }{\frac{1}{n-1}\sum_{i=1}^{n-1}\tilde{\psi}_{2}(Y_{i})f(Y_{i+1})}\end{array}$ . In the context of HMM, however, the sample cannot be split into two independent parts. Fortunately this is not too worrisome. As explained in Section $\mathrm{A},$ it is possible to split the sample $(Y_{1},\ldots,Y_{n})$ into three parts, and then use the first third to estimate $\tilde{\psi}_{2}$ and the last third for empirical averages. This way, deviation inequalities for the empirical averages of functions involving $\tilde{\psi}_{2}$ can be achieved as if $\tilde{\psi}_{2}$ were independent of the observations used in the empirical averages, up to a term $C e^{-c\gamma^{*}n}$ for $C$ and c universal constants. Thus, to facilitate reading, we will throughout assume that $\tilde{\psi}_{2}$ is estimated using a sample $(\tilde{Y}_{1},\ldots,\tilde{Y}_{n})\sim P_{\phi,\psi}^{(n)}$ independent of $(Y_{1},\ldots,Y_{n})$
