Notations. For any positive integer n we let [n] denote the set $\{1,\ldots,n\}$ . For any set A we let $\Delta(A)$ denote the set of probability measures over A. For sets $A,B,$ we let $A \times B$ be the Cartesian product of the two. During the whole paper, we use $k \in [ K ]$ to refer to an episode and $h \in [ H ]$ to refer to a horizon. In addition, we use $\tilde{k}$ to refer to a bufer period associated with the k-th episode. We consider a repeated (lazy) multi-phase second-price auction with personalized reserve prices. Particularly, we assume that there are N rational bidders, indexed by [N], and one seller participating in the auction. For ease of presentation, we use “he” to refer to a specific bidder and “she” to the seller. Second Price Auction with Personalized Reserve Prices. We begin by describing a single round of the auction. Each bidder $i \in [ N ]$ submits some bid $b_{i}\in\mathbb{R}_{\geq 0}$ and the seller determines the personalized reserve prices for the bidders in the form of reserve price vector $\boldsymbol{\rho}\in\mathbb{R}_{>0}^{N}$ , with $\rho_{i}$ denoting bidder i’s reserve price. The bidder with the highest bid only wins if he also clears his personal reserve price, i.e., $b_{i}\geq\rho_{i}$ . If the bidder i receives the item, he pays the seller the maximum of his personalized reserve and the second highest bid, namely max $\{\rho_{i},\operatorname*{max}_{j\neq i}b_{j}\}$ , which we dub $m_{i}$ for simplicity. When the bidder with the highest bid fails to clear his personalized reserve price, the auction fails, the seller gains zero, and the item remains unsold. In summary, bidder i receives the item if and only if $b_{i}\geq m_{i}$ and the price he pays is $m_{i}$ . For any round of auction, we let $q_{i}=11(\mathrm{bidder}\ i$ receives the item) indicate whether bidder i received the item or not. For the sake of convenience, throughout the paper, we assume that there are no ties in the submitted bids. A Multi-Phase Second Price Auction. We now characterize the dynamics of the multiphase auction setting we study. Assume that the transition dynamic between rounds can be modeled as an episodic Markov Decision Process $(\mathrm{MDP})^{1}$ . A multi-phase second price auction with personalized reserves is parameterized as $(\mathcal{S},\Upsilon,H,\mathbb{P},\{r_{i}\}_{i=1}^{N})$ , with the state space denoted by S, seller’s item choice space $\Upsilon^{2}$ , horizon H, transition kernel $\mathbb{P}=\{\mathbb{P}_{h}\}_{h=1}^{H}$ where $\mathbb{P}_{h}:\mathcal{S}\times\Upsilon\Delta(\mathcal{S})$ , and the individual bidders’ reward functions $r_{i}=\{r_{i h}\}_{h=1}^{H}$ for all $i \in [ N ]$ . The choice of item $\upsilon \in \Upsilon$ afects the bidders’ rewards as well as the transition. The interaction between the bidders and the seller is then defined as follows. We assume without loss of generality that the state at the initial step is fixed at some $x_{1}\in S$ . For each $h \in [ H ]$ , the seller and the bidders engage in a single round of the second-price auction. Given the seller’s item choice at step $h,v_{h}$ , nature transitions to the next state according to the transition kernel $\mathbb{P}_{h}$ Bidder Rewards. We assume that for each bidder $i \in [ N ]$ at time $h \in [ H ]$ , his reward3 depends on both the state x and item being auctioned of at that round $\upsilon \in \Upsilon$ , which we formalize as $$ r_{i h}(x,\upsilon)=1+\mu_{i h}(x,\upsilon)+z_{i h},\text{where} z_{i h}\stackrel{\mathrm{i.i.d.}}{\sim}F. $$ Here, $z_{i h}$ denotes the randomness within bidders’ rewards and is drawn i.i.d. from the market noise distribution $F(\cdot)$ . We assume that $F(\cdot)$ is supported on [−1, 1] and has mean 0. Let $\mu_{i,h}:S\times\Upsilon [0,1]$ denote the conditional expectation of the reward less one, where the constant is added to ensure $r_{i h}(x,v)\in [0,3]$ Policies and Value Functions. Before we describe the seller’s policy, we first discuss the action space $\mathcal{A}=\Upsilon\times\mathbb{R}_{\ge 0}^{N}$ . At each $h \in [ H ]$ , the seller chooses some action $a_{h}=(v_{h},\rho_{h})$ ， comprising of item choice $\upsilon \in \Upsilon$ and reserve price vector $\rho\in\mathbb{R}_{\geq 0}^{N}$ . The seller’s policy is then $\pi=\{\pi_{h}\}_{h=1}^{H}$ , where $\pi_{h}:S\to\Delta({\mathcal{A}})$ . We let $\pi^{v}$ and $\pi^{\rho}$ denote the marginal item choice and reserve price policies, respectively. Recall that the seller garners revenue only when the item is sold to a bidder. At each $h \in [ H ]$ , her per-step expected revenue is then $$ R_{h}=\mathbb{E}_{\{z_{i h}\}_{i=1}^{N}}\left[\sum_{i=1}^{N}m_{i h}\mathbb{1}(m_{i h}\leq b_{i h})\right]\tag{1} $$ as we recall that $m_{i h}=\operatorname*{max}\{\rho_{i h},\operatorname*{max}_{j\neq i}b_{j h}\}$ and bidder i pays the seller $m_{i h}$ if and only if $b_{i h}\geq m_{i h}$ . The value function (V-function) of the seller’s revenue for any policy π and the action-value function (Q-function) is $Q_{h}^{\pi}:\mathcal{S}\times\mathcal{A}\mathbb{R}$ are then $$ V_{h}^{\pi}(x)=\mathbb{E}_{\pi}\left[\sum_{h^{\prime}=h}^{H}R_{h^{\prime}}(x_{h^{\prime}},a_{h^{\prime}})\mid x_{h}=x\right] $$ and $$ Q_{h}^{\pi}(x,a)=\mathbb{E}_{\pi}\left[\sum_{h^{\prime}=h}^{H}R_{h^{\prime}}(x_{h^{\prime}},a_{h^{\prime}})\mid x_{h}=x,a_{h}=a\right], $$ respectively. Since the bidder reward only depends on state x and the choice of item υ instead of reserve $\rho,$ we have a family of mappings from $\mathcal{S}\times\Upsilon$ to $\mathbb{R}_{\geq 0}^{N}$ that determines $\rho .$ Therefore, with a slight abuse of notation, we can rewrite our Q-function as $Q(x,a)=Q(x,(v,\rho(x,v)))$ , restricting the role of setting reserve prices using such mappings without loss of generality. From now on, we use $Q(x,v)$ to denote the Q-function for simplicity. For any function $f:{\mathcal{S}}\mathbb{R}$ , we define the transition operator $\mathcal{P}$ and the Bellman operator $\boldsymbol{B}$ as $$ (\mathcal{P}_{h}f)(x,a)=\mathbb{E}[f(x_{h+1})\mid x_{h}=x,a_{h}=a],(\mathcal{B}_{h}f)(x,a)=\mathbb{E}[R_{h}(x_{h},a_{h})]+(\mathbb{P}_{h}f)(x,a), $$ respectively. Finally, we let $\pi^{\star}$ denote the optimal policy when the bidders’ reward functions, the MDP’s underlying transition, and the market noise distribution are all known to the seller. We remark that when these parameters are known, second price auctions with personalized reserve prices are inherently incentive compatible and rational bidders will bid truthfully. Impatient Utility-Maximizing Bidders. We assume the bidders are equipped with some discount rate $\gamma\in(0,1)$ while the seller’s reward is not discounted. For the sake of simplicity, we assume $\gamma$ is common knowledge. Drutsa (2020) consider a scenario where $\gamma$ is unknown but with a strictly less than one upper bound. We highlight that it also works with our CLUB algorithm as long as we replace $\gamma$ with its upper bound. We can have regret bounds with the same order because we adopt more conservative estimators, and buyers won’t violate as much as the corresponding results of $\gamma$ . Then all results in our paper hold up to some changes of absolute constants. Rational bidder i’s utility at step h is given by $(r_{i h}(x_{h},v_{h})-m_{i h})\mathbb{1}(b_{i h}\geq m_{i h})$ , as we note that he only receives nonzero utility upon winning the auction. His objective is to maximize his discounted cumulative utility $$ \mathrm{Utility}_{i}=\sum_{k=1}^{K}\gamma^{k}\mathbb{E}_{\pi_{k}}\left[\sum_{h=1}^{H}(r_{i h}(x_{h}^{k},v_{h}^{k})-m_{i h}^{k})\mathbb{1}(b_{i h}^{k}\geq m_{i h}^{k})\mid x_{1}^{k}=x_{1}\right]. $$ Linear Markov Decision Process. We consider a Markov Reward Process $(\mathrm{M R P^{1}}$ , Bellman (1957); Puterman (2014)) with a state space ${\mathcal{S}}\subseteq\mathbb{R}^{K}$ for some $K\in\mathbb{N}$ . The MRP employs an initial distribution $p_{0}:B(S)[0,1]$ , where B denotes the Borel algebra. The dynamics of the $\mathrm{MRP}$ are characterized by a transition kernel $p:B({\mathcal{S}})\times{\mathcal{S}}[0,1]^{2}$ The $\mathrm{MRP}$ also adopts a measurable and bounded reward function $r:{\mathcal{S}}\mathbb{R}$ . At time step $t,$ suppose the agent is at state $S_{t}.$ . It transitions to the next state $S_{t+1}\sim p(\cdot|S_{t})$ following the transition kernel. At the same time, the environment emits a reward $R_{t+1}\doteq r(S_{t})$ to the agent for transitioning out of $S_{t}$ . Note that $(p,p_{0})$ defines a Markov chain $\{S_{t}\}$ . We further define a p-induced operator $P_{\pi}:{\mathcal{F}}{\mathcal{F}}$ , where ${\mathcal{F}}\doteq\{f:S\to\mathbb{R}^{n}\mid f$ is measurable and integrable}, as $(P_{\pi}f)(s)\doteq\int_{S}f(s^{\prime})p(\mathrm{d}s^{\prime}\mid s)$

The state-value function $v_{\pi}:S\mathbb{R}$ is defined as $\begin{array}{ r }{v_{\pi}(s)\doteq\mathbb{E}\bigl [\sum_{t=0}^{\infty}\gamma^{t}R_{t+1}|S_{0}=s\bigr]}\end{array}$ , where $\gamma\in [0,1)$ is a discount factor. The state-value function maps each state to the expected cumulative reward the agent gets starting from that state. We consider a linear function approximation of $v_{\pi}$ with a feature mapping $x:S\mathbb{R}^{d}$ and a weight vector $w\in\mathbb{R}^{d}$ . The function x maps each state $s\in{\mathcal{S}}$ to a d-dimensional real vector $x(s)$ . One simply takes $x(s)^{\top}$ w to compute the approximated state value for s. The goal is thus to adjust w such that $x(s)^{\top}w\approx v_{\pi}(s)$ for all $s\in{\mathcal{S}}$ . Linear TD updates the weight w iteratively as

$$
w_{t+1}=w_{t}+\alpha_{t}\Big(R_{t+1}+\gamma x(S_{t+1})^{\top}w_{t}-x(S_{t})^{\top}w_{t}\Big)x(S_{t}).\qquad(\text{Linear TD})
$$

where $\alpha_{t}$ is the learning rate and we recall that $\{S_{t}\}$ is a Markov chain evolving as $S_{t+1}\sim$ $p(\cdot|S_{t})$ and $S_{0}$ is sampled from an arbitrary initial distribution. The following assumptions are commonly made in analyzing linear TD (Tsitsiklis and Roy, 1996).

Assumption 2.1 The learning rates $\left\{\alpha_{t}\right\}$ is a decreasing sequence of positive real numbers such that $\begin{array}{ r }{\sum_{t=0}^{\infty}\alpha_{t}=\infty,\sum_{t=0}^{\infty}\alpha_{t}^{2}<\infty}\end{array}$ , and lim $\begin{array}{ r }{t\to\infty\left(\frac{1}{\alpha_{t+1}}-\frac{1}{\alpha_{t}}\right)<\infty}\end{array}$

Assumption 2.2 The Markov chain $\{S_{t}\}$ admits a well-defined and unique stationary distribution $\mu:B(S)\to [0,1]$ , such that $\textstyle\mu(Z)=\int_{S}p(Z\mid s)\mu(\mathrm{d}s)$ for all $Z\in B({\cal S})$ and $\mu(U)>0$ for all non-empty open sets $U \subseteq S$

The sequence $\textstyle\left\{{\frac{1}{(t+1)^{k}}}\right\}$ where $k\in(0.5,1]$ satisfies Assumption 2.1 as a valid example. In light of Assumption 2.2, we define an inner product $\langle\cdot,\cdot\rangle_{\mu}$ induced by $\mu$ as $\langle f,g\rangle_{\mu}\doteq$ $\begin{array}{ r }{\int_{S}\langle f(s),g(s)\rangle\mu(\mathrm{d}s)}\end{array}$ , where $f:S\mathbb{R}^{n}$ and $g:S\mathbb{R}^{n}$ are measurable functions. The inne product $\langle\cdot,\cdot\rangle_{\mu}$ further induces a semi-norm $\|f\|_{\mu}^{2}\doteq\langle f,f\rangle_{\mu}$

Assumption 2.3 The feature function and reward function are bounded, $i . e .$ sup ∥x(s)∥ < ∞, sup |r(s)| < ∞.

We use $L_{p}(S,\mu)$ to denote the set of functions defined on $s$ that are p-integrable with respect to $\mu .\mathrm{~A~}$ direct consequence of Assumption 2.3 is that $x\in L_{p}(S,\mu)$ for $p\in [1,\infty)$ because $\begin{array}{ r }{\big(\int_{S}\|x(s)\|^{p}\mu(\mathrm{d}s)\big)^{1/p}\leq\big((\operatorname*{sup}_{s\in S}\|x(s)\|)^{p}\int_{S}\mu(\mathrm{d}s)\big)^{1/p}=\operatorname*{sup}_{s\in S}\|x(s)\|<\infty .}\end{array}$

Assumption 2.4 Given any $f:{\mathcal{S}}\mathbb{R}^{n}$ and $f = 0 \ a . e$ . with respect to µ, it holds that $P_{\pi}f=0~a . e$ . with respect to $\mu$ as well.

In the rest of the paper, we use $\because_{\mathrm{a . e .}}\ d s^{\prime}$ to denote “a.e. with respect to $\mu^{\dag}$ for simplifying notations. Notably, Assumptions 2.2 - 2.4 trivially hold when S is finite and {S<sub>t</sub>} is irreducible.

Intuitively, when {S<sub>t</sub>} reaches the stationary distribution and the learning rate α is “small”, linear TD behaves like a deterministic algorithm as $w_{t+1}=w_{t}+\alpha_{t}(A w_{t}+b)$ , where

$$
\begin{array}{l}A\doteq\mathbb{E}_{S\sim\mu,S^{\prime}\sim p(\cdot|S)}\left[x(S)\big(\gamma x(S^{\prime})^{\top}-x(S)^{\top}\big)\right]\\ =\int_{\mathcal{S}}x(s)\left(\gamma\left(P_{\pi}x\right)(s)^{\top}-x(s)^{\top}\right)\mu(\mathrm{d}s)\in\mathbb{R}^{d\times d}\tag{1}\\ \end{array}
$$

$$
b\doteq\mathbb{E}_{S\sim\mu}[x(S)r(S)]=\int_{\mathcal{S}}x(s)r(s)\mu(\mathrm{d}s)\in\mathbb{R}^{d}.\tag{2}
$$

We can then further relate the stochastic and discrete iterative updates (Linear TD) with deterministic and continuous trajectories of the following ordinary diferential equation (ODE)

$$
\frac{\mathrm{d}w(t)}{\mathrm{d}t}=A w(t)+b,\tag{3}
$$

which is known as the ODE method in stochastic approximation (Benveniste et al., 1990; Kushner and Yin, 2003; Borkar, 2009; Borkar et al., 2025; Liu et al., 2025a).

Lemma 2 Let Assumptions 2.2 & 2.3 hold. Then A is negative semi-definite.

As previously discussed, linear TD is approximately a stochastic discretization of ODE (3). The fixed points of linear TD, commonly referred to as TD fixed points (Tsitsiklis and Roy, 1996; Sutton and Barto, 2018), are linked to the equilibria of this ODE. We hence consider the linear system

$$
A w+b=0,\tag{4}
$$

Without assuming linear independence, matrix A is merely negative semi-definite (Lemma 2), so (4) can potentially adopt infinitely many solutions. In light of this, we refer to all solutions to the linear system as TD fixed points. Namely, we define $\mathcal{W}_{*}\doteq\{w_{*}|A w_{*}+b=0\}$ and refer to W as the set of TD fixed points. We shall give afirmative answers to all the questions above in the rest of the paper. We use

context:
Let $X_{1},\ldots,X_{n}$ be n independent and identically distributed random vectors from an unknown distribution with probability density function $f_{0}$ on $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb{R}^{d}$ . The task is to estimate $f_{0}$ nonparametrically based on the observed data $\{X_{i}\}_{i=1}^{n}$

Our proposed data-augmented nonparametric noise contrastive density estimation is to first convert the unsupervised density estimation problem into a supervised task of classification, building on the ideas from Hastie et al. (2009) and Gutmann and Hyv¨arinen (2012). The key diference is that we estimate a mixture density $f_{\mathcal{M}}$ by classification, instead of estimating the target density $f_{0}$ directly. To achieve this, we need to introduce external data points sampled from some known density $f_{\mathcal{R}}$ . Specifically, our proposed procedure consists of three main steps:

Let $f_{\mathcal{R}}$ be a known density function on $\Omega_{;}$ termed as the reference density. We generate a random sample $\{\tilde{Z}_{1},\dots,\tilde{Z}_{\rho n}\}$ from the reference density $f_{\mathcal{R}}$ , independent of the observed data $\{X_{i}\}_{i=1}^{n}$ , where $\rho$ is a positive constant such that $\rho n\in\mathbb{Z}_{+}$ and $\mathbb{Z}_{+}$ denotes the set of positive integers. Given the observed data $\{X_{i}\}_{i=1}^{n}\sim f_{0}$ and the reference data $\{\tilde{Z}_{i}\}_{i=1}^{\rho n}\sim$ $f_{\mathcal{R}}$ , we term $\{Y_{i}\}_{i=1}^{n+\rho n}: -\{X_{i}\}_{i=1}^{n}\cup\{\tilde{Z}_{i}\}_{i=1}^{\rho n}$ as the augmented data.

We assign a binary label ${\tilde{C}}_{i}$ to each $Y_{i}$ according to whether it is the observed data. That is, we assign $\tilde{C}_{i}=1\mathrm{if}Y_{i}\in\{X_{j}\}_{j=1}^{n}$ and $\tilde{C}_{i}=0\mathrm{if}Y_{i}\in\{\tilde{Z}_{j}\}_{j=1}^{\rho n}$ . Then, the conditional densities of $Y$ are

$$
f(y\mid\tilde{C}=1)=f_{0}(y),\quad f(y\mid\tilde{C}=0)=f_{\mathcal{R}}(y).
$$

Note that the probability mass of label $\tilde{C}$ is $\operatorname*{Pr}(\tilde{C}=1)=1/(1+\rho)$ and $\mathrm{Pr}(\tilde{C}=0)=$ $\rho/(1+\rho)$ . Then, the marginal density of the augmented data $Y$ is

$$
\begin{array}{l}f(y)=f(y\mid\tilde{C}=1)\mathrm{Pr}(\tilde{C}=1)+f(y\mid\tilde{C}=0)\mathrm{Pr}(\tilde{C}=0)\\ =\frac{1}{1+\rho}f_{0}(y)+\frac{\rho}{1+\rho}f_{\mathcal{R}}(y): -f_{\mathcal{M}}(y).\tag{1}\\ \end{array}
$$

Here $f_{\mathcal{M}}$ is referred to as the mixture density. It can be easily derived from (1) that $f_{0}=(1+\rho)f_{\mathcal{M}}-\rho f_{\mathcal{R}}$ . We can obtain an estimator for $f_{0}$ once the estimator for the mixture density $f_{\mathcal{M}}$ is available.

Step 2. Estimating the mixture density $f_{\mathcal{M}}$ with a noise contrastive estimation.

We generate an additional set of reference data $\{Z_{i}\}_{i=1}^{\nu(n+\rho n)}$ from $f_{\mathcal{R}}$ independent of $\{\tilde{Z}_{i}\}_{i=1}^{\rho n}$ , termed as the contrastive noise. Here ν is the ratio of sample sizes between the contrastive noise and the augmented data. We let $\nu\in\mathbb{Z}_{+}$ for convenience. Henceforth, we write the union of the augmented data and the contrastive noise as $S=\{Y_{1},\ldots,Y_{n+\rho n}\}$ $Z_{1},\dots,Z_{\nu(n+\rho n)}\}$ , the sample used for density estimation.

Similar to Step 1, we rewrite S as $\{U_{t}\}_{t=1}^{(1+\nu)(n+\rho n)}$ and assign a binary label $C_{t}$ to each $U_{t}$ according to whether it is the augmented data. That is, we assign $C_{t}=1\mathrm{~i f~}U_{t}\in\{Y_{i}\}_{i=1}^{n+\rho n}$ 2 and $C_{t}=0{\mathrm{~i f~}}U_{t}\in\{Z_{i}\}_{i=1}^{\nu(n+\rho n)}$ . Then, the conditional densities of U are:

$$
f(u\mid C=1)=f_{\mathcal{M}}(u),\quad f(u\mid C=0)=f_{\mathcal{R}}(u).
$$

The prior marginal probability mass of label C in the combined data S is $\operatorname*{Pr}(C=1)=$ $1/(1{+}\nu)$ and $\operatorname*{Pr}(C=0)=\nu/(1{+}\nu)$ . Then, by the Bayes’ formula, the posterior probabilities for the labels are

$$
\operatorname*{Pr}(C=1\mid u)=\frac{f_{\mathcal{M}}(u)}{f_{\mathcal{M}}(u)+\nu f_{\mathcal{R}}(u)},\quad\operatorname*{Pr}(C=0\mid u)=\frac{\nu f_{\mathcal{R}}(u)}{f_{\mathcal{M}}(u)+\nu f_{\mathcal{R}}(u)}.
$$

Then, the log-likelihood of $f$ for the sample $S$ is

$$
\begin{array}{l}\ell(f;S)=\sum_{t=1}^{(1+\nu)(n+\rho n)}\left\{C_{t}\log\Pr(C_{t}=1\mid U_{t};f)+(1-C_{t})\log\Pr(C_{t}=0\mid U_{t};f)\right\}\\ =\sum_{i=1}^{n+\rho n}\log\Pr(C_{i}=1\mid Y_{i};f)+\sum_{i=1}^{\nu(n+\rho n)}\log\Pr(C_{i}=0\mid Z_{i};f),\\ \end{array}
$$

where $\operatorname*{Pr}(C=1\mid u;f): -f(u)/\{f(u)+\nu f_{\mathcal{R}}(u)\}$ and $\operatorname*{Pr}(C=0\mid u;f): -\nu f_{\mathcal{R}}(u)/\{f(u)+$ $\nu f_{\mathcal{R}}(u)\}$ . Intuitively, an estimator for $f_{\mathcal{M}}$ can be obtained by maximizing the log-likelihood function $\ell(f;S)$ over $f\in\mathcal{F}_{n}$ , a prespecified function class. Equivalently, we minimize

$$
\begin{array}{l}\hat{R}_{S}(f): - -\frac{1}{(1+\rho)n}\left\{\sum_{i=1}^{(1+\rho)n}\log\Pr\left(C_{i}=1\mid Y_{i};f\right)+\sum_{i=1}^{\nu(1+\rho)n}\log\Pr\left(C_{i}=0\mid Z_{i};f\right)\right\}\\ = -\frac{1}{(1+\rho)n}\Bigl\{\sum_{i=1}^{(1+\rho)n}\log\frac{f(Y_{i})}{f(Y_{i})+\nu f_{\mathcal{R}}(Y_{i})}+\sum_{i=1}^{\nu(1+\rho)n}\log\frac{\nu f_{\mathcal{R}}(Z_{i})}{f(Z_{i})+\nu f_{\mathcal{R}}(Z_{i})}\Bigr\},\\ \end{array}
$$

which equals to $-\ell(f;S)/\{(1+\rho)n\}$ . We refer to $\hat{R}_{S}(f)$ as the empirical noise contrastive risk given sample S, which is also written as $\hat{R}(f)$ to suppress its dependence on sample S when there is no confusion.

As a result, we define the estimator for the mixture density as the empirical risk minimizer:

$$
\hat{f}_{\mathcal{M}}\in\underset{f\in\mathcal{F}_{n}}{\arg\min}\hat{R}(f).\tag{3}
$$

Step 3. Deriving the estimator for the target density $f_{0}$ .

In view of (1) and the estimator $\hat{f}_{\mathcal{M}}$ defined in (3), our proposed estimator for $f_{0}$ is given by

$$
\tilde{f}_{n}=(1+\rho)\hat{f}_{\mathcal{M}}-\rho f_{\mathcal{R}},\tag{4}
$$

which is referred to as data-augmented nonparametric noise contrastive estimation.

Remark 1 For any $f\in\mathcal{F}_{n}$ , the population-level noise contrastive risk corresponding to (2) is

$$
\begin{array}{l}R(f)= -\bigl\{\mathbb{E}_{Y\sim f_{\mathcal{M}}}\log P r(C=1\mid Y;f)+\nu\mathbb{E}_{Z\sim f_{\mathcal{R}}}\log P r(C=0\mid Z;f)\bigr\}\\ = -\Bigl\{\mathbb{E}_{Y\sim f_{\mathcal{M}}}\log\frac{f(Y)}{f(Y)+\nu f_{\mathcal{R}}(Y)}+\nu\mathbb{E}_{Z\sim f_{\mathcal{R}}}\log\frac{\nu f_{\mathcal{R}}(Z)}{f(Z)+\nu f_{\mathcal{R}}(Z)}\Bigr\}.\\ \end{array}
$$

We now introduce the class of neural networks used for density function approximation. In recent years, advancements on the approximation theory of the feedforward neural networks with Rectified Linear Unit (ReLU) activation function are reported by Yarotsky (2017), Chen et al. (2019), Shen et al. (2020), Farrell et al. (2021), and Lu et al. (2021). In this paper, we consider multi-layer perceptron, an important and widely-used subclass of feedforward neural networks. The following expression characterizes the architecture of multi-layer perceptron:

$$
f_{\theta}(x)=\mathcal{L}_{\mathcal{D}}\circ\pmb{\sigma}\circ\mathcal{L}_{\mathcal{D}-1}\circ\pmb{\sigma}\circ\dots\circ\mathcal{L}_{1}\circ\pmb{\sigma}\circ\mathcal{L}_{0}(x),x\in\mathbb{R}^{p_{0}},
$$

where $\sigma$ is the component-wise version of ReLU activation function $\sigma(x)=\operatorname*{max}\{0,x\}$ , and $\mathcal{L}_{i}(x)=W_{i}x+b_{i},i=0,\ldots,D$ are linear transformations with weight matrices $W_{i}\in\mathbb{R}^{p_{i+1}\times p_{i}}$ and bias vectors $b_{i}~\in~\mathbb{R}^{p_{i+1}}$ . Here, D is the depth of the neural network, that is, the number of hidden layers. The (D + 2)-tuple $(p_{0},\ldots,p_{\mathcal{D}+1})$ denotes the number of neurons in each layer, and specifically, $p_{0}=d,p_{D+1}=1$ . The width of the network is defined as $\mathcal{W}=\operatorname*{max}\{p_{1},...,p_{D}\}$ . The total number of parameters $\begin{array}{ r }{S=\sum_{i=0}^{\mathcal{D}}p_{i+1}(p_{i}+1)}\end{array}$ is referred to as the size of the network. We denote the collection of networks $f_{\theta}$ described above as $\mathcal{N N}(\mathcal{D},\mathcal{W},\mathcal{S})$ . Note that the architecture parameters of the network class satisfies max $\{\mathcal{W},\mathcal{D}\}\le\mathcal{S}\le\mathcal{W}(d+1)+(\mathcal{W}^{2}+\mathcal{W})(\mathcal{D}-1)+\mathcal{W}+1=O(\mathcal{W}^{2}\mathcal{D})$

We take ${\mathcal{F}}_{n}$ to be the following class of neural networks:

$$
\mathcal{F}(\mathcal{D},\mathcal{W},\mathcal{S},\gamma,\Gamma): -\{f_{\theta}\in\mathcal{N N}(\mathcal{D},\mathcal{W},\mathcal{S}):\gamma\leq f_{\theta}\leq\Gamma\},
$$

for some positive constants $\gamma,\Gamma$ . Note that the architecture parameters $\mathcal{D},\mathcal{W}_{:}$ , and $\boldsymbol{\mathcal{S}}$ can depend on n, and we suppress the subscript n for simplicity. Furthermore, the output range constraint $\gamma\leq f_{\theta}\leq\Gamma$ can be satisfied by adding an additional layer $\phi(x)=\sigma(x-\gamma)-\sigma(x-$ $\Gamma)+\gamma$ at the end of the network. Then, the network depth will increase by 1 accordingly. Such adjustment will only afect the constant prefactors in our non-asymptotic error bounds and will not afect the convergence rate, and thus the details are omitted for simplicity.

In this section, we provide a theoretical analysis of the proposed data-augmented nonparametric noise contrastive estimator. We will study the convergence properties of the mixture density estimator $\hat{f}_{\mathcal{M}}$ , which can imply the convergence properties of $\tilde{f_{n}}$ , the estimator for the target density $f_{0}$

To evaluate the quality of an estimator $\hat{f}$ for a target function $f_{*},$ we use the expected $L_{2}.$ -risk $\mathbb{E}\Vert\hat{f}-f_{*}\Vert_{L_{2}(f_{*})}^{2}$ , where the expectation is taken with respect to training sample and

$$
\|f-f_{*}\|_{L_{2}(f_{*})}^{2}: -\mathbb{E}_{X\sim f_{*}}|f(X)-f_{*}(X)|^{2}=\int_{\Omega}|f(x)-f_{*}(x)|^{2}f_{*}(x)d x.
$$

The main procedure for the error analysis is to decompose the expected $L_{\mathrm{{2^{-}}}}\mathrm{risk}$ of $\hat{f}_{\mathcal{M}}$ into stochastic error and approximation error, and bound them separately. Thereafter, an upper bound of $\mathbb{E}_{S}\Vert\tilde{f}_{n}-f_{0}\Vert_{L_{2}(f_{0})}^{2}$ can be established based on that of $\mathbb{E}_{S}\Vert\hat{f}_{\mathcal{M}}-f_{\mathcal{M}}\Vert_{L_{2}(f_{\mathcal{M}})}^{2}$

We first present some conditions imposed on the target density $f_{0}$ and reference density $f_{\mathcal{R}}$ . We take the domain Ω of $f_{0}$ and $f_{\mathcal{R}}$ to be the d-dimensional hypercube $[0,1]^{d}$ for simplicity. Extension to accommodate density with unbounded domain will be discussed in Section 3.5.

Assumption 3 The reference density $f_{\mathcal{R}}$ is positive and continuous on $[0,1]^{d}$ , and there exists a positive constant $L_{0}$ such that $f_{0}\leq L_{0}$

Lemma 4 For any $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb{R}^{d}$ , the data-augmented nonparametric noise contrastive estimator ${\tilde{f}}_{n}$ defined in $(4)$ satisfies

$$
\mathbb{E}_{S}\|\tilde{f}_{n}-f_{0}\|_{L_{2}(f_{0})}^{2}\leq(1+\rho)^{3}\mathbb{E}_{S}\|\hat{f}_{\mathcal{M}}-f_{\mathcal{M}}\|_{L_{2}(f_{\mathcal{M}})}^{2},
$$

where $S$ is the training sample.

Lemma 5 (Calibration) Under Assumption 3, there exist positive constants $c_{1}$ and $c_{2}$ such that, for all $f\in\mathcal{F}_{n}$ 2

$$
c_{1}\|f-f_{\mathcal{M}}\|_{L_{2}(f_{\mathcal{M}})}^{2}\leq R(f)-R(f_{\mathcal{M}})\leq c_{2}\|f-f_{\mathcal{M}}\|_{L_{2}(f_{\mathcal{M}})}^{2}.\tag{5}
$$

Moreover, $c_{1}$ and $c_{2}$ only depend on $\nu,\rho,L_{0},\gamma,\Gamma$ , and $f_{\mathcal{R}}$ .

Lemma 6 (Error decomposition) Under Assumption 3, we have

$$
\mathbb{E}_{S}\|\hat{f}_{\mathcal{M}}-f_{\mathcal{M}}\|_{L_{2}(f_{\mathcal{M}})}^{2}\leq\frac{1}{c_{1}}\mathbb{E}_{S}[R(\hat{f}_{\mathcal{M}})-\hat{R}(\hat{f}_{\mathcal{M}})]+\frac{c_{2}}{c_{1}}\inf_{f\in\mathcal{F}_{n}}\|f-f_{\mathcal{M}}\|_{L_{2}(f_{\mathcal{M}})}^{2},\tag{6}
$$

where $c_{1},c_{2}$ are the same constants as in Lemma ${ 5 . }$

The stochastic error of the density estimator $\hat{f}_{\mathcal{M}}$ will be controlled by the complexity measures of the neural network class ${\mathcal{F}}_{n}$ . The definitions of uniform covering number and pseudo-dimension are given in Appendix B.

Lemma 7 (Stochastic error) Let $\mathcal{F}_{n}=\mathcal{F}(\mathcal{D},\mathcal{W},\mathcal{S},\gamma,\Gamma)$ be the class of feedforward neural networks activated by continuous piecewise linear activation function with finitely many inflection points. Let $\begin{array}{ r }{\hat{f}_{\mathcal{M}}\in\arg\operatorname*{min}_{f\in\mathcal{F}_{n}}\hat{R}(f)}\end{array}$ be the empirical risk minimizer over $\mathcal{F}_{n}$ Suppose that Assumption 3 holds. Then $f o r n\ge P d i m(\mathcal{F}_{n})/\{(1+\nu)(1+\rho)\}$

$$
\mathbb{E}_{S}[R(\hat{f}_{\mathcal{M}})-\hat{R}(\hat{f}_{\mathcal{M}})]\leq c_{3}\mathcal{S D}\log\mathcal{S}\frac{\log n}{n},
$$

where $c_{3}$ is a constant depending only on $\nu,\rho,L_{0},\gamma,\Gamma$ , and $f_{\mathcal{R}}$ .

To bound the approximation error inf ${\ L}_{f\in\mathcal{F}_{n}}\parallel f-f_{\mathcal{M}}\parallel_{L_{2}(f_{\mathcal{M}})}^{2};$ , we impose some smoothness conditions on the target density $f_{0}$ and the reference density $f_{\mathcal{R}}$ . In this paper, we assume that both $f_{0}$ and $f_{\mathcal{R}}$ belong to some H¨older class (Definition 28, Appendix B).

Assumption 8 (H¨older smoothness) The densities $f_{0},f_{\mathcal{R}}\in\mathcal{H}^{\beta}([0,1]^{d},B_{0})$ for a given $\beta > 0$ and some finite constant $B_{0}>0$

The assumption on $f_{\mathcal{R}}$ in Assumption 8 is not restrictive, as many popular distributions satisfy this assumption, such as the uniform distribution on $[0,1]^{d}$ . Notably, Assumption 8 implies that the mixture density $f_{\mathcal{M}}\in\mathcal{H}^{\beta}([0,1]^{d},B_{0})$

In this subsection, we establish non-asymptotic error bounds for our proposed density estimator under the total variation distance. Specifically, we consider the expected total variation distance $\mathbb{E}_{S}\mathrm{TV}(\tilde{f}_{n},f_{0})$ between our proposed estimator ${\tilde{f}}_{n}$ and the target density $f_{0}$ , where

$$
\mathrm{TV}(f,f_{*})=\frac{1}{2}\int_{\Omega}|f(x)-f_{*}(x)|d x.
$$

In this subsection, we extend our method to handle densities with unbounded supports. Specifically, we let the target density $f_{0}$ and the reference density $f_{\mathcal{R}}$ be functions on $\Omega=\mathbb{R}^{d}$ , the entire d-dimensional Euclidean space. To tackle the challenges associated with unbounded support, we consider a truncated version of noise contrastive risk.

We define the truncated domain $\Omega_{t}$ as a d-dimensional hypercube $[-t,t]^{d}$ , where t is a positive constant (the truncation level) and can depend on the sample size n. Then, the truncated noise contrastive risk is defined as

$$
R_{t}(f)= -\Big\{\mathbb{E}_{Y\sim f_{\mathcal{M}}}\Big [\log\frac{f(Y)}{f(Y)+\nu f_{\mathcal{R}}(Y)}\mathbb{1}_{\Omega_{t}}(Y)\Big]+\nu\mathbb{E}_{Z\sim f_{\mathcal{R}}}\Big [\log\frac{\nu f_{\mathcal{R}}(Z)}{f(Z)+\nu f_{\mathcal{R}}(Z)}\mathbb{1}_{\Omega_{t}}(Z)\Big]\Big\},
$$

where $\mathbb{1}_{A}$ denotes the indicator function on a set $A,$ , i.e $\mathbb{1}_{A}$ is equal to 1 on A and 0 outside A. Given the training sample ${\cal S}=\{Y_{1},\dots,Y_{n+\rho n},Z_{1},\dots,Z_{\nu(n+\rho n)}\}$ , the truncated empirical risk is defined by replacing the expectations in $R_{t}$ by sample averages:

$$
\hat{R}_{t}(f)= -\frac{1}{(1+\rho)n}\left\{\sum_{i=1}^{(1+\rho)n}\log\frac{f(Y_{i})}{f(Y_{i})+\nu f_{\mathcal{R}}(Y_{i})}\mathbb{1}_{\Omega_{t}}(Y_{i})+\sum_{i=1}^{\nu(1+\rho)n}\log\frac{\nu f_{\mathcal{R}}(Z_{i})}{f(Z_{i})+\nu f_{\mathcal{R}}(Z_{i})}\mathbb{1}_{\Omega_{t}}(Z_{i})\right\}.
$$

We define the estimator for the mixture density $f_{\mathcal{M}}$ as the minimizer of the truncated empirical risk, that is, $\begin{array}{ r }{\check{f}_{\mathcal{M}}\in\arg\operatorname*{min}_{f\in\mathcal{F}_{n}}\hat{R}_{t}(f)}\end{array}$ . Then, similar to (4), the resulting estimator for the target density $f_{0}$ is given by

$$
\bar{f}_{n}=(1+\rho)\check{f}_{\mathcal{M}}-\rho f_{\mathcal{R}}.\tag{9}
$$

Lemma 19 (Approximation error) Suppose that Assumptions 3 and 8 hold, and $\gamma \leq$ $\rho l/(1+\rho),\Gamma\geq L_{0}\vee L$ where l, L are positive constants such that $l\le f_{\mathcal{R}}\le L$ . Then for any $P,Q\in\mathbb{Z}_{+}$ , there exists a function $f_{*}\in\mathcal{F}_{n}=\mathcal{F}(\mathcal{D},\mathcal{W},\mathcal{S},\gamma,\Gamma)$ with width $\mathcal{W}=$ $38(\lfloor\beta\rfloor+1)^{2}d^{\lfloor\beta\rfloor+1}P\lceil\log_{2}(8P)\rceil$ and depth $\mathcal{D}=21(\lfloor\beta\rfloor+1)^{2}Q\lceil\log_{2}(8Q)\rceil$ such that

$$
\|f_{*}-f_{\mathcal{M}}\|_{L_{2}(f_{\mathcal{M}})}^{2}\leq 324B_{0}^{2}(\lfloor\beta\rfloor+1)^{4}d^{2\lfloor\beta\rfloor+\beta\vee 1}(PQ)^{-4\beta/d}.

In this subsection, we present an error analysis of our estimator for estimating densities with unbounded support, with a focus on the diferences between the theoretical analysis in this setting and the bounded case. First, a positive and continuous reference density supported on a compact domain is lower bounded, while this property does not hold for unbounded domains. Second, conventional neural network approximation theory for approximating function with compact domain and is not directly applicable to the unbounded support case. To address the complications associated with unbounded support, we will leverage the truncation technique and assume that the target distribution has a sub-exponentially decaying tail.

In the following, we denote the target distribution (probability measure) as $\mu_{0};$ that is, $\mu_{0}(d x)=f_{0}(x)d x$ . We make the following assumptions on the target density $f_{0}$ and the reference density $f_{\mathcal{R}}{}^{\mathrm{~}}$

Assumption 20 The target distribution $\mu_{0}$ is sub-exponential in the sense that

$$
\mu_{0}(\mathbb{R}^{d}\setminus [-x,x]^{d})\leq C d\exp(-a x),\forall x>0,\tag{22}
$$

for some positive constants a and $C$ . Furthermore, there exist positive constants $L_{0}$ and $L_{\mathcal{R}}$ such that $f_{0}\leq L_{0}$ and $0<f_{\mathcal{R}}\le L_{\mathcal{R}}$ on $\mathbb{R}^{d}$ . In addition, there exists a positive number $l_{\mathcal{R}}$ that depends on t and $d,$ such that $f_{\mathcal{R}}\geq l_{\mathcal{R}}$ on $\Omega_{t}$

Since the integral of $f_{\mathcal{R}}$ over $\Omega_{t}$ is upper bounded by 1, it follows that $l_{\mathcal{R}}\leq(2 t)^{-d}$ . Therefore, $l_{\mathcal{R}}$ depends on both t and d. We also select the lower bound of the neural network, $\gamma,$ to be a function of t and $d .$ In our theoretical results, we establish the dependence of the error bounds on $l_{\mathcal{R}}$ and $\gamma$ explicitly.

Suppose the entire dataset $\mathbf{D}=(Y_{i})_{i\in [N]}$ consists of independent (not necessarily identically distributed) observations $Y_{1},\dots,Y_{N}$ . The dataset is partitioned into $T$ mini-batches of equal size $n,$ so that the total sample size up to the t-th mini-batch is given by $N_{t}=n t$ for all $t\in\{0,1,2,\ldots,T\}$ . The t-th mini-batch and the collection of all samples up to the t-th mini-batch are denoted as $$ \mathbf{D}_{t}=(Y_{N_{t-1}+1},Y_{N_{t-1}+2},...,Y_{N_{t}}),\quad \text{and}\quad\mathbf{D}_{1:t}=(\mathbf{D}_{1},\mathbf{D}_{2},...,\mathbf{D}_{t})=(Y_{i})_{i\in [N_{t}]}. $$ For $i \in [ N ]$ , let $p_{\theta,i}(\cdot)$ be the probability density function for $Y_{i}$ parametrized by $\theta \in$ $\Theta\subset\mathbb{R}^{p}$ , and let $\ell_{\theta,i}(y)=\log p_{\theta,i}(y)$ be the log density. For $t \in [ T ]$ ], let $$ L_{t}(\theta)=L_{t}(\theta;\mathbf{D}_{t})=\sum_{i=N_{t-1}+1}^{N_{t}}\ell_{\theta,i}(Y_{i}). $$ Let $\mathbb{P}_{\theta}^{(N)}$ denote the joint probability measure corresponding to the product density function $(y_{1},y_{2},...,y_{N})\mapsto\prod_{i=1}^{N}p_{\theta,i}(y_{i})$ . We assume that the model is well-specified; that is, D is generated from $\mathbb{P}_{\theta_{0}}^{(N)}$ for some true parameter $\theta_{0}\in\Theta$ . Let $\mathbb{P}_{0,t}(\cdot)$ denote the joint probability measure corresponding to the product density $$ (y_{N_{t-1}+1},y_{N_{t-1}+2},\dots,y_{N_{t}})\mapsto\prod_{i=N_{t-1}+1}^{N_{t}}p_{\theta_{0},i}(y_{i}), $$ and let $\mathbb{E}_{t}$ denote the expectation under $\mathbb{P}_{0,t}$ . Since the model is assumed to be well-specified, we have $\theta_{0}=\operatorname{argmax}_{\theta\in\Theta}\mathbb{E}_{t}L_{t}(\theta)$ for all $t \in [ T ]$ Now, we introduce our online learning procedure. Let Q be the collection of all Gaussian measures with nonsingular covariance matrices. Given an initial prior $\Pi_{0}$ and the log-likelihood $L_{t}(\theta)$ for the t-th mini-batch data $\mathbf{D}_{t}.$ , we iteratively define the posterior distribution $\widetilde{\Pi}_{t}(\cdot\mid\mathbf{D}_{t})$ and the corresponding variational approximation $\Pi_{t}(\cdot)$ as described in (1) and (2). We denote by $\widetilde{\pi}_{t}(\cdot\mid\mathbf{D}_{t})$ and $\pi_{t}(\cdot)$ the density functions of $\widetilde{\Pi}_{t}(\cdot\mid\mathbf{D}_{t})$ and $\Pi_{t}(\cdot)$ respectively. In particular, we consider a normal distribution $\mathcal{N}(\mu_{0},\Omega_{0}^{-1})$ as the initial prior $\Pi_{0}$ • where $\mu_{0}\in\mathbb{R}^{p}$ and $\Omega_{0}\in{S}_{+ +}^{p}$ . For such a diferentiable $L_{t}(\cdot)$ , we introduce some notations used for posterior analysis. For $t \in [ T ]$ and $\theta \in \Theta$ , define $$ \mathbf{F}_{t,\theta}= -\nabla^{2}L_{t}(\theta)\in\mathbb{R}^{p\times p},\quad\widetilde{\mathbf{F}}_{t,\theta}=\boldsymbol{\Omega}_{t-1}+\mathbf{F}_{t,\theta},\tag{5} $$ where $\Omega_{t-1}$ is defined in (4). For $\theta_{\mathrm{c}}\in\mathbb{R}^{p},r\geq 0$ and $\mathbf{F}\in S_{+ +}^{p}$ , let $$ \Theta\left(\theta_{\mathrm{c}},\mathbf{F},r\right)=\left\{\theta\in\Theta:\left\|\mathbf{F}^{1/2}\left(\theta-\theta_{\mathrm{c}}\right)\right\|_{2}\leq r\right\}\tag{6} $$ denote the local elliptical vicinity of $\theta_{\mathrm{c}}$ . For notational simplicity, let $$ \Theta(\mathbf{F},r)=\Theta(0,\mathbf{F},r).\tag{7} $$ Given the prior distribution $\Pi_{t-1}$ , which reflects the information in $\mathbf{D}_{1:t-1}$ , we define the penalized log-likelihood function as $$ \widetilde{L}_{t}(\theta)=L_{t}(\theta)-\frac{1}{2}\left\|\boldsymbol{\Omega}_{t-1}^{1/2}\left(\theta-\mu_{t-1}\right)\right\|_{2}^{2}.\tag{8} $$ For each $t \in [ T ]$ , the penalized maximum likelihood estimator (pMLE) and its population version are defined as $$ \widehat{\theta}_{t}=\underset{\theta\in\Theta}{\operatorname{argmax}}\widetilde{L}_{t}(\theta),\quad\theta_{t}^{*}=\underset{\theta\in\Theta}{\operatorname{argmax}}\mathbb{E}_{t}\widetilde{L}_{t}(\theta).\tag{9} $$ Now, we formalize the notion of smoothness. Let $f:\Theta\to\mathbb{R}$ be a four-times diferentiable function. For some $\mathbf{F}\in S_{+ +}^{p}$ and $\tau_{3},r\geq 0$ , we say that $f$ satisfies the third order smoothness at $\theta \in \Theta$ with parameters $(\tau_{3},\mathbf{F},r)$ if $$ \sup_{u\in\Theta(\mathbf{F},r)}\sup_{z\in\mathbb{R}^{p}}\frac{\left|\langle\nabla^{3}f(\theta+u),z^{\otimes 3}\rangle\right|}{\left\|\mathbf{F}^{1/2}z\right\|_{2}^{3}}\leq\tau_{3}.\tag{10} $$ In this section, we demonstrate that the posterior distribution $\widetilde{\Pi}_{t}\left(\cdot\mid\mathbf{D}_{t}\right)$ is well approximated by its variational approximation $\Pi_{t}$ . Before establishing the precise relation between $\Pi_{t}$ and $\widetilde{\Pi}_{t}\left(\cdot\mid\mathbf{D}_{t}\right)$ , we first show that the posterior can be accurately approximated by its Laplace approximation, defined as $$ \Pi_{t}^{\mathsf{LA}}=\mathcal{N}\left(\widehat{\theta}_{t},\widetilde{\mathbf{F}}_{t,\widehat{\theta}_{t}}^{-1}\right),\quad\forall t\in [T], $$ which admits a density function $\pi_{t}^{\tt L A}(\cdot)$ . Although our primary focus is on $\Pi_{t}$ rather than $\Pi_{t}^{\mathtt{LA}}$ , understanding the concentration behavior of the pair $(\widehat{\theta}_{t},\widetilde{\mathbf{F}}_{t,\widehat{\theta}_{t}})$ allows us to facilitate the theoretical analysis needed to establish $\Pi_{T}\approx\Pi(\cdot\mid\mathbf{D})$ . We will revisit this issue in Section 8. Our main results and the corresponding proofs in this section are largely inspired by those in Spokoiny (2023). Notably, for the total variation (TV) metric, we refine the dimension dependency of Theorem 2.4 in Spokoiny (2023) by leveraging advanced analysis in Spokoiny (2024). Moreover, for the KL divergence, we significantly improve the convergence rate presented in Theorem 2.6 of Spokoiny (2023); see the discussion following Theorem 3. Since the variational posterior $\Pi_{t}$ minimizes the KL divergence, obtaining a sharp upper bound for the KL divergence between $\Pi_{t}^{\mathtt{LA}}$ and $\widetilde{\Pi}_{t}(\cdot\mathrm{~\bf~|~D}_{t})$ is a crucial step in bounding $K(\Pi_{t};\widetilde{\Pi}_{t}(\cdot{|\textbf{ D }_{t})})$ ). A detailed proof of this section is provided in Appendix B, where we present self-contained non-asymptotic proofs adapted to the online learning framework. As discussed in Section 2.3, to accurately approximate $\widetilde{\Pi}_{t}(\cdot\mathrm{~\bf~|~}\mathbf{D}_{t})$ , we adopt selfconcordance-type smoothness conditions. To this end, we impose the following assumption: (A0) For every $t \in [ T ]$ , assume that the map $\theta\mapsto L_{t}(\theta)$ is concave on $\Theta$ and at least four times continuously diferentiable with probability 1. For the remainder of this paper, every event is treated as the intersection with the event under which assumption (A0) holds, without further explicit restatement. Let $$ \begin{array}{l}r_{\mathrm{LA}}=2\sqrt{p}+\sqrt{2\log N}\\ \widehat{\tau}_{3,t}=\inf\left\{\tau\in\mathbb{R}_{+}:\sup_{u\in\Theta\left(\widetilde{\mathbf{F}}_{t,\widehat{\theta}_{t}},4 r_{\mathrm{LA}}\right)}\sup_{z\in\mathbb{R}^{p}}\frac{\left|\langle\nabla^{3}\widetilde{L}_{t}\left(\widehat{\theta}_{t}+u\right),z^{\otimes 3}\rangle\right|}{\left\|\widetilde{\mathbf{F}}_{t,\widehat{\theta}_{t}}^{1/2}z\right\|_{2}^{3}}\leq\tau\right\},\tag{19}\\ \end{array} $$ $$ \widehat{\tau}_{4,t} = \inf \left\{\tau \in \mathbb{R}_{+}:\sup_{u\in \Theta (\widetilde{\mathbf{F}}_{t,\widehat{\theta}_{t}},4r_{\mathrm{LA}})}\sup_{z\in \mathbb{R}^{p}}\frac{\left|\langle\nabla^{4}\widetilde{L}_{t}(\widehat{\theta}_{t} + u),z^{\otimes 4}\rangle\right|}{\left\| \widetilde{\mathbf{F}}_{t,\widehat{\theta}_{t}}^{1 / 2}z\right\|_{2}^{4}}\leq \tau \right\}. $$ Then, with probability 1, $\widetilde L_{t}(\cdot)$ satisfies the third and fourth order smoothness at $\widehat{\theta}_{t}$ with parameters $(\widehat{\tau}_{3,t},\widetilde{\mathbf{F}}_{t,\widehat{\theta}_{t}},4r_{\mathrm{LA}})$ and $(\widehat{\tau}_{4,t},\widetilde{\mathbf{F}}_{t,\widehat{\theta}_{t}},4r_{\mathrm{LA}})$ , respectively. Note that $\widehat{\tau}_{3,t}$ and $\widehat{\tau}_{4,t}$ are finite almost surely under (A0) because $\widetilde{L}_{t}$ is four times continuously diferentiable and $\widetilde{\mathbf{F}}_{t,\widehat{\theta_{t}}}\in S_{+ +}^{p}$ For two probability distributions $P$ and $Q,$ , the total variation (TV) distance is defined as $$ d_{V}(P,Q)=\sup_{\mathcal{A}}|P(\mathcal{A})-Q(\mathcal{A})|,\tag{20} $$ where the supremum is taken over all measurable sets $\mathcal{A}$ . Theorem 2 (Laplace approximation: TV distance) Suppose that (A0) holds. $Then,$ with probability 1, we have $$ d_{V}\left(\Pi_{t}^{\mathrm{LA}}(\cdot),\widetilde{\Pi}_{t}(\cdot\mid\mathbf{D}_{t})\right)\leq K\epsilon_{n,t,\mathrm{TV}},\quad\forall t\in [T],\tag{21} $$ where $$ \epsilon_{n,t,\mathbf{TV}}=\left(\widehat{\tau}_{4,t}+\widehat{\tau}_{3,t}^{2}\right)p^{2}+\widehat{\tau}_{3,t}p+\widehat{\tau}_{3,t}^{3}\log^{3}N+e^{-8\log N-8p} $$ and $K > 0$ is a universal constant. Recently, Spokoiny (2012, 2017, 2024) developed advanced techniques for analyzing statistical behaviors of M-estimators with finite-sample guarantees. Accordingly, we adopt these techniques with modifications to adapt them to our framework. We say the model is stochastically linear if the map $\theta\mapsto\zeta_{t}(\theta)=L_{t}(\theta)-\mathbb{E}_{t}L_{t}(\theta)$ is linear for every $t ;$ that is, $\zeta_{t}(\theta)=a^{\top}\theta+b$ for some (random) quantities $a\in\mathbb{R}^{p}$ and $b\in\mathbb{R}$ . Note that stochastic linearity implies that $\nabla^{k}L_{t}(\theta)$ is non-random for all $t \in [ T ]$ and $k\in\{2,3,4\}$ Also, since $\nabla\zeta_{t}({\boldsymbol{\theta}})$ does not depend on $\theta,$ we hereafter denote this random vector by $\nabla{\zeta}_{t}$ The stochastically linear framework encompasses many important statistical models, such as the logistic regression, Poisson regression, nonparametric regression (Spokoiny and Panov, 2025), nonlinear inverse problem (Spokoiny, 2019), and covariance estimation (Puchkin et al., 2025). See Section 1.3 in Spokoiny (2024) for a detailed discussion. We now introduce the assumptions and notations used in the estimation procedure. (A1) The model is stochastically linear. For this purpose, we define the following quantity: $$ \tau_{3,t}^{*}=\inf\left\{\tau_{3}\in\mathbb{R}_{+}:\sup_{u\in\Theta(\widetilde{\mathbf{F}}_{t,\theta_{t}^{*}},4 r_{\mathrm{eff},t})}\sup_{z\in\mathbb{R}^{p}}\frac{\left|\langle\nabla^{3}\mathbb{E}_{t}\widetilde{L}_{t}(\theta_{t}^{*}+u),z^{\otimes 3}\rangle\right|}{\left\|\widetilde{\mathbf{F}}_{t,\theta_{t}^{*}}^{1/2}z\right\|_{2}^{3}}\leq\tau_{3}\right\}.\tag{29} $$ Note that $\tau_{3,t}^{*}$ is random because both $\theta_{t}^{*}$ and $\Omega_{t}$ −1 depend on $(\mathbf{D}_{1},...,\mathbf{D}_{t-1})$ . (Est) On an event ${\mathcal{E}}_{2}$ , the following inequality holds uniformly for all $t \in [ T ]$ $$ \tau_{3,t}^{*}r_{\mathrm{eff},t}\leq 1/16.\tag{30} $$ To state the main theorem in this section, let $\mathcal{E}_{\mathrm{{e s t},1}}^{\mathcal{O}}$ be the event on which the following inequality holds: $$ \left\|\widetilde{\mathbf{F}}_{t,\theta_{t}^{*}}^{-1/2}\nabla\zeta_{t}\right\|_{2}\leq r_{\text{eff},t}\quad \text{for all} t\in [T].\tag{32} $$ Then, $\mathbb{P}_{0}^{(N)}(\mathcal{E}_{\mathrm{est},1})\geq 1-n^{-1}$ under (A1). The event $\mathcal{E}_{\mathrm{{e s t},1}}^{\mathcal{o}}$ plays a crucial role throughout this paper, as it ensures the statistical validity of the online estimation procedure. For $t \in [ T ]$ , let $$ \begin{array}{l}\Delta_{t}=\left\|\boldsymbol{\Omega}_{t}^{1/2}\left(\mu_{t}-\widehat{\theta}_{t}\right)\right\|_{2}\vee\left\|\widetilde{\mathbf{F}}_{t,\widehat{\theta}_{t}}^{1/2}\left(\mu_{t}-\widehat{\theta}_{t}\right)\right\|_{2}\tag{100}\\ \vee\left\|\boldsymbol{\Omega}_{t}^{-1/2}\widetilde{\mathbf{F}}_{t,\widehat{\theta}_{t}}\boldsymbol{\Omega}_{t}^{-1/2}-\mathbf{I}_{p}\right\|_{\mathrm{F}}\vee\left\|\widetilde{\mathbf{F}}_{t,\widehat{\theta}_{t}}^{-1/2}\boldsymbol{\Omega}_{t}\widetilde{\mathbf{F}}_{t,\widehat{\theta}_{t}}^{-1/2}-\mathbf{I}_{p}\right\|_{\mathrm{F}}.\\ \end{array} $$ In this subsection, assume we are given a function $f:\Theta\to\mathbb{R}$ that is four times continuously diferentiable. For $\theta \in \Theta$ , let $\mathbf{F}_{\theta}= -\nabla^{2}f(\theta)$ , and assume $\mathbf{F}_{\theta}$ is nonsingular in this subsection. Lemma 40 For a given $\theta \in \Theta$ , suppose that f satisfies the third order smoothness at θ with parameters $(\tau_{3},\mathbf{F}_{\theta},r)$ . Then, $$ \sup_{\theta^{\prime}\in\Theta(\theta,\mathbf{F}_{\theta},r)}\left\|\mathbf{F}_{\theta}^{-1/2}\mathbf{F}_{\theta^{\prime}}\mathbf{F}_{\theta}^{-1/2}-\mathbf{I}_{p}\right\|_{2}\leq\tau_{3}r. $$ Consequently, for every $u\in\mathbb{R}^{p}$ and $\theta^{\prime}\in\Theta(\theta,\mathbf{F}_{\theta},r)$ , we have $$ (1-\tau_{3}r)\left\|\mathbf{F}_{\theta}^{1/2}u\right\|_{2}^{2}\leq\left\|\mathbf{F}_{\theta^{\prime}}^{1/2}u\right\|_{2}^{2}\leq(1+\tau_{3}r)\left\|\mathbf{F}_{\theta}^{1/2}u\right\|_{2}^{2}. $$ Lemma 44 For $\mu_{1},\mu_{2}\in\mathbb{R}^{p}$ and $\Omega_{1},\Omega_{2}\in{\mathcal{S}}_{+ +}^{p}$ , let $Q_{1}={\mathcal{N}}(\mu_{1},\Omega_{1}^{-1}),Q_{2}={\mathcal{N}}(\mu_{2},\Omega_{2}^{-1})$ Suppose that $$ d_{V}\left(Q_{1},Q_{2}\right)\leq\frac{1}{600}. $$ Let $$ \Delta=\left\|\boldsymbol{\Omega}_{1}^{1/2}\left(\mu_{1}-\mu_{2}\right)\right\|_{2}\vee\left\|\boldsymbol{\Omega}_{2}^{-1/2}\boldsymbol{\Omega}_{1}\boldsymbol{\Omega}_{2}^{-1/2}-\mathbf{I}_{p}\right\|_{\mathrm{F}}. $$ Then, $$ \frac{\Delta}{200}\leq d_{V}\left(Q_{1},Q_{2}\right)\leq\frac{\Delta}{\sqrt{2}}. $$

$$
d_{V}\left(\Pi_{t}^{\mathsf{LA}}(\cdot),\widetilde{\Pi}_{t}\left(\cdot\mid\mathbf{D}_{t}\right)\right)\leq K_{1}\epsilon_{n,t,\mathtt{TV}},\quad K\left(\Pi_{t}^{\mathsf{LA}}(\cdot),\widetilde{\Pi}_{t}\left(\cdot\mid\mathbf{D}_{t}\right)\right)\leq K_{2}\epsilon_{n,t,\mathtt{KL}}^{2},
$$

where $K_{1}$ and $K_{2}$ denote the constant K in Theorems 2 and 3, respectively. By the definition of $\Pi_{t}(\cdot)$ , it follows that

$$
K\left(\Pi_{t}(\cdot);\widetilde{\Pi}_{t}(\cdot\mid\mathbf{D}_{t})\right)\leq K\left(\Pi_{t}^{\mathrm{LA}}(\cdot);\widetilde{\Pi}_{t}(\cdot\mid\mathbf{D}_{t})\right)\leq K_{2}\epsilon_{n,t,\mathrm{KL}}^{2}.
$$

By Pinsker’s inequality, we have

$$
\begin{array}{l}d_{V}\left(\Pi_{t}(\cdot),\widetilde{\Pi}_{t}\left(\cdot\mid\mathbf{D}_{t}\right)\right)\leq\sqrt{\frac{1}{2}K\left(\Pi_{t}(\cdot),\widetilde{\Pi}_{t}\left(\cdot\mid\mathbf{D}_{t}\right)\right)}\leq\sqrt{\frac{K_{2}}{2}}\epsilon_{n,t,\mathrm{KL}},\\ d_{V}\left(\Pi_{t}^{\mathrm{LA}}(\cdot),\widetilde{\Pi}_{t}\left(\cdot\mid\mathbf{D}_{t}\right)\right)\leq\sqrt{\frac{1}{2}K\left(\Pi_{t}^{\mathrm{LA}}(\cdot),\widetilde{\Pi}_{t}\left(\cdot\mid\mathbf{D}_{t}\right)\right)}\leq\sqrt{\frac{K_{2}}{2}}\epsilon_{n,t,\mathrm{KL}}.\\ \end{array}
$$
By taking the constant K in Theorem 4 as $K=K_{2}\vee\sqrt{K_{2}/2}$ , we complete the proof.

$$

where the last inequality holds by $\tau_{3,t}^{*}r_{\mathrm{eff},t}\leq 1/16$ .
This completes the proof.

context:
We consider error-in-variables regression in a high-dimensional setting with fixed design. Formally, we observe a labeled dataset of size $n,$ denoted as $\{(y_{i},z_{i}):i\le n\}$ . Here, $y_{i}\in$ R is the response variable and $z_{i}\in\mathbb{R}^{p}$ is the observed covariate. For any $i \geq 1$ , we posit that

$$
y_{i}=\left\langle\boldsymbol{x}_{i},\boldsymbol{\beta}^{*}\right\rangle+\varepsilon_{i},\tag{1}
$$

where $\beta^{*}\in\mathbb{R}^{p}$ is the unknown model parameter, $\pmb{x}_{i}\in\mathbb{R}^{p}$ is a fixed covariate, and $\varepsilon_{i}\in\mathbb{R}$ is the response noise. Unlike traditional settings where $z_{i}={\pmb x}_{i}$ , the error-in-variables (EiV) setting reveals a corrupted version of the covariate $\mathbf{\delta}_{\mathbf{\mathcal{X}}_{i}}$ . Precisely, for any $i \geq 1$ , let

$$
\boldsymbol{z}_{i}=(\boldsymbol{x}_{i}+\boldsymbol{w}_{i})\circ\boldsymbol{\pi}_{i},\tag{2}
$$

where $\pmb{w}_{i}\in\mathbb{R}^{p}$ is the covariate measurement noise, $\pi_{i}\in\{1,\mathsf{NA}\}^{p}$ is a binary mask with NA denoting a missing value, and ◦ is the Hadamard (entrywise) product. Further, we consider a high-dimensional setting where n and p are growing with n possibly smaller than p.

For a matrix $\pmb{A}\in\mathbb{R}^{a\times b}$ , we denote its operator (spectral), Frobenius, and max element-wise norms as $\|A\|_{2},\|A\|_{F}$ , and $\|A\|_{\operatorname*{max}}$ , respectively. By rowspan(A), we denote the subspace of $\mathbb{R}^{b}$ spanned by the rows of A. Let $A^{\dagger}$ denote the pseudoinverse of A. For a vector $\pmb{v}\in\mathbb{R}^{a}$ , let $\|\pmb{v}\|_{p}$ denote its $\ell_{p}{\mathrm{-n o r m}}$ for $p\in [1,\infty]$ . We define the sub-gaussian (Orlicz) norm as $\lVert\pmb{v}\rVert_{\psi_{2}}$ . Let $\langle\cdot,\cdot\rangle$ and $\otimes$ denote the inner and outer products, respectively. For any two numbers $a,b\in\mathbb{R}$ , we use $a \wedge b$ to denote min(a, b) and $a \lor b$ to denote $\operatorname*{max}(a,b)$ . Let $[a]=\{1,\dots,a\}$ for any positive integer a.

Let f and g be two functions defined on the same space. We say that $f(n)=O(g(n))$ if and only if there exists a positive real number M and a real number $n_{0}$ such that for all $n\geq n_{0},|f(n)|\leq M|g(n)|$ |. Analogously we say $f(n)\ : =\ :\Theta(g(n))$ if and only if there exists positive real numbers m, M such that for all $n\geq n_{0},\ m|g(n)|\leq|f(n)|\leq M|g(n)|$ ; $f(n)=o(g(n))$ if for any $m > 0$ , there exists $n_{0}$ such that for all $n\geq n_{0},|f(n)|\leq m|g(n)|$ ; $f(n)=\omega(g(n))$ if for any $m > 0$ , there exists $n_{0}$ such that for all $n\geq n_{0},|f(n)|\geq m|g(n)|$ |. ${\bar{O}}(\cdot)$ is defined analogously to $O(\cdot)$ , but ignores log dependencies.

As described in Section 1, our in-sample (train) data consists of n labeled observations $\{(y_{i},z_{i}):i\leq n\}$ . By contrast, our out-of-sample (test) data consists of $m \geq 1$ unlabeled observations. That is, for $i ~ > ~ n$ , we observe the covariates $z_{i}$ but do not observe the associated response variables $y_{i}$ . Let $\pmb{Z}=[\pmb{z}_{i}^{\top}:i\leq n]\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times p}$ and $Z^{\prime}=[z_{i}^{\top}:i>n]\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times p}$ denote the matrices of in- and out-of-sample covariates, respectively.

We describe PCR, as introduced in Jollife (1982), with a variation to handle missing data.

I: Parameter estimation. Let $\widehat{\rho}$ denote the fraction of observed entries in $Z .$ Replace all missing values (NA) in the covariate matrices with zero. Let $\begin{array}{ r }{\widetilde{\pmb{Z}}=(1/\widehat{\rho})\pmb{Z}=\sum_{i=1}^{n\wedge p}\widehat{s}_{i}\widehat{\pmb{u}}_{i}\otimes\widehat{\pmb{v}}_{i}}\end{array}$ 2 where $\widehat{s}_{i}\in\mathbb{R}$ are the singular values (in decreasing order) and $\widehat{\pmb{u}}_{i}\in\mathbb{R}^{n},\widehat{\pmb{v}}_{i}\in\mathbb{R}^{p}$ are the corresponding left and right singular vectors, respectively. For a hyperparameter $k \in [ n \land p ]$ ， let $\begin{array}{ r }{\widetilde{Z}^{\bar{k}}=\sum_{i=1}^{k^{-}}\widehat{s}_{i}\widehat{\pmb{u}}_{i}\otimes\widehat{\pmb{v}}_{i}}\end{array}$ and define the estimated model parameter as

$$
\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}=(\widetilde{\boldsymbol{Z}}^{k})^{\dagger}\boldsymbol{y}=\Big(\sum_{i=1}^{k}(1/\widehat{s}_{i})\widehat{\boldsymbol{v}}_{i}\otimes\widehat{\boldsymbol{u}}_{i}\Big)\boldsymbol{y}.\tag{3}
$$

Property 2.1 The PCR solution, ${\widehat{\beta}},$ , as given in (3), is

1. the unique solution to the following program:

$$
\text{minimize}\quad\|\boldsymbol{\beta}\|_{2}\quad \text{over}\quad\boldsymbol{\beta}\in\mathbb{R}^{p}\quad \text{such that}\quad\boldsymbol{\beta}\in\underset{\boldsymbol{b}\in\mathbb{R}^{p}}{\arg\min}\|\boldsymbol{y}-\widetilde{\boldsymbol{Z}}^{k}\boldsymbol{b}\|_{2}^{2}.
$$

2. embedded within the rowspan(Ze<sup>k</sup>).

This section formalizes our problem setup. Let $\pmb{X}=[\pmb{x}_{i}^{\top}:i\leq n]\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times p}$ and $\pmb{X}^{\prime}=[\pmb{x}_{i}^{\top}$ $i>n]\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times p}$ represent the underlying in- and out-of-sample covariates, respectively.

Collectively, we assume (1) and (2) are satisfied. We make the additional assumptions.

Assumption 3.1 (Response noise) Let $\{\varepsilon_{i}:i\leq n\}$ be a sequence of independent mean zero subgaussian random variables with $\|\varepsilon_{i}\|_{\psi_{2}}\leq\sigma$

Assumption 3.1 is a standard assumption in the regression literature that posits the idiosyncratic response noise to be independent draws from a subgaussian distribution.

Assumption 3.2 (Covariate noise and missing values) Let $\{w_{i}:i\leq n+m\}$ be a sequence of independent mean zero subgaussian random vectors with $\|\pmb{w}_{i}\|_{\psi_{2}}\ \leq\ K$ and $\|\mathbb{E}[\pmb{w}_{i}\otimes\pmb{w}_{i}]\|_{2}\le\gamma^{2}$ . Let $\pi_{i}\in\{1,\mathsf{NA}\}^{p}$ , where NA denotes a missing value, be a vector of independent Bernoulli variables with parameter $\rho\in\left(0,1\right]$ . Further, let $\varepsilon_{i},\ w_{i},\ \pi_{i}$ be mutually independent.

Consistent with standard assumptions in the error-in-variables (EiV) regression literature, Assumption 3.2 posits the idiosyncratic EiV vector-valued noise ${\pmb w}_{i}$ to be subgaussian and independent across measurements; note, however, that the noise is allowed to be dependent within a measurement, i.e., the coordinates of ${\pmb w}_{i}$ can be correlated. Finally, we require missing entries in the observed covariate vector to be missing completely at random (MCAR). In Section 4.3.1, we discuss ways to allow for more heterogeneous missingness patterns.

Assumption 3.3 (Bounded covariates) Let $\|X\|_{\operatorname*{max}}\leq 1\ a n d\ \|X^{\prime}\|_{\operatorname*{max}}\leq 1$

This section addresses Q1–Q2. For ease of notation, let $C,c>0$ be absolute constants whose values may change from line to line or even within a line. Let $H=X^{\dagger}X\in\mathbb{R}^{p\times p}$ and ${\pmb{H}}_{\perp}={\pmb{I}}-{\pmb{H}}$ denote the projection matrices onto the rowspace and nullspace of $\boldsymbol{X}$ respectively. Let ${\pmb H}^{\prime},{\pmb H}_{\perp}^{\prime}\in\mathbb{R}^{p\times p}$ be defined analogously with respect to $X^{\prime}$ . We define $\tilde{\beta}^{*}=H\beta^{*}$ as the projection of $\beta^{*}$ onto the linear space spanned by the rows of $\boldsymbol{X}$

Q1: “When $p > n$ , is there a model parameter that PCR consistently identifies?”

The model parameter $\beta^{*}$ is not identifiable in the high-dimensional regime as infinitely many solutions satisfy (1). Among all feasible parameters, we show that PCR recovers $\tilde{\beta}^{*}$ the unique parameter with minimum $\ell_{2}{\mathrm{-n o r m}}$ that is entirely embedded in the rowspace of $\boldsymbol{X}$ , provided the number of principal components k is aptly chosen.

From Property 2.1, recall that PCR enforces $\widehat{\beta}\in\mathrm{rowspan}(\widetilde{Z}^{k})$ . Hence, if $k = r =$ rank(X) and the rowspace of $\widetilde{\pmb{Z}}^{r}$ is “close” to the rowspace of X, then ${\widehat{\beta}}\approx{\widetilde{\beta}}^{*}$ . The “noise” in $z$ arises from the missingness pattern induced by $\pi$ and the measurement error $W ;$ meanwhile, the “signal” in $z$ arises from $\boldsymbol{X}$ , where its strength is captured by the magnitude of its singular values. Accordingly, we define the snr as

$$
\mathrm{snr}:=\frac{\rho s_{r}}{\sqrt{n}+\sqrt{p}}.\tag{5}
$$

Here, $s_{r}$ is the smallest nonzero singular value of $X,\rho$ determines the fraction of observed entries, and ${\sqrt{n}}+{\sqrt{p}}$ is induced by the perturbation in the singular values from W. As one would expect, the signal strength snr scales linearly with $\rho .$ From standard concentration results for sub-gaussian matrices, it follows that $\|\boldsymbol{W}\|_{2}=\widetilde{O}(\sqrt{n}+\sqrt{p})$ (see Lemma 9). With this notation, we state the main result on model identification.

Theorem 4.1 Let Assumptions 3.1–3.3 hold. Consider $(i)$ PCR with $k=r=\mathrm{rank}(X)$ )， $(i i)\rho\geq c(n p)^{-1}\log^{2}(n p)$ , and $(iii)$ snr $\ge C(K+1)(\gamma+1)$ . Then w.p. at least $1-O((np)^{-10})$ ,

$$
\|\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}-\tilde{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{*}\|_{2}^{2}\leq C_{\text{noise}}\log(n p)\cdot\left\{\frac{\|\tilde{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{*}\|_{2}^{2}}{\mathsf{snr}^{2}}+\frac{\sqrt{n}\|\tilde{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{*}\|_{1}}{(n\vee p)\mathsf{snr}^{2}}+\frac{r(1\vee\|\tilde{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{*}\|_{1}^{2})}{(n\vee p)\mathsf{snr}^{2}}+\frac{\|\tilde{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{*}\|_{1}^{2}}{\mathsf{snr}^{4}}\right\},\tag{6}
$$

where $C_{\mathrm{noise}}=C(K+1)^{4}(\gamma+1)^{2}(\sigma^{2}+1)$ . Further, if $\langle\pmb{x}_{i},\beta^{*}\rangle\in [-d,d]$ for all $i \leq n$ , then

$$
\|\tilde{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{*}\|_{2}\leq s_{r}^{-1}\cdot d\sqrt{n}\quad a n d\quad\|\tilde{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{*}\|_{1}\leq s_{r}^{-1}\cdot d\sqrt{n p}.\tag{7}
$$

We start with some useful notation. Note $\pmb{X}\beta^{*}=\pmb{X}\tilde{\beta}^{*}$ . Let $\pmb{y}=\pmb{X}\tilde{\beta}^{*}+\varepsilon$ be the vector notation of (1) with $\pmb{y}=[y_{i}:i\le n]\in\mathbb{R}^{n},\varepsilon=[\varepsilon_{i}:i\le n]\in\mathbb{R}^{n}$ . Throughout, let $\pmb{X}=\pmb{U}\pmb{S}\pmb{V}^{\top}$ denote the singular value decomposition (SVD) of X. Recall that we write $\widetilde{Z}=\widehat{\rho}^{-1}Z=\widehat{U}\widehat{S}\widehat{V}^{\top}$ for the SVD of $\widetilde{\boldsymbol{z}}$ Its truncation using the top k singular components is denoted as $\widetilde{Z}^{k}=\widehat{U}_{k}\widehat{S}_{k}\widehat{V}_{k}^{\top}$

Further, we will often use the following bound: for any $\pmb{A}\in\mathbb{R}^{a\times b},\pmb{v}\in\mathbb{R}^{b}$ ，

$$
\|\boldsymbol{A}\boldsymbol{v}\|_{2}=\|\sum_{j=1}^{b}\boldsymbol{A}._{j}v_{j}\|_{2}\leq\left(\max_{j\leq b}\|\boldsymbol{A}._{j}\|_{2}\right)\left(\sum_{j=1}^{b}|v_{j}|\right)=\|\boldsymbol{A}\|_{2,\infty}\|\boldsymbol{v}\|_{1},\tag{S1}
$$

where $\|A\|_{2,\infty}=\operatorname*{max}_{j}\|A_{\cdot j}\|_{2}$ with $A ._{j}$ representing the $j\mathrm{-t h}$ column of A.

Lemma 16 (Modified Hoefding Inequality) Let $\ b{X}\in\mathbb{R}^{n}$ be random vector with independent mean-zero sub-Gaussian random coordinates with $\|X_{i}\|_{\psi_{2}}\leq K$ . Let $\mathbf{\pmb{a}}\in\mathbb{R}^{n}$ be another random vector that satisfies $\|\mathbf{a}\|_{2}\leq b$ almost surely for some constant $b \geq 0$ . Then for all $t \geq 0$ ，

$$
\mathbb{P}\Big(\Big|\sum_{i=1}^{n}a_{i}X_{i}\Big|\geq t\Big)\leq 2\exp\Big(-\frac{c t^{2}}{K^{2}b^{2}}\Big),
$$

where $c > 0$ is a universal constant.

Lemma 17 (Modified Hanson-Wright Inequality) Let $\ b{X}\in\mathbb{R}^{n}$ be a random vector with independent mean-zero sub-Gaussian coordinates with $\|X_{i}\|_{\psi_{2}}\leq K$ . Let $\ b{A}\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times n}$ be a random matrix satisfying $\|A\|_{2}\leq a$ and $\|A\|_{F}^{2}\le b$ almost surely for some $a,b\geq 0$ . Then for any $t \geq 0$

$$
\mathbb{P}\left(\left|\boldsymbol{X}^{\top}\boldsymbol{A}\boldsymbol{X}-\mathbb{E}[\boldsymbol{X}^{\top}\boldsymbol{A}\boldsymbol{X}]\right|\geq t\right)\leq 2\cdot\exp\Big(-c\min\left(\frac{t^{2}}{K^{4}b},\frac{t}{K^{2}a}\right)\Big).
$$

theorems.statement:
Lemma 2 Consider the setup of Theorem 4.1, and PCR with parameter $k = r$ . Then, for any $t > 0$ , the following holds w.p. at least $1-\exp\bigl(-t^{2}\bigr)$

$$
\|\boldsymbol{U}\boldsymbol{U}^{\top}-\widehat{\boldsymbol{U}}_{r}\widehat{\boldsymbol{U}}_{r}^{\top}\|_{2}\leq C(K+1)(\gamma+1)\frac{\sqrt{n}+\sqrt{p}+t}{\rho s_{r}},
$$

$$
\|\boldsymbol{V}\boldsymbol{V}^{\top}-\widehat{\boldsymbol{V}}_{r}\widehat{\boldsymbol{V}}_{r}^{\top}\|_{2}\leq C(K+1)(\gamma+1)\frac{\sqrt{n}+\sqrt{p}+t}{\rho s_{r}}.
$$

Here, $s_{r}>0$ represents the r-th largest singular value of X.

steps.claim: Recall that U, V denote the left and right singular vectors of X (equivalently, $\rho X)$ , respectively; meanwhile, $\widehat{U}_{k},\widehat{V}_{k}$ denote the top k left and right singular vectors of Ze (equivalently, $z)$ , respectively. Further, observe that $\mathbb{E}[Z]=\rho X$ and let $\tilde{W}=Z-\rho X$ . To arrive at our result, we recall Wedin’s Theorem (Wedin, 1972).

Theorem C.1 (Wedin’s Theorem) Given $\boldsymbol{A},\boldsymbol{B}\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times p}$ , let $\boldsymbol{A}=\boldsymbol{U}\boldsymbol{S}\boldsymbol{V}^{\top}$ and $\boldsymbol{B}=\widehat{\boldsymbol{U}}\widehat{\boldsymbol{S}}\widehat{\boldsymbol{V}}^{\top}$ be their respective SVDs . Let $U_{k},V_{k}$ (respectively, $\widehat{U}_{k},\widehat{V}_{k})$ correspond to the truncation of U, V (respectively, ${\widehat{U}},{\widehat{V}})$ that retains the columns corresponding to the top k singular values of A (respectively, B). Let $s_{k}$ denote the k-th singular value of A. Then,

$$
\max\left(\|\boldsymbol{U}_{k}\boldsymbol{U}_{k}^{\top}-\widehat{\boldsymbol{U}}_{k}\widehat{\boldsymbol{U}}_{k}^{\top}\|_{2},\|\boldsymbol{V}_{k}\boldsymbol{V}_{k}^{\top}-\widehat{\boldsymbol{V}}_{k}\widehat{\boldsymbol{V}}_{k}^{\top}\|_{2}\right)\leq\frac{2\|\boldsymbol{A}-\boldsymbol{B}\|_{2}}{s_{k}-s_{k+1}}.
$$

Using Theorem C.1 for $k = r$ , it follows that

$$
\max\left(\|\boldsymbol{U}\boldsymbol{U}^{\top}-\widehat{\boldsymbol{U}}_{r}\widehat{\boldsymbol{U}}_{r}^{\top}\|_{2},\|\boldsymbol{V}\boldsymbol{V}^{\top}-\widehat{\boldsymbol{V}}_{r}\widehat{\boldsymbol{V}}_{r}^{\top}\|_{2}\right)\leq\frac{2\|\tilde{\boldsymbol{W}}\|_{2}}{\rho s_{r}},\tag{S24}
$$

where $s_{r}$ is the smallest nonzero singular value of X. Next, we obtain a high probability bound on $\|\tilde{W}\|_{2}$ . To that end,

$$
\frac{1}{n}\|\tilde{\boldsymbol{W}}\|_{2}^{2}=\frac{1}{n}\|\tilde{\boldsymbol{W}}^{\top}\tilde{\boldsymbol{W}}\|_{2}\leq\frac{1}{n}\|\tilde{\boldsymbol{W}}^{\top}\tilde{\boldsymbol{W}}-\mathbb{E}[\tilde{\boldsymbol{W}}^{\top}\tilde{\boldsymbol{W}}]\|_{2}+\frac{1}{n}\|\mathbb{E}[\tilde{\boldsymbol{W}}^{\top}\tilde{\boldsymbol{W}}]\|_{2}.\tag{S25}
$$

We bound the two terms in (S25) separately. We recall the following lemma, which is a direct extension of Theorem 4.6.1 of Vershynin (2018) for the non-isotropic setting, and we present its proof for completeness in Section C.5.

Lemma 6 (Independent sub-gaussian rows) Let A be an $n \times p$ matrix whose rows $A_{i}$ are independent, mean zero, sub-gaussian random vectors in $\mathbb{R}^{p}$ with second moment matrix $\Sigma=(1/n)\mathbb{E}[A^{\top}A]$ . Then for any $t \geq 0$ , the following holds w.p. at least $1-\exp(-t^{2})$

$$
\|\frac{1}{n}\boldsymbol{A}^{\top}\boldsymbol{A}-\boldsymbol{\Sigma}\|_{2}\leq K^{2}\max(\delta,\delta^{2}),\quad \text{where}\delta=C\sqrt{\frac{p}{n}}+\frac{t}{\sqrt{n}};\tag{S26}
$$

here, $K=\operatorname*{max}_{i}\|A_{i}\|_{\psi_{2}}$

The matrix $\tilde{W}=Z-\rho X$ has independent rows by Assumption 3.2. We state the following Lemma about the distribution property of the rows of $\tilde{W}$ , the proof of which can be found in Section C.6.

Lemma 7 Let Assumption 3.2 hold. Then, $z_{i}-\rho x_{i}$ is a sequence of independent, mean zero, sub-gaussian random vectors satisfying $\|\mathbf{\cdot}\mathbf{-}\rho\mathbf{x}_{i}\|_{\psi_{2}}\leq C(K+1)$

From Lemmas 6 and 7, w.p. at least $1-\exp\bigl(-t^{2}\bigr)$

$$
\frac{1}{n}\|\tilde{\boldsymbol{W}}^{\top}\tilde{\boldsymbol{W}}-\mathbb{E}[\tilde{\boldsymbol{W}}^{\top}\tilde{\boldsymbol{W}}]\|_{2}\leq C(K+1)^{2}\left(1+\frac{p}{n}+\frac{t^{2}}{n}\right).\tag{S27}
$$
Finally, we claim the following bound on $\lVert\mathbb{E}[\tilde{\mathbf{W}}^{\top}\tilde{\mathbf{W}}]\rVert_{2}$ , the proof of which is in Section C.7.

Lemma 8 Let Assumption 3.2 hold. Then, we have

$$
\|\mathbb{E}[\tilde{\boldsymbol{W}}^{\top}\tilde{\boldsymbol{W}}]\|_{2}\leq C(K+1)^{2}n(\rho-\rho^{2})+n\rho^{2}\gamma^{2}.
$$

From (S25), (S27) and Lemma 8, we have w.p. at least $1-\exp(-t^{2})$ for any $t > 0$

$$
\|\tilde{\boldsymbol{W}}\|_{2}^{2}\leq C(K+1)^{2}(n+p+t^{2})+n(\rho(1-\rho)(K+1)^{2}+\rho^{2}\gamma^{2}).
$$
For this, we conclude the following lemma.

Lemma 9 For any $t>0_{i}$ , the following holds w.p. at least $1-\exp\bigl(-t^{2}\bigr)$

$$
\|\boldsymbol{Z}-\rho\boldsymbol{X}\|_{2}\leq C(K+1)(\gamma+1)(\sqrt{n}+\sqrt{p}+t).
$$
Using the above and (S24), we conclude the proof of Lemma 2.

Lemma 12 (Weyl’s inequality) Given A, $\pmb{{B}}\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times n}$ , let $\sigma_{i}$ and $\widehat{\sigma}_{i}$ be the i-th singular values of A and B, respectively, in decreasing order and repeated by multiplicities. Then for all $i \in [ m \land n ]$ 2

\left|\sigma_{i}-\widehat{\sigma}_{i}\right|\leq\left\|\boldsymbol{A}-\boldsymbol{B}\right\|_{2}.
$$

Let $\tilde{s}_{k}$ be the k-th singular value of Z. Then, $\widehat{s}_{k}=(1/\widehat{\rho})\widetilde{s}_{k}$ since it is the k-th singular value of $\widetilde{Z}=(1/\widehat{\rho})Z$ . By Lemma 12, we have

$$

recall that $s_{k}$ is the k-th singular value of X. As a result,

steps.claim:
We need to bound $\langle\widetilde{Z}^{k}(\widehat{\beta}-\widetilde{\beta}^{*}),\varepsilon\rangle$ . To that end, we recall that $\widehat{\beta}=\widehat{V}_{k}\widehat{S}_{k}^{-1}\widehat{U}_{k}^{\top}y,\widetilde{Z}^{k}=$ $\widehat{U}_{k}\widehat{S}_{k}\widehat{V}_{k}^{\top}$ , and $\pmb{y}=\pmb{X}\tilde{\beta}^{*}+\varepsilon$ . Thus,

$$
\widetilde{\boldsymbol{Z}}^{k}\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}=\widehat{\boldsymbol{U}}_{k}\widehat{\boldsymbol{S}}_{k}\widehat{\boldsymbol{V}}_{k}^{\top}\widehat{\boldsymbol{V}}_{k}\widehat{\boldsymbol{S}}_{k}^{-1}\widehat{\boldsymbol{U}}_{k}^{\top}\boldsymbol{y}=\widehat{\boldsymbol{U}}_{k}\widehat{\boldsymbol{U}}_{k}^{\top}\boldsymbol{X}\tilde{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{*}+\widehat{\boldsymbol{U}}_{k}\widehat{\boldsymbol{U}}_{k}^{\top}\boldsymbol{\varepsilon}.
$$

Therefore,

$$
\langle\widetilde{\boldsymbol{Z}}^{k}(\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}-\widetilde{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{*}),\boldsymbol{\varepsilon}\rangle=\langle\widehat{\boldsymbol{U}}_{k}\widehat{\boldsymbol{U}}_{k}^{\top}\boldsymbol{X}\widetilde{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{*},\boldsymbol{\varepsilon}\rangle+\langle\widehat{\boldsymbol{U}}_{k}\widehat{\boldsymbol{U}}_{k}^{\top}\boldsymbol{\varepsilon},\boldsymbol{\varepsilon}\rangle-\langle\widehat{\boldsymbol{U}}_{k}\widehat{\boldsymbol{S}}_{k}\widehat{\boldsymbol{V}}_{k}^{\top}\widetilde{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{*},\boldsymbol{\varepsilon}\rangle .\tag{S34}
$$

Now, ε is independent of $\widehat{U}_{k},\widehat{S}_{k},\widehat{V}_{k}$ since $\widetilde{Z}^{k}$ is determined by Z, which is independent of ε. As a result,

$$
\begin{array}{l}\mathbb{E}\big [\langle\widehat{\boldsymbol{U}}_{k}\widehat{\boldsymbol{U}}_{k}^{\top}\boldsymbol{\varepsilon},\boldsymbol{\varepsilon}\rangle\big]=\mathbb{E}\big [\boldsymbol{\varepsilon}^{\top}\widehat{\boldsymbol{U}}_{k}\widehat{\boldsymbol{U}}_{k}^{\top}\boldsymbol{\varepsilon}\big]\\ =\mathbb{E}\big [\operatorname{tr}\Big(\boldsymbol{\varepsilon}^{\top}\widehat{\boldsymbol{U}}_{k}\widehat{\boldsymbol{U}}_{k}^{\top}\boldsymbol{\varepsilon}\Big)\big]=\mathbb{E}\big [\operatorname{tr}\Big(\boldsymbol{\varepsilon}\boldsymbol{\varepsilon}^{\top}\widehat{\boldsymbol{U}}_{k}\widehat{\boldsymbol{U}}_{k}^{\top}\Big)\big]\\ =\operatorname{tr}\left(\mathbb{E}\left[\boldsymbol{\varepsilon}\boldsymbol{\varepsilon}^{\top}\right]\widehat{\boldsymbol{U}}_{k}\widehat{\boldsymbol{U}}_{k}^{\top}\right)\leq C\operatorname{tr}\left(\sigma^{2}\widehat{\boldsymbol{U}}_{k}\widehat{\boldsymbol{U}}_{k}^{\top}\right)\\ =C\sigma^{2}\|\widehat{\boldsymbol{U}}_{k}\|_{F}^{2}=C\sigma^{2}k.\tag{S35}\\ \end{array}
$$

Therefore, it follows that

$$
\mathbb{E}[\langle\widetilde{\boldsymbol{Z}}^{k}(\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}-\tilde{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{*}),\boldsymbol{\varepsilon}\rangle]\leq C\sigma^{2}k,\tag{S36}
$$

where we used the fact $\mathbb{E}[\varepsilon]=\mathbf{0}$ . To obtain a high probability bound, using Lemma 16 it follows that for any $t > 0$

$$
\mathbb{P}\left(\langle\widehat{\boldsymbol{U}}_{k}\widehat{\boldsymbol{U}}_{k}^{\top}\boldsymbol{X}\tilde{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{*},\varepsilon\rangle\geq t\right)\leq\exp\left(-\frac{c t^{2}}{n\|\tilde{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{*}\|_{1}^{2}\sigma^{2}}\right)\tag{S37}
$$

due to Assumption 3.1, and

$$
\|\widehat{\boldsymbol{U}}_{k}\widehat{\boldsymbol{U}}_{k}^{\top}\boldsymbol{X}\tilde{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{*}\|_{2}\leq\|\boldsymbol{X}\tilde{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{*}\|_{2}\leq\|\boldsymbol{X}\|_{2,\infty}\|\tilde{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{*}\|_{1}\leq\sqrt{n}\|\tilde{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{*}\|_{1};
$$

note that we have used the fact that $\widehat{U}_{k}\widehat{U}_{k}^{\top}$ is a projection matrix and $\|X\|_{2,\infty}\leq{\sqrt{n}}$ due to Assumption 3.3.

Similarly, for any $t > 0$

$$
\mathbb{P}\left(\langle\widehat{\boldsymbol{U}}_{k}\widehat{\boldsymbol{S}}_{k}\widehat{\boldsymbol{V}}_{k}^{\top}\tilde{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{*},\boldsymbol{\varepsilon}\rangle\geq t\right)\leq\exp\Big(-\frac{c t^{2}}{\sigma^{2}(n+\|\widetilde{\boldsymbol{Z}}^{k}-\boldsymbol{X}\|_{2,\infty}^{2})\|\tilde{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{*}\|_{1}^{2}}\Big),\tag{S38}
$$

due to Assumption 3.1, and

$$
\begin{array}{l}\|\widehat{\boldsymbol{U}}_{k}\widehat{\boldsymbol{S}}_{k}\widehat{\boldsymbol{V}}_{k}^{\top}\tilde{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{*}\|_{2}=\|(\widetilde{\boldsymbol{Z}}^{k}-\boldsymbol{X})\tilde{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{*}+\boldsymbol{X}\tilde{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{*}\|_{2}\leq\|(\widetilde{\boldsymbol{Z}}^{k}-\boldsymbol{X})\tilde{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{*}\|_{2}+\|\boldsymbol{X}\tilde{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{*}\|_{2}\\ \leq\left(\|\widetilde{\boldsymbol{Z}}^{k}-\boldsymbol{X}\|_{2,\infty}+\|\boldsymbol{X}\|_{2,\infty}\right)\|\tilde{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{*}\|_{1}.\\ \end{array}
$$

Finally, using Lemma 17 and (S36), it follows that for any $t > 0$

$$
\mathbb{P}\left(\langle\widehat{\boldsymbol{U}}_{k}\widehat{\boldsymbol{U}}_{k}^{\top}\boldsymbol{\varepsilon},\boldsymbol{\varepsilon}\rangle\geq\sigma^{2}k+t\right)\leq\exp\Big(-c\min\left(\frac{t^{2}}{k\sigma^{4}},\frac{t}{\sigma^{2}}\right)\Big),\tag{S39}
$$

since $\widehat{U}_{k}\widehat{U}_{k}^{\top}$ is a projection matrix and by Assumption 3.1.

From (S34), (S37), (S38), and (S39), we conclude that w.p. at least $1-O(1/(np)^{10})$

$$
\langle\widetilde{\boldsymbol{Z}}^{k}(\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}-\widetilde{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{*}),\boldsymbol{\varepsilon}\rangle\leq\sigma^{2}k+C\sigma\sqrt{\log(n p)}\left(\sigma\sqrt{k}+\sigma\sqrt{\log(n p)}+\|\widetilde{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{*}\|_{1}(\sqrt{n}+\|\widetilde{\boldsymbol{Z}}^{k}-\boldsymbol{X}\|_{2,\infty})\right).
$$

This completes the proof of Lemma 5.

context:
In this paper, we consider the following bilevel optimization problem:

$$
\min_{x\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{x}}}\varphi(x):=f(x,y^{*}(x)),\quad \text{where} y^{*}(x)=\arg\min_{y\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{y}}}g(x,y).\tag{1}
$$

We call f the upper-level problem, $g$ the lower-level problem, and $\varphi$ the hyper-objective. This formulation covers many applications, including but not limited to hyperparameter tuning (Franceschi et al., 2018; Pedregosa, 2016; Bae and Grosse, 2020; Mackay et al., 2018), neural architecture search (Liu et al., 2019; Wang et al., 2022b; Zoph and Le, 2016; Zhang et al., 2021), meta-learning (Finn et al., 2017; Fallah et al., 2020; Andrychowicz et al., 2016; Mishchenko et al., 2023; Rajeswaran et al., 2019; Chandra et al., 2022; Ji et al., 2022; Zhou et al., 2019), adversarial training (Zhang et al., 2022; Br¨uckner and Schefer, 2011; Wang et al., 2021; Bishop et al., 2020; Wang et al., 2022a; Robey et al., 2023) and data hyper-cleaning (Gao et al., 2022; Zhou et al., 2022; Ren et al., 2018; Yong et al., 2022; Shu et al., 2019; Li et al., 2022).

Here $g^{*}(x)=g(x,y^{*}(x))$ is usually called the value-function. The Lagrangian with a multiplier $\lambda > 0$ for this inequality-constrained problem takes the form of:

$$
\mathcal{L}_{\lambda}(x,y):=f(x,y)+\lambda\left(g(x,y)-g^{*}(x)\right).\tag{4}
$$

Kwon et al. (2023) further defines the following auxiliary function:

$$
\mathcal{L}_{\lambda}^{*}(x):=\mathcal{L}_{\lambda}(x,y_{\lambda}^{*}(x)),\text{where} y_{\lambda}^{*}(x)=\arg\min_{y\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{y}}}\mathcal{L}_{\lambda}(x,y),\tag{5}
$$

and showed that $\mathcal{L}_{\lambda}^{*}(x)$ is a good proxy of $\varphi(x)$ with

$$
\|\nabla\mathcal{L}_{\lambda}^{*}(x)-\nabla\varphi(x)\|=\mathcal{O}\left(\kappa^{3}/\lambda\right).
$$

Notations. We follow the notations of tensors used in Kolda and Bader (2009).
