As we are in the agnostic setting, there may be no w that achieves zero loss. We can split the loss function $L(w)$ into two components, one of which is $F(w)$ defined by

\begin{array}{ r }{F(w): =\frac{1}{2}\mathbb E\left[(\sigma(w^{\top}x)-\sigma(v^{\top}x))^{2}\right],\nabla F(w): =\mathbb E\left[(\sigma(w^{\top}x)-\sigma(v^{\top}x))\sigma^{\prime}(w^{\top}x)x\right].}\end{array}\tag{5}

We will often refer to $F(w)$ as the realizable loss, since it captures the difference between w and $v ;$ in the realizable setting $\dot{L}(w)=F(w)$ . Note that $F(v)=0$

Gradient of the Loss. The gradient of $L(w)$ with respect to w is

\nabla L(w)=\mathbb{E}\left[(\sigma(w^{\top}x)-y)\sigma^{\prime}(w^{\top}x)x\right]\tag{6}

where $\sigma^{\prime}(\cdot)$ is the derivative of $\sigma(\cdot)$ , defined as $\sigma^{\prime}(z)=\mathbb{1}\{z\geq 0\}$ . Note that the ReLU function $\sigma(z)$ is differentiable everywhere except at $z = 0$ Following standard convention in this literature, we define $\sigma^{\prime}(0)=1$ . Note that the exact value of $\sigma^{\prime}(0)$ will have no effect on our results.

We can also decompose $\nabla L(w)$ as

\nabla L(w)=\mathbb{E}\left[(\sigma(w^{\top}x)-\sigma(v^{\top}x))\sigma^{\prime}(w^{\top}x)x\right]+\mathbb{E}\left[(\sigma(v^{\top}x)-y)\sigma^{\prime}(w^{\top}x)x\right]\tag{7}

\mathrm{Therefore},\nabla L(w)=\nabla F(w)+\mathbb{E}\left[(\sigma(v^{\top}x)-y)\sigma^{\prime}(w^{\top}x)x\right]\tag{8}

Gradient Descent. Finally, our paper focuses on the standard gradient descent algorithm with a fixed learning rate $\eta > 0$ We initialize at some point $w_{0}\in\mathbb{R}^{d+\bar{1}}$ , and at each iteration $t\in\mathbb{N}$ we have $w_{t+1}=w_{t}-\eta\nabla F(w_{t})$ . We do not optimize the iteration count in this paper; hence it will be instructive to think of  as a non-negligible parameter that can be set to be sufficiently small (e.., an inverse polynomial for polynomial time guarantees).

Simplification. For sake of exposition we will assume that $\|\tilde{v}\|_{2}=1$ ; the same analysis goes through when $\lVert\tilde{v}\rVert_{2}\in [1/C_{1},C_{1}]$ as well. Moreover Proposition1shows that assuming that $\|\tilde{v}\|_{2}$ is normalized is without loss of generality. Note that we cannot make such a simplifying assumption about the vectors $\boldsymbol{w}_{t}=\left(\boldsymbol{\tilde{w}_{t}},\boldsymbol{b_{w}}\right)$ in the intermediate iterations.

Finally, please see Section Bfor the weaker distributional guarantees and guarantees.

4 Overview of the Analysis (Proof of Theorem 1)

We now provide an overview of our analysis. For complete proofs of the lemmas and propositions, please refer to the supplementary material (Appendix A). Recall that our goal throughout the learning process is to find a $\mathcal{w}\in\mathbb{R}^{d+1}$ such that $L(w)$ achieves a comparable performance to $OPT=L(v)$ In order to accomplish this, we aim to find w such that it is close to $v,\mathrm{i . e .}\parallel w-v\parallel$ is small. Note that approximating v suffices to achieve an error close to $O P T$ , since we can upper-bound $L(w)$ as

\begin{array}{ c }{\displaystyle\boldsymbol{L}(\boldsymbol{w})=\frac 1 2\mathbb E\left[\big(\sigma(\boldsymbol{w}^{\top}\boldsymbol{x})-y)^{2}\right]=\frac 1 2\mathbb E\left[\big(\sigma(\boldsymbol{w}^{\top}\boldsymbol{x})-\sigma(\boldsymbol{v}^{\top}\boldsymbol{x})+\sigma(\boldsymbol{v}^{\top}\boldsymbol{x})-y)^{2}\right]}\\ {\le 2\cdot\frac 1 2\mathbb E\left[\big(\sigma(\boldsymbol{w}^{\top}\boldsymbol{x})-\sigma(\boldsymbol{v}^{\top}\boldsymbol{x}))^{2}\right]+2\cdot\frac 1 2\mathbb E\left[\big(\sigma(\boldsymbol{v}^{\top}\boldsymbol{x})-y)^{2}\right]=~2 F(\boldsymbol{w})+2 O P T}\end{array}

through Young's inequality. The realizable portion of the loss $F(w)$ becomes $O(OPT)$ when $\|w-v\|\leq O({\sqrt{O P T}})$ (see Lemma1for a proof), and as a consequence we will get $O(OPT)$ ) error in total.

To formalize our intuition above, we adopt a similar proof strategy used inFrei et al. (2020). Namely, we argue that when optimizing with respect to the agnostic loss $L(w_{t})$ , we are always making some non-trivial progress due to a decrease in $\lVert\boldsymbol{w}_{t}-\boldsymbol{v}\rVert$ and due to a decrease in $F(w_{t})$ (which is just the realizable portion of the loss). Moreover, whenever we stop making progress, we will argue that at this point either $\lVert w_{t}-v\rVert\leq O({\sqrt{O P T}})$ or $\begin{array}{ r }{\|\nabla F(w_{t})\|\leq O(\sqrt{O P T});}\end{array}$ in both cases, this iterate already achieves an error of $O(OPT)$ due to Lemma 1and Lemma 2

Challenges in arguing progress. At a high-level the analysis of gradient descent follows a similar approach toFrei et al. (2020) which only handles zero bias. Yet there are several new ideas needed to obtain the stronger $\overline{{O(O P T)}}$ guarantee even for the zero-bias case. Moreover, allowing non-zero bias terms imposes extra technical challenges. For example, the probability measure of $\{w^{\top}x\geq 0,v^{\top}x\geq 0\}$ under Gaussian distributions, which is vital to deriving the gain in each gradient descent step, does not have a closed-form expression when bias is present. Furthermore we cannot afford to lose any dimension dependent factors or assume boundedness. Thus, to address these difficulties, more detailed analyses (e.g. Lemma3 4) are needed to facilitate our argument.

Moreover tackling non-zero bias terms requires additional assumptions when initializing $w_{0}$ as well. The initializer finds a $w_{0}$ such that $F(w_{0})$ is strictly less than $F(0)$ by a constant amount $\delta > 0$ (this is inspired by Vardi et al.(2021), however δ in their case can have an inverse-polynomial dependence on the dimension ). In fact our multiscale random initialization and the improved analysis is crucial to obtaining a dimension-independent bound on the error. The high-level intuition behind why this property is useful is that it ensures that gradient descent does not get trapped around a highly non-smooth region (e.g. when $w=0)$ by making it start at somewhere better than it, so that w keeps moving closer to v. Moreover, in our case the analysis is more challenging to implement compared to Vardi et al. (2021)because of the agnostic setting. This is becauseVardi et al. (2021heavily relies on the realizability assumption to simplify its analysis.

We also highlight our improvements on the dependency of the dimension d. In previous works, the guarantees of the algorithm has a dependence on d either explicitly or implicitly. For instance, inFrei et al.(2020the $O({\sqrt{O P T}})$ guarantee for ReLU neurons includes a coefficient in terms of $B_{X}$ (the upper-bound for $\lVert x\rVert)$ , which for Gaussian inputs is in fact ${\sqrt{d}};$ or for example inVardi et al. the gain for each gradient descent iteration γ comes with a dependency on c (the upper-bound for $\|{\boldsymbol{x}}\|)\operatorname{of}c^{-8}$ , which for Gaussian is $d^{-4}$ . In contrast, we avoid such dependencies on the dimension d in order to obtain our guarantees.

4.1 Main Proof Strategy

With these two key lemmas, we are now ready to discuss the proof overview of the main theorem (Theorem[1). We inductively maintain two invariants in every iteration of the algorithm:

\begin{array}{ r }{\mathrm{(A)}\quad\|w_{t}-v\|_{2}\leq O(1),\quad\mathrm{and}\quad\mathrm{(B)}\ F(0)-F(w_{t})=\Omega(1).}\end{array}

These two invariants are true at $t = 0$ due to our initialization $w_{0}$ Lemma 5guarantees with at least constant probability $\Omega(1)$ , both the invariants hold for $w_{0}$ . The proof that both the invariants continue to hold follows from the progress made by the algorithm due to a decrease in both $\lVert\boldsymbol{w}_{t}-\boldsymbol{v}\rVert_{2}$ and $F(w_{t})$ (note that we only need to show they do not increase to maintain the invariant).

The argument consists of two parts. First, assuming $F(w_{t})\le F(0)-\delta$ holds (for some constant $\delta>0)$ , we establish that whenever $\|w_{t}-v\|^{2}>\gamma\breve{O}P T$ for some constant $\gamma > 0 .$ gradient descent always makes progress i.e. $\|w_{t}-v\|^{2}-\|w_{t+1}^{\cdot}-\dot{v}\|^{2}$ is lower bounded. Next, we argue that if $w_{0}$ is initialized such that $F(w_{0})\leq F(0)-\delta$ for some constant $\delta > 0$ , then throughout gradient descent $F(w_{t})$ always decreases, i.e. the inequality $F(w_{t})\leq F(w_{0})\leq F(0)-\delta$ always holds.

error_explanation: Step 3 asserts the decomposition $F_2 = \cos(\alpha)F_1 + \sin(\alpha)F_2^{\perp}$ for arbitrary (non-unit-norm) vector fields $F_1,F_2$. This identity holds only when each row vector has unit $L^2$-norm. Since $F_2^{\perp}$ is defined as the NORMALIZED perpendicular component, the expression $\cos(\alpha)F_1 + \sin(\alpha)F_2^{\perp}$ reproduces the parallel part $F_2^{\parallel}$ correctly but fixes the perpendicular magnitude to $\sin(\alpha)$ instead of the true magnitude $k=\|F_2 - F_2^{\parallel}\|$. For a general vector these differ ($\|F_2\|\neq 1$), so the decomposition — and hence the identity $F_2^{\theta=0}=F_2$ derived from it in step 5 — fails. The rotation therefore does not preserve the field even at zero angle. The fix is to require unit $L^2$-norm rows (use $\hat{F}_1,\hat{F}_2$), under which $\hat{F}_2=\cos(\alpha)\hat{F}_1+\sin(\alpha)\hat{F}_2^{\perp}$ holds exactly.

context:
2 Designing a Dataset Difficulty Measure

For supervised learning across data modalities such as images and text, data samples can usually be viewed as feature-label pairs (x, y) where $x\in\mathcal{X}\subset\mathbb{R}^{d_{x}}$ , and $y\in\mathcal{V}$ . We focus on classification problems where the labels y are discrete, i.e., $\mathcal{V}\subset\mathbb{Z}^{+}$ . We denote the joint distribution of the feature-label pairs as $\mathcal{P}_{\mathcal{X}\mathcal{Y}}$ . The marginal distributions of the features and labels are denoted as $\mathcal{P}_{\mathcal{X}}$ and $\mathcal{P}_{\mathcal{Y}}$ respectively. We make the following widely adopted assumption from learning theory literature about how samples are generated:

Assumption 2. The feature-label pairs $(x,y)$ in the datasets, both training and testing, are sampled i.i.d. from a static distribution $(x,y)\sim{\mathcal{P}}_{\chi y}$

Intuitively, there are many possible indicators for the potential difficulty of a dataset: the number of features, the number of classes, the number of samples, the distinguishability of samples across classes, as well as the difference between the data distributions of the training set and the testing set. However, none of these indicators alone can fully describe the relative difficulty of a dataset.

From Assumption 2, if the samples $(x,y)$ are sampled i.i.d. from $\mathcal{P}_{\mathcal{X}\mathcal{Y}}$ , where Y is discrete, a natural measure that characterizes the difficulty of the data distribution is the best probability of the 0-1 error that can be achieved by any estimator.

Definition 2 (Model-Agnostic Error). $\begin{array}{ r }{\mathcal{P}_{e}=\operatorname*{inf}_{f}\mathcal{P}_{x,y\sim\mathcal{P}x y}\left[f(x)\neq y\right]}\end{array}$

The measure 1 is straightforward but unfortunately it is hard to compute since it involves evaluations against all possible estimators. However, with mild assumptions, it can be lower bounded by terms related to the conditional entropy, which is much easier to evaluate.

2.1 Discrete Features

In the case where the features $x\in\mathcal{X}$ are discrete, according to Fano's theorem, $\mathcal{P}_{e}$ is lower bounded: Fano's inequality. If both X and Y are discrete random variables, then $\begin{array}{ r }{\mathcal{P}_{e}\ge\frac{\mathbb{H}(Y|X)-1}{\log|\mathcal{V}|}}\end{array}$ , where |V| is the cardinality of the label set Y, and $\mathbb{H}(Y|X)$ is the conditional entropy.

However, even though data can be represented using discrete integers, treating the features as discrete random variables leads to the following difficulties:

1.The cardinality of the feature space becomes extremely large if discrete features are used. For image data, since each pixel is represented as an integer, the (raw) feature dimension would bee he mber  pixel in tage, whic can b xtey rSmilarly, or n data, when the sequence length is long, the feature dimension becomes large very quickly.

2Given the large feature space, finding a matching set of features between training and testing data from the limited number of training and test samples would be unlikely. As a result, probability mass estimation on each discrete value would be impractical, since we may only see at most one sample for each discrete configuration.

2.2 Continuous Features

As opposed to treating the features x as discrete random variables, if we view them as i.i.d. samples from a continuous distribution with probability density $p_{x},$ we can estimate the conditional entropy $\mathbb{H}(Y|X)$ under some smoothness assumptions and also infer the model-agnostic error $\mathcal{P}_{e}$

However, classical Fano's inequality only holds for discrete random variables. For the case with the continuous features and discrete labels, it has not been shown how $\mathcal{P}_{e}$ can be controlled. In this paper, we prove a generalized version of Fano's inequality that holds for the continuous-featurediscrete-label scenario. Formally, for the continuous-X-discrete-Y case:

Definition 3. Hybrid Conditional Entropy

$$
\mathbb{H}(Y|X): =\mathbb{E}_{X}\left[-\sum_{y=1}^{|\mathcal{V}|}\mathbb{P}(Y=y|X)\log\mathbb{P}(Y=y|X)\right],\tag{2}
$$

where $\mathbb{P}(Y=y|X): =\mathbb{E}[\mathbf{1}(Y=y)|X]$

This definition of $\mathbb{H}(Y|X)$ is consistent with the classical definition, in the sense that both of them give the intuition that how much information or uncertainty is left for Y given X.

Next, to connect $\mathcal{P}_{e}$ and the hybrid $\mathbb{H}(Y|X)$ , we introduce an assumption on the function f

Definition 4. Smooth Discretization Property: The function $f:\mathcal{X}\mathcal{Y}$ satisfies the smooth discretization property if for every $y\in\mathcal{V},$ almost every $x\in\mathcal{X}$ (x a.e. in $\mathcal{X})$

$$
f(x)=y\iff\exists\delta>0\quad s . t .\quad\forall\tilde{x}\in B_{\delta}(x),\quad f(\tilde{x})=y,
$$

where $B_{\delta}(x): =\{\tilde{x}\in\Omega:\|\tilde{x}-x\|_{2}<\delta\}$ is a δ—neighborhood of x in X.

This assumption on the classifier function f is not unnatural considering f maps a continuous variable to a discrete variable. Without this assumption, it would be extremely hard to quantify the population error probability $P(f(X)\neq Y)$ since the behavior of f may be erratic. Furthermore, in the real data setting, this assumption is always satisfied for every classifier $f,$ as we can always construct a small enough neighborhood of each data point such that they are disjoint and assume f is a constant in each neighborhood. In this sense the assumption on $f$ is pretty minimal. Now we are ready to extend Fano's inequality:

Theorem 2. Fano's Inequality for Continuous Features: Let $\mathcal{P}_{e}$ be the minimum error probability, i.e.,

$$
{\mathcal{P}}_{e}=\operatorname*{inf}_{f}P(f(X)\neq Y)
$$

where f is any estimator of Y based on the observation X that satisfies the smooth discretization property. Then we have

$$
\mathbb{H}(\mathcal{P}_{e})+\mathcal{P}_{e}\log(m-1)\geq\mathbb{H}(Y|X),\tag{3}
$$

where $\mathbb H(\mathcal P_{e}): = -\mathcal P_{e}\log\mathcal P_{e}-(1-\mathcal P_{e})\log(1-\mathcal P_{e}).$

Proof. See appendix B.

3 Estimating the Lower Bound

It is natural to consider $\mathcal{P}_{e}$ defined in Theorem 2 as a measure of dataset difficulty. Unfortunately, direct estimation of $\mathcal{P}_{e}$ is impractical since one has to evaluate the estimation error against all possible estimators. However, theorem 2 provides an alternative towards estimating a lower bound on $\mathcal{P}_{\epsilon}$ through estimating the hybrid conditional entropy $\mathbb{H}(Y|X)$ defined in Equation (2).

3.1 Conditional Entropy Estimation

In real applications, direct calculation of hybrid conditional entropy $\mathbb{H}(Y|X)$ according to Definition 3 is impossible since $\mathbb{P}(Y=y|X)$ is unknown. However, similar to the conditional entropy for discrete random variables, the hybrid conditional entropy H $[(Y|X)$ can also be written as

$$
\mathbb{H}(Y|X)=\mathbb{H}(Y)-\sum_{y=1}^{|\mathcal{D}|}P(Y=y)\mathbb{K}\mathbb{L}(X|Y=y| |X).\tag{4}
$$

Please refer to Appendix A for a detailed proof of Equation (4). We also define the hybrid mutual information $\mathbb{I}(X;{\bar{Y}})$ , which is compatible with H(Y |X):

$$
\mathbb{I}(X;Y)=\sum_{y=1}^{|\mathcal{V}|}P(Y=y)\mathbb{K L}(X|Y=y| |X)\tag{5}
$$

In some benchmark datasets with balanced classes (e.g., CIFAR-10 and MNIST), $\mathbb{H}(Y|X)\ =$ log $\begin{array}{ r }{|\mathcal{V}| -\frac{1}{|\mathcal{V}|}\sum_{y=1}^{|\mathcal{V}|}\mathbb{K}\mathbb{L}(X|Y=y| |X)}\end{array}$ . This indicates that if a dataset has more classes and the features for different classes are closer to each other on average, then $\mathbb{H}(Y|X)$ would be larger.

3.2 A Variational KL Divergence Estimator using Neural Networks

We now discuss the practical design of an estimator for $\mathbb{K L}(X|Y)$ . Even though there are nonparametric KL divergence estimators such as kNN based techniques (Noshad et al., 2017; Perez-Cruz, 2008; Wang et al., 2009), they rely on some knowledge of the internal dimension of the data manifold. However, the internal dimension of the data manifold is usually much smaller than the dimension of the raw features and is hard to estimate. As an alternative, we design a neural networkbased estimator for KL divergence estimation, inspired by Belghazi et al. (2018). The estimator is based on the following theorem:

Donsker-Varadhan representation.

$$
\mathbb{K L}(\mathcal{P}| |\mathcal{Q})=\operatorname*{sup}_{T:\mathcal{X}\mathbb{R}}\mathbb{E}_{\mathcal{P}}[T]-\log\mathbb{E}_{\mathcal{Q}}[e^{T}]\tag{6}
$$

If we parameterize the function T using a neural network, we obtain:

$$
\mathbb{K L}(\mathcal{P}| |\mathcal{Q})\geq\operatorname*{sup}_{\theta\in\Theta}\mathbb{E}_{\mathcal{P}}[T_{\theta}]-\log\mathbb{E}_{\mathcal{Q}}[e^{T_{\theta}}],\tag{7}
$$

where θ represents the neural network parameters.

In our empirical evaluation, we optimize the empirical average instead of the expectation. However this may cause issues such as overftting. To mitigate this issue, we split the data into separate training and validation sets. The neural network models are trained on the training set and the estimation is made using the validation set. See Algorithm 1 for details.

3.3 DIME as a Difficulty Measure

Given that we are using a neural network model to estimate the KL divergence between $\mathcal{P}(X|y)$ and ${\mathcal{P}}(X)$ , according to Equation $(7),{\widehat{\mathbb{K L}}}(X|y| |X)\leq{\mathbb{K L}}(X|y| |X)$ . As a consequence, the estimated mutual information $\widehat{\mathbb{I}}(X;Y)\leq\mathbb{I}(X;Y)$ , which leads to a larger ${\widehat{\mathbb{H}}}(Y|X)$ . In the end, DIME could be larger as compared to true lower bound on $\mathcal{P}_{e}$

The caveat is that $\mathcal{P}_{e}$ is defined as a model-agnostic measure, but we use a neural network model to estimate its lower bound instead. The hope is, if the function class of the neural network is large enough, the gap between ${\widehat{\mathbb{K L}}}(X|y| |X)$ and $\mathbb{K L}(X|y| |X)$ is small enough so that DIME won't deviate too much from the true lower bound of $\mathcal{P}_{e}$ . We now describe our experiments for DIME using vision and language benchmark datasets.

A Hybrid Conditional Entropy

Consider the usual classification setting, X, representing the feature, is a random vector in $\mathbb{R}^{p};Y$ representing the label, is a random variable(or vector) in $\{1,\ldots,|\mathcal{V}|\}$ . Assume X is a continuous variable with density $p_{X}(x)$ for x in some compact domain $\Omega\subset\mathcal{X}\subset\mathbb{R}^{p}$ Can we define a hybrid conditional entropy $\operatorname{\mathbb{H}}(Y|X)$ while X is continuous and Y is discrete? We give a formal definition for this mixed-pair case and demonstrate that $\mathbb{H}(Y|X)$ defined in our way can be a good indicator for the hardness of classification on the data $(X,Y)$ , which is consistent with the classical definition in the sense that both of them give the intuition that how much information or uncertainty is left for Y given X.

Our definition is

$$
\mathbb{H}(Y|X): =\mathbb{E}_{X}\left[-\sum_{y=1}^{|\mathcal{V}|}\mathbb{P}(Y=y|X)\log\mathbb{P}(Y=y|X)\right],\tag{8}
$$

where $\mathbb{P}(Y=y|X): =\mathbb{E}[\mathbf{1}(Y=y)|X]$ . By the definition of conditional expectation (or probability), it is easy to check that

$$
\mathbb{E}[{\bf 1}(Y=y)|{X}]=\frac{P(Y=y)p(X|{Y=y})}{p_{X}(X)},\tag{9}
$$

where $p(x|Y=y),x\in\mathbb{R}^{p}$ is the conditional density function of X given $Y = y$ .Denote $p_{y}: =$ $P(Y=y)$ , we have

$$
\begin{array}{ l }{\displaystyle\mathbb{H}(Y|X)=\int_{\Omega}-\sum_{y=1}^{|\mathcal{V}|}p_{y}p(x|Y=y)\log\frac{p_{y}p(x|Y=y)}{p_{X}(x)}d x}\\ {\displaystyle= -\sum_{y=1}^{|\mathcal{V}|}p_{y}\log p_{y}-\sum_{y=1}^{|\mathcal{V}|}p_{y}\int_{\Omega}p(x|Y=y)\log\frac{p(x|Y=y)}{p_{X}(x)}d x}\\ {\displaystyle=\mathbb{H}(Y)-\sum_{y=1}^{|\mathcal{V}|}p_{y}\mathbb{E}\mathbb{L}(X|Y=y| |X).}\end{array}\tag{10}
$$

This proves (4).

We summarize some basic properties of $\mathbb{H}(Y|X)$ under our definition (8):

B Proof of Fano's Inequality for Continuous Features

We see the above essential properties for $\mathbb{H}(Y|X)$ have been preserved for the mixture case. Furthermore, we prove Fano's inequality still holds for our case. Let us restate Theorem 2 here:

steps.claim: For each class $c$, a network $T_{\theta_c}$ is trained by $\theta_c = \arg\max_{\theta_c} \frac{1}{|S_c|}\sum_{S_c} T_{\theta_c}(x_i) - \log[\frac{1}{b}\sum_j \exp T_{\theta_c}(x_j)]$, and the KL is then evaluated on the held-out set as $\widehat{\mathbb{KL}}_{\theta_c} = \frac{1}{|S_c^e|}\sum_{S_c^e} T_{\theta_c}(x_i^e) - \log[\frac{1}{b}\sum_j \exp T_{\theta_c}(x_j^e)]$.

This estimator is the finite-sample version of the neural-network KL bound of Eq. (7): the population term $\log \mathbb{E}_{\mathcal{Q}}[e^{T}]$ is replaced by the empirical Monte-Carlo quantity $\log[\frac{1}{b}\sum_j \exp T_{\theta_c}(x_j)]$.

The population Donsker-Varadhan / MINE bound (Eq. 7) gives $\mathbb{KL}(\mathcal{P}||\mathcal{Q}) \geq \sup_{\theta \in \Theta} \mathbb{E}_{\mathcal{P}}[T_\theta] - \log \mathbb{E}_{\mathcal{Q}}[e^{T_\theta}]$.
According to Equation (7), the neural-network estimate satisfies $\widehat{\mathbb{KL}}(X|y \,||\, X) \leq \mathbb{KL}(X|y \,||\, X)$.
Consequently the estimated hybrid mutual information satisfies $\widehat{\mathbb{I}}(X;Y) \leq \mathbb{I}(X;Y)$.
Therefore the estimated conditional entropy satisfies $\widehat{\mathbb{H}}(Y|X) \geq \mathbb{H}(Y|X)$ (DIME yields a larger $\widehat{\mathbb{H}}(Y|X)$).
Hence DIME, obtained by solving Fano's inequality (Eq. 3) with $\widehat{\mathbb{H}}(Y|X)$, is $\geq$ and thus a valid conservative estimate of the true lower bound on $\mathcal{P}_e$.

label: flawed
error_explanation: Step 4 asserts $\widehat{\mathbb{KL}} \leq \mathbb{KL}$ "according to Equation (6)", but Eq. (6) is the POPULATION Donsker-Varadhan bound, in which $\log\mathbb{E}_{\mathcal{Q}}[e^{T}]$ is an exact expectation. Algorithm 1's estimator replaces this with a Monte-Carlo average inside the log, $\log[\frac{1}{b}\sum_j \exp T_{\theta_c}(x_j)]$. By Jensen's inequality, a Monte-Carlo estimate of a log-expectation is a stochastic LOWER bound of the true log-expectation; subtracting it therefore makes $\widehat{\mathbb{KL}}$ a stochastic UPPER bound of the proposed KL lower bound, so $\widehat{\mathbb{KL}} \leq \mathbb{KL}$ is NOT guaranteed. This severs the entire downstream chain ($\widehat{\mathbb{I}} \leq \mathbb{I} \Rightarrow \widehat{\mathbb{H}}(Y|X) \geq \mathbb{H}(Y|X) \Rightarrow$ DIME lower-bounds $\mathcal{P}_e$): the procedure computes an upper bound of a lower bound, which does not preserve the inequality direction. The empirical MINE estimator is biased and, even de-biased, cannot in general be claimed to bound $\mathcal{P}_e$.

A missing additive term $\epsilon_{CS}$ (the cost-sensitive learner's regret, called $\epsilon_{approx}$ in the corrected paper) must appear additively in Eq. context:
Q-learning and Deep Q-Networks (DQNs). Markov decision processes (MDPs) are at the core of RL. Our focus is on discounted discrete-time MDPs, which are defined by tuple $(S,\mathcal{A},R,P,\gamma,d_{0})$ where S is a set of states (each with dimensionality N), A represents a set of discrete actions, $R:S\times\mathcal{A}\mathbb{R}$ is the reward function, and $P:\bar{S\times A}\bar{\mathcal{P}(S)}$ is the transition function with P(·) defining the set of probability measures, $\gamma\in [0,1]$ is the discount factor, and $d_{0}\in{\mathcal{P}}(S)$ is the distribution over the initial state. At time step t, the agent is in the state $s_{t}\in S$ After choosing action $a_{t}\in A .$ , the agent transitions to the next state $s_{t+1}\sim P(s_{t},a_{t})$ and receives reward $R(s_{t},a_{t})$ . The goal is to learn ${\mathrm{a~p o l i c y~}}\pi:S{\mathcal{P}}(A)$ that maximizes the expected cumulative reward $\mathbb{E}[\sum_{t}\gamma^{t}r_{t}]$ .

Definition 2 (Certification for per-state action). Given a trained network $Q^{\pi}$ with policy π, we define the robustness certification for per-state action as the maximum perturbation magnitude , such that for any perturbation $\delta\in B^{\bar{\varepsilon}}$ , the predicted action under the perturbed state will be the same as the action taken in the clean environment, $i . e .,\pi(s+\delta)=\pi(s),\mathcal{\overline{{\forall}}}\delta\in\mathcal{B}^{\bar{\varepsilon}}$

Definition 3 (Cumulative reward). Let $P:\mathcal{S}\times\mathcal{A}\mathcal{P}(\mathcal{S})$ be the transition function of the environment with $\mathcal{P}(\cdot)$ defining the set of probability measures. Let $R,d_{0},\gamma,Q^{\pi}$ , π be the reward function, initial state distribution, discount factor, a given trained Q-network, and the corresponding greedy policy as introduced in Section $2,J(\pi)$ represents the cumulative reward and $J_{\varepsilon}(\pi)$ represents the perturbed cumulative reward under perturbations $\delta_{t}\in B^{\varepsilon}$ at each time step t:

$$
J(\pi): =\sum_{t=0}^{\infty}\gamma^{t}R(s_{t},\pi(s_{t})),
$$

$$
\mathrm{where}\ s_{t+1}\sim P(s_{t},a_{t}),s_{0}\sim d_{0},
$$

and

$$
J_{\varepsilon}(\pi): =\sum_{t=0}^{\infty}\gamma^{t}R(s_{t},\pi(s_{t}+\delta_{t})),\tag{4}
$$

$$
\mathrm{where}\ s_{t+1}\sim P(s_{t},\pi(s_{t}+\delta_{t})),s_{0}\sim d_{0}.
$$

The randomness of $J(\pi)$ arises from the environment dynamics, while that of $J_{\varepsilon}(\pi)$ includes additional randomness from the perturbations $\{\delta_{t}\}$ . We focus on a finite horizon H in this paper, where a sufficiently large H can approximate $J(\pi)$ and $J_{\varepsilon}(\pi)$ to arbitrary precision when $\gamma < 1$

Definition 4 (Robustness certification for cumulative reward). The robustness certification for cumulative reward is the lower bound of perturbed cumulative reward J such that $\underline{{J}}~\leq~J_{\varepsilon}(\pi)$ under perturbation in $B^{\varepsilon}=\{\delta\in\mathbb{R}^{n}\mid\|\delta\|_{2}\leq\varepsilon\}$ applied to all time steps.

Let $Q^{\pi}$ be the action-value function given by the trained network Q with policy π. We derive a smoothed function ${\widetilde{Q}}^{\pi}$ through per-state local smoothing. Specifically, at each time step t, for each action $a\in{\mathcal{A}}$ , we draw random noise from a Gaussian distribution $\mathcal{N}(\mathrm{~0~},\sigma^{2}I_{N})$ to smooth $Q^{\pi}(\cdot,a)$

$$
\widetilde{Q}^{\pi}(s_{t},a): =\mathbb{E}_{\Delta_{t}\sim\mathcal{N}(0,\sigma^{2}I_{N})}Q^{\pi}(s_{t}+\Delta_{t},a)\quad\forall s_{t}\in\mathcal{S},a\in\mathcal{A},\mathrm{~a n d~}\tilde{\pi}(s_{t}): =\operatorname*{argmax}_{a}\widetilde{Q}^{\pi}(s_{t},a)\quad\forall s_{t}\in\mathcal{S}.\tag{5}
$$

Definition 5 (σ-randomized trajectory and σ-randomized policy). Given a state trajectory $\left(s_{0},s_{1},\ldots,s_{H-1}\right)$ of length H where $s_{t+1}\sim P(s_{t},\pi(s_{t})),s_{0}\sim d_{0}.$ with π the greedy policy of the action-value function $Q^{\pi}$ , we derive a σ-randomized trajectory as $(s_{0}^{\prime},s_{1}^{\prime},\ldots,s_{H-1}^{\prime})$ , where $s_{t+1}^{\prime}\sim$ $P(s_{t}^{\prime},\pi(s_{t}^{\prime}+\Delta_{t})),\Delta_{t}\sim\mathcal{N}(0,\sigma^{2}I_{N})$ , and $s_{0}^{\prime}=s_{0}\sim d_{0}$ We correspondingly define a σ-randomized policy π' based on π in the following form: $\overline{{\pi}}^{\prime}(s_{t}): =\pi(s_{t}+\Delta_{t})$ where $\bar{\Delta_{t}}\sim\mathcal N(0,\sigma^{2}I_{N})$ .

Let the operator $\oplus$ concatenates given input states or noise that are added to each state. The sampled noise sequence is denoted by $\Delta\bar{=}\oplus_{t=0}^{H-\bar{1}}\Delta_{t}$ , where $\Delta_{t}\sim\mathcal{N}(0,\sigma^{2}I_{N})$

Definition 6 (Perturbed return function). Let $R,P,\gamma,d_{0}$ be the reward function, transition function, discount factor, and initial state distribution in Definition 3. We define a bounded perturbed return function $F_{\pi}:\mathbb{R}^{H\times N}[J_{\operatorname*{min}},J_{\operatorname*{max}}]$ representing cumulative reward with potential perturbation $\delta \colon$

$$
F_{\pi}\left(\oplus_{t=0}^{H-1}\delta_{t}\right): =\sum_{t=0}^{H}\gamma^{t}R(s_{t},\pi(s_{t}+\delta_{t})),\quad{\mathrm{w h e r e~}}s_{t+1}\sim P(s_{t},\pi(s_{t}+\delta_{t})),s_{0}\sim d_{0}.\tag{6}
$$

We can see when there is no perturbation $(\delta_{t}=\mathbf{0}),F_{\pi}(\oplus_{t=0}^{H-1}\mathbf{0})=J(\pi)$ ; when there are adversarial perturbations $\delta_{t}\in B^{\varepsilon}$ at each time step, $F_{\pi}(\oplus_{t=0}^{H-1}\delta_{t})=J_{\varepsilon}(\pi)$ ,i.e., perturbed cumulative reward.

Mean Smoothing: Expectation bound. Here we propose to sample noise sequences $\Delta$ to perform global smoothing for the entire state trajectory, and calculate the lower bound of the expected perturbed cumulative reward $\mathbb{E}_{\Delta}\left[J_{\varepsilon}(\pi^{\prime})\right]$ under all possible $\ell_{2}$ -bounded perturbations within magnitude ε. The expectation is over the noise sequence $\Delta$ involved in the σ-randomized policy $\pi^{\prime}$ in Definition 5.

theorems.statement: Lemma 2 (Lipschitz continuity of the smoothed value function). Given the action-value function $Q^{\pi}:S\times{\mathcal{A}}[V_{\operatorname*{min}},V_{\operatorname*{max}}]$ , the smoothed function ${\widetilde{Q}}^{\pi}$ with smoothing parameter σ is L-Lipschitz continuous with $\begin{array}{ r }{L=\frac{V_{\mathrm{max}}-V_{\mathrm{min}}}{\sigma}\sqrt{2/\pi}}\end{array}$ w.r.t. the state input.

steps.claim:
Proof. To prove Lemma 2, we leverage the technique in the proof for Lemma 1 of Salman et al.   
(2019) in their Appendix A.

For each action $a\in{\mathcal{A}}.$ ,our smoothed value function is

$$
\widetilde{Q}^{\pi}(s,a): =\underset{\Delta\sim\mathcal{N}(0,\sigma^{2}I_{N})}{\mathbb{E}}Q^{\pi}(s+\Delta,a)=\frac{1}{(2\pi)^{N/2}\sigma^{N}}\int_{\mathbb{R}^{n}}Q^{\pi}(t,a)\exp\left(-\frac{1}{2\sigma^{2}}\|s-t\|^{2}\right)d t .
$$

Taking the gradient w.r.t. s, we obtain

$$
\nabla_{s}\widetilde{Q}^{\pi}(s,a)=\frac{1}{(2\pi)^{N/2}\sigma^{N}}\int_{\mathbb{R}^{n}}Q^{\pi}(t,a)\frac{1}{\sigma^{2}}(t-s)\exp\left(-\frac{1}{2\sigma^{2}}\|s-t\|^{2}\right)d t .
$$

For any unit direction u, we have

$$
\begin{array}{ r l }&{u\cdot\nabla_{s}\widetilde{Q}^{\pi}(s,a)\leq\displaystyle\frac{1}{(2\pi)^{N/2}\sigma^{N}}\int_{\mathbb R^{n}}\frac{V_{\operatorname*{max}}-V_{\operatorname*{min}}}{\sigma^{2}}\displaystyle|u(s-t)|\exp\left(-\frac{1}{2\sigma^{2}}\|s-t\|^{2}\right)d t}\\ &{\quad\quad\quad=\displaystyle\frac{V_{\operatorname*{max}}-V_{\operatorname*{min}}}{\sigma^{2}}\cdot\int_{\mathbb R^{n}}\frac{1}{(2\pi)^{1/2}\sigma}|s_{i}-t|\exp\left(-\frac{1}{2\sigma^{2}}|s_{i}-t|^{2}\right)d t}\\ &{\quad\quad\quad\cdot\displaystyle\prod_{j\neq i}\int_{\mathbb R^{n}}\frac{1}{(2\pi)^{1/2}\sigma}\exp\left(-\frac{1}{2\sigma^{2}}|s_{j}-t|^{2}\right)d t}\\ &{\quad\quad\quad=\displaystyle\frac{V_{\operatorname*{max}}-V_{\operatorname*{min}}}{\sigma}\sqrt{\frac{2}{\pi}}}\end{array}
$$
Thus, ${\widetilde{Q}}^{\pi}$ is L-Lipschitz continuous with $\begin{array}{ r }{L=\frac{V_{\mathrm{max}}-V_{\mathrm{min}}}{\sigma}\sqrt{2/\pi}}\end{array}$ w.r.t. the state input.

Theorem 2. Let $Q^{\pi}:S\times{\mathcal{A}}[V_{\operatorname*{min}},V_{\operatorname*{max}}]$ be a trained value network, ${\widetilde{Q}}^{\pi}$ be the smoothed function with (5). $$
r_{t}=\frac{\sigma}{2}\left(\Phi^{-1}\left(\frac{\widetilde{Q}^{\pi}(s_{t},a_{1})-V_{\operatorname*{min}}}{V_{\operatorname*{max}}-V_{\operatorname*{min}}}\right)-\Phi^{-1}\left(\frac{\widetilde{Q}^{\pi}(s_{t},a_{2})-V_{\operatorname*{min}}}{V_{\operatorname*{max}}-V_{\operatorname*{min}}}\right)\right),\tag{7}

error_explanation: The certified lower bound is asserted for every perturbation sequence, including one chosen ADAPTIVELY, i.e. where the adversary picks $\delta_t$ as a function of the smoothed actions/states already observed at steps $0,\ldots,t$. However, the proof of this bound at Step 7 lifts the single-shot Lipschitz / randomized-smoothing argument, whose validity requires generating the $m$ randomized trajectories from a KNOWN, pre-committed noise sequence $\{\delta_t\}_{t=0}^{H-1}$. This silently assumes a NON-ADAPTIVE adversary. As the reviewer put it, 'the presented Lemma 2 only holds if the attacker commits to the values of $\zeta_t$ beforehand,' and the authors concede it 'cannot be applied against an adaptive attacker' (a stated limitation of CROP-GRe). The underlying Lipschitz constant established earlier (Step 3) is itself correct as a property of a fixed input; the missing-assumption error is that Step 7 uses it to certify against an ARBITRARY adaptive adversary without assuming the perturbation/noise sequence is fixed and known in advance.

An algorithm has no-regret if lim $_{N\to\infty}\mathrm{Regret}(N)/N\to 0$ for any sequence of losses with bounded gradients. For example, Kingma & Ba (2015) prove that Adam has no-regret:

Theorem 2 (Adam has no-regret, (Kingma & Ba, 2015)).

Suppose the the losses $\ell^{n}$ have bounded gradients $\|\nabla_{\mathbf{W}}\ell^{n}(\mathbf{W})\|_{2}\leq G a n d\|\nabla_{\mathbf{W}}\ell^{n}(\mathbf{W})\|_{\infty}\leq G$ for all $\mathbf{W}\in\mathcal{H}$ and suppose that the weights chosen by the algorithm $\ L\ L_{\{a t i s f y}\|\mathbf{W}^{m}-\mathbf{W}^{n}\|_{2}\leq D$ and $\|\mathbf{W}^{m}-\mathbf{W}^{n}\|_{\infty}\leq D$ for all $m,n\in\{1,\ldots,N\}$ . Then Adam satisfies

$$
\mathsf{Regret}(N)/N\le O\left(1/\sqrt{N}\right)\quad f o r a l l N\ge 1 .\tag{3}
$$

The regret of gradient descent, AdaGrad (Duchi et al., 2011), mirror descent and a variety of related algorithms satisfy (3), albeit with different constant terms that are hidden in the big-O notation. Finally, the $1/\sqrt{N}$ rate is also lower-bound. It cannot be improved without additional assumptions.

Consider a network with $L - 1$ hidden layers and weight matrices $\mathbf{W}: =\{\mathbf{W}_{1},\dots,\mathbf{W}_{L}\}$ . Let $\mathbf{x}_{\mathrm{0}}$ denote the input. For hidden layers $l\in\{\bar{1},\ldots,L-1\bar\}$ }, set $\mathbf{a}_{l}=\mathbf{W}_{l}\cdot\mathbf{x}_{l-1}$ and ${\mathbf x}_{l}=s({\mathbf a}_{l})$ where $s(\cdot)$ is applied coordinatewise. The last layer outputs $\mathbf{x}_{L}=\mathbf{a}_{L}=\mathbf{W}_{L}\cdot\mathbf{x}_{L-1}$ . Let $p_{l}$ denote the size of the $l^{\mathrm{th}}$ layer; $p_{0}$ is the size of the input and $p_{L}$ is the size of the output. Suppose the loss $\ell(\mathbf{f},y)$ is smooth and convex in the first argument. The training data is $(\mathbf{x}^{d},y^{d})_{d=1}^{D}.$ The network is trained on stochastic samples from the training data on a series of rounds $n=1,\ldots,N$ For simplicity we assume minibatch size $1 ;$ the results generalize without difficulty.

We recall backprop using notation from Martens et al. (2012). Let $\mathbf{J_{b}^{a}}$ denote the Jacobian matrix of the vector a with respect to the vector b. By the chain rule the gradient decomposes as

$$
\nabla_{\mathbf{W}_{l}}\ell\big(\mathbf{f}_{\mathbf{W}}(\mathbf{x}_{0}),y\big)=\underbrace{\mathbf{J}_{L}^{\mathcal{E}}\cdot\mathbf{J}_{L-1}^{L}\cdot\cdot\cdot\mathbf{J}_{l}^{l+1}}_{\delta_{l}}\otimes\mathbf{x}_{l-1}=\underbrace{\mathbf{J}_{L}^{\mathcal{E}}}_{\nabla_{\mathbf{f}}\ell(\mathbf{f},y)}\cdot\underbrace{\mathbf{J}_{l}^{L}\otimes\mathbf{x}_{l-1}}_{\nabla_{\mathbf{W}_{l}}\mathbf{f}_{\mathbf{W}}(\mathbf{x}_{0})= :\mathbf{G}_{l}}\tag{4}
$$

where $\delta_{l}=\mathbf{J}_{l}^{\varepsilon}$ is the backpropagated error computed recursively via $\delta_{l}=\delta_{l+1}\cdot\mathbf{J}_{l}^{l+1}.^{2}$ The middle expression in (4) is the standard representation of backpropagated gradients. The expression on the right factorizes the backpropagated error $\delta_{l}=\mathbf{J}_{L}^{\varepsilon}\cdot\mathbf{\hat{J}}_{l}^{L}$ into the gradient of the loss $\mathbf{J}_{L}^{\mathcal{E}}$ and the Jacobian $\mathbf{J}_{l}^{L}$ between layers, which describes gradient flow within the network.

The first-order Taylor approximation to a differentiable function $f:\mathbb{R}\mathbb{R}$ near a is $T_{a}(x)=$ $f(a)+f^{\prime}(a)\cdot(x-a)$ . The neural Taylor approximation for a fully connected network is as follows. Definition 2. The Jacobian tensor of layer $l,{\bf G}_{l}: ={\bf J}_{{l}}^{L}\otimes{\bf x}_{l-1}$ , is the gradient of the output of the neural network with respect to the weights of layer l. It is the outer product of a $\left(p_{L}\times p_{l}\right)$ -matrix with a pl−1-vector, and so is a $(p_{L},p_{l},p_{l-1})– t e n s o r$

Given $\mathbf{G}_{l}$ and $\left(p_{l}\times p_{l-1}\right)$ -matrix V, the expression $\langle\mathbf{G}_{l},\mathbf{V}\rangle: =\mathbf{J}_{l}^{L}\cdot\mathbf{V}\cdot\mathbf{x}_{l-1}$ is the pL-vector computed via matrix-matrix-vector multiplication. The neural Taylor approximation to f in a neighborhood of $\mathbf{W}^{n}$ , given input $\mathbf{x}_{0}^{n}$ , is the first-order Taylor expansion

$$
\mathbf{T}^{n}(\mathbf{V}): =\mathbf{f}_{\mathbf{W}^{n}}(\mathbf{x}_{0}^{n})+\sum_{l=1}^{L}\left.\mathbf{G}_{l},\mathbf{V}_{l}-\mathbf{W}_{l}^{n}\right.\approx\mathbf{f}_{\mathbf{V}}(\mathbf{x}_{0}^{n}).
$$

Finally, the Taylor loss of the network on round n is $\mathcal{T}^{n}(\mathbf{V})=\ell(\mathbf{T}^{n}(\mathbf{V}),y^{n})$

The Taylor approximation to layer l is $\mathbf{T}_{l}^{n}(\mathbf{V}_{l}): =\mathbf{f}_{\mathbf{W}^{n}}\big(\mathbf{x}_{0}^{n}\big)+\big\langle\mathbf{G}_{l},\mathbf{V}_{l}-\mathbf{W}_{l}^{n}\big\rangle$ . We can also construct the Taylor approximation to neuron α in layer l. Let the pL-vector $\mathbf{J}_{\alpha}^{L}: =\mathbf{\dot{J}}_{l}^{L}[:,\alpha]$ denote the Jacobian with respect to neuron α and let the $\left(p_{L}\times p_{l-1}\right)$ -matrix $\mathbf{G}_{\alpha}: =\mathbf{J}_{\alpha}^{L}\otimes\mathbf{x}_{l-1}$ denote the Jacobian with respect to the weights of neuron α. The Taylor approximation to neuron α is $\mathbf{T}_{\alpha}^{n}(\mathbf{V}_{\alpha}): =\mathbf{f}_{\mathbf{W}^{n}}(\mathbf{x}_{0}^{n})+\left.\mathbf{G}_{\alpha},\mathbf{V}_{\alpha}-\mathbf{W}_{\alpha}^{n}\right.$

The Taylor losses are the simplest non-trivial (i.e. non-affine) convex functions encoding the information generated by backprop, see section A.4.

2.3 Empirical Analysis of Online Neural Optimization and Regret

This section empirically investigates the Taylor optimum and regret terms in theorem 3 on two tasks:

Autoencoder trained on MNIST. Dense layers with architecture $784\to 50\to 30\to 20\to 30\to$ 50 → 784 and ReLU non-linearities. Trained with MSE loss using minibatches of 64.

Convnet trained on CIFAR-10. Three convolutional layers with stack size 64 and $5 \times 5$ receptive fields, ReLU non-linearities and $2 \times 2$ max-pooling. Followed by a 192 unit fully-connected layer with ReLU before a ten-dimensional fully-connected output layer. Trained with cross-entropy loss using minibatches of 128.

For both tasks we compare the optimization performance of Adam, RMSProp and SGD (figure 6). Learning rates were tuned for optimal performance. Additional parameters for Adam and RMSProp were left at default. For the convnet all three methods perform equally well: achieving a small loss and an accuracy $\mathrm{of}\geq 99\%$ on the training set. However, SGD exhibits slightly more variance. For the autoencoder, although it is an extremely simple model, SGD with the best (fixed) learning rate performs significantly worse than the adaptive optimizers.

The neuronal and layer-wise regret are evaluated for each model. At every iteration we record the training error  the left-hand-side of eq. (5). To evaluate the Taylor loss, we record the input to the neuron/layer, it's weights, the output of the network and the gradient tensor $\mathbf{G}_{l}$ After training, we minimize the Taylor loss with respect to V to find the Taylor optimum at each round. The regret is the difference between the observed training loss and the optimal Taylor loss.

3.1 The Role of Activation Configurations in Optimization

We describe how configurations of active neurons relate to smooth regions of rectifier networks and to neural Taylor approximations. Recall that the loss of a neural net on its training data is $\begin{array}{ r }{\hat{\ell}(\mathbf{W})=\frac{1}{D}\sum_{d=1}^{D}\ell\big(f_{\mathbf{W}}(\mathbf{x}^{d}),y^{d}\big)}\end{array}$

Definition 3. Enumerate the data as $[D]=\{1,\dots,D\}$ and neurons as $[ M ]$ .The activation configuration A(W) is a $(D\times M)$ binary matrix representing the active neurons for each input. The set of all possible activation configurations corresponds to the set of all $(D\times M)$ binary matrices.

Observation 3 (activation configurations correspond to smooth regions in rectifier networks).

A parameter value exhibits a kink in iff an infinitesimal change alters the of activation configuration, i.e.  is not smooth at W iff there is a V s.t. $\pmb{\mathcal{A}}(\mathbf{W})\neq\pmb{\mathcal{A}}(\mathbf{W}+\delta\mathbf{V})$ for all $\delta > 0 .$

---

A.1 Background on Convex Optimization

A continuous function $f$ is smooth if there exists a $\beta > 0$ such that $\|\nabla f(\mathbf{x})-\nabla f(\mathbf{y})\|_{2}\ \leq$ $\beta\cdot\|\mathbf{x}-\mathbf{y}\|_{2}$ for all x and y in the domain. Rectifiers are not smooth for any value of β.

Nonsmooth convex functions. Let $X\subset\mathbb{R}^{p}$ be a convex set contained in a ball of radius R. Let $\ell : X \to$ R be a convex function. Section 3.1 of (Bubeck, 2015) shows that projected gradient descent has convergence guarantee

$$
\ell\left({\frac{1}{N}}\sum_{n=1}^{N}\mathbf{w}^{n}\right)-\ell(\mathbf{w}^{*})\leq O\left({\frac{1}{\sqrt{N}}}\right)
$$

where $\mathbf{w}^{n}$ are generated by gradient descent and $\mathbf{w}^{*}: =\mathrm{argmin}_{\mathbf{w}\in X}\ell(\mathbf{w})$ is the minimizer of l. It is also shown, section 3.5, that

$$
\operatorname*{min}_{1\le n\le N}\ell(\mathbf{w}^{n})-\ell(\mathbf{w}^{*})\geq\Omega\left(\frac{1}{\sqrt{N}}\right)
$$

where the weights are in the span of the previously observed gradients: $\mathbf{w}^{n}\in$ span $\left\{\nabla\ell(\mathbf{w}^{1}),\ldots,\nabla\ell(\mathbf{w}^{n-1})\right\}$ for all $n\in\{1,\ldots,\bar{N}\}$ •

The gradient of a convex function increases monotonically. That is

$$
\left.\nabla\ell(\mathbf{w})-\nabla\ell(\mathbf{v}),\mathbf{w}-\mathbf{v}\right.\geq 0
$$

for all points w, v where the gradient exists. Gradients at one point of a nonsmooth convex function therefore do contain information about other points, although not as much information as in the smooth case. In contrast, the gradients of nonsmooth nonconvex functions can vary wildly as shown in Fig. 1.

Smooth convex functions. In the smooth setting, gradient descent converges at rate $\textstyle{\frac{1}{N}}$ . The lower bound for convergence is even better, $\scriptstyle{\frac{1}{N^{2}}}$ . The lower bound is achieved by Nesterov's accelerated gradient descent method.

theorems.statement: Observation 3 (activation configurations correspond to smooth regions in rectifier networks). Assume the per-example loss $\ell(\mathbf{f},y)$ is smooth in its first argument. theorems.statement:
Theorem 3 (no-regret relative to Taylor optimum).

Suppose, as in Theorem 2, the Taylor losses have bounded gradients and the weights of the neural network have bounded diameter during training. Suppose the neural net is optimized by an algorithm with Regret $(N)\leq O({\sqrt{N}})$ such as gradient descent, AdaGrad, Adam or mirror descent.

Network guarantee: The running average of the training error of the neural network satisfies

$$
\underbrace{\frac{1}{N}\sum_{n=1}^{N}\ell\left(f_{\mathbf{W}^{n}}\left(\mathbf{x}_{0}^{n}\right),y^{n}\right)}_{\text{ running average of training errors }}\leq\underbrace{\min_{\mathbf{V}}\left\{\frac{1}{N}\sum_{n=1}^{N}\mathcal{T}^{n}(\mathbf{V})\right\}}_{\text{ Taylor optimum }}+\underbrace{O\left(\frac{1}{\sqrt{N}}\right)}_{\mathrm{Regret}(N)/N}.\tag{6}
$$

• Layer-wise / Neuron-wise guarantee: The Taylor loss of [layer-l / neuron-α] is $\mathcal{T}_{l/\alpha}^{\bar{n}}(\mathbf{V}_{l/\alpha}): =\ell(\mathbf{T}_{l/\alpha}^{n}(\mathbf{V}_{l/\alpha}),y^{n})$ . Then,

$$
\underbrace{\frac{1}{N}\sum_{n=1}^{N}\ell\left(f_{\mathbf{W}^{n}}\left(\mathbf{x}_{0}^{n}\right),y^{n}\right)}_{\text{ running average of training errors }}\leq\underbrace{\min_{\mathbf{V}_{l/\alpha}}\left\{\frac{1}{N}\sum_{n=1}^{N}\mathcal{T}_{l/\alpha}^{n}(\mathbf{V}_{l/\alpha})\right\}}_{\text{ layer-wise/neuronal Taylor optimum }}+\underbrace{O\left(\frac{1}{\sqrt{N}}\right)}_{\mathrm{Regret}(N)/N}.\tag{5}
$$

steps.claim:
The Taylor loss has three key properties by construction: T1. The Taylor loss $\mathcal{T}^{n}$ coincides with the loss at $\mathbf{W}^{n}$

$$
\ell(\mathbf{f}_{\mathbf{W}^{n}}(\mathbf{x}_{0}^{n}),y^{n})=\mathcal{T}^{n}(\mathbf{V})_{|\mathbf{V}=\mathbf{W}^{n}}
$$

T2. The Taylor loss gradient ${\mathcal{T}}^{n}$ coincides with the loss gradient at $\mathbf{W}^{n}$

$$
\nabla_{\mathbf{W}}\ell(\mathbf{f}_{\mathbf{W}^{n}}(\mathbf{x}_{0}^{n}),y^{n})=\nabla_{\mathbf{V}}\mathcal{T}^{n}(\mathbf{V})_{|\mathbf{V}=\mathbf{W}^{n}}
$$

T3. The Taylor losses are convex functions of V because $\ell(\mathbf{f},y)$ is convex in its first argument and convexity is invariant under affine maps. If  is a convex function, then so is $g(x)=$ $\ell(Ax+b)$ , where $A\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times n}$ and $b\in\mathbb{R}^{m}$ •

By T1, the training loss, i.e. the left-hand side of (6), exactly coincides with the Taylor losses. By T2, the gradients of the Taylor losses exactly coincide with the errors computed by backpropagation on the training losses. That is, the training loss over n rounds is indistinguishable from the Taylor losses to the first order:

$$

error_explanation: Step 1 claims that to prove $\{a_n\}$ converges it suffices to show the successive differences vanish, $\lVert a_n - a_{n+1}\rVert \to 0$. This sufficiency claim is invalid: successive differences tending to zero does NOT imply the sequence is Cauchy and hence does NOT imply convergence. Being Cauchy requires the strictly stronger condition $\lVert a_n - a_m\rVert \to 0$ for ALL $m>n$ (equivalently $\sup_{m>n}\lVert a_n-a_m\rVert\to 0$ in a complete space). Classic counterexamples where $\lVert a_n-a_{n+1}\rVert\to 0$ yet the sequence diverges include the partial sums of the harmonic series and $a_n=\sqrt{n}$. The false reduction is introduced here at step 1; steps 2-3 merely establish the successive-difference condition and draw the unwarranted convergence conclusion from it.

The dataset is denoted by $\{(x_i,y_i)\}_{i=1}^n$ where $x_i\in\mathbb R^d$ and $y_i\in\{-1,+1\}$. For simplicity, we assume that $\|x_i\|_2=1$ for any $1\le i\le n$.

The two-layer network has weight matrices $W\in\mathbb R^{m\times d}$ and $a\in\mathbb R^m$. We use the following parameterization:

$$
f(x;W,a):=\frac{1}{\sqrt m}\sum_{s=1}^m a_s\sigma\big(\langle w_s,x\rangle\big),
$$

with initialization

$$
w_{s,0}\sim\mathcal N(0,I_d),\quad\text{and}\quad a_s\sim\mathrm{unif}\big(\{-1,+1\}\big).
$$

Note that $w_{s,t}$ denotes the $s$-th row of $W$ at step $t$. We fix $a$ and only train $W$. We consider the ReLU activation $\sigma(z):=\max\{0,z\}$.

We use the logistic (binary cross entropy) loss $\ell(z):=\ln\big(1+\exp(-z)\big)$ and gradient descent. For any $1\le i\le n$ and any $W$, let $f_i(W):=f(x_i;W,a)$. The empirical risk and its gradient are given by

$$
\widehat{\mathcal R}(W):=\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n\ell\big(y_if_i(W)\big),\quad\text{and}\quad\nabla\widehat{\mathcal R}(W)=\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n\ell'\big(y_if_i(W)\big)y_i\nabla f_i(W).
$$

For any $t\ge0$, the gradient descent step is given by $W_{t+1}:=W_t-\eta_t\nabla\widehat{\mathcal R}(W_t)$. Also define

$$
f_i^{(t)}(W):=\big\langle\nabla f_i(W_t),W\big\rangle,\quad\text{and}\quad\widehat{\mathcal R}^{(t)}(W):=\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n\ell\Big(y_if_i^{(t)}(W)\Big).
$$

Note that $f_i^{(t)}(W_t)=f_i(W_t)$. This property generally holds due to homogeneity: for any $W$ and any $1\le s\le m$,

$$
\frac{\partial f_i}{\partial w_s}=\frac{1}{\sqrt m}a_s\mathbb 1\big[\langle w_s,x_i\rangle>0\big]x_i,\quad\text{and}\quad\Big\langle\frac{\partial f_i}{\partial w_s},w_s\Big\rangle=\frac{1}{\sqrt m}a_s\sigma\big(\langle w_s,x_i\rangle\big),

In this section, we consider a fixed training set and empirical risk minimization. We first state our assumption on the separability of the NTK, and then give our main result and a proof sketch.

The key idea of the NTK is to do the first-order Taylor approximation:

$$
f(x;W,a)\approx f(x;W_{0},a)+\left.\nabla_{W}f(x;W_{0},a),W-W_{0}\right..
$$

In other words, we want to do learning using the features given by $\nabla f_{i}(W_{0})\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times d}$ A natural assumption is that there exists $\overline{{U}}\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times d}$ which can separate $\{(\nabla f_{i}(W_{0}),y_{i})\}_{i=1}^{n}$ with a positive margin:

$$
\operatorname*{min}_{1\leq i\leq n}\left(y_{i}\left.\overline{{U}},\nabla f_{i}(W_{0})\right.\right)=\operatorname*{min}_{1\leq i\leq n}\left(y_{i}\frac{1}{\sqrt{m}}\sum_{s=1}^{m}a_{s}\langle\bar{u}_{s},x_{i}\rangle\mathbb{1}\left[\langle w_{s,0},x_{i}\rangle>0\right]\right)>0 .\tag{1}
$$

The infinite-width limit of eq. (1) is formalized as Assumption 1, with an additional bound on the $(2,\infty)$ norm of the separator. A concrete construction of $\overline{U}$ using Assumption 1 is given in eq. (2).

Let $\mu_{\mathcal{N}}$ denote the Gaussian measure on $\mathbb{R}^{d}$ , given by the Gaussian density with respect to the Lebesgue measure on $\mathbb{R}^{d}$ . We consider the following Hilbert space

$$
\mathcal{H}: =\left\{w:\mathbb{R}^{d}\to\mathbb{R}^{d}\bigg|\int\|w(z)\|_{2}^{2}\mathrm{d}\mu_{\mathcal{N}}(z)<\infty\right\}.
$$

For any $x\in\mathbb{R}^{d}$ , define $\phi_{x}\in\mathcal{H}$ by

$$
\phi_{x}(z): =x\mathbb{1}\left[\langle z,x\rangle>0\right],

and particularly define $\phi_{i}: =\phi_{x_{i}}$ for the training input $x_{i}$

$$

$$

As discussed in Section 5, the space H is the reproducing kernel Hilbert space (RKHS) induced by the infinite-width NTK with respect to $W$ , and $\phi_{x}$ maps x into H. Assumption 1 supposes that the induced training set $\{(\phi_{i},y_{i})\}_{i=1}^{n}$ can be separated by some $\bar{v}\in\mathcal{H}.$ with an additional bound on $\left.\bar{v}(z)\right._{2}$ which is crucial in our analysis. context: While quantum theory encompasses a broad scope of subjects, quantum information theory or quantum Shannon theory is a sub-field that focuses on the quantum equivalent of Shannon information theory (Wilde, 2013).A brief introduction is provided in Appendix A.Among the extensive results, we utilize only the basic concepts of von Neumann entropy, conditional entropy, and mutual information in this work. While Shannon entropy is calculated for a classical probability distribution, von Neumann entropy (also called quantum entropy) is calculated for a density operator ρ (Nielsen & Chuang, 2002), a positive semidefinite hermitian matrix in a Hilbert space H with the trace value of one. More details can be found in Appendix A. Similar to Shannon information theory, it measures the uncertainty associated with a quantum system. Definition 1 (von Neumann entropy (Nielsen & Chuang, 2002)). The von Neumann entropy (quantum entropy) of a quantum state with density operator p is defined as below. $$ S(\rho)\equiv-t r(\rho\log\rho)= -\sum_{x}\lambda_{x}\log\lambda_{x},w h e r e\lambda_{x}\ a r e\ t h e\ e i g e n\nu a l u e s\ o f\rho . $$ In case some of the singular values are zero, we exclude the corresponding dimensions with $\overline{{0\cdot log(0)=0.5(\rho)}}$ ranges from zero (when $\rho$ is a pure state) to log d (when $\rho$ is uniformly mixed), where ρ is in a d-dimensional space. The von Neumann entropy agrees with the Shannon entropy if and only if the states $|\psi_{i}\rangle$ are orthogonal (Nielsen & Chuang, 2002). When we have two quantum systems A and $B,$ their composite system is called AB. The corresponding density operators are denoted as $\rho_{A},\rho_{B}$ , and $\rho_{A B}$ , respectively. Then, conditional entropy and mutual information are defined as below, where the quantum system name instead of the density operator is used as the argument's notation. Definition 2 (Conditional entropy and mutual information (Nielsen & Chuang, 2002)). The quantum conditional entropy and mutual information of a composite system AB with components A and B are defined as below. $$ \begin{array}{ c }{{S(A|B)\equiv S(A B)-S(B).}}\\ {{S(A;B)\equiv S(A)-S(A|B).}}\end{array} $$ The value of conditional entropy S(A|B) is reduced as the two systems become entangled. In fact, it can be even negative (Cerf & Adami, 1997). In general, measuring quantum entanglement is computationally challenging (Huang, 2014). The quantum mutual information $S(A;B)$ can be understood in a similar way as in Shannon information theory, and it is a measure of shared information between the two systems. In this section, we provide the derivation of von Neumann entropy lower bound for $H(\mathbf{Z})$ and derive the negative cosine similarity upper bound for $H(\mathbf{Z}_{1}|\mathbf{Z}_{2})$ . In Section 5, the two bounds are combined to form a new lower bound of mutual information.non-contrastive loss for unsupervised learning. Consider two random variables $\mathbf{Z}_{1}$ and $\mathbf{Z}_{2}$ , where $\mathbf{Z}_{2}$ is assumed to be on a unit hypersphere in $\mathbb{R}^{d}$ If $\mathbf{Z}_{1}$ is an augmented version of $\mathbf{Z}_{2}$ with a weak Gaussian perturbation, the two random variables are related as $\mathbf{\bar{Z}}_{1}\sim\mathcal{N}(\mathbf{Z}_{2},\mathbf{\Sigma}\mathbf{)}$ . For this special augmentation, the main result of Theorem 1 can be proved. For the two lemmas, it is assumed that Σ is a symmetric positive definite matrix whose eigendecomposition is $\pmb{\Sigma}=\pmb{Q}\pmb{\Lambda}\pmb{Q}^{T},\pmb{\Lambda}=\mathrm{diag}(\lambda_{1},...,\lambda_{d}),$ ,and $0<\dot{\lambda}_{d}\leq ...\leq\lambda_{1}\ll 1$ Also, note T that $| |z_{1}| |^{2}\approx| |z_{2}| |^{2}=1$ and $\begin{array}{ r }{z_{1}\cdot z_{2}\approx\frac{z_{1}^{\prime}z_{2}}{| |z_{1}| |\cdot| |z_{2}| |}=\cos{(z_{1},z_{2})}>0}\end{array}$ due to the weak Gaussian noise perturbation condition. Lemma 2. $-\frac{1}{2}(z_{1}-z_{2})^{T}\Sigma^{-1}(z_{1}-z_{2})\geq-1/\lambda_{d}+z_{1}\cdot z_{2}/\lambda_{1}$ . The Theorem 2 was derived for random variables $\mathbf{Z}_{1}$ and $\mathbf{Z}_{2}$ . For unsupervised representation learning, however, augmentation is applied to input random variables $\mathbf{X}_{1}$ and $\mathbf{X}_{2}$ . Therefore, we assume the commonly used ReLU as the activation vector and utilize its piecewise linearity to prove the following theorem.

error_explanation: The step concludes $z_1 \sim \mathcal{N}(z_2, \Sigma)$ with $\Sigma = cAA^T$ by treating the piecewise-linear map $f$ as a single fixed affine map $Ax+b$ on the whole noise neighborhood. This is invalid: a piecewise-linear $f(x)=\sum_i (A_i x + b_i)\mathbb{1}(x\in\mathcal{B}_i)$ does not preserve Gaussianity, because conditional on $x_1$ the region indicators $\mathbb{1}(x_1+e\in\mathcal{B}_i)$ are random (Bernoulli). No matter how small the noise variance $c$, the support of the perturbation $e$ is all of $\mathbb{R}^d$, so there is nonzero probability of crossing a linear-region boundary; hence $e_f = f(x_2)-f(x_1)$ is not Gaussian and $\Sigma$ is not a single fixed matrix $cAA^T$. Consequently the Gaussian conditional-entropy machinery of Theorem 4.4 cannot legitimately be applied here. (Compounding this, $\alpha=\tfrac{d}{2}\log 2\pi\lambda_1+\tfrac{1}{\lambda_d}$ and $\beta=\tfrac{1}{\lambda_1}$ are built from the eigenvalues of the local $\Sigma$ at one $x_2$, so they cannot serve as global constants; by Proposition A, $h(z_2|z_1)=\tfrac{1}{2}\log((2\pi e)^d\det\Sigma)$ is unbounded over $\Sigma$, so no fixed $\alpha,\beta$ can bound $H(\mathbf{Z}_1|\mathbf{Z}_2)$ for all augmentations.)

Hence $g_{ti}$ as defined does not dominate the estimation error of the price-dependent extended feature, invalidating bounds (13)-(14). 3.3 Double-Momentum Method for Lower-Level Constrained Bilevel Optimization

Equipped with the hypergradient $\bar{\nabla}f_{\delta}(x,y;\bar{\xi})$ , our next endeavor is to design a single-loop singletimescale algorithm to solve the constrained bilevel optimization problem (1). Our main idea is to adopt the double-momentum-based method and adaptive step-size method developed in (Huang & Huang, 2021; Khanduri et al., 2021; Shi et al., 2022). Our algorithm is summarized in Algorithm 1. Since we use the double-momentum method to solve the lower-level constrained bilevel optimization problem, we denote our method as DMLCBO.

Define $\alpha\in(0,1)$ and $\beta\in(0,1)$ . For the lower-level problem, we can utilize the following projected gradient method with the momentum-based gradient estimator and adaptive step size to update y,

$$
y_{k+1}=(1-\eta_{k})y_{k}+\eta_{k}\mathcal{P}y(y_{k}-\frac{\tau}{\sqrt{\|v_{k}\|}+G_{0}}v_{k}),v_{k+1}=(1-\beta)v_{k}+\beta\nabla_{y}g(x_{k},y_{k}),
$$

where $\eta_{k}>0,\tau>0 . G_{0}>0$ is used to avoid to prevent the molecule from being equal to 0. Here, we initialize $v_{1}=g(x_{1},y_{1})$ . Similarly, for the upper-level problem, we can utilize the following gradient method with the momentum-based gradient estimator and adaptive step size to update x,

$$
x_{k+1}=(1-\eta_{k})x_{k}+\eta_{k}\mathcal{P}_{\lambda}(x_{k}-\frac{\gamma}{\sqrt{\|w_{k}\|}+G_{0}}w_{k}),\ w_{k+1}=(1-\alpha)w_{k}+\alpha\bar{\nabla}f_{\delta}(x_{k},y_{k};\bar{\xi}_{k}),
$$

and we initialize $w_{1}=\bar{\nabla}f_{\delta}(x_{1},y_{1};\bar{\xi}_{1})$

In this section, we discuss the convergence performance of our DMLCBO (All the detailed proofs are presented in our Appendix). We follow the theoretical analysis framework in (Huang & Huang, 2021; Huang et al., 2020; Shi et al., 2022; Khanduri et al., 2021) (For easy understanding, we also provide a route map of the analysis in Appendix E). Before proceeding to the main results, we present an additional assumption and a useful lemma.

$$
\mathbf{A s s u m p t i o n 5 .~}W e\ln a v e\ c_{l}\leq 1/(\sqrt{\|v_{k}\|}+G_{0})\leq c_{u}\ a n d\ c_{l}\leq 1/(\sqrt{\|w_{k}\|}+G_{0})\leq c_{u}.
$$

The above assumption is used to bind the adaptive terms in our method which has been widely used in convergence analysis (Shi et al., 2022; Guo et al., 2021b). error_explanation: The claim $\sqrt{G}=\tilde{\mathcal{O}}(\sqrt{d_2})$ is false for the original potential function. In the original proof the constant/potential $G$ inherits $L_0=\max(L_1(\sqrt{d_2}/\delta),L_2(\sqrt{d_2}/\delta))$, so $G$ scales like $\sqrt{d_2}/\delta$ (and higher powers), not $\tilde{\mathcal{O}}(d_2)$. Hence $\sqrt{G}$ is NOT $\tilde{\mathcal{O}}(\sqrt{d_2})$; it actually carries a $1/\delta$ factor. Propagating the true dependence, Eqn 11 implies $K=\tilde{\mathcal{O}}(d_2^2/(\delta^4\epsilon^4))$, and with the required $\delta=\mathcal{O}(\epsilon d_2^{-3/2})$ (so $\delta^4=\epsilon^4 d_2^{-6}$) this becomes $K=\tilde{\mathcal{O}}(d_2^8/\epsilon^8)$ — an 8th-power dependence on both $d_2$ and $\epsilon$, far worse than the advertised $\tilde{\mathcal{O}}(d_2^2\epsilon^{-4})$. Recovering $\tilde{\mathcal{O}}(d_2^2/\epsilon^4)$ required replacing the potential with a new $\Phi_{k+1}$ and setting $a=0$ to genuinely decouple $G$ from $1/\delta$.

Definition 1 (Differential Privacy (Dwork & Roth, 2014)). A randomized algorithm M $i s \ \varepsilon -$ differentially private if for any neighboring datasets D and D' and any measurable subset $S \subseteq$ range(M), we have

$$
\mathbb{P}\left\{\mathcal{M}(D)\in S\right\}\leq e^{\varepsilon}\mathbb{P}\left\{\mathcal{M}(D^{\prime})\in S\right\},

Neighboring datasets (Section 1.1):
In this paper, we use Definition 1 on data matrix $\mathbf{X}\in\mathbb{R}^{d\times n}$ . We say two data matrices $\mathbf{X},\mathbf{X}^{\prime}$ are neighboring datasets if X and $\mathbf{X}^{\prime}$ differ on only one column. We follow the setting and notation in (He et al., 2023) as follows. let $(\Omega,\rho)$ be a metric space. Consider a dataset $\mathbf{X}=[X_{1}^{-},\ldots,X_{n}]\in\Omega^{n}$ We aim to construct a computationally efficient differentially private randomized algorithm that outputs synthetic data $\mathbf{Y}=\hat{[}Y_{1},\ldots,Y_{n}^{\cdot}]\in\Omega^{m}$ such that the two empirical measures

$$
\mu_{\mathbf{X}}=\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\delta_{X_{i}}\quad\mathrm{and}\quad\mu_{\mathbf{Y}}=\frac{1}{m}\sum_{i=1}^{m}\delta_{Y_{i}}
$$

are close to each other. Here $\delta_{X_{i}}$ denotes the Dirac measure centered on $X_{i}$ . We measure the utility of the output by $\mathbb{E}W_{1}(\mu_{\mathbf{X}},\mu_{\mathbf{Y}})$ , where the expectation is taken over the randomness of the algorithm.

Section 3.2 setup (private mean vector and metric projection):
3.2 Adding a Private Mean Vector and Metric Projection

Since we shift the data by its private mean before projection, we need to add another private mean vector back, which shifts the dataset $\widehat{\mathbf X}$ to a new private affine subspace close to the original dataset X. The output data vectors in $\mathbf{X}^{\prime\prime}$ (defined in Algorithm 1) are not necessarily inside $[0,1]^{d}$ . The subsequent metric projection enforces all synthetic data inside $[0,1]^{d}$ . Importantly, this post-processing step does not have privacy costs.

After metric projection, dataset Y from the output of Algorithm 1 is close to an affine subspace, as shown in the next proposition. Notably, (2) shows that the metric projection step does not cause the largest accuracy loss among all subroutines.

Definition 2 (p-Wasserstein distance). Consider a metric space $(\Omega,\rho)$ . The p-Wasserstein distance (see e.g., (Villani, 2009) for more details) between two probability measures $\mu,$ ν is defined as

$$
W_{p}(\mu,\nu): =\left(\operatorname*{inf}_{\gamma\in\Gamma(\mu,\nu)}\int_{\Omega\times\Omega}\rho(x,y)^{p}\mathrm{d}\gamma(x,y)\right)^{1/p},

where $\Gamma(\mu,\nu)$ is the set of all couplings of µ and $\nu .$
