Lemma 3 (Stability of noisy projection). Let X be a d × n matrix and A be a d × d Hermitian matrix. Let $\begin{array}{ r }{\mathbf{M}=\frac{1}{n}\mathbf{X}\mathbf{X}^{\mathsf{T}}}\end{array}$ with eigenvalues $\sigma_{1}\geq\sigma_{2}\geq\cdot\cdot\cdot\geq\sigma_{d}.$ Let $\begin{array}{ r }{\widehat{\mathbf{M}}=\frac{1}{n}\mathbf{X}\mathbf{X}^{\mathsf{T}}+\mathbf{A},}\end{array}$ $\widehat{\mathbf{V}}_{d^{\prime}}$ be a $d\times d^{\prime}$ matrix whose columns are the first d' orthonormal eigenvectors of ${\widehat{\mathbf{M}}},$ and $\mathbf{Y}=\widehat{\mathbf{V}}_{d^{\prime}}\widehat{\mathbf{V}}_{d^{\prime}}^{\mathsf{T}}\mathbf{X}$ Let $\mu_{\mathbf{X}}$ and $\mu_{\mathbf{Y}}$ be the empirical measures of column vectors of X and Y, respectively. Then

$$
W_{2}^{2}(\mu_{\mathbf{X}},\mu_{\mathbf{Y}})\leq\frac{1}{n}\|\mathbf{X}-\mathbf{Y}\|_{F}^{2}\leq\sum_{i>d^{\prime}}\sigma_{i}+2 d^{\prime}\|\mathbf{A}\|.\tag{4}
$$

steps.claim:
Proof. Let $\widehat{v}_{1},\ldots,\widehat{v}_{d}$ be a set of orthonormal eigenvectors for $\widehat{\bf M}$ with the corresponding eigenvalues $\widehat{\sigma}_{1},\ldots,\widehat{\sigma}_{d}$ . Define four matrices whose column vectors are eigenvectors:

$$
\mathbf{V}=[v_{1},\ldots,v_{d}],\qquad\widehat{\mathbf{V}}=[\widehat{v}_{1},\ldots,\widehat{v}_{d}],
$$

$$
\mathbf{V}_{d^{\prime}}=[v_{1},\ldots,v_{d^{\prime}}],\qquad\widehat{\mathbf{V}}_{d^{\prime}}=[\widehat{v}_{1},\ldots,\widehat{v}_{d^{\prime}}].
$$

By orthogonality, the following identities hold:

$$
\sum_{i=1}^{d}\|v_{i}^{\mathsf{T}}\mathbf{X}\|_{2}^{2}=\sum_{i=1}^{d}\|\widehat{v}_{i}^{\mathsf{T}}\mathbf{X}\|_{2}^{2}=\|\mathbf{X}\|_{F}^{2}.
$$

$$
\sum_{i>d^{\prime}}\|v_{i}^{\mathsf{T}}\mathbf{X}\|_{2}^{2}=\|\mathbf{X}-\mathbf{V}_{d^{\prime}}\mathbf{V}_{d^{\prime}}^{\mathsf{T}}\mathbf{X}\|_{F}^{2}.
$$

$$
\sum_{i>d^{\prime}}\|\widehat{v}_{i}^{\mathsf{T}}\mathbf{X}\|_{2}^{2}=\|\mathbf{X}-\widehat{\mathbf{V}}_{d^{\prime}}\widehat{\mathbf{V}}_{d^{\prime}}^{\mathsf{T}}\mathbf{X}\|_{F}^{2}.
$$

Separating the top d' eigenvectors from the rest, we obtain

$$
\sum_{i\leq d^{\prime}}\|v_{i}^{\mathsf{T}}\mathbf{X}\|_{2}^{2}+\|\mathbf{X}-\mathbf{V}_{d^{\prime}}\mathbf{V}_{d^{\prime}}^{\mathsf{T}}\mathbf{X}\|_{F}^{2}=\sum_{i\leq d^{\prime}}\|\widehat{v}_{i}^{\mathsf{T}}\mathbf{X}\|_{2}^{2}+\|\mathbf{X}-\widehat{\mathbf{V}}_{d^{\prime}}\widehat{\mathbf{V}}_{d^{\prime}}^{\mathsf{T}}\mathbf{X}\|_{F}^{2}.
$$

Therefore

$$
\begin{array}{ r l }{\|{\mathbf{X}}-\widehat{{\mathbf{V}}}_{d^{\prime}}\widehat{{\mathbf{V}}}_{d^{\prime}}^{\mathsf{T}}{\mathbf{X}}\|_{F}^{2}=\displaystyle\sum_{i\leq d^{\prime}}\|v_{i}^{\mathsf{T}}{\mathbf{X}}\|_{2}^{2}-\displaystyle\sum_{i\leq d^{\prime}}\|\widehat{v}_{i}^{\mathsf{T}}{\mathbf{X}}\|_{2}^{2}+\|{\mathbf{X}}-{\mathbf{V}}_{d^{\prime}}{\mathbf{V}}_{d^{\prime}}^{\mathsf{T}}{\mathbf{X}}\|_{F}^{2}}&{}\\ {=n\displaystyle\sum_{i\leq d^{\prime}}\sigma_{i}-n\displaystyle\sum_{i\leq d^{\prime}}\widehat{v}_{i}^{\mathsf{T}}{\mathbf{M}}\widehat{v}_{i}+n\displaystyle\sum_{i>d^{\prime}}\sigma_{i}}&{}\\ {=n\displaystyle\sum_{i\leq d^{\prime}}\sigma_{i}-n\displaystyle\sum_{i\leq d^{\prime}}\widehat{v}_{i}^{\mathsf{T}}(\widehat{\mathbf{M}}-{\mathbf{A}})\widehat{v}_{i}+n\displaystyle\sum_{i>d^{\prime}}\sigma_{i}}&{}\\ {=n\displaystyle\sum_{i\leq d^{\prime}}(\sigma_{i}-\widehat{\sigma}_{i})+n\displaystyle\operatorname{tr}({\mathbf{A}}\widehat{\mathbf{V}}_{d^{\prime}}\widehat{\mathbf{V}}_{d^{\prime}}^{\mathsf{T}})+n\displaystyle\sum_{i>d^{\prime}}\sigma_{i}.}&{}\end{array}\tag{5}
$$

By Weyl's inequality, for $i\leq d^{\prime}$

$$
|\sigma_{i}-{\widehat{\sigma}}_{i}|\leq\|\mathbf{A}\|.\tag{6}
$$

By von Neumann's trace inequality,

$$
\mathrm{tr}(A\widehat{\mathbf{V}}_{d^{\prime}}\widehat{\mathbf{V}}_{d^{\prime}}^{\mathsf{T}})\leq\sum_{i=1}^{d^{\prime}}\sigma_{i}({\mathbf{A}}).\tag{7}
$$

From (5), (6), and (7),

$$
\frac 1 n\|{\bf X}-\widehat{{\bf V}}_{d^{\prime}}\widehat{{\bf V}}_{d^{\prime}}^{\top}{\bf X}\|_{F}^{2}\leq\sum_{i>d^{\prime}}\sigma_{i}+d^{\prime}\|{\bf A}\|+\sum_{i=1}^{d^{\prime}}\sigma_{i}({\bf A})\leq\sum_{i>d^{\prime}}\sigma_{i}+2 d^{\prime}\|{\bf A}\|.
$$

Let $Y_{i}$ be the i-th column of Y. We have

$$
W_{2}^{2}(\mu_{\mathbf{X}},\mu_{\mathbf{Y}})\leq{\frac{1}{n}}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\|X_{i}-Y_{i}\|_{2}^{2}={\frac{1}{n}}\|\mathbf{X}-\mathbf{Y}\|_{F}^{2}.
$$

theorems.statement:
Proposition 1. The subroutine Algorithm 4 is ε-differentially private. For any $d^{\prime}\geq 2,$ with the input as the projected data $\widehat{\mathbf{X}}$ and the range $\Omega^{\prime}$ with radius R, Algorithm 4 has an accuracy bound

$$
\mathbb{E}W_{1}(\mu_{\widehat{\mathbf{X}}},\mu_{\mathbf{X}^{\prime}})\leq C R(\varepsilon n)^{-1/d^{\prime}},
$$

where the expectation is taken with respect to the randomness of the synthetic data subroutine, conditioned on R.

steps.claim: The privacy guarantee follows from (He et al., 2023, Theorem 1.1).
For accuracy, note that the region Ω' is a subregion of a d'-dimensional ball. Algorithm 4 enlarges the region to a $\bar{d}^{\prime}.$ -dimensional hypercube with side length 2R.
By re-scaling the size of the hypercube and applying (He et al., 2023, Corollary 4.4), we obtain the accuracy bound.

theorems.statement: Consider a data matrix $\mathbf{X}=[X_1,\ldots,X_n]\in\mathbb{R}^{d\times n}$ with each $X_i\in[0,1]^d$, where two data matrices are neighboring if they differ on only one column, and a randomized algorithm $\mathcal{M}$ is $\varepsilon$-differentially private if $\mathbb{P}\{\mathcal{M}(D)\in S\}\leq e^{\varepsilon}\,\mathbb{P}\{\mathcal{M}(D')\in S\}$ for all neighboring $D,D'$ and measurable $S$. Algorithm 1 releases synthetic data via steps $\mathcal{M}_1$ (private covariance matrix $\widehat{\mathbf{M}}$, Alg. 2), $\mathcal{M}_2(\mathbf{X})=\overline{X}+\lambda$ (private sample mean, with $\overline{X}=\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^n X_i$ and $\lambda\in\mathbb{R}^d$ having i.i.d. $\mathrm{Lap}(1/(\varepsilon n))$ components), $\mathcal{M}_3$ (private projection onto the top $d'$ principal components plus a DP synthetic-data subroutine), $\mathcal{M}_4$ (shifting the data back by $\overline{X}_{\mathrm{priv}}$), and a final metric projection. Theorem 1 (Privacy): Algorithm 1 is $\varepsilon$-differentially private.

steps.claim: Algorithm 1 can be decomposed into steps $\mathcal{M}_1(\mathbf{X})=\widehat{\mathbf{M}}$ (private covariance via Algorithm 2), $\mathcal{M}_2(\mathbf{X})=\overline{X}+\lambda$ (private sample mean), $\mathcal{M}_3(\mathbf{X},y,\Sigma)$ (project the shifted data $\{X_i-y\}$ onto the first $d'$ principal components of $\Sigma$ plus a DP subroutine), $\mathcal{M}_4(\mathbf{X},\mathbf{X}')$ (shift the dataset to $\{X_i'+\overline{X}_{\mathrm{priv}}\}$), and a final metric projection.
It suffices to show that the data before the metric projection is already differentially private.

The private-mean release $\mathcal{M}_2(\mathbf{X})=\overline{X}+\lambda$ uses noise $\lambda=(\lambda_1,\ldots,\lambda_d)$ with i.i.d. $\mathrm{Lap}(1/(\varepsilon n))$ entries, and $\mathbb{E}\|\lambda\|_2^2=\sum_{j=1}^d\mathbb{E}|\lambda_j|^2=\frac{2d}{\varepsilon^2 n^2}$ (eq (3)).
Each of $\mathcal{M}_1,\mathcal{M}_2,\mathcal{M}_3,\mathcal{M}_4$ is $\varepsilon/4$-differentially private with respect to the input $\mathbf{X}$ while fixing the other input variables.
The private sample mean $\mathcal{M}_2(\mathbf{X})=\overline{X}+\lambda$ with entry-wise noise $\mathrm{Lap}(1/(\varepsilon n))$ attains its stated $\varepsilon/4$-differential privacy.

The composition $\mathcal{M}_4(\mathbf{X},\mathcal{M}_3(\mathbf{X},\mathcal{M}_2(\mathbf{X}),\mathcal{M}_1(\mathbf{X})))$ satisfies $\varepsilon$-differential privacy, and hence Algorithm 1 is $\varepsilon$-differentially private.

theorems.statement: Theorem 3. Algorithm 2 is ε-differentially private.

steps.claim:
Proof. Before applying the definition of differential privacy, we compute the entries of M explicitly. One can easily check that

$$
\mathbf{M}=\frac{1}{n}\sum_{k=1}^{n}X_{k}X_{k}^{\mathsf{T}}-\frac{1}{n(n-1)}\sum_{k\neq\ell}X_{k}X_{\ell}^{\mathsf{T}}.\tag{8}
$$

Now, if there are neighboring datasets X and $\mathbf{X}^{\prime}.$ ,suppose $X_{k}=(X_{k}^{(1)},\ldots,X_{k}^{(d)})^{\top}$ is a column vector in X and $X_{k}^{\prime}=(X_{k}^{\prime}{}^{(1)},\ldots,X_{k}^{\prime}{}^{(d)})^{\mathsf{T}}$ is a column vector in $\mathbf{X}^{\prime}.$ , and all other column vectors are the same. Let M and $\ddot{\mathbf{M}}^{\prime}$ be the covariance matrix of X and $\mathbf{X}^{\prime}$ , respectively. Then we consider the density function ratio for the output of Algorithm 2 with input X and $\mathbf{X}^{\prime}\colon$

$$
\begin{array}{ l }{\displaystyle\frac{\mathrm{den}_{\boldsymbol{A}}(\widetilde{\mathbf{M}}-\mathbf{M})}{\mathrm{den}_{\boldsymbol{A}}(\widetilde{\mathbf{M}}-\mathbf{M^{\prime}})}=\displaystyle\prod_{i<j}\frac{\mathrm{den}_{\boldsymbol{A}j}\left((\widetilde{\mathbf{M}}-\mathbf{M})_{i j}\right)}{\mathrm{den}_{\boldsymbol{A}j}\left((\widetilde{\mathbf{M}}-\mathbf{M^{\prime}})_{i j}\right)}\displaystyle\prod_{i=j}\frac{\mathrm{den}_{2\boldsymbol{A}j}\left((\widetilde{\mathbf{M}}-\mathbf{M})_{i j}\right)}{\mathrm{den}_{2\boldsymbol{A}j}\left((\widetilde{\mathbf{M}}-\mathbf{M^{\prime}})_{i j}\right)}}\\ {=\displaystyle\prod_{i<j}\frac{\exp\left(-\frac{|(\widetilde{\mathbf{M}}-\mathbf{M})_{i j}|}{\sigma}\right)}{\exp\left(-\frac{|(\widetilde{\mathbf{M}}-\mathbf{M^{\prime}})_{i j}|}{\sigma}\right)}\displaystyle\prod_{i}\frac{\exp\left(-\frac{|(\widetilde{\mathbf{M}}-\mathbf{M})_{i i}|}{2\sigma}\right)}{\exp\left(-\frac{|(\widetilde{\mathbf{M}}-\mathbf{M^{\prime}})_{i i}|}{2\sigma}\right)}}\\ {\leq\exp\left(\displaystyle\sum_{i<j}\left|\mathbf{M}_{i j}-\mathbf{M}_{i j}^{\prime}\right| /\sigma+\displaystyle\sum_{i}\left|\mathbf{M}_{i i}-\mathbf{M}_{i i}^{\prime}\right| /(2\sigma)\right)}\\ {=\exp\left(\displaystyle\frac{1}{2\sigma}\displaystyle\sum_{i,j}\left|\mathbf{M}_{i j}-\mathbf{M}_{i j}^{\prime}\right|\right).}\end{array}
$$

As the datasets differs on only one data $X_{k},$ ,consider all entry containing $X_{k}$ in (8), we have

$$
\begin{array}{ r }{\left|{\bf M}_{i j}-{\bf M}_{i j}^{\prime}\right|\leq\displaystyle\frac{1}{n}\Big|X_{k}^{(i)}X_{k}^{(j)}-{X_{k}^{\prime}}^{(i)}X_{k}^{\prime}{}^{(j)}\Big| +\frac{1}{n(n-1)}\displaystyle\sum_{\ell\neq k}\left|X_{k}^{(i)}-{X_{k}^{\prime}}^{(i)}\right|X_{\ell}^{(j)}}\\ {+\frac{1}{n(n-1)}\displaystyle\sum_{\ell\neq k}X_{\ell}^{(i)}\Big|X_{k}^{(j)}-X_{k}^{\prime}{}^{(j)}\Big|}\end{array}
$$

$$
\leq{\frac{2}{n}}+{\frac{2}{n(n-1)}}\cdot 2(n-1)={\frac{6}{n}}.
$$

Therefore, substituting the result in the probability ratio implies

$$
\frac{\mathrm{den}_{A}(\widehat{\mathbf{M}}-\mathbf{M})}{\mathrm{den}_{A}(\widehat{\mathbf{M}}-\mathbf{M}^{\prime})}\leq\exp\left(\frac{1}{2\sigma}\cdot d^{2}\cdot\frac{6}{n}\right)=\exp\left(\frac{3 d^{2}}{\sigma n}\right),
$$
and when $\begin{array}{ r }{\sigma=\frac{3 d^{2}}{{\varepsilon}n}}\end{array}$ , Algorithm 2 is ε-differentially private.

theorems.statement:
Proposition 2 (Y is close to an affne subspace). The function $f:\mathbb{R}^{d}[0,1]^{d}$ is the metric projection to $[0,1]^{d}$ with respect $t o\parallel\cdot\parallel_{\infty}$ and the accuracy error for the metric projection step in Algorithm 1 is dominated by the error of the previous steps:

$$
W_{1}(\mu_{\mathbf{Y}},\mu_{\mathbf{X}^{\prime\prime}})\leq W_{1}(\mu_{\mathbf{X}},\mu_{\mathbf{X}^{\prime\prime}}),\tag{2}
$$

where the dataset $\mathbf{X}^{\prime\prime}$ defined in Algorithm 1 is in a d'-dimensional affine subspace. And we have

$$
\mathbb{E}W_{1}(\mu_{\mathbf{Y}},\mu_{\mathbf{X}^{\prime\prime}})\lesssim_{d}\sqrt{\sum_{i>d^{\prime}}\sigma_{i}(\mathbf{M})}+(\varepsilon n)^{-1/d^{\prime}}.
$$

steps.claim: Proof. For the function f defined in Algorithm 1, we know $f(x)$ is the closest real number to x in the region $[0,1]$ for any $x\in\mathbb{R}$ Furthermore, if $v\in\mathbb{R}^{d}$ is a vector, then $f(v)$ is the closest vector to v in $[\breve{0},1]^{d}$ with respect to $\|\cdot\|_{\infty}$ . Thus $f:{\mathbb{R}^{d}}\to [0,1]^{d}$ is indeed a metric projection to $[0,1]^{d}$

We first assume that the synthetic data $\mathbf{X}^{\prime\prime}$ also has size n. Then for any column vector $X_{i}^{\prime\prime}$ , we know that $Y_{i}=f(X_{i}^{\prime\prime})$ is its closest vector in $[0,1]^{d}$ under the $\ell^{\infty}$ metric. For the data $X_{1},X_{2},\ldots,X_{n},$ suppose that the solution to the optimal transportation problem for $W_{1}(\mu_{\mathbf{X}},\mu_{\mathbf{X}^{\prime\prime}})$ is to match $X_{\tau(i)}$ with $X_{i}^{\prime\prime}$ , where τ is a permutation on [n]. Then

$$
W_{1}(\mu_{{\bf Y}},\mu_{{\bf X}^{\prime\prime}})\leq\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\bigl\|Y_{i}-X_{i}^{\prime\prime}\bigr\|_{\infty}\leq\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\Bigl\|X_{\tau(i)}-X_{i}^{\prime\prime}\Bigr\|_{\infty}=W_{1}(\mu_{{\bf X}},\mu_{{\bf X}^{\prime\prime}}).
$$

In general, if the synthetic dataset has m data points and $m \neq n$ , we can split the points and regard both the true dataset and synthetic dataset as of size mn, then it's easy to check that the inequality still holds.
The expectation bound follows from (9) and (10).

label: flawed
error_explanation: Step 4 already asserts the false claim before Step 5 restates it: it says "Each of M1,M2,M3,M4 is epsilon/4-differentially private with respect to the input X while fixing the other input variables" -- an unqualified blanket claim that includes M2 (the private-mean release). This is false for the same reason given for Step 5: the L1-sensitivity of the d-dimensional mean X-bar is d/n, not 1/n, so releasing X-bar with epsilon-DP requires entry-wise noise Lap(d/(epsilon*n)), not the Lap(1/(epsilon*n)) used in the proof (per eq. C.7). Using the too-small noise scale means M2 only achieves (d*epsilon)-DP, a factor d too weak, so Step 4's blanket epsilon/4-DP claim already fails for M2 -- this is the same false statement that the record previously located at Step 5, but Step 5 is merely a restatement /elaboration of the identical error already asserted at Step 4, making Step 4 the first genuine error. (Reviewer quote and the authors' own admission of the underlying d/n-vs-1/n sensitivity error are unchanged and still apply.)

context: 2.1 Variational Autoencoder and Theoretical Analysis In VAE, ELBO is maximized instead of maximizing the log-likelihood directly. Let ${\pmb x} \in \mathbb{R}^m$ be a point in a dataset. The original VAE model consists of a latent variable with fixed prior ${\pmb z} \sim p({\pmb z}) = \mathcal{N}({\pmb z}; {\pmb 0}, {\pmb I}_n) \in \mathbb{R}^n$, a parametric encoder $\mathrm{Enc}_\phi:{\pmb x}\Rightarrow{\pmb z}$, and a parametric decoder $\mathrm{Dec}_\theta : {\pmb z} \Rightarrow \hat{\pmb x}$. In the encoder, $q_\phi({\pmb z}|{\pmb x}) = \mathcal{N}({\pmb z}; {\pmb \mu}_{({\pmb x})}, {\pmb \sigma}_{({\pmb x})})$ is provided by estimating parameters ${\pmb \mu}_{({\pmb x})}$ and ${\pmb \sigma}_{({\pmb x})}$. Let $L_{\pmb x}$ be a local cost at data ${\pmb x}$. Then, ELBO is described by $$ \mathrm{ELBO} = E_{{\pmb x} \sim p({\pmb x})} \left[ E_{{\pmb z} \sim q_\phi({\pmb z}|{\pmb x})} [\log p_\theta({\pmb x}|{\pmb z})] - D_{\mathrm{KL}}(q_\phi({\pmb z}|{\pmb x}) \| p({\pmb z})) \right] .\tag{14} $$ In $E_{{\pmb x} \sim p({\pmb x})}[\,\cdot\,]$, the first term $E_{{\pmb z} \sim q_\phi({\pmb z}|{\pmb x})}[\,\cdot\,]$ is called the reconstruction loss. The second term $D_{\mathrm{KL}}(\cdot)$ is a Kullback–Leibler (KL) divergence. Let $\mu_{j({\pmb x})}$, $\sigma_{j({\pmb x})}$, and $D_{\mathrm{KL}j({\pmb x})}$ be $j$-th dimensional values of ${\pmb \mu}_{({\pmb x})}$, ${\pmb \sigma}_{({\pmb x})}$, and KL divergence. Then $D_{\mathrm{KL}}(\cdot)$ is derived as: $$ D_{\mathrm{KL}}(\cdot)=\sum_{j=1}^{n}D_{\mathrm{KL}j({\pmb x})},\quad \text{where } D_{\mathrm{KL}j({\pmb x})}=\frac{1}{2}\left({\mu_{j({\pmb x})}}^2+{\sigma_{j({\pmb x})}}^2-\log{\sigma_{j({\pmb x})}}^2-1\right). $$ $D({\pmb x}, \hat{\pmb x})$ denotes a metric such as sum square error (SSE) and binary cross-entropy (BCE) as log-likelihoods of Gaussian and Bernoulli distributions, respectively. In training VAE, the next objective is used instead of Eq. 14, where $\beta$ is a parameter to control the trade-off (Higgins et al., 2017). $$ L_{\pmb x} = E_{{\pmb z} \sim q_\phi({\pmb z}|{\pmb x})} [D({\pmb x}, \hat{\pmb x})] + \beta D_{\mathrm{KL}}(\cdot) . $$ 3.1 Hypothesis of Mapping VAE to the Implicit Orthonormal Transform Figure 1 shows the mapping of VAE to the implicit isometric embedding. Assume the data manifold is smooth and differentiable. Let $S_{\mathrm{input}}\mathopen{}\mathclose\bgroup\left(\mathsf{C}\bar{\mathbb{R^{m}}}\aftergroup\egroup\right)$ be an input space of the dataset. $D({\pmb x},{\acute{\pmb x}})$ denotes a metric for points x, $\acute{\pmb{x}}\in S_{\mathrm{input}}.$ Using the second order Taylor expansion, $D({\pmb x},{\pmb x}+\delta{\pmb x})$ can be approximated by tδx $G_{x}\delta x$ , where $G_{x}$ and δx are an x dependent positive definite Hermitian metric tensor and an arbitrary infinitesimal displacement in $S_{\mathrm{{i n p u t}}}$ , respectively. The derivations of $G_{x}$ for SSE, BCE, and SSIM are shown in Appendix H.2. Next, an implicit isometric embedding space $S_{\mathrm{Iso}}(\subset\mathbb{R}^{m})$ is introduced like the isometric latent space in RaDOGAGA (Kato et al., 2020), such that the entropy of data representation is minimum in the inner product space of $G_{x}$ Let y and $y_{j}$ be a point in $S_{\mathrm{{I s o}}}$ and its $j$ -th component, respectively. Because of the isometricity, $p({\pmb x})\simeq p({\pmb y})$ will hold. We will also show the posterior variance of each dimensional component $y_{j}$ is a constant $\beta / 2$ In addition, the variance of $y_{j}$ will show the importance like PCA when the data manifold has a disentangled feature by nature in the metric space of $G_{x}$ and the prior covariance is diagonal. Then, $S_{\mathrm{{I s o}}}$ is nonlinearly scaled to the VAE's anisometric orthogonal space $S_{\mathrm{VAE}}(\subset\ \mathbb{R}^{n})$ on a variable-by-variable basis. Let z be a point in $S_{\mathrm{VAE}}$ , and $z_{j}$ denotes the j-th component of z. Let $p(y_{j})$ and $p(z_{j})$ be the probability distribution of the j-th variable in $S_{\mathrm{{I s o}}}$ and $S_{\mathrm{VAE}}$ . Each variable $y_{j}$ is nonlinearly scaled $\mathrm{to}~z_{j}$ ,such that $\mathrm{d}z_{j}/\mathrm{d}y_{j}=\bar{p}(y_{j})/p(z_{j})$ to fit the cumulative distribution. $\mathrm{d}z_{j}/\mathrm{d}y_{j}$ is $\sigma_{j(\pmb{x})}/\sqrt{\beta/2}$ , the ratio of posterior's standard deviations for $z_{j}$ and $y_{j}$ , such that KL divergences in both spaces are equivalent. In addition, dimensional components whose KL divergences are zero can be discarded because such dimensions have no information. 3.2 Reformulation of Objective to the Form Using $\partial\pmb{x}/\partial z_{j}$ and $\partial\pmb{x}/\partial z$ We reformulate the objective $L_{x}$ to the form using $\partial\pmb{x}/\partial z_{j}$ and ∂x $/ \partial z$ . Here, the dimensions of x and z, i.e., m and n, are set as the same. The condition to reduce n is shown in section 3.3. Reformulation of $D(\pmb{x},\hat{\pmb{x}})$ loss: In accordance with Kato et al. (2020), the loss $D(\pmb{x},\hat{\pmb{x}})$ can be decomposed into $D(\breve{\pmb{x}},\hat{\pmb{x}})+D(\pmb{x},\breve{\pmb{x}})$ where denotes $\mathrm{Dec}_{\theta}(\pmb{\mu}_{(\pmb{x})})$ The first term $\boldsymbol{D}(\breve{\pmb{x}},\hat{\pmb{x}})$ is a distortion between the decoded values of ${\pmb\mu}_{({\pmb x})}$ with and without noise ${\pmb\sigma}_{({\pmb x})}$ . We call this term as a coding loss. This term is expanded as follows. δx denotes $\hat{\mathbf{x}}-\breve{\mathbf{x}}$ .Then, $D(\breve{\pmb x},\hat{\pmb x})$ term can be approximated by tδ $\mathbf{\Pi}_{G_{x}\delta\breve{\mathbf{x}}}$ . Let $\mathbf{\boldsymbol{x}}_{z_{j}}$ be ∂x/∂zj at $z_{j}=\mu_{j(\pmb{x})}$ , and $\delta z_{j}\sim\mathcal{N}(0,\overset{\cdot}{\sigma}_{j(\pmb{x})})$ be an added noise in $z_{j}$ . Then, δx is approximated by $\begin{array}{ r }{\delta\breve{\pmb{x}}\simeq\sum_{j=1}^{m}\delta z_{j}\ \pmb{x}_{z_{j}}}\end{array}$ . Because $\delta z_{j}$ and $\delta z_{k}$ for $j \neq k$ are uncorrelated, the average of $D(\breve{\pmb x},\hat{\pmb x})$ over $z\sim q_{\phi}(z|\mathbf{x})$ can be finally reformulated by $$ E_{z\sim q_{\phi}(z|\mathbf{x})}\left[D(\check{\mathbf{x}},\hat{\mathbf{x}})\right]\simeq E_{z\sim q_{\phi}(z|\mathbf{x})}\left[{^t\delta\check{\mathbf{x}}\ G_{\mathbf{x}}\delta\check{\mathbf{x}}}\right]\simeq\sum_{j=1}^{n}\sigma_{j(\mathbf{x})}{^2\ ^{t}}x_{z_{j}}G_{x}x_{z_{j}}.\tag{3} $$ The second term $D({\pmb x},{\breve{\pmb x}})$ is a loss between the input data and $\mathrm{Dec}_{\theta}(\pmb{\mu}_{(\pmb{x})})$ . We call this term a transform loss. We presume VAE is analogous to the Wiener filter (Wiener, 1964; Jin et al., 2003) where the coding loss is regarded as an added noise. From the Wiener filter theory, the ratio between the transform loss and coding loss is close to the ratio between the coding loss and the variance of the input data. The coding loss, approximately $n \beta / 2$ as in Eq. 4, should be smaller than the variance of the input data to capture meaningful information. Thus the transform loss, usually small, is not considered in the following discussion. Appendix B explains the detail in a simple 1-dimensional VAE. We show the exhaustive and quantitative evaluation of coding loss and transform loss in the toy dataset in appendix E.2 to validate this approximation. Reformulation of KL divergence: When $\sigma_{j(x)}\ll 1,{\sigma_{j(x)}}^{2}\ll-\log{\sigma_{j(x)}}^{2}$ is observed. For example, when ${\sigma_{j(\pmb x)}}^{2}<0.1$ , we have $-({\sigma_{j(x)}}^{2}/\log{\sigma_{j(x)}}^{2})<0.05$ . In such dimensions, $D_{\mathrm{KL}j(x)}$ can be approximated as Eq. 5 by ignoring the ${\dot{\sigma}_{j(\pmb{x})}}^{2}$ term and setting $p(\mu_{j({\pmb x})})$ to $\mathcal{N}(z_{j};0,1)$ •• $$ D_{\mathrm{KL}j(x)}\simeq\frac{1}{2}\left(\mu_{j(x)}{}^{2}-\log\sigma_{j(x)}{}^{2}-1\right)= -\log\left(\sigma_{j(x)}p\big(\mu_{j(x)}\big)\right)-\frac{\log 2\pi e}{2}.\tag{5} $$ Eq. 5 can be considered as a rate of entropy coding for a symbol with mean $\mu_{j({\pmb x})}$ allowing quantization noise ${\sigma_{j(\pmb x)}}^{2}$ , as shown in Appendix H.3. Thus, in the dimension with meaningful information, ${\sigma_{j(\pmb x)}}^{2}$ is much smaller than the prior variance 1, and the approximation in Eq.5 is reasonable.

theorems.statement: Minimum entropy of implicit isometric representation: Let $L_{\operatorname*{min}{x}}^{\prime}$ be a minimum of $L_{x}^{\prime}$ at x. $D_{\operatorname*{min}{\pmb x}}$ and $R_{\operatorname*{min}{x}}$ denote a coding loss and KL divergence in $L_{\mathrm{min}\alpha}^{\prime},$ respectively. By applying Eqs. 6-7 and $p(z_{j})=(\mathrm{d}y_{j}/\mathrm{d}z_{j})p(y_{j})$ to Eqs. 3 and 8, the following equations are derived: $$ L_{\operatorname*{min}\ x}^{\prime}=D_{\operatorname*{min}\ x}+\beta R_{\operatorname*{min}\ x},{\mathrm{~w h e r e~}}D_{\operatorname*{min}\ x}={\frac{n\beta}{2}},R_{\operatorname*{min}\ x}= -\log p(y)-{\frac{n\log\left(\beta\pi e\right)}{2}}.\tag{9} $$ Here, $D_{\operatorname*{min}{\boldsymbol x}}$ is derived as $\begin{array}{ r }{\sum_{j=1}^{n}(\beta/2)\ ^{t}x_{y_{j}}G_{x}x_{y_{j}}=n\beta/2}\end{array}$ ,implying each dimensional posterior variance of the implicit isometric variable is a constant $\beta / 2$ In addition, $\exp(-L_{\operatorname*{min}{x}}^{\prime}/\beta)=$ $p(\pmb{y})\exp(\mathrm{C o n s t .})\propto p(\pmb{y})\simeq p(\pmb{x})$ will hold in the inner product space of $G_{x}$ from the isometricity. By averaging $L_{\mathrm{min}\alpha}^{\prime}$ over $\begin{array}{ r }{\pmb{x}\sim p(\pmb{x})}\end{array}$ and approximating this average by the integration over $\mathbf{\mu}_{\mathbf{\mu}_{y}\sim}$ $p(\pmb{y})$ , the global minimum $L_{\mathrm{G}}^{\prime}$ is derived as: $$ L_{\mathrm{G}}^{\prime}=D_{\mathrm{G}}+\beta R_{\mathrm{G}}\mathrm{,~w h e r e~}D_{\mathrm{G}}=\frac{n\beta}{2}\mathrm{,~}R_{\mathrm{G}}=\operatorname*{min}_{p(y)}\left(-\int p(y)\log p(y)\mathrm{d}y\right)-\frac{n\log\left(\beta\pi e\right)}{2}.\tag{4} $$

error_explanation: The change-of-variables relation for probability densities is $p(\mu_{(x)}) = p(x)\,|\det(\partial x/\partial z)|$ — the density ratio is the ABSOLUTE VALUE of the Jacobian determinant, not the bare determinant. Writing $p(\mu_{(x)}) = p(x)\,\det(\partial x/\partial z)$ (Step 2) is only valid when $\det(\partial x/\partial z) > 0$; a Jacobian determinant need not be positive. If $\det(\partial x/\partial z) < 0$ this equates a nonnegative density with a negative quantity, and it propagates to Eq. 8 where $p(x)\,\det(\partial x/\partial z)\prod_j \sigma_{j(x)}$ becomes negative, making its logarithm undefined and invalidating the objective. The correct relation and objective use $|\det(\partial x/\partial z)|$; the author admission confirms 'Eq.8 is incorrect. We revise it to the absolute value of the Jacobian determinant.'

Problem formulation. Let $D=(x_{1},\ldots,x_{n})$ be a database of size $n,$ where each of $i,i\in\lceil n\rceil$ is a data instance. $x_{i}$ is a d-dimensional vector, $x_{i}\in\mathbb{R}^{d}$ and w.l.o.g., normalized to be $| |x_{i}| |_{2}\in [\mathrm{0 .\bar{1}}]$

Gaussian mechanism G with variance $\sigma^{2}$ is applied to each $x_{i}.$ resulting in $\tilde{x_{i}}$ .Then, all $\tilde{x_{i}}\mathrm{\tilde{s}}$ undergo shuffling; let $S_{n}:\mathcal{V}^{n}\mathcal{V}^{n}$ be the shuffling operation which takes $\tilde{x_{i}}\mathrm{:s}$ as input and outputs a uniformly and randomly permuted $\tilde{x_{i}}\mathrm{:s}$ . The randomization mechanism M of interest is therefore

$$
\mathcal{M}(D)=S_{n}(\mathcal{G}(x_{1}),\ldots,\mathcal{G}(x_{n})).
$$

Our purpose is to characterize and quantify the DP of M through RDP.

Definition 1 (Rényi Differential Privacy (RDP) (Mironov, 2017)). A randomization mechanism $\mathcal{M}:\mathcal{D}\mathcal{S}$ is said to satisfy $(\lambda,\epsilon){\tt RDP}$ for $\lambda\in(1,\infty)$ , if for any adjacent databases D, $D^{\prime}\in\mathcal{D}$ the Rényi divergence of order λ between $\mathcal{M}(D)$ and $\mathcal{M}(D^{\prime})$ , as defined below, is upper-bounded by e:

$$
D_{\lambda}(\mathcal{M}(D)| |\mathcal{M}(D^{\prime})): =\frac{1}{\lambda-1}\log\left(\mathbb{E}_{y\sim\mathcal{M}(D^{\prime})}\left[\left(\frac{\mathcal{M}(D)(y)}{\mathcal{M}(D^{\prime})(y)}\right)^{\lambda}\right]\right)\leq\epsilon,\tag{1}
$$

where $\mathcal{M}(\mathcal{D})(y)$ denotes M taking $D$ as input to output y with certain probability.

Definition 2 (Gaussian mechanism). Given $x\in\mathbb{R}^{d}$ , the Gaussian mechanism applied to x is a mechanism with parameter σ that adds zero mean isotropic Gaussian perturbation of variance $\sigma^{2}$ to x, outputting $\mathcal{M}(x)=x+\mathcal{N}(0,\sigma^{2}I_{d})$ .

3 The RDP of Shuffle Gaussian

We first derive the Rényi divergence (of order λ) of the shuffle Gaussian mechanism in this section. Subsequently, an upper bound on the notion is given, followed by a description of the numerical technique used for evaluating the RDP.

The main result of this paper is given by the following theorem.

Upper bound of shuffle Gaussian RDP. Using the above exact expression, we next give an upper bound on the shuffle Gaussian RDP.

We first consider the mechanism where a fixed number of data instances, $m,$ is sampled randomly from n data instances to participate in training. Each data instance is randomized with Gaussian noises before being shuffled. We call this overall procedure the subsampled (without replacement) shuffle (Girgis et al., 2021b) Gaussian mechanism. Let subsamp $\mathbf{\Delta}_{m}^{n}:\mathcal{V}^{n}\mathcal{V}^{m}$ be the subsampling operation mentioned above. Then, the mechanism can be written as

$$
{\mathcal{M}}({\mathcal{D}})=S_{n}\circ\operatorname{subsamp}_{m}^{n}({\mathcal{G}}(x_{1}),\dots,{\mathcal{G}}(x_{n})).
$$

The RDP of the subsampled shuffle Gaussian mechanism is given by the following theorem.

theorems.statement: Corollary 2 (Upper bound of shuffle Gaussian RDP). The shuffle Gaussian RDP (λ) is upperbounded by $\lambda/2\dot{\sigma}^{2}$

noting that $\begin{array}{ l }{{\sum_{k_{1}+\ldots+k_{n}=\lambda;}{\binom{\lambda}{k_{1},\ldots,k_{n}}}=n^{\lambda}}}\end{array}$ . Substituting this to Equation 1, we get the desired expression.

theorems.statement: Let $D=(x_1,\ldots,x_n)$ be a database of $n$ data instances $x_i\in\mathbb{R}^d$ with $\|x_i\|_2\in[0,1]$, and let $\mathcal{M}(D)=S_n(\mathcal{G}(x_1),\ldots,\mathcal{G}(x_n))$ be the shuffle Gaussian mechanism, where the Gaussian mechanism $\mathcal{G}$ adds zero-mean isotropic Gaussian noise of variance $\sigma^2$ to each instance and $S_n$ uniformly randomly permutes the noisy instances. For any two adjacent databases $D,D'$ (differing by replacement of one instance) with $n$ instances, the Rényi divergence of order $\lambda$ between $\mathcal{M}(D)$ and $\mathcal{M}(D')$ is $$D_{\lambda}(\mathcal{M}(D)\|\mathcal{M}(D'))=\frac{1}{\lambda-1}\log\left(\frac{e^{-\lambda/2\sigma^2}}{n^{\lambda}}\sum_{\substack{k_1+\ldots+k_n=\lambda;\\k_1,\ldots,k_n\geq 0}}\binom{\lambda}{k_1,\ldots,k_n}e^{\sum_{i=1}^{n}k_i^2/2\sigma^2}\right).$$

steps.claim: It suffices, without loss of generality, to consider the specific canonical adjacent databases $D,D'\in\mathbb{R}^n$ with one-dimensional instances $D=(0,\ldots,0)$ and $D'=(1,0,\ldots,0)$; equivalently in vector notation $D=0$ (the all-zeros $n$-vector) and $D'=e_1$ (a unit vector).

The shuffled output of $D$ distributes as $\mathcal{M}(D)\sim(\mathcal{N}(0,\sigma^2),\ldots,\mathcal{N}(0,\sigma^2))$, an $n$-tuple of $\mathcal{N}(0,\sigma^2)$, and by the homogeneity of $D$ this is written $\mathcal{M}(D)\sim\mathcal{N}(0,\sigma^2 I_n)$.
The shuffled output of $D'$ distributes as the uniform mixture $\mathcal{M}(D')\sim\frac{1}{n}(\mathcal{N}(e_1,\sigma^2 I_n)+\ldots+\mathcal{N}(e_n,\sigma^2 I_n))$.

The neighbouring distributions of interest are $\mathcal{M}(D)\sim\mathcal{N}(0,\sigma^2 I_n)$ and $\mathcal{M}(D')\sim\frac{1}{n}(\mathcal{N}(e_1,\sigma^2 I_n)+\ldots+\mathcal{N}(e_n,\sigma^2 I_n))$ (Equation 3).

Using the Gaussian density $\mathbb{P}(\mathcal{N}(0,\sigma^2))=\exp[-x^2/2\sigma^2]/\sqrt{2\pi\sigma^2}$ and the mixture density for $\mathcal{M}(D')$, the Rényi divergence integrand for the pair reduces to a power of a sum of exponentials, namely $\left(\sum_{i=1}^{n}\exp[(2x_i-1)/2\sigma^2]\right)^{\lambda}$ (Equation 4).

By the multinomial theorem, $\left(\sum_{i=1}^{n}\exp[(2x_i-1)/2\sigma^2]\right)^{\lambda}=\sum_{\substack{k_1+\ldots+k_n=\lambda;\\k_1,\ldots,k_n\geq 0}}\binom{\lambda}{k_1,\ldots,k_n}\prod_{i=1}^{n}\exp[k_i(2x_i-1)/2\sigma^2]$, where $\binom{\lambda}{k_1,\ldots,k_n}=\frac{\lambda!}{k_1!\cdots k_n!}$ and $k_i\in\mathbb{Z}^{+}$ (Equation 5).

Taking the expectation and simplifying yields $\frac{1}{n^{\lambda}}\sum_{\substack{k_1+\ldots+k_n=\lambda;\\k_1,\ldots,k_n\geq 0}}\binom{\lambda}{k_1,\ldots,k_n}\prod_{i=1}^{n}\exp[(k_i^2-k_i)/2\sigma^2]=\frac{e^{-\lambda/2\sigma^2}}{n^{\lambda}}\sum_{\substack{k_1+\ldots+k_n=\lambda;\\k_1,\ldots,k_n\geq 0}}\binom{\lambda}{k_1,\ldots,k_n}e^{\sum_{i=1}^{n}k_i^2/2\sigma^2}$ (Equation 2).

Combining Equation 2 with Equation 1 gives $D_{\lambda}(\mathcal{M}(D)\|\mathcal{M}(D'))=\frac{1}{\lambda-1}\log\left(\frac{e^{-\lambda/2\sigma^2}}{n^{\lambda}}\sum_{\substack{k_1+\ldots+k_n=\lambda;\\k_1,\ldots,k_n\geq 0}}\binom{\lambda}{k_1,\ldots,k_n}e^{\sum_{i=1}^{n}k_i^2/2\sigma^2}\right)$, i.e. Equation 6, as desired.

Theorem 3 (Subsampled Shuffle Gaussian RDP). Let n be the total number of users, m be the number of subsampled users in each round of training, and γ be the subsampling rate, $\gamma = m / n$ Also let $\epsilon_{m}^{\mathrm{{\tiny\breve{S}G}}}(\lambda)$ be the shuffle Gaussian RDP given in Theorem 2. The subsampled shuffle Gaussian mechanism satisfies $(\lambda,\epsilon_{\gamma,m}^{\mathrm{{S S G}}}(\lambda))– R D P,$ where

$$
\epsilon_{\gamma,m}^{\mathrm{SG}}(\lambda)\leq\frac{1}{\lambda-1}\log\left(1+\gamma^{2}{\binom{\lambda}{2}}\operatorname*{min}\left\{4(e^{\epsilon_{m}^{\mathrm{SG}}(2)}-1),2e^{\epsilon_{m}^{\mathrm{SG}}(2)}\right\}+\sum_{j=3}^{\lambda}2\gamma^{j}{\binom{\lambda}{j}}e^{(j-1)\epsilon_{m}^{\mathrm{SG}}(j)}\right)\tag{7}
$$

steps.claim: The proof is a direct application of Theorem 2 and the subsampled RDP results of Wang et al. (2019).
The full proof can be found in Appendix B.

label: flawed
error_explanation: Step 1 claims that computing the Rényi divergence for the single canonical adjacent pair $D=(0,\ldots,0), D'=(1,0,\ldots,0)$ suffices 'without loss of generality' for arbitrary adjacent databases, justifying this by normalizing/applying a unitary (affine) transform to the data instances. This is invalid because that affine normalization does NOT commute with the shuffling operation $S_n$: once the per-instance data are permuted by $S_n$, a fixed affine transform applied before shuffling no longer yields the canonical configuration. Hence the RDP computed for the canonical pair neither equals nor upper-bounds the RDP for general adjacent databases, so the result holds only for the specific pair $D=(0,\ldots,0), D'=(1,0,\ldots,0)$ and not in the generality Theorem 1 (Eq. 4) claims. The authors conceded this and withdrew the submission; no general fix exists.

Sequential approximation as a functional approximation problem. The goal of sequential modeling is to learn a relationship between an input sequence $\textbf{ x }=\ \{\mathbf{x}_{t}\}$ and a corresponding output sequence $\{y_{t}\}$ . The time index t can be discrete or continuous. For ease of analysis, we adopt the continuous-time setting in (Li et al., 2021), where $t \in \mathbb R$ This is also a natural setting for irregularly sampled time series (Lechner & Hasani, 2020). We consider the d-dimensional input space $\breve{\mathscr{X}}=\breve{C}_{0 . T . K}^{1}(\mathbb{R},\mathbb{R}^{d})$ , which is continuously differentiable with respect to time and vanishes at infinity in the sense that $\mathbf{x}_{t}~=~\mathbf{x}_{\infty}$ for some $0 < T \leq t \leq \infty$ , with the supremum norm $\begin{array}{ r }{\|\mathbf{x}\|_{\mathcal{X}}: =\operatorname*{sup}_{t\in\mathbb{R}}\|\mathbf{x}_{t}\|_{\infty}}\end{array}$ Without loss of generality, we also assume $\mathbf{x}_{t}~=~0$ for $t \leq 0$ and the derivatives of input is bounded: $\|\frac{d{\bf x}_{t}}{d t}\|_{\infty}\leq K,\forall t$
We assume the input and output sequences are related by a family of underlying functionals

$$
y_{t}=H_{t}(\{\mathbf{x}_{t}\}),\quad t\in\mathbb{R},\tag{2}
$$

where $H_{t}:\mathcal{X}\mapsto\mathbb{R}$ is a functional. Now, the sequential approximation problem can be formulated as the approximation of target functionals $\{H_{t}:t\in\mathbb{R}\}$ by model functionals $\{\widetilde{H}_{t}:t\in\mathbb{R}\}$ , where $\widetilde{H}_{t}(\cdot)$ is contained in certain hypothesis space $\widetilde{\mathcal{H}},$ such as various classes of neural networks. We say a sequence of target functionals $\{H_{t}:t\stackrel{\cdot}{\in}\mathbb{R}\}$ can be uniformly approximated by model functionals, if for any tolerance $\epsilon > 0$ , there exists $\{\widetilde{H}_{t}:t\in\mathbb{R}\}\in\widetilde{\mathcal{H}}$ such that

$$
\operatorname*{sup}_{t\in\mathbb{R}}\operatorname*{sup}_{\|\mathbf{x}\|\mathbf{x}\leq 1}|H_{t}(\mathbf{x})-\widetilde{H}_{t}(\mathbf{x})|\leq\epsilon .\tag{3}
$$
The continuous-time RNN architecture. First, we introduce the same continuous-time formulation of RNNs as (Li et al., 2021):

$$
\frac{d h_{t}}{d t}=\sigma(W h_{t}+U{\bf x}_{t}),\tag{4}
$$

$$
\hat{y}_{t}=c^{\top}h_{t}.\tag{5}
$$

Here, $\hat{y}_{t}\in\mathbb R$ is the prediction, and $\boldsymbol{h}_{t}\in\mathbb{R}^{m}$ denotes the hidden state. As a common practice, we set the initial hidden state $h_{0}=0 .{}^{1}$ The hyper-parameter m is also known as the hidden dimension of recurrent neural networks. For different hidden dimensions $m$ , the RNN is parameterized by trainable weights $(c,W,U)$ , where $c\in\mathbb{R}^{m}$ is the readout, $W\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times m}$ is the recurrent kernel and $U\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times d}$ is the input kernel. Obviously, the complexity of the RNN hypothesis space is characterized by the hidden dimension m. The nonlinearity arises from the activation $\sigma(\cdot)$ , which is a scalar nonlinear function performed element-wisely, such as tanh, hardtanh, sigmoid, ReLU and so on. The hypothesis space of RNNs with different activations are denoted by $\mathcal{H}^{\sigma(\cdot)}$

1. (Linear) $H_{t}$ is linear if for any $\lambda,\lambda^{\prime}\in\mathbb{R}a n d\mathbf{x},\mathbf{x}^{\prime}\in\mathcal{X},H_{t}(\lambda\mathbf{x}+\lambda^{\prime}\mathbf{x}^{\prime})=\lambda H_{t}(\mathbf{x})+$ $\lambda^{\prime}H_{t}(\mathbf{x}^{\prime})$

R(m)=\operatorname*{sup}_{t\in\mathbb{R}}\|{H}_{t}-\bar{H}_{t}\|\equiv\operatorname*{sup}_{t\in\mathbb{R}}\operatorname*{sup}_{\|{\bf x}\||{x}\leq 1}|{H}_{t}({\bf x})-\bar{H}_{t}({\bf x})|\leq\frac{C(\alpha)\gamma d}{\beta m^{\alpha}}.\tag{10}
$$
Proposition 2 (Universal approximation for linear RNNs by nonlinear RNNs) For any linear $R N N\left\{\hat{H}_{t}:t\in\mathbb{R}\right\}$ there exists a sequence of nonlinear RNN $\{\widetilde{H}_{t}:t\in\mathbb{R}\}$ with activations satisfying Equation (11) that can approximate the linear RNN with the following error bound:

$$
\operatorname*{sup}_{t\in\mathbb{R}}\operatorname*{sup}_{\|\mathbf{x}\|_{\mathcal{X}}\leq 1}|\bar{H}_{t}(\mathbf{x})-\widetilde{H}_{t}(\mathbf{x})|\leq\frac{\epsilon}{2}.\tag{12}
$$

theorems.statement:
Theorem 3 (Universal approximation of linear functionals) Let $\{H_{t}:t\in\mathbb{R}\}$ be a family of linear, continuous, causal, regular and time-homogeneous functionals on X. Assume the activation $\sigma(\cdot)$ is continuous and monotonically-increasing, and satisfies the following assumptions

$$
\sigma(0)=0,\sigma^{\prime}(0)=1,|\sigma^{\prime}(z)|\leq M,|\sigma^{\prime}(z)-\sigma^{\prime}(0)|\leq M|\sigma(z)|,|\sigma^{\prime\prime}(z)|\leq M|\sigma^{\prime}(z)|\tag{11}
$$

for some constant $M > 0$ Then, for any $\epsilon>0,$ there exists a sequence of nonlinear RNNs $\{\widetilde{H}_{t}$ $t\in\mathbb{R}\}\in\widetilde{\mathcal{H}}^{\sigma}$ such that

$$
\operatorname*{sup}_{t\in\mathbb{R}}\|H_{t}-\widetilde{H}_{t}\|\equiv\operatorname*{sup}_{t\in\mathbb{R}}\operatorname*{sup}_{\|\mathbf{x}\|_{\mathcal{X}}\leq 1}|H_{t}(\mathbf{x})-\widetilde{H}_{t}(\mathbf{x})|\leq\epsilon .\tag{13}
$$

One can verify that tanh, which is commonly-used in practice for RNNs, is an activation satisfying the conditions (11). The proof of Theorem 3 is given in Appendix A.3.

steps.claim: By the universal approximation theorem for linear functionals by linear RNNs (Theorem 1), and the universal approximation theorem for linear RNNs by tanh RNNs (Proposition 2), we have

$$
\operatorname*{sup}_{t\in\mathbb{R}}\|H_{t}-\hat{H}_{t}\|\equiv\operatorname*{sup}_{t\in\mathbb{R}}\operatorname*{sup}_{\|\mathbf{x}\|_{\boldsymbol{x}}\leq 1}|H_{t}(\mathbf{x})-\hat{H}_{t}(\mathbf{x})|\leq\frac{\epsilon}{2},
$$

$$
\operatorname*{sup}_{t\in\mathbb{R}}\|\hat{H}_{t}-\widetilde{H}_{t}\|\equiv\operatorname*{sup}_{t\in\mathbb{R}}\operatorname*{sup}_{\|\mathbf{x}\|_{x}\leq 1}|\hat{H}_{t}(\mathbf{x})-\widetilde{H}_{t}(\mathbf{x})|\leq\frac{\epsilon}{2},
$$
which yields the desired estimate

$$
\operatorname*{sup}_{t\in\mathbb{R}}\|H_{t}-\widetilde{H}_{t}\|\equiv\operatorname*{sup}_{t\in\mathbb{R}}\operatorname*{sup}_{\|\mathbf{x}\|_{\mathcal{X}}\leq 1}|H_{t}(\mathbf{x})-\widetilde{H}_{t}(\mathbf{x})|\leq\epsilon .
$$

theorems.statement:
Theorem 4 (Approximation rate of linear functionals) Assume the same conditions as in Theorem 3. Consider the output of constant signals

$$
y_{i}(t)=H_{t}(\mathbf{e}_{i}),\quad i=1,\ldots,d .\tag{14}
$$

Suppose there exist constants $\alpha\in\mathbb{N}_{+},\beta,\gamma>0,$ such that $fori=1,\ldots,d,k=1,\ldots,\alpha+1$ $y_{i}(t)\in C^{(\alpha+1)}(\mathbb{R})$ , and

$$
e^{\beta t}y_{i}^{(k)}(t)=o(1)\quad a s t\to+\infty,\tag{15}
$$

$$
\operatorname*{sup}_{t\geq 0}\frac{|e^{\beta t}y_{i}^{(k)}(t)|}{\beta^{k}}\leq\gamma .\tag{16}
$$

Then, there exists a universal constant C(α) only depending on α, such that for any m $\in\mathbb{N}_{+}$ , there exists a sequence of width-m nonlinear RNN functionals $\{\widetilde{H}_{t}:t\in\mathbb{R}\}\in\widetilde{\mathcal{H}}_{m}^{\sigma}$ such that

$$
R(m)=\operatorname*{sup}_{t\in\mathbb{R}}\|{H}_{t}-\widetilde{H}_{t}\|\equiv\operatorname*{sup}_{t\in\mathbb{R}}\operatorname*{sup}_{\|{\mathbf x}\|{x}\leq 1}|{H}_{t}({\mathbf x})-\widetilde{H}_{t}({\mathbf x})|\leq\frac{C(\alpha)\gamma d}{\beta m^{\alpha}}.\tag{17}
$$

The proof is included in Appendix A.4. Theorem 4 shows that, as long as the activation function $\sigma(\cdot)$ satisfies the conditions in Equation (11), such as the tanh activation, nonlinear RNNs can obtain the same approximation rate as linear RNNs.

steps.claim: By the approximation rate theorem for linear functionals by linear RNNs (Theorem 2), and proper rescaling from the universal approximation theorem for linear RNNs by tanh RNNs (Proposition 2), we have

$$
\operatorname*{sup}_{t\in\mathbb{R}}\|H_{t}-\bar{H}_{t}\|\equiv\operatorname*{sup}_{t\in\mathbb{R}}\operatorname*{sup}_{\|\mathbf{x}\|_{x}\leq 1}|H_{t}(\mathbf{x})-\bar{H}_{t}(\mathbf{x})|\leq\frac{C(\alpha)\gamma d}{\beta m^{\alpha}},
$$

$$
\operatorname*{sup}_{t\in\mathbb{R}}\|\bar{H}_{t}-\widetilde{H}_{t}\|\equiv\operatorname*{sup}_{t\in\mathbb{R}}\operatorname*{sup}_{\|\mathbf{x}\|_{x}\leq 1}|\bar{H}_{t}(\mathbf{x})-\widetilde{H}_{t}(\mathbf{x})|\leq\epsilon\frac{C(\alpha)\gamma d}{\beta m^{\alpha}},
$$
which gives

$$
\operatorname*{sup}_{t\in\mathbb{R}}\|{\cal H}_{t}-\widetilde{{\cal H}}_{t}\|\equiv\operatorname*{sup}_{t\in\mathbb{R}}\operatorname*{sup}_{\|{\bf x}\|_{\cal x}\leq 1}|{\cal H}_{t}({\bf x}-\widetilde{{\cal H}}_{t}({\bf x}))|\leq(1+\epsilon)\frac{C(\alpha)\gamma d}{\beta m^{\alpha}}.
$$
Let the quantity M in Proposition 2 go to infinity, we get $\epsilon  0 .$ This completes the proof.

theorems.statement: Consider the $d$-dimensional input space $\mathcal{X}$ of continuously differentiable signals vanishing at infinity, with supremum norm $\|\mathbf{x}\|_{\mathcal{X}}:=\sup_{t\in\mathbb{R}}\|\mathbf{x}_t\|_\infty$, and the continuous-time tanh RNN hypothesis space defined by $\frac{dh_t}{dt}=\sigma(Wh_t+U\mathbf{x}_t)$, $\hat y_t=c^\top h_t$ (with $\sigma=\tanh$, $h_0=0$). Uniform approximation of target functionals $\{H_t\}$ by model functionals $\{\widetilde H_t\}$ means: for any $\epsilon>0$ there exists $\{\widetilde H_t\}$ with $\sup_{t\in\mathbb{R}}\sup_{\|\mathbf{x}\|_{\mathcal{X}}\le 1}|H_t(\mathbf{x})-\widetilde H_t(\mathbf{x})|\le\epsilon$. A family $\{H_t\}$ is homogeneous of degree $p>0$ if $H_t(\kappa\mathbf{x})=\kappa^p H_t(\mathbf{x})$ for all $\kappa$. Claim (Proposition 1): There exists a sequence of homogeneous functionals $\{H_t : t\in\mathbb{R}\}$ with a homogeneity degree $p>1$ and an $\epsilon>0$, such that there is no tanh RNN $\{\widetilde H_t : t\in\mathbb{R}\}$ approximating $\{H_t : t\in\mathbb{R}\}$ uniformly with an approximation error smaller than $\epsilon$.

steps.claim: Assume, for contradiction, the universal approximation theorem holds for homogeneous functionals by tanh RNNs. Then for any $\epsilon>0$ there exists a tanh RNN $(c,W,U)$ with $\sup_t\sup_{\|\mathbf{x}\|_{\mathcal{X}}\le 1}|H_t(\mathbf{x})-\widetilde H_t(\mathbf{x})|\le\epsilon$.
Take an input $\mathbf{x}$ with $H_t(\mathbf{x})\neq 0$ for $t\ge 0$; WLOG $H_t(\mathbf{x})>0$ for $t\ge 0$.
Set $\epsilon=\frac12|H_t(\kappa\mathbf{x})|=\frac12|\kappa^2 H_t(\mathbf{x})|$, with the constant $\kappa$ to be fixed later.

By the (assumed) universal approximation theorem, there exists $\widetilde H_t$ such that for any $t$: $|H_t(\kappa\mathbf{x})-\widetilde H_t(\kappa\mathbf{x})|\le\epsilon$ and $|H_t(\mathbf{x})-\widetilde H_t(\mathbf{x})|\le\epsilon$.
Construct a linear RNN $\bar H_t$ with the same parameters $(c,W,U)$ (i.e. the RNN with the tanh nonlinearity removed). Then $\bar H_t(\mathbf{x})=\widetilde H_t(\mathbf{x})\equiv 0$ for $t\le 0$.

There always exists a $t>0$ such that, for $\delta=\frac12$: $|\bar H_t(\kappa\mathbf{x})-\widetilde H_t(\kappa\mathbf{x})|\le\delta|\widetilde H_t(\kappa\mathbf{x})|$ and $|\bar H_t(\mathbf{x})-\widetilde H_t(\mathbf{x})|\le\delta|\widetilde H_t(\mathbf{x})|$; hence $\bar H_t(\mathbf{x})\ge(1-\delta)\widetilde H_t(\mathbf{x})$.
Take $\kappa=\frac{1}{10},\ \delta=\frac12$; then by continuity $(1-\delta)(1-\frac12\kappa^2)>(1+\delta)\frac1\kappa(\kappa^2+\frac12\kappa^2)$.

$\bar H_t(\mathbf{x})\ge(1-\delta)\widetilde H_t(\mathbf{x})\ge(1-\delta)\big(H_t(\mathbf{x})-\frac12\kappa^2 H_t(\mathbf{x})\big)>(1+\delta)\frac1\kappa\big(\kappa^2 H_t(\mathbf{x})+\frac12\kappa^2 H_t(\mathbf{x})\big)=(1+\delta)\frac1\kappa\big(H_t(\kappa\mathbf{x})+\frac12\kappa^2 H_t(\mathbf{x})\big)\ge(1+\delta)\frac1\kappa\widetilde H_t(\kappa\mathbf{x})\ge\frac1\kappa\bar H_t(\kappa\mathbf{x})$.

However, the linear RNN satisfies exactly $\bar H_t(\mathbf{x})=\frac1\kappa\bar H_t(\kappa\mathbf{x})$, and $\bar H_t(\mathbf{x})>(1-\delta)(1-\frac12\kappa^2)H_t(\mathbf{x})>0$, contradicting the strict inequality $\bar H_t(\mathbf{x})>\frac1\kappa\bar H_t(\kappa\mathbf{x})$ derived in Step 8.

theorems.statement:
Theorem 5 (Inverse approximation theorem) Assume that the activation function $\sigma(\cdot)$ is tanh, and $\{H_{t}:t\in\mathbb{R}\}$ is a family of linear, continuous, causal, regular and time-homogeneous functionals on X. Consider the output of constant signals

$$
y_{i}(t)=H_{t}(\mathbf{e}_{i})\in C^{(\alpha+1)}(\mathbb{R}),\quad i=1,\dots,d,\alpha\in\mathbb{N}_{+}.\tag{18}
$$

Suppose there exists a sequence of nonlinear RNNs $\{\widetilde{H}_{t}:t\in\mathbb{R}\}\in\widetilde{\mathcal{H}}^{\sigma}$ with an increasing hidden dimension m approximating $\{H_{t}:t\in\mathbb{R}\}$ in the following sense:

$$
\operatorname*{lim}_{m\to\infty}\operatorname*{sup}_{t\geq 0}|\tilde{y}_{i,m}^{(k)}(t)-y_{i}^{(k)}(t)| =0,\quad i=1,\ldots,d,k=1,\ldots,\alpha+1,\tag{19}
$$

where

$$
\widetilde{y}_{i,m}(t)=\widetilde{H}_{t}(\mathbf{e}_{i}),\quad i=1,\ldots,d .\tag{20}
$$

Moreover, assume that the recurrent kernel matrix $W_{m}$ in the nonlinear RNN is a special Hurwitz matrix, that is, there exists a diagonal positive-definite matrix $D_{m}$ and a negative-definite matrix $N_{m}$ such that $W_{m}=D_{m}N_{m}$ . Define $n_{m}=\mathrm{max}_{j\in [m]}$ Re(λj), where $\{\lambda_{j}\}_{j=1}^{m}$ collects all the eigenvalues of $N_{m}$ . Define $\begin{array}{ r }{d_{m}=\operatorname*{min}_{j\in [m]}(D_{m})_{j j}.}\end{array}$ Assume that the parameters in nonlinear RNNs are uniformly bounded and there exits constants $\bar{\beta},\theta>0$ such that lim $\begin{array}{ r }{\operatorname*{sup}_{m\infty}\frac{n_{m}}{\theta d_{m}}< -\beta}\end{array}$ , then we have

$$
e^{\beta t}y_{i}^{(k)}(t)=o(1)a s t\to+\infty,\quad i=1,\ldots,d,k=1,\ldots,\alpha+1 .\tag{21}
$$

Here, we only give the proof sketch to show the meaning and implications of Theorem 5. For the detailed proof, see Appendix A.7. Similar results can also be obtained for the sigmoid activation.

steps.claim:
Without loss of generality, we give the proof for $\alpha \ : = \ : 0$ and $k \ = \ 1$ The dynamics of hidden states of tanh RNNs are described by the following differential equations:

$$
\begin{array}{ r }{\frac{d h_{t}}{d t}=\sigma(W h_{t}+U{\bf x}_{t}),}\\ {h_{0}=0 .\qquad}\end{array}
$$

Define $\begin{array}{ r }{v_{t}=\frac{d h_{t}}{d t}}\end{array}$ , then we have $v_{t}=\sigma(W h_{t}+U\mathbf{x}_{t})$ . Notice that $\sigma^{\prime}(z)=1-\sigma(z)^{2}$ holds for the tanh activation, the dynamics of $v_{t}$ satisfies

$$
\begin{array}{ l }{\displaystyle\frac{d v_{t}}{d t}=\sigma^{\prime}({\boldsymbol{W}}h_{t}+{\boldsymbol{U}}\mathbf{x}_{t})({\boldsymbol{W}}v_{t}+{\boldsymbol{U}}\frac{d\mathbf{x}_{t}}{d t})}\\ {\displaystyle\ }\\ {\displaystyle=(I-\mathrm{diag}(\sigma({\boldsymbol{W}}h_{t}+{\boldsymbol{U}}\mathbf{x}_{t}))^{2})({\boldsymbol{W}}v_{t}+{\boldsymbol{U}}\frac{d\mathbf{x}_{t}}{d t}),}\\ {\displaystyle\ }\\ {\displaystyle=(I-\mathrm{diag}(v_{t})^{2})({\boldsymbol{W}}v_{t}+{\boldsymbol{U}}\frac{d\mathbf{x}_{t}}{d t}),}\\ {\displaystyle v_{0}=0 .}\end{array}
$$

We also consider a special class of constant inputs $\pmb{x}_{t}=x_{0}1_{\{t\geq 0\}},x_{0}\in\mathbb{R}^{d}.$ Then for any $t > 0$

$$
\begin{array}{ c }{\frac{d v_{t}}{d t}=(I-\mathrm{diag}(v_{t})^{2})W v_{t},}\\ {v_{0}=\sigma(W x_{0}).}\end{array}
$$

The proof is based on the construction of the Lyapunov function. Define

$$
V(v)=\sum_{i=1}^{m}\sum_{j=1}^{\infty}\frac{1}{2 j D_{i i}}v_{i}^{2 j},
$$

where $v_{i}$ is the i-th coordinate of v. It is straightforward to verify that $V(v)\geq 0$ , and $V(v)=0$ if and only if $v = 0$

Since the special Hurwitz matrix W can be decomposed into $W = D N .$ ,where D is a positive diagonal matrix and N is a negative definite matrix. We can derive the global stability of $v_{t}$ as

follows:

$$
\begin{array}{ l }{\displaystyle\frac{d V(v_{t})}{d t}=\sum_{i=1}^{m}\sum_{j=1}^{\infty}\frac{1}{D_{i i}}v_{i,t}^{2 j-1}\frac{d v_{i,t}}{d t}}\\ {\displaystyle\quad\quad=v_{t}^{\top}D^{-1}\bigg(\sum_{j=1}^{\infty}\mathrm{diag}(v_{t})^{2 j-2}\bigg)\frac{d v_{t}}{d t}}\\ {\displaystyle\quad=v_{t}^{\top}D^{-1}(I-\mathrm{diag}(v_{t})^{2})^{-1}(I-\mathrm{diag}(v_{t})^{2})W v_{t}}\\ {\displaystyle\quad=v_{t}^{\top}D^{-1}W v_{t}}\\ {\displaystyle\quad=v_{t}^{\top}N v_{t}\leq 0 .}\end{array}
$$

For any bounded input, we get $\left\|v_{0}\right\|\le 1-\iota$ for some $\iota > 0$ Therefore, we further have

$$
\frac{d V(v_{t,m})}{d t}\leq-\alpha_{m}V(v_{t,m}),
$$

where m is the hidden dimension, $\begin{array}{ r }{\alpha_{m}=\frac{n_{m}}{\theta d_{m}}}\end{array}$ with $\textstyle\theta=\sum_{j=1}^{\infty}{\frac{1}{2 j}}(1-\iota)^{2 j-2}$ as a constant related to t. Define $\beta=\mathrm{inf}_{m\in\mathbb{N}_{+}}\alpha_{m}$ .

Based on the Lyapunov exponential stability theorem, we establish the exponential stability of $v_{t,m},$ i.e. $e^{\alpha_{m}t}v_{t,m}=o(1)$ . Since $\tilde{y}_{i,m}^{(1)}(t)=c^{\top}v_{t,m}$ , we get $e^{\beta t}\tilde{y}_{i,m}^{(1)}(t)=$ o(1) for all $m\in\mathbb{N}_{+}$ , which gives $e^{\beta t}y_{i}^{(1)}(t)=o(1)$ for $i=1,\cdots,d.$

label: flawed
error_explanation: Step 3 sets $\epsilon = \tfrac12|H_t(\kappa\mathbf{x})|$ with $t$ still unbound -- no $t$ has been fixed anywhere in Steps 1-2. Step 4 then invokes the universal-approximation assumption as though $\epsilon$ were already a well-defined positive real, but $H_t(\mathbf{x})$ is generically not constant in $t$, so $\epsilon$ cannot actually be pinned down until $t$ is known -- yet $t$ is only fixed in step 6, *after* the RNN built from this ill-defined $\epsilon$ already exists. This is a genuine quantifier/scope circularity ($\epsilon$ must depend on the $t$ that hasn't been chosen yet), not mere terseness. The authors' own withdrawal note confirms this exact issue: 'the selection of $\epsilon$ should not depend on $\kappa$ and $t_0$' -- precisely describing step 3's construction. Step 6 (the previously-labeled error step) only inherits this problem; it is not itself the first failure.

context:
We consider a physical system specified by a state variable s and a parameter variable θ. The system is also influenced by an external input $\mathrm{v},\mathrm{e}.\mathrm{g}.$ in the supervised setting $\mathrm{~v~}=\mathrm{~(x,y)~}$ where y is the target that the system wants to predict given x. Let $s\mapsto\mu(\theta,\mathrm{v},s)$ be a vector field in the state space and $C(\theta,\mathrm{v},s)$ a cost function. We assume that the state dynamics induced by µ converges to a stable fixed point $s_{\theta,\mathrm{v}}^{0},$ corresponding to the "prediction" from the model and characterized by

$$
\begin{array}{ r }{\mu\left(\boldsymbol{\theta},\mathrm{v},\boldsymbol{s}_{\boldsymbol{\theta},\mathrm{v}}^{0}\right)=0 .}\end{array}\tag{1}
$$

The objective function that we want to optimize is the cost at the fixed point

$$
\begin{array}{ r }{J(\theta,\mathrm{v}): =C\left(\theta,\mathrm{v},s_{\theta,\mathrm{v}}^{0}\right).}\end{array}\tag{2}
$$

Note the distinction between J and $C { : }$ the cost function is defined for any state s whereas the objective function is the cost at the fixed point. Before defining ν we first introduce the "extended vector field"

$$
\mu^{\beta}(\boldsymbol{\theta},{\mathrm v},s): =\mu(\boldsymbol{\theta},{\mathrm v},s)-\beta\ \frac{\partial C}{\partial s}(\boldsymbol{\theta},{\mathrm v},s),\tag{3}
$$

where $\beta$ is a real-valued scalar called "influence parameter". Then we extend the notion of fixed point for any value of $\beta$ For any $\beta$ we define the β-fixed point $s_{\theta,\mathrm{v}}^{\beta}$ such that

$$
\mu^{\beta}\left(\theta,\mathrm{v},s_{\theta,\mathrm{v}}^{\beta}\right)=0 .\tag{4}
$$

Under mild regularity conditions on µ and $C .$ , the implicit function theorem ensures that, for a fixed data sample v, the funtion $(\theta,\beta)\mapsto s_{\theta,\mathrm{v}}^{\beta}$ is differentiable.

Now for every θ and v we define the vector $\nu(\theta,\mathrm{v})$ in the parameter space as

$$
\nu(\theta,{\bf v}): = -\frac{\partial C}{\partial\theta}\left(\theta,{\bf v},s_{\theta,\mathrm{v}}^{0}\right)+\frac{\partial\mu}{\partial\theta}\left(\theta,{\bf v},s_{\theta,\mathrm{v}}^{0}\right)\cdot\left.\frac{\partial s_{\theta,\mathrm{v}}^{\beta}}{\beta}\right|_{\beta=0}.\tag{5}
$$

In this section, we attempt to understand why the proposed algorithm is experimentally found to optimize the objective function J (Figure 3). We say that $W$ is a "good parameter" if:

1. for any initial state for the neurons, the state dynamics $\begin{array}{ r }{\frac{d h}{d t}=\mu\left(W,\mathbf{x},h\right)}\end{array}$ converges to a fixed point - a condition required for the algorithm to be correctly defined,

2. the scalar product $\frac{\partial J}{\partial W}\cdot\nu(W)$ at the point $W$ is negative - a desirable condition for the algorithm to optimize the objective function J.

Experiments show that the dynamics of h (almost) always converges to a fixed point and that J consistently decreases (Figure 3). This means that, during training, as the parameter W follows the update rule $\Delta W\propto\nu(W)$ , all values of W that the network takes are "good parameters". In this section we attempt to explain why.

Theorem 3. The gradient of J can be expressed in terms of µ and C as

$$
\frac{\partial J}{\partial W}= -\frac{\partial C}{\partial h}\cdot\left(\frac{\partial\mu}{\partial h}\right)^{-1}\cdot\frac{\partial\mu}{\partial W}.\tag{6}
$$

Similarly, the vector field ν (Eq. 7) is equal to

$$
\nu(W)=\frac{\partial C}{\partial h}\cdot\left(\left(\frac{\partial\mu}{\partial h}\right)^{T}\right)^{-1}\cdot\frac{\partial\mu}{\partial W}.\tag{8}
$$

In these expressions, all terms are evaluated at the fixed point $h^{0}$

Theorem 3 is proved in Appendix A. Note that the formulas show that $\nu(W)$ is related to $\frac{\partial J}{\partial W}$ and that the angle between these two vectors is directly linked to the "degree of symmetry" of the Jacobian of $\mu .$ .

An important particular case is the setting of Equilibrium Propagation (Scellier & Bengio, 2017), in which the vector field $\mu$ is a gradient field $\begin{array}{ r }{\mu= -\frac{\partial E}{\partial h}}\end{array}$ , meaning that it derives from an energy function $E .$ In this case the Jacobian of $\mu$ is symmetric since it is the Hessian of E.

We argue that the set of "good parameters" covers a large proportion of the weight space and that they contain the matrices W that present a form of symmetry or "alignment". In the next subsection, we discuss how this form of symmetry may arise from the learning procedure itself.

Experiments show that a form of symmetry between feedforward and feedback weights arises from the learning procedure itself (Figure 3). Although the causes for this phenomenon aren't understood very well yet, it is worth pointing out that similar observations have been made in previous work and different settings.

Lemma 1. Let $s\mapsto\mu^{\beta}(\theta,s)$ be a differentiable vector field, and $s_{\theta}^{\beta}$ a fixed point characterized by

u(W)$ optimizes $J$, because during training every $W$ visited is a 'good parameter' — meaning the dynamics converges AND $ rac{\partial J}{\partial W}\cdot

Comparing Eq. 6 and Eq. 8, $\nu(W)=-\frac{\partial J}{\partial W}$ holds when the Jacobian $\frac{\partial\mu}{\partial h}$ is symmetric (e.g. gradient/energy-based dynamics with tied weights); more generally the angle between $\nu(W)$ and $\frac{\partial J}{\partial W}$ is governed by the 'degree of symmetry' of $\frac{\partial\mu}{\partial h}$.
Experiments (Figure 3) show that the dynamics of $h$ almost always converges to a fixed point and that $J$ consistently decreases during training.

Therefore, during training, as $W$ follows the update rule $\Delta W\propto\nu(W)$, all values of $W$ that the network takes are 'good parameters' (the dynamics converges AND $\frac{\partial J}{\partial W}\cdot\nu(W)<0$), and the set of good parameters covers a large proportion of the weight space — those matrices $W$ that present a form of symmetry or 'alignment' — with this symmetry arising from the learning procedure itself.
Hence the STDP-compatible update $\Delta W\propto\nu(W)$ optimizes the objective function $J$.

This section presents and explains our main results on Transformers' capability in deductive reasoning and backtracking with CoT. To rigorously state our results, we first formally define decision problems, decision procedures, and what it means for a model to "solve" a decision problem using CoT:

Algorithm 1: Greedy Decoding
Input: Model $M:\mathcal{V}^{*}\to\mathcal{V}$ , prompt $s_{1:n}=(s_{1},s_{2},\ldots,s_{n})$ , stop tokens $\mathcal{E}\subseteq\mathcal{V}$ , $t \leftarrow n$
1: while $t \leftarrow t + 1$ do
2: $s_{t}\leftarrow M(s_{1:t-1})$ ; // Obtain model output and append to string
3: if $s_{t}\in\mathcal{E}$ return $s_{1:t}$
4: end

In this paper, we refer to the full generated sequence of tokens as the Chain-of-Thought, and the number of chain-of-thought tokens in Algorithm 1 is $t - n$ .

Definition 1 (Decision Problem). Let V be a vocabulary, $\Sigma \subseteq \nu$ be an alphabet, $L\subseteq\Sigma^{*}$ be a set of valid input strings. We say that a mapping $f:L\{0,1\}$ is a decision problem defined on L.

Definition 2 (Decision Procedure). We say that an algorithm A is a decision procedure for the decision problem f, if given any input string x from $L,A$ halts and outputs 1 if $f(x)=1$ , and halts and outputs 0 if $f(x)=0$

Definition 3 (Autoregressive Decision Procedure). For any map $M:\mathcal{V}^{*}\mathcal{V}.$ ,which we refer to as an auto-regressive next-token prediction model, and $\mathcal{E}=\{\bar{\mathcal{E}}_{0},\bar{\mathcal{E}}_{1}\}\subset\mathcal{V}$ , define procedure $\mathcal{A}_{M,\mathcal{E}}$ as follows: For any input $s_{1:n},$ run Algorithm 1 with stop tokens $\mathcal{E}.\ A_{M,\mathcal{E}}$ outputs 0 if $s_{1:t}$ ends with ${\mathcal{E}}_{0}$ and $\mathcal{A}_{M,\mathcal{E}}$ output 1 otherwise. We say M autoregressively decides decision problem f if there is some $\mathcal{E}\subset\mathcal{V}$ for which $\mathcal{A}_{M,\mathcal{E}}$ decides $f .$

Definition 4 ($3\text{-}\mathrm{SAT}_{p,c}$). Let $\mathrm{DIMACS}(p,c)$ denote the set of valid DIMACS encodings of 3-SAT instances with at most p variables and c clauses with a prepended [BOS] token and an appended [SEP] token. Define $3\text{-}\mathrm{SAT}_{p,c} : \mathrm{DIMACS}(p,c) \to \{0,1\}$ as the problem of deciding whether the 3-SAT formula encoded in the input in $\mathrm{DIMACS}(p,c)$ encoding is satisfiable.

With the above definition, we're ready to present a formal statement of our theoretical construction of a Transformer model that performs SAT Solving:

Remarks on Theorem 1

The upper bound on the CoT length $p\cdot 2^{p+1}$ is a worst-case upper bound which assumes that the model is unable to make any logical deductions have to try all $2^{p}$ assignments. However, this upper bound is never reached in practice, and in Figure 4 we show that the number of CoT tokens is no greater than $8p\cdot 2^{0.58p}$ for most formulas. If the number of backtracking steps is bounded by T then the CoT is no longer than $(2p+1)(T+1)$

Positional encodings are not included in the number of parameters. The positional encoding at position i is the numerical value i at a particular dimension.

Each parameter can be represented with $O(p+\log c)$ bits

In this section, we present adapted versions of several lemmas from Feng et al. (2023). Specifically, an MLP with ReGLU can exactly simulate ReLU, linear operations, and multiplication without error. For Self-attention lemmas, we directly adapt from Feng et al. (2023).

This section shows several lemmas showing the capabilities of the self-attention operation and MLP layers to approximate high-level vector operations. These high-level operations are later used as building blocks for the Transformer SAT-solver. Specifically, with appropriate weight configurations, a 2-layer MLP with ReGLU activation $f({\pmb x})=\bar{\pmb W_{2}}[({\pmb W_{1}\pmb x}+{\pmb b})\otimes\bar{\mathrm{\ r e l u}(\pmb V x+\pmb c)}]$ can approximate the following vector operations for arbitrary input x:

Simulate a 2-layer MLP with ReLU activation: $W_{\mathrm{2}}\mathrm{ReLU}(W_{1}^{\prime}x+b_{1}^{\prime})+b_{2}^{\prime}$

•Simulate any linear operation Wx

Simulate element-wise multiplication: $\pmb{x}_{1}\otimes\pmb{x}_{2}$

theorems.statement: Lemma 1 (Simulating Linear Operations with ReGLU MLP). A 2-layer MLP with ReGLU activation can compute any linear operation $f({\pmb x})={\pmb W}{\pmb x}+{\pmb b}.$

Since $V x+b_{2}=b_{2}=\mathbf{1}$ , we have: $$ \mathrm{ReLU}(V x+b_{2})=\mathrm{ReLU}({\bf 1})={\bf 1}. $$
Then, the ReGLU MLP computes: $$ f(\pmb{x})=I\left[\left(\pmb{W}\pmb{x}+\pmb{b}\right)\otimes\pmb{1}\right]=\pmb{W}\pmb{x}+\pmb{b}. $$

theorems.statement: Theorem 1 (Decoder-only Transformers can solve SAT). For any $p,c\in\mathbb{N}^{+}$ , there exists a Transformer model M : $\nu^{*}\to\nu$ that autoregressively decides ${\mathrm{3-S A T}}_{p,c}$ in no more than $p\cdot 2^{p+1}$ CoT iterations. M requires L = 7 layers, $H = 5$ heads, $d_{e m b}={\cal O}(p)$ , and $O(p^{2})$ parameters.

steps.claim: The construction uses adapted versions of lemmas from Feng et al. (2023) as basic building blocks. Here we provide a proof sketch of the core operations in our theoretical construction.

Proof Sketch In Figure 1 we illustrate the CoT process used by our theoretical construction, which uses CoT tokens to simulate various operations including unit propagation (i.e., logical deduction), variable decision, and backtracking.

To process clauses and partial assignments with attention operations, the initial layers of the theoretical construction compute the binary vector encodings of clauses and partial assignments and store them in the hidden states. We formally define the encoding scheme for clauses and partial assignments below:

Definition 5 (Encoding of clause). Let $C$ be a clause. Define encoding $E(C)\in\{0,1\}^{2p}$ of clause $C$ as the following: For $v\in[p]$, $E(C)_v=1$ iff $x_v$ is a literal in $C$, and $E(C)_{p+v}=1$ iff $\neg x_v$ is a literal in $C$. All positions in $E(C)$ are 0 otherwise.

Definition 6 (Encoding of partial assignment). Let $A:\{x_1,\ldots,x_p\}\to\{\mathrm{True},\mathrm{False},\mathrm{None}\}$ be a partial assignment. Define encoding $E(A)\in\{0,1\}^{2p}$ of clause $C$ as the following: For $v\in[p]$, $E(A)_v=1$ iff $A(x_v)=\mathrm{True}$ , and $E(A)_{p+v}=1$ iff $A(x_v)=\mathrm{False}$. All positions in $E(C)$ are 0 otherwise.

We also define a variant of the partial assignment encoding as an affine Transformers of $E(A)$, which sets both positions corresponding to a variable to 1 if the variable is unassigned:

Proposition 1. For partial assignment $A$, define $E_{\textit{not-false}}(A)=M_{\textit{not-false}}\cdot E(A)+\mathbf{1}^{2p}$ where $M_{\textit{not-false}}=\begin{bmatrix}\mathbf{0}&-\mathbf{I}_p\\-\mathbf{I}_p&\mathbf{0}\end{bmatrix}\in\mathbb{R}^{2p\times 2p}$ and $\mathbf{1}^{2p}$ is the all ones vector. Then, for $v\in[p]$:
$$
E_{\textit{not-false}}(A)_v=1 \text{ iff } A(x_v)\in\{\mathrm{True},\mathrm{None}\},\quad E_{\textit{not-false}}(A)_{p+v}=1 \text{ iff } A(x_v)\in\{\mathrm{False},\mathrm{None}\}.
$$

We now show that the relationship between a 3-SAT formula and a partial assignment can be established using their binary encoding:

Lemma 4. Let $F$ be a 3-SAT formula over variables $\{x_1,\ldots,x_p\}$ with $c$ clauses $\{C_1,\ldots,C_c\}$ and $A$ a partial assignment defined on variables $\{x_1,\ldots,x_p\}$, then the following properties hold:

1. Satisfiability Checking: The partial assignment $A$ satisfies the formula $F$ if and only if:
$$
\forall i\in[c],\quad E(C_i)\cdot E(A)\geq 1.
$$

2. Conflict Detection: The partial assignment $A$ contradicts the formula $F$ if and only if:
$$
\exists i\in[c],\quad E(C_i)\cdot E_{\textit{not-false}}(A)=0.
$$

3. Deduction: If partial assignment $A$ does not contradict formula $F$, then

(a) A variable $x_v$ is implied to be true under $A$ and $F$ if:
$$
\exists i\in[c],\quad E(C_i)\cdot E_{\textit{not-false}}(A)\leq 1,\quad E(C_i)_v=1,\quad \text{and}\quad E(A)_v=E(A)_{p+v}=0.
$$

(b) A variable $x_v$ is implied to be false under $A$ and $F$ if :
$$
\exists i\in[c],\quad E(C_i)\cdot E_{\textit{not-false}}(A)\leq 1,\quad E(C_i)_{p+v}=1,\quad \text{and}\quad E(A)_v=E(A)_{p+v}=0.
$$

Recall that an attention head computes a query and key vector from the hidden states and the attention weight between two positions is based on the dot product between the query vector of the source position and the key vector of the target position. If the Transformer weights are configured such that the query vectors are Figure 1 is $E(A)$ or $E_{\mathrm{not\text{-}false}}(A)$ for partial assignments $A$ in the Chain-of-Thought illustrated, and the key vectors are $E(C_i)$ for positions of clauses $C_i$ in the formula, then the attention weight (before softmax) would be proportional to $E(C_i)\cdot E(A)$ or $E(C_i)\cdot E_{\mathrm{not\text{-}false}}(A)$ respectively, which are values crucial for the operations in 4. We can then scale the attention weights so that the the attention weights focus on only the extremal values of $E(C_i)\cdot E(A)$ or $E(C_i)\cdot E_{\mathrm{not\text{-}false}}(A)$. We illustrate the consequence of this correlation with the following informal lemma, which considers an idealized input that contains only the positions with encoding vectors and auxiliary values:

Lemma 5 (Parallel Processing of Clauses, Informal). Let $F$ be a 3-SAT formula over variables $\{x_1,\ldots,x_p\}$ with $c$ clauses $\{C_1,\ldots,C_c\}$ and $A$ a partial assignment defined on variables $\{x_1,\ldots,x_p\}$. Let
$$
X_{encoding}=\begin{bmatrix}0&1&1\\E(C_1)&0&1\\\vdots&\vdots&\vdots\\E(C_c)&0&1\\E(A)&0&1\end{bmatrix}\in\mathbb{R}^{(c+2)\times(2p+2)}
$$
which includes encoding of clauses in $F$ and partial assignment $A$ as well as added auxiliary values. Let $\mathbf{1}_{A\models F}$ denote the indicator variable of whether $A$ satisfy formula $F$, $\mathbf{1}_{A\not\models F}$ denote the indicator variable of whether $A$ constradict $F$, and $e_{UP}\in 0,1^{2p}$ denote the encoding of all variable assignments that can be deduced from $A$ and $F$, then with $X_{encoding}$ as input and any $1>\epsilon>0$ there exists:

- An attention head that outputs $\mathbf{1}_{A\models F}$ with approximation error bounded by $\epsilon$
- An attention head that outputs $\mathbf{1}_{A\not\models F}$ with approximation error bounded by $\epsilon$
- An attention head followed by a MLP layer that outputs $e_{UP}$ with $\|\cdot\|_\infty$ error bounded by $\epsilon$

and all weight values are bounded by $O(poly(p,c,\log(1/\epsilon)))$

Lemma 5 essentially shows that, when given the binary encoding of clauses and a partial assignment, a single Transformer layer can perform satisfiability checking, conflict detection, and deduction over all clauses in the formula in parallel, which is the core reasoning our theoretical construction uses drastically less CoT tokens than step-wise simulation of Turing Machines.

The remaining parts of the construction performs indexing operations that translates DIMACS encodings into our encoding of clauses and partial assignments and selects the correct output token from the results of the operations described in Lemma 5.

theorems.statement: There exists a decoder-only Transformer $M:\mathcal{V}^*\to\mathcal{V}$ that solves 3-SAT via Chain-of-Thought reasoning, i.e. that reliably decides whether an arbitrary 3-SAT formula in DIMACS encoding is satisfiable.

steps.claim: By Theorem 1, for any $p,c \in \mathbb{N}^+$ there exists $M:\mathcal{V}^*\to\mathcal{V}$ autoregressively deciding $3\text{-}\mathrm{SAT}_{p,c}$ in at most $p\cdot 2^{p+1}$ CoT iterations, with $L=7$, $H=5$, $d_{emb}=\mathcal{O}(p)$, $\mathcal{O}(p^2)$ parameters.

By Definition 4, for each fixed $(p,c)$ this $M$ decides $3\text{-}\mathrm{SAT}_{p,c}$: it determines satisfiability of every formula with at most $p$ variables and $c$ clauses in $\mathrm{DIMACS}(p,c)$.

The constructions above share one architecture template ($L=7$, $H=5$, $d_{emb}=\mathcal{O}(p)$, $\mathcal{O}(p^2)$ parameters), doing logical deduction on all clauses in parallel and backtracking via CoT.

Theorem 4.5 only builds, for each bounded size $(p,c)$, an input-size-dependent model $M$ (with $d_{emb}=\mathcal{O}(p)$ and $\mathcal{O}(p^2)$ parameters that grow with $p$) that decides only $3\text{-}\mathrm{SAT}_{p,c}$, i.e. instances of at most $p$ variables and $c$ clauses. This is a non-uniform / bounded-input result; it does not imply the existence of one uniform Transformer solving general SAT. The step silently drops the boundedness (non-uniformity) assumption. The correct statement is that one constructs a non-uniform class of decoder-only Transformers, one per input size, deciding all 3-SAT instances of at most $p$ variables and $c$ clauses.

2 Preliminaries

Neural ODE and Continuous Normalizing Flow: A Neural ODE is a continuous model where the trajectory of data is modeled as the solution of an ordinary differential equation (ODE). Formally, in $\mathbf{\mathbb{R}}^{d}$ , given an input $x(t_{0})=x_{0}$ at time $t_{0}$ , the transformation to the output $x(T)$ is governed by:

$$
\frac{d x(t)}{d t}=\mathbf v(x(t),t),\tag{2}
$$

where $\mathbf{v}(x(t),t)$ represents the velocity field, which is of the same dimension as $x(t)$ and is parameterized by a neural network with input $x(t)$ and t.

A Continuous Normalizing Flow (CNF) is a class of normalizing flows where the transformation of a probability density from a base distribution $p(x)$ (at $t=0)$ to a target distribution $q(x)$ (at $t=T)$ is governed by a Neural ODE. The marginal density of $x(t)$ , denoted as $\rho(x,t)$ , evolves according to the continuity equation derived from the ODE in Eq. (2). This continuity equation is written as:

$$
\partial_{t}\rho(x,t)+\nabla\cdot(\rho(x,t)\mathbf{v}(x,t))=0,\quad\rho(x,0)=p(x),\tag{3}
$$

where the divergence $\nabla\cdot(\rho\boldsymbol{v})$ accounts for the change in density as the flow evolves over time.

Dynamic Optimal Transport $(O T){\mathrm{{z}}}$ The Benamou-Brenier equation (Benamou & Brenier, 2000) below provides the dynamic formulation of Optimal Transport $\tau .$

$$
\begin{array}{ r l }&{\underset{\rho,v}{\operatorname*{inf}}\int_{0}^{1}\mathbb{E}_{\boldsymbol{x}(t)\sim\rho(\cdot,t)}\|\mathbf{v}(\boldsymbol{x}(t),t)\|^{2}d t}\\ &{\mathrm{s . t .}\quad\partial_{t}\rho+\nabla\cdot(\rho v)=0,\quad\rho(\cdot,0)=p,\quad\rho(\cdot,1)=q,}\end{array}\tag{4}
$$

The optimization problem seeks to find the optimal transport map that moves mass from the base density p to the target density $q,$ subject to the continuity equation (3) to ensure that $\rho(\cdot,t)$ evolves as a valid probability density over time. Additionally, the constraint $\rho(\cdot,1)=q$ ensures that the target density is reached by the end of the time horizon. The time horizon is scaled to $[0,1]$

3 Annealing Flow Model

The annealing philosophy (Gelfand et al., 1990; Neal, 2001; Sorkin, 1991; Van Groenigen & Stein, 1998) refers to gradually transitioning an initial fattened distribution to the target distribution as the temperature decreases. Building on this idea, we introduce Annealing Flow (AF), a sampling algorithm that learns a continuous normalizing flow to gradually map an initial easy-to-sample density $\pi_{0}(x)$ to the target density $q(x)$ through a set of intermediate distributions.

We define $q(x)=Z\tilde{q}(x)$ where $\tilde{q}(x)$ represents the unnormalized target distribution given in explicit form. Next, we define a sequence of intermediate distributions $f_{k}(x)$ that interpolate between an easy-to-sample initial distribution $\pi_{0}(x)$ (e.g., a Gaussian) and the target $q(x)$ . These intermediate distributions are formulated as:

$$
f_{k}(x)=\pi_{0}(x)^{1-\beta_{k}}q(x)^{\beta_{k}}=Z_{k}{\tilde{f}}_{k}(x),\tag{5}
$$

Here $\tilde{f}_{k}(x)=\pi_{0}(x)^{1-\beta_{k}}\tilde{q}(x)^{\beta_{k}}$ , and $\beta_{k}$ is an increasing sequence with $\beta_{0}=0$ and $\beta_{K}=1$ . This formulation ensures that $\tilde{f}_{0}(x)=\pi_{0}(x)$ and $\tilde{f}_{K}(x)=\tilde{q}(x)$ . The sequence $0=\beta_{0}<\beta_{1}<\cdots<$ $\beta_{K}=1$ controls the gradual transition between the two distributions.

The above construction aligns with the annealing philosophy. As $\beta_{k}$ increases, $\tilde{f}_{k}(x)$ gradually sharpens toward the target $\bar{\tilde{q}(\boldsymbol{x})}$ , starting from the initially flattened distribution around $\pi_{0}(x)$ . These annealed densities serve as a bridge, providing a gradual flow path from the easy-to-sample distribution $\pi_{0}(x)$ to the target density $q(x)$ . Figure 1 provides an intuitive illustration of this process, where $\pi_{0}(x)$ is a standard Gaussian, and $q(x)$ is a Gaussian mixture model with six modes.
