Let $\sigma_{S}[\pmb{v}]$ and $\sigma_{H}[\pmb{v}]$ for any input vector v be the softmax function and hardmax function, respectively. Note that when there are multiple indices with maximum values, the hardmax function is defined such that the sum of the values at these indices equals one. By abuse of notation, for any input matrix $A,\sigma_{S}\left[A\right]$ and $\sigma_{H}\left[\boldsymbol{A}\right]$ are defined as column-wise softmax and column-wise hardmax, respectively. We denote the ReLU activation function by $\sigma_{R}$ . Unlike $\sigma_{S}$ and $\sigma_{H},\sigma_{R}$ is always an element-wise operator, regardless of whether the input is a vector or a matrix. Let | · |lbe the $\bar{\ell}^{2}$ norm and $\|\cdot\|_{p}\left(1\overset{\_}{\leq}p<\infty\right)$ be the $\ell^{p\ }$ norm.

2.2 Transformer Block

Transformer was first introduced in Vaswani et al. (2017). Here we follow the definitions adopted in Kim et al. (2023): the Transformer block is composed of the self-attention mechanism and the feed-forward neural network, each accompanied by a skip connection. Given an input sequence $\boldsymbol{Z}\in\mathbb{R}^{d\times n}$ − composed of n tokens each with an embedding dimension of size $d,$ a dot-product self-attention mechanism with h heads outputs the following values:

$$
\mathcal{F}_{S}^{(S A)}(Z)=Z+\sum_{i=1}^{h}W_{i}^{(O)}\left(W_{i}^{(V)}Z\right)\sigma_{S}\left[\left(W_{i}^{(K)}Z\right)^{\top}\left(W_{i}^{(Q)}Z\right)\right]\in\mathbb{R}^{d\times n},\tag{1}
$$

where ${\bf W}_{i}^{(V)},{\bf W}_{i}^{(K)},{\bf W}_{i}^{(Q)}\in\mathbb{R}^{s\times d}$ and $W_{i}^{(O)}\in\mathbb{R}^{d\times s}$ are the weight matrices, and s is the head size. In contrast, given an input $H\in\mathbb{R}^{d\times n}$ , the output of feed-forward neural network with a skip connection at index $k \in [ n ]$ is

$$
\mathcal{F}^{(F F)}(H)_{:,k}=H_{:,k}+W^{(2)}\sigma_{R}\left[W^{(1)}H_{:,k}+b^{(1)}\right]+b^{(2)}\in\mathbb{R}^{d},
$$

where q is the hidden dimension, $W^{(1)}\in\mathbb{R}^{q\times d}$ and $W^{(2)}\in\mathbb{R}^{d\times q}$ are weight matrices, and $b^{(1)}\in\mathbb{R}^{q}$ and $b^{(2)}$ are bias terms. On the basis of the above definition, the Transformer block is represented as a composition of a self-attention mechanism and a feed-forward neural network: for any input sequence $Z\in\mathbb{R}^{d\times n}$ , composed of n tokens each with an embedding dimension of size d, the Transformer block $\mathcal{F}:\mathbb{R}^{d\times n}\to\mathbb{R}^{d\times n}$ outputs

$$
\mathcal{F}(Z)=\mathcal{F}^{(F F)}\left(\mathcal{F}_{S}^{(S A)}(Z)\right).
$$

3.1 Problem Setting

Let $(\pmb{X}^{(1)},\pmb{Y}^{(1)}),\dots,(\pmb{X}^{(1)},\pmb{Y}^{(1)})\subset\mathbb{R}^{d\times n}\times [\pmb{C}]^{d\times n}$ be an N input-output pairs of sequences, each of which consists of a sequence $\pmb{X}^{(i)}$ of n tokens with embedding dimension d, and an output $\mathbf{\nabla}\mathbf{\mathbf{{Y}}}^{(i)}$ , where $Y_{:,k}^{(i)}$ corresponds to the label of the token $X_{:,k}^{(i)}$ at index k. In addition, we define the i-th vocabulary set for $\begin{array}{ r }{i\in [N]\mathrm{~b y~}\mathcal{V}^{(i)}=\bigcup_{k\in [n]}X_{:,k}^{(i)}\subset\mathbb{R}^{d}}\end{array}$ , and the whole vocabulary set $\nu$ is defined by $\begin{array}{ r }{\mathcal{V}=\bigcup_{i\in [N]}\mathcal{V}^{(i)}\subset\mathbb{R}^{d}}\end{array}$

3.2 Background

Definition 2 (Tokenwise Separatedness). Let $m\in\mathbb{N}$ and $Z^{(1)},\ldots,Z^{(N)}\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times n}$ be input sequences. Then, ${Z}^{(1)},\ldots,{Z}^{\bar{(N)}}$ are called tokenwise $(r_{\operatorname*{min}},r_{\operatorname*{max}},\delta)$ -separated if the following three conditions hold.

1. For any $i \in [ N ]$ and $k\in [n],\left\|Z_{:,k}^{(i)}\right\|>r_{\operatorname*{min}}$ holds.

2. For any $i \in [ N ]$ and $k\in [n],\left\|Z_{:,k}^{(i)}\right\|<r_{\operatorname*{max}}$ holds.

3. For any $i,j\in [N]$ and $k,l\in [n]$ with $Z_{:,k}^{(i)}\neq Z_{:,l}^{(j)},\left. Z_{:,k}^{(i)}-Z_{:,l}^{(j)}\right.>\delta$ holds.

Note that we refer to ${Z}^{(1)},\ldots,{Z}^{(N)}$ as tokenwise $(r_{\operatorname*{max}},\epsilon)$ -separated instead if the sequences satisfy conditions 2 and 3.

Definition 3 (Contextual Mapping). Let $\pmb{X}^{(1)},\ldots,\pmb{X}^{(N)}\in\mathbb{R}^{d\times n}$ be input sequences. Then, a map $q:\mathbb{R}^{d\times n}\bar{\mathbb{R}}^{d\times n}$ is called an $(r,\delta)$ -contextual mapping if the following two conditions hold:

1. For any $i \in [ N ]$ and $k\in [n],\left\|q\left(\mathbf{X}^{\left(i\right)}\right)_{:,k}\right\|<r$ holds.

2. For any $i,j\in\mathsf{\Gamma}[N]$ and $k,l~\in~[n]$ such that $\mathcal{V}^{(i)}~\neq~\mathcal{V}^{(j)}$ or $X_{:,k}^{(i)}~\neq~X_{:,l}^{(j)}$ $\left\|\boldsymbol{q}\left(\boldsymbol{X}^{(i)}\right)_{:,k}-\boldsymbol{q}\left(\boldsymbol{X}^{(j)}\right)_{:,l}\right\|>\delta$ holds.

In particular, $\boldsymbol{q}(\boldsymbol{X}^{(i)})$ for $i \in [ N ]$ is called a context id of $\pmb{X}^{(i)}$

3.3 Self-Attention with Hardmax

In previous studies analyzing the memorization capacity of Transformers (Yun et al., 2019; Kim et al., 2023), the softmax function is taken to be an approximation of the hardmax function. However, we show here that the attention block with the hardmax function is not a contextual mapping.

First we define the attention block with the hardmax function: for an input sequence $\boldsymbol{Z}\in\mathbb{R}^{d\times n}$ , the attention with the hardmax function is calculated as

$$
\mathcal{F}_{H}^{(S A)}(Z)=Z+\sum_{i=1}^{h}W_{i}^{(O)}\left(W_{i}^{(V)}Z\right)\sigma_{H}\left[\left(W_{i}^{(K)}Z\right)^{\top}\left(W_{i}^{(Q)}Z\right)\right],\tag{2}
$$

where $\pmb{W}_{i}^{(V)},\pmb{W}_{i}^{(K)},\pmb{W}_{i}^{(Q)}\in\mathbb{R}^{s\times d}$ and $W_{i}^{(O)}\in\mathbb{R}^{d\times s}$ are the weight matrices

The following theorem holds for such a model. The proof is in Appendix A.1.

3.4 Self-Attention with Softmax

In this subsection, we show that a softmax-based 1-layer attention block with low-rank weight matrices is a contextual mapping for almost all input sequences.

4.1 Memorization Capacity of One-Layer Transformer

As a first application of Theorem 1, we prove that a 1-layer Transformer can completely memorize finite samples, each of which has no duplicate token. This result emphasizes that in contrast to the proof of Kim et al. (2023), which requires 2n self-attention layers for Transformer memorization, one layer of self-attention is actually sufficient. In addition, it is worth noting that the hardmaxbased Transformers do not have a memorization capacity, which is implied straightforwardly from Theorem 2.

In addition, it is straightforward to show that a 1-layer Transformer with trainable positional encodings has a memorization capacity for arbitrary input sequences possibly with duplicate tokens.

B.2 Properties of Boltzmann Operator

For any vector $\pmb{a}=(a_{1},\ldots,a_{n})\in\mathbb{R}^{n}$ , let denote $\pmb{p}=(p_{1},\ldots,p_{n})=\sigma_{S}[\pmb{a}]$ . In addition, we define the Boltzmann operator, partition function, and entropy as follows.

$$
\mathbf{boltz}(\pmb{a})=\sum_{i=1}^{n}a_{i}p_{i},
$$

$$
\mathcal{L}(\pmb{a})=\log\left(\sum_{i=1}^{n}e^{a_{i}}\right),
$$

$$
\mathcal{S}(\pmb{p})= -\sum_{i=1}^{n}p_{i}\log p_{i}.
$$

context:
Our key insight is that the relation between factors in a representation with data can be described from the perspective of containing information. Since each factor in a disentangled representation corresponds to a single factor of variation in data, each factor only contains the information of the corresponding factor of variation in data. In other words, different factors in a disentangled representation contain absolutely different information about data, and the containing information about data in a single factor is irrelevant to other factors. Motivated by this insight, we aim at proposing an information-based assumption to describe the relation between factors in a disentangled representation with factors of variation in data. For mathematical analysis of the information terms, we adopt mutual information to measure the information of a variable contained by another:

$$
I(\mathbf{x};\mathbf{z})=H(\mathbf{z})-H(\mathbf{z}|\mathbf{x})\tag{5}
$$

where entropy $H(\mathbf{z})= -\mathbb{E}_{q(\mathbf{z})}[\log q(\mathbf{z})]$ and conditional entropy $H(\mathbf{z}|\mathbf{x})= -\mathbb{E}_{q(\mathbf{z},\mathbf{x})}[\log q(\mathbf{z}|\mathbf{x})]$ are measures of uncertainty. Hence mutual information measures the uncertainty reduction of one variable when another is given. The mutual information satisfies the symmetry $I(\mathbf{x;z})=I(\mathbf{z;x})$

Therefore, for a single factor $\mathbf{Z}_{j}$ in a disentangled representation $\mathbf{z},$ its containing information about the corresponding underlying factor of variation in data x can be expressed as $I({\bf z};{\bf x})$ . To represent the irrelevance of $\mathbf{Z}_{j}$ to other information in data, we involve conditional mutual information:

$$
I(\mathbf{z}_{j};\mathbf{x}|\mathbf{z}_{i\in S_{-j}})=H(\mathbf{z}_{j}|\mathbf{z}_{i\in S_{-j}})-H(\mathbf{z}_{j}|\mathbf{x},\mathbf{z}_{i\in S_{-j}})\tag{6}
$$

where $j\in\{1,2,...,J\},S_{-j}$ is any subset of $\{1,\dotsc,j-1,j+1,\dotsc,J\}$ and $\mathbf{z}_{i\in S_{-j}}$ denotes all factors with subscript index in $S_{-j}$ .The conditional mutual information is the difference of two conditional entropy, representing the containing information of $\mathbf{Z}_{j}$ on the corresponding underlying factor of variation in data x when other factors $\mathbf{z}_{i\in S_{-j}}$ are given. Considering the corresponding factors of variation in data of $\mathbf{z}_{i\in S_{-j}}$ , they are fixed when $\mathbf{z}_{i\in S_{-}}$ are given. Hence the conditional mutual information term above can describe the their relation with $\mathbf{Z}_{j}$

Assumption. Suppose $\mathbf{z}\in\mathbb{R}^{J}$ is a disentangled representation of data x and $I({\bf z};{\bf x})>0$ , then for any single factor $\mathbf{z}_{j},$ its containing information in data is irrelevant to other factors $z_{i\in S_{-j}},i . e .$

$$
I(\mathbf{z}_{j};\mathbf{x}|\mathbf{z}_{i\in S_{-j}})=I(\mathbf{z}_{j};\mathbf{x})\tag{7}
$$

where $j\in\{1,2,\dots,J\}$ and $S_{-j}$ is any subset of $\{1,\dotsc,j-1,j+1,\dotsc,J\}$

On condition of independence, the proposed assumption is equivalent to conditional independence. In this section we analyze the inductive biases about conditional independence, and then propose a simple architecture to improve disentanglement based on our assumption and the inductive biases.

Figure 1: Structure of vanilla encoder and split encoder. The blue and short-dash box denotes sharing-parameter block, and the red and long-dash box represents no-sharing-parameter block.

Motivated by our proposed assumption, we find that there are some inductive biases on encoders of VAEs to ensure conditional independence. Considering $q(\mathbf{z})$ is pushed to match a factorized prior $p(\mathbf{z})$ in VAE-based models and thus encourages independence and the common assumption is satisfied, this discovery shows that our assumption is also satisfied in these models.

In VAEs, the encoders encode data into a Gaussian distribution of representation $q(\mathbf{z}|\mathbf{x})$ via reparameterization trick. Specifically, the data is encoded into a mean $\mu(\mathbf{x})$ and a variance $\sigma(\mathbf{x})$ , then the representation is sampled from $\mathcal{N}(\mathbf{z};\pmb{\mu}(\mathbf{x}),\sigma^{2}(\mathbf{x})\pmb{I})$ with reparameterization trick:

$$
z\sim q(\mathbf{z}|\mathbf{x})\Leftrightarrow z=\mu(\mathbf{x})+\sigma(\mathbf{x})\odot\epsilon,\epsilon\sim\mathcal{N}(0,I)\tag{8}
$$

For analyzing the outputs of those encoders, we divide them into two blocks: if the parameters of several layers are shared for different factors in a representation, the block consists of these layers is called "sharing-parameter block". Conversely, those layers without shared parameters for different factors form "no-sharing-parameter block". In vanilla VAE, the last layers in encoders are fullyconnected nets, which are no-sharing-parameter block (see Fig. 1).

theorems.statement: In VAEs the encoder outputs $z=\mu(\mathbf{x})+\sigma(\mathbf{x})\odot\epsilon$, $\epsilon\sim\mathcal{N}(0,I)$ (Eq. 8), where $j\in\{1,2,\dots,J\}$ indexes the factors of $\mathbf{z}$. The encoder's last layers form a 'no-sharing-parameter block' (parameters not shared across factors). Claim: this block, together with the independence of the reparameterization noise, is a source of the conditional independence $q(\mathbf{z}|\mathbf{x})=\prod_{j=1}^{J} q(\mathbf{z}_j|\mathbf{x})$ of the representation factors; removing the no-sharing-parameter block violates conditional independence.

steps.claim: Encoder samples $z=\mu(\mathbf{x})+\sigma(\mathbf{x})\odot\epsilon$, $\epsilon\sim\mathcal{N}(0,I)$ (Eq. 8).
The encoder's last (fully-connected) layers constitute a no-sharing-parameter block (parameters not shared across factors); vanilla VAE, Fig. 1.
Factors output by the no-sharing-parameter block are independent conditioned on $\mathbf{x}$, hence the factors of $\mu(\mathbf{x})$ and of $\sigma(\mathbf{x})$ are conditionally independent.
$q(\mu|\mathbf{x})=\prod_{j=1}^{J} q(\mu_j|\mathbf{x})$, $q(\sigma|\mathbf{x})=\prod_{j=1}^{J} q(\sigma_j|\mathbf{x})$, $q(\epsilon)=\prod_{j=1}^{J} q(\epsilon_j)$ (Eq. 10).
Hence $q(\mathbf{z}|\mathbf{x})=\prod_{j=1}^{J} q(\mathbf{z}_j|\mathbf{x})$ (Eq. 11), originating from the no-sharing-parameter block and the independent reparameterization noise.
Removing the no-sharing-parameter block (sharing-parameter encoder) violates conditional independence and degrades disentanglement.

label: flawed
error_explanation: Step 3 asserts that the factors output by the 'no-sharing-parameter block' are independent conditioned on the input, and hence that the factors of $\mu(\mathbf{x})$ and of $\sigma(\mathbf{x})$ are conditionally independent. This attribution is false. Eq. 9, $q(\mathbf{z}|\mathbf{x})=\prod_j q(\mathbf{z}_j|\mathbf{x})$, is the defining property of the factorized (diagonal) Gaussian variational family and follows ENTIRELY from the factorized reparameterization noise $q(\epsilon)=\prod_j q(\epsilon_j)$ (Eq. 7); it does not follow from, and does not require, parameters being un-shared across factors. Parameter sharing and (conditional) independence are different concepts: if one sets every mean equal, $\mu_j=f(\mathbf{x})$ for all $j$ (all parameters fully shared, so no no-sharing-parameter block at all), Eq. 9 still holds because the per-coordinate noise is independent. Thus the no-sharing-parameter block is neither necessary nor a source of conditional independence, and the premise that a shared-parameter encoder violates conditional independence is false. Correctly, conditional independence comes solely from the factorized noise of the chosen variational family; a valid experiment must genuinely remove the no-sharing-parameter block (e.g. sharing the last fully-connected layer's bias across factors), not merely replace FC layers with conv layers whose last-layer parameters are still un-shared across factors. Steps 5-6 only restate and apply this same invalid attribution.

context:
We follow a similar (though not identical) theoretical setup to (Mandt et al., 2017), approximating SGD with a continuous-time stochastic process, which we now outline.

Let us consider a model parameterized by $\pmb{\theta}=\{\theta_{1},...,\theta_{q}\}$ . For $N$ training examples $\mathbf{\Psi}_{{\pmb{x}}_{i},i}\in\mathbf{\Psi}$ $\{1,...,N\}$ , the loss function, $L(\theta)$ , and the corresponding gradient ${\bf g}(\pmb{\theta})$ , are defined based on the sum over the loss values for all training examples. Stochastic gradients ${\bf g}^{(S)}(\pmb{\theta})$ arise when we consider a batch B of size $S < N$ of random indices drawn uniformly from $\{1,...,N\}$ and form an (unbiased) estimate of loss and gradient based on the corresponding subset of training examples

$$
L^{(S)}(\pmb{\theta})=\frac{1}{S}\sum_{n\in\mathcal{B}}l(\pmb{\theta},\pmb{x}_{n})\ ,\qquad\mathbf{g}^{(S)}(\pmb{\theta})=\frac{\partial}{\partial\pmb{\theta}}L^{(S)}(\pmb{\theta})\ .
$$

We consider stochastic gradient descent (SGD) with learning rate η, as defined by the update rule

$$
\pmb{\theta}(t+1)=\pmb{\theta}(t)-\eta\pmb{g}^{(S)}(\pmb{\theta})\ .
$$

We now make the following assumptions:

(1 By the central limit theorem (CLT), we assume the noise in the stochastic gradient is Gaussian with covariance matrix $\scriptstyle{\frac{1}{S}}\mathbf{C}({\boldsymbol{\theta}})$

$$
{\bf g}^{(S)}(\pmb{\theta})={\bf g}(\pmb{\theta})+\frac{1}{\sqrt{S}}\Delta{\bf g}(\pmb{\theta}),\mathrm{where}\Delta{\bf g}(\pmb{\theta})\sim N(0,{\bf C}(\pmb{\theta})).
$$

We note that the covariance is symmetric positive-semidefinite, and so can be decomposed into the product of two matrices $\mathbf{C}(\pmb\theta)=\mathbf{\dot{B}}(\pmb\theta)\mathbf{B}^{\top}(\pmb\theta)$

(2) We assume the discrete process of SGD can be approximated by the continuous time limit of the following stochastic differential equation (known as a Langevin equation)

$$
\frac{d\pmb{\theta}}{d t}= -\eta\pmb{g}(\pmb{\theta})+\frac{\eta}{\sqrt{S}}\mathbf{B}(\pmb{\theta})\mathbf{f}(t)\tag{3}
$$

where $\mathbf f(t)$ is a normalized Gaussian time-dependent stochastic term.

Note that the continuous time approximation of SGD as a stochastic differential equation has been shown to hold in a weak approximation on the condition that the learning rate is small (Li et al., 2017).

Note that we have not made Assumption 4 of (Mandt et al., 2017), where they assume the loss can be globally approximated by a quadratic. Instead, we allow for a general loss function, which can have many local minima.

The Langevin equation is a stochastic differential equation, and we are interested in its equilibrium distribution which gives insights into the behavior of SGD and the properties of the points it converges to. Assuming isotropic noise, the Langevin equation is well known to have a Gibbs-Boltzmann distribution as its equilibrium distribution. This equilibrium distribution can be derived by finding the stationary solution of the Fokker-Planck equation, with detailed balance, which governs the evolution of the probability density of the value of the parameters with time. The Fokker-Planck equation and its derivation is standard in the statistical physics literature. In Appendix A we give the equation in the machine learning context in Eq. (4) and for completeness of presentation we also give its derivation. In Appendix C we restate the standard proofs of the stationary distribution of a Langevin system, and provide the resulting Gibbs-Boltzmann equilbirium distribution here, using the notation of this paper:

Discussion: Here $P(\pmb\theta)$ defines the density over the parameter space. The above result says that if we run SGD for long enough (under the assumptions made regarding the SGD sufficiently matching the infinitesimal limit), then the probability of the parameters being in a particular state asymptotically follows the above density. Note, that $\textstyle n\equiv{\frac{\eta}{S}}$ is a measure of the noise in the system set by the choice of learning rate η and batch size S. The fact that the loss is divided by n emphasizes that the higher the noise $n,$ the less granular the loss surface appears to SGD. The gradient variance $\mathbf{C}(\pmb\theta)$ on the other hand is determined by the dataset and model priors (e.g. architecture, model parameterization, batch normalization etc.). This reveals an important area of investigation, i.e., how different architectures and model parameterizations affect the gradient's covariance structure. We note that in the analysis above, the assumption of the gradient covariance $\mathbf{C}(\pmb\theta)$ being fixed and isotropic in the parameter space is unrealistic. However it is a simplification that enables straightforward insights regarding the relationship of the noise, batch size and learning rate in the Gibbs-Boltzmann equilibrium. We empirically show that various predictions based on this relationship hold in practice.

Returning to SGD as an optimization method, we can ask, given the probability density $P(\pmb\theta)$ can we derive the probability of ending at a given minimum, $\pmb{\theta}_{A}$ , which we will denote by lowercase $p_{A}={\tilde{p}}_{A}C$ , where C is a normalization constant which is the same for all minima (the unnormalized probability ${\tilde{p}}_{A}$ A is all we are interested in when estimating the relative probability of finishing in a given minimum compared to another one). This probability is derived in Appendix D, and given in the following theorem, which is the core insight from our theory.

Discussion: For this analysis, we qualitatively categorize a minima $\theta_{A}$ by its loss $L_{A}$ (depth) and the determinant of the Hessian det $\mathbf{H}_{A}$ (a larger determinant implies a sharper minima). The above result shows that the probability of landing in a specific minimum depends on three factors - learning rate, batch-size and covariance of the gradients. The two factors that we directly control only appear in the ratio given by the noise $n = \eta / S$ Note that the proof of this result utilizes a Laplace Approximation in which the loss near a given minimum can be approximated using a second order Taylor series in order to evaluate an integral. We emphasize this is not the same as globally treating the loss as a quadratic.

In this appendix we derive the Fokker-Planck equation. For any stochastic differential equation, since the evolution is noisy we can't say exactly where in parameter space the parameter values will be at any given time. But we can talk about the probability $P(\boldsymbol{\theta},t|\boldsymbol{\theta}_{0},t_{0})$ that a parameter takes a certain value θ at a certain time t, given that it started at $\theta_{0},t_{0}$ That is captured by the Fokker-Planck equation, which reads

$$
\frac{\partial P(\pmb{\theta},t)}{\partial t}=\nabla_{\pmb{\theta}}\cdot\left[\eta\pmb{g}(\pmb{\theta})P(\pmb{\theta},t)+\frac{\eta^{2}}{2 S}\nabla_{\pmb{\theta}}\cdot [\mathbf{C}(\pmb{\theta})P(\pmb{\theta},t)]\right].\tag{4}
$$

In this appendix we will not be interested in pure mathematical rigour, but intend the proof to add intuition for the machine learning audience.

For brevity we will sometimes write the probability just as $P(\theta,t)$ . We will sometimes make use of tensor index notation, where a tensor is denoted by its components, (for example $\theta_{i}$ are the components of the vector $\pmb\theta)_{\backslash}$ , and we will use the index summation convention, where a repeated index is to be summed over.

In order to prove this is the equilibrium distribution, we need to solve the Fokker-Planck equation (4) with the left hand side set equal to zero (which would give a stationary distribution) and further we require for equilibrium that detailed balance holds. To do this, we begin by writing the Fokker-Planck equation in a slightly different form, making use of a probability current J, defined

$$
{\pmb J}\equiv\eta{\pmb g}({\pmb\theta})P({\pmb\theta},t)+\frac{\eta^{2}}{2 S}\nabla_{{\pmb\theta}}\cdot({\bf C}({\pmb\theta})P({\pmb\theta},t))\tag{5}
$$

in which the Fokker-Planck equation becomes

$$
\frac{\partial P(\pmb{\theta},t)}{\partial t}=\nabla_{\pmb{\theta}}\cdot\pmb{J}.\tag{6}
$$

We emphasize this is not the same as Assumption 4 of (Mandt et al., 2017), where they assume the loss can be globally approximated by a quadratic. In contrast, we allow for a general loss, with multiple minima, and locally to each minima approximate the loss by its second-order Taylor expansion in order to evaluate the integral in the Laplace method.

The distribution $P_{A}(\pmb\theta)$ is a probability density, while we are interested in the discrete set of probabilities of ending at a given minimum, which we will denote by lowercase $p_{A}$ . To calculate this discrete set of probabilities, for each minimum we need to integrate this stationary distribution over an interval containing the minimum.

For any stochastic differential equation, since the evolution is noisy we can't say exactly where in parameter space the parameter values will be at any given time. But we can talk about the probability $P(\boldsymbol{\theta},t|\boldsymbol{\theta}_{0},t_{0})$ that a parameter takes a certain value θ at a certain time t, given that it started at $\theta_{0},t_{0}$ That is captured by the Fokker-Planck equation, which reads

$$
\frac{\partial P(\pmb{\theta},t)}{\partial t}=\nabla_{\pmb{\theta}}\cdot\left[\eta\pmb{g}(\pmb{\theta})P(\pmb{\theta},t)+\frac{\eta^{2}}{2 S}\nabla_{\pmb{\theta}}\cdot [\mathbf{C}(\pmb{\theta})P(\pmb{\theta},t)]\right].\tag{4}
$$

steps.claim:
We start with the stochastic differential equation

$$
\frac{d\pmb{\theta}}{d t}= -\eta\pmb{g}(\pmb{\theta})+\frac{\eta}{\sqrt{S}}\mathbf{B}(\pmb{\theta})\mathbf{f}(t).\tag{7}
$$

A formal expression for the probability for a given noise function f is given by $P(\pmb\theta,t)=\delta(\pmb\theta-\pmb\theta_{\mathbf f})$ but since we don't know the noise, we instead average over all possible noise functions to get

$$
P(\pmb\theta,t)=\mathbb{E}[\delta(\pmb\theta-\pmb\theta_{\mathbf f})].\tag{8}
$$

We now consider a small step in time $\delta t,$ working at first order in $\delta t .$ and ask how far the parameters move, denoted δθ, which is given by integrating (7)

$$
\delta\pmb{\theta}= -\eta\pmb{g}\delta t+\frac{\eta}{\sqrt{S}}\mathbf{B}\int_{t}^{t+\delta t}\mathbf{f}(t^{\prime})d t^{\prime}\tag{9}
$$

We now look at expectations of δθ. Using the fact that the noise is normalized Gaussian, $\mathbb{E}({\bf f}(t))=0$ ,we get (switching to index notation for clarity)

$$
\mathbb{E}(\delta\theta_{i})= -\eta g_{i}\delta t\tag{10}
$$

and using that the noise is normalized Gaussian again, we have that $\mathbb{E}({\bf f}(t){\bf f}(t^{\prime}))={\bf I}\delta(t-t^{\prime})$ leading to

$$
\mathbb{E}(\delta\theta_{i}\delta\theta_{j})=\frac{\eta^{2}}{S}C_{i j}\delta t+\mathcal{O}(\delta t^{2}).\tag{11}
$$

If at time t we are at position $\pmb{\theta}^{\prime}$ and end up at position $\pmb{\theta}=\pmb{\theta}^{\prime}+\delta\pmb{\theta}$ at time $t + \delta t$ , then we can take ) with $\theta_{\mathbf{f}}=\theta^{\prime}$ and Taylor expand it in $\delta\theta_{i}$

$$
P(\pmb\theta,t+\delta t|\pmb\theta^{\prime},t)=\left(1+\mathbb{E}(\delta\pmb\theta_{i})\frac{\partial}{\partial\theta_{i}^{\prime}}+\frac{1}{2}\mathbb{E}(\delta\pmb\theta_{i}\delta\pmb\theta_{j})\frac{\partial^{2}}{\partial\theta_{i}^{\prime}\partial\theta_{j}^{\prime}}+\mathcal{O}(\delta t^{2})\right)\delta(\pmb\theta-\pmb\theta^{\prime}).\tag{12}
$$

We will use the following identity, called the Chapman-Kolmogorov equation, which reads

$$
P(\theta,t+\delta t|\theta_{0},t_{0})=\int_{-\infty}^{+\infty}d\theta^{\prime}P(\theta,t+\delta t|\theta^{\prime},t^{\prime})P(\theta^{\prime},t^{\prime}|\theta_{0},t_{0})\tag{13}
$$

for any $t^{\prime},$ such that $t_{0}\leq t^{\prime}\leq t+\delta t$ This identity is an integral version of the chain rule of probability, stating there are multiple paths of getting from an initial position $\pmb{\theta}_{0}$ to $\pmb \theta$ at time $t + \delta t$ and one should sum all of these paths.

We will now substitute (12) into the first term on the right hand side of (13) with $t^{\prime}$ set to be $t,$ and apply integration by parts (assuming vanishing boundary conditions at infinity) to move the derivatives off of the delta functions and onto the other terms. We end up with

$$
\begin{array}{ r l }&{P(\pmb{\theta},t+\delta t|\pmb{\theta}^{\prime},t)=P(\pmb{\theta},t|\pmb{\theta}_{0},t_{0})-\displaystyle\frac{\partial}{\partial\theta_{i}}\left(\mathbb{E}(\delta\theta_{i})P(\pmb{\theta},t|\pmb{\theta}_{0},t_{0})\right)}\\ &{\qquad+\displaystyle\frac{1}{2}\frac{\partial^{2}}{\partial\theta_{i}^{\prime}\partial\theta_{j}^{\prime}}\left(\mathbb{E}(\delta\theta_{i}\delta\theta_{j})P(\pmb{\theta},t|\pmb{\theta}_{0},t_{0})\right).}\end{array}\tag{14}
$$

We can then take the first term on the right hand side of (14) to the other side, insert (10) and (11), divide by δt and take the limit $\delta t  0$ ,getting a partial derivative with respect to time on the left hand side, leading directly to the Fokker-Planck equation quoted in the text (4) (where we have reverted back to vector notation from index notation for conciseness)

$$
\frac{\partial P(\pmb{\theta},t)}{\partial t}=\nabla_{\pmb{\theta}}\cdot\left[\eta\pmb{g}(\pmb{\theta})P(\pmb{\theta},t)+\frac{\eta^{2}}{2 S}\nabla_{\pmb{\theta}}\cdot [\mathbf{C}(\pmb{\theta})P(\pmb{\theta},t)]\right].\tag{15}
$$

theorems.statement: Consider SGD with learning rate $\eta$ and batch size $S<N$, whose update $\pmb\theta(t+1)=\pmb\theta(t)-\eta\mathbf{g}^{(S)}(\pmb\theta)$ is approximated by the Langevin SDE $\frac{d\pmb\theta}{dt}=-\eta\mathbf{g}(\pmb\theta)+\frac{\eta}{\sqrt{S}}\mathbf{B}(\pmb\theta)\mathbf{f}(t)$ (Eq. 3), where the stochastic gradient noise is Gaussian with covariance $\frac{1}{S}\mathbf{C}(\pmb\theta)$, $\mathbf{C}(\pmb\theta)=\mathbf{B}(\pmb\theta)\mathbf{B}^\top(\pmb\theta)$, and $\mathbf{f}(t)$ is a normalized Gaussian time-dependent term. Assume that the gradient covariance is isotropic, i.e. $\mathbf{C}(\pmb\theta)=\sigma^2(\pmb\theta)\mathbf{I}$. Then the equilibrium distribution of the SDE (Eq. 3) is $P(\pmb\theta)=P_0\exp\left(-\frac{2L(\pmb\theta)}{n\sigma^2}\right)$, where $n\equiv\eta/S$ and $P_0$ is a normalization constant (well defined for loss functions with $L_2$ regularization).

steps.claim: The current is $\pmb J\equiv\eta\mathbf{g}(\pmb\theta)P(\pmb\theta,t)+\frac{\eta^2}{2S}\nabla_{\pmb\theta}\cdot(\mathbf{C}(\pmb\theta)P(\pmb\theta,t))$ (Eq. 5), so $\partial_tP=\nabla_{\pmb\theta}\cdot\pmb J$ (Eq. 6).
With $\mathbf{C}(\pmb\theta)=\sigma^2(\pmb\theta)\mathbf{I}$, $\mathbf{C}(\pmb\theta)P=\sigma^2(\pmb\theta)P$.

So $
abla_{\pmb	heta}\cdot(\sigma^2(\pmb	heta)P)=\sigma^2
abla_{\pmb	heta}P$, giving $\pmb J=\eta\mathbf{g}(\pmb	heta)P(\pmb	heta,t)+ rac{\eta^2\sigma^2}{2S}
abla_{\pmb	heta}P(\pmb	heta,t)$ (Eq. 16).
Equilibrium requires detailed balance, $\pmb J=0$: $\eta\mathbf{g}(\pmb\theta)P=-\frac{\eta^2\sigma^2}{2S}\nabla_{\pmb\theta}P$.
$\nabla_{\pmb\theta}\log P=-\frac{2S}{\eta\sigma^2}\mathbf{g}(\pmb\theta)=-\frac{2S}{\eta\sigma^2}\nabla_{\pmb\theta}L(\pmb\theta)$.
Integrating, $P(\pmb\theta)=P_0\exp\left(-\frac{2S}{\eta\sigma^2}L(\pmb\theta)\right)=P_0\exp\left(-\frac{2L(\pmb\theta)}{n\sigma^2}\right)$ (Eq. 17).

theorems.statement:
Theorem 3 (Probability of ending in region near minima $\pmb{\theta}_{A})$ . Assume the loss has a series of separated local minima. Consider one such minima, with Hessian $\mathbf{H}_{A}$ and loss $L_{A}$ at a minimum $\theta_{A}$ . Then the unnormalized probability of ending in a region near minima $\pmb{\theta}_{A}$ is

$$
\tilde{p}_{A}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{\operatorname*{det}\mathbf{H}_{A}}}\exp\left(-\frac{2 L_{A}}{n\sigma^{2}}\right)\tag{18}
$$

where $\begin{array}{ r }{n=\frac{\eta}{S}}\end{array}$ is the noise used in the SGD process to reach $\theta_{A}$

steps.claim:
We work locally near $\theta_{A}$ and take the following approximation of the loss function, since it is near a minimum,

$$
L(\pmb\theta)\Big|_{R_{A}}\approx L_{A}+\frac{1}{2}(\pmb\theta-\pmb\theta_{A})^{\top}\mathbf{H}_{A}(\pmb\theta-\pmb\theta_{A}).\tag{19}
$$

Integrating (20) in some region $R_{A}$ around $\theta_{A}$ and using (19)

$$
p_{A}\approx P_{0}\int_{R_{A}}\exp{\left(-\frac{2 S}{\eta\sigma^{2}}L(\pmb\theta)\Big|_{R_{A}}\right)}\tag{21}

context:
Dec-MDPs. We consider a fully cooperative multi-agent task in which a team of cooperative agents choose sequential actions in a stochastic environment. It can be modeled as a decentralized Markov decision process (Dec-MDP), defined by a tuple $\{\mathcal{N},\mathcal{S},\mathcal{A},P,r,\rho_{0},\gamma\}$ , where $\mathcal{N}\triangleq\{1,\dots,N\}$ denotes the set of N agents and s $\in\mathcal{S}\triangleq\mathcal{S}^{1}\times\mathcal{S}^{2}\times\ldots\times\mathcal{S}^{N}$ describes the joint state of the environment. The initial state $s_{0}\sim\rho_{0}$ is drawn from distribution $\rho_{0}$ , and at each time step t, all agents $k \in \mathcal N$ choose simultaneously one action $a_{t}^{k}\in\mathcal{A}^{k}$ , yielding a joint action $\begin{array}{ r }{\pmb{a}_{t}\triangleq a_{t}^{1}\times a_{t}^{2}\times ...\times a_{t}^{N}\in\mathcal{A}\triangleq}\end{array}$ $\mathcal{A}^{1}\times\mathcal{A}^{2}\times\ldots\times\mathcal{A}^{N}$ . After executing the joint action $\mathbf{}\mathbf{a}_{t}$ in state $\mathbf{}_{s_{t},}$ the next state $\pmb{s}_{t+1}\sim P(\pmb{s}_{t},\pmb{a}_{t})$ is drawn from transition kernel P and a collaborative reward $r_{t}=r(s_{t},{\boldsymbol{a}}_{t})$ is returned. In a Dec-MDP, each agent $k \in \mathcal N$ has a local state $s_{t}^{k}\in S^{k}$ , and chooses its actions with a decentralized policy $a_{t}^{k}\sim\pi_{k}(\cdot|s_{t}^{k})$ based only on its local state. The collaborating team of agents aims to learn a joint policy, $\begin{array}{ r }{\mathbf{\sigma}:\left(\mathbf{a}_{t}|\mathbf{s}_{t}\right)\triangleq\prod_{k=1}^{N}\pi_{k}\big(a_{t}^{k}|s_{t}^{k}\big)}\end{array}$ , that maximizes their expected discounted return, $\begin{array}{ r }{\eta(\pmb{\pi})\triangleq\mathbb{E}_{(\pmb{s}_{t},\pmb{a}_{t})}[\sum_{t=0}^{\infty}\gamma^{t}r_{t}]}\end{array}$ , where $\gamma\in [0,1)$ is a discount factor.

Let the advantage function be $A_{\pi}(s,a)=Q_{\pi}(s,a)-V_{\pi}(s)$ ; the following useful identity expresses the expected return of another policy  in terms of the advantage over π (Kakade & Langford, 2002): $\begin{array}{ r }{\eta(\tilde{\pi})=\eta(\pi)+\sum_{s}\rho_{\tilde{\pi}}(s)\sum_{a}\tilde{\pi}(a|s)A_{\pi}(s,a)}\end{array}$ , where $\rho_{\tilde{\pi}}(s)$ is the state distribution induced by π.

Define $\begin{array}{ r }{D_{\mathrm{TV}}^{\operatorname*{max}}(\pi,\tilde{\pi})\triangleq\operatorname*{max}_{s}D_{\mathrm{TV}}\big(\pi(\cdot|s),\tilde{\pi}(\cdot|s)\big)}\end{array}$ , where $D_{\mathrm{TV}}$ is the total variation (TV) divergence.

To analyze the non-stationarity in decentralized policy optimization, we first consider the Markov chain for the local state $s^{k}$ induced by the underlying MDP for agent k. When all agents’ policies are updated from $\pi_{1},\dots,\pi_{N}$ to $\tilde{\pi}_{1},\dots,\tilde{\pi}_{N}$ , the state transition distribution of this Markov chain also shifts. We denote such transition shift from $s^{k}$ to $\tilde{s}^{k}$ for agent k as

$$
\Delta_{\pi_{1},\dots,\pi_{N}}^{\tilde{\pi}_{1},\dots,\tilde{\pi}_{N}}(\tilde{s}^{k}|s^{k})\triangleq\sum_{a^{k}}\big [p_{\tilde{\pi}_{1},\dots,\tilde{\pi}_{N}}(\tilde{s}^{k}|s^{k},a^{k})\tilde{\pi}_{k}(a^{k}|s^{k})-p_{\pi_{1},\dots,\pi_{N}}(\tilde{s}^{k}|s^{k},a^{k})\pi_{k}(a^{k}|s^{k})\big],
$$

where $p_{\pi_{1},\dots,\pi_{N}}$ and $p_{\tilde{\pi}_{1},\dots,\tilde{\pi}_{N}}$ refer to the transition dynamics before and update π is updated.

Define the surrogate objective for decentralized policy $\pi_{k}$ as

$$
L_{\pi_{1},\pi_{2},...,\pi_{N}}^{(k)}(\tilde{\pi}_{k^{\prime}})=\sum_{s^{k}}\rho_{\pi_{1},\pi_{2},...,\pi_{N}}(s^{k})\sum_{a^{k}}\tilde{\pi}_{k^{\prime}}(a^{k}|s^{k})A_{\pi_{k^{\prime}}}(s^{k},a^{k}),
$$

and the expected return of decentralized policy $\pi_{k}$ as

$$
\eta_{\pi_{1},\ldots,\pi_{N}}(\pi_{k})=\mathbb{E}_{(s^{k},a^{k})\sim\rho_{\pi_{1},\ldots,\pi_{N}}(s^{k},a^{k})}\left[r_{k}(s^{k},a^{k})\right].
$$

In practice, $r_{k}(s^{k},a^{k})$ is usually unknown. As the state transition shift decomposes into the sum of transition shifts caused by each decentralized policy, we can bound this state transition shift with a centralized trust region constraint as in equation 1.

Proposition 1. In a Dec-MDP, $\begin{array}{ r }{D_{\mathrm{TV}}^{\operatorname*{max}}(\pi,\tilde{\pi})\leq\sum_{k=1}^{N}D_{\mathrm{TV}}^{\operatorname*{max}}(\pi_{k},\tilde{\pi}_{k})}\end{array}$

This proposition is a direct result of the fact that the joint policy in a Dec-MDP factors as a product of decentralized policies, i.e., $\begin{array}{ r }{\pi=\prod_{k=1}^{N}\pi_{k}}\end{array}$

Proposition 2. $\begin{array}{ r }{D_{\mathrm{TV}}^{\operatorname*{max}}(\pi_{k},\tilde{\pi}_{k})=\operatorname*{max}_{s\in\mathcal{S}}\sum_{\tilde{\pi}_{k}(a^{k}\mid s^{k})\geq\pi_{k}(a^{k}\mid s^{k})}\big [\tilde{\pi}_{k}(a^{k}\vert s^{k})-\pi_{k}(a^{k}\vert s^{k})\big].}\end{array}$

This useful identity follows from a property of $\begin{array}{ r }{D_{\mathrm{TV}}\colon D_{\mathrm{TV}}(\mu(x),\nu(x))=\sum_{\mu(x)>\nu(x)}[\mu(x)-\nu(x)]}\end{array}$ where $\mu$ and v are two distributions. This proposition indicates that a decentralized trust region is also defined by the sum of probability differences over a special subset. We use this to upper bound the trust region in the following analysis.

Assumption 2. Assume the advantage function $A_{\pi_{k}}(s_{k},a_{k})$ converges to a fixed point for ∀k.

error_explanation: In going from eq (13) to eq (14) the proof asserts that the bracketed quantity $r(s_i)+\sum_{s_i'}p_{\tilde\pi_1,\dots,\tilde\pi_{j-1},\pi_j,\dots,\pi_N}(s_i'|s_i,a_i)\gamma v(s_i')-v_{\tilde\pi_1,\dots,\tilde\pi_{j-1}}(s_i)$ equals the advantage $A_{\pi_j}(s_i,a_i)$. This is not true: the equality is forced only by an ad-hoc redefinition of $A_{\pi_j}$ with a baseline $v_{\tilde\pi_1,\dots,\tilde\pi_{j-1}}(s_i)$ engineered so that $L^{(i)}(\pi_j)=0$. The resulting object is not an advantage function (it does not match the IPPO/MAPPO advantage) — 'it does not have any actual meaning, just a function by definition.' Crucially, the true value $v(s_i')$ in eq (11) is action-independent and, as the matrix notation $G^{s_i}\rho_0$ shows, is NOT changed by the policy update, so the value $v(s_i')$ inside the bracket differs from the value used to form the baseline; the $v$ for state $s'$ and the $v$ for state $s$ are different functions. Hence the second term in eq (15) does not vanish and the claim $L^{(i)}(\pi_j)=0$ fails. context:
In RL, the task environment is modeled as an MDP $M=(S,A,T,R,\gamma)$ , where S is the state space, A is the action space, $T:S\times A\times S[0,1]$ is the transition function, $R : S \times A $ R is the reward function, and γ is the discount factor. At every step t, the RL agent observes state $s_{t}$ and takes an action $a_{t}\in A$ As a result, the agent progresses to state $s_{t+1}$ with probability $T(s_{t},a_{t},s_{t+1})$ , and receives a reward $r_{t}$ The goal is to search for a policy that maximizes the expected cumulative reward. We use π to denote a policy as a mapping from S to A. The Q function of the optimal policy $\pi^{*}$ is defined by:

$$
Q_{R}^{*}(s,a)=\operatorname*{max}_{\pi}\left[\mathbb{E}\left[\sum_{t=0}^{\infty}\gamma^{t}r_{t}|s_{0}=s,a_{0}=a,\pi\right]\right]\tag{2}
$$

Our solution to RA is related to a variant of the Q function, which we refer to as Q-min (note the min operator below), denoted by $Q_{R}^{\mu}$ •.

$$
Q_{R}^{\mu}(s,a)=\operatorname*{min}_{\pi}\left[\mathbb{E}\left[\sum_{t=0}^{\infty}\gamma^{t}r_{t}|s_{0}=s,a_{0}=a,\pi\right]\right]\tag{3}
$$

Intuitively, $Q_{R}^{\mu}$ above represents the Q function of the policy that leads to the minimum expected return, in contrast to ${Q}_{R}^{\bar{*}}$ that corresponds to the maximum expected return. Furthermore, the following lemma establishes a connection between $Q_{R}^{\mu}$ and a max form of Q. Throughout the paper, proofs, if omitted, are included in the appendix.

Lemma 2.

$$
Q_{R}^{\mu}(s,a)= -Q_{-R}^{*}(s,a)\tag{4}
$$

where $Q_{-R}^{*}(s,a)$ denotes the Q function of the optimal policy in Eq. 2 under —R.

Definition (Reward Adaptation (RA)). Given a set of source behaviors trained under an MDP $M\setminus R=(S,A,T,\cdot,\gamma)$ with different source reward functions, compute the optimal policy for a target reward function under $M \setminus R$ .

Definition 1 (Reward Adaptation with Q Variants). Given a reward adaptation problem where $Q_{R_{i}}^{*}$ and $Q_{-R_{i}}^{*}$ are accessible for each source domain indexed by i, compute the optimal policy under a target reward function that is a polynomial function of the source reward functions:

$$
\mathcal{R}=\sum_{i_{1}+i_{2}+i_{3}+\ldots i_{n}\leq m}a_{i_{1}i_{2}\ldots i_{n}}R_{1}^{i_{1}}R_{2}^{i_{2}}\cdots R_{n}^{i_{n}}\tag{5}
$$

where $R_{i}$ is the source reward function for the $i^{t h}$ domain.

To derive bounds under R, we start with simpler forms of Eq. 5 and then combine the results. In the following, we denote the upper bound as $\mathbb{Q}_{\mathcal{R}}^{\ast}$ and the lower bound as $\mathbb{Q}_{\mathcal{R}}^{\mu}$ . We refer to a reward function as positive when all rewards are non-negative. We also assume in the following that the influence of discounting can be safely ignored, e.g., when MDPs with absorbing states are considered.

Lemma 6. When $\mathcal{R}=R^m$ and $R$ is positive, an upper and lower bounds of the expected return under $\mathcal{R}$ are given, respectively, by:

$$
\mathbb{Q}_{\mathcal{R}}^{*}=(Q_R^{*})^{m}\ge Q_{R^m}^{*}=Q_{\mathcal{R}}^{*}
$$

$$
\mathbb{Q}_{\mathcal{R}}^{\mu}=-|Q_{-R}^{*}|^{m}\le -Q_{-R^m}^{*}=Q_{\mathcal{R}}^{\mu}
$$

Lemma 5. When $\mathcal{R}=R_i\times R_j$, and both $R_i$ and $R_j$ are positive, an upper and lower bounds of the expected return under $\mathcal{R}$ is given, respectively, by:

$$
\mathbb{Q}_{\mathcal{R}}^{*}=Q_{R_i}^{*}\times Q_{R_j}^{*}\ge Q_{R_iR_j}^{*}=Q_{\mathcal{R}}^{*}
$$

$$
\mathbb{Q}_{\mathcal{R}}^{\mu}=-|Q_{-R_i}^{*}|\times|Q_{-R_j}^{*}|\le -Q_{-R_iR_j}^{*}=Q_{\mathcal{R}}^{\mu}
$$

Intuitively, the smaller the distance between the bounds is, the more pruning opportunities there may be. Even though we cannot tighten the bounds without additional information, in the following, we show that we can "effectively" achieve the same effect by reward shaping Ng et al. (1999). Reward shaping has been widely used to support more informative reward functions to guide learning. In our case, however, we apply it with the objective to reduce the distance between the computed bounds.

A shaping function of a reward function R has the form of $\mathcal{F}=\gamma *\Phi(s^{\prime})-\Phi(s)$ following Ng et al. (1999), where Φ is referred to as a potential function. The shaped reward function, denoted by $R_{F},$ satisfies $R_{F}=R+\mathcal{F}$ Applying reward shaping this way does not affect the optimal policy, i.e., the optimal policy remains invariant. Next, we first establish the effects of applying reward shaping to the target reward function R on $Q_{\mathcal{R}}^{\ast}$ and $Q_{\mathcal{R}}^{\mu}$ below.

Let $\mathcal{F} = \gamma \cdot \Phi(s') - \Phi(s)$ be a potential-based shaping function (Ng et al. 1999) with potential $\Phi$, and let $\mathcal{R}_{\mathcal{F}} = \mathcal{R} + \mathcal{F}$ be the shaped reward. Assume the influence of discounting can be safely ignored (e.g., MDPs with absorbing states). Then after applying reward shaping to $\mathcal{R}$ with $\mathcal{F}$, the shaped optimal and Q-min functions are $Q_{\mathcal{R}_{\mathcal{F}}}^{*}(s,a) = Q_{\mathcal{R}}^{*}(s,a) - \Phi(s)$ (Eq. 12) and $Q_{\mathcal{R}_{\mathcal{F}}}^{\mu}(s,a) = Q_{\mathcal{R}}^{\mu}(s,a) + \Phi(s)$ (Eq. 13).

steps.claim: $Q_{\mathcal{R}_{\mathcal{F}}}^{*}(s,a) = Q_{\mathcal{R}}^{*}(s,a) - \Phi(s)$
$Q_{\mathcal{R}_{\mathcal{F}}}^{\mu}(s,a) = -\left[Q_{-\mathcal{R}_{\mathcal{F}}}^{*}(s,a)\right]$
$Q_{\mathcal{R}_{\mathcal{F}}}^{\mu}(s,a) = -\left[Q_{-\mathcal{R}}^{*}(s,a) - \Phi(s)\right]$
$Q_{\mathcal{R}_{\mathcal{F}}}^{\mu}(s,a) = -Q_{-\mathcal{R}}^{*}(s,a) + \Phi(s)$
$Q_{\mathcal{R}_{\mathcal{F}}}^{\mu}(s,a) = Q_{\mathcal{R}}^{\mu}(s,a) + \Phi(s)$

theorems.statement:
Theorem 2: Given R in the form of Eq. 5 where every $a_{i_{1}i_{2}... i_{n}}>0$ and every source reward function is positive, an upper and lower bounds of the expected return under $\mathcal{R}$ are given, respectively, by:

$$
\mathbb{Q}_{\mathcal{R}}^{*}=\sum_{i_{1}+i_{2}+i_{3}+\ldots i_{n}\leq m}a_{i_{1}i_{2}\ldots i_{n}}|Q_{R_{1}}^{*}|^{i_{1}}\times|Q_{R_{2}}^{*}|^{i_{2}}\times\ldots\times|Q_{R_{n}}^{*}|^{i_{n}}\geq Q_{\mathcal{R}}^{*}
$$

$$
\mathbb{Q}_{\mathcal{R}}^{\mu}= -\left[\sum_{i_{1}+i_{2}+i_{3}+\ldots i_{n}\leq m}a_{i_{1}i_{2}\ldots i_{n}}|Q_{-R_{1}}^{*}|^{i_{1}}\times|Q_{-R_{2}}^{*}|^{i_{2}}\times\ldots\times|Q_{-R_{n}}^{*}|^{i_{n}}\right]\leq Q_{\mathcal{R}}^{\mu}
$$

steps.claim:
Substituting $R_{k}^{i_{k}}=\bar{R_{k}}$ in Eq. 14, we obtain

$$
Q_{a_{i_{1}i_{2}\ldots i_{n}}R_{1}^{i_{1}}\times R_{2}^{i_{2}}\ldots R_{n}^{i_{n}}}^{*}\leq a_{i_{1}i_{2}\ldots i_{n}}|Q_{R_{1}}^{*}|^{i_{1}}\times|Q_{R_{2}}^{*}|^{i_{2}}\times\ldots\times|Q_{R_{n}}^{*}|^{i_{n}}\mathrm{[L e m m a~6]}\tag{15}
$$

Now we can derive the following for $\begin{array}{ r }{{\mathcal{R}}=\sum_{i_{1}+i_{2}+i_{3}+... i_{n}\leq m}a_{i_{1}i_{2}... i_{n}}R_{1}^{i_{1}}R_{2}^{i_{2}}\cdot\cdot\cdot R_{n}^{i_{n}}{\mathrm{.}}}\end{array}$

$$
Q_{{\mathcal R}}^{*}\leq\sum_{\substack{i_{1}+i_{2}+i_{3}+\ldots i_{n}\leq m}}a_{i_{1}i_{2}\ldots i_{n}}|Q_{{\cal R}_{1}}^{*}|^{i_{1}}\times|Q_{{\cal R}_{2}}^{*}|^{i_{2}}\times\ldots\times|Q_{{\cal R}_{n}}^{*}|^{i_{n}}\quad\quad [\mathrm{L e m m a~}3]\tag{16}
$$

Similarly we can derive the lower bound:

$$
\mathbb{Q}_{\mathcal{R}}^{\mu}= -\left[\sum_{i_{1}+i_{2}+i_{3}+... i_{n}\leq m}a_{i_{1}i_{2}... i_{n}}|Q_{-R_{1}}^{*}|^{i_{1}}\times|Q_{-R_{2}}^{*}|^{i_{2}}\times ...\times|Q_{-R_{n}}^{*}|^{i_{n}}\right]\leq Q_{\mathcal{R}}^{\mu}\tag{17}
$$

theorems.statement: Theorem 3 (optimality). Given a problem of reward adaptation with Q variants (Def. 1), the optimal policies under R remain invariant under Q-Manipulation.

steps.claim: To retain all optimal policies, it must be satisfied that none of the optimal actions under each state are pruned.

Assuming that a pruned action $\widehat{a}$ under s is an optimal action, we must have

$$
\forall a~Q_{\mathcal{R}_{\mathcal{F}}}^{*}(s,a)\leq Q_{\mathcal{R}_{\mathcal{F}}}^{*}(s,\widehat{a})
$$

Given that Q-Manipulation only prunes an action $\widehat{a}$ under s when $\exists a$ $\mathbb{Q}_{\mathcal{R}_{\mathcal{F}}}^{\mu}(s,a)>\mathbb{Q}_{\mathcal{R}_{\mathcal{F}}}^{*}(s,\widehat{a})$ , we can derive that

$$
\begin{array}{ r }{Q_{\mathcal{R}_{\mathcal{F}}}^{\mu}(s,a)\geq\mathbb{Q}_{\mathcal{R}_{\mathcal{F}}}^{\mu}(s,a)>\mathbb{Q}_{\mathcal{R}_{\mathcal{F}}}^{*}(s,\widehat{a})\geq Q_{\mathcal{R}_{\mathcal{F}}}^{*}(s,\widehat{a})\geq Q_{\mathcal{R}_{\mathcal{F}}}^{*}(s,a),}
\end{array}
$$

resulting in a contradiction that

$$
Q_{\mathcal{R}_{\mathcal{F}}}^{\mu}(s,a)>Q_{\mathcal{R}_{\mathcal{F}}}^{*}(s,a)
$$
As a result, we know that all optimal actions and hence policies are retained.

label: flawed
error_explanation: The step asserts $Q_{-\mathcal{R}_{\mathcal{F}}}^{*}(s,a) = Q_{-\mathcal{R}}^{*}(s,a) - \Phi(s)$ by reusing Eq. (13). This is wrong because the shaping function applied to the negated reward $-\mathcal{R}$ is $-\mathcal{F}$ (its potential is $-\Phi$, since $-\mathcal{R}_{\mathcal{F}} = -\mathcal{R} + (-\mathcal{F})$). By Ng et al. (1999) the correct value is $Q_{-\mathcal{R}_{\mathcal{F}}}^{*}(s,a) = Q_{-\mathcal{R}}^{*}(s,a) + \Phi(s)$, giving a $+\Phi(s)$ term rather than $-\Phi(s)$. Propagating the correct sign through the outer negation yields $Q_{\mathcal{R}_{\mathcal{F}}}^{\mu}(s,a) = -[Q_{-\mathcal{R}}^{*}(s,a) + \Phi(s)] = Q_{\mathcal{R}}^{\mu}(s,a) - \Phi(s)$, i.e. the lower bound shifts DOWN by $\Phi(s)$, the SAME direction as the upper bound in Eq. (13) — not the opposite direction. The proof effectively uses two different shaping functions ($\mathcal{F}$ for $\mathcal{R}$ but implicitly $+\mathcal{F}$ instead of $-\mathcal{F}$ for $-\mathcal{R}$). A counter-example: in a 1-state, 1-action MDP all policies coincide, so min and max Q-values are equal and stay equal after adding a constant potential, contradicting Eq. (14).

context: We consider the problem of verifying the local robustness of piecewise-linear neural networks for a given $\ell_p$ bound. Precisely, given a point, $x$, network, $F$, and norm bound, $\epsilon$, this entails determining whether Equation 2 holds. $$\forall x' . \|x - x'\|_p \le \epsilon \Longrightarrow F(x) = F(x') \tag{2}$$ In this section we give a high-level overview of our proposed algorithm, and present some implementation heuristics that improve its performance (Section 2.2). We also propose a variant (Section 2.3) to compute certified lower bounds of the robustness radius. Correctness proofs for all of the algorithms discussed in this section are provided in Appendix A. Because our algorithm applies to arbitrary $\ell_{p}$ norms, we use the un-subscripted notation $\| \cdot \|$ to refer to a general $\ell_{p}$ norm for the remainder of this section. We propose the Fast Geometric Projections (FGP) algorithm, which takes a model, $F,$ an input, x, and a bound, $\epsilon,$ and either proves that Equation 2 is satisfied (i.e., e-local robustness), finds an adversarial input at distance less than  from x, or returns unknown. Our algorithm assumes $F(x)=\operatorname{argmax}\{f(x)\}$ , where $f:\mathbb{R}^{m}\mathbb{R}^{n}$ is the function computed by a neural network composed of linear transformations with ReLU activations $(\mathrm{i . e .,}f$ is a feed-forward ReLU network). The algorithm relies on an analysis of all possible activation regions around x. An activation region is a maximal set of inputs having the same activation pattern of ReLU nonlinearities. Formally, let $f_{u}(x)$ denote the pre-activation value of neuron u in network $F$ when evaluating x. We say that neuron u is activated if $f_{u}(x)\geq 0$ . An activation pattern, A, is a Boolean function over neurons that characterizes whether each neuron is activated. Then the activation region, A, associated with pattern A is the set of inputs that realize A: $\bar{A}: =\{x\mid\forall u .(f_{u}(x)\geq 0)\iff A(u)\}$ Because we assume that F is a piecewise-linear composition of linear transformations and ReLU activations, we can associate the activation status $A(u)$ of any neuron with a closed half-space of $\mathbb{R}^{m}$ (Jordan et al., 2019). The activation constraint, $C_{u}$ , for neuron u and pattern A is the linear inequality $w_{u}^{T}x+b_{u}\leq 0$ , where $w_{u}$ and $b_{u}$ satisfy $\forall x\in\mathbb{R}^{m}. w_{u}^{T}x+b\leq 0\iff A(u)$ . The coefficients, $w_{u}$ are equal to the gradient of $f_{u}$ with respect to its inputs, evaluated at a point in Å. Crucially, because the gradient is the same at every point in Å, the constraints can be computed from the activation pattern alone via backpropagation. More details on this computation are given in Appendix B. The intersection of these constraints yields the activation region ${\bar{A}}.$ and the facets of Å correspond to the non-redundant constraints. The convexity of activation regions follows from this observation, as does the fact that the decision boundaries are also linear constraints of the form $f(x)_{i}\geq f(x)_{j}$ for classes i and $j$ . The FGP algorithm performs a search of all activation regions that might be at distance less than from x. We begin by analyzing the region, ${\bar{A}}_{0}$ , associated with the activation pattern of the input, x, as follows. First, we check to see if ${\bar{A}}_{0}$ contains a decision boundary, C, that is at distance less than  from x; if so, we take the projection, $p,$ from x onto C. Intuitively, the projection is an input satisfying C that is at minimal distance from $x,$ i.e., $\forall x^{\prime}. C(x^{\prime})\Longrightarrow\|x-p\|\dot{\leq}\|\dot{x}-x^{\prime}\|$ . Similarly we define the distance, d, from x to a constraint or decision boundary, C, as $d(x,C): =\mathrm{min}_{x^{\prime}:C(x^{\prime})}\left\|x-x^{\prime}\right\|$ , i.e., d is the distance from x to its projection onto C. If p does not have the same class as x according to $F$ (or lies directly on the decision boundary between classes), then p is an adversarial example. $\operatorname{If}p$ has the same class as x, it means that the projection to the decision boundary is outside of the activation region we are currently analyzing; however, this is not sufficient to conclude that no point on the decision boundary is inside both the current activation region and the e-ball (see Figure 1b). Therefore, we return unknown. Otherwise, we collect all activation constraints in ${\bar{A}}_{0};$ there is one such activation constraint per neuron u in the network; thus each constraint corresponds to the neighboring region, ${\bar{A}}_{0}^{u}$ , which has the same activation pattern as ${\bar{A}}_{0},$ except with neuron u flipped, i.e., $\ \bar{A}_{0}(u^{\prime})\ \bar{\neq}\ \bar{A}_{0}^{u}(u^{\prime})\iff u=u^{\prime}$ For each constraint $\bar{C}_{u},$ we check whether it might be at distance less than e from x using a geometric projection. Although $C_{u}$ is only valid in the polytope corresponding to the activation region ${\bar{A}}_{0}$ , we compute the distance to the hyperplane corresponding to the infinite prolongation of $C_{u}$ . As such, we only obtain a lower bound on the distance from x to $C_{u}.$ If the computed distance is smaller than e, we enqueue the corresponding activation region if it has not been searched yet. Thus the queue contains unexplored regions that might be at distance less than  from x. The algorithm continues to analyze each enqueued region in the same way, each explored region enqueuing neighbouring regions that might be at distance less than  from x, until the queue is empty. Exhausting the queue means that we did not find any adversarial examples in any activation region that might intersect with the -ball centered at x. We therefore conclude that x is locally e-robust. We show that when the FGP algorithm returns not_robust, there exists an adversarial example, and when it returns robust, the model is locally robust at x, with radius e. However, the algorithm may also return unknown, in which case we do not claim anything about the robustness of the model. A complete proof of Theorem 2 is provided in Appendix A.1. As mentioned previously, our focus is on feed-forward ReLU networks. Such networks contain an ordered hierarchy of layers. Therefore, for a neuron $u$, the activation constraint corresponding to the condition $f_u(x) > 0$ only depends on the activations of neurons in previous layers. In particular, if we fix the activations of all neurons at previous layers, then this constraint becomes linear. Our crucial observation is that, if two activations patterns $A$ and $A'$ differ only in the activation of one neuron, $u$, in layer $N$, the activation constraints for all neurons up to layer $N$ remain identical in $A$ and $A'$, as they do not depend on neurons deeper in the network such as $u$. We leverage this hierarchy to enhance FGP with a tree-based exploration of the network to prove that an input $x$ is $\epsilon$-robust. Each node in our exploration tree corresponds to the activation pattern of neurons at a layer. Nodes are ordered similarly to the layers in the network: if layer $N$ has $k$ neurons, the vertices at depth $N-1$ have degree $2^k$, with one child for each possible activation pattern of these $k$ neurons. Leaf nodes give a complete characterization of an activation pattern for the entire network. Leaves that share an ancestor at depth $N$ in the tree correspond to activation patterns that share an *activation prefix*, i.e., the activations of all neurons in the layers up to layer $N$ are the same in both activation patterns. An illustration of such a tree is shown in panel (a) of the figure below. The version of the FGP algorithm given in Section 2.1 systematically explores all regions that might be at distance less than $\epsilon$ from $x$; a region $\bar{A}_i$ is explored if it is reachable from a previously explored region (starting with the one containing $x$) by flipping the activation of exactly one neuron. Exploration of $\bar{A}_i$ consists of collecting all activation constraints and decision boundaries at distance less than $\epsilon$ from $x$ w.r.t the activation pattern $A_i$, and enqueuing the corresponding neighboring regions to analyze them. In our optimized variant, when enqueuing a region, $\bar{A}_{i+1}$, we additionally keep track of its predecessor in the exploration, $\bar{A}_i$, i.e., the region from which $\bar{A}_{i+1}$ was discovered. Crucially, when exploring $\bar{A}_{i+1}$, we only enqueue neighboring regions belonging to the subtree of the lowest common ancestor (LCA) of $\bar{A}_i$ and $\bar{A}_{i+1}$ in the tree. Supposing neuron $u$ was flipped to obtain $A_{i+1}$ from $A_i$, this corresponds to considering only activation constraints in $\bar{A}_{i+1}$ that are associated with the layer $u$ belongs to or deeper. To understand how this approach helps prune unnecessary regions that the basic FGP algorithm would otherwise have searched, an example is provided in panel (b) of the figure below. In practice, for efficiency, we do not construct the tree in memory. Instead, it is sufficient to use a regular queue of regions to explore, enriched with information about which layer the last flipped neuron belongs to. When exploring a region, we filter out all collected constraints that belong to earlier layers. This preserves the inherent parallelism from the basic version of FGP, leading to a more efficient implementation. In the correctness argument for this tree-based variant, the paper fixes the following notation: we consider the case where we are exploring a region $\bar{A}$, reached from a previously explored region $\bar{A}_{prev}$ by flipping a neuron $u$ at layer $N$. Figure: (a) Illustration of the "tree" of activation pattern prefixes for the network shown on the left. Each leaf corresponds to an activation pattern, each level corresponds to a layer, and internal nodes correspond to activation pattern prefixes at the respective layer. (b) Example of the tree-based exploration on a simple network with two internal neurons. The constraint for neuron 1, $C_1$, is linear and the constraint for neuron 2, $C_2$, is piecewise linear, as it depends on the activation of neuron 1. The initial region, $\bar{A}_{00}$, has been explored, its neighbor obtained by flipping neuron 1, $\bar{A}_{10}$, is enqueued, and its neighbor obtained by flipping neuron 2, $\bar{A}_{01}$, is being explored. The LCA in the tree of $\bar{A}_{01}$ and its predecessor in the exploration ($\bar{A}_{00}$) is shown in red. $\bar{A}_{11}$ (which is not in the $\epsilon$-ball) is not searched from $\bar{A}_{01}$, despite the fact that $C_1$ is in the $\epsilon$-ball, because it is not a child of the LCA in the tree. We now consider the related problem of finding a lower bound on the local robustness of the network. A variant of the FGP algorithm can provide certified lower bounds by using a priority queue; constraints are enqueued with priority corresponding to their distance from x, such that the closest constraint is always at the front of the queue. We keep track of the current certified lower bound in a variable, β. At each iteration, we set $\boldsymbol{\beta}$ to the maximum of the old β and the distance from x to the constraint at the front of the queue. The algorithm terminates either when all constraints at distance less than the initially specified  were handled, or when a decision boundary for which the initial algorithm returns unknown or not_robust is found. In the first case, we return e; in the second, we return the value stored in $\beta$ at this iteration. The proof of this variant is similar to the proof of the FGP algorithm. It relies on the following loop invariant, which we prove in Appendix A.2. We define a path of activation regions as a sequence, $\bar{A}_{0},\ldots,\bar{A}_{k}.$ , of activation regions such that the underlying activation patterns $\bar{A_{i}}$ and $A_{i+1}$ differ in exactly one neuron for all i, and there exists at least one input, $x_{i},$ that has activation pattern $A_{i}$ for all i.

theorems.statement: Theorem 2 (general position). Assume the ReLU network is in general position: distinct neurons have distinct pre-activation boundary hyperplanes $\{z : f_u(z)=0\}$, and their arrangement is simple (any $k$ distinct such boundaries meet in codimension $k$). Then (1) when the FGP algorithm returns not_robust, there exists an adversarial example $p$ with $\|x - p\| \le \epsilon$ and $F(x) \neq F(p)$; (2) when it returns robust, $x$ is locally robust with radius $\epsilon$ (Equation 2 holds).

steps.claim: If FGP returns not_robust, the claim is immediate; the substance is the robust case, where we show x is locally robust with radius epsilon by contradiction.
Assume for contradiction FGP returns robust yet some $p$ has $\|x-p\| \le \epsilon$ and $F(x) \neq F(p)$; let $A_x$, $A_p$ be the activation regions of $x$ and $p$.
A path of activation regions is a sequence $A_0,\ldots,A_k$ in which consecutive activation patterns differ in exactly one neuron and each $A_i$ is realized by some input $x_i$.

The proof rests on three facts: (1) a path $P$ from $A_x$ to $A_p$ exists with every region containing an input within $\epsilon$ of $x$ and (if $A_x \neq A_p$) all regions distinct; (2) FGP visits every region of $P$; (3) any visited region containing an adversarial input makes FGP return not_robust or unknown.

Existence of a path $P$ from $A_x$ to $A_p$, in general position, all traversed regions within $\epsilon$ of $x$ and pairwise distinct. Consider the segment going from $x$ to $p$ in a straight line. As $\|x - p\| \le \epsilon$, all points on this segment are also at distance less than $\epsilon$. As $f$ is a neural network with ReLU activations, $f$ is a continuous function, as are the activation functions, $f_u$ for each of its internal neurons, $u$. Furthermore, input points at the boundary between two activation regions (i.e., $z$, such that $f_u(z) = 0$) belong to both activation regions. Therefore, listing all activation regions on the segment between $x$ and $p$ yields a path, $P$, from $A_x$ to $A_p$, with each region on the path containing an input point, $x_i$, on the segment, such that $\|x - x_i\| \le \epsilon$. That each $A_i, A_j$ in $P$ is unique follows from the convexity of activation regions: If there exist $A_i = A_j$ in $P$ such that there exists an $A_k$ in between, then $A_i = A_j$ cannot be convex, as there exists a line segment with its end points in $A_i$ and $A_j$ that is not entirely contained within the region $A_i = A_j$. This ensures that paths are of finite length.

FGP visits every region of P when it returns robust, by induction on path length. We proceed by induction on the length of paths induced (similarly to as above) by a line segment included in the $\epsilon$-ball centered on $x$. In the base case, if the path is of length one, then it contains only $A_x$, and the claim holds trivially since FGP starts by visiting $A_x$. In the inductive case, let us assume that for any path with length at most $k$ induced by a segment, $s$, beginning at $x$ with $\|s\| \le \epsilon$, FGP visits all regions in the path. Now consider a path, $P' = A_0, \ldots, A_k$, of length $k+1$, induced by a segment, $s'$, beginning at $x$ with $\|s'\| \le \epsilon$. Since $A_{k-1}$ is on the path, there exists a point, $x_{k-1}$, on $s'$ such that the sub-segment from $x$ to $x_{k-1}$ induces a path of length $k$; thus we can apply our induction hypothesis to conclude that FGP visits $A_0, \ldots, A_{k-1}$. Now, since $A_{k-1}$ and $A_k$ are neighbors in $P'$, they must share some boundary, $C$, that is intersected by $s'$. Thus, since $\|s'\| \le \epsilon$, $d(x, C) \le \epsilon$; thus when FGP visits $A_{k-1}$, it will add $A_k$ to the queue via $C$. Therefore, since FGP returns robust only when all regions in the queue have been visited, FGP will visit $A_k$.

If a visited region holds an adversarial example, FGP returns not_robust or unknown. If $p$ in $A_p$ is an adversarial example, then $F(x) \neq F(p)$. By continuity of $f$, this means that there exists an input, $p'$ on the segment from $x$ to $p$ that is exactly on a decision boundary, $C$. As $\|x - p'\| \le \|x - p\| \le \epsilon$, $C$ must have been analyzed when exploring $A_p$. However, when analyzing a decision boundary, FGP always returns either not_robust or unknown.

theorems.statement: The tree-based exploration heuristic, which prunes which neighboring activation regions are enqueued, is sound: every region filtered out when exploring from a region is either unreachable within the $\epsilon$-ball or is still explored through a different path in the tree. Hence pruning cannot cause FGP to skip a region that could contain an adversarial example, and Theorem 2 continues to hold for the tree-based variant.

steps.claim: It suffices to consider adjacent activation regions differing by exactly one flipped neuron, and trace how a filtered-out region is recovered through another branch of the tree.
$\bar{A}_{10}$ is visited by the tree search.
From $\bar{A}_{10}$, the neighboring region $\bar{A}_{11}$ is in turn explored (enqueued) by the search.
So a region $\bar{A}_{11}$ pruned when exploring from some other branch (e.g. from $\bar{A}_{prev}/\bar{A}$) is still reachable, since it is explored through the $\bar{A}_{10}$ branch.
Hence no reachable region within the $\epsilon$-ball is dropped by the heuristic, and the tree-based variant preserves the soundness guarantee of Theorem 2.

theorems.statement: Loop Invariant 2. (1) All activation regions at distance less than β from x were previously visited, (2) β is always smaller than e, and (3) there is no adversarial point at distance less than $\beta .$

steps.claim: Loop Invariant 2 trivially holds on entry of the loop since bound is initialized to 0. Proving that the invariant is maintained is more interesting.
Suppose that bound increases to $\mathrm{\it~b o u n d^{\prime}}$ . It must then be shown that there is no unvisited activation region at distance less than bound'.

We proceed again by contradiction: assume there was such a region, ${\bar{A}},$ containing a point, $p,$ such that $\lvert | x - p \rvert | \leq$ bound'. Again, let us consider the segment from x to $p,$ and the path, $P_{\mathrm{:}}$ it induces.

Let us consider ${\bar{A}}_{i}.$ , the first region of $P$ at distance greater than bound that was not previously visited. If no such region exists, then Å is at distance less than bound from $x,$ and so by our induction hypothesis, it was already visited.

otherwise, $\bar{A}_{i-1}$ was visited, and the activation constraint, $C,$ between $\bar{A}_{i-1}$ and $\bar{A}_{i}$ is such that $d(x,C)\leq b o u n d^{\prime}\leq\epsilon$ . Therefore, $C$ (which leads to ${\bar{A}}_{i})$ was already added to the queue with priority less than bound', and by virtue of the priority queue, it was explored before the current iteration, which yields a contradiction.

If bound does not increase, the invariant still trivially holds. This case can happen because our computation of the distance to constraints is an underapproximation of the true distance to the feasible portion of the constraint.

label: flawed
error_explanation: The step asserts that once $\bar{A}_{10}$ is visited, the neighboring region $\bar{A}_{11}$ is enqueued and explored from $\bar{A}_{10}$ — but this is only assumed, never proved. The tree-based heuristic prunes which neighbors are enqueued, so visiting $\bar{A}_{10}$ does not entail that $\bar{A}_{11}$ is reached from it. The counterexample shows $\bar{A}_{11}$ may fail to be explored from $\bar{A}_{10}$: exactly as boundary $GC$ between $\bar{A}_{prev}$ and $\bar{A}'$ does not pass inside the $\epsilon$-ball (so $\bar{A}'$ is never explored from $\bar{A}_{prev}$), $\bar{A}_{11}$ can be unreachable via the $\bar{A}_{10}$ branch. If such a region is also pruned on every other path, a reachable region that could contain an adversarial example is dropped, and the pruned search can return robust when an adversarial example actually exists. The proof needed, but never established, the assumption that every pruned region is recovered along some retained path; hence the soundness claim (Theorem 1 for the tree-based variant) is unsound. There is no valid fix — the authors removed the tree-based exploration heuristic entirely.
